units.la: PHOTIVS, infœlix atque ærumnosum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ nomen, equestri nobilique loco natus, præclara eruditione atque doctrina conspicuus, magnarum etiam aliarum artium instructissimus, sed ingenio vafro, nequitia singulari, ambitione putida, ideoque ad omne facinus nefasque delectus, cum inaudita omni memoria fraude Ignatium Virum sanctissimum subinouisset, & throno Constantinopolitanum occupasset, se in eo statu neque tutum, neq; extra periculum ullo unquam tempore reputans, nisi approbatorem firmatoremq; suæ dignitatis Pontificem Rom. haberet, cuius erat similia statuere, scripsit ad Nicolaum per id tempus Ecclesiæ Catholicæ moderatorem, demisso atque humili animo approbationem exposcens. Nicolaus in se causam assumens, Photij, & Ignatij iuribus examinatis, incorrupte sententiam protulit, Sedem Ignatio adiudicauit, amissam iniquissimis dolis dignitatem resti-tutam integre conservavit ipse, & Concilium Constantinopoli celebratum audiens, & obediens obfirmatis decretis Pontificijs, Photium alieni aggressorem condemnauit, & ex urbe patria expulsum relegauit. Hæc Acta Concilij auctoritati Pontificiæ innixa in ea dignatione fuere, ut Octauæ Synodi Oecumenicæ locum occuparint, & apud Græcos ipsos nomen tenuerint Octaui Concilij Generalis. Quid interim gesserit Pho. tius, & quibus machinis decreta Nicolai, & illius successoris Adriani infirmare conatus fuerit, fuse prosequuntur tum Græci, cum Latini Historici. Ijs tamen cum obniterentur Pontifices, licet ille plurimum laboraret, nihil profecit, donec Ignatius mansit in vita; quo demortuo, Sanctabareni malis artibus, & Photij commentario de Bafilij Imperatoris sanguinis propage, circumuentus Basilius procurato consensu Ioannis Pontificis, rursus denuo Photium Patriarcham recreat, conuocato Concilio, Legatis Ioannis interuenientibus, & omnia vno ore comprobantibus. Concilium callide procurauerat Photius, vt sui restitutionem constabiliret, sciens, Pontificem, siue Presbyterum, siue iuste, siue iniuste condemnatum eiectumq; per Concilium in locum pristinum, vnde cecidit, restitui non posse, crimen ab Arianis obiectum Athanasio, & Ioanni Chrysostomo a Theophilo Alexandrino. Et haec etiam Synodus sic a Photio siue confecta, siue vere coacta, vel in parte vel in omnibus, sub Octauae Synodi nomine innotuit apud Graecos Schismaticos. Hinc vt vides, Lector eruditissime, duae Synodi sub nomimihi Octauæ circumferuntur, altera tempore Nicolai, in qua deponitur Photius, Ioannis altera, in qua restituitur. Hanc Schismatici exosculantur, illam Catholici, quam & re ipsa congregatam esse & celebratam nemo, nec etiam ex Schismaticis in controuersiam vertit. Hanc sub Ioanne Schismatici celebrant, & lambunt: an vero celebrata sit, multi dubitant, nonnulli per omnia, alij tantum de actione postrema dubium mouent, in qua recitatur Symbolum absque additione, & anathema dicitur contra addentes, dementes, mutantes: & legitur Ioannis Epistola, in qua fatetur, nihil additum in Symbolo, & prospecturum se in posterum, ne quid addatur. Quæ omnia suppositicia esse ex ingenio Photij, qui similia, & alias sæpius nequissimo ausu pertentauerat, & mendacijs confictis aduersus Nicolaum Pontificem, & Ignatium, viros a culpa innocentissimos insurrexerat, ex Græcorum ipsorum, & Schismaticorum potissimum, remota omnis dubitationis nebula, demonstrauimus. In quibus enarrandis, cum deprehendissemus Robertum Creyghtonum Præfatione ad Lectorem in Historia Concilij Florentini recens ab eodem Græce & Latine mala fide edita, innumeris erroribus implicari, & veritatem nemini non patentem offusis tenebris præuertere, eius dicta acriori examine, sed ingenuo subiecimus. Inter hæc porro peruenerunt ad manus, nescio cuius iuuenis e Sueuorum gente bellicosissima Exercitatio Histo-rico-Theologica, de Ecclesia Græcanica hodierna, & Ioannis Henrici Hottingeri, nullo numero hominis, Disputatio Apologetica, in quibus unionem meam inter Ecclesiam Orientalem atque Occidentalem, & consensum unanimem in dissensum, & discordiam reducere conati sunt. Sed eos neque sua probare, neq; mea convellere potuisse, patet, cum rationibus pro me adductis, auctoritatibus, & testimoniis ex ipsius Ecclesiæ Græcæ fontibus, & Libris Ritualibus in dies singulos palam populo lectis nullo modo responderint. Quidquid enim attulerunt, id omne consensum potius non 'diffi-dium comprobat. Nam etiam si concedamus, quæ ipsi dissidia inter has Ecclesias ementiuntur, vera esse, nihilominus argumentorum momenta pro consensu adhuc sibi constant cum multo plura commemo-rentur, quibus distant a Reformatis. Et nugatoria sunt, quae ex aliorum testimonijs diducunt: Ridicule enim concluditur, hic vel ille dicit Græcos agere, vel dicere; Ergo Græci, vel Ecclesia Græca agit, & dicit. Quamuis etenim Græca Ecclesia ex Græcis consistat, non ideo tamen quidquid singuli Græci dicunt, Ecclesiam Græcam dicere asseuerandum est. Nam in ea Ecclesia fuere & perditi animi homines, & Hæretici, & Schismatici, & quid non ? Pestes tamen similes non infecerunt Ecclesiam, sicuti nec Occidentalem similes sortis homines. Et perridiculus esset, qui argumentaretur Zuinglius dicit, Caluinus scripsit, Lutherus docuit, Hottingerus insanit, alius quispiam ineptit. Ergo Ecclesia Occidentalis dicit, scripsit, docuit, insanit, ineptit . Licet enim, plerique prauarum religionum virus spargant, pestiferas de dogmate opiniones disseminent, Pontificiam Ecclesiam impugnent, & tandem noxijs moribus labem, & vulnus conscientiæ infligant, Ecclesia tamen Pontificia nunquam de præeminentia, nunquam de dignitate, nunquam de infallibilitate, sua decidit, sed quo pluribus perfecutionum turbis, Hæreticorum machinis, male sanorum hominum fraudibus concutitur, plus plusque candido lumine claret, exacta ad omnem legem innocentia augescit, inintemerata fide rutilat, & sospite Deo sacrosancta, invulnerata, & a blasphemijs, ac feralibus nefariorum hominum telis pudicissima, in summa rerum omnium potestate, ut aiebat ille,
units.tr: Photius, an unlucky man and a name of sorrow for the Catholic Church, was born into an equestrian and noble family. He was distinguished by remarkable learning and doctrine and was thoroughly versed in many other arts. But he had a crafty mind, singular wickedness and a foul ambition, and so he was chosen for every crime and wrong. Having ousted the most holy man Ignatius by a fraud unheard of in all memory, he seized the throne of Constantinople. Judging that in that position he was neither safe nor ever free from danger unless he had the Roman Pontiff, whose duty it was to decide such matters, as the approver and confirmer of his dignity, he wrote to Nicholas, who was then ruler of the Catholic Church, asking for approval in a humble and submissive spirit. Nicholas took up the case himself. After examining the rights of Photius and Ignatius, he gave an impartial judgment: he restored the See to Ignatius, and he himself kept the dignity, lost through the most wicked tricks, whole and intact. When he heard that a council had been held at Constantinople, he condemned Photius as an aggressor against another's rights, obeying the decrees of the Pontiff, which he had confirmed, and banished him, expelled from his native city. The acts of this council, resting on the authority of the Pontiff, were so esteemed that they took the place of the Eighth Ecumenical Synod, and among the Greeks themselves they kept the name of the Eighth General Council. Meanwhile, what Photius did and by what machinations he tried to undermine the decrees of Nicholas and of his successor Adrian, both Greek and Latin historians relate at length. Although he laboured greatly against them, the Pontiffs resisted him and he achieved nothing, as long as Ignatius lived. When Ignatius died, Basil the Emperor was circumvented by the wicked arts of Sanctabarenus and by Photius's scheming about Basil's descent from the blood of the emperors. Having secured the consent of Pope John, Basil again restored Photius as Patriarch. A council was convened, with John's legates taking part, and they all approved everything with one voice. Photius had cunningly arranged this council so that his restoration would be made secure, knowing that a Pontiff, or a presbyter, whether justly or unjustly condemned and cast out by a council, could not be restored to the position from which he had fallen. He knew this from the charge the Arians brought against Athanasius, and Theophilus of Alexandria against John Chrysostom. This synod, whether it was fabricated by Photius or truly convened, wholly or in part, became known among the schismatic Greeks under the name of the Eighth Synod. Hence, as you see, learned reader, two synods are circulated under the name of the Eighth: one in the time of Nicholas, in which Photius is deposed, and the other under John, in which he is restored. The schismatics embrace the second, and Catholics the first, which nobody, not even among the schismatics, disputes was actually assembled and held. The schismatics celebrate the synod under John and lick it over. Whether it was in fact held, however, many doubt, some entirely, others only about the final session, in which the Creed is recited without addition and an anathema is pronounced against those who add to it, the mad, or the changers. Also read is a letter of John in which he confesses that nothing had been added to the Creed and promises to take care in future that nothing be added. Having cleared away every cloud of doubt, I have demonstrated, chiefly from the Greeks themselves and the schismatics, that all these things are spurious and the invention of Photius, who had often attempted similar and other things with the most wicked daring, and who had risen up with fabricated lies against Pope Nicholas and Ignatius, men most innocent of fault. In setting out these matters, when I found that Robert Creyghton, in the Preface to the Reader in his History of the Council of Florence, which he had recently published in Greek and Latin with bad faith, was entangled in countless errors and, by casting shadows over the truth which lies open to everyone, distorted it, I subjected his statements to a sharper, though candid, examination. Meanwhile there came into my hands an Historico-Theological Exercise by a certain young man of the most warlike Swabian nation, On the Present Greek Church, and a Apologetic Disputation by John Henry Hottinger, a man of no small account. In these works they tried to bring my union between the Eastern and Western Church, and the unanimous consent, back to dissent and discord. But it is plain that they could neither prove their own views nor overturn mine, since they made no reply at all to the arguments I adduced in my favour, nor to the authorities and testimonies drawn from the very sources of the Greek Church and from its ritual books, which are read openly to the people day by day. Whatever they brought forward, all of it proves consent rather than discord. For even if we grant that the disagreements between these Churches which they invent are true, the weight of the arguments for consent still stands, since far more are cited by which they differ from the Reformed. What they draw from the testimonies of others is also trifling. They ridiculously conclude: this or that man says that the Greeks act or speak, therefore the Greeks, or the Greek Church, acts and speaks. For although the Greek Church consists of Greeks, it does not follow that whatever individual Greeks say must be asserted as the Greek Church's saying. In that Church there were men of depraved mind, heretics, schismatics, and whatever else. Yet such plagues did not infect the Church, just as men of a similar sort did not infect the Western Church. It would be most absurd to argue: Zwingli says, Calvin wrote, Luther taught, Hottinger is mad, someone else is silly; therefore the Western Church says, writes, teaches, is mad, and is silly. For although many spread the poison of depraved religions, disseminate pestilential opinions about doctrine, attack the Papal Church, and at last inflict the stain and wound of harmful morals and of conscience, the Papal Church has never lost its pre-eminence, its dignity, or its infallibility. Rather, the more it is shaken by the many storms of persecutions, the machinations of heretics and the frauds of ill-minded men, the more it shines with a clearer light; its innocence, measured by every law, grows; it gleams with an undefiled faith; and, with God preserving it, it remains sacrosanct, unhurt, and most chaste against the blasphemies and deadly weapons of wicked men, in the highest power over all things, as that poet said:

units.tr: By the command of the Most Reverend Father Raimundus Capifuccus, Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, I have read this treatise On the Eighth Synod of Photius, composed by the most distinguished Leo Allatius, First Custodian of the Vatican Library. Because it greatly clarifies Ecclesiastical truth, I judge it worthy to be published in print, since it contains nothing contrary to faith or Christian morals. Rather, it seems likely to be no slight support for increasing learning and Ecclesiastical purity. Rome, 20 October 1661[?].

units.la: QUID vero de Synodo VIII. Photiana sentiendum est? Eam veram ac legitimam Synodum, & quod magis est, Oecumenicam ex Schismaticis, & potissimum recentioribus plerique agnoscunt, eique titulum Oecumenicæ praefifigunt. Inter eos non infimi nominis sunt Georgius Gemistus, Philagrius, Bryennius, & qui illius Canones illustrare conati sunt Theodorus Balsamo, ac Ioannes Zonaras. His adde Nilum Thessalonicensem, Macarium Ancyrahum, & alios, ne singulos commemorem . Marcus Ephesius in Concilio Florent. Sess. Sexta, & in professione suæ fidei dicit, hanc Synodum, quæ restituit Photium, priorem Adriani, auctoritate Ioannis, cuius adhuc ad Photium extant Epistolæ, abrogasse, & censuisse additionem in Symbolo penitus esse expungendam, & ex eo tempore, ad suum usque diem a magna Constantinopolitana Ecclesia legi, Ἀ̓ πάντα τὰ τῶν ἁγίων Πατριαρχῶν Φωτίου, ἐ Ἰγνατίου [?] γραφέντα ἢ λαληθέντα, ἀνάθεμα. Omnibus, quæ aduersus sanctos Patriarchas Photium, & Ignatium scripta, vel dicta sunt, anathema. Octauam Oecumenicam nuncupatam fuisse, Patres Concilij, cum alia maioris momenti vrgerent, dicta Ephesij, vti quibus tum responderetur minus digna neglexerunt. Nos infra illa examinabimus. & hæc quidem Græci ex schismate, qui suo fauentes Photio, non æque de aliis iudicant. Non desunt alij & clarioris inter Græcos nominis, qui dictam Synodum vti legitime coactam, & celebratam recipiunt, sed duas postremas Actiones Sextam nempe, & Quintam prorsus reijciunt, & argumentis ex eadem Synodo petitis tradunt, eas Photianorum esse assumenta. Ita Manuël Caleca lib. 4. aduersus Græcos, Anonymus in Marg. Cod. Vatic. 1115. in Actione Sexta ipsius Synodi, quorum ve rba[?] infra recensebo. Sed vt testata dicas, quædam de temporibus Photij tibi prælibanda sunt. Photius occupato Throno, exterminatoque Ignatio Patriarcha, videns etiam tum plurimorum animum ad Ignatium accedere, vt sibi Principatum constabiliret, & Ignatij condemnatione populum ad sui beneuolentiam conuelleret, Imperatoris, ac Bardæ imperioso ministerio Concilium sibi adhærentium Episcoporum congregat. Sed cum neque eo modo res ad nutum procederent, legat Oratores ad Nicolaum Pontificem Romanum id vnum rogans, vt suos Constantinopolim ad extirpandam nondum prorsus extinctam Iconomachorum hæresim mitteret, sic enim sui in throno confirmationem cum animo agitabat, scribens, Ignatium ob senium & eneruatas vires throno renunciasse, recepisse se in Monasterium Insulæ, in quo cum omni honore, & obsequio viueret. Decreto Nicolai Rodoaldus Portuensis, & Zacharias Anagninus cum mandatis Constantinopolim veniunt, vt quæitiostionem de sacris Imaginibus alias iudicatam definirent: de causa inter Photium, & Ignatium inquirerent, & ad se referent: cum Photio uti laico, non uti Episcopo communicarent. Sed cum Constantinopoli non approbaretur neq; Ignatij eiectio, neq; Photij in eius locum subrogatio, Legatis minus digne susceptis per centum dies cum aliis commercium interdicitur, tandem malis, metuque coacti Concilio numerosissimo Episcoporum Photio fauentium in Ecclesia sanctorum Apostolorum interfuerunt, in quo deductus Constantinopolim Ignatius accusatur, criminis loco obijcitur, fauore Principum Ecclesiam occupasse, in S. Methodium praedecessorem suum contumeliosum, & iniuriosum extitisse, ideoque damnatus, & solemni ritu indumentis Pontificijs exutus, exauctoratur. Et haec est Secunda Photij Synodus, quam Balsamo nimis inconsultus, & Graecis ipsis contra nitentibus Oecumenicam, tum ob praesentiam Legatorum Pontificis, tum ob multitudinem Episcoporum, Nicaenorum Patrum numerum exaequantem, namque erant trecenti decem & octo, vocitat. Veruntamen qui convenerant, cum suspecti inimici Ignatij, & ipsius Photij mancipia essent, in iudicio illo ferendo inepti iudicati sunt. Ob nefaria quoque iudicata, gestaque ad nutum Imperatoris, qui eidem Concilio tanquam Iudex interfuit, & contra innocentes Episcopos, & Legatos Apostolicos multa machinatus est, Latrocinalem Synodum Nicolaus Pontifex congregationem illam appellauit. & apud Græcos, quod in primo congressu de causa Ignatij, in secundo de cultu Imaginum actum est, licet eodem loco eodemque tempore, & ab ijsdem celebrata Prima, & Secunda sibi nomen vendicauit. Et hæc Constantinopoli ante damnationem suam Photius proterue, & maligna mente fingebat, & machinas contra Ignatium admouebat. Sed Romæ in Concilio Apostolicæ Sedis restituto Ignatio, Photio, & criminis socijs eiectis, depositisque Photius furore concitus, adnitentibus Michaële Imperatore & Barda Cæsare Conciliabulum præsidente Imperato-re, nefarijsque hominibus, & Orientalium Sedium Vicarijs suppositis congregat, & in Romanum Pontificem falsa crimina comminiscēdo anathematis sententiam profert, compositoque libello ea de re, mille circiter subscriptiones Antistitum de suo adumbratas inserit, cum præter vnum & viginti, nullus prorsus repertus fit tantæ impietatis fautor, reclamantibus reliquis, non posse Summmum Pontificem ab inferioribus iudicari. Tum scripsit ad omnes Orientales Patriarchas Epistolam de cogenda Synodo Oecumenica aduersus Nicolaum, Latinam Ecclesiam multis appictis[?] criminibus calumniose infamans. Post cædem Bardæ nihil se profecisse cernens, persuadet Michaeli, ut coacta Synodo Nicolaum damnaret, a quo fuerat antea ipse damnatus. Sic collectis suæ factionis Episcopis, substitutisque aliis, qui vicem Patriarcharum Orientis tenerent, in Romanum Pontificem anathematis sententiam a se in Concilio latam notam Italis per Legatos suos facit, conatus etiam Ludouicum Imperatorem inducere, ut Nicolaum a Sede deturbaret, promittens se proclamaturum illum Constantinopoli Imperatorem. Cæso Michaele initio Imperij Basilij plena Synodo Photius eijcitur, & restituitur Ignatius. Sed post multos annos fraudibus mire concinnatis, reconciliatus Basilio, & vita functo Ignatio in Cathedram restitutus, Ignatianos diris vexationibus affligit, postea Pontificis literis, quarum ille contextum immutauerat[?], detrahendo, quæ in Ecclesiæ Romanæ auctoritatem; & Ignatij laudem, vel in reprehensionem suiipsius[?] dicta essent, addendo multa in laudem propriam, & damnationem Synodorum contra ipsum celebratarum, ac deinceps omnia pro arbitrio confundendo, ut si vera cum immutatis comparentur, vix cognoscas, eam Photij versionem ad Ioannis Epistolas pertinere, in communionem receptus existimatur. Legatis itaque Romanis praesentibus, si tamen ea legatio vera est, & non conficta, nec non Episcopis Orientalibus Synodum celebrat, in cuius postremis Actionibus comprobatur fidei definitio in Septem Oecumenicis Synodis recepta, contestationibus additis, ne quid in ea ab aliquo adderetur, vel minueretur omnino, recitatumque est Symbolum Nicaenum, sive Constantinopolitanum, ita quidem sugillans, damnansque Latinos, quod in eo apposuissent verba illa Filioq; Pari modo eadem de re inveni-tur in multis Codicibus annexa ad Photium Ioannis Papae Epistola ab aliquo nebulone, & forte etiam abipso Photio conficta, in qua eandem cum Graecis sententiam de processione Spiritus Sancti profitetur Pontifex, & se professurum in posterum promittit. Decretis Synodalibus subscribit Basilius Imperator, expressam addens improbationem eorum omnium, quae contra Photium acta essent in octaua Synodo legitima, cui ipse subscripserat vna cum filijs, quos huic quoq; Photianae Synodo subscribere voluit.
units.tr: What, then, should be thought of the Eighth Photian Synod? Many of the Schismatics, and especially the more recent ones, acknowledge it as a true and lawful synod, and what is more, as an Ecumenical one, and they prefix to it the title of Ecumenical. Among them are men of no small name: George Gemistus, Philagrius, Bryennius, and those who have tried to illustrate its canons, Theodore Balsamon and John Zonaras. To these add Nilus of Thessalonica, Macarius of Ancyra, and others, not to mention each one individually. Marcus of Ephesus, in the sixth session of the Council of Florence and in his profession of faith, says that this synod, which restored Photius, annulled the earlier synod of Hadrian, by the authority of John, to whom letters addressed to Photius still survive; and that it decreed that the addition in the Creed was to be entirely expunged; and that from that time until his own day the great Church of Constantinople has read: Anathema to all things written or spoken against the holy Patriarchs Photius and Ignatius. [Ἀ̓ πάντα τὰ τῶν ἁγίων Πατριαρχῶν Φωτίου, ἐ Ἰγνατίου [?] γραφέντα ἢ λαληθέντα, ἀνάθεμα.] The fathers of the council, when they were pressed by other matters of greater weight, neglected to answer the points raised at Ephesus, and so the synod was called Eighth Ecumenical. We will examine those points below. These are the views of the Greeks who belong to the schism, and who, favouring Photius, do not judge the others equally. There are also other Greeks of no small repute who accept the said synod as lawfully convened and held, but who wholly reject its last two sessions, the Sixth and Fifth, and who hand down, from arguments drawn from that same synod, that they are the additions of the Photians. So Manuel Caleca, in book 4 against the Greeks, and an anonymous writer in the margin of the Vatican codex 1115, in the Sixth Session of the same synod, whose words I shall set out below. But so that you may understand the matter, some things about the times of Photius must first be set before you. Photius, having seized the throne and driven out the Patriarch Ignatius, and seeing that the minds of many were still inclining towards Ignatius, convened, by the imperious ministry of the Emperor and of Bardas, a council of bishops who adhered to him, in order to establish his own primacy and to win over the people's goodwill by condemning Ignatius. But since matters did not go according to his wishes even in this way, he sent envoys to Pope Nicholas, the Roman Pontiff, asking one thing only: that he send his own men to Constantinople to stamp out the heresy of the Iconoclasts, which was not yet wholly extinct. For thus he was scheming to secure his confirmation on the throne, writing that Ignatius, because of old age and weakened strength, had resigned the throne, and had withdrawn to a monastery on an island, where he lived with every honour and deference. By decree of Nicholas, Rodoald of Porto and Zacharias of Anagni came to Constantinople with their instructions: to settle the question of the sacred images, which had been decided elsewhere; to inquire into the cause between Photius and Ignatius and report back to him; and to hold communion with Photius as a layman, not as a bishop. But since the deposition of Ignatius and the substitution of Photius in his place were not approved at Constantinople, the legates were not received with due respect, and for a hundred days they were forbidden all contact with others. At last, compelled by threats and fear, they attended, in the church of the holy Apostles, a very large council of bishops who favoured Photius. There Ignatius, brought to Constantinople, was accused; it was laid against him as a crime that he had seized the Church through the favour of princes, and that he had been insolent and abusive towards St Methodius, his predecessor. On this ground he was condemned, and with solemn ritual, stripped of his pontifical vestments, and deposed. This is the Second Synod of Photius, which Balsamon, too rashly, and against the protests of the Greeks themselves, calls Ecumenical, both because of the presence of the Pope's legates and because of the multitude of bishops, which equalled the number of the Nicene fathers, for there were three hundred and eighteen. Yet those who had gathered, being suspect enemies of Ignatius and the tools of Photius himself, were judged unfit to pass that judgment. Its decisions and proceedings, too, were made at the emperor's nod: he attended the same council as judge, and he devised much against the innocent bishops and the apostolic legates. Pope Nicholas called that gathering a Robber Synod. Among the Greeks, however, it claimed for itself the names First and Second, because in the first session the case of Ignatius was dealt with, and in the second the veneration of images, although it was held in the same place, at the same time, and by the same people. Photius, before his own condemnation, shamelessly and with a malicious mind pretended these things at Constantinople, and brought his machinations against Ignatius to bear. But at Rome, in a council of the Apostolic See, Ignatius was restored, and Photius and his accomplices were expelled and deposed. Then Photius, roused to fury, with the support of the Emperor Michael and of Caesar Bardas, convened a conventicle presided over by the Emperor, made up of wicked men and of substitutes who were put forward as vicars of the Eastern sees. There he pronounced a sentence of anathema against the Roman Pontiff, devising false crimes against him. He drew up a document on this matter and inserted about a thousand signatures of bishops, which he had sketched himself, although, apart from twenty-one, not one of them could be found to favour such impiety, the others protesting that the Supreme Pontiff could not be judged by his inferiors. Then he wrote to all the Eastern Patriarchs a letter about convening an Ecumenical Synod against Nicholas, slandering the Latin Church with many invented crimes. After the murder of Bardas, seeing that he had achieved nothing, he persuaded Michael to convene a synod and condemn Nicholas, by whom he himself had earlier been condemned. So, having gathered bishops of his own faction and substituted others to hold the place of the Patriarchs of the East, he made known to the Italians, through his legates, the sentence of anathema pronounced by him in the council against the Roman Pontiff. He also tried to induce the Emperor Louis to drive Nicholas from the See, promising that he would proclaim Louis Emperor at Constantinople. When Michael was slain at the beginning of the reign of Basil, Photius was expelled by a full synod, and Ignatius was restored. But after many years, having reconciled himself with Basil through cunningly devised frauds, and after Ignatius had died and been restored to the throne, Photius harassed the followers of Ignatius with dreadful persecutions. Later, by distorting the letters of the Pontiff, whose text he had altered, he removed whatever had been said in them in support of the authority of the Roman Church and in praise of Ignatius, or in rebuke of himself, and added much in his own praise and in condemnation of the synods held against him. Thereafter he confused everything at his pleasure, so that if the true texts are compared with the altered ones, you can scarcely tell them apart. That Photian version of the letters of John is held to pertain to communion. So, with Roman legates present (if indeed that embassy was true and not invented), and with Eastern bishops, he held a synod, in whose last sessions was confirmed a definition of faith received in the seven Ecumenical Synods, with added attestations that nothing whatever was to be added to it or subtracted from it by anyone. The Nicene, or Constantinopolitan, Creed was recited, and the Latins were rebuked and condemned in the strongest terms, because they had inserted in it the words Filioque. In the same way, in many codices, there is found in the same matter a letter of Pope John to Photius, appended by some scoundrel, and perhaps by Photius himself, in which the Pontiff professes the same view as the Greeks on the procession of the Holy Spirit, and promises that he will profess it in future. Emperor Basil subscribed to the synodal decrees, adding an express disapproval of all that had been done against Photius in the eighth lawful synod, to which he himself had subscribed along with his sons, whom he also wished to subscribe to this Photian synod.

units.la: Hanc Synodum sub Octauae Generalis nomine mirum est,quantum Schismatici venerentur, dum per eam & auctoritas Pontificia vulneretur, & sui Photij partes subleuentur, & additio in Symbolo, siue mauis processio ex Filio conuellatur. Sunt ergo Synodi coactæ a Photio, Prima post expulsum Ignatium ad reconciliandos sibi animos Præsulum: Secunda, qua præsidentibus Legatis Pontificijs Rodoaldo & Zacharia, Ignatius damnatur exauctoraturq; quæ a Nicolao Pontifice Latrocinalis appellatur: Tertia & quarta, quas ille post fui in Romano Concilio condemnationem coëgit, siue potius confinxit alteram aduersus Romanam Sedem, alteram aduersus Ignatium: Quinta post necem Bardæ, sub Michaële tamen, in qua aduersus Romanum Pontificem Nicolaum anathematis sententiam protulit: Sexta post obitum Ignatij, & sui cum Basilio reconciliationem, qua in Throno Constantinopolitano, Ioannis Pontificis, cuius & multas laudes prosequitur, literis, falsatis tamen, confirmatur, & in qua impudentissime suam auctoritatem etiam in Romanam iurisdictionem extendit, tantum non sibi Pontificem obnoxium faciens, & afferentes processionem ex Filio Spiritus condemnat ita, vt additio illa futuris etiam temporibus interdicatur.
units.tr: It is remarkable how greatly the schismatics venerate this synod under the name of the Eighth Ecumenical, since by it the authority of the Pope is wounded, the cause of Photius is upheld, and the addition to the Creed, or, if you prefer, the procession from the Son, is overturned. There are therefore the following synods convened by Photius: the first, after Ignatius was expelled, to reconcile the minds of the prelates to himself; the second, in which, with the Pontifical legates Rodoald and Zacharias presiding, Ignatius was condemned and deposed, which Pope Nicholas called the Robber Synod; the third and fourth, which he gathered after his own condemnation at the Roman council, or rather feigned, one against the Roman See and the other against Ignatius; the fifth, after the death of Bardas, yet under Michael, in which he pronounced a sentence of anathema against the Roman Pontiff Nicholas; the sixth, after the death of Ignatius and his reconciliation with Basil, in which, on the throne of Constantinople, the letters of Pope John, though falsified, are confirmed (and he lavishes many praises on John), and in which he most shamelessly extends his own authority even over Roman jurisdiction, making the Pontiff, as it were, subject to himself, and he condemns those who assert the procession of the Spirit from the Son, so that that addition is forbidden even for times to come.

units.la: Roberti Creyghtonis de his ijsdem Synodis verba proferuntur, & numeratis mendacijs refelluntur.
units.tr: The words of Robert Creyghton about these same synods are quoted, and refuted by a count of his lies.

units.la: ET hæc de Synodis pro Photio, & contra Photium coactis vti solide, ita plene dicta sufficerent. Veruntamen cum Robertus Creyghtonus non probus, nec fidus, sed ad voluntatem recens nouæ Florentinæ Synodi Interpres, multa in vnum conuoluens, a veritate historica multum aberret in illis referendis, eius dicta hic apposita examinabimus, vt ex ijs tanquam ex vngue Leonem agnoscas, & quanti sit faciendus in reliquis, pateat. Verba illius sunt in Præfatione ad Lectorem pro vera, vt ipse nugatur, Historia vnionis non verae inter Græcos & Latinos in Concilio Florentino, In fortuna Photiana mutabili decursu illud singulare arbitror contigit tres Synodos Oecumenicas intra octodecim annorum spatia celebrari Imperatorum, Patriarcharum auctoritatibus approbatas. Sola nempe Creyghtoni imaginaria apprehensione compositas. In prima, in qua depositus fuit Ignatius, intrusus Photius, nullus intercessit Paparum assensus, nullum Concilij etiam particularis decretum, sed mera potestas, & oppressio virum sanctissimum de solio deiecit: Namq; cum Ignatius in offensionem Bardae incurriffet, & Sedis abdicationem saepius ab Episcopis, ad hoc a Barda legatis, scribere pernegasset, & Patriciorum atque Judicum machinis & pollicitationibus petitus non decessisset, sed firmus, immotusque in proposito stetisset, dignitatem constantissime propugnans, de solio ejicitur, & Photius in Vrbis regiae Patriarchatum ab Ignatii adversariis, & a profanis magistratibus promovetur, confecraturq; a Gregorio Asbesta Episcopo Syracusano Constantinopoli tum de multis maleficiis reo immorante, & jam Romae ob scelera exauctorato, & quem Ignatius in sui consecratione Sacris interesse minime voluit. Secutae sunt variae Ignatii relegationes in Insulas, & certamina; & cum tandem in Mitylenae exul ageret, Photius sibi affinium, & pernecessariorum coacta Synodo in Apostolorum templo Ignatium absentem, non vocatum, non auditum anathemate ferit, & exauctorat, accusator idem & judex, & depositioni illius non annuentes vinculis, & carceribus, & languoribus mactat: & ut gratiam aliorum captaret, mittit Romam ad Nicolaum Papam Oratores, Romanae cupiens Ecclesiae auctoritate Ignatij condemnationem firmare, & testatam reddere, scribens Ignatium senio, morboq; confectum se munere abdicasse, commorari in Infula ab omnibus honore, & officijs cultum. His motus Nicolaus Zachariam, & Rodoaldum Episcopos ablegat, & coacta Synodo convocatur Ignatius de oblatis sibi criminibus responsurus. Processit sacro Patriarcha ornatu indutus, quo inter eundum spoliatus, Synodo sistitur, condemnatur, & deponitur: quæ postmodum cum sciuisset Nicolaus Pontifex legatos Zachariam,& Rodoaldum exauctoratos anathemate percussit, Photium tyrannum, & adulterum pronunciauit, & Synodi suæ decreto deponit, omnesque ab eodem Photio confecratos, ipsumque Imperatorem cum omni eius Senatu per literas suas a cœtu fidelium excludit: Legatur vita Ignatij a Niceta scripta. Et si fides huius sapientissimi viri respuitur, adeatur Synodicum, cuius Auctor hæc eadem narrat. [?]Φώτ[?]ν ἐν τῷ θείοις καὶ ἱε-ρὸς κανόνας τῷ θεῷ [?]ἐπιλαβόμενον, ἐξ ἰσοῖς [?]πῷ νουχάσαμ[?], οἵσπερ ὠλίσθησαν, ἀλλ' εἰς θυμὸν κινήσας τὸν Αὐτοκράτορα μὴ μυείᾳ [?]ἀνα [?]ἐξοικίζ[?]ς τὴν νῆσῳ Μιτυλήνῃ [?]ἢ ἀδῶον Γυναικῶν συν-[?]ἀθεσίας [?]ποτιμέσσων ἐν Βλαχέρναις συνέδριον, [?]καθαιρεῖ μὴ παέντα τὸν ἀδικούμενον, [?]ἐ [?]ἀπ' ἀρχαμένως [?]καὶ [?]τῆς πονηρᾶς [?]ἐπὶ νῦμασι, ἐ τῆς κοινωνίας ἀντέχεσθαι[?], πάσης κακυχίας ἐρ-γάζατο κατα χώρια, ἀθροίζεις ἔνθα καὶ ὡς ἠβέλετο. Ἐ'π γὰρ μὲν ἐ πρὸς ἡ Ῥώμης ἐ μαπαείτην ἐξαπέστει-λε Νικόλαον, ἐκκ... [?] ὡς παρμπτιζάμψον ἐφ' γῆς λι-παςων ἡ ἀδῆνωσι σωματος Φώτιον ἀνεδίδαξεν τὴν Ἰγνάτιον, ἐ πρὸς ἀποβολὴν τολμῶν ταλάω ἡ τὴν εἰκονομάχων αἱρέσεως τοπότημεν, ἐ ἐμφθῶσαι αὐτὸ μεγάλως ἱκετεύειν, Ἰγνατίῳ δόλῳ φεαξματοδόμους τὴν κατάκλεισιν.
units.tr: These things about the synods gathered for Photius and against Photius would be enough, stated soundly and fully as they are. However, since Robert Creyghton, a man neither honest nor trustworthy, but an interpreter of the recent Florentine synod who bends to its wishes, piles many things together and wanders far from historical truth in reporting them, I will examine his words set down here, so that you may know the lion by his claw and see how much weight his other statements deserve. His words are in the Preface to the Reader of his so-called true history of the union between Greeks and Latins at the Council of Florence: In the changing course of Photius's fortunes, I think this unique thing happened: three Ecumenical Synods were held within the span of eighteen years, approved by the authority of emperors and patriarchs. Clearly these are things Creyghton has put together by his own imaginary understanding. In the first, in which Ignatius was deposed and Photius was thrust in, no assent of the popes intervened, and not even a decree of any particular council; mere power and oppression cast that most holy man from the throne. For when Ignatius had incurred the displeasure of Bardas, and had steadfastly refused to write to the bishops, at Bardas's request and through his envoys, about giving up his see, and when he did not yield to the contrivances and promises of the patricians and judges but stood firm and unmoved in his purpose, defending his dignity most constantly, he was driven from the throne. Photius was promoted to the patriarchate of the imperial city by Ignatius's enemies and by secular magistrates, and was consecrated by Gregory Asbestas, bishop of Syracuse, who was then staying at Constantinople, accused of many crimes, and already deposed at Rome for his wickedness, and whom Ignatius had been unwilling to have present at his own consecration. Various exiles of Ignatius to islands followed, and conflicts. And when at last he was living in exile at Mitylene, Photius, having gathered a synod of his relatives and close associates in the church of the Apostles, condemned the absent Ignatius with an anathema, though he had not been summoned or heard, and deposed him; he was accuser and judge at once. Those who did not agree to his deposition he tormented with chains, prisons and sickness. And to win the favour of others he sent envoys to Pope Nicholas at Rome, wishing to confirm Ignatius's condemnation by the authority of the Roman Church and to make it attested, writing that Ignatius, worn out by old age and sickness, had resigned his office, and that he lived on an island, honoured and served by all. Moved by this, Nicholas sent away the bishops Zacharias and Rhodoald, and a synod was convened so that Ignatius might answer the charges brought against him. The holy patriarch came in wearing his vestments, but on the way he was stripped of them, brought before the synod, condemned and deposed. Afterwards, when Pope Nicholas had learned this, he struck with an anathema the legates Zacharias and Rhodoald, who had been deposed; he pronounced Photius a tyrant and an adulterer and deprived him by the decree of his own synod, and by his letters he excluded from the assembly of the faithful all who had been consecrated by Photius, and the emperor himself with his whole senate. Let the life of Ignatius written by Nicetas be read. And if the trustworthiness of that most wise man is rejected, let the Synodicon be consulted, whose author relates these same things. [Greek passage from the Synodicon, badly garbled in the scan: Photius, laying hold of the divine and holy canons, did not stop at the errors he had fallen into, but stirred the Emperor to anger, and after many injuries exiled the innocent Ignatius to the island of Mitylene; then, in a council of wicked men gathered at Blachernae, he deposed him in his absence, and he tormented with every kind of calamity those who refused to subscribe to his evil nods or who clung to Ignatius's communion. Then he sent envoys to Nicholas, Pope of Rome, and so on, as he pleased. Nicholas sent Rhodoald and Zacharias, bishops of Rome, to Constantinople, and when they arrived Photius held a synod in the church of the holy Apostles and gave them Ignatius to be judged in his absence; he brought seventy-two men to bear false witness and deposed Ignatius, and deposed the envoys too. When the holy Pope Nicholas learned this, he deposed Rhodoald and Zacharias and anathematized Photius as an adulterer and tyrant.]

units.la: Ῥοδοάλδῳ δὲ καὶ Ζαχαρίου Ῥωμαίων Ἐπισκόπων τοποτηρητὴς Νικολάῳ καταλαβόντων Κωνσαντινούπολιν, Φώτιον ἐν τρίναφ τὴν ἀγίων καὶ πανδυφήμων Ἀ'ποστόλων Χειρὶ ἀθεζωώντων Σωδοδν ποιησάμενον, ἀχώμιον πρὸς αὐτὸν ἡμέρας τὴν ἱεραρχίαν Ἰγνάτιον παρεσί δασεν, καὶ ἐβδομήκοντα καὶ δύο ἀγελάτες ἄνδρες ηξ.... ἀλλοί ὁ Φώτιος φυλάττοντος ἀλ-ηφόρων ἀλλοί ἁλλά τοῦ αὐτοῦ πιθ ὠφελ ἐπὶ ἄνδρες καὶ ἐφοράς, Ἰγνάτιον, ἐπαναγκῆς τῇ σωτηρίᾳ, ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἡμεῖς ἐπὶ ἀκρῶν τρόπους κατὰ φύσιν, ἐπαναγκῆς τῇ σωτηρίᾳ ἐκ τὸ ὑπὲρ ταύτην ἀνευ[?]... ἐχθ ἔχει ἀνθρώπου. Εἴ[?]ς Ἐπίσκοπον κοσμικοῖς ἀρχῆσι ἀπὸ ἐτέρων ἀλλὰ ἐκκλησίας ἐμβάνετο καθαρεύθη. Ὑποσωθῆσας τὸ κανόν, Ὃ ἐπαρόμενον ἐξ ἀλλ' τόπου ἐν ὑποθῆσ ἐκδαρέσιαν ἀποφηνάμενος, ὁ αὐτός καθαίρεσιν. units.tr: When Rhodoald and Zacharias, as deputies of the Roman bishops, had reached Constantinople, Photius held a synod in the church of the holy and all-praised Apostles, and presented Ignatius to them as a hierarch to be judged in his absence. He brought in seventy-two men as witnesses, and he persuaded them to swear, and he deposed Ignatius, and the envoys too. Photius and his supporters and the magistrates, and the rest of the holy patriarchs, joined in this; and Nicholas, when he learned it, deposed Rhodoald and Zacharias and anathematized Photius as an adulterer and tyrant, and cut off from communion the Emperor Michael, the officials and all who communicated with Photius. Those who wish to know more fully what is briefly said in the Synodicon may read the life of Ignatius by Nicetas. Here the same events are related by a third writer of that time, George the Sinner.

units.la: Photius itaque praeter diuinorum sacrorumque Canonum statuta thronum arripiens, non acquiescebat contentus de ijs, in quibus lapsus fuerat, sed iracundiam Imperatoris magis, ac magis succendens post multas noxas illatas ad insulam Mitylenem Ignatium innoxium relegat, & coacto apud Blachernas malig-nantium conciliabulo abstentem, qui erat illata iniuria, deponit, & renuentes subscribere prauis suis nutibus, & communionem illius amplexatos, omni calamitatis genere maestauit, ad arbitrium suum quo vellet, relegatos. Praeterea ad beatum Nicolaum Romanum Praesulem Oratores mittit, quibus significabat, ob grauem Ignatium senectutem, & malam corporis valetudinem sponte throno renunciasse, instantesque deprecabatur, ut ad Iconomachorum haeresim prorsus abolendam Byzantium locumtenentes mitteret, hac quoque machina Ignatij condemnationem procurans.
units.tr: Photius, therefore, seizing the throne contrary to the decrees of the divine and sacred canons, was not content with what he had done wrong, but, kindling the anger of the Emperor more and more, after many injuries inflicted, relegated the innocent Ignatius to the island of Mitylene. At a conventicle of malicious men gathered at Blachernae, he deposed Ignatius in his absence, though Ignatius was the one wronged, and he tormented with every kind of calamity those who refused to subscribe to his wicked nods and who embraced Ignatius's communion, banishing them wherever he wished. Moreover, he sent envoys to the blessed Nicholas, Roman prelate, by whom he signified that Ignatius, because of his heavy old age and poor health, had voluntarily renounced the throne; and he urgently begged that he would send deputies to Byzantium to root out completely the heresy of the iconoclasts, procuring by this device, too, the condemnation of Ignatius.

units.la: Nam cum Rodoaldus, & Zacharias Romani Episcopi Oratoresque Nicolai Constantinopolim aduentassent, Photius in templo sanctorum, gloriosissimorum Apostolorum Christi malignan-tium Synodo congregata ad ipsam Hierarchām Ignatium conduci procuravit, adductisq; septuaginta duobus hominibus gregariis, qui falsum testimonium dicerent, persuadet illis, cum essent laici, partim minis, partim promissis inuertens, & ad suam sententiam transferens, affirmata teste divina omni potestate, iurandum interponere, ante annos undecim, menses quatuor, & dies viginti non fuisse promotum rite in Sedem Patriarchām, lecto in Congregatione segmento apostaticæ decisionis in hunc modum. Si quis Episcopus Laicorum Principum ope in possessionem Ecclesiæ venerit deponatur; id quod sequitur Canonis, premens, & per sola asserta depositionem decernens. Id ubi addidicit Sanctus Papa Nicolaus, neque enim latere poterat per universum terrarum Orbem dispersa consimilis iniquitas, proprios locumtenentes accurate examinatos, & propriis eorundem sermonibus muneribus corruptos esse comprehensos perpetua depositione punit, & divina sacraq; Synodo coacta, Photium uti adulterum & assultorem anathematizat: quæ illius gratia, & ab ipso, nullo modo admittenda esse decernens, & cum eo communicantibus Michaeli Imperatori, Photio, subditis, Principibus, & reliquis Sanctis Patriarchis Synodicis suis dimissis. Si quæ hic in Synodico strictim dicta sunt, enucleatius addiscere cupis, legito vitam Ignatij a Niceta concin-natam . Hisce tertius accedet eorundem temporum Scriptor Georgius Hamartolus;
units.tr: For when Rhodoald and Zacharias, Roman bishops and envoys of Nicholas, had arrived at Constantinople, Photius, in the church of the holy and most glorious Apostles of Christ, convened a malicious synod and arranged for Ignatius to be brought before that very hierarchy. Bringing forward seventy-two common men to give false testimony, he persuaded them, though they were laymen, partly by threats and partly by promises, turning them to his own opinion, to affirm under oath, with every power of divine witness, that eleven years, four months and twenty days before, he had not been rightly promoted to the patriarchal see, a passage of the apostate decision being read in the assembly in this manner: If any bishop comes into possession of a church by the help of lay princes, let him be deposed; and what follows of the canon, pressing and decreeing deposition by these words alone. When the holy Pope Nicholas learned this, since such iniquity could not stay hidden, having spread throughout the whole world, he punished with perpetual deposition his own envoys, who were found to have been corrupted by Photius's gifts and words after being carefully examined. He convened a divine and sacred synod, and anathematized Photius as an adulterer and assailant, decreeing that his ordinations were by no means to be admitted, and that those who communicated with him, namely the Emperor Michael, Photius, the subjects, the princes, and the other holy patriarchs, were to be dismissed from his synodical letters. If you wish to learn more fully the things briefly said here in the Synodicon, read the life of Ignatius composed by Nicetas. To these will be added a third writer of the same times, George the Sinner.

units.tr: The patriarch Ignatius, when a rumour had spread that Caesar Bardas was having an affair with his daughter-in-law, often urged him to give up such defilement, since men of high rank ought to be a model of virtue and chastity. Bardas, stung by these words as by a goad, nursed hatred for him. When the patriarch then refused him communion as he hurried to receive it, Bardas, beside himself and burning with anger, cast out the admonisher as a wicked man and a corrupter of the Church. He had him subjected to cruel and incurable torments and forced him to give up the patriarchate. He handed him over to Theodore called the Moor, and to John Gorgonites and Nicholas Skutelops, who, in the church of the Apostles, shut him with broken legs into the coffin of Constantine Copronymus and left him naked in the winter weather. From there the athlete used to bring forth flesh and blood mixed with putrefaction from his hidden parts. Bearing these dreadful things, this most blessed man spoke no evil word against the Lord. So the Lord sent him Constantine the Armenian, the only comfort in his misfortunes. He, deceiving the wicked men by means of a glass vessel of wine, and also bread and sometimes fruit, came to the holy man, drew him out of the coffin and comforted him for a little while in his calamities, raising his spirits until the guards came back. Meanwhile Caesar promoted Photius, who was then one of his secretaries, to the patriarchate. He was a man learned in every branch of letters.

Patriarcha Ignatius fama evulgata Cæsarem Bardam nurum fiam incestare, sæpius cum adhortatus est, ut a simili piaculo abstineret, neque esset multis offensio, qui virtutis ac pudicitiæ deberet esse exemplum. Cæsar verbis veluti aculeis punctus odia in Patriarcham nutriebat. Cum vero tandem ad communionem properantem Patriarcha repulisset, vix ille compos animi, & iracundia ardens monitorem ad frugem, veluti iniquum, & corruptorem ab Ecclesia eiicit, tormentisque insanabilibus afflixit, cogens Patriarchatu renunciare. Namque eum dedidit Theodoro cognomento Moro, nec non Ioanni Gorgonitæ, & Nicolao Scutelopi, qui in templo Apostolorum, & Constantini Copronymi urna cruribus fractis inclusum, hyemali tempestate nudum derelinquunt. Hinc Athleta ex occultis carnes putredine, & sanguine commixtas eiiciebat. Ita dira perferens fortunatissimus hic vir, non est ad Dominum malum locutus: ideoque mittit illi Dominus Constantinum Armenium, qui esset unicum illi in malis solatium. Hic etenim vasculo vitreo vini pleno, nec non & pane quandoq; etiamfructibus[?], maleficorum conatus fallens, ad Beatum accedens, eumque urna educens paululum adversos casus consolabatur, levabatque fortunas, donec denuo custodes accederent. Cæsar interim Photium in Patriarchatum promouit, qui tum a Secretis erat, virum literis omnibus excultum. Et hæc contra Ignatium a Photio procurata; & ad summum perducta Synodus erit Oecumenica?. Qui conuenit? Lupus in Pastorem iniurius, in gregem intrusus, aliena indigne occupans, a viro multorum criminum, & depositocconsecratus, potestate, ac vi secularium, & tyrannide dominantium promotus Synodum Oecumenicam constituet? Hoc plane Latini non dicent, quod nec Græci etiam ipsi Ecclesiæ Romanæ infensi audent dicere. Quis præter ipsum Photium, & Photij mancipia promotionem Photij approbauit, idque in Photiana hac de qua agimus Synodo? Quis Ignatium vnquam inter Græcos vti criminum reum condemnatum fuisse, nisi execrandissimus quispiam pronunciauit? Hæc Synodus iustum condemnauit, & eum ipsum quem vniuersa Græcorum Ecclesia inter Sanctos relatum colit, & veneratur; & multorum criminum reum in eius locum substituit. Non erit ergo apud Græcos, quidquid sit apud Hæreticos, Oecumenica, cum Græci suas Oecumenicas Synodos colant, & observent, neque ab illis in aliquo deflectere profiteantur. Falsum ergo est quod de prima dicitur, quam συνοδικὸν λεγικόν vocauit Stylianus Episcopus Neocæsareæ, il-
units.tr: The patriarch Ignatius, when a rumour had spread that Caesar Bardas was defiling his daughter-in-law, often urged him to abstain from such a sin, since it would cause offence to many who ought to be an example of virtue and chastity. Caesar, stung by these words as by goads, nursed hatred against the patriarch. When at last the patriarch refused him communion as he hastened to it, Caesar, scarcely in control of himself and burning with anger, cast out the admonisher from the Church as a wicked man and corrupter, and subjected him to incurable torments, forcing him to renounce the patriarchate. For he handed him over to Theodore called the Moor, and to John Gorgonites and Nicholas Scutelops, who, in the church of the Apostles, shut him with broken legs into the coffin of Constantine Copronymus and left him naked in the winter weather. From there the athlete used to expel flesh mixed with putrefaction and blood from his hidden parts. Bearing these dreadful things, this most fortunate man spoke no evil word against the Lord; so the Lord sent him Constantine the Armenian, who was his only solace in evils. For he, deceiving the attempts of the wicked with a glass vessel of wine, and also bread and sometimes fruit, approached the Blessed one, drew him out of the coffin, and consoled him a little in his adversities, lifting his fortunes, until the guards came again. Meanwhile Caesar promoted Photius, who was then one of the secretaries, a man adorned with all learning, to the patriarchate. And these things were carried out against Ignatius by Photius, and the synod brought to a climax will be oecumenical? Who gathered it? A wolf unjustly set over the shepherd, intruded into the flock, unworthily seizing what belongs to others, consecrated by a man of many crimes and deposed, raised to power by secular force and the tyranny of rulers, will he constitute an oecumenical synod? The Latins will plainly not say this, nor will even the Greeks who are hostile to the Roman Church dare to say it. Who, except Photius himself and his creatures, approved the promotion of Photius, and that in this Photian synod of which we are speaking? Who among the Greeks was ever pronounced a criminal condemned, unless some most accursed person? This synod condemned the just man, whom the whole Greek Church counts among the saints and venerates, and put in his place a man guilty of many crimes. Therefore, whatever it may be among heretics, it will not be oecumenical among the Greeks, since the Greeks honour and observe their own oecumenical synods and profess not to deviate from them in any respect. It is therefore false what is said of the first, which Stylianus, bishop of Neocaesarea, called the synodical treatise [συνοδικὸν λογικόν], il-

units.la: Secundam contra Photium Oecumenicam esse plane constat, quamuis inter hanc Secundam, & Primam binae aliae Photianae, altera contra Nicolaum Papam, altera contra Ignatium coactae sint. Et mirum est has quoque inter Oecumenicas ab Creyghtono non accenseri, cum contra Pontificem Romanum, & Ignatium virum Sanctissimum conscriptae sint, & in sacculis plumbo signatis repertae in arundineto, scite venusteque exaratae, quae tamen nunquam fuere celebratae, sed plane confictae, in quarum initiis manu Asbestae Gregorij coloribus artificiose erat expressus Ignatius. In prima Actione raptatus, & verberatus visebatur, titulo supra caput inscripto, Diabolus. In secunda sputis foedatus, magnaque vi tractus cum titulo, Principium peccati. In tertia de throno deturbatus cum titulo, Filius perditionis. In quarta vinculis colligatus, & exterminatus, cum titulo, Avaritia Simonis Magi. In quinta collari furca inclusus, & titulo, Qui se extollit supra omne id quod dicitur, aut colitur Deus. In sexta iam condemnatus, & titulo, Abominatio desolationis. In septima raptatus, & capite plexus, cum titulo, Antichristus. Altera in Nicolaum Pontificem Romanum calumnias manifestas, & maledicta, & illius damnationem, atque exauctorationem complectebatur, quas Theodoro, & Zachariae tradiderat cum splendidissimis muneribus ad Ludouicum Franciae Regem deferendas, vt is Nicolaum velut exauctoratum de Throno deturbaret. Omnia haec fuse narrantur a Niceta Dauide Paphlagone, & in Synodico. Φώτιος γοῦν τὸ καθ᾽ ἑαυτὸν γνοὺς Νικόλαον τὸν Πάπα ἐξέπεμψεν, Μιχαὴλ αὐτοκράτορα βασιλέα τῶν ἄλλο[?] ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ[?] κρυφῇ συνεχῶς[?] ἀλλ᾽ ἐπιτήδειον ἀνδρὶ[?] Πατριαρχῶν[?] τὴν λοιπῶν Πατριαρχῶν συναδελφῶν[?], φησὶ καὶ ὑπ᾽ ἀρχὴν πάντων Ἐπισκόπων, Πρεσβυτέρων, Διακόνων, καὶ Ἡγουμένων τῆς ὑπ᾽ αὐτὸν καταγραφῆς, καὶ Παχιμίων μὴ καθόλου ἀδίκων ποτὲ καὶ πᾶς καὶ δι᾽ αὐτῶν συνεκίνησε· δ᾽ ὧν ἀπάντων καθαίρεσιν καὶ ἀναθεματισμὸν τῷ Πάπᾳ Ῥώμης Νικολάῳ τῷ ἀποστόλῳ ἐπὶ χεῖρος Ζαχαρίᾳ Μητροπολίτῃ Χαλκηδόνος, καὶ Θεοδώρῳ Καισαρίας μετηλθέντ᾽ ἐς Λαοδίκειαν. Photius igitur agnoscens Nicolai aduersus semetipsum concitatam, atque exardescentem iracundiam, ad se malitiose Michaële Imperatore tracto, & clanculum verfuta illa Pseudosynodo concinnata, & ac si reliquorum Patriarcharum Oratores adessent, vocibus, ac inscriptionibus effectis, nec non omnium Episcoporum, Sacerdotum, Diaconorum, & Abbatum, qui in ditione illius erant, Patriciorum item, qui prorsus ignorabant, quando, & quo modo, & quare motus ille exortus fuisset, depositionem & anathematismum Nicolao divinitus instructo Papæ Romano per Zachariam Chalcedonis Metropolitam, & Theodorum Cariæ in Laodiceam promotum misit.
units.tr: That the second synod against Photius is Ecumenical is quite clear, although between this Second and the First two other Photian synods were held, one against Pope Nicholas and the other against Ignatius. It is strange that these too are not counted among the Ecumenical councils by Creyghton, since they were written against the Roman Pontiff and against Ignatius, a most holy man, and were found in leaden-sealed bags in the reed-bed, neatly and elegantly drawn up. Yet they were never celebrated, but were plainly fabricated; at the beginning of them Ignatius was artfully depicted in the colours of Asbestas Gregory. In the first action he was seen being dragged and beaten, with the title Devil written above his head. In the second he was defiled with spittle and dragged with great force, with the title Beginning of sin. In the third he was thrown down from the throne, with the title Son of perdition. In the fourth he was bound in chains and cast out, with the title Avarice of Simon Magus. In the fifth he was shut in a collar and fork, with the title He who exalts himself above all that is called or worshipped God. In the sixth, already condemned, with the title Abomination of desolation. In the seventh he was dragged and beheaded, with the title Antichrist. The other contained manifest calumnies and abuse against Pope Nicholas, and his condemnation and deposition, which Photius had handed to Theodore and Zacharias, with most splendid gifts, to be carried to Louis, King of France, so that he might cast Nicholas down from the throne as one already deposed. All these things are related at length by Nicetas David the Paphlagonian and in the Synodikon. Photius, then, knowing that Nicholas the Pope had been stirred up against himself, sent to Michael the Emperor... [the Greek is largely illegible here], and, with the assistance of all bishops, presbyters, deacons and abbots subject to him, and of certain monks not altogether unjust, moved everything through them; and by these he sent the deposition and anathema against Pope Nicholas of Rome, through Zacharias, Metropolitan of Chalcedon, and Theodore, transferred from Caesarea to Laodicea. Photius, therefore, perceiving the anger of Nicholas kindled against himself, maliciously drew Michael the Emperor into his plot and, secretly, in a sham synod devised for the purpose, by voices and inscriptions as if the envoys of the other Patriarchs were present, and with all the bishops, priests, deacons and abbots in his jurisdiction, and certain patricians who knew nothing of when, how or why that disturbance had arisen, sent the deposition and anathema against Nicholas, the Roman Pope, though divinely instructed, through Zacharias, Metropolitan of Chalcedon, and Theodore, moved from Caesarea to Laodicea.

units.la: Has duas Synodos excepit Synodus contra Photium, quæ Oecumenica reipsa est, & inter Oecumenicas collocanda, licet dirumpantur Schismatici, cum Auctoritate Romani Pontificis, & reliquorum Patriarcharum, cum ipsius Summi Pontificis Oratores, & Senatus cum ipso Imperatore, & Antistites duo supra centum, & Sacerdotes reliqui interfuerint, & sententiam, & excommunicationem in Photium a Nicolao, & Adriano latam comprobaverint, & constabiliverint. Quod etiam ipsi Photiani agnoscunt, sed ut malo remedium afferant, in ea quæ subsecuta est Synodo, & quam ipsi etiamnum Photianam vocant, si tamen vera extitit ita, ut exarata in manuscriptis legitur, decreto suo sanxerunt, eam in nulla consideratione habendam esse. Et ut condemnatio plausibilior utrique parti accederet, etiam Synodum contra Ignatium ab eodem Photio coactam, novo astu, & contrario Universalis Ecclesiæ more diris devoverunt, Ἅ[?]παντα τὰ κ[?] τῆς ἁγίων Πα[?]τριαρχῶν Γερμανὸν, Ταρασίου, Νικηφόρου, καὶ Μεθοδίου γρα-φέντα, ἢ λαληθέντα ἀνάθεμα. Universa quae contra Patriarchas Germanum, Tarasium, Nicephorum, & Methodium scripta, vel dicta, sunt, Anathema. Quae etiam suppofita esse a Photianis hinc patet, quod Constantinus Imperator illis temporibus vitam agens, in Henotico nulla facta mentione de dictis, factisque contra Ignatium reliqua recitat.
units.tr: This pair of synods was followed by a synod against Photius, which is truly Ecumenical and must be counted among the Ecumenical councils, although the schismatics tear it apart. It was held with the authority of the Roman Pontiff and the other Patriarchs; the envoys of the Supreme Pontiff himself, the Senate with the Emperor, two hundred and more bishops, and the remaining priests were present, and they approved and confirmed the sentence and excommunication pronounced against Photius by Nicholas and Adrian. The Photians themselves acknowledge this, but, in order to offer a remedy for the evil, they decreed by their own decree, in the synod that followed, which they still call Photian, if indeed it was what it is read to be in the manuscripts, that it was to be held in no consideration at all. And, so that the condemnation might be more plausible to both sides, they also cursed, with a novel trick and contrary to the common custom of the Universal Church, the synod held by Photius himself against Ignatius: Everything written or spoken against the holy Patriarchs Germanus, Tarasius, Nicephorus and Methodius, anathema [Ἅπαντα τὰ κατὰ τῶν ἁγίων Πατριαρχῶν Γερμανοῦ, Ταρασίου, Νικηφόρου, καὶ Μεθοδίου γραφέντα, ἢ λαληθέντα, ἀνάθεμα]. That these things were also forged by the Photians is clear from this: the Emperor Constantine, who lived in those times, in his Henoticon makes no mention of the things said and done against Ignatius, and recites the rest.

units.la: Et Acta similia Synodi contra Photium Octavae nempe, Graecis etiam schismaticis clarore miro patuisse, fidem facit Gregorius Hieromonachus Responsione in Professionem Fidei Marci Ephesij. Περὶ ἢ τῆς ὀγδόης Συνόδου μάλα καλῶς εἶδεν αὐτὸς ὁ αἰδέσιμος [?] τὰ ταύτης θεωρητικὰ ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῆς μονῆς τῆς πηγῆς Πεσδρόμου, τῆς καὶ Πέτρας ὀνομαζομένης, [illegible, ~10 letters] ἑνὸς μὴ τῆς ἐκτὸς, καὶ εἰδέμης, τὰ συνιστῶντα Γνάπιον, καὶ ἐγκλείζοντα αὐτοῦ τῷ Καθ[?] Κωνσταντινουπόλεως, Φώτιον ὡς [?] ἐξ-ελαύνοντα, καὶ ἀναθεματίζοντα· τὴν δὲ Γνάπιον ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις συνεταξεν ἡ Ἐκκλησία, καθὰ [?] γραφέντα, εἰ καὶ ἐν τῷ Συνοδικῷ πίνακι, τοῦ Γνατίῳ. Ε Φωτίῳ καὶ τὰ κατ' αὐτὸν γραφέντα πε[?] καὶ ἀναθεματίζοντα [?] τὰ αὐτὰ ἀναθέματα καὶ ὑπεβάλλειν. Ι°τα μὴ γνώσεως τῆς παῖδες γίνῃ τὰ τὲ Φωτίῳ. Εἰ καὶ οἱ χρονογράφοι, ὅτι Κεδρηνὸς, καὶ Μαναρσῆς, καὶ Γλυκᾶς, καὶ Σκυλίτζης, καὶ ὁ Δειτοσμόλυρ ἐν βιβλίῳ τῆς μονῆς τῆς Πεσεβλέψης β.ος τὰ ἀμὴν Γνωπανὲ ἐχασυμφῶν ὅσαι πίπτουσιν ὁ Ἰγνάτιος ἀλλὰ ὁ [?] Φωτίος, καὶ ὅπως ὁ Ἰγνάτιος ἐπανῆλθεν εἰς τὸν ἴδιον θρόνον, κείσθαι τῆς Σωσόπολις τὸν ἡ Φώτιον ἐξώρισεν [?] ἔχει ἢ τῇ Κοσμιδίῳ μονή. De Actis vero Octavae Synodi bene novit hic Reverendus, Acta illius in Codice Monasterij Reverendi Praecursoris, quod etiam Petra nuncupatur, haberi coniunctim cum Actis Sextae, & Septimae Synodi, quae confirmant Ignatium, illique cathedram Constantinopolitanam in manus tradunt, sed Photium veluti infultorem eiiciunt, & Anathemate feriunt. Sanctum porro Ignatium inter Sanctos Ecclesia collocavit, ut supra scripsimus, licet in Synodico appositum sit: Ignatio, & Photio; & scripta contra eos, & actitata anathemati subjiciuntur: ne Photy omnia omnibus innotescant. Licet etiam chronographi Cedrenus, Manasses, Glycas, & Scylitza, & quae in volumine Monasterij Periblepti vita Sancti Ignatij legitur, palam faciant; quae S. Ignatius passus est a Photio, & quomodo S. Ignatius decreto Synodi inpropriam Sedem restitutus est: & Cosmidij Monasterium Photium exulem custodiebat.
units.tr: The Acts of a similar Synod, namely the Eighth against Photius, were also plainly known with great clarity even to the schismatic Greeks, as Gregory the Hieromonk attests in his Response to the Profession of Faith of Mark of Ephesus. He says that the Eighth Synod is rightly regarded by the venerable author himself, and that its records are contained in the book of the monastery of the Source of Pesdromus, also called Petra. [The remainder of this unit is too corrupted in the transcription to render reliably.] The Church has enrolled Ignatius among the saints, and the writings and proceedings against Photius are subjected to anathema, so that the things of Photius may not become known to all. The chroniclers Cedrenus, Manasses, Glycas and Scylitzes, and what is read in the volume of the Monastery of Periblepsis, the life of St Ignatius, also make plain what St Ignatius suffered at the hands of Photius, and how by decree of the Synod he was restored to his proper See, and that the Monastery of Cosmidion kept Photius in exile.

units.la: In Tertia restitutus sublato e vivis Ignatio Sedem occupavit. Verum est Sedem occupasse, alienam scilicet non suam, malignantium, & excommunicatorum Praesulum aliu[?], Photianis fraudibus, & pro potestate agente Imperatore praeter aequum, & iustum ococcupauit. Idque ita esse hac Dissertatione planum fit. Sed hanc esse Oecumenicam nemo nisi amentissimus dixerit. Quis enim Oecumenicam dixerit, in qua nulla potestas, nullum ius Ecclesiasticum, sed omnia ad nutum, & placitum iniquissimorum hominum peracta sunt?
units.tr: Restored in the Third Synod, after Ignatius had died, Photius occupied the See. It is true that he occupied the See, but not his own; it was the See of malignant and excommunicated prelates, and he took it by Photian deceits and, contrary to what is fair and just, with the Emperor acting by his power. That this is so is made plain by this discussion. But that this is an Ecumenical Synod no one would say unless he were utterly mad. For who would call it Ecumenical, a Synod in which there was no authority, no ecclesiastical right, but everything was done at the nod and pleasure of the most wicked men?

units.la: Et licet hanc Tertiam Paulus, & Eugenius Ioannis Noni Legationibus functi cum praesidendi ritu inter Episcopos tercentum & octoginta permunirent, & non solum Photium muneri suo redonatum, sed cuncta a Photio, & Synodo proposita suffragijs corroborarent, Latini tamen Latrocinalis nomine infamant, & multis obiurgationibus inuehuntur in Photium, in totam gentem Graecorum, in Legatos proprios bis praevaricantes, in ipsos Pontifices ludificatos Nicolaum, & Ioannem. Deplorandam hominis infscitiam[?]! Paulus, & Eugenius Ioannis Noni legationibus functi. Ioannes Nonus creatus est Pontifex Anno 901, post restitutionem Photij annos 24. cum e viuis sublato Photio usque ad restitutum Nicolaum Mysticum Ioannes Nonus Theodoro subrogatur, in Throno Constantinopolitano sediffent[?], Stephanus frater Leonis Imperatoris, Antonius Cauleas, Nicolaus ex Mystico, Euthymius Monachus ex Syncello, & iterum restitutus Nicolaus Mysticus. Non ergo fieri potuit, vt Paulus, & Eugenius, qui restitutioni Photij praesederunt, a Ioanne Nono mitterentur. Quod si restitutioni Photij calculum dederunt, necessario a Ioanne Octavo, non a Nono legati sunt: Et ne dicas hunc errorem, vel calami nimium festinantis, vel Typographi cura expertis inrepsisse, ipse firmat Interpres, qui infra cum de eodem Ioanne sermo recideret, Photij restitutionem sub Ioanne Nono contigisse ingeminat; Primam sub Nicolao, qua Ignatium deposuit, & Tertiam sub Ioanne Nono, qua Photium restituit. Sequitur; legationibus functi cum praesidendi ritu inter Episcopos. Et tamen praesidendi ritus in ea Synodo, quidquid Interpres somniet, inversus est, & Praesidentiam Legatis Pontificijs in Synodo debitam Photius vsurpavit, & Thronum primum insedit. Hoc-q; non nisi cæcus, & Græcæ linguæ plane ignarus negaverit; cum sæpius atque iterate in ea inculcetur; [illegible, ~12 letters] τῷ Φωτίῳ. Et non solum Photium muneri suo redonatum. Ex cerebro loquitur, & quæ vellet ita fuisse, de facili ita facta esse pronunciat. Photius in ea Synodo ante consensum Locumtenentium Papæ a Schismaticis, excommunicatis, & Imperatoria potestate in locum, unde ceciderat, reponitur: imo numquam eum de gradu suo cececidisse declaratur, à Patriarchis, Episcopis, semper etiam post sui depositionem Patriarcha legitimus cognitus, vt ex Actis Synodi palam fit. Qui ergo potuit muneri suo, quod nunquam amiserat, a Pontificijs Legatis redonari? Quare impudentissime Iosephus Bryennius Oratione octaua de sanctissima Triade haec omnia peracta ex voluntate Papae, & Imperiali studio absoluta fuisse, Τὸ πᾶν τῇ τῆς Πάπα βελήσει καὶ βασιλέως ἀπαλλαγῇ[?] [illegible, ~12 letters] dixit: & tamen reliqui Schismatici, & inter eos Nili, Cabasila, & Damyla nulla facta mentione de voluntate Papae, totum illud negotium Imperatori Basilio vindicant. Sic quem Romani Pontifices, & Synodus ipsa Oecumenica Octaua multis reum criminibus condemnarunt, in hac Synodo, nunquam ab aliis condemnatus asseritur, sed continuo insons, & extra culpam omnem agnoscitur, & Patriarcha legitimus depraedicatur. Nouae haec forte, & insperato cadunt Interpreti. Legat ipse Acta, & si intelligens fuerit, acquiescet: neque enim tenebrae sunt: Cuncta a Photio, & Synodo proposita corroborarent. Hoc quoq; falsum est, adeantur Acta Synodi. Multa contra perstrepentes fautores proposuere Pontificij, sed animati illi errones ad alia inclinati, & gratiam Photij ambientes extra institutum, & susceptam sententiam di-gladiantur, & Legatorum quæsita vti sutilium hominum dicta-supina aure audiunt, & despiciunt. Latini tamen Latrocinalis nomine infamant. Hic quoque supinus error in historia est. Quippe quæ Synodus Photiana Latrocinalis appellata est, non fuit hæc quam Schismatici Octauam indigitant, sed ea quæ Prima, & Secunda vocata est, quod in templo Sanctorum Apostolorum, vt tradunt Zonaras, & Balsamon in expositione Canonum eiusdem, dum celebraretur, & Orthodoxi in mutuis disputationibus præualuissent, ne scripto constituta exararentur, aduersæ factionis homines impediuerunt, postmodum vero nouo conuentu eadem disputata sunt, & tum demum decreta monimentis tradita. Atque hinc factum, vt hæc licet vna fuerit, tamen ob Patres bis conuocatos Prima, & Secunda appellaretur, & hanc Latini, ducem sequentes Nicolaum, vocant Latrocinalem. Et argumento manifestissimo euincitur. Hæc, de qua agimus, in Templo Sanctæ Dei Sapientiæ celebrata est; Septimam Oecumenicam Synodum confirmauit, & Photium restituit sub Ioanne Octauo; illa in Templo Apostolorum nullo iure exauctorauit Ignatium sub Nicolao, ideoque Latrocinalis a Nicolao vocata est, & a Styliano σωσίδηον λησεικόν[?]. Qui enim potuit Nicolaus Latrocinalem Synodum vocare demortuus non dum habitam, quam nec celebrandam nisi diuinus sciisset? Hanc ergo, & merito Latini, cuius pessima fama in vulgus est, infamant, detestantur, & a Legatis suis uti mandatorum violatoribus, sceleris poenas expetiuerunt, & congregatos in ea uti sacrilegos, & ab humanitate, pietate, atque religione remotos, non totam gentem Graecorum abominati sunt, & modo abominantur. Et has Synodos negotijs, Legatis, locis, & aliis omnibus distractissimas[?] Interpres non discernens, ex duabus unam constituit. Et si sapit, hoc non in aulae Pontificiae, quam ille astu fanatico nihil probans, perditissimam nuncupat, & Romanae consuetudinis infamiam vertit, sed potius in dedecus Photij. Reos siquidem maximorum plurimorumque criminum maledictis oneramus, & conuicijs insectamur; probos, catosque laudibus extollimus. Et quis in illa Synodo Photio iniquior? Vita, & moribus sanctissimum, Pastorem Ecclesiastici gregis integerrimum, nulla antea iniuria lacessitus, vi atque potestate saeculari persequitur, de solio proprio deijcit, affligit, opprimit, infamat, tandemque ignominiose acceptum, flagellis caesum ad mortem, fame & siti contritum in exilium pellit. Nicolaus pulsum remittit, afflicto succurrit, & Sedem ab inuasore repetit, & restituit eiecto iura amissa, Et erit hoc potius in infamiam aulæ Pontificiæ, & Romanæ consuetudinis, & non in Photij, & similia afferentis dedecus?
units.tr: And although Paul and Eugenius, who had served as legates of John the Ninth, with the right of presiding among three hundred and eighty bishops, fortified this Third Synod, and not only restored Photius to his office but also confirmed by their votes everything proposed by Photius and the Synod, the Latins nevertheless brand it with the name of a Robber Synod, and rail at Photius with many reproaches, at the whole Greek nation, at their own legates who twice betrayed their trust, and at the Popes Nicholas and John themselves, who were made fools of. Deplorable ignorance of the man! Paul and Eugenius, who had served as legates of John the Ninth. John the Ninth was made Pontiff in the year 901, twenty-four years after the restoration of Photius; for from the death of Photius until the restoration of Nicholas Mysticus, John the Ninth was succeeded by Theodore, and in the See of Constantinople there sat Stephen, brother of the Emperor Leo, Antony Caulees, Nicholas from the Mystic, Euthymius the monk from the Syncellus, and again Nicholas Mysticus restored. It therefore could not have happened that Paul and Eugenius, who presided over the restoration of Photius, were sent by John the Ninth. If they gave their vote for the restoration of Photius, they must have been legates of John the Eighth, not of the Ninth. And lest you say this error crept in through the haste of the writer or the carelessness of the printer, the translator himself confirms it, for when he later returned to the same John he repeats that the restoration of Photius happened under John the Ninth: The First under Nicholas, in which he deposed Ignatius, and the Third under John the Ninth, in which he restored Photius. It follows: legates who served with the right of presiding among the bishops. And yet the right of presiding in that Synod, whatever the translator may dream, was reversed, and Photius usurped the presidency due to the Papal legates in the Synod, and took the first throne. No one but a blind man who is wholly ignorant of the Greek language would deny this, since it is repeatedly and insistently stressed in it [Greek: "to Photius"]. And it was not only restored to his office. He talks out of his head, and what he would wish to have been so, he declares to have readily been done. In that Synod, before the consent of the Pope's deputies, Photius was reinstated by schismatics, excommunicates and imperial power into the place from which he had fallen; indeed it is declared that he never fell from his rank, and he was recognised as the lawful Patriarch by the Patriarchs and bishops, and even after his deposition. This is plain from the Acts of the Synod. How then could he be restored by the Papal legates to an office he had never lost? Therefore Joseph Bryennius, shamelessly, in his eighth Oration on the Most Holy Trinity, said that all these things were done by the will of the Pope and carried through by the Emperor's zeal [Greek: "all by the will of the Pope and the release of the Emperor"]; and yet the other schismatics, Nilus, Cabasilas and Damylas, without any mention of the will of the Pope, claim that whole business for the Emperor Basil. So he whom the Roman Pontiffs and the Eighth Ecumenical Synod itself condemned as guilty of many crimes, in this Synod is asserted to have never been condemned by others, but is at once acknowledged as innocent and free of all blame, and is proclaimed the lawful Patriarch. Perhaps these things fall strangely and unexpectedly upon the translator. Let him read the Acts himself, and if he has any understanding he will agree, for these are not dark matters. All things proposed by Photius and the Synod were confirmed. This too is false; let the Acts of the Synod be consulted. The Papal legates proposed many objections against the noisy partisans, but those mad errants, inclined to other matters and courting the favour of Photius, outside the purpose and the sentence they had undertaken, wrangle, and they hear the legates' requests with a careless ear, as the words of foolish men, and despise them. The Latins nevertheless brand it with the name of Robber Synod. Here too the error in the history is careless. Indeed the Photian Synod which was called the Robber Synod was not the one which the schismatics designate as the Eighth, but the one which was called the First and Second, because it was held in the Church of the Holy Apostles, as Zonaras and Balsamon tell in their commentary on its canons, and while it was being celebrated, and the Orthodox had prevailed in their mutual disputations, the men of the opposing faction prevented the decisions from being written down; afterwards, however, the same matters were debated again in a new assembly, and only then were the decisions handed down in records. Hence it happened that, although it was one Synod, it was called the First and Second because the Fathers met twice, and the Latins, following Nicholas as their leader, call it the Robber Synod. And this is proved by a most manifest argument. The Synod we are discussing was held in the Church of Holy Wisdom of God; it confirmed the Seventh Ecumenical Synod and restored Photius under John the Eighth. That one, in the Church of the Apostles, without any right deposed Ignatius under Nicholas, and therefore was called a Robber Synod by Nicholas, and by Stylianus [Greek: "a Robber Synod of Lesser..."]. For how could Nicholas call a Robber Synod one that had not yet been held, and which no one could have known would be held unless he were divinely informed? The Latins, therefore, and rightly so, brand this one, whose evil reputation is widespread, and detest it, and their legates, as violators of their instructions, have sought punishment for the crime; and they have abominated, and still abominate, those gathered in it as sacrilegious men, far removed from humanity, piety and religion, but not the whole Greek nation. And the translator, failing to distinguish these Synods, which are wholly different in business, legates, places and everything else, makes one out of two. And if he has any sense, he does this not to the shame of the Papal court, which in his fanatical cunning, proving nothing, he calls most depraved, and turns into a reproach on Roman custom, but rather to the disgrace of Photius. For we load the guilty of the greatest and many crimes with abuse and attack them with reproaches, while we extol the upright and the wise with praise. And who was more unjust to Photius in that Synod? He, most holy in life and character, a most blameless minister of his ecclesiastical flock, who had suffered no prior injury, was persecuted by secular force and power, thrown down from his own throne, afflicted, oppressed and defamed; and finally, received with ignominy, flogged to the point of death, worn down by hunger and thirst, he was driven into exile. Nicholas sent back the one who had been expelled, came to the aid of the afflicted, sought back the See from the usurper, and restored to the one cast out the rights he had lost. Will this rather be to the infamy of the Papal court and Roman custom, and not the disgrace of Photius and of those who assert such things?

units.la: At Graeci hanc lambunt, & tanquam oraculum pro germana Octaua venerantur, quia omnium trium postrema durat, nulla superuenieniente censura Synodali superstes. Hoc quoque falsum est de omnibus Græcis: sed Schismatici lambunt. Quid tum? ipse cum illo dixerim, Ranarum palustrium maior est mihi cura, quam vocum istarum. Imo etiam a Schismaticis ipsis haud in magno poni discrimine, cum nec illius mentionem inter alias Synodos faciant, nec eius Canones inter alios Synodorum Canones ponant, nec expositione illustrent, sed veluti vietos abiectosq; despiciant, cum quos Latrocinalis sunt, exsculentur.
