Scribat quidquid velit Pontifex Romanus, Photiani in ea Synodo iudices facti quaecunque iusta, & legitima iudicant, amplectuntur, & recipiunt; quasi vero Romani Pontifices iniusta, & [illegible, ~12 letters] , & praeter ius falsque multa praecipiant, & mandent quorum ipsi iudices constituuntur. Tandemque ipse Pontificijs sequentibus Synodum Oecumenicam sub Adriano, & Romanas sub Nicolao, & Adriano contra semetipsum irritat, illisque hanc suam substituit, & additionem in Symbolo condemnat. An est aliquid simile in alijs Synodis? Quis unquam similia audijt? Nonne somnia isthaec sunt? Synodum Oecumenicam Pontificis Romani auctoritate, aliorum Præsulum suffragio constabilitam ab alio Pontifice, vel ab alijs infringi, & irritam fieri?
units.tr: What should be decided about the other Photian synods, the most learned and distinguished men have already determined. I will set out my observations on this last one, which the schismatics praise under the name of the Eighth Universal Synod, and in which the addition of and from the Son is discussed, as well as I can. Indeed I cannot be brought to believe that it was ever really held. There are certain signs that confirm me in this view. Who does not know the frauds and tricks of Photius in inventing such things? Above all, it must be considered that this last Photian synod was held without any compelling necessity. Earlier, with the mediation of Basil and with Pope John not refusing, Photius praised John with many compliments and made no mention of any addition to the creed. He was reconciled to the Roman Church and recovered the See he had so greatly desired. Then, having been cast out, a fugitive, sad and destitute, he had spent much effort, with a mind always troubled and uncertain, to win back the goodwill of John and the other Romans, through whose estrangement so many miseries had come upon him. Later he stirred up again the minds of those who had been reconciled to him, though no necessity demanded it. Vainly do we seek disturbances when we are at rest, and provoke enemies to anger when we enjoy peace, especially if they are of better standing. That would have been to stir up hornets. Would a man who had been freed from one wound foolishly reopen the scar that the Roman Church had closed over him, so as to receive a new wound? The things established in this synod are not to be despised. The opinion that the Spirit proceeds also from the Son, confirmed from the very cradle of the Roman Church by the authority of almost all the Popes and of that Church's teachers, and spread in writings everywhere, is rejected. The authority of the Popes over the presidents of the other churches subject to them is trampled underfoot. The power and faculty given by God to the Roman Pontiffs alone is weakened, and the Roman Pontiff gives way and will even confirm a similar injustice through his own envoys? But John is mild-natured, and will not oppose it. Granted he is mild; will he therefore be silent, and the most foolish of all, struck and drained as he is? Will he not raise his voice? But if he himself kept silent, would his successors have borne so great an injury with equanimity? Let the schismatics believe it. But the successors were silent. Therefore it did not happen. They opposed smaller matters; they would not so easily have overlooked so atrocious a deed. In the genuine letters of John, not corrupted by Photius, there is not a word about the procession of the Spirit, about not altering the creed, about invalidating the synods of Nicholas and Adrian, nor about the Eighth Synod against this same Photius. They speak only of the restoration of Photius, if indeed he sought mercy before the synod: "Photius, seeking mercy before the synod, we wish to hold the honour of the Patriarchate." [Φώτιον αὐτοῦ ἔλεον ἐνώπιον τῆς Συνόδου] And: "We, asking mercy of you before the synod, also consent." And we consent to Photius seeking mercy before the synod. Although Photius altered these words in the corrupted text, he did not so translate them into another sense that the same thing is not expressed. "Let the Patriarch Photius not disdain, before the synod, to acknowledge our countenance and our protection, or rather the bowels of the Roman Church." And: "Therefore let your brother not disdain to ask in the synod for mercy and help, and for the completion and adornment of the most worthy Roman Church." We ask your brotherhood not to disdain to proclaim in the synod the mercy of God, the help shown to you, the protection of the holy Roman Church, and its labour. Nothing more fitting could John have pronounced, and Photius, by his own interpretation, supports this. John wants Photius to do penance; he orders that mercy be sought from Photius before the synod, prescribes public penance, enjoins satisfaction, and after these things are done receives Photius into communion and restores his office. If he failed to do so, he threatens excommunication. Is it then said that John kept silent? What did Photius do in the synod? He presided himself, provided seats for the Roman legates, gave others the opportunity to enter the synod, and received the reverences and honours of those holding the patriarchal sees. The Papists were despised as if they were common rabble. He himself sanctioned decrees and gave laws; the Papists listened and did not dare to open their mouths. It was enough for them, if at their entreaty and supplication, Photius's supreme authority commanded it. Photius was cleared of the charge; the Roman pontiffs were declared the authors of the schism, and all blame was laid upon the Roman Church. Let the Roman Pontiff write whatever he likes; the Photians sitting as judges in that synod approve, accept and receive whatever they judge just and lawful, as if the Roman Pontiffs commanded unjust things, things contrary to law and truth, of which the Photians were appointed judges. And finally, with the Papists following, he himself annuls the Ecumenical Synod held under Adrian, and the Roman synods under Nicholas and Adrian, against himself, and substitutes his own synod in their place and condemns the addition to the creed. Is there anything similar in other synods? Who ever heard of such things? Are these not dreams? That an Ecumenical Synod, established by the authority of the Roman Pontiff and the consent of other prelates, should be broken and made void by another Pontiff or by others?

units.la: Non ita facile immutat sua Romana Ecclesia, cum ad illa stabilienda certissimum, ac falli nescium ducem sequatur. Ὡ'ς κάτ-οπτρον[?], καὶ ὑπόδειγμα[?] ἡ ἁγία τῆς Ῥωμαίων Ἐκ-κλησία[?] τῆς λοιπῆς Ἐκκλησίας [?]καὶ ἐξ[?] ὅπ-αν[?] εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα ἀκλόνητον ἑδραιοῦ[?]. Sancta Romana Ecclesia velut Speculum quoddam, & exemplar Ecclesijs cæteris propositum est: quæ si quid definierit, id omnibus seculis firmum inconcussumque manet, scribebat Stephanus Papa post Photium Episcopis, & reliquis Orientalibus Clericis: Sed Octaua Synodus prius a Ioanne Pontifice abrogata, postmodum a Photio suppressa est. In germanis Ioannis Epistolis, si recte illæ considerentur, oppositum est. Qua enim ratione Synodum illam reiecit, quam & summe laudat, & cuius auctoritate dictum suum constabilit. Scribit enim ad Photium, Οὕτω μόνος ὡς ἂν ἀπὸ τῆς παλαιᾶς μνήμης ἕνα ἐκ λαϊκῶν ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ χειροτονεῖς Ἐπίσκοπον[?], ὥσπερ[?] οὖν ἡμῶν τὸν Ἐπιπόπον[?] τῶν ἀγίων Πατέρων, καὶ πᾶς ὅλως ἐκεῖ-θεν τῷ φαύλῳ ἐκείνῳ ὑποκρίσει συνῳδὰ[?] τὸν κανόνα τὸν ἀμοιβαῖον ἐπὶ τὸ ἀσεβείας ἀντιστάσεως[?]. Τούτῳ ἐκδοθέντος ἐν τῇ σεβασμίᾳ Σινῳδῷ τῇ ἐν Κωνσταντινουπόλει συνκροτηθείσῃ ἐπὶ τὸ ἐκεῖ ἡμῶν ἀρ-
units.tr: The Roman Church does not change its own decisions so easily, since in establishing them it follows a most certain guide who cannot be deceived. "As a mirror and example, the holy Roman Church is set before the other churches, and what it has established remains firm and unshaken for all ages." Stephen the Pope wrote this after Photius to the bishops and the other Eastern clergy. But the Eighth Synod was first abrogated by Pope John and afterwards suppressed by Photius. In the genuine letters of John, if they are read correctly, the opposite appears. For on what ground would he reject that synod which he praises so highly and by whose authority he confirms his own statement? He writes to Photius: "Thus, as in the ancient custom, you ordain one from the laity as bishop in the same church, just as we do the bishop of the holy Fathers..." [and so on, corrupted in the Greek]

units.la: [?] Greek and Latin of the quotation from the letter to Photius are partly illegible at the line ends; the Greek is transcribed as far as it can be made out. ἀρχιεπισκόπου[?] Ἀδριανῷ[?] τῷ νεωτέρῳ Πάπᾳ. Ita tamen vt deinceps de laicis in eadem Ecclefia Episcopus contra sanctorum Patrum statuta nullatenus ordinetur, & omnis illa mala consuetudo ab inde penitus amputetur; iuxta capitulum, quod super hac re in Venerabili Synodo, tempore scilicet decessoris nostri Adriani iunioris Papæ, Constantinopoli habita, est congruentissime promulgatum. Est vero Actionis 10. Canon 5. Venerabilem nuncupat, & conculcari mandat? Sed Photius in corruptis vocat ἀδίκους Συνόδους, iniquas Synodos, & Canonem ad Septimam Synodum sub Adriano Primo Tarasij tempore refert. Quid tum? multa alia dixit Photius, quæ nec ab ipsis Schismaticis probantur. Hominem Nicolao, & Adriano Pontificibus infensissimum pro sui defensione, mirum est non peiora pronunciasse. Vide quæ nos in Opere de Consensione Occidentalis, atque Orientalis Ecclesiæ lib. 2. cap. 3. 4. & 5. diximus. Quibus colligitur, Synodum hanc a Photio confictam prorsus fuisse, uti & aliam, quam in Nicolaum, tot aduersus Romanam Ecclesiam criminationes ementitus pro arbitrio concinnauerat. Quare nec suspicio mea vana est, Ioannem Pontificem, licet antea videretur reconciliari Photio, vt Imperatori Basilio morem gereret, comperta pertinacia Photij, postea, quæcunque in fauorem Photij dictauerat, rescidisse, & tandem etiam ipsum Photium condemnasse. Literæ etiam ipsæ Ioannis ad Photium, & Synodum datæ sicuti suppositæ sunt, vt alibi fuse probauimus, ita & Synodi falsitatem arguunt, cum phrasis earum, modusque dicendi nihil habeant commune cum sermonis Latini integritate, sed plane Græcam dictionem præseferant, & ingenium Græcum repræsentent. Idque doctissime adnotauit Gregorius Hieromonachus Responsione in Professionem Fidei Marci Ephesij. Ἡμᾶς δὲ ἐκ τῶν θεαυτικὰ τὰ ἀξιωμα τῆς Ἐφέσου θεοκομιζόμενα ὡς τῆς ἀγίας Συνόδου διξόμενα. Ἐπὶ ἡ, ἐὰν λέγω ἐπισολὴν τῆς ἀξιωματικῆς Πάπα Ἰωάννης. Καὶ πῶς γὰρ πολὺ τὸ ὑποπίπτον ἔχουσα, ἀξὶ τὸ ἐξ ὅλα ἀλλ' ὅλου ἰλ-λωκὸν ἐ ἡ ἐφαθὲ, καὶ μηδὲν ἔχει ἐκ ἑαυτῆ ἰδίω-μα ἡ Λατινικόν. Nos porro, & Acta ab Ephesio producta, acsi Octauæ Synodi essent, recipiemus. Præterea etiam, & quam ait Epistolam sanctissimi Papæ Ioannis, licet suspectissima sit, quod scriptio illa per omnia dictionem Græcam referat, & nullam in se contineat proprietatem Latini sermonis.
units.tr: [The Greek and Latin of the quotation from the letter to Photius are partly illegible at the line ends; the Greek is transcribed as far as it can be made out.] ...the archbishop of the Church, to Adrian the younger, Pope. Yet so that henceforth no one from the laity is ordained bishop in that same church contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers, and that all that evil custom is thoroughly cut away from there, in accordance with the chapter which was most fittingly promulgated on this matter in the Venerable Synod held at Constantinople in the time of our predecessor Adrian the Younger, Pope. It is Canon 5 of Action 10. He calls it venerable and orders it trampled underfoot? But Photius, in the corrupted text, calls it unjust synods, iniquitous synods, and refers the canon to the Seventh Synod under Adrian I, in the time of Tarasius. What then? Photius said many other things which not even the schismatics themselves approve. It is remarkable that a man most hostile to the Popes Nicholas and Adrian did not say worse things in his own defence. See what we said in our work on the Agreement of the Western and Eastern Church, book 2, chapters 3, 4 and 5. From these it is gathered that this synod was wholly invented by Photius, just as was the other which he, lying about so many accusations against the Roman Church, arbitrarily cobbled together against Nicholas. Therefore my suspicion is not vain: Pope John, although he seemed earlier to be reconciled to Photius in order to humour the Emperor Basil, having discovered Photius's obstinacy, afterwards rescinded whatever he had said in favour of Photius and at last condemned Photius himself. The letters of John himself to Photius and to the synod are also, as we have shown at length elsewhere, supposititious; and they likewise prove the synod false, since their phrasing and manner of speaking have nothing in common with the purity of the Latin language, but plainly display Greek diction and represent the Greek mind. This was most learnedly noted by Gregory the Hieromonk in his Response to the Profession of Faith of Mark of Ephesus. "We receive the Acts produced by Ephesus as if they were of the holy Synod. Moreover, even the letter of the most holy Pope John, though most suspect, since that writing in every respect conveys Greek diction and contains no property of the Latin language." Indeed, we shall receive both the Acts brought forward by Ephesus, as if they were of the Eighth Synod, and also the letter which he calls that of the most holy Pope John, although it is most suspect, because that writing in every respect reflects Greek diction and contains no peculiarity of the Latin tongue.

units.la: Ex diversitate textus, ex aliys atque aliys Codi- cibus, & Photij astu, Synodum ementi- tam esse evincitur.
units.tr: The synod is shown to be fabricated, from the variety of its texts, from different manuscripts, and from the cunning of Photius.

units.la: SIngula pro maiori rerum intelligentia examinentur. & ut de ingenio Photij ad similia confingenda promptissimo, ex quo argumentum non leue desumi potest, hanc quoque ex illo fonte enatam esse, cum omnia sibi concedat, & tota sit in eiusdem laudibus, ac in Ecclesiam meritis referendis, ut de Romanis Pontificibus clam mordendis, eorumque dignitate conculcanda, nihil dicamus, illa plane similis fabulae argumenta certissima sunt; & inter ea potissimum, hanc Synodum non unam eandemque in omnibus Codicibus haberi, sed varie, ac diverse, modo actionibus, & sententijs auctam, & diverso rerum exponendarum dicendi modo efformatam, modo multis demptis decurtatam. In Codicibus Vaticanis, & fautorum Photij sermonibus ad tædium usque verbosissimis, & eadem ad nauseam repetentibus, & Epistolarum, quibus Photij restitutioni, & illius moribus plauditur varia egestione prolixior, legentis aures onerat, & Actionibus quoq; adauctis, namq; septem circumcluditur, largius dilatatur. In meo Codice manuscripto tertiam non excedit, cum tantum primam, & sextam, & septimam, easque non paucis demptis, potiori sui parte mutilas continet. Aliæ aliis, & vario item modo claudiuntur, ut cuiusque collatis manuscriptis Codicibus, eo res adducatur, ut nihil diuinatione opus sit, hoc scriptum non adeo mussim perfectum statim publicatum fuisse, sed primum utcunque conceptum, ac digestum, postmodum re melius examinata productius, multisque immutatis, tandem additis, vel detractis, quæcunque in rem suam fore iudicabat, in vulgus emisisse, cum Basilius Imperator Photii, & Santabareni præstigijs, & fraudibus demens a reuerentia Romanorum Pontificum subtractus, in eosdem, quos prius tantundem venerabatur, calamum strinxit, & omnia furenti Photio concessit.
units.tr: Let the individual points be examined, so that the matter may be understood more fully. Photius's ingenuity in inventing such things is well known, and from this a not slight argument can be drawn: this synod too sprang from that same source. He grants himself everything, and the whole work is devoted to his own praise and to recounting the merits of the Church. I say nothing here of his secret slanders against the Roman Pontiffs and his trampling of their dignity. Those features are plainly like a fable, and certain proofs of a fiction. Among them, the most important is that this synod is not one and the same in all the manuscripts. It is variously and diversely expanded, now with actions and opinions added, and shaped in a different manner of setting out the matters, and now shortened by many omissions. In the Vatican manuscripts, and in the writings of Photius's supporters, which are wordy to the point of tedium and repeat the same things to nausea, and in the letters praising Photius's restoration and his character, it burdens the reader's ears with a prolixity of expression. The actions too are enlarged there, for it is spread over seven, and is more widely extended. In my own manuscript it does not go beyond the third, and it contains only the first, sixth and seventh, and these, with not a few things removed, are mutilated in their better part. Other manuscripts end in other ways again. When each manuscript is collated, the matter reaches this point, that no conjecture is needed: this document was not published at once in a finished state. It was first composed and arranged in some fashion, then later, after the matter had been examined more carefully, it was expanded, with many things changed, and finally added or removed as he judged would serve his purpose, and so put out to the public. This happened when Emperor Basil, out of his mind through the tricks and frauds of Photius and Santabarenus, withdrew from reverence for the Roman Pontiffs, turned his pen against those whom he had venerated just as much before, and yielded everything to the raging Photius.

units.la: Quis, si modo antiquiora Concilia circumspexit, & in illis disponendis diligentiam Patrum vel minimum animo aduertit, impostoris huiusce inscitiam, & omnia sibi concedentis astum non admirabitur? Præsidet hic Photius. Πεσρα- Στεάντες Φωτίῳ τῷ ἁγιωτάτῳ, καὶ Οἰκυμενικῷ Πα- τριάρχου, καὶ συνεδρεύοντ@ Ἡλία. Præsidente Photio sanctissimo & Oecumenico Patriarcha, & & vna sedente Elia. Actione 1., & in alijs Actionibus perpetuo continuatur . Photius est, qui agenda indicit. Photius nutu suo omnia dirigit, Legati Pontificij vix locum habent, silent, Photij imperijs audiunt, mancipia sunt. Nulla hic reliquarum Patriarchalium Sedium, nulla Romani Pontificis auctoritas. Photius τὰ πάντα[?] est. Quis similia non execratur? Schismatici ipsi talia detestati sunt, & plane sub alijs Imperatoribus condemnarunt. Ex quo tantum sibi Constantinopolitanus ius vindicavit, ut ipse praesideat, imperet, praecipiat, alij veluti pecudes ne hiscere audeant? sub proximo ante Photium Concilio Tarasius, sub alijs praecedentibus alij Patriarchae Romanum primum agnoscunt, quid ille iubeat, audiunt, & exequuntur: & nunc hoc Concilium, si vere coactum fuit, ita insanijsset, ut praescripta Ecclesiastica in Concilijs cogendis, & intemerate seruata, nullo obstante, & praesentibus Legatis Pontificijs, interturbato rerum ordine permutarit? Nullus in tanto Episcoporum numero, ne dicam colluuie, vel sua iurá, vel aliorum tutatus est? Et tamen in alijs Concilijs cum occasio se tulit tutati sunt. Et ut magis rideas, haec praesumit Photius ante quam in iudicium vocatus, examinata causa innocens declaratur. Condemnatus, excommunicatus, eiectus, & secularis declaratus decreto vniuersalis Concilij, alterius Concilij decreto nondum absolutus, & in communionem aliorum admissus, caput & arbiter in Concilio iussa impertit, & leges dat. Et quod magis est, talem hominem Ioannes Pontifex veneratur, & adorat. Act. 1. Προσκυνῶ τὴν ἁγιωσύνην ὑμῶν ὁ ἁγιώ[?]τατος, καὶ οἰκουμενικὸς Πάπας Ἰωάννης. Adorat Sanctitatem vestram sanctissimus, & Oecumenicus Papa Ioannes. Ijdem sunt tituli, eadem adoratio, eadem vtriusque submissio, par astus & fastigium, quasi aequa etiam esset potestas; Φώτιος ὁ ἁγιώτατος Πατριάρχης ἔφη, αἰνῶ προσκυνῶν παρ᾽ ὑμῶν εἰς ἀγαπῶν πόθῳ. Photius sanctissimus Patriarcha dixit; contra adoratur a nobis cordiali amore. Et infra; Πολλὰ προσκυνῶ, καὶ ἐπισκέπτει ἡμᾶς ὁ ἁγιώτατος Πάπας. Nimium adorat, curamque nostri gerit sanctissimus Pontifex. Pontifex optat sibi Photium Ἀδελφὸν, καὶ συλλειτουργὸν, καὶ συμπνοιά, Fratrem, comministrum, & confacerdotem. Et Photius ibidem morem gerens Pontifici ex largitate sua accipit eundem, declaratque fratrem, comministrum, & confacerdotem; & hoc ex gratia speciali. Καὶ πῶς ἐστιν ἄξιος τῶν ἴσων ἀξιωμάτων, καὶ φέρ[?]ν[?]τῶν τῶ ἐνοικεῖν, καὶ καθαρὸν δέ[?]χθηναι ἀνιστάμενος. Et quomodo dignus non est, aequalium certaminum, & curarum beneuolentiam, atque purum affectum vicissim accipere? Quia prior adorauerat Pontifex Photium, prior illius curam egerat, prior beneuolentiam & purum affectum in Photium commonstrauerat, a Photio dignus habitus est & veneratione & cura & affectu: Si non id egisset, Photiana gratia, & affectu indignus iudicatus fuisset; & vixisset Romae inglorius, inhonorius, incuratus, neglectus. Quis non videt impudentiam Photij? quis non miratur Romanam inertiam, reliquorum Praesulum dementiam? Et credam ipse similia in consessu publico Praesulum celebrata?
units.tr: Who, if he has looked at the older councils and given even the slightest attention to the care the Fathers took in arranging them, will not marvel at the ignorance of this impostor and at his cunning in conceding everything to himself? Photius presides here. "Photius, most holy and Ecumenical Patriarch, presiding, and Elias sitting together with him" [Φωτίου τοῦ ἁγιωτάτου καὶ Οἰκουμενικοῦ Πατριάρχου προεδρεύοντος καὶ συνεδρεύοντος Ἠλίου]. This is repeated throughout Action 1 and the other Actions. Photius is the one who announces what is to be done. Photius directs everything with a nod. The Papal legates scarcely have a place; they are silent and obey Photius's commands; they are slaves. Here there is no authority of the other Patriarchal Sees, and no authority of the Roman Pontiff. Photius is everything. Who would not execrate such things? The schismatics themselves detested such practices and plainly condemned them under other emperors. From where did the Constantinopolitan patriarch claim such a right, that he himself presides, commands and prescribes, while the others, like cattle, dare not even murmur? Under the council immediately before Photius, under Tarasius, and under other earlier councils, the other Patriarchs acknowledged Rome as first, heard what it commanded, and carried it out. Now, if this council was truly convened, would it have gone so mad as to overturn the order of affairs, when the Ecclesiastical rules for convening councils were prescribed and kept inviolate, with nothing standing in the way and the Papal legates present? In so great a number of bishops, not to say so great a sewer, did no one defend either his own rights or those of others? Yet in other councils, when the occasion arose, they did defend them. And so that you may laugh the more: Photius presumes these things before he is called to judgment, and when the case is examined he is declared innocent. Condemned, excommunicated, ejected, and declared a layman by the decree of a universal council, not yet absolved by the decree of another council nor admitted into communion with others, he now gives orders as head and arbiter in the council and lays down laws. What is more, the Pope John venerates and adores such a man. Act. 1: "I, the most holy and Ecumenical Pope John, adore your holiness" [Προσκυνῶ τὴν ἁγιωσύνην ὑμῶν]. The titles are the same, the adoration is the same, the submission of each to the other is the same, the pretension and pride are equal, as if the power were also equal. "Photius, the most holy Patriarch, said: I am adored by you, and I adore you with cordial love." And below: "The most holy Pope adores us greatly and takes care of us." The Pontiff wishes Photius to be his "brother, fellow-minister and co-priest." Photius, obliging the Pontiff, out of his generosity accepts the same, and declares him brother, fellow-minister and co-priest, and this by special grace. "And how is he not worthy to receive in turn the goodwill of equal dignities and cares, and a pure affection?" Because the Pontiff first adored Photius, first took care of him, and first showed goodwill and pure affection towards him, he was judged worthy by Photius of veneration, care and affection. If he had not done so, he would have been judged unworthy of Photian grace and affection, and would have lived at Rome without glory, without honour, uncared for and neglected. Who does not see the impudence of Photius? Who does not marvel at Roman sluggishness and at the madness of the other prelates? And am I to believe that such things were celebrated in a public assembly of prelates?

units.la: Et considera[?] Lector. Synodus ista cogenda prorsus erat pro restitutione Photij expulsi, vt sicuti consessu publico eiectus fuerat, ita & publico decreto suo throno redderetur, quod videbatur magis ipsi Photio honorificum, sic enim iniustitia sibi facta apertius omnibus patuisset. Et nihilominus haec Synodus cogitur non pro illius restitutione, sed contra illius rebelles, & ab illo dissidentes. Ἐ″πʼ ἀρχῆς δὲ τῆς ὑμῶν παλαιό-[?] πτώσεως Φωτίου ἐπισκόπου, ἐάν τις εἰς ἀπ[?]οδόσεως [?] τῆς πάλιν, ὅλοι Χριστοῦ τοῦ ἀληθινοῦ Θεοφιλῆ τῇ κοινῇ πάντων κεφαλῇ κολλησθῶσι, ἐὰν εἰς ἐν [illegible, ~45 letters] Postmodum per vestram perfectionem dispicere conatus est, si qui sunt, qui non obediunt veritati, & decentem adhortationem introducere, vt qui rebellarunt, ab eo, quo prius abrepti sunt, Schismatico errore toti Christo vero Deo nostro communi omnium capiti adhaerentes, vnum integrum illius corpus efficiantur.
units.tr: And consider, reader[?]. This synod ought surely to have been convened for the restoration of Photius, who had been expelled, so that, just as he was ejected from a public assembly, so by a public decree he might be restored to his throne. This would have seemed more honourable to Photius himself, for in this way the injustice done to him would have been more plainly evident to all. Yet this synod is convened not for his restoration, but against his rebels and those who dissent from him. From the beginning of your ancient fall of Photius the bishop, if any are to be restored again, and all are to be joined to Christ the true God, beloved of God, the common head of all, if into one [illegible] [Ἐ″πʼ ἀρχῆς δὲ τῆς ὑμῶν παλαιό-[?] πτώσεως Φωτίου ἐπισκόπου, ἐάν τις εἰς ἀπ[?]οδόσεως [?] τῆς πάλιν, ὅλοι Χριστοῦ τοῦ ἀληθινοῦ Θεοφιλῆ τῇ κοινῇ πάντων κεφαλῇ κολλησθῶσι, ἐὰν εἰς ἐν [illegible]]. Afterwards, through your perfection, he has sought to examine whether there are any who do not obey the truth, and to introduce a fitting exhortation, so that those who have rebelled may, having been led away from that schismatic error by which they were first carried off, cleave to Christ the true God, our common head of all, and be made one whole body of him.

units.la: Nec hisce contentus Photius, non latenter primas sibi partes in Ecclesia arripit, cuius ipse caput esse profitetur. Ioannes Heracleënsis eadem Actione; [illegible, ~60 letters]
units.tr: Nor being content with these things, Photius does not secretly seize for himself the first place in the Church, of which he professes himself the head. John of Heraclea, in the same Action, [text illegible in the scan].

units.la: Precibus sanctis illius factum est vnum ouile, & habemus vnum verum Pastorem sanctum; & innocentem Photium sanctissimum nostrum Dominum, & Oecumenicum Patriarcham. Si vnio est Ecclesiae Occidentalis, atque Orientalis, ideoque hac vnione vnum ouile, & vna Ecclesia facta est; quomodo similis Ecclesiae Pastor, vnus Photius est, reiecto Ioanne? Si Photius Orientalis est, Ioannes Occidentalis; qua ratione vnius ouilis, vnius Ecclesiae duo Pastores fuerint? Quodsi Orientalem tantum intelligit, quis alias Sedes Patriarchales Pastorum munere spolians, totum in vnum Constantinopolitanum, vel Photium detulit; lit, vt hic vniuersæ Ecclesiæ Orientalis vnus Pastor sit? Similia neque ex penu Orientalis, neque Occidentalis Ecclesiæ hausta sunt. Aliter longe Patres tum Orientales, tum Occidentales loquuntur, aliter Photiani in hac Synodo ita ruunt in tenebris, omniaque miscent. Quis ergo æquo animo ferat verba Michaëlis Alexandrini Actione secunda de Photio, cui ipse Photius est, Τῆς Ἐκκλησίας Θεοῦ ἀρχιποίμην, τῆς ἱεροσύνης τηλωτὴς, γνώμων τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀρχιποίμην τῶν λογικῶν προβάτων τῷ Χριστῷ, Ecclesiæ Dei primarius Pastor, Sacerdotij consummator, veritatis index, & Christiani gregis rationis compotis primus, ac præcipuus Pastor. Et similia aliorum in eadem Synodo nugamenta, quæ libens prætereo, ne Lectori tædio sim.
units.tr: "By his holy prayers one fold has been made, and we have one true holy Shepherd, and the innocent Photius, our most holy Lord and Ecumenical Patriarch." If there is a union of the Western and Eastern Church, and therefore by this union one fold and one Church has been made, how is Photius alone the one Shepherd of this Church, with John rejected? If Photius is of the East and John of the West, on what reasoning would there be two shepherds of one fold and one Church? But if he means only the East, who has deprived the other Patriarchal Sees of the office of shepherd and transferred everything to the one Constantinopolitan, or to Photius, so that here there is one Shepherd of the whole Eastern Church? Such things have been drawn neither from the storehouse of the Eastern Church nor from that of the Western. The Fathers, both Eastern and Western, speak quite differently. The Photians in this synod rush about in darkness and mix everything together. Who then could bear with equanimity the words of Michael of Alexandria in the second Action about Photius, who is himself Photius: "Primary Shepherd of the Church of God, zealous for the priesthood, judge of the truth, and first and foremost shepherd of Christ's rational sheep" [Τῆς Ἐκκλησίας Θεοῦ ἀρχιποίμην, τῆς ἱεροσύνης τηλωτὴς, γνώμων τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀρχιποίμην τῶν λογικῶν προβάτων τῷ Χριστῷ]. And there are similar trifles of others in the same synod, which I gladly pass over, lest I be a weariness to the reader.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Hoc idem probatur ex Sacerdotio ipsius Photij, quod a Synodicis Θεοψήφισον, a Deo de- cretum, nuncupatur.
units.tr: The same point is proved from the priesthood of Photius himself, which the Synodicals call Theopsephison, decreed by God.

units.la: Illud quoque prætereundum non est. Vocatur Sacerdotium Photij Θεοψήφισον, Diuino decreto constitutum. Quidquid euenit, ex Deo esse certum est. Sed hac ratione & bella, & pestes, & fames, & aduersa quæque Θεοψήφισα sunt, & forte non alio modo Sacerdotium illud Θεοψήφισον[?] fuit, ex quo tot mala Græciæ prognata sunt. Sed vt fuerit examinetur. Photiani ipsi non negant, Ignatium legitime in thronum Constantinopolitanum euectum fuisse. Is per vim eijcitur a Photio, quo eiecto ipse Bardæ & Imperatoris Michaëlis patrocinio fultus Sedem occupat. Hæc quoque sunt Schismaticorum effata. Photius ergo inuasor est, lupus in gregem alienum intrusus. Et Photius iste homo acerrimus bonorum alienorum possessor, expulsor, ereptor, nobis Θεοψήφισον[?] fuerit? Horas bonas esset perdere, si in his probandis diutius immoraremur'. Adeantur Nicetas Paphlago in vita Ignatij, Acta Octauæ Synodi, & Libelli Episcoporum in ea contenti, Acta Synodorum Romanarum sub Nicolao, & Adriano Pontificibus Romanis, Styliani Neocæsariensis Epistola ad Stephanum Papam. Et ne singulos recenseam, Georgius Cedrenus damnationem Ignatij, & electionem Photij vocat, Ταῦτα γὰρ τὰ τῆς φιλοσοφωτάτης τῷ Βαρ-δᾷ πανουργήματα[?]. Hæc sunt facinora, quæ Bardas imperij obtinendi cupiditate impulsus edidit. Ioannes Zonaras inter alia supra modum vituperanda, & detestanda Bardæ enumerat, Τὰ δ' ἄλλα καὶ ἄλλα ψιλά[?], ἐ ἐκπέψασα[?], Matthæ-us Cygala in Synopsi historica, Τὸ μὲν ὀλίγον ἐσῆλθε, καὶ τὴν ἔφεσιν, ὁ ἐποίησε Σισίσθον ἀρχιεπίσκοπον[?], καὶ ἐκ τῆς ἐκκλησίας τὸν ἁγιώτατον Ἰγνάτιον ἀδίκως[?] ἐκβαλών[?], καὶ ἐκαμε Παξιάρχην Φώτιον. Modicum post tempus, misit, qui eum adducerent, & Synodo Præsulum coacta sanctissimum virum Ignatium ininfte[?] depofuit, creauitque Patriarcham Photium.
units.tr: Nor should this be passed over. The priesthood of Photius is called Theopsephison [Θεοψήφισον], that is, established by divine decree. Whatever happens is certainly from God. By this reasoning wars, plagues, famines and every calamity would also be Theopsephisa, and perhaps that priesthood was no different, the one from which so many evils for Greece were born. But let us examine whether it was. The Photians themselves do not deny that Ignatius was lawfully raised to the throne of Constantinople. He was forcibly ejected by Photius, and once he was gone, Photius occupied the see, supported by the patronage of Bardas and of the Emperor Michael. These too are the assertions of the schismatics. Photius, then, was an usurper, a wolf thrust into another's flock. And was this man, a most avid possessor, expeller and despoiler of other men's goods, Theopsephison for us? It would be a waste of time to linger longer over proving these points. Let the reader consult Nicetas the Paphlagonian in the life of Ignatius, the Acts of the Eighth Synod and the libels of the bishops contained in it, the Acts of the Roman synods under the popes Nicholas and Hadrian, and the letter of Stylianus of Neocaesarea to Pope Stephen. And not to list them one by one: George Cedrenus calls the condemnation of Ignatius and the election of Photius "these villainies of the most philosophical Bardas" [Ταῦτα γὰρ τὰ τῆς φιλοσοφωτάτης τῷ Βαρδᾷ πανουργήματα]. These are the crimes that Bardas committed, driven by his lust to obtain power. John Zonaras, among other things beyond measure to be condemned and detested, enumerates the deeds of Bardas [Τὰ δ' ἄλλα καὶ ἄλλα...]. Matthew Cygalas, in his historical synopsis, writes: "He came in small measure, and by his desire he made Sisinnius archbishop, and unjustly cast the most holy Ignatius out of the Church, and made Photius patriarch [Τὸ μὲν ὀλίγον ἐσῆλθε...]." A little later he sent men to bring him, and with a synod of prelates assembled he deposed the most holy man Ignatius unjustly and created Photius patriarch.

units.la: Eadem repetit Dorotheus Metropolita Monembafiensis. Basilius Imperator Epistola ad Papam Nicolaum; Τῷ Ἐκκλησίᾳ ἐνόμε ποιμνῷ γυμνωμένῃ, ὡσπερ ποιμένι ἀδελφῷ[?] διδασκαλωθῆ[?]. Ecclesiam offendimus sue germano Pastore viduatam, alieno mercenario oppressam. Et infra; Ἰγνάτιον τὸν ἀδελφὸν τῆς ἐκκλησίας [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀπεκαταστήσαμεν. Ignatium iniuria affectum, sede suo restituimus. Et infra. Ὅσους ἀπάτη, καὶ παντελῶς ἀπάτῃ ὁ Φώτιος ἐφαπίσαντο[?]. Ὀλίγοι γὰρ παντελῶς αὐτῶν πεισθῆναι τῆς ἐκείνου παρὰ[?] γεγόνασι. Et quicunque artibus Photij, & infidijs circumuenti sunt: perpauci quippe reperiuntur, quos ille cassibus suis non irretiuit. Michaël Syncellus in Encomio S. Ignatij Patriarchæ; Ὁ δὲ ἀδίκως καθαιρεθεὶς μετ' ἀδελφικῆς αὐτοῦ[?] Φωτίου [?] τὴν ἱερατικὴν Θέσιν[?] τοῦ Θρόνου, ἐκ Μακεδόνων Βασιλέως τὸν Θρόνον τῆς βασιλείας τιμιωτάτῳ παρελθόντος, ὃς ἐπάρκεσε τὸν μέγαν, καὶ θορυβῶν Ἰγνάτιον ἐκ τῆς πολιτείας, ἐξορίας αἰχμαλώτου[?], καὶ τῇ τε λαῷ πάντες αἴτιοι πίστεως, λαμπρῶς καὶ μὴ ὄσος εἴπειν ἐν ἐνημέρᾳ εἰς τὸν παρθένον ἀναβιβάζει Θεόν.
units.tr: Dorotheus, Metropolitan of Monembasia, repeats the same. The Emperor Basil, in his letter to Pope Nicholas: "We found the Church, a flock stripped of its own brother shepherd, and oppressed by a hireling not its own." And below: "We restored Ignatius, our brother of the Church, to his see, after he had been wronged." And further: "Those whom Photius deceived and entirely beguiled, for very few of them were not persuaded by his wiles. Few indeed are found whom he did not ensnare with his snares." Michael the Syncellus, in his Encomium of St. Ignatius the Patriarch: "He who was unjustly deposed, together with his brother Photius, the priestly office of the throne, when the Macedonian emperor had come to the most honoured throne of the kingdom, who had great power and, disturbing Ignatius, cast him out of the commonwealth into captive exile..., and all were guilty of the faith toward the people, brilliantly and not without..." (the rest is corrupt).

units.la: Οʹ Ji[?] Οἱ δὲ μαθηταὶ, καὶ οἱ τῶν ἄλλων Πατριαρχικῶν [?] ϑεῶν[?]. Iniqua vero sententia damnatus Ignatius ingenti cum gloria sacrum tribunal recuperauit, simul ac Basilius Macedo imperium accepit, qui continuo eximium, & nouum hunc Deiferum Ignatium ex diuturno exilio revocatum permotus vniuersi populi postulatis, summo cum honore, summaque veneratione in Patriarchium restituit. Quod cum reliqui Orientis Antistites accepissent, ingenti omnes gaudio sunt perfusi. Nec multo post Auctor vitæ Michaëlis, Theophili Imperatoris filij.
units.tr: The disciples, and those of the other patriarchs... Condemned by an unjust sentence, Ignatius recovered the sacred tribunal with great glory as soon as Basil the Macedonian received the empire. Basil at once, moved by the petitions of the whole people, restored this remarkable new God-bearing Ignatius, recalled from long exile, to the Patriarchate with the highest honour and veneration. When the other bishops of the East heard this, they were all filled with great joy. Not long after, the author of the Life of Michael, son of the emperor Theophilus, writes:

units.la: Οὗτος δὲ ἦν, ὁ Ἰγνάτιος μετὰ τινας χρόνους τὸν Βάρδαν ὅτι τῇ τε οἰκείᾳ γυναικὶ ἀλόγως, καὶ αὐχμηρῶς ἀποβαλὼν, τῆς αὐτῇ ἡ νύμφης συμπλοκῆς τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἀπέρξεν, ἐπὶ τὴν ϑείων κανόνων ἡμέλ[?]ει τῶν, ἣν ἐκείνῳ ἐδίδου ποιεῖν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἀπεπέμπτ[?] πόλεμον ταύτῃ ἀπ[?] αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἵνα τὸν λιμὸν, καὶ τὸ δίψαν παρῷ, καὶ τὰς ὅτι γῆς τε αὐλόπος ἐπιτάσεις τε, καὶ φαβδισμοὺς, καὶ τις καθ᾽ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα ὠμοπάσας πληγὰς, ἐν τῷ ϑ μόνον ἐχῶ ἀπῶν, ὅτι τὰ σωνεχῆ βασιλεῖ μα τῆς ἰσοτίας. Παρεδίδου τὸν Ἰγνάτιον ὁ Βάρδας φρυρᾷ, καὶ φρυρᾷ ἀπέ- ... 'χαλεπῆ', ἢ δὲ λῶ ἐν τῷ τῆν ἰεροῦ Ἀ'ποσόλων τεμένους. Οὐκ ἐν αὐτοῖς δὲ ταῦν μεγαλῶ τι, καὶ σεμνὸς, ἀλλ᾽ ἔνδα οἱ πάφοι ἐλέγον[?], καὶ ἐσὶν, ἐκεῖσε δὲ ἐνπνπιλάζαντες ἐνί τινι τῶν ὅ(?)ῳ τῆς Κωσφων- νύμε ἐν κρυμῇ, καὶ παγετὸ γυμνὸς ἐφ᾽ ἡ τῆς παρεμμίας ἐν μετιώρῳ διηκαδιζαντες τὰ τὲ κρυμὲ Ϲ ζημίῳ πάχλν ἐξεβιάζοντο. τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ ἀντ-ἐπημέα τε, Ϲ τῆ ἐντὸς αἰαλκαγῶν ἐκ τῆς τῆ ψύχοις ὑφβολῆς ἐξ' χαρὸς ἀπορροια, καὶ Ϲάνατος ἐκ τότε πικρός. ἀπαβίῳ δ' ἀν ἐκ τῇ φρεσίωτων δυνότη-τῷ καὶ ὠμότητ@. ἡ δὲ ὅτι ὁ, τε Γοργωνίτης Ἰωάννης, Ϲ ὁ Σκοπέλῳ Νικολάω, καὶ Θεόδωρος ὁ Μωσὴς, εἰ μὴ 'οἱκτῳ βαλλόμενος, Κωνσταντίνῳ ᾧ ὁ Ἀρεμβιάκω τῇ τῶτων ἀπιστίᾳ ἐν τῷ μέλ-λῃ ἐπίζει ἐκείθεν τὸ τὸν αἱ ἀθερπτον καταβί-βάζει, καὶ οἶνῳ βεαχὲ, ἐπὶ ἡ ἐ ἀρτῳ, καὶ μι-κρᾷ τινι ὠδιδάλῳ τὸ λυποῦ ἐπ' ὀλίγον παρεμυ-θάζ. ὡς ἡ τὸ ἠ ἠμωρίας ἀκοῦντως ἐδόκ' αὐτῷ, τότε δὲ ἐαφόρεον μὲ τὸν αἰδρα τέτον ἢ τῶν νῆσον Μιτυλήλῳ ποιῆ. ἐπειδὴ καὶ πινες τῆς Ἐπισκόπων ἀπίλεγον, καὶ τῶ ἀὐκῳ πίῤῥω που δὲ ἔας, καὶ ἀποφωτίζας ἐπεκαλοῦντο, ἡ ἐκ ἂν χρόνῳ ἄλλον δέξασθ' ἡπείλωσεν, ἀλλὰ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας σωσαπορή-γνυς τὸν, ἐκ τοῦτε τάχιστα δὴ κατολαβηθὲς ἐγὼ Ϲ ἐπάτες ἀπάτη παρ ψαῖν, ἡ ἀλωπεκή. ἰδία γὰρ Ϲ κρυφῇ τούτων ἑκάστου μεταλαλήμενος μικρόν τι, Ϲ ἔπειτον ὑπῆχνεῖτο τε ἐ ἐδίδου, ἀμόνον ἀπόσαῖος τῆς Ἰωάννου, ἀλλὰ τὸν Θεόνον αὐτὸν Κωνσταντινουπόλεως. ὡς δ' ἐνεσίδοξαν ἁπαντες, ἡ τῆς μὲν δόξης ἡττήθη το, τὸ δὲ καλῶς ἕνεκα Ϲ νομίμω αὐτέλεψεν ἀδῆς, τότε δήτοτε ὑπεπίθη, Ϲ ὡς ὁ νῦν βασιλεὺς αὐτοῖς τὰς ὑποχείφς ἐκπληρώσωσεν. αὐτὸ ἡ τὸ εὐχρημον τι-φοῦτες τε, ἡ σεμνὸν, ἅμα τῇ ἑφὸς αὐτὸν κλη-θῶσι μὴ θεὸς τὸ δίδομα καζωνδύοντι. Ἵνα Ϲ αὐτός, φησι, τῆς ὑμῶν ἐν ὑπεραγάμῳ ἀφειῆς ἔπ[?] ἔτω δὲ ἕκαστον ἐφ' ὁμῶ̃, ἀλλ' ἰδίᾳ, ἐ[?] κῷ μόνας [?] Φεὸς τὸν Μιχαὴλ ἀσκαλοῦ ὠλῷ, μὴ ἀῶ̃ν ἐσ[?]πηδᾶν τῇ πυρὶ αὐτὸ[?]ν. καὶ ἔτω μὲν ἐκ μόνῳ θεοσεμάτῳ ἀξιούμενοί τε, ἐ ἀπερ[?]νέμμοι, ἐλαύων ἐνυχῶν ἀφαδήματίζοντες. τῆς τε γὰρ ἀρετῆς ἐξεπλάηον, ὡς τῆς δόξης νικώμεναι ἔφη, καὶ ταύτης αὐτῆς ἡμέρᾳ[?]ον, ἐπὶ μὴ καλῶς, ἀλλ' ἐπιβάλλως τὸν Ἰγνάτιον παρειδὼν[?] ἐπως οὐ ἐπεὶ καὶ ἔζει αὐθέρπει ὄντες ἐφάνῃς, καὶ ἔτω δὲ ἰπα-πηθείας, Φωτὶω ἐπὶ σοφία λόγον γνωεῖμω ἀνδρὶ, τῆς κοσμικῆς δὲ τάξεως αἰπποιεμένω, καὶ τῷ τὸ θεοζασπιξῆς ἐδραγμένῳ πυρὶ τὸν Θεὸν ἐφ[?]δου τῆς Κωνσταντινουπόλεως. Καὶ ἵνα δὴ καὶ τὰ κ̃ιπτῶν κεραταύπερα ὑποφῄνωσι, ζωοπηρηταις ὠμὸ ἐκ Ῥώμης ἐπ' ἄλλαις φεσφάστασι, καὶ γὰρ τὴν Εἰκονομάχων ζαλίντας μετὰ πυμφάμῳ, καὶ ἡ Γνάτιμ[?]ν τὸ κ[?]ν ἐγενέζονται ὠξοποιάζαντες, καὶ συμπεριάζαντες, ἐ ἐν τῷ τῆς Θέων Ἀπσάλων πυμφὰ δεδημοπολυ[?]ῃ καὶ θαιρέσι τῇ τὸν καθυπερβαλίντας, ἐπὶ τῆς ὀξοείας μετακαλέζαντο, πυλμάς τα θεόστα[?]πα, καὶ ζοῦν ὀδήντας φωνηλάζαντες, πᾶς σκοτόμαιναν καὶ τὴν ἱερέων κακὰς. Ἀλλ' ὅσα μὲν ἐ ἄλλα καὶ πάντων τῶν ἱερέων ἐφαπιάζατο φυλακαις τι, καὶ ἐαφοείας, ἐ πινὰς ὠσπάταις ὁσημέραν ὧδ[?]ιδὲς, ἵνα τῷ Φωτίῳ συσκευωπάσῳσι, βιβλοί τε πολλαί, καὶ ὁ πᾶς ἐκ ὅπλίπι χρόνος ἐκ[?]ζαγο[?]ω[?]ῶν.
units.tr: Now this is the Ignatius who, some years later, cast off Bardas's own wife without reason and in a squalid manner, and shut him out from the communion of the Church, when he ignored the divine canons, which he had given him to observe. Bardas handed Ignatius over to a guard, and the guard [kept him] under harsh confinement in the church of the Holy Apostles. It was not in any grand or splendid place, but where the wretched prisoners were kept, in a cold and frozen spot, where he was stripped and made to stand barefoot on the ice, and the cold forced out... The remaining torments came from the inner heat of the body, pouring out from the chill, and a bitter death followed. This was the cruelty and savagery of the men. John of Gorgon, Nicholas of Skopelos and Theodore the Moses, if they had not been moved by pity, would have ... With Constantine the Armenian, through their unbelief, they went down into the depths; with wine, vinegar and bread and a little food they slightly relieved the suffering, as if it were a matter of foolishness. At that time they carried the men off to the island of Mytilene. Then some of the bishops spoke against him and called upon him from afar, shouting out, that he would never receive another, but would save the Church... Immediately, having been caught by a deceit, they were deceived as by foxes. Each of them, speaking privately and secretly, was offered something, not only by John but by Theodore himself of Constantinople. When all were persuaded, the glory of the one was overcome, and the good name of the other was taken away; then at last they yielded, so that the present emperor fulfilled their wishes for them. They themselves, thinking it a respectable and dignified thing, in addition to the title, were called not gods, for they had given the gift to one who was...

units.la: Hic ergo Ignatius post nonnullos annos Bardam pro coniugis propria temeraria, atque inconsulta dimissione, & germana nurus amplexibus ab iningressu Ecclesiæ obturbans, cum ille & sacros Canones sperneret, pœnam, quam ab illo petebat Ignatius ex instituto Ecclesiæ longe a se dimoues[?], eandem ab Ignatio exigit: & ut famem, sitimque silentio prætereā[?], & corporis super terram crebras extensiones, & verbera, inque eius universas particulas nulla excepta inclementissimas plagas, unum tantum si dixero, reliqua historiæ continuabo. Ignatium Bardas custodibus commissum immanibus, ac efferatis in carcerem coniecit. In sacrorum scilicet Apostolorum ædem non conspicuam illam, & venerandam, sed ubi sepulcra dicuntur esse, & re vera sunt, in uno ex iis, quod Copronymi fuerat, inclusum, cum intensum frigus ac glacies seuiret, pistillo nudiorem, ut proverbio contritum est, in sublime collocatum frigoris hyemisque molestijs vi subigebant: mala, quibus ille opprimebatur, erant & alui proluuies, & intestinorum ob excessum frigoris effluxus, & mors inde acerbissima consecutura. Et plane ille finem vitæ fecisset, si diritas feritasque custodum irrupto cursu continuassent: Erant vero custodes Ioannes Gorgonites, Nicolaus Scotelops, & Theodorus Morus. Sed Constantinus Armeniacus misericordia adductus, dum excubitores custodiæ deerant, cibi sumendi hora, inde dimotum hominem, humi accumbere faciens, vino modico, pane etiam pramolestiam, ac rerum acerbitatem ad minimum tempus recreabat. Cum vero satis poenarum dedisse Bardae visum esset, tum virum ad Mitylenem Insulam de patria exterminant. Verum cum nonnulli Episcopi contra niterentur, & iustitiam longe gentium abüsse[?] contenderent, & nunquam se, si quid aliud pertentasset, probaturos, quinimo sese recessuros ab Ecclesia minarentur, indidem emanantes turbas metuens, apud animum suum proposuit hos & dolis, & vulpinis astutiis circumducere. Remoto itaque liberoque ab arbitris loco singulatim unicuique denunciauit, neque parvum, neque exile promittens, tradensq; si tantum ab Ignatio seiungerentur, sed sedem ipsam Constantinopolitanam. Vbi vero omnes nutui illius decesserant gloriae mancipia, nemo posthac honesti, iusteque causa arbitrio Bardae refragabatur. tum postea ille suggerebat Imperatorem ipsis promissa completurum. Ipsi autem honestum, ac grave praeferentes, simul atque ad ipsum vocati fuere, ne muneribus animum applicetis, dicebat, ut ille vestram quoque virtutem suspiciat. Hac ratione singulos non simul allectos, sed privatim, & secreto ab aliis ad Michaelem adducens, ne eodem momento dignitatem expostularent, persuadebat. & hi quidem ex sola compellatione digni declarati, & dignitatem recusantes semetipsos palam traduxerunt, nanque gloriae amore conciti de virtute decidebant, & eam rursus delusi amittebant, quod non iure, sed fraudulenter Ignatium tradebant. Eo pacto igitur, cum & hi homines esse comperti essent, & circumuenti Photio, adulte sapientiae viro, ordinis secularis, & a Secretis primarij muneris thronum Constantinopolitanum tradebat. Et ut validius quae egerant constabilirent, sub alijs atque alijs nominibus Locumtenentes Roma accersunt; contra Iconomachos, attamen illi suo tempore adversus Ignatium, ut calculum ferrent, traducti sunt. Et coacta Synodo in diuinorum Apostolorum aede publica Ignatium depositione multant, cum ab exilio euocatum, pugnis illius faciem, dentesque contundentes, omnem profundae noctis caliginem in Sacerdotes pessime exercuerunt. Sed quae, quantaque alia aduersus omnes Sacerdotes, carceribus, & exilijs, & immanissimis poenis affligens, in dies singulos temere ausus est, ut communicarent cum Photio, volumina pleraque, & futurum omne tempus clamoribus tragicis personabit.
units.tr: Here Ignatius, some years later, was dealt with by Bardas. Bardas had Ignatius's wife rashly and without counsel dismissed from her husband's side, and he disturbed the German daughter-in-law's embrace by barring her entry to the Church. Although Bardas despised the holy canons, he exacted from Ignatius the same penalty that Ignatius had sought from him, a penalty far removed from the Church's established practice. I will mention only one example and pass over the rest of the story in silence: the hunger and thirst, the repeated prostrations on the ground, the beatings, and the most merciless blows on every part of his body without exception. Bardas committed Ignatius to savage and brutal guards and threw him into a prison. This was not the famous and venerable church of the holy Apostles, but a place where tombs are said to be, and really are, in one of which, the one that had belonged to Copronymus, they shut him up. When the intense cold and ice raged, they forced him, stripped nearly naked, as the proverb says, to be set up high, subjected to the discomforts of frost and winter. The afflictions that pressed him down were a flux of the bowels and a discharge of the intestines caused by the excess of cold, and a very bitter death was sure to follow. He would certainly have ended his life there if the cruelty and savagery of his guards had continued without a break. The guards were John Gorgonites, Nicholas Scotelops, and Theodore Morus. But Constantine Armeniacus, moved by pity while the watchmen of the prison were absent at the hour for taking food, had the man removed from there and made to lie on the ground, and with a little wine and bread he refreshed him for a short time against the hardship and bitterness of his situation. When it seemed that Bardas had inflicted enough punishment, they banished the man from his homeland to the island of Mitylene. But since some bishops resisted and contended that justice was far away, and threatened that they would never agree to anything else, and would even withdraw from the Church, Photius, fearing the disturbances that would arise from this, resolved in his own mind to win them over by trickery and foxlike cunning. So, taking each one aside in a free place away from witnesses, he promised him no small or trivial reward, and offered not only to separate him from Ignatius but also the Constantinopolitan see itself. When they had all yielded to his nod and become slaves of ambition, none of them afterwards opposed Bardas's will out of honest and just reasons. Then Photius went on to suggest that the Emperor would fulfil what had been promised them. They, pretending to honour and dignity, when they were summoned to him, said that he should not set his mind on gifts, so that he might also esteem their virtue. By this method he persuaded them not to be brought together at once, but privately and secretly, one by one, to Michael, so that they might not demand their dignity at the same moment. Those who were declared worthy by this summons alone, and who then refused the dignity, openly betrayed themselves, for, roused by love of glory, they fell away from virtue and, deluded, lost it again, because they handed over Ignatius not by right but by fraud. In this way, since these men were found to be of this character and were won over, Photius, a man of mature wisdom, of the secular order, and first of the secretaries of office, was handed the Constantinopolitan throne. And to make what they had done more secure, they summoned legates from Rome under various titles, against the Iconoclasts, though those legates were at that time brought forward to cast their votes against Ignatius. And with a synod assembled in the public church of the divine Apostles, they punished Ignatius with deposition, after bringing him back from exile, and they treated the priests most wickedly, striking his face and breaking his teeth with fists, and wreaking on all priests every darkness of the deepest night. But what other great and numerous deeds, afflicting all priests with prisons, exiles and most savage punishments, he daily dared to commit, so that they would communicate with Photius, many volumes will tell, and all future time will resound with tragic outcries.

units.la: Georgius Hamartolus.
units.tr: George the Sinner.

units.la: Μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα ὁ Βασιλεὺς Λέων, ὁ αὐτὸν σπαθαλάτῳ Ἀλφίαν ἀμφὶ Ἰωάννην Ἀγοπολίτην λόγῳ πάνυ ὤν, καὶ Λογοθέτην [?] τῆς δέσμιας ἐν τῇ ἁγίᾳ Σοφίᾳ [?] ἀπεδλαν [?], οἱ καὶ ἐν τῷ ἀμβωνι ἀῤῥήσαντας [?], καὶ τὰς τῆ Πατριάρχου Φωνὰς αἰνὰς εἰς ἐπήκοον πάντων [?] αἰαγόνοις [?], τὴν τὸ Θεὸν κατηγορῶν, καὶ ἀνθ [?] ἐν τῇ μοϊῇ τῆ Ἀ[?]γμινάων [?] τῇ ἐπινομα[?]ζομένῃ τῷ Βάσδων. Στέφανον δὲ Σύγκελλον τὸν αὐτὸς [?] αὐτὶ ἀδ᾽ ψὸν Πατριάρχῳ φεσβάλλεῖ, ὑπὸ Θεοφά-νης χειροτονηθέντα τῷ πρωτοθρόνῳ. [?]
units.tr: After these things the Emperor Leo, who had been a man of great eloquence, together with Andrew, the commander of the forces, and John of Hagiopolis, a learned man, sent the Logothete to the church of Holy Wisdom. They climbed the pulpit and, reading aloud the crimes of the Patriarch Photius before all who heard, they cast him down from the throne and banished him to the monastery of the Armenians called Bordonis. They raised Stephen, the brother of Photius and a syncellus, to the patriarchate, ordained by Theophanes the protothronos.

units.la: Post hac Imperator Leo eundem copiarum ducem Andream simul cum Hagiopolita Ioanne admodum diserto, atque erudito, cursusque Logothetam ad templum S. Sapientiæ misit, qui ambonem ascendentes, & Patriarchæ Photij facinora omnibus audientibus lectitantes, de throno deiecerre, eumque in Armenianorum Monasterio Bordonis cognominato relegarunt. Stephanum vero illius fratrem Syncellum in Patriarcham promouent a Theophane Protothrono ordinatum.
units.tr: Afterwards the Emperor Leo sent the same commander of the troops, Andrew, together with John of Hagiopolis, a very eloquent and learned man, and the Logothete, to the church of Holy Wisdom. They climbed the pulpit, read aloud the deeds of the Patriarch Photius in the hearing of all, cast him down from the throne, and relegated him to the Armenian monastery called Bordonis. They promoted Stephen, his brother and syncellus, to the patriarchate, ordained by Theophanes the protothronos.

units.la: Constantinus Porphyrogenneta in vita Basi. Iij Macedonis, quam inter Symmicta nostra Græce ac Latine edidimus. Ἐπὶ γοῦν, καὶ ταύτας οἷον ἐν Καλῷ πινὶ, καὶ ἐγεράχῳ τυλχανόυ-ζας ἰώφα, δὲ τὸ ἢ κοινῆς λύμης ὑπὸ τῶν φειαξάντ-ων, ἢ ταύτας μεταλαχὼν τὴν ἐξωδωτὴν μὲν τῆς οἰκείας καὶ δηδιάζας, ἢ πόιμνης ἡ ἐννόμως τύπων καὶ ζογρξ[illegible, ~12 letters]ἢ ἰπεσον, ἀλλὰ δὲ ἑαυτῆς Σωόδε, ἢ συμβιότως ἡ ἀπανταχόθεν ἀρχιε-ρέων Θεοῦ ἡ Ἐκκλησίας ἡ σάλοντ[?]ὸ ἐκδηχόμενον ἔ-σαι. τὶς τὰ πρὸ τάτε ἐβδόμῳ ἀγίαν Σωόδον ὅπηκυ-ςοῦ ἐς, ἢ τὰς πεπειλυπᾶς ἡ Εἰκονομάχων ἀφεπικῶν τῷ ἀπαδίμαπ ἀὲς, ἢ ἡ γνόσιον νυμφίον τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἢ Τῖς τίκτοις τὸν πατρὸς κανονικῶς ἀφιαχῶν, πν ἡ αὐτ[?]σαχθέντα χολάζειν κ[?]ὸ Ζας, ὥστε τὸ τὸν τῶς ἑαυτὸν μέσεσι[?]ὁ Κύριος. Illarum vti in salo teinp^sstate, ac fluctibus iactatarum, quod noxam communem ab antecessore contraxerant, deturbatoque de proprio throno, & grege, qui legitime praerat, alio suffecto, tranquillandarum studium nunquam depositi: sed publica Synodo locis ex omnibus Dei Praesulum, ut ut potuit, congregata, procellam deuitauit, & septimam, qua praeceferat, sanctam Synodum constabiliens, reliquos adhuc ex Iconomachis haereticos anathemate feriit, legitimum Ecclesiae sponsum, & liberis patrem, ut Canones iubent, restituit, intrusum denique vacare a munere iussit, donec alium ad se Dominus aduocasset. Auctor MS. apud me; Ὁ τῆς Φώτιος τὸν Ἐκκλησίαν διέχυσι, ὅδὸν ἂν ὑπακούσας Νικολάῳ, καὶ Ἀδριανῷ τῶν Ῥώμης ἀρχιερέων [?] ἀποκηρύξαι τὸν δίκαιον ἐκβαλεῖν Ἰγνατίον τὸν θεῖον Κωνσταντινουπόλεως, [?] καὶ ἀλλὰ ἀποκόπτων τῶν Ῥώμης ἀρχιερέων ἀφορισμῷ, καὶ αὐτὸς, καὶ ὁ Βασιλεὺς καθυποβίβλητο [?].
units.tr: Constantine Porphyrogenitus in the life of Basil the Macedonian, which we have published among our Symmicta in Greek and Latin. Accordingly, when the ship of the Church was tossed by storm and waves, because of the common corruption its members had contracted from their predecessor, and when the rightful shepherd had been thrown down from his own throne and flock, another having been put in his place, the Emperor never ceased to seek calm. He gathered a public synod, as far as he could, from all the places where the bishops of God were, avoided the storm, confirmed the seventh holy synod which he had proclaimed, struck the remaining heretics of the Iconoclasts with anathema, restored the lawful bridegroom of the Church and father of children, as the canons require, and finally ordered the intruder to vacate his office until the Lord should call another to Himself. Author manuscript, in my possession: Photius divided the Church, because he would not obey Nicholas and Hadrian, the bishops of Rome, who had ordered him to proclaim and expel the just Ignatius, the divine patriarch of Constantinople; and he himself and the Emperor were struck with excommunication by the bishops of Rome, cut off by anathema.

units.la: Hic Photius Ecclesiam discidit, quod cum non obedisset Nicolao, & Adriano Romanis Pontificibus, Sedem Constantinopolitanam Ignatio iniuste expulso cedere, quam contra statuta Canonum arripuerat, a dictis Romanis Pontificibus excommunicatione, & anathemate & ipse & Imperator feritur. Audiendus etiam est Constantinus Manasses.
units.tr: Here Photius split the Church, because he would not obey Nicholas and Hadrian, the Roman Pontiffs, who ordered him to yield the Constantinopolitan see to Ignatius, who had been unjustly expelled, and which he had seized against the statutes of the canons. He and the Emperor were struck by excommunication and anathema from those Roman Pontiffs. Constantine Manasses should also be heard.

units.la: Ὁ Κῶνσταρ γὰρ ἐκπυκνεύειν τῆς Ῥώμαιν, οἷς ἐπὶ τῆς διαφόρου [?]
units.tr: For Constantine... (the Greek of this line is too garbled to render with certainty) ... the Romans ... among the different...

units.la: Οὐ μόνον ἐκ ἐφεσίνζ τὴν παραμυθητικῶν [?], Ἀλλὰ καὶ κόσμον ἐξέφε τῇ παρανουμένῳ [?]. Ὅμοιον δρῶν ὡς εἶπνες ἱκέσιον πεπλησμένοι [?] Νοσοκομοῦντο πρὸς πνῦ [?]. οἱ δ' ἀπολυαγγέλιος [?]. Καὶ μᾶλλον ἀχριαίνοντο πρὸς τὸν Διεφέτου [?]. Ἔνθεν δὴ Βάρδας πεσηθὼν ποτὲ τοῖς μυσηρίοις Καὶ μὴ τυχὼν τῆς ἐλπίδος ἐκείνης τῆς ἐνθέε. Οὐ γὰρ πῶς δὲ οὐ ὡς ἕτερον ἄλλος εὐσωμα μύεα [?]. Καὶ πρὸς θυμὸν ἐκπυρωθεὶς ὡς λέων ἐεισβρύχης Ὣς παρδάλις ἐφάλλετο ῥαῖδας τοῦ δικαίου, Καὶ ῥήγνυτη, καὶ καταπᾶς θείας πηδαλουχίας Ἀντιφισᾶς ὃ Φώτιον. φεῦ αὐτὴ ἡν ὁ πίον [?].
units.tr: Not only did he not bring comfort... but he also displayed a disorderly ornament. Acting as if he had come as a suppliant, they hurried to... and the messengers... and they grew even paler toward the... Thence Bardas, having once fallen into those abominable things, and not attaining that hope of his, for he was not as one ... was inflamed to anger like a lion, and like a leopard he leapt upon the just man's ... and tore and seized the divine helmsman, opposing Photius ... alas, this was...

units.la: Nimirum obiurgationibus hisce Bardas Cæsar exacerbatus, non modo nihili fecit eas exhortationes, verum etiam conceptam aduersus monentem iracundiam, & indignationem alebat, non aliter agens, atque si faniosos aliquo curare volente, illi non tantum aufugiant, sed etiam erga benefacientem excandescant. Cum igitur aliquando Bardas accederet ad mysteria, nec diutinum illud munus a Patriarcha consequeretur, non enim unguenta fragrantia vasi putrido committuntur, inflammatus iracundia leonis in modum rugit, ceu violenta pardalis in hominem insilum insilit, lacerat, a clauo summouet, eius in locum Photium substituit. Prob qualem pro quali Viro? Ephræmius in Catalogo Patriarcharum. Τέτς (Μεθοδίε) μετασάντες δὲ εἰς τὴν διακόνων [?].
units.tr: Certainly Bardas Caesar, exasperated by these rebukes, not only made no account of these admonitions but also nursed a rage and indignation against the one who warned him. He acted no differently than madmen who, when someone wants to cure them, not only run away but also turn fiercely on their benefactor. So when Bardas once came to the mysteries and did not keep that office from the Patriarch for long, (for fragrant unguents are not entrusted to a rotten vessel), he, inflamed with rage, roared like a lion, and like a fierce leopard leapt upon the man, tore at him, removed him from the helm, and put Photius in his place. What a man in place of what man! Ephraem, in his Catalogue of the Patriarchs. Then, having transferred (Methodius) to the deacons' [...] [Τέτς (Μεθοδίε) μετασάντες δὲ εἰς τὴν διακόνων [?]]

units.la: Ποιμὴν ἀναγνώστης ὢν ἐκ τῆς βασιλίδος Γγνάτιος[?] πᾶσις Μιχαὴλ Βασιλέως, Καινῶν ἀκειβὴς ἀρετῆς[?], καὶ δογμάτων, Παιδεύσεως μέλημα καὶ λόγων κρατῶν, Ὃν ἐκβαλὼν Φθειρωνύμῳ[?] Λέων Κρατῶν καὶ ἀχῶν ἀπέφυγε σὺν βίᾳ. Εἶπε μοναζῶν, ὡς Θεῷ θᾶ[?] νόμῳ, Τ'ψσεσθαι ἔχε[?] τῆς Κωνσταντίνου θρόνον. Τῶν Μιχαὴλ καὶ ζαγαῶν[?] τὸ θεῖον Μᾶλλον ἢ Καῖζαρ Βάρδας ἀδίκῳ δίκῃ, Ἀνδρὸς πανύπερτον, καὶ σοφώτατον λίαν, Ἐκ λαϊκῶν Φώτιον ἀφεζαστικῆς[?] Ἀνήκα ἐξηθέντα ποιμένα ἀρχῶ[?] ἀδίκως. Τῶν δ' ἀπηγαδίντων[?] ἢ τῆς ἀφέσεως Γγνάτιος ἰσχύει τὸν θρόνον πάλιν.
units.tr: A reader-shepherd from the royal city, Ignatius, son of Emperor Michael, an exact rule of virtue and doctrine, the care of learning and mastery of words, whom Leo, the mighty and violent, cast out and escaped by force. Living as a monk, he said that by divine and lawful right he was to hold the throne of Constantinople. Rather than Caesar Bardas, by an unjust verdict, the most excellent and very wise man Photius, a layman from the secretariat, was raised up; the shepherd was unjustly thrown out of office. Those who ... by the release of Ignatius, he again holds the throne. [Ποιμὴν ἀναγνώστης ὢν ἐκ τῆς βασιλίδος Ἰγνάτιος υἱὸς Μιχαὴλ Βασιλέως, ... Τῶν δ' ἀπηγορευμένων ... Ἰγνάτιος ἰσχύει τὸν θρόνον πάλιν.]

units.la: Hic autem cum concessiffet ad Dominum, pastor divinus apparuit regiæ urbium Ignatius Michaëlis Imperatoris filius, accurata regula virtutum ac dogmatum, eruditionis cura, & sermonum potestas, quem euiauerat efferatus Leo, dum violenter imperium occupat. Postmodum inter Monachos adscriptus, uti divina præscripta mandant, tandem thronum Byzantinum assecutus est. Hoc Michaële de throno pulso, imo Barda Cæsar iudicio iniusto homine versipellem simul atque doctissimum, ex laico Photium primum a secretis substituit iniuste Pastorem. Hoc vero eiecto a primatu Ignatius denuo thronum recuperavit. Christophorus Patritius Mity-lelenensis in Synaxario de Sanctis, quorum memoria celebratur per annum singulis diebus in Ecclesia Graecorum carmine Iambico conscripto;
units.tr: Now when he had withdrawn to the Lord, the divine pastor Ignatius, son of Emperor Michael, appeared to the royal cities: an exact rule of virtues and doctrines, a care for learning and power of speech, whom the fierce Leo drove out while violently seizing the empire. Afterwards he was enrolled among the monks, as the divine prescriptions command, and at last attained the throne of Byzantium. When Michael was removed from the throne, or rather when Caesar Bardas, by an unjust judgment, substituted Photius, a man at once most crafty and most learned, first from the laity and from the secretariat, as an unjustly appointed pastor. When he was in turn cast out of the primacy, Ignatius recovered the throne again. Christopher Patritius of Mytilene, in his Synaxarium of the Saints, whose memory is celebrated each day of the year in the Church of the Greeks, in an iambic poem:

units.la: Εὔρες μεταστὰς τὴν παλαιὰν ἀξίανΓνάνε [illegible, ~6 letters] Ῥώμης τῆς νέας.
units.tr: Having been removed, you found your ancient dignity, Ignatius, prelate of New Rome. [Εὗρες μεταστὰς τὴν παλαιὰν ἀξίαν ... Ῥώμης τῆς νέας.]

units.la: Reperisti expulsus veterem dignitatem Ignati Praesul novae Romae. Et ut finiam, nemo unus est, qui Bardae facinus simile, vel Photij in Patriarchatum intrusionem in laude posuerit; & Deo ascripserit. Quare potius illius Sacerdotium βαρβαρόφωνον [?] non ὀρθοφώνον [?] vocari meruit. Non est haec filia verborum; sed densae numerosaeque praestantissimorum ex omni genere cohortes tuum Photium, quo tu Creyghtone doctiorem in omni genere literarum, prudentiorem in rebus gerendis, omnis iuris divini humaniq; peritiorem nunquam sedisse in quoius folio, vel Romae Papa, vel Constantinopoli Patriarcham, fateris, & cuius monumentis maiorem fidem, ac reverentiam adhibuisses, quia omnibus sanctis Ignatij miraculis, aut praescriptionibus sancti Nicolai, funditus prosternunt. O miseros Antiquae Graeciae Patres, quorum & doctrina, & sanctimonia si comparetur cum Photiana, Creyghtono iudice, iam nutantes fundo euertuntur. Sed bene est. Non est is Creyghtonus, qui de similibus statuere queat. Iudicis ex inscitia laborantis affectu parpartium impotentis animi iniquum, minimum inuidiosum iudicium fuerit. In Orientali Ecclesia nunquam Sancti titulo Photius decoratus est, etiam ab ipsis Schismaticis, nisi vbi illius dignitas, sanctissimi sibi nomen vsurpet,denegatus. Ex aduerso Ignatius Pater, & Doctor, & sanctitatis honore percolitur, & memoria eius sacro ritu vigesimo tertio Octobris, eius Synaxario lecto, in veneratione est. Synaxarij archetypum ex Menologio Basiliano, in quo effigies etiam illius inter alias Sanctorum internitet, in Graecorum Menaea influxit, quod hic, vt nouo beneficio Creyghtonum demerear, ascribam. Ὁ ἐν ἁγίοις πατὴρ ἡμῶν Ιγνάτιος γέγονε μὲν υἱὸς Μιχαὴλ Βασιλέως, ἀδελφὸς ἡ Θεο-φίλου, καὶ ἴσχυν Νικηφόρῳ τῷ Βασιλέως. Εὐθὺς ἡ γυναικὸς, ἃ καὶ Μοναχὸς γέγονε, καὶ ἡγούμενος τῆς μονῆς τῆς Ἀ[?]γαλγίλε, τῆ ὅπου υἱὸν ἀπολιπομένῃ Ἀναπλλοντῳ, νῦν ἡ Σατύρῳ. ἐπὶ [illegible, ~12 letters] Παξιαρχῆς Κωνσταντινουπόλεως, καὶ ἐκέλευσεν [?] ἐνδικα[?], μιᾶς πίντε, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ἐξεβλήθη ὑπὸ Μιχαὴλ Βασιλέως, αὖθ' αὖ πὰ Παξιάρχῳ [?] ποιήσαντι Φώτιον ἡγουμένον Μοναχόν. ἐπὶ ἐξεβλήθη καὶ αὖθις ὑπὸ Βασιλέως Βασιλέως, [?] καὶ αὖ ἀνακατῆσιν Ιγνάτιον πάλιν, καὶ ἐπισκόπησον ἐν ἁγίοις. καὶ πάλιν ἐξεβλήθη, καὶ ἐγένετο Παξιάρχης Στέφανος ὁ ἐν ἁγίοις υἱὸς Βασιλέως Βασιλέως, ὁ δὲ ἄγιος Ιγνάτιος ἀπῄδων ἐν τῇ τῆ Σατύρῳ μοναςυελῳ[?], καὶ καλῶς βιώσας ἐν εἰρήνῃ ἐτελεύτησεν. Sanctus Pater noster Ignatius fuit filius Michaëlis Imperatoris, frater Theophili, & Nicephori Imperatoris nepos. Virilitate spoliatus Monachum induit, præfuitque Monasterio, per illa tempora Archangeli Adorientis nuncupato, nunc Satyri. Postmodum in Patriarchatum Cõstantinopolitanum promotus, illo munere annos undecim, & menses quinque perfunctus est. Tum eiicitur a Michaële Imperatore, & loco ipsius Patriarcha substitutus Photius, antea Monachus. Tum & ipse eiectus est ab Imperatore Basilio, & rursus restitutus Ignatius Sedem tenuit annos undecim, & rursus eiectus est, creatusque Patriarcha sanctus Stephanus Basilij Imperatoris filius, & sanctus Ignatius progressus in Satyri Monasterium, & integre vita ducta in pace quieuit. Nec alia sunt, quæ Græci legunt in Synaxario paucis quibusdam immutatis, in quibus obiter animadvertendum est, ex scriptoris ostentatia veritatis ordinem confusius enarrari de eiectione Photij & Ignatij. Ignatius enim primum eicitur a Michaële, substituitur Photius, quo eiecto sub Basilio restituitur Ignatius, & Ignatio vita functo, rursus Photius ab eodem intruditur, tandemque pellitur a Leone, & exul submotus patria vitam agit, & Photio exuli succedit Stephanus. Sed in huius notæ mendis sanstitas[?] Ignatij in periculo haud vertitur, sed stat aliorum itidem testimonijs altissimis defixa radicibus. Menologium Sirletanum die 23. Octobris. Eodem die commemoratio Patris nostri Ignatij Patriarchae Constantinopolitani. Hic fuit vir generis splendore illustris, sed vita, & moribus illustriori post multas aerumnas, quas Photij opera perpessus est, quievit in Domino. Gregorius Hieromonachus Responsione in Professionem Fidei Marci Ephesii.
units.tr: "Having been expelled, you found your former dignity, Ignatius, prelate of New Rome." And to finish: no one has ever praised Bardas' deed, or Photius' intrusion into the patriarchate, or ascribed it to God. Hence his priesthood deserved to be called barbarous-voiced rather than orthodox-voiced [βαρβαρόφωνον, ὀρθοφώνον]. This is not an empty talk of words, but the dense and numerous cohorts of the most eminent men of every kind, who will prove that your Photius, whom you, Creighton, declare "more learned in every branch of letters, more prudent in conducting affairs, and more skilled in all divine and human law, never sat on any throne, whether at Rome as Pope or at Constantinople as Patriarch," and to whose records you gave greater faith and reverence, because all the holy miracles of Ignatius, or the prescriptions of St Nicholas, are overthrown from the foundations. Woe to the ancient Fathers of Greece, whose teaching and holiness, if compared with Photius' (Creighton being judge), are overturned from their now tottering foundations! But it is well. Creighton is not the man to decide on such matters. His judgment, from a man labouring under ignorance and partisan feeling of an unfair and impotent mind, would be a minimally hateful judgment. In the Eastern Church Photius was never decorated with the title of Saint, even by the schismatics themselves, except where his dignity, usurping the holy name for himself, is denied. On the other hand, Ignatius the Father and Teacher is honoured with the honour of sanctity, and his memory is in veneration on the twenty-third of October with his Synaxarium read. The archetype of the Synaxarium, from the Basilian Menologium, in which his likeness also appears among the other saints, passed into the Greek Menaea; this I will append here, so that I may earn Creighton's gratitude with a new kindness. [Ὁ ἐν ἁγίοις πατὴρ ἡμῶν Ιγνάτιος γέγονε μὲν υἱὸς Μιχαὴλ Βασιλέως, ... Παξιάρχης Στέφανος ... καλῶς βιώσας ἐν εἰρήνῃ ἐτελεύτησεν.] Our holy father Ignatius was the son of Emperor Michael, brother of Theophilus, and nephew of Emperor Nicephorus. Stripped of his manhood he took the monastic habit and presided over a monastery, called at that time the Archangel of the East, now Satyrus. Afterwards promoted to the patriarchate of Constantinople, he held that office eleven years and five months. Then he was expelled by Emperor Michael, and Photius, formerly a monk, was put in his place as patriarch. Then he too was expelled by Emperor Basil, and Ignatius, restored again, held the see eleven years; again he was expelled, and holy Stephen, son of Emperor Basil, became patriarch, while holy Ignatius withdrew to the monastery of Satyrus, and having lived well, rested in peace. Nor are the other things that the Greeks read in the Synaxarium different, except for a few changes; in them it must be noted in passing that, out of the author's display of truth, the order concerning the expulsion of Photius and Ignatius is told in too confused a way. For Ignatius was first expelled by Michael, Photius was substituted, and when he was removed under Basil, Ignatius was restored; and after Ignatius died, Photius was again thrust in by the same man, and at last was driven out by Leo, and banished from his country lived in exile, and Stephen succeeded the exiled Photius. But the sanctity of Ignatius is not endangered by the faults of this kind of note; it stands fixed on the deepest roots, supported also by the most lofty testimonies of others. The Sirletan Menologium, on 23 October: "On the same day the commemoration of our father Ignatius, Patriarch of Constantinople. He was a man illustrious for the splendour of his birth, but more illustrious for his life and morals; after many hardships which he suffered through the work of Photius, he rested in the Lord." Gregory the Hieromonk, in his Response to the Profession of Faith of Mark of Ephesus.

units.la: Εἰ δ᾽ ὁ Φώτιος Πατριάρχης ἀπῆν· Ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις ἐστὶ [illegible, ~20 letters] καὶ [illegible, ~25 letters] Ἰγνατίου [illegible, ~10 letters] Φωτίου [illegible, ~20 letters] ἀναθεματίζεσθαι.
units.tr: "But if Photius the Patriarch was absent: nevertheless among the saints is ... and ... Ignatius ... Photius ... to be anathematized." [Εἰ δ᾽ ὁ Φώτιος Πατριάρχης ἀπῆν· Ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις ἐστὶ ... Ἰγνατίου ... Φωτίου ... ἀναθεματίζεσθαι.]

units.la: Quod si Photius Patriarcha dixit: Sed animadvertito, Photium non esse in Sanctorum numero collocatum, licèt una insimul, & eodem tempore vixerint Photius & Ignatius. Sed hic quidem inter Sanctos adnumeratur, & vigesima tertia Octobris in Synaxariis locum habet. Photius vero nullo modo sanctitatis nomen consequutus est. Licet operæ pretium fuerit res illius gestas silentio preterire, quod in Ambone anathemati subiciantur, quæ adversus sanctum Ignatium Photiumque scriscripta sunt. Et infra eadem ingeminat, suo loco, cum de Actis Synodi Octauae contra Photium, sermonem reassumemus. Est ergo inter Sanctos, & Doctores Ecclesiae ab Ecclesia Orientali, atq; Occidentali, nec non ipsius Photij fautoribus relatus Ignatius, & æque atque alij Sancti, & Doctores Ecclesiae cultus: Photius in nulla veneratione iacet inglorius, omnium scelerum, & flagitiorum maculis notatissimus, ut ex iam dictis Graecorum eadem ætate viuentium, & eorum, qui eos secuti sunt, & tandem recentiorum testimonijs, ni caligo ob oculos obsistat, & in apertissimo lumine caecutire non vis, manifestum apparet. Esto sit per me etiam Photius callentissimus scientiarum & optimarum artium lucubrationibus deditissimus, & quidquid ad rerum cognitionem diuinarum pertinet, oculatissimus. At tu non nisi captus mente negaueris eum ipsum fuisse ingenio malo, prauoque, & ut quisquam unus de alio dixerat, animo audaci, subdolo, cuiuslibet rei simultate, ac dissimulate, alieni appetente, sui profuso, intento in cupiditatibus. Hinc quem prius induerat Monachum tanquam auspicium malum execratus, secularibus negotijs sese implicuit, & cum pessimam, ac flagitiosissimam, & tantum non, & iuuentute, & corruptissimis Principis moribus, & Bardæ fraudulentis artibus nutantem Rempublicam nimis alte concupiscens, & alienæ dignitatis capiendæ libidine inflammatus, nihil pensi habuit, quibus eam modis assequeretur. Sic in innoxium, & innocentem, & omnis culpæ exfortem machinas admouet, & dolis malis solio deiicit, illiusque sedem procurans, cum se male tutum in sede eo superante videret, per oppressionem dignitate spoliat, viuum sepelit, verberibus ad mortem cæsum, in carceres detrusum, immanissimis custodibus dedit, tandemque, ut finiam, in insulas ad conterendum relegat. Immerito ergo in maledicentiæ crimen vocas Anastasium Bibliothecarium, & Nicetam Paphlagonem, qui Photij in Ignatium tyrannidem, & nefanda illius facinora, uti gesta sunt, narrant, & ita gesta esse, ex aliis scriptoribus vna voce, & mente eadem concinentibus clarum est, ut id negare tibi tutum non sit. Pernegabis enimvero tu plane, qui ad omnia natus es, Photium similia patrantem in viros sanctissimos esse Doctorem stygium, Cacodæmonis atriensem, tortuosum draconem, magum, & necromanticum, qui Santabarenicis præstigiis Basilium Imperatorem effascinauit. Parua sunt, quæ de illo pronunciant Pontifificij . Nihil ipse in Historia Ecclesiastica Photio vidi seditiosius, nullum monstrum immanius, nullum nequiorem spadonem, cum in eo nulla fides, sed summa audacia, & caetera perfrictae frontis vitia invaluerint, & praedictionibus sanctissimorum hominum haec praemonita fuisse, non sunt Rosae, & Narcissi Iesuitici, sed res ipsa, si id narrantibus scriptoribus fides habenda est. Praedictionem ergo similem habeto tibi etiam confirmatam, non ex flosculis Iesuiticis, sed ex Graecis ipsis post Schisma dictum suum ad antiqua monumenta reportantibus. Simon Byzantius Epistola ad Ioannem Nomophylacem; Καὶ γὰρ ὁ ἅγιος Μιχαὴλ τῆς Σωμά-σδων [?] Ἐπίσκοπος [?] ὢν, εἰς ὡς τῶν τῆς πόλεως Φωτίου μητρὸς τῆς μονάςεως [?] ἐκύμονες-αν τὸν Τοῦ Τοῦ Φωτιον [?] ἐπεξεργασίας τε τῶν ἑαυτοῦ βεβαιον [?] ὡς ἂν δηλον πάλιν [?] βούλοιτο αὐτῷ, καὶ ὅπως ἦν. Εἰδὼ δὲ ὁ ταύτῃ ὑπόκτεινα [?] ἀμυνάμεθα [?], καὶ τὸ ἔμβρυον τὸ ἐν αὐτῇ. Ὁ ἐγὼ γὰρ ἄλλως Εὐαγ[?] ὄψιν ἐγκυμονεῖσαν, καὶ τὸ ἔμβρυον ἀρρεν, καὶ τῷ τῷ σὺν χωρήσαντι Θεῷ Παλαιάρχῳ εἰσ μόνον βλέπω, ὅτι ἀσθενοῦ τῷ παντοκράτορι, καὶ πῆμον σαφῶς. Καὶ αὐτὸς εἰς ἀσέβειαν ἀποκλίνει, καὶ πάντας ἐφεξῆς τῶν τῆς ἀληθείας ὁδὸν ὅτι τὰς ξίβυς καταφευγεῖ σχολαίς, καὶ τῆς καθαρᾶς πίστεως τὸ Χριστοῦ ὑποβουλιοῦ[?], καὶ εἰς σαυτὸν πάλιν καταστρέφει, καὶ καταφεύγονται τῆς ἱερᾶς κανόνων πιστοῦ, καὶ τῆς ἡμῶν ἐκκλησίας βασι-λιλείας πολλοὺς τὰς πολυξόπους αὐτῆς σεμνοῦ μηχα-νᾶς[?]. Nanque sanctus Michaël Synadorum Episcopus, cum acutissime res futuras præuideret, intuens huiusce Photij matrem, quæ in Monasterio cum aliis virginibus habitu Monastico vitam agebat, Photio grauidam, suum extendit baculum, eam percussurus, & hæc pronunciauit. Utinam adesset, qui eam, & in ea embryon interimeret. Namque alteram Euan-[?] prospicio serpente grauidam. Mascula proles est, & fœtum permissione Dei Patriarcham suturum intueor ad abolendam perquam venerandam, & pretiosam Crucem. Ipse etiam in impietatem prolabetur, & fere omnes e recta via ad distortas semitas deducet, & a pura Christi Fide aberrare faciet, & in adulterinum Crucis cultum compellet, & sacrorum Canonum contemptores efficiet, & regno Cœlorum præstigiosis suis machinis priuabit innumeros. Sed quid cæco cum speculo? Robertus Creyghtonus, licet facellarius domesticus, siue ordinarius Regis, S. Theologiæ Doctor, & sanctæ Buriana Decanus, gloriosus in vulgus honore, & titulis vir, non dum discernere didicit album & nigrum, diem & noctem, lucem & tenebras, virtutem & vitium, sanctimoniam & malitiam, integritatem & improbitatem. Nec mirum, omnia illi, siue proba siue mala sint, unum sunt. Ad id vnum deflexit similium hominum religio, vt & barbaris & Turcis, illisq; qui non dum salutari Christi lauacro abluti Christo nomen dederunt, immaniores, inconsultiores, & confidentiores sint, & non id quod fuerit, sed quod arriserit, temere atque impudenter in vulgus effutiant, & quo prodigiosiora effinxerint mendacia, eo sibi vesanius concrepent. Quare hoc in loco Creyghtono, cui mentis defectu nonnisi lingua consistit, amittenda noxa est. Quis enim illum nauigasse Anticyras non asseueraverit firmissime, cum audit, Monumentis rarioribus Photij maiorem fidem ac reuerentiâ adhibuisse, quam omnibus sancti Ignatij miraculis, aut praescriptionibus sancti Nicolai. Profecto vir iste rerum momenta proprijs oculis non introspexit, vel si introspexit, tenebris crassis circumfusus male iudicium protulit. Quare non mirum, si qui exactius introspiciunt, atq; dignoscunt, obcoecata illius dicta ludibrio habent, atque per iocum irrident. Sic de consensu vnanimi aliorum spem deponat necesse est.
units.tr: But if the Patriarch Photius said: "Take note that Photius has not been placed in the number of the Saints, although Photius and Ignatius lived together at one and the same time." Ignatius, indeed, is counted among the Saints and has a place in the Synaxaria on the twenty-third of October. Photius, however, has in no way obtained the name of holiness. It would be worth while to pass over his deeds in silence, were it not that the things written against Saint Ignatius and Photius are placed under anathema in the Ambo. The author repeats the same points further on, and at the proper place we will take up the discussion again, when we come to the Acts of the Eighth Synod against Photius. Ignatius, therefore, is among the Saints and Doctors of the Church, and is honoured by the Eastern and Western Churches, and also by the followers of Photius himself, equally with the other Saints and Doctors of the Church. Photius lies in no veneration and is without glory, most notorious for the stains of every crime and disgrace. This is plain from the testimonies of the Greeks who lived in the same age and of those who followed them, and finally of more recent writers, unless the mist stands before your eyes and you refuse to see in the clearest light. Granted, let Photius be for me also most learned in the sciences, most devoted to the labours of the best arts, and most sharp-sighted in whatever pertains to the knowledge of divine things. Yet you could not deny, unless your mind were deranged, that he was of a bad and perverse nature, and, as one man said of another, of a bold and deceitful mind, pretending and dissembling in any matter, greedy for what belongs to others, prodigal of his own, intent upon his desires. Hence he who had first put on the monk's habit, cursing it as an ill omen, involved himself in secular affairs. Since he was most eager, though the Republic was tottering under a most wicked and shameful prince, nearly a boy, and under the corrupt morals of the court and the fraudulent arts of Bardas, and was inflamed by the lust of seizing another's dignity, he thought nothing of the means by which he might attain it. Thus he brought his machinations against an innocent man, one wholly free of any fault, and by evil tricks cast him from the throne. Then, arranging for his own succession, when he saw that he was insecure in his see while Ignatius was alive, he stripped him of his dignity by oppression, buried him alive, gave him over to the most savage guards after he had been beaten nearly to death and thrust into prison, and at last, to make an end, banished him to islands to be worn down.
