Existimamus vero tuam sanctitatem non ignorare, cum prudens sit, & sapientia abundet, reliquis nostris Episcopis, vt ita teneant, persuadere, maximis difficultatibus esse inuolutum, quod rem similem in aliud atque aliud immutare, nullus ita facile poterit, licet non ante multum tempus principium suum habuerit, neque suam firmitatem multorum annorum curriculo possederit. Propterea ita visum est nobis, ne quis per nos violenter cogatur additionem deserere, quam iam in Symbolo adscriptam recitat: sed potius cum prudentia paulatim præparare, adhortantes, vt blasphemiam eiurent, Pascite enim gregem, qui in vobis est, non coacte, sed suauiter, neque ut prædominatores in clero, sed veluti exemplaria facti, Princeps Apostolorum Petrus dixit. & quæ sequuntur. Et hæc quidem ex ea Epistola sunt. Quis vero adeo ieiunus est in rebus Latinorum, ut nesciat, eos igne potius, quam rebus alijs castigare non recte sentientes? Quare non anathemate ferijt simili ratione blasphemantes? & quanam in re potius quam in depravatis dogmatibus locum habet, non prædominari in clero. Hoc siquidem Arius, & Macedonius, & eorum assecla [?] dixisse, scriptum esse, ne prædominemini clero, & omnes alij, qui recta dogmata aspernantur. Et ubi nam fuerit canon, qui decernit: Communicans separato & ipse sit separatus. Hinc manifestum est hæresim non esse appositum in divino Symbolo. Nanque si hæresis esset, qui id concinunt, anathemati subiycerentur, licet ignis condemnationem effugissent. Sed beatissimus Papa Ioannes, cum sua ipsius Synodo hoc non fecit, licet in rebus Ecclesiasticis enodandis etiam atque etiam consideratissimus esset, & ita exactus, ut Orientalem Ecclesiam, quod Anthimi nomen in diptychis apposuerit, a semetipsa Romana Ecclesia separauerit.
units.tr: But the most blessed Pope John, and the bishop Sosthenes [?] ... and the one in the ecclesiastical ... as also in the synod ... the name of Anthimus in the diptychs ... the Eastern Church ... by this Roman Church. We will also receive the Acts that are produced from Ephesus, as if they were of the Eighth Synod. Moreover, we will receive also the letter of the most holy Pope John that they cite, although it is most suspect, because that writing reproduces Greek idiom throughout and contains no characteristic of the Latin language. Undoubtedly in that synod this letter ought to have been read first of all, and afterwards Photius ought to have been received, and those things admitted that would advance him to the see of Constantinople. But this was not done. Instead, as soon as the papal legates had assembled and presented the gifts, the omophorion, the sticharion, and the sandals, Photius at once received them without any prior examination, and the gifts sent to him, as the Acts of the Synod attest, and also that saying: "May Christ our God, who wraps the heavens in clouds, and who willed to be clothed in our nature in order to restore and cleanse it, grant safe custody and holy salvation in the present life to our brother, fellow minister and spiritual father, and clothe him in the future age in the wedding garment, showing him worthy of that blessed bridal chamber." It was therefore fitting first to read the letter in the hearing of all, and to receive the written confession of the legates, and only then to admit those things that signified the restoration of the throne and the pontificate. Nevertheless we will receive that letter most willingly as ecumenical, and the letter itself. What, moreover, is contained in it? We think, however, that your holiness, since you are prudent and abound in wisdom, does not fail to know that it is a matter of the greatest difficulty to persuade our other bishops to hold thus; that no one can easily change such a thing from one thing into another, although it may not have had its beginning long ago, nor possessed its firmness through the course of many years. Therefore it has seemed good to us that no one be violently compelled by us to abandon the addition which he now recites as written in the Creed; but rather that they be prepared gradually and with prudence, exhorting them to renounce the blasphemy. "Feed the flock that is among you, not under compulsion but willingly, nor as lords over the clergy, but becoming examples," said the Prince of the Apostles, Peter, and what follows. And these things are from that letter. But who is so ignorant of the affairs of the Latins as not to know that they punish those who think incorrectly with fire rather than with other penalties? Why, then, did they not strike with anathema those who blaspheme in a similar way? And in what matter does "not lording it over the clergy" have its place rather than in corrupt doctrines? For Arius, and Macedonius, and their followers, said this, that it is written, "Do not lord it over the clergy," and all others who scorn right doctrines. And where is the canon that decrees: "Whoever communicates with one who is separated, let him also be separated"? Hence it is clear that heresy is not appended in the divine Creed. For if it were heresy, those who sing it would be subjected to anathema, even though they escaped condemnation by fire. But the most blessed Pope John, with his own synod, did not do this, although he was most carefully and repeatedly thoughtful in settling ecclesiastical matters, and so exact that, because Anthimus's name had been placed in the diptychs, he separated the Eastern Church from the Roman Church itself.

units.la: Et ut verius, ac planius loquar, ex verbis Photianæ Synodi hoc unum elicitur, non alium fuisse illius scopum, nec aliud consilium, quam privatis, & singularibus personis non licere Symbolum a Nicæno, & Constantinopolitano diversum, illique, ut ita dicam, disparile, ac dissociabile, & ex male prognata hæresi confictum Catholicis, vel ex hæresi conversis publice recitandum proponere, qua ratione Theodorum Mopsuestanum, vel etiam Nestorium fecisse cum conversis Tessarescaedecatitis, quibus erroribus scatens Symbolum tradiderant, in Ephesina Synodo euincitur, cuius verba hæc Photiana usurpat. Plena siquidem sunt Conciliorum acta, & extra Concilia Patrum, piorumque hominum scripta Professionum fidei, in quibus fere omnia, & singula inter se longissime diversa continentur, a nullo tamen in crimen vocata, quinimo in laude omnium posita: quæ vero de errore suspecta, vel male sana mente hæreticorum prolata fuere, & reiecta, & condemnata. Decretis vero, & fidei professionibus in Conciliis generalibus nomine omnium expositis, ac pronunciatis nunquam vel Synodus alia, vel quispiam cui cor saperet, sese opposuit, probri, vel criminis ea insimulando, sed veneratione prosequutus coluit, & observavit. Hinc machinæ technaeque Photianorum omnes adversus Romanam Ecclesiam ruunt, Photianæ huiusce Synodi fauor exolescit, & ementitæ inaniæ ac fraudes deprehenduntur.
units.tr: To speak more truly and plainly, from the words of the Photian Synod this one thing is drawn out: its aim and purpose was nothing other than that private and individual persons may not propose to the Catholics, or to those converted publicly from heresy, a creed different from that of Nicaea and Constantinople, unlike it and, so to speak, discordant and dissociated, and devised from a badly begotten heresy, to be recited publicly. It is shown in the Council of Ephesus that Theodore of Mopsuestia, or even Nestorius, did this with the converted Quartodecimans, to whom they had handed over a creed teeming with their errors; and the Photian Synod uses these very words. For the Acts of the Councils, and the writings of professions of faith outside the Councils, of the Fathers and pious men, are full, and in them nearly all and each of the items are contained that differ greatly from one another; yet none of them was called into accusation by anyone, but all were set in praise; whereas those things which were suspected of error, or put forward by the heretics in an unsound mind, were both rejected and condemned. Yet no other synod, nor anyone who had sense, ever opposed the decrees and professions of faith set forth and proclaimed in the general Councils in the name of all, accusing them of disgrace or crime, but rather followed and observed them with veneration. Hence all the machinations and devices of the Photians collapse against the Roman Church, the favour of this Photian synod fades, and its feigned emptiness and frauds are exposed.

units.la: CAPUT XIII. Hottingerana Disputationis Apologetica con- tra Allatium de consensu Græcæ Roma- næque Ecclesiæ sordes, atque men- dacia eluuntur.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. Hottinger's apologetic disputation against Allatius, on the agreement of the Greek and Roman Church, is cleansed of filth and lies.

units.la: DUm hæc Exercitationi extrema lineamenta adderem, & ad metam properaret oratio, en ecce ad me literæ Illustrissimi, ac Reuerendissimi Domini Ferdinandi Furstembergij Episcopi Paderbornensis, & Sacri Romani Imperij Principis, cum humanitatis sparsæ suauitate, tum in-insignes amoris notis perferuntur, vnaque cum iis Disputatio Apologetica Hottingeri contra Leonem Allatium de consensu Orientalis, & Occidentalis Ecclesiarum perpetuo. Non est quod amplius dicam, actutum attento animo lectioni me dedi, neque intermisi, donec ad exitum Disputatio illa adducta est: Quid tum? Magnopere admiratus sum hominis infantiam putidam, audaciam inconsultam, temeritatem inverecundam, & vt verbo explepleam, in rebus omnibus πανυεχίαν[?] nequissimam. Licet enim in aliis quicquam Hottingerum nosse, vel intelligere, & quod ipse non nosset, ab aliis traditum gratias agendo excipere, exceptum palam defendere, nec alia atque alia commiscendo insulse pervertere, nonnemo deputarit; attamen post huiusce Disputationis lectionem, & accuratum examen perhilum illius fortis commiferebitur.
units.tr: While I was adding the final touches to this Exercitatio and my discourse was hurrying toward its close, there arrived for me a letter from the most illustrious and reverend lord Ferdinand, Fürstenberg, Bishop of Paderborn and Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, which, with its wide-ranging courtesy and its distinct marks of affection, came together with Hottinger's Apologetic Disputation against Leo Allatius, on the perpetual agreement of the Eastern and Western Churches. I need say no more. I at once gave myself to reading it with an attentive mind, and I did not stop until that disputation was brought to its end. And what then? I was greatly astonished at the stinking puerility of the man, his unconsidered boldness, his shameless rashness and, to put it in one word, his most wicked utter carelessness [πανυεχίαν] in all matters. For although some have thought that Hottinger knows or understands something from others, and that by thanking them he takes up what he himself did not know, openly defends what he has taken, and does not foolishly distort it by mixing one thing with another, yet after reading and carefully examining this disputation, anyone will pity that man's great lack of sense.

units.la: Ille siquidem argumenta, rationesque Allatii, & allata ab eodem ex universae Ecclesiae Orientalis Doctoribus testimonia putat iam elusisse, si dicat, se observare Orientales vel reformatis per omnia accedere, vel in circumstantiis tantum variare, vel ubi Pontificiis videntur fauere partibus, illud aut ex principiis fluere Pontificiorum etiam opinione erroneis, aut φανταςιώσως[?] potius quam ὄντως, verbis, quam rebus assensum testari maiorem, atque sic non negamus Orientales Ecclesias cum Romana aliquod habere simile (difficulter obtinebunt, plura tamen nobiscum.)
units.tr: He clearly thinks he has already overthrown the arguments and reasoning of Allatius, and the testimonies brought forward by him from the teachers of the whole Eastern Church, if he says that he observes that the Orientals either agree with the Reformed in every respect, or differ only in circumstances, or, where they seem to favour the Papists, that this either flows from principles which the Papists themselves hold erroneous, or is apparent [φανταστικῶς] rather than real [ὄντως], and that by words rather than by facts they show greater assent; and so, he says, we do not deny that the Eastern Churches have some resemblance to the Roman Church (though they will hardly maintain this, yet they have more in common with us).

units.la: Et non videt Hottingerus, dum similia pronunciat, nullum se stolidius esse saxum.
units.tr: And Hottinger does not see that, in declaring such things, he proves himself to be the most stupid stone of all.

units.la: Homines in rebus eruditionis volutati, vel solum dictorum eiusmodi auditione nonne percutientur animo, & tantam subtilitatem ingenii, ne dicam stupiditatem deplorabunt? Nunc etiam ipse comprehendo mente memori diuinum illud eloquium non contradices veritati, & de mendacio ineruditionis tuæ confundere. Ipse tamen tua non omnia spectabo: neque enim mihi tantum otij est vniuersas tuas ineptias, ac deliramenta pellere, & ἀνηφλυαρῶν[?], quod æque atque anguem auersor. Verùntamen tuo etiam arbitratu Hottingere, quoniam ita conceßum est, licet non fit tui stomachi, de nonnullis responsionem ineam. Sed antequam aggrediar, ad ea, quæ disputanda sunt, ex te ipse sciscitor.
units.tr: Men who are steeped in learning, will they not be struck in mind merely by hearing such statements, and will they not lament such a small subtlety of wit, not to say stupidity? Now I too bear in mind that divine saying: Do not contradict the truth, and be ashamed of your ignorance. Yet I shall not look into all your points: I have not so much leisure as to drive away all your silliness and ravings, and to talk nonsense, which I shun just as I would a snake. Nevertheless, Hottinger, since it has been granted by your own judgement, although it does not sit well with your temper, I will make a reply to some points. But before I begin, I will question you about what is to be disputed.

units.la: Quæ vis, aut necessitas, aut amentia, quæ festinatio, quæ immaturitas tanta te compulit, vt mora remota inconsideratissime responsionem ad obiecta Allatij præcipitares? Næ tu inconsulte procedere visus es, & famæ tuæ parum consuluisse: Poteras in aliud tempus rem differendo dexterius vti fortuna tua, & per decennium, & si in animo erat, etiam longiori tempore cogitationes percoquendo solidius aliquid comminisci, tum denique in Allatium vti iam fecisti, maledicentiæ, & malignitatis tela, & si quid his est acerbius, retorquere. Sed effrænis malæ mentis impetus in rabiem versus in longiora tempora extrahere non permisit. Hinc factum est, vt subuersis cogitationibus non quæ debebas, sed quæ celeriritas ipsa, & mixta cum rabie inconsiderantia suggerebant, sed [illegible, ~9 letters] omnia effudisti, & canis properans cœcos genuisti catulos. Sicque, vt video, maiorem differtationis tuæ partem ad astruendum inter Græcos, & Latinos dissidium, hinc inde ex varijs auctoribus Latinis, Græcis, Orientalibus, etiam Pontificijs, recentioribus quoque Romanensibus, Allatio [illegible, ~8 letters], & alijs vndique cogis, & auxilia comparas, in quibus magnum quid tibi polliceris, cum posthinc ad obiecta tibi ab Allatio deuolas, vel non respondens, vel in alia atque alia intempestiue subsultans, & nihil ad rem afferens, ita vt vbi ratio, & verba opus sunt, mutus atque elinguis deprehendaris. Quamuis modice me similia tangant, attamen vt tua nunc recens dicta priori congressu omnes noscant, habeto tibi quas infra scripsi notulas, cogor siquidem respondere stulto iuxta stultitiam suam, sed non stulte.
units.tr: What force, or necessity, or madness, what haste, what great immaturity compelled you, with all thought of delay set aside, to hurry in the most thoughtless way into a reply to the objections of Allatius? Indeed you seem to have proceeded rashly, and to have taken little care for your reputation. You could have deferred the matter to another time, used your fortune more skilfully, and for a decade, or even longer if you had intended it, have thought things over and devised something more solid; then at last you might have hurled back at Allatius the weapons of slander and malice, and anything even more bitter than these, as you have now done. But the unbridled impulse of an evil mind, turning to rage, did not allow you to draw it out over a longer time. Hence it came about that, with your thoughts in disorder, you poured out everything, not what you ought to have, but what mere haste and recklessness mixed with rage suggested, [illegible, ~9 letters], and, like a dog hurrying, you have borne blind puppies. And so, as I see, you gather and assemble the greater part of your dissertation, to establish a split between the Greeks and the Latins, from various authors on all sides, Latin, Greek, Oriental, even Papist, and recent Roman writers too, [illegible, ~8 letters] against Allatius and others; and in these you promise yourself something great. Yet afterwards you fly off to the objections raised against you by Allatius, either not answering them, or leaping out at other and irrelevant points at the wrong time, bringing nothing to the matter; so that where reason and words are needed, you are caught dumb and tongue-tied. Although such things touch me only slightly, nevertheless, so that everyone may know your recent statements from our earlier encounter, take the notes I have written below. For I am compelled to answer a fool according to his folly, but not foolishly.

units.la: Leo Allatius Roma a Pontifice Romano huc ablegatus eam Bibliothecam diripuit. Bibliothecam Palatinam, & multitudine manuscriptorum Codicum tum Græcorum, tum Latinorum, aliarumque etiam linguarum, & singularium Codicum copia fuisse celeberrimam, non nego. Eam tamen a milite Bauaro spolium factam, Maximilianus tum Bauariæ Dux trophæum misit Gregorio XV. Pontifici Maximo, qui ad eam auehendam Leonem transmisit, & Leo bona fide iussis obtemperans per hyemem, & per medios hostes, Vrbem Heidelbergam non sine discrimine, & vitæ alea penetrans conseruatam a milite Tillio, & Henrico de Metternich, sibique traditam, impensis Pontificijs integram, ne minima quidem illius chartula deperdita, Romam inuexit in Vaticanam, in qua nunc perhonorifice custoditur vniuscuiusque commoditati, sicuti & Vaticana ipsa. Et hoc est Bibliothecam diripuisse Allatium? Nonne vides Lector, Hottingerum innata sibi vecordia maligni improbique viri officio fungi?
units.tr: Leo Allatius, sent here from Rome by the Roman Pontiff, plundered that library. That the Palatine Library was very famous for the great number of its manuscript codices, both Greek and Latin, and also in other languages, and for the richness of its single codices, I do not deny. Yet when it had been made booty by a Bavarian soldier, Maximilian, then Duke of Bavaria, sent it as a trophy to Gregory XV, the Supreme Pontiff, who sent Leo to carry it away. Leo, obeying the orders in good faith, through the winter and through the midst of enemies, not without danger and staking his life, came into the city of Heidelberg, which had been preserved by the soldier Tilly and by Henry of Metternich and handed over to him. At Papal expense, with not even the smallest scrap of its paper lost, he brought it to Rome to the Vatican, where it is now most honourably kept for the use of everyone, just as the Vatican itself is. And is this what Allatius's plundering of the library amounts to? Do you not see, reader, that Hottinger is performing the duty of a wicked and dishonest man, by the madness innate in him?

units.la: Plane ut Herostratus ex incendio Ephesino.
units.tr: Just as Herostratus did with the burning of Ephesus.

units.la: Nepacatam[?] quidem nequitiam Hottingeri quis ferre posset? quid Leoni cum Herostrato? Ille volens, & gloriæ cupidus infami scelere se commaculauit: Leo datam a vero possessore, & a Domino sibi rem traditam ad deportandam conuexit. Herostratus in Maiestatem diuinam iniurius templum exussit, Allatius ex hostium manibus illa abutentium, ereptum thesaurum ad piorum manus detulit, qui commodis Ecclesiæ deseruiunt. Sed esto, Diripui. Annon item Allatij ea maxima laus est, qui collegatus consociatusque cum Duce Bauaro Heidelbergam diripuit, Bibliothecam expiliauit, & vna secum Romam induxit? Sed haec minima laus Bauaro est, qui Leonis ad diripiendam Bibliothecam ope indiguit, illiusque auxilio tantum opus perpetrauit; & tum non vt Herostratus ex incendio Ephesino infamiam, sed laudem Leo captasset.
units.tr: Who could bear the sheer wickedness of Hottinger? What has Leo to do with Herostratus? The one, eager for glory, stained himself with an infamous crime; Leo carried off a treasure entrusted to him by its true owner and handed to him by his Lord, to be taken away. Herostratus, acting outrageously against the divine majesty, burned down a temple. Allatius took those treasures, seized from the hands of enemies who misused them, and brought them into the hands of the pious, who serve the advantage of the Church. But grant it: "He plundered." Is it not likewise the greatest praise of Allatius that he, allied and joined with the Duke of Bavaria, plundered Heidelberg, stripped the library, and brought it with him to Rome? Yet this is only a minor credit to Bavaria, who needed Leo's help to plunder the library and accomplished so great a work only with his aid. And then Leo would have sought not infamy, as Herostratus did with the burning of Ephesus, but praise.

units.la: Sed eandem in perniciem causae reformatae Religionis conuertere coepit. Quomodo ipse Bibliothecam illam in perniciem Reformatae Religionis conuerterim, non dum capio. Si intelligit, me illius Codicibus usum, & eorum dictis, ac testimonijs Reformatorum causam confutasse, & illius patronos, & praecipue Hottingeri saltum[?], & fraudes libris meis editis fregisse, mihi gratulor, iam assecutus, quod tamdiu desideraueram; & cum in eodem proposito sim, continuo illos evoluam, ut Reformatae causae pernicies atq; alastor sim. Sed, ne sis nescius Hottingere, Codices omnes Palatinos, quemadmodum & Vaticanos Allatius singulis fere diebus, omnibus omnium generum hominibus, aeque ac si expositi essent, a mane usque ad meridiem foribus apertis eorundem Custos primarius a Summo Pontifice Alexandro VII., quo nomine nemo sanctior, neque probior, neque in omnibus officijs retinendis diligentior esse potest, constitutus promptos tenet, voluntati locum interuisentium obsecuturus, & desiderio, curiositatique responsurus. Nullus hinc excluditur, nulli prohibetur aditus, nullius conatus interrumpitur. Tanta est in adiuuandis literatorum studijs summi Pontificis munificentia. Non credis? Rogita tuos omnes, etiam ex Reformata religione, qui Romam venere, a quibus plane disces & humanitatem, qua excepti sunt, & promptitudinem in porrigendis voluminibus, & obsequia in ministrando, & solicitudinem, vt eis ex sententia satis sint. Longum tibi catalogum texerem, si eorum nomina animus esset referre. Improbe igitur perniciem causæ Deformatæ, Reformatæ volui dicere, Religionis deploras. Porro illud quoque velim animaduertas, ex Palatinis illis Codicibus multa erbi[?] literato obtrusse, quæ tua sunt, illorum Codicum nullum unquam usum Allatio suisse. Nihil enim in illis est alicuius momenti, quod non in Vaticana melius, & speciosius eniteat. Et vt securius posthac verba profundas, & cesses dare sonum sine mente: si Heidelbergensis cum Romana comparetur, Heidelbergensis nulla prorsus iudicabitur. Romana siquidem ad illam collata, & quantitate, & qualitate multo Heidelbergenfi superior est. Romana numerat solum Græca volumina supra duo millia, Heidelbergensis quadringentorum numerum non explet, vt nihil dicam de Codicibus Orientalium Linguarum. Sed quidquid sit de hoc, age Hottingere, si quid est, quod tibi dubitationem moueat, vel suspectam fidem diuerberet, quare vel præteritum aliquod verbum, vel ambigue positum, vel sententiam immutatam suspicaris, signato locum Auctoris, conceptis a te verbis iusiurandum do, & sincera fide polliceor, me ex autographo, etiam si Vaticanum est, verba, & sententiam, vt in illo concepta sunt, integra, & incorrupta daturum, vt in illa inquirere possis; ne exemplarium absentia peiorem Reformatorum causam efficias.
units.tr: But he has begun to turn it to the ruin of the cause of the reformed religion. I do not yet grasp how I have turned that library to the ruin of the reformed religion. If he means that I used its codices and their sayings and testimonies to refute the cause of the Reformers, and that in my published books I broke the defenders of that cause, and especially Hottinger's leaps and frauds, I congratulate myself, since I have already achieved what I had long desired; and since I remain of the same purpose, I shall keep unrolling them, so that I may be the bane and pest of the reformed cause. But, lest you be ignorant, Hottinger, the Chief Keeper of all the Palatine codices, as also of the Vatican ones, which Allatius holds ready almost every day, open to every kind of person, as if they were on display, from morning until midday with the doors open, appointed by Pope Alexander VII (than whom no one can be holier, more upright, or more diligent in keeping all his duties), is ready to comply with the wishes of those who visit and to satisfy their desire and curiosity. No one is shut out from here, no one is denied access, no one's effort is interrupted. Such is the generosity of the Supreme Pontiff in supporting the studies of scholars. Do you not believe it? Ask all your own people, even from the reformed religion, who have come to Rome; from them you will learn plainly both the courtesy with which they were received, the readiness in handing over volumes, the services in attending to them, and the care that they had all they wanted. I would weave you a long catalogue if I had the mind to recount their names. So you wickedly deplore the ruin of the cause of the Reformed religion, which I wished to call the ruin of the deformed cause. Furthermore, I would also have you note this: you have foisted many of your own words word for word upon the literal text of those Palatine codices, and Allatius never made any use of those codices at all. For nothing in them is of any importance that does not shine more fully and splendidly in the Vatican. And so that you may in future pour out words more carefully and stop giving sound without sense: if the Heidelberg collection is compared with the Roman, the Heidelberg one will be judged to be nothing at all. For the Roman, compared with that one, surpasses it by far both in quantity and in quality. The Roman holds more than two thousand Greek volumes alone, while Heidelberg does not reach four hundred, not to mention the codices of the Oriental languages. But whatever the case, come now, Hottinger: if there is anything that troubles you with doubt, or casts suspicion on the faithfulness of the text, whether you suspect some word omitted, or ambiguously placed, or the sense altered, mark the place of the author, set down the words in your own hand, and I give my oath and promise in good faith that I will supply the words and sense, exactly as they stand, whole and uncorrupted, from the autograph, even if it is in the Vatican, so that you may examine it there; lest by the absence of the copies you make the cause of the Reformers worse.

units.la: Quod postmodum addis, multa obtrusisse maiori astu, quam successu, hoc vero ex tua nequitia est, qui damnas quod non intelligis, & de fraude arguis quod non vidisti, & sola tui asseueratione vis ita rem se habere, vt tu oscitanter consomnias. Nihil enim de veritate inde decedit, sed Speciosum tantum mendacio schema inducitur. De Catholica veritate verum est: de Deformata falsum; donec rationibus, & auctoritatibus ab Allatio productis respondendo non satisfeceris, & verbis solummodo aërem diuerberandi intercapedinem posueris. Sed agnosco vulpeculae ingenium. Testimonia ab Allatio ex Græcæ Ecclesiæ Doctoribus, Patribus, Ritualibus, & Schismaticorum contra Ecclesiam Romanam scriptis prolata, quæ Græci ipsi non negabunt, adeo clara, & manifesta sunt, vt Hottingerus, etiam si medius dirumpatur, ea infirmare, & eorum fidem præcidere nequeat, & cum rationes, quibus contrarium stabiliat, in promptu non habeat, satius duxit ignorantiam suam absentia librorum, & Bibliothecæ direptione obtegere, quam culpam fateri. Hoc persæpe facis Hottingere, vt cum in aliquod Leonis incideris, quod diluere non valeas, vel reprehensionem effugere potis non es, aliquod afferas, quod omnino ne fieri quidem possit; vt satius fuerit id ipsum, de quo ambigebatur, concedere, quam tam impudenter resistere.
units.tr: As for what you add afterward, that he foisted many things "with greater cunning than success," this indeed comes from your own wickedness: you condemn what you do not understand, accuse of fraud what you have not seen, and by your mere assertion you want things to stand as you drowsily dream them. For nothing is taken away from the truth by this, but only a specious appearance is brought in by a lie. That is true of the Catholic truth; of the deformed cause it is false, until you answer the arguments and authorities adduced by Allatius, and not merely set a gap in the air by beating it with words. But I recognize the fox's nature. The testimonies that Allatius has brought forward from the teachers, Fathers, and ritual writers of the Greek Church, and from the writings of the schismatics against the Roman Church, which the Greeks themselves will not deny, are so clear and manifest that Hottinger, even if he burst in the middle, cannot weaken them or cut off their credit. And since he has no arguments ready with which to establish the opposite, he has thought it better to cover his ignorance by the absence of books and the plundering of the library than to confess his fault. You do this very often, Hottinger: when you have run into some point of Leo's that you cannot dilute, nor escape reproof, you put forward something that could not possibly be done at all, so that it would have been better simply to concede the very point in question than to resist so shamelessly.

units.la: Tale eius scriptum est de perpetua consensione Occidentalis, & Orientalis Ecclesiæ, Βιβλίον μέγα, ἥτοι[?] κακόν. Non dum Disputationem exorsus es, & quam decreuisti viam ingredi non persequeris, & dum a mente consilioque deducto[?] conaris scribere, imprudens villam præterijsti: nil mirum itaque, si tibi magnus liber in κακὸν μέγα euaserit, qui, quis sit magnus liber, vel paruus, in comperto non habes; sed tantum ex chartis quantitatem illius pendis. Rei grauitas passa non est, vt liber coarctioribus terminis restringeretur, hinc molimine suo ingens euasit. Annon ista tua Disputatio quatuor tantum foliorum quaternionibus expansa, cum nihil boni in se contineat, perniciosius malum est?
units.tr: Such is his writing on the perpetual agreement of the Western and Eastern Church: Βιβλίον μέγα, ἥτοι κακόν [Great Book, that is, Evil]. You have not yet begun your disputation, and you do not pursue the path you had decided to follow; while you try to write from a mind and plan that has been led astray, you have unwittingly passed over the village. It is no wonder, then, if your great book has turned out to be a great evil [κακὸν μέγα]. You do not even know whether it is a great book or a small one; you judge its size only by the amount of paper. The gravity of the subject did not allow the book to be confined within narrower limits, and so by its own effort it became huge. Is your disputation, spread out in just four quires of leaves, and containing nothing good in itself, not rather a more pernicious evil?

units.la: Ambabus manibus ceu Apollinis Oraculum exceperunt. Quomodo liber meus de perpetua consensione exceptus sit, clarum testatumque est in libris clarissimorum hominum post illum passim peruulgatis, interque eos literis datis receptisque, in quibus perhonorifica cum Scriptoris, tum argumenti laus conspicitur, quam Auctor facit vel maximi, sicuti contra Hottingeri nihilum æstimat, cum semper magni fecerit, a magnis laudatisque viris laudari, non a sciolis, & impudentibus.
units.tr: They received it with both hands, as though it were an oracle of Apollo. How my book on the perpetual agreement was received is clear and attested in the books of most distinguished men, published widely since then, and among the letters given and received by them, in which the highest praise, both for the writer and for the subject, is seen; the author thinks very highly of it himself, just as he sets little store by Hottinger's praise, since he has always valued being praised by great and renowned men, not by smatterers and shameless people.

units.la: Utque illis potius sit succensendum librorum censoribus, qui etiam Romae talia edi, atque ipsi Papae Alexandro offerri patiuntur, & approbant, cum tamen sint coniuncta cum Pontificiae sedis, & vniuersae Romanae Ecclesiae summo dedecore. Succensendum potius tibi fuerit, qui non vereris quasi superior Iudex, legem censoribus Romanis ponere, qua ratione debeant libros examinare, quae probare, quæ reprobare, hominibus in doctrinis versatissimis, omnium scientiarum genere spectatissimis, in hoc negotio multum & in aliis etiam causis exercitatissimis. Voluptati interim mihi est, si tamen mente constans loqueris, Alexandrum Papam agnoscere, & eum nunquam passurum, ut improba sibi offerantur. Cum ergo ille bona atque probatissima excipiat, mala & quæ coniuncta sunt cum Pontificiæ sedis, & universæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ summo dedecore reiiciat, & oblatus illi Hottingerus frau-dis, & manifesta impostura convictus, approbantibus Romanis Censoribus, nec ab Alexandro Papa reiectus, sed humanissime exceptus fuerit, argumentare, Allatii Hottingerus celebrandus venit, & ea, quæ in ipso continentur, non sunt coniuncta cum Pontificiæ sedis, & universæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ summo dedecore. Infans es Hottingere, si credis, Ecclesiam Romanam dedecus sibi procurasse, & semel, atque iterum, & sæpius, & anxie quod sibi inhonorum esset, quæsiuisse. Studia Ecclesiæ Romanæ ad devincendos sibi Græcorum animos, & ad unionem convellendos, quæ vel pueri sciunt, tu solus ignoras. Recentioris, & antiquioris historiæ monumenta similis curæ, & sollicitudinis Romanorum Pontificum plena sunt. Quare cum Censorum Romanae Curiae tam sanctam, atque sollemnem dignitatem comminuere tentas, eam in summo loco ponis, & Allatium repugnante natura celebras, & temetipsum incaute, ut alias saepe facis, sine iudicio & modo vituperas.
units.tr: And so the censors of books, who allow such things to be published even at Rome and offered to Pope Alexander himself, and approve them, should rather be angry with them, since these things are linked with the great disgrace of the Papal See and of the whole Roman Church. Rather, you should be angry, who, as though you were a superior judge, do not hesitate to set a law for the Roman censors, by what method they ought to examine books, what to approve and what to reject, men most versed in doctrines, most highly regarded in every branch of learning, and very practised in this business, and in other matters too. Meanwhile it gives me pleasure, if indeed you speak with a consistent mind, to acknowledge Pope Alexander, and that he will never allow wicked things to be offered to him. Since he therefore accepts good and most approved works, and rejects bad ones and those linked with the great disgrace of the Papal See and of the whole Roman Church, and since Hottinger, convicted of fraud and manifest imposture, was offered to him, and was not rejected by Pope Alexander, with the Roman censors approving, but was most courteously received, argue, then, that Hottinger ought to be praised as an Allatius, and that what is contained in it is not linked with the great disgrace of the Papal See and of the whole Roman Church. You are a child, Hottinger, if you believe that the Roman Church has brought disgrace upon itself, and has sought once, twice, and often, and anxiously, what would be dishonourable for it. The efforts of the Roman Church to win over the minds of the Greeks to itself, and to overturn their unity, which even children know about, you alone do not know. The records of both recent and older history are full of the same care and concern of the Roman Pontiffs. Therefore, when you try to diminish the so holy and solemn dignity of the censors of the Roman Curia, you place it in the highest position, and you praise Allatius against your own nature, and rashly, as you often do elsewhere, you disparage yourself without judgment or measure.

units.la: Propterea quod repugnante Oriente, & Occidente reclamante experientia, dissentientibus primis, medijs, & postremis Ecclesiae Romanae Doctoribus perpetuum sustineret Ecclesiarum Occidentalis, & Orientalis consensum. Hoc probandum erat, non temere effutiendum. Quos tu hic adducis ad peruincendum diffidium inter Ecclesiam Graecam, & Pontificios, eos multo ante Allatius in libris de consensione, & alibi saepius laudauit: neq; enim illum fugit, & Orientales, & Occidentales multa de dissidio, & studio in partes diducto in eorum monumentis decertasse. Sed hoc extra consilium Allatij est, qui non ex corrupti iudicij falsis rumoribus, sed ex ijs, qui legem sibimetipsis indixerunt, innocentiae, integritatis, & ab alijs eandem rationem vitae reposcunt, nec non ex libris ipsis Graecorum Ecclesiasticis, qui non mentiuntur, quia causa cur mentiantur non est, sed rem uti est, ex oraculo denarrant; & quando iam Sectarijs ita com-plaplacitum est, Pontificiorum testimonia vti suspecta reijcientibus ex Papomastigū scriptis, qui tempore schismatis ab eisdem schismatis patronis clarissimi, atq; eloquentissimi habiti sunt, ne asperior atq; inhumanior in te tuosque videretur, verba eorum referens, atque examinans dissidium[?] convellere nixus est, quod conspicere poteras in Hottingero fraudis, & impostura manifesto, qui ex aduersarijs Pontificiorum regimen ipsum Pontificiorum probari contendit, & ad hoc stabiliendum tum ipse, tum illi similes Patres Græcos, & Latinos reijciunt. nouum, ac vetus fœdus, & verbum ipsum diuinum repudiant, cum testes ipsi, quos exoptant, non loquantur, sed verba ineptissime funditent[?], vt aliquid dicere possint argutius, tamen eorum vti Ecclesiæ Romanæ perditissimorum hostium testimonia reiectamus. Tuum erat Hottingere tuorum testium dictorum factorumque constantiam tueri ad hoc, vt producti in iudicium fidem facerent, quando meos iam respuis. Non enim hic vi, non scelere, non latrocinio, non denique omnibus potius, quam iure, quam officio, quam pudore res discutitur.
units.tr: Because, with the East opposing and the experience of the West protesting, and with the first, middle and last teachers of the Roman Church disagreeing, he maintained a perpetual consensus of the Western and Eastern Churches. This was to be proved, not blurted out carelessly. The witnesses you bring forward to overturn the division between the Greek Church and the Papists, Allatius praised long before, in his books on the consensus and elsewhere, and often. For it did not escape him that both Easterners and Westerners have wrangled much, in their own records, about the division and about the factions that split them. But this lies outside Allatius's purpose. He did not draw on the false rumours of a corrupt judgement, but on those who have laid down a law for themselves, who demand innocence and integrity of others, and who take the same rule of life; nor did he draw only on the Greek ecclesiastical books themselves, which do not lie, since there is no reason for them to lie, and which report the matter as it is, as from an oracle. Since the sectaries have now been pleased to reject the testimonies of the Papists as suspect, and to rely on the writings of the Papomastix, who at the time of the schism were held by the patrons of the schism to be most famous and most eloquent, Hottinger, so as not to seem harsher or less civil toward you and yours, has tried to overturn the division by quoting and examining their words. In this you could see Hottinger's fraud and imposture plainly. He strove to prove from the adversaries of the Papists the very government of the Papists, and to establish this both he and men like him reject the Greek and Latin Fathers. They repudiate the New and Old Covenant and the divine Word itself, since the witnesses they desire do not speak, but pour out words most inanely, so that they may say something more subtly; yet we reject the testimonies of these men, the most desperate enemies of the Roman Church. It was your duty, Hottinger, to defend the consistency of the sayings and deeds of your own witnesses, so that, having been produced in court, they might give credit, since you now spurn mine. For here the matter is not being decided by force, by crime, by robbery, or finally by everything rather than by right, duty and shame.

units.la: & quando de rebus Græcis, & potissimum Ecclesiasticis agendum erat, & laudatos ab Allatio non excipiebas hilaris, quare non nonominatim prosecutus es tuos? Si meliori mente audisses hæc mea, multis plane incommodis a te tuisque debilitata veritas tandem aliqua ratione recreata fuisset. Sed hic teneo te: noluisti immanissima, ac foedissima monstra conclamare. Sed antequam ulterius progrediar, quando jam hic fumus, & de testibus constitutum est, quædam alia statuenda sunt, in quibus conveniendum est inter nos, quæ ipse si fateris, conatum iracundiæ tuæ, ut decet virum bonum, fedasti; si negas, stulto stultior es, & insigniter improbus. Primum erit, Græcos Conciliorum, Græcorum sanctorum dicta, eaque quæ in Ritualibus libris suis legunt, dummodo non sint recentiorum nebulonum assumenta, post divina eloquia venerari, eorumque auctoritati firmam fidem tribuere προπαρασκευαστὰς[?] edocti sunt; eorumque insistentes institutis, prout illis suggeritur, proni atque morigeri multa discunt, atque dediscunt. Secundum tum veram unionem, atque consensum inter duos intercedere dici, cum uno ore consentiunt, & una mente unum, idemque comprobant, improbantque, nec inter eos voluntatum altercatio est. Temere enim uniri sententijs dicentur, qui rem eandem ijsdem, vel alijs idem tamen valentibus verbis non exprimit. Quare vbi Ecclesiæ Orientalis, atque Occidentalis eadem verba deprehendimus, eandem quoque sententiam concinere dicemus. Tertium, ritum, & cæremoniarum diuersitatem, siue quæ ex hominum arbitrio pendent, nullum inferre dissidium, neque vtentes illis alio, atque alio modo, in partes deduci: quod aliter fit de dogmate, quod cum non innitatur institutis humanis, sed decreto diuino, semper firmum, atque immutabile est; ideo scindit in factiones, & pietatem atque religionem in Deum dissoluit, & quæ antea vnum erant, in diuersa studia concisa, diuersam quoque religionem ingenerant. Hinc fit, vt in Pontificio dominatu, licet vnum regimen sit, vnaque Ecclesia, attamen in ea recitandi officij diuersus ordo non vnus apud omnes est, & quod magis est, in eadem ciuitate a diuersis religiosorum communibus diuersis, atque interstinctis tenoribus variatur. Imo in eodem ipso Ecclesiæ Romanæ foro, ne extra cancellos, quos mihi ipse circumdedi, egredi videar, Breuiarium Romanum ex decreto sacrosancti Concilij restitutum, & Pij V. summi Pontificis iussu publicatum, multis additis vel detractis correctisque a subsequentibus Pontificibus semel atq; iterum luci datum, nunnunquam ex Ecclesiasticorum manibus deponitur. Quod idem in Græcorum Ecclesia locum habuit, postquam ab antiquissimis Patribus omnibus suis numeris, & partibus absoluta officia in communionem Christianorum venere, & potissimum post Theodori Studitæ tempora non tantum in Hierosolymitana Ecclesia, a qua videtur prima commutatio facta, ut ex Dissertatione mea de Libris Ecclesiasticis Græcorum plene potest intelligi, sed in aliis etiam Patriarchiis immutata sunt adeo, ut aliud atq; aliud officium scioli non vereantur afferere: & ut compressione rerum brevis sim, percurre, si tibi commodum fuit Librum, quem Græci vocant Typicon, in quo singulis diebus recitandi officii modus præscribitur. In eo siquidem longissime inter se diversum recitandi officii ordinem deprehendes, & illius ope ex his turbis te expedies.
units.tr: And since the question concerned Greek matters, and especially ecclesiastical ones, and you did not receive cheerfully the men praised by Allatius, why did you not follow up your own by name? If you had heard my words with a better mind, the truth, weakened by many plain disadvantages from you and yours, would at last have been restored by some means. But here I have you: you did not want to cry out against the most monstrous and foul portents. Yet before I proceed further, since the smoke is now here and the question of witnesses has been settled, certain other points must be laid down on which we must agree. If you admit them, you have, as a good man should, sullied the attempt of your anger; if you deny them, you are more foolish than a fool and notoriously wicked. First: the Greeks are taught to venerate, after the divine oracles, the decisions of the Councils, the sayings of the Greek saints, and whatever they read in their Ritual books, provided these are not additions of more recent scoundrels; and to grant firm faith to their authority. They are eager and compliant, following their institutions as these are presented to them, and they learn and unlearn much. Second: a true union and consent is said to exist between two parties when they agree with one voice and in one mind, approve and disapprove the same things, and there is no quarrel of wills between them. For those would be said to be rashly united in opinion who do not express the same thing in the same words, or in other words of the same force. Therefore, where we find the same words in the Eastern and Western Churches, we shall say that the same opinion also agrees. Third: a diversity of rites and ceremonies, whether they depend on human judgement, brings in no division, and those who use them in one way or another are not divided into parties. It is otherwise with dogma, which, since it does not rest on human institutions but on the divine decree, is always firm and unchangeable; therefore it splits into factions, dissolves piety and religion toward God, and what was previously one, cut into diverse pursuits, also engenders a diverse religion. Hence it comes about that under Papist domination, although there is one government and one Church, yet the order of reciting the office is not one among all, and what is more, in the same city it varies among the different communities of religious orders, with differing and distinct tones. Indeed, in that very forum of the Roman Church, so that I may not seem to leave the bounds I have set myself, the Roman Breviary, restored by decree of the most sacred Council and published by order of Pius V, the supreme Pontiff, after many things were added, removed or corrected by later Popes, and brought to light once and again, is sometimes taken out of the hands of the clergy. The same has happened in the Greek Church: after all the offices were completed by the most ancient Fathers in all their numbers and parts and came into the communion of Christians, and especially after the time of Theodore the Studite, changes were made not only in the Church of Jerusalem, where the first alteration seems to have been made, as can be fully understood from my Dissertation on the Ecclesiastical Books of the Greeks, but also in the other patriarchates, so much so that smatterers do not hesitate to assert one office after another. And to be brief in summarising, run through, if it was convenient for you, the book the Greeks call the Typicon, in which the manner of reciting the office for each day is prescribed. In it you will find the order of reciting the office differing widely from one place to another, and by its help you will extricate yourself from these confusions.

units.la: Et ut plenius hoc quoque pateat. In Legibus ab Imperatoribus præscriptis hanc quoque immutationem prævaluisse ex dictis doctorum hominum, & Novellis novis antiquum usum obliterantibus percipi potest .. Cum enim leges ad commodum Reipublicæ referantur, & ad utilitatem civium, ex eiusdem commodo, atq; utilitate ponderantur. & cum quod hodie commodum cadit, & plurimum prodest urbibus, varijs rerum obortis euentibus in perniciem vertitur & contra, factum est, ut lex quae modo Reipublicae seruiebat, uti noxia repudietur, & in aliam nouo exemplo factam infundatur. eandem subiere fortunam ritus, & consuetudines Ecclesiasticae. Cum enim illae sint de iure, quod dicitur positiuum, nec dogma respiciant, qua ratione nec eædem apud omnes, sed pro qualitate gentium, & Ecclesiarum distinguantur, & varient, ita nouis semper emergentibus causis pro nutu Pontificum alias, atque alias formas induunt, neque propterea qui illis seruiunt, licet dispares sint, dicuntur animis, atque voluntatibus dissociari, sed in una Ecclesia coniungi. & tum dissidium nullum est, aut si quando fuerit, non apparet, illud dedita opera esse quaesitum. Quod aliter de dogmate, vel de iis, quae ad dogmata pertinent, usu venit. tum siquidem vel minima sententiarum variatio maximam voluntatum atque animorum dissimilitudinem infert, & unus alium uti sibi refragantem condemnat, fugat, tandemque perdere nititur. Hinc concluditur, sicuti qui variant in dogmate, & pugnant sententijs, unionem non astruunt, ita cum eadem dicunt, & sentiunt unionem in-cocolumem & integram firmant.
units.tr: And that this may be made clearer still: that this change also prevailed in the laws prescribed by the emperors can be perceived from the sayings of learned men and from the new Novels that blot out ancient usage. For since laws are referred to the advantage of the commonwealth and weighed by its advantage and utility to the citizens, and since what today falls out as advantageous and greatly benefits cities is turned to ruin when various events arise, and conversely, it has come about that a law which once served the commonwealth is rejected as harmful and replaced by another made on a new model. The rites and customs of the Church have undergone the same fate. For since these belong to what is called positive law and do not touch dogma, they are distinguished and vary, not identically among all, but according to the character of peoples and churches; and so, as new causes always emerge, they take on different forms at the will of the Popes. Nor, for that reason, are those who serve them, although unlike one another, said to be divided in minds and wills, but are joined in one Church. Then there is no division, or if there ever is one, it does not appear, and it has not been sought on purpose. It is otherwise with dogma, or with what pertains to dogma. For then even the smallest variation of opinion brings the greatest dissimilarity of wills and minds, and one condemns and drives out the other as opposing him, and at last strives to destroy him. Hence it is concluded that, just as those who vary in dogma and clash in opinions do not establish union, so those who say and think the same things affirm union intact and whole.

units.la: His positis Hottingere, quae indubitata apud omnes sunt, Allatius, ut probaret unionem, dicta Graecorum, & Latinorum una inter se contulit in libris de Consensione, & in illis continuatam constantiam a principio Ecclesiasticae Hierarchiae eorundem testimoniis fultam ad haec tempora demonstrauit. Id tibi, tuisque indoluit, neque enim abalienati animo ab Ecclesia Romana ad Graecam, quasi illi repugnantem, effugere valetis. Ideoque temeritatis Allatium detulisti, & ne absque ratione id facere videreris, Capita illa tua ad probandum dissidium concinnasti, & magis probans fidem tuam aphoristice. Sed quo fructu? Jam qui lumine mentis destituti non sunt, vident, & iudicant, te certe quid sit dissidium, & quid unio, plane incompertum habere. Illis numeratis Allatius, & meditate discussis, quam in eo temeritatem arguebas, in te detorsit, & adductis ex ritualibus libris Graecorum testimoniis, quae illi non negant, si sapiunt, & quod magis est, ex Schismaticis ipsis Capita illa tua non dissensionem cum Ecclesia Romana, sed unionem per singula luce clarius, & causam suam te iudice superiorem esse probauit, cum Hottingerus fraudis, atque imimpostura manifestæ convictus prodijt. propterea que ut videreris aliquid egisse, rursus versus in rabiem, non considerans quid in Allatium dicere poteras, præcipitando dicta sententiasque tuas, quas furor propinabat, præproperanter, turbulenteq; istam tuam Disputationem Apologeticam proiecisti. Non ergo mirum est, si non respondes ad argumenta Allatij, sed ea aliorum dictis confertis densatisque frustra tentas eludere, quod infra examinabitur, cum ad argumenta Allatij revertemur.
units.tr: These things being laid down, Hottinger, which are beyond doubt among all, Allatius, in order to prove the union, brought together in his books on the Consensus the sayings of the Greeks and Latins, and in them he demonstrated a continuous constancy from the beginning of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, supported by their testimonies, down to these times. This displeased you and yours, for you cannot escape by turning your mind away from the Roman Church toward the Greek, as if it opposed her. Therefore you accused Allatius of rashness, and, so as not to seem to do so without reason, you compiled those chapters of yours to prove the division, and you confirmed your faith aphoristically, more than proving it. But to what profit? Those who are not deprived of the light of the mind see, and judge, that you clearly have no reliable grasp of what division is and what union is. Allatius, having enumerated those chapters and examined them with care, turned back upon you the rashness you charged him with, and by bringing forward from the Greek ritual books testimonies which they do not deny, if they have sense, and, what is more, from the schismatics themselves, he showed that those chapters of yours clearly prove, point by point, not dissension from the Roman Church but union, and that his cause, with you as judge, is the stronger. Hottinger came forth convicted of manifest fraud and imposture. Therefore, so that you might seem to have accomplished something, you turned again to rage, not considering what you could say against Allatius, and in haste and with confusion you threw forth that turbulent Apologetic Disputation of yours, hurrying the sayings and opinions which fury poured out for you. It is no wonder, then, that you do not answer Allatius's arguments, but vainly try to evade them by piling up and crowding together the sayings of others. This will be examined below, when we return to Allatius's arguments.

units.la: Fateor me forte modestiori, quam merebatur, iudicio, Allatij conatum nimis appellasse temerarium. Mirum te non negare id etiam dixisse, sed agnosco modestiam Hottingeri, qui aphoristice loquens, & nihil probans, nimiam temeritatem Allatij criminatus est. Sed Allatius tractat de unione, ergo nimis temerarius est. En Aristophanis, & Cleanthis lucernam? Disceptationes, contentiones, & certamina literaria quis unquam prohibuit? Quis litibus scholasticis silentium imposuit? Quis ista iura tam aequa decernit? Quis id statuit, quod aequum est in Hottingero, & aliis illis similibus, id temerarium esse in Allatio? Vidit Allatius, examinauitque Heterodoxorum conatus, qui ut se non absque ratione ab Ecclesia Romana desciuisse ostenderent, ut socios criminis haberent, & sic culpam prætextu aliquo non inhonesto cuitarent, ad Græcorum Ecclesiam confugisse, ut quam ipsi defectionem ab Ecclesia Romana perpetrarunt, non sibi appingerent, causam prætexentes, ob violatum dogma, & rectas consuetudines, quæ Græca scilicet non violaverat, abilla fe feparaffe. Quod probatu illis erat difficile, nisi dissidium inter Romanam, & Græcam constabiliuissent.
units.tr: I confess that I judged Allatius's undertaking too leniently, since it deserved a harsher verdict, and called it rash. It is remarkable that you do not deny having said this, but I recognise Hottinger's moderation, for he speaks in aphorisms, proves nothing, and accuses Allatius of excessive rashness. But Allatius treats of union, therefore he is excessively rash. Behold the lamp of Aristophanes and Cleanthes! Who has ever forbidden disputations, contentions and literary battles? Who has imposed silence on scholarly quarrels? Who decrees such fair laws? Who has ruled that what is fair in Hottinger, and in others like him, is rash in Allatius? Allatius saw and examined the attempts of the heterodox, who, to show that they had not left the Roman Church without reason, and to have partners in their crime, and so to escape blame under some respectable pretext, fled to the Greek Church. They did this so that they would not impute to themselves the defection from the Roman Church which they had themselves committed, alleging as their cause a violated dogma and right customs, which the Greeks, of course, had not violated, and on account of which they had separated themselves from them. This would have been hard for them to prove, unless they had first established a disagreement between the Roman and the Greek Churches.

units.la: Et hoc iniquum, falsumque reputans Allatius, libros de consensione conscripsit.
units.tr: Judging this to be unjust and false, Allatius wrote books on the consensus.

units.la: Qua ergo causa Allatius urgens unionem nimis temerarius fuerit, Hottingerus urgens dissidium non item? Modeftiffimum fuit Hottingeri iudicium, qui nec nominatus unquam, nec notus Allatio, nullis impulsus inimicitijs, nulla privatim læsus iniuria Allatium, uti temerarium nimis, quia de unione scriptum ediderat, & magnum alastorem, & fumos vendere magnos magno libro de consensione Occidentalis, & Orientalis Ecclefiæ, hominem innocuum, & quem albus anater fuerit, non noverat, ut ipse scribit L. B. S. eiusmodi titulis insignire, minus quam nihil existimas, emunctæ naris homo; & tantilla trium syllabarum vocula absque causa in Allatium omnia malignæ tuæ linquæ venena coniecisti, quæ parata sunt in eos, qui permulta scelera male agendo fraudandoq; fecerunt. Si hoc modestius ingenium est, quid expectandum de immodestiori? Et nunc crimen maledicentiæ dissoluere conaris, temeritatem Allatij sæpiuscule in medium producens, merito in Allatium iactatam contendis, de Alastore semel enunciās; quasi temerarium esse minus quid sit, quam Alastorem, vt hinc quoque singulare genus fraudis, & nouam rationem insidiarum Lector cognoscat.
units.tr: For what reason, then, would Allatius, in urging union, be too rash, while Hottinger, in urging disagreement, would not be? Hottinger's judgement was most moderate. He had never been named or known to Allatius, was driven by no private enmity, and had suffered no personal injury, yet he called Allatius "too rash," because he had published a book on union, and "a great alastor," and said he "sells great smoke in a great book on the consensus of the Western and Eastern Church," and he marked a harmless man, whom he "did not know from a white raven" (as he himself writes), with such titles. You, a man of keen nose, think this of less account than nothing, and with that tiny little word of three syllables, without cause, you have poured all the poisons of your slanderous tongue upon Allatius, which are kept ready for those who have committed many crimes by evil dealing and deceit. If this is the more moderate temper, what can be expected of the less moderate? And now you try to wipe away the charge of slander, bringing forward Allatius's rashness again and again, and you insist that it was thrown at Allatius with good reason, having once mentioned the alastor. As if being rash were a lesser thing than being an alastor! So that the reader may also learn this singular kind of deceit and new method of ambush.

units.la: Sed lixarum, & calonum hæc dicendi methodus est. Concludamus itaque cum primus Hottingerus nulla antea ab Allatio exulceratus iniuria, in ipsum Allatium sæuierit, & immanissime debacchatus fit, erit procul dubio & lixa, & calo, & quidquid aliud in Allatium rependit in hac sua Disputatione; nec illi iniucundum fit, si vapulauerit ab Allatio, & quæ voluit locutus, audiuerit quæ noluit.
units.tr: But this is the method of speaking of camp-followers and hucksters. Let us conclude, then: since Hottinger first, though never provoked by any prior injury from Allatius, raged against Allatius himself and raved most savagely, he will undoubtedly be a camp-follower, a huckster, and whatever else one might pay back to Allatius in this your Disputation. Nor will it be unwelcome to him if he is thrashed by Allatius, and hears in return what he did not wish to hear, having spoken what he wished.

units.la: Nihil equidem viro graui indignius est, quam turpi diuortio Musas a charitibus separare.
units.tr: Nothing is more unworthy of a serious man than to separate the Muses from the Graces by a shameful divorce.

units.la: En Hottingerum factum de repente de Momo Philosophum, & ex cathedra boni summique viri officia deprædicantem, & Zoilum agentem, & itâ se gerentem in alios, vt in eo & humanitas desideretur, & bonorum virorum instituta requirantur. Eodem ipso momento qui humanitatem insinuat, humanitate exuit, & dum candorem in aliis exoptat improbissima ipse conuicia excreat, ut ex hac sua Disputatione addiscitur. Reprehensit in Allatio, in quo ipse reprehensibilior deprehenditur. Bonorum orationem, frustra tamen, cum imitatur, vultque eorum documentis viuere, innatam sibi obiurgandi mentiendique conditionem non dediscit. Quare sua ipse, quae in alios aggerat maledicta, & conuicia habeat: nosenim ea non grauate, sed summa cum voluptate illi, quae sua sunt, concedimus. & Leo ipse fuerit, & insulso latratu, & horrido rictu canem prodat.
units.tr: Behold Hottinger, suddenly turned from Momus into a philosopher, preaching from the chair the duties of good and great men, and playing the Zoilus, and conducting himself toward others in such a way that humanity is lacking in him, and the practices of good men are missed. At the very moment he recommends humanity, he strips himself of it, and while he longs for candour in others, he himself spews the most shameless insults, as is learned from this Disputation of his. He finds fault with Allatius, in whom he himself is found more blameworthy. When he imitates the speech of good men, and wishes to live by their teaching, he does not unlearn his innate habit of railing and lying, though in vain. Let him, therefore, keep for himself the abuse and reproaches he heaps on others, for we willingly and with the greatest pleasure leave to him what is his own: let him be a lion, if you like, and betray a dog with his silly barking and his horrid snarl.

units.la: Qui nullo Ecclesiarum Graeca, & Latina authentico munitus priuilegio dense testium nubi se audet opponere. Rides scilicet Leonis amentiam, qui in te vel sal, vel lumen mentis, vel micam prudentiae inesse negat. Ecce fateor me nullo priuilegio munitum de vnione tractasse, ostende tu tuum, quo munitus de dissidio tractas. Ergo nonnisi priuilegio muniti in hoc tam erudito seculo literis mandare aliquid possunt? Quis ingenia mancipat, ne se in disciplinis exerceant? Quis manus deligat, ne calamis chartam illiniant? Quis linguam remoratur, ne in disputationibus sensa animi exprimat? Quis iudicio tam diro de fortunis omnibus literatorum, atque eruditorum decernit? Potuit igitur Allatius, sicuti & nunc potest, licet ringatur[?] Hottingerus, etiam absque priuilegio communis Ecclesiæ de unione, & de aliis, uti libuerit, scribere. Mirum est, hanc facultatem in se non subtraxisse Hottingerum, qui stultissime opponit Allatio afferens, Ostendendum ergo Allatio, ne Andabatarum more pugnetur, quo Synodi decreto huius de Dogmatibus, & Ritibus constanter hactenus negata contentionis, probandi onus ita sibi esse impositum euincat, ut iudicio eius & cadere velit & stare. Sed hæc [illegible, ~9 letters] & præter rem argutula Hottingero, ut aliquid dicere videatur, relinquamus, & ad rem, unde digressi sumus, reuertamur.
units.tr: Who, supported by no authentic privilege of the Greek or Latin Churches, dares to oppose himself to a thick cloud of witnesses. You evidently laugh at the madness of the lion, who denies that there is in you either salt, or light of mind, or a crumb of prudence. Behold, I confess that I treated of union without any privilege, show yours, by which you are supported in treating of disagreement. Can only those supported by privilege commit anything to writing in this so learned age? Who enslaves minds, lest they exercise themselves in the disciplines? Who binds hands, lest they smear paper with pens? Who holds back the tongue, lest it express the feelings of the mind in disputations? Who decrees with such a harsh judgement concerning the fortunes of all the literate and learned? Therefore Allatius could, as he still can, write on union and on other matters as he pleases, even without a privilege of the common Church, though Hottinger rages. It is remarkable that Hottinger did not withdraw this faculty from himself, he who most foolishly opposes Allatius, asserting: It must be shown to Allatius, lest we fight in the manner of the Andabatae, by what decree of the Synod, constantly denied hitherto in this contention about dogmas and rites, the burden of proof is so imposed on him that by its judgement he must either fall or stand. But let us leave these [illegible, about nine letters] and what is trivial and beside the point to Hottinger, who wants to seem to say something, and return to the matter from which we digressed.

units.la: Qui quod totus affirmat Orbis, unus conatur in dubium vocare, Thomas, Antoninus, Nauclerus, & alij antiquiores, & non ita pridem Cafalius, Honoratus Fabri, Scriptores Romani. Dissensum inter Græcos, & Romanam Ecclesiam firmissime asseuerant. Nunquam id inficias iuerit Allatius. Is primus tentat dissensum in assensum conuertere. Id vero absonum fidei est? Nunquam Allatius verum, & falsum unum fecit. cit . Dicit Romanus , Spiritum ex Filio quoque procedere, Græcus ex solo Patre. alterum veritas Catholica est, alterum hæresis. Quare inter hæc afferentes apertum dissidium fuerit: & plane stultus est, qui dixerit, hæc duo vnum esse, dum vnum cum altero pugnat. Et fatetur plane Allatius, nec se, nec alios, licet operam insumant suam, hæc duo distracta, aduersaque inter se in concordiam adducere posse, & quæ inter ipsa est discordiam, & ex dissensu assensum constituere. Veruntamen cum Latina dicat, Spiritum etiam ex Filio procedere, Græca vero, procedere ex Patre non exprimendo Filium, imo etiam sæpius in suis Ritualibus libris procedere ex Patre per Filium, quod & approbatum est in Synodo septima, quam Græci omnes, etiam Schismatici inter vniuersales collocant, & apud Patres Græcos Basilium, & Cyrillum potissimum, cum in creatis, tum in diuinis præpositiones Ex, & Per eandem vim habere certum est: tibi ne tamen temerarium, & perabsurdum, si duorum similium dictorum consensum, in quibus dissidium, licet omnia experiaris, nunquam deprehendes, Allatius consensum procurat? An non satius esset tibi, Asino dare ossa, & cani paleam, quam de rebus Ecclesiasticis scrsermocinari ? Ita philosophandum est de Purgatorio, & de visione beatifica, & aliis. Male ergo & temerarie vrget concordiam. Hoc est non comprehendere animo, quid dicat Allatius, vel verba illius devorare inconsiderate, atque absumere. Quid ergo agit? Dicit, Romanos Spiritum sanctum asferere ex Filio procedere, hoc item fateri Græcos. Purgatorium etiam per ignem Romanos, Græcos hoc quoque affirmare: visione beatifica iustos demortuos ante iudicium vniuersale perfrui, hoc idem Græcos instare. Ergo Græci, & Latini cum eadem dicunt, & eadem omni asseueratione affirmant, concordes animis sunt. Qui enim dissentiunt, dictis inter se non congruunt. Quid igitur ludis operam in tot confarcinandis testibus, vt dissensum astruas? Testes enarrant, quæ Græci extra Romanam Ecclesiam viuentes dictitant, & ea in capita plura, vel pauciora reducunt. Allatius quid illi dicant, haud in magno ponens discrimine, illud probare curat, Græcam Ecclesiam, & Romanam eandem dicere, & dixisse perpetuo. Hinc nascitur perpetua consensio. Quare ad demonstrandum dissidium, male a te opera luditur, si quid dixerint alij de dissidijs Græcorum, & Latinorum, & potissimum Schismatici, in medium afferas . Proba, illos non dicere eadem, & tum duc in triumphum Allatium. Tu porro vt huius ratiocinationis vim effugias de dictorum congruentia, nihil de Capitibus dissidij, de auctoribus vero illud asserentibus multa in vnum exagerās. Hic Rhodus. hic salta[?]. Hinc exemptus est tibi scrupulus, postquam ad monomachiam Allatium provocasti.
units.tr: Who alone attempts to call into doubt what the whole world affirms: Thomas, Antoninus, Naucler, and other older writers, and, not so long ago, Casalius and Honoratus Fabri, Roman writers. They firmly assert a dissent between the Greeks and the Roman Church. Allatius would never deny this. He is the first to attempt to turn dissent into assent. But is this something absurd to faith? Allatius never made the true and the false one. The Roman says that the Spirit proceeds also from the Son, the Greek from the Father alone. The one is Catholic truth, the other heresy. Therefore, between those who affirm these things, there will be an open disagreement, and he is plainly foolish who says these two are one, when one fights with the other. And Allatius plainly admits that neither he nor others, however much effort they expend, can bring these two, divided and opposed to each other, into concord, and make assent out of the dissent that lies between them. Yet, while the Latin says that the Spirit proceeds also from the Son, and the Greek says proceeds from the Father, without naming the Son, indeed, in their Ritual books they often say proceeds from the Father through the Son, which was also approved in the Seventh Synod, which all Greeks, even the schismatics, count among the ecumenical councils, and as Basil and Cyril especially among the Greek Fathers show, it is certain that the prepositions from and through have the same force both in created and in divine things. Yet Allatius seeks agreement between two similar statements, in which there is disagreement, though you try everything and will never find it. Is it rash and utterly absurd to you? Would it not be better for you to give bones to an ass and chaff to a dog than to chatter about ecclesiastical matters? So one must philosophise about Purgatory, the beatific vision, and the rest. Therefore he urges concord badly and rashly. That is, he does not grasp in his mind what Allatius says, or he devours and consumes his words carelessly. What, then, does he do? He says that the Romans assert the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, and that the Greeks confess this too. That the Romans affirm a purgatory by fire, and the Greeks affirm this also; that the just departed enjoy the beatific vision before the universal judgement, and the Greeks insist on the same. Therefore the Greeks and the Latins say the same things, and affirm them with the same assurance, and are agreed in mind. For those who dissent do not agree with one another in what they say. Why, then, do you labour in stuffing together so many witnesses to prove a dissent? The witnesses recount what the Greeks living outside the Roman Church keep saying, and they reduce these to more or fewer heads. Allatius, placing little weight on what they say, takes care to prove that the Greek Church and the Roman say the same and have always said it. From this a constant consensus arises. Therefore, in order to demonstrate the dissent, it is wasted effort on your part to bring forward whatever others have said about the disagreements of Greeks and Latins, especially the schismatics. Prove that they do not say the same things, and then lead Allatius in triumph. Moreover, to escape the force of this reasoning about the agreement of statements, you pile up much about the heads of disagreement, and about authors who assert it, all in one heap. Here is Rhodes, here jump! Thus the scruple has been removed from you, now that you have challenged Allatius to single combat.

units.la: Generaliter primum, & in thesi recte Allatium temeritatis accusari, quod imprudenter argumenti suscipiat patrocinium, & toti orbi contradicat vehementer, & Ecclesiae Romanae vehementissime, ad oculum demonstrabo. Sed iam tandem ad thesim probandam accessisti. Examinemus conatus, quibus redarguatur Allatius, & imprudentiae, ac temeritatis, cum argumenti susceperit patrocinium, quo toti orbi, & Romanae Ecclesiae contradicit: & primum praxis: Photius auctor Schismatis, Michael Cerularius, aliique Patriarchae Constantinopolitani excommunicati sunt a Romanis Pontificibus. Hoc ante te signavit Allatius. Hinc excommunicatorum in Romanam Ecclesiam reposita iurgia, & Graeci in factiones diuisi vnus aduersus alium scriptis inuehitur. Hinc natus Nilus, Niceta Choniata, Niceta Stethatus, alij, qui inter se & Romanam Ecclesiam cleclesiam productis dissensionis capitibus schisma disseminarunt. An non & ante dictos Patriarchas alij cum Romanis varijs exortis contentionibus delitigarunt, & concertatorijs artibus compugnarunt? Sed semper a Romana vti a superiore poenis indictis, & contra pertinaces etiam publicatis, repressi, & peracta poenitentia in antiquam concordiam etiam nolentes redacti sunt. Non est quod hic agam exemplis. Inde est quod Latinis multa Græci obijcerent, & contra Latini Græcis reponerent, & progressu temporis crescente pertinacia in immensum, vt ita dicam, crimina quoque creuerint, quæ licet inter particulares homines vage dispergerentur, non inde tamen factum est, vt vniuersa Ecclesia Græca a Romana, profitendo capita dissidij, separaretur, & in sua professione, vel libris Ritualibus, & officijs in Ecclesia recitandis aliquid adderet, quod Ecclesiæ Romanæ probrum obijceret. Quod si etiam obiecissent, & permansisset per aliquod tempus in Schismate, subsecuti alij Patriarchæ in frugem redacti, erroribus dimissis conciliatis animis ad benevolentiam Romani se adiunxerunt. & ea dissensio non adeo in ea Ecclesia saeuijt, vt vel Symbolo adderetur Ex solo Filio, vel de Purgatorio contra Romanam Ecclesiam in suis Professionibus fidei aliquid affirmaret, & sic de alijs. Et qui dicit Spiritum ex Patre procedere* non negat eum etiam ex Filio procedere› & qui rogat pro mortuis, ut liberentur abpoenis & igne, non negat in Purgatorio poenas, & ignem. Et hoc eodem modo de alijs edisserendum est. An non vides te prosanae mentis esse, qui cum sequi Græcam Ecclesiam debeas, quid sequendum sit illi, ipse constituis? & temeritatis notam, quam appingis Allatio, putas te effugere? O caput!
units.tr: First, in general and in principle, I will clearly demonstrate that Allatius is rightly accused of rashness, since he imprudently takes up the defence of an argument and vehemently contradicts the whole world, and the Roman Church most vehemently. But you have now at last come to prove your thesis. Let us examine the attempts by which you refute Allatius and charge him with imprudence and rashness, since he has taken up the defence of a position that contradicts the whole world and the Roman Church. First, the practice: Photius, the author of the schism, Michael Cerularius, and other Patriarchs of Constantinople were excommunicated by the Roman Pontiffs. Allatius has already noted this before you. From this, quarrels arose between the excommunicated and the Roman Church, and the Greeks, divided into factions, attacked one another in writing. From this came Nilus, Niceta Choniates, Niceta Stethatus, and others, who, by putting forward the heads of dissension, spread the schism between themselves and the Roman Church. Did not others before the Patriarchs mentioned also quarrel with the Romans over various disputes and fight with contentious arts? But they were always restrained by the Roman authority, which imposed penalties on them, published them even against the obstinate, and, once penance was done, brought them back to the old concord even against their will. There is no need for me to go through examples here. Hence it is that the Greeks would raise many objections against the Latins, and the Latins would answer the Greeks; and as time went on, obstinacy grew beyond measure, and, if I may say so, the accusations grew too. Although these were scattered loosely among private individuals, it did not follow that the whole Greek Church separated from the Roman Church by professing the heads of dissension, or added anything to its profession, or to its ritual books and the offices recited in church, that would bring reproach upon the Roman Church. Even if they had made such objections, and had remained in schism for some time, later Patriarchs were brought to their senses, dropped their errors, and, with minds reconciled, joined themselves to the Romans in goodwill. Nor did that dispute rage so fiercely in that Church that either the words *from the Son alone* were added to the Creed, or it affirmed anything against the Roman Church about Purgatory in its professions of faith, and so on for other points. And whoever says that the Spirit proceeds from the Father does not deny that he also proceeds from the Son; and whoever prays for the dead that they may be freed from penalties and fire does not deny penalties and fire in Purgatory. The same method should be applied to other points. Do you not see that you are of a profane mind, since, though you ought to follow the Greek Church, you yourself decide what is to be followed? And do you think you escape the mark of rashness which you fix upon Allatius? O head!

units.la: Dogma Græcorum de Processione Spiritus sancti, expresse vocat hæresim. Nonne hoc est, dissentire? Hæresim esse quis negat? Et hoc non est dissentire? ergo inter Ecclesiam Græcam, & Latinam dissidium intercedit; hoc vero probandum. Ecclesia Græca non negat, sequitur suos Patres, & Concilia, a quorum auctoritate pendet, & suis etiam ritualibus Libris confitetur, Spiritum sanctum esse ex Filio, esse per Filium, Profluere, exilire, profundi ex Filio, Procedere per Filium, quod idem est, id afferentibus Basilio, Cyrillo, alijs, esse ex essentia Filij, quod notat productionem ad intra, id Schismaticis Synodali decreto decernentibus. Et tu Hottingere audes dicere, Dogma Græcorum, Ecclesiæ Græcæ scilicet esse hæresim, & hoc esse dissentire?
units.tr: The Greeks' dogma on the procession of the Holy Spirit you expressly call heresy. Is this not to dissent? Who denies that it is heresy? And this is not to dissent? Therefore there is a dissension between the Greek and Latin Church; but this has yet to be proved. The Greek Church does not deny this; it follows its Fathers and Councils, on whose authority it depends, and it confesses in its ritual books: that the Holy Spirit is from the Son, is through the Son, flows forth, springs forth, and is poured forth from the Son, proceeds through the Son, which is the same thing, as Basil, Cyril and others affirm; that he is from the essence of the Son, which denotes production within the Godhead, as the schismatics decree by synodal decree. And do you, Hottinger, dare to say that the dogma of the Greeks, that is, of the Greek Church, is heresy, and that this is to dissent?

units.la: Recentissimi etiam Leone posteriores. Scriptorum similium dicta quomodo intelligenda sint, iam diximus. Sed quidam ex his dicunt, Ecclesiam Græcam, non conflugem, aut colluuiem Schismaticorum, quæ perpetua, & sola Allatij exceptio est. Addendum erat, & vere. Sed καθαρμάτα[?] hæc Leoni sunt, & capita sacra, quæ Ecclesiam Græcam non faciunt. Hoc quoque sunt ex tuis, & ad Allatium non pertinent.
