Si Hæresis est dicere, Spiritum sanctum ex Filio non procedere, Ecclesia Græca id asserens Hæretica est; sed quæ Ecclesia Hæretica Ecclesia est? Ergo quisquis id dicit, Ecclesiam Græcam id credere, non loquitur de Ecclesia Græca, quæ nulla est; sed intelligit conflugem, & colluuiem Schismaticorum, quæ vera Ecclesia non est. Vt si quis diceret Ecclesiam Lutheranam, & Caluinisticam, næ illi de Ecclesia vera sermo non esset, sed de vulgo Hæreticorum, & purgamentorum receptaculo.
units.tr: Even the most recent writers after Leo. We have already said how the statements of such writers are to be understood. But some of them say that the Greek Church is not a gathering or sink of schismatics, which is the constant and sole exception of Allatius. It should have been added, and truly so. But these are the refuse [καθάρματα] of Leo, and sacred heads, which do not make up the Greek Church. These too are among your own, and do not pertain to Allatius. If it is heresy to say that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, and the Greek Church, asserting this, is heretical, yet what heretical church is a church? Therefore whoever says that the Greek Church believes this is not speaking of the Greek Church, which does not exist, but means the gathering and sink of schismatics, which is not a true church. It would be as if someone said that the Lutheran and Calvinist Church: he would not be speaking of the true Church, but of the common herd of heretics and the receptacle of refuse.

units.la: Solus est Allatius, qui contra testimonium, sensus, & consensus pene omnium. An Allatius solus est alij dicant. Quod ipse exposuit, id certum est. Sin minus, ostendat Hottingerus, quodnam ex Capitibus, quæ ille prourgendo dissidio attulit, Ecclesia Græca in suis Ritualibus libris, vel in Professionibus fidei firmiter teneat, & fateatur.
units.tr: Allatius alone stands against the testimony, the sense, and the consensus of almost everyone. Whether Allatius is alone, others may say. What he has set out is certain. If not, let Hottinger show which of the heads which he brought forward in support of the dissension the Greek Church firmly holds and confesses in its ritual books or in its professions of faith.

units.la: Pag. 9. & sequentibus, totus est in astruendo dissidio ex Historia Siluestri Syropuli: sed frustra labor consumitur: de Syropuli hac historia, Notis in eam, & versione Creyghtoni nostris in eundem exercitationibus, quas iam paramus, fuse dicemus. Et pudendum est Hottingere, te speculatorem venatoremque sagacem historiæ, quam scriptis etiam editis profiteris, ab animis consuetudine Schismaticis, & Latinos capitali odio aspernantibus, atque abhorrentibus petere testimonium veritatis, & defendere ista tua absurda, & quod magis mirum est, hominem in primis acutum, quæ per se sunt falsa, & inter sese repugnantia non perspicere.
units.tr: On page 9 and the following pages, you are wholly engaged in establishing the dissension from the history of Silvester Syropulus; but your labour is spent in vain. We will speak at length about this history of Syropulus, and about the notes on it and Creighton's translation, in our own exercises on the same subject, which we are now preparing. And it is shameful, Hottinger, that you, a keen spy and hunter of history, which you profess even in your published writings, should seek testimony to the truth from men who are by custom schismatics, who regard the Latins with deadly hatred and abhor them, and should defend those absurdities of yours; and what is more surprising, that you, a man especially keen, should not see that these things are false in themselves and inconsistent with one another.

units.la: Et primo quidem illi, qui ἀσεβῶν[?] Romæ indixerunt bellum, magno referuntur numero. Non negauit unquam Allatius magnum eorum numerum extitisse, quos ipse ex scriptis eorum in Pontificios commemoratis Commentarijs de nomine, tum in libris de Confensione, tum alibi sæpius ingenue in medio posuit, & quod magis, ac magis indolet, singulis diebus de nouo aliquis emergit e tenebris, qui ne lateant, & facilius cum eduntur in publicum, fucum simplicioribus faciant, Allatius, cum sese occasio tulerit, nomen, & Commentarium indicat. Sed καθάρματα hec Leoni sunt, & capita sacra, quæ Ecclesiam Græcam non faciunt, Schismatici, & pacis perturbatores. Et in dubio ponis, Allatium simile genus hominum uti καθάρματα abijcere, qui auita Patrum & Conciliorum religione neglecta, & fide promissa in Baptismo eiurata, in innocentissimam matrem linguam exacuunt, & ab illius decretis summo scelere filios distrahunt, unde postmodum oritur in Ecclesia perturbatio vitæ, & magna confusio? Sed Reformatis fauent, & Pontificios vulnerant: & propterea sunt καθάρματα putida, & ut verbo expediam, odium terræ. Non nunc primum mos invaluit, sed ab antiquo tempore in Ecclesia Græca, iuxta atque in Latina, similes pestes, & mala auspicia, execrandi, detestandi, fugandique poenis etiam inflictis, e solo patrio exterminandi, & relapsos & pugnaces in hæresi perdendi, & comburendi.
units.tr: And first, those who declared war on Rome against the impious are cited in great number. Allatius has never denied that there were a great many of them; from their writings he has frequently and openly set before the reader, in his commentaries on the Papists, in his book on the Confession, and elsewhere, those whom he named. And what is more and more grievous, every day someone new emerges from the darkness, and, so that they may not lie hidden, and so that, when published, they may more easily deceive the simple, Allatius, whenever occasion offers, names them and their commentary. But these men are refuse [καθάρματα], as Leo says, and sacred heads who do not make up the Greek Church: schismatics and disturbers of peace. And do you doubt that Allatius casts out a similar kind of men as refuse [καθάρματα], who, neglecting the ancestral religion of the Fathers and Councils, and renouncing the faith promised at Baptism, sharpen their tongues against their most innocent mother tongue, and by its decrees wickedly separate sons from it, whence afterwards disturbance of life and great confusion arise in the Church? But they favour the Reformed and wound the Papists, and therefore they are rotten refuse [καθάρματα], and, to put it in a word, the hatred of the earth. This custom is not new; from ancient times in the Greek Church, just as in the Latin, similar plagues and evil omens have been punished, cursed, detested and driven out, with penalties even imposed, banished from their native soil, and the relapsed and contentious in heresy have been destroyed and burned.

units.la: Quis iudicem Leonem constituit, ut de Ecclesia Græca vel vera, vel falsa iudicaret? Non satis est te semel insanisse, Hottingere. De auctoritate Allatij in dijudicandis rebus fifidei supra etiam eundem rogasti . Præter ea, quæ dicta sunt, addo. Illi ijdem, qui tibi id onus imposuerunt, vt pietatis, sanctitatis, ac religionis hostes defenderes. Quasi vero non omnibus liberum sit pronunciandi, proferendique sententiam. Tu tu Hottingere tuis illis mendaciloquijs excitasti Allatium, non socordem ad veri inuestigandi cupiditatem. & cum verum inuenisset, quid obstat, ne illud in publicum edat? Sed id Hottingero non placet, id propter Allatius edidit. Verum dic Hottingere, quis te Allatio iudicem constituit, vt ex eo poscas, cur id potius quam illud ageret? Edit, quia ita illi complacet. Sed stulte egit. cum a stultissimo enunciatur, nihil moror. Dum nugas de me concilias, nihil interdico. Dicant te sapere.
units.tr: Who appointed Leo judge to decide whether the Greek Church was true or false? It is not enough, Hottinger, for you to have gone mad once. You asked the same thing earlier about Allatius's authority in judging matters of faith. Besides what has been said, I add this: those same men who imposed that burden on you, so that you would defend the enemies of piety, sanctity and religion. As if it were not free for everyone to pronounce and give an opinion! You, Hottinger, with your lying words, roused Allatius, who was not lazy in his desire to investigate the truth. And when he had found the truth, what prevents him from publishing it? But this does not please Hottinger; he published it because it pleased him. But tell me, Hottinger, who appointed you judge over Allatius, that you may demand from him why he did this rather than that? He publishes because it pleases him. But he acts foolishly. When it is said by the most foolish man, I do not care. While you gather trifles about me, I forbid nothing. Let them say you are wise.

units.la: Et qui sic de Ecclesia sunt meriti, in Diuorum Catalogum esse relatos, quod exemplo probatur Palama. Inter Græcos fuisse plurimos, qui Allatio καθαρμὰς[?] sunt, non ambigitur. Qui tamen in Diuorum catalogum relati sint; hoc vero purum putum mendacium est. Numera vnum, si potes. Auctor Schismatis Photius, Sergius Photio sanguine coniunctus, Sifinnius[?], Michaël Cerularius, Michaël Anchiali, Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani, Nilus, Nicolaus Cabasilæ, Simeon Thessalonicensis, Iosephi Bryennius, & Philagrius, Marcus Ephesius, & alij schisma propugnarunt, in Romanam Ecclesiam inuecti sunt, magnæ apud Græcos schismaticos existimationis Viri.
units.tr: That those who deserved so well of the Church were enrolled in the catalogue of saints is proved by the example of Palamas. That there were very many Greeks who, in Allatius's phrase, were purged clean is not in doubt. But that they were enrolled in the catalogue of saints is a plain and downright lie. Name one, if you can. Photius, the author of the schism; Sergius, related to Photius by blood; Sifinnius[?]; Michael Cerularius; Michael Anchialus, patriarchs of Constantinople; Nilus; Nicholas Cabasilas; Simeon of Thessalonica; Joseph Bryennius; Philagrius; Mark of Ephesus; and others who defended the schism and attacked the Roman Church were men of great repute among the schismatic Greeks.

units.la: Nullus ex his in catalogum Sanctorum relatus est, licet relati sint, qui Pontificiam dignitatem agnouerunt, & vnionem cum illa conseruarunt ad vltimum vsque spiritum.
units.tr: None of these has been enrolled in the catalogue of saints, although those have been enrolled who acknowledged the Papal dignity and kept up union with it to their last breath.

units.la: Hoc certe magnum est, & forte id non confiderauit, sicut & alia multa, Hottingerus. Inspice Græcorum Sanctorum catalogum, reuolue libros Rituales illius Ecclesiæ, interroga Critopulum illum tuum, cuius authoritati tantum defers. Quare fateasimilis necesse est, dum hæc scriberes, te vel sopore solutum, vel in maxima veritatis ignoratione versatum fuisse. Probas id de Palama ex mea Græcia Orthodoxa pag. 809.
units.tr: This is certainly a great point, and perhaps Hottinger did not consider it, as he has not considered many other things. Look at the catalogue of Greek saints, turn over the ritual books of that Church, and question that Critopulus of yours, on whose authority you rely so heavily. Because of this, you must confess that when you wrote these things you were either drowsy with sleep or in the greatest ignorance of the truth. You support this about Palamas from my Graecia Orthodoxa, p. 809.

units.la: Hic etiam schismaticos sequeris, quorum ductu necesse est, vt persæpe in mendacia decidas. Vellem in apertis, & manifestis non impegisses. Quare antequam protulisses sententiam, allata ibi ab Allatio oculis apertis non lectitasti? Ibi collocatæ sunt sententiæ in Palamam a nonnullis Græcorum in numerum Sanctorum ascitum.
units.tr: Here too you follow schismatics, and by their guidance you must often fall into falsehood. I wish you had not stumbled on things that are open and plain. Why, before you pronounced your judgement, did you not read with open eyes the passages that Allatius cites there? There are gathered the opinions of some Greeks who admitted Palamas into the number of the saints.

units.la: Nonnulli Græcorum non sunt vniuersi Græci, nec ipsa Ecclesia Græca. Titulum sequuntur Gregorij Acindyni Iambi, quibus Palamae haereses quamplurimae exponuntur. Excipiunt ex Dissertatione mea de libris Ecclesiasticis Graecorum, Ioannis Patriarchae Constantinopolitani in Palamam sententia Synodica, incerti disceptatio de Haeresibus Palamae, alia alterius de iisdem, & ex libris de consensione Tomus Synodicus contra Palamam, & illius haereses, de Barlaamo, Palama, & Isidoro Hypopsephio Thessalonicensi Tomus alius Synodicus: quae si recte consideraretur, Palamam inter Sanctos, secutus quorundam incognitorum hominum levitatem, non collocasses, nisi etiam id conaris ostendere, quales, quos ipse veneraris, Sancti esse debeant. Vide etiam quae in Historia non dum edita Nicephori Gregorae, disputationes adversus illius haereses, sive potius colluvium haeresum. Ego ne prolixior sim, ut sanctitas huius hominis qua in opinione habenda fit, pateat, ad dictam Gregorae historiam provoco, quam concludo ex libro 29. eiusdem.
units.tr: Some Greeks are not all the Greeks, nor is the Greek Church itself. They follow the title of Gregory Akindynos's Iambs, in which the many heresies of Palamas are set out. From my Dissertatio de libris ecclesiasticis Graecorum they take the synodal judgement of John, Patriarch of Constantinople, against Palamas; an anonymous disputation on the heresies of Palamas; another by a different author on the same subject; and from the books De consensione, the Synodal Tome against Palamas and his heresies; and another synodal Tome on Barlaam, Palamas, and Isidore Hypopsephius of Thessalonica. If these were rightly considered, you would not have counted Palamas among the saints, following the levity of certain unknown men, unless you also wished to show what sort of men, whom you yourself revere, ought to be saints. See also what is in the history of Nicephorus Gregoras, not yet published, and his disputations against the heresies of Palamas, or rather the jumble of heresies. To keep this short, and so that the holiness of this man, and the opinion in which he is to be held, may be made plain, I appeal to the said history of Gregoras, which I quote from its 29th book.

units.la: [illegible, ~60 letters] Θεσσα-[illegible, ~75 letters] ἐνταῦθα δ' αὐτὸς λίξαντος, ͨ οἷον εἰπεῖν γενεραθέντος [?] ἐξαιφνης, νηνεμία κακεὰ κατέχε τὸ πέλαγος, καὶ ἀκίνητον ἔχε τὴν ὁλκάδα τῆς γῆς ἐκείνων ἐπ' αἰσχύ-ρας μᾶς ἡμέραν δυοῖν ζαλάδες [?]. Τῇ δ' ἑξῆς παρασχούσης ἐκ δυοῖν ποταμοῖν Σκαμάνδρου τε, καὶ Σιμόεντος, οἱ πόλεως [?] καταρρέοντες ἐφ' ἑκάτερα πεζαικοῖς [?] ποτὲ λέμβοις, οἱ βάρβαροι ταύτῃ αἱρεῖσιν αἱματώτ[?]ς, ͨ καὶ ὡς εἰς ἁμάλας καθηγούμενος ἐκείνης, ἔνθα καὶ τὴν Τ'ρῶκην τὸ σαξάπου υἱὸν τὸν Πρεσβύτερον ἐπὶ ταῦτα συμπεπτωκέναι παρεῖναι, τὸν τῆς ὁλκάδος ἀπαιτοῦσι φόρον ἐκείνῃ βλέποντος ἐξιστάμεναί τε, καὶ ἐξεφόουν. μετ' ὧν ἤδη καὶ Παλαμῆς ἀξίωμα, καὶ γνωσθεὶς ὡς τις εἴη τὸν ξόνον καὶ τῶν ἀξίων, ͨ μόνον ἐκ τῆς δαψιλῆς ἐκείνης ὑλαί-αἰ ἀποσκιὰς, ἀλλὰ καίζων ἐν τοῖς κέλλοις ἐκρυ-πτειν ἀργύρια, καὶ χρυσῦ νομισμάτων ταμιόλων[?], πολλοῖς δὲ ἠδὴ θεὸς τῆς βαρβάρων[?], ἐβάλλετο τοῖς σκώμμασι[?], καὶ πολλοῖς τὰ ὧδε ἐμπέπληκεν χλαδίης[?], λεγόντων, ὡς διδάσκειν ὀφείλων ἑτέρας ἀν-θρώπῳ, τῇ σῶν διδασκάλων νομοθεσίαν τὸν ἀσκὸν τε, καὶ ἄχαλκον βίον, ἔρχοις αὐτοῖς αὐ-τὸς τὰ τῆς σῆς ἀνακαλύπτεις ψυχῆς μοχθυρίας, καὶ ἅμα ταῦτα πάθης εἰς ἐπομένης σοι δρᾶν.
units.tr: [illegible, ~60 letters] at Thessalonica … and when he had sailed there, as one might say, suddenly a calm held the sea, and kept the merchant ship fixed still off that shore for a day and two nights. On the following day, the waters of the two rivers, Scamander and Simois, flowing down from the city on either side, were carried by barbarian rowing-boats; the barbarians, so they say, captured it bloodily, and as they led it to the shore, where the son of the sebastos, the elder Trokes, had come together with them, they demanded the tribute of the ship. Those who saw this were astonished and terrified. Among them was Palamas, with his reputation, and once he was recognised as who he was, and the donkey and the people were revealed, not only from that abundant wood-shade, but also in the cells he had hidden silver and gold coins in secret… and many mocked him, and many filled the hills with jeers, saying that a man who ought to teach others should first overturn the law of his own teachers, the wineskin and the unbronzed life, and that by his own acts he revealed the faults of his soul, and at the same time showed that he would do the same in the future.

units.la: ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς βίβλων αὐτοῦ ἐχρημοζοίουσαν ἠρώ-ᾳ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ὁ βάρβαρος, ὅ, τι τε ἐκ καὶ ὅπου ἔρχον. Καὶ ἕπω μὲν μανθάνων, τὰ μὲν αὐτῷ Παλαμᾶς συνεφέρετα τῇ μίσει φαδαζῆμα κῆρ[?] εἰφθυῶν θαλάσσης, οἷμαι δὲ θείας ἀοφέσεως θεὸς τὸ κινύσης ἀεφυνείας, ἵνα μὴ σεσωσμένα, πολλῆς τε, καὶ νεωτέρας τῆς ἀσωτίας ἐμπλήσωσι ταύτῃ τὴν ἀπλυστέρων ψυχάς, καὶ αὐτά. Τὸ γε μὲν Θεὸν τῇ Χριστῷ Εὐαγγέλιον μὴ τῷ Δαυϊτικῷ Ψαλτηρίῳ ἀξιοῦ πολλῇ σὺν οἰκείας πηρᾶν ἐπεπλάτω. ἐώθασ[?] δὲ καὶ Γ'Ζμανλίται ἡμᾶς Πεφήτας τε ἀπαναζας, καὶ ἅμα τὸν σωτῆρα Χριστὸν ὡς ἕνα τῆς Πεφητῆς. πῶς δ' αὐτὸν γυμνωθῆναι μὴ τῆς οἰκείων φωσ-τεράχως[?] ἱματίων, ἐπεὶ ἡ Ἀερρωγότα μετεσθωαι[?], κωνοζόφοις[?] ποὶν αὐτὸν εἰς φεᾶσιν εἰσδώκ[?] πηρᾶν, τὰς τε ἄλλας εἰκῆ δ(ὲ)[?] μύρου μάστης ἐπάγλν αὐτᾷ πυμάτου[?] ἔνεκα πλέον[?] ἐς ὠνῶ. καὶ ἅμα τὸ σοδομπακὸν, καὶ ὠδρ[?] φύσιν πάθος τῆς ἀρρενομανίας, ἐκ οἶδ' ὁποῖος ἐπ' εἰωθὼς σοφοὶ[?] ποιεῖν ὡς ἐμπαιγμὸν τῆς ἀλισκομένων Χεισιανῶν, εἰ ἐν-δὴ[?] σωκ[?] ὑρ[?] ὁ[?] ἀδρ[?] Κατὰ ὄνομα, μακεδωμ[?] ὡς ὅπαρ[?] ἐ μέλλε[?] ἀναχωρῆσις, ἡ τὸν ἀλιτήριον ὡς ἀρχηγὸν τῆς νῶ ὑπολαξζῶν[?] ἀσεβείας, χειρὸς βαρβάρων παρείπεμ[?]φεν, ἵνα μὴ λάθῃ, μηδ' τῆς ἀμαθίστεραν[?], ἢ ἀμελέστεραν ὡς τὰ Θεία δρακμένων[?] τὸ τῆς αὐτοῦ γ' αἰρέσεως ἀχιστον, ἀλλ' ὑβεὶς ὕβειν ἀμανὴν[?] ἀνοῖγ[?] καὶ τὸ τῆς αὐτῆς κακίας κακκαλύμμένων[?] ἀχέσθω, τὰ τὲ σαρκικὰ, καὶ φαντασμύσ[?] πάθος ἀχίσω, ἀταξικώτεραν[?] τὴν ἐμπνευμένην[?] ὕδρων[?] ὁ[?] ἀλλαξέσματα[?] ὁ[?] Θέλων ἐκ τῆς τυφλῆς κῶ[?] Ζων ... ἐκ[?] τὴν πολυθείας ἀπόπμα ζαφῶς ἐξηγέλεται τε, καὶ ἰσηλίτδ[?]).
units.tr: From his books the barbarian asked, one by one, what he was and where he came from. I learned that Palamas was brought to the sea by the … of the sea, but I think by the divine permission of God, so that the things that were not saved might fill the souls of the more ignorant with many and recent licentiousness, and themselves as well. Indeed, he set the Gospel of Christ no higher than the Psalter of David, and mocked it with his own … He was accustomed to call us Pephetae, and at the same time to call the Saviour Christ one of the Pephetae. And how could he be stripped of his own clothing… since the Aerrhogotae … he entered into the world before him … and he poured the ointment of other ... for the sake of more … Along with this, the Sodomite and male-loving passion, I know not what sort of, ... accustomed to make a mockery of the captured Christians, if ... by name ... he was about to withdraw, and the barbarians sent that accursed man on his way, as the leader of his impious faction, so that he would not escape, nor be the more ignorant or careless of divine things, the most vile of his heresy... and let him be cleansed of the same wickedness, let him shed the carnal and phantasmal passion, and let the inspired ... of the waters ... the one who wishes from blind ... and from the polytheistic ... is clearly and plainly declared.

units.la: Pudor meus me revocat a similium versio-ne, quam tibi libens relinquo, ut tuum hunc ingenuum virum a tua pietate inter Sanctos relatum, si aliquando opus fuerit, in cælum extollas.
units.tr: My modesty holds me back from translating such things. I leave them to you willingly, so that if ever there is need, you may exalt to heaven this man of yours, who has been enrolled among the saints by your piety.

units.la: Concordiam sæpe quæsitam fuisse. Non negó tam a Græcis, quam a Pontificijs. Sed de his, nostris ad Syropulum, & Creyghtonum exercitationibus diligentius dicemus.
units.tr: That concord has often been sought I do not deny, either by the Greeks or by the Papists. But about these matters we shall speak more carefully in our Exercitationes against Syropulus and Creyghton.

units.la: Hoc vero non ne est fumos vendere, & sub insidiosis involucris ξυνάσμον μελίκρατον [?] propinare? Quis est qui fumos vendit? quis μελίκρατον propinat? Certe neque Veccus, neque Allatius id fecerit. Si veritas ipsa tibi tenebræ sunt, iam in vitio tuo es, & sumos vendis, eosque densissimos, & ξυνάσμον μελίκρατον, ut tuis utar verbis, propinas.
units.tr: Is this not to sell smoke, and to serve up ξυνάσμον μελίκρατον [a honeyed draught] under insidious wrappings? Who is it that sells smoke? Who serves up μελίκρατον [honey-mead]? Certainly neither Veccus nor Allatius did so. If the truth itself is darkness to you, you are already at fault, and you sell smoke, and very thick smoke at that, and serve up, to use your own words, ξυνάσμον μελίκρατον.

units.la: Nam Præside Constantinopolitano Veccus, & Michaële Palæologo regnante, cum de pace ineunda inter Græcos, & Pontificios tractaretur, qui pacem & vnionem auersabantur, tota vrbe clamitare non desistebant, scriptis etiam diuulgare, indignissime pacem futuram, tanquam quæ in perniciem consuetudinum, & dogmatum Græcæ Ecclesiæ tenderet; Veccus, qui pacem suadebat, vt similem opinionem ex animis Græcorum euelleret, scribit, pacem procurari, non ad refellendos ritus, & dogmata Græcorum, ideoque maledicta in eos conjecit, qui consuetudines & dogmata Græcæ Ecclesiæ contemnentes asserent, Romanam Ecclesiam magis pie sentire, & credere, quam Ecclesiam Græcam, non verebantur. Illos cum Iuda, & Christi crucifixoribus connumerat. Veccus ergo, ut vides, cum pietatem Romanam, tum Græcam, & ambarum consuetudines easdem esse promulgat inter suos, neque patitur, ut una altera integrior reputetur, & qui aliter tenet, maledictis subiaceat. Si non diuersæ secundum hunc auctorem tum Græcæ, tum Romanæ Ecclesiæ sunt consuetudines, & eadem dogmata, unde nam tu, nisi fumos vendere vis, dissidium hariolaris? Sed non sunt eædem consuetudines, & dogmata. Dogmata unum sunt, cum pietas illa & fides essentiam dogmati non mutat, neque alterat. Magis, & minus consuetudines admittunt, & licet de illis aliqua dissensione certetur, certamen illud Ecclesiarum dissidium non parit: sed in cultu diuino ritus tam varij, & consuetudines dissidentes, magis, ac magis Deo uniunt, reddunntque Ecclesiam pulchriorem. Quare habeat sibi suos fumos, vendatque Hottingerus. Nos qui in meridiana luce veritatis versamur, similem fumorum nundinationem detestamur.
units.tr: For under the Constantinopolitan Prefect Veccus, in the reign of Michael Palaeologus, when peace was being negotiated between the Greeks and the Papists, those who opposed peace and union would not stop shouting through the whole city, and even spreading in writing, that a peace would be most unworthy, since it tended to the ruin of the customs and doctrines of the Greek Church. Veccus, who urged peace, in order to tear such an opinion from the minds of the Greeks, wrote that the peace was being arranged not to refute the rites and doctrines of the Greeks; and therefore he hurled curses at those who, despising the customs and doctrines of the Greek Church, asserted without hesitation that the Roman Church thought and believed more piously than the Greek Church. He numbers them with Judas and the crucifiers of Christ. Veccus, then, as you see, proclaims among his own people that Roman piety and Greek piety, and the customs of both, are the same, and he does not allow that one should be reckoned purer than the other, nor that whoever holds otherwise should lie under curses. If, according to this author, the customs of the Greek and Roman Churches are not different, and their doctrines the same, whence, unless you wish to sell smoke, do you conjure up a disagreement? But the customs and doctrines are not the same. Doctrines are one, since that piety and faith do not change or alter the essence of the doctrine. Customs admit more and less, and although some disagreement may be contested about them, that contest does not produce a schism between Churches; rather, in the worship of God, rites and customs that are so varied, even when they differ, unite men more and more to God and make the Church more beautiful. So let Hottinger keep his smoke and sell it. We, who live in the noonday light of truth, detest such hawking of smoke.

units.la: Quid inde a Reformatione factum fuerit, ubi ex Graecis alij [illegible, ~8 letters] πίστιν[?] ἡμῶν, publicis etiam scriptis testati sunt; alij communem contra Pontificios nobiscum susceperunt causam. Cyrillus adhuc vel ex aduersariorum hypothesi γνώμῳ ἄλλῳ [?], Patriarcha Alexandrinus hoc saxum strenue, & feliciter voluit. De unione Græcorum cum Reformatis suo loco cumulate egi. De Cyrilli Professione fidei Reformatorum esto iudicium. Res ipsa, quid de eo Græci sentirent, plane demonstrauit. Depositus est a Græcis Synodali decreto, de throno petentibus id Græcis etiam erogata pecunia lictoribus traditus, fune strangulatus in mare proiectus est, & usque in nostra tempora ut hæreticus ob hanc, vel solam fidei suæ professionem, uti Reformatis coniunctus, anathemate feritur. Ex Zygomala quid colligas, tute ipse videris. Ego video palpatorem pessimum, non re, factisque, sed lingua tantum, & verbo tenus Crusio gratificantem, tantum ut nummos emungat. An non vides eum non dum absoluta narratione de Fratribus, vel Monachis eodem loci, & temporis vestigio subiungere; Indigentes autem nos subsidio pecuniario, & tua humanitate intercedentibus a munifica manu eorum, qui potentia isthic valent. Nam, ut Demosthenes ait, opus est pecuniis, nec absque his quicquam confici potest. Petimus autem propter magnas necessitates nostras, & tributa, quæ quotannis pendimus his, qui apud nos dominantur. Et de eo Crusius; Hic siquidem cum D. Gerlachio aliquo iret, aut navigaret, monstrato inani marsupio ἀδεινᾶ[?]. tum ille pro ipso persoluebat. Et nundinantibus adeo palam fidem suam Græcis credis, & in testes aduocas: illis, qui pro Pontificijs stant, fidem adimis, & offas opiparas, & lenocinium obijcis, & testimonium reijcis? Quod Zygomala tradit de Fratribus seu Monachis Papistis, nullum ipse reputo. etiam iurató non credam. Proba tu, si poteris.
units.tr: What happened after the Reformation, when some of the Greeks, [illegible], also bore witness in public writings to our faith [πίστιν ἡμῶν]; and others took up the common cause with us against the Papists. Cyril, even on his opponents' own hypothesis, wished to hold this rock stoutly and successfully, as Patriarch of Alexandria. I have dealt fully with the union of the Greeks and the Reformed in its proper place. As for Cyril's confession of faith among the Reformed, let that be judged as it will. The event itself plainly showed what the Greeks thought of it. He was deposed by the Greeks by synodal decree; those who sought the throne had paid money to the Greeks for it; he was handed over to the lictors, strangled with a cord, and thrown into the sea. And to this day, for this one confession of faith, by which he was joined with the Reformed, he is struck with anathema as a heretic. What you infer from Zygomalas, you must judge for yourself. I see a most wicked flatterer, who pleases Crusius not in deeds but in word and tongue only, so that he may wring out money. Do you not see that, before he has finished his account of the brothers or monks in the same place and time, he adds: Being in need of financial help, and with your kindness interceding, from the generous hand of those who have power there. For, as Demosthenes says, money is needed, and nothing can be done without it. We ask this because of our great needs and the taxes we pay every year to those who rule among us. And Crusius says of him: when he went somewhere with Mr Gerlach, or sailed, showing his empty purse, the other paid for him. Do you believe the Greeks so openly, who sell their faith, and summon them as witnesses? Do you deny credit to those who stand for the Papists, and object to them sumptuous bribes and flattery, and reject their testimony? What Zygomalas reports about the Papist brothers or monks I myself count as nothing; I would not believe it even under oath. Prove it, if you can.

units.la: Et tales quidem ex ipsis Pontificijs multi &c. Azorius Instit. Moral. lib. 5. cap. 11. Dubitari non potest. Non nego, Azorium, aliosque Pontificios multa dissidij capita inter Græcos, & Latinos recensere. Inter ea pleraq; esse, quæ illis falsò attribuuntur, quemadmodum a Græcis Pontificijs, quæ cum re vera falsa sint, non sunt assumenda ad probandum discrimen: multa esse vera, quæ cum non contineant errorem, nec hæresim, in eodem gradu collocanda sunt. Alia etiam ex professo in Ecclesiam Latinam iactantur a schismati deditis Græcis, quæ cum in Ecclesia Græca, neque in professionibus fidei, neque in Ritualibus libris continentur; quin imo inter officia solemnia non alia, quam quæ Latina Ecclesia recitat, fit vt inter eas consensus sit, & non dissensus . maximeque errare eos, qui asserunt, Græcos, & Pontificios re discrepare, verbis consentire, ideoque eos non nomine, sed genere toto disiungunt. Sic enim erit non verborum parua, sed rerum quoque permagna dissensio.
units.tr: And indeed many such things among the Papists themselves, etc. Azorius, Institutiones Morales, book 5, chapter 11. It cannot be doubted. I do not deny that Azor and other Papists list many heads of dispute between the Greeks and the Latins. Among them, most are things falsely attributed to them; just as things that are really false must not be taken up to prove a difference, so many things that contain neither error nor heresy must be placed on the same level. Other things too are openly thrown at the Latin Church by Greeks given to schism, which are not contained in the Greek Church, neither in its confessions of faith nor in its ritual books. Indeed, among the solemn offices there are none other than what the Latin Church recites, so that there is agreement between them and not disagreement. Those err most who assert that the Greeks and the Papists differ in substance but agree in words, and so separate them not by name but wholly by kind. For thus the disagreement would be not small in words, but very great in matters too.

units.la: An ad Liturgiam ritus spectant, quæ de Processione Spiritus sancti, de Purgatorio, Potestate Papæ hactenus fuerunt ἀκαταλλακτα[?]; & quid si ritibus tantum differrent, differrent tamen. De processione Spiritus sancti, Purgatorio, & præeminentia Romani Pontificis in alias Ecclesias, quæ tu vocas ἀκαταλλακτα[?], sed non probas, plura dicta sunt a nobis in Hottingero, & alibi, ad quæ tu nec verbum quidem. Si quæ fuerunt mendacia, quare non euertisti rationes? Quare si probabiliora habebas, si certiora, si firmiora, non produxisti? Sed neutrum fecisti: vna tui insita negatione, & inverecunda taciturnitate transiluisti omnia, quia sic es in antilogijs luctator emeritus. Quæ non potes refellere pro causa tua respondens, irrefutata hæc tanquam foveam prætergrediens relinquis. Sed Latini dicunt, ex Filio quoque procedere Spiritum, Græci negant, asseruntque non procedere ex Filio, sed ex Patre solo. Paruum ne id discrimen est? De Latinis non dubito, nanque id expressis verbis recitant in Symbolo, sed Græci non recitant. Sapienter. Ergo negant. obtundam aures tuas saepius de eadem re, ut melius intelligas. Quæ est ista ratiocinatio? Possem aliquid in Hottingerum inclementius dicere; sed reprimo me. Christus non dixit in Evangelio, Spiritum ex se procedere, ergo negavit. Quare ergo tu cum tuis, qui tantum Verbum Dei obtenditis, cum illud in verbo Dei planum non fit, ut verbum Dei aliis propinatis? Sed agam tecum liberaliter. Esto negent Græci. Ne invideas nobis tantum mysterium. Indica, ubi loci id negent. Ego Patriarcharum, Imperatorum, Episcoporum, aliorum professiones fidei, Symbolum quod singulis diebus inter Missarum solemnia recitant, & attentius, sæpiusque libros Græcorum Rituales post schisma, & ante schisma concinnatos evolui, nunquam usquam ullo in loco, sedulo licet quærerem, investigavi. Sed veniam dabis morosò seni, qui oculorum acie non valet. Tu qui naso plus vides, quam oculis, haud scio an videris in Synaxario Xanthopuli, quod habetur in Triodio, Spiritum esse ex solo Patre. Sed debuisti scire etiam inter Schismaticos collocari Xanthopulum, quod ex principio suæ historiæ addiscere poteras, non autem inter Patres illius Ecclesiæ haberi, Xanthopuli illa Synaxaria publice in Ecclesijs non legi. Incertum prætereà esse, an illa additio Xanthopuli sit, cum in nonnullis editionibus non contineatur, nescirique, a quo facta sit.
units.tr: Or do the following belong to the liturgy and rites: what about the procession of the Holy Spirit, Purgatory, and the power of the Pope, which hitherto have been irreconcilable; and what if they differed only in rites, they would still differ. Concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, Purgatory, and the pre-eminence of the Roman Pontiff over other Churches, which you call irreconcilable but do not prove, much has been said by us in Hottinger and elsewhere, and to these you do not answer even a word. If there were falsehoods, why have you not overturned the arguments? Why, if you had more probable, more certain, or firmer things, did you not bring them forward? But you have done neither: by your ingrained denial and shameless silence you have leapt over everything, because you are a veteran wrestler in contradictions. What you cannot refute in answering for your cause, you leave unrefuted, passing by it as if it were a pit. But the Latins say that the Spirit proceeds also from the Son, while the Greeks deny it, and assert that he proceeds not from the Son but from the Father alone. Is that a small difference? I have no doubt about the Latins, for they recite this in express words in the Creed; but the Greeks do not recite it. Wisely so. Therefore they deny it? I shall wear out your ears more often on the same matter, so that you may understand better. What kind of reasoning is this? I could say something harsher against Hottinger, but I restrain myself. Christ did not say in the Gospel that the Spirit proceeds from himself; therefore he denied it. Why then do you and your people, who hold up only the Word of God, when that is not plain in the Word of God, offer your own word as if it were God's word? But I shall deal with you generously. Grant that the Greeks deny it. Do not begrudge us so great a mystery. Show where they deny it. I have carefully examined, again and again, the confessions of faith of the patriarchs, emperors, bishops and others, the creed which they recite every day during the solemn Masses, and the Greek ritual books compiled both after and before the schism; but nowhere, in any place, though I searched diligently, have I found it. Yet you will pardon an old man, who is not sharp of sight. You, who see more with your nose than with your eyes, perhaps have seen in the Synaxary of Xanthopulus, which is found in the Triodion, that the Spirit is from the Father alone. But you ought to have known that Xanthopulus is counted among the schismatics, as you could have learned from the beginning of his history, and not among the Fathers of that Church; and that those Synaxaries of Xanthopulus are not read publicly in the churches. Moreover, it is uncertain whether that addition is Xanthopulus's, since it is not contained in some editions, and it is not known by whom it was made.

units.la: Quid si dicam etiam si Christus dixisset, ex solo Patre, non excludi Filium ab illa procefsione. Dixit Christus, de die illa nescire se neque diem, neque horam, Patrem solum Deum vocauit, & ne alia referam Ecclesia Græca conuersa ad Christum enunciat; οὐδὲ μόνος ἅγιος, μόνος κύριος[?]. quibus respondent illa Latinæ. Tu solus Sanctus, tu solus Dominus. Ergo conclude tu cum aliis Hæreticis, Christum nescisse horam, neque diem, non esse Deum Patrem, & Spiritum sanctum, non esse neq; Sanctum, neq; Dominum. Id licet tu concludas, Græcorum tamen, & Pontificiorum Ecclesia sententijs non discrepant, cum vtraq; teneat & Christum, & Spiritum sanctū, & diem, & horam compertam habuisse, & esse Deum; esse sanctum & Dominum Patrem, & Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: What if I say that even if Christ had said from the Father alone, the Son would not thereby be excluded from that procession? Christ said that he did not know that day or hour, and called the Father alone God; and not to mention other things, the Greek Church, turned to Christ, declares: [οὐδὲ μόνος ἅγιος, μόνος κύριος], to which the Latin answers: You alone are holy, you alone are Lord. So you conclude, with other heretics, that Christ did not know the hour or the day, that he is not God the Father and the Holy Spirit, that he is neither holy nor Lord. Although you draw this conclusion, the teaching of the Greek and the Papist Church does not differ, since both hold that Christ and the Holy Spirit both knew the day and the hour, and that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are God, holy and Lord.

units.la: Adde, apud Græcos vulgo, illud axioma certissimum esse, quod etiam Synodico decreto stabilitum est; aliud indicari, cum dicitur in diuinis, ex essentia alicuius esse, & aliud cum dicitur, ex Deo esse: hoc enim ad creaturas referri, illud ad existentiam diuinam significandam, vt cum dicitur, Filius ex essentia Patris, notare genitam existentiam ex Patre; Spiritus ex essentia Patris productam existentiam ex Patre per processionem; secus autem cum ex Patre, vel Filio, vel Spiritu tacita essentia: tum enim vt plurimum indicare creaturas productas. Sed Spiritum sanctum esse ex essentia Filij persæpe habetur in Patribus, & in Ritualibus hodiernis Græcorum. Ergo cum publice ea recitent, & profiteantur similia, eodem tempore tenent, & profitentur, Spiritum sanctum ex Filio etiam procedere. Dicunt præterea Filium effluere, produci, emanare, exilire, & similia ex Patre, & generationem Filij ex Patre designant. Hæc eadem pronunciant de Spiritu sancto ex Patre, & Spiritus processionem ex Patre significant. Ergo cum pronunciant, & creberrime eadem de Spiritu sancto ex Filio, cum Spiritus productio generatio non sit, tum enim esset Spiritus Filius, & Filius Pater, processionem Spiritus etiam ex Filio notant. Sic etiam vbi Patres explicitis verbis decernunt, Spiritum sanctum esse ex Filio, & in Filio. Ergo si ex Filio est, habet suam existentiam, & si existentia essentialis est, ergo procedit essentialiter ex Filio. Si enim non esset essentialis processio, Spiritus esset creatura, quod in Ecclesia Græca, atque Pontificia, quae tenent Spiritum verum Deum, Patri Filioque consubstantialem, sacrilegium, ac impium verbum est. Lege attentius quae de hoc argumento disseruimus contra te, Patrum testimoniis Græcæque Ecclesiæ auctoritate firmata, tum dijudica, & statue serio[?]. Et in essentialibus, ut hic articulus esse videtur, Græcam Ecclesiam cum Romana similia tenere, licet inficetus[?] fateberis. Et hæc veritas profecta est a Christo, & ab Apostolis, repetita a sanctis Ecclesiæ Græcæ, & Latinæ Doctoribus, confirmata a Conciliis, & usque ad hanc nostram ætatem, quidquid Schismatici Hæreticique oblatrent, viget. Quare si his refragaris, bona venia me audies, prius te quispiam de omni vitæ statu, quam de ista tua adeo dementi opinione deiecerit.
units.tr: Add that among the Greeks it is commonly held as a most certain axiom, which has also been established by synodal decree, that one thing is indicated when it is said of divine things that something is from the essence of someone, and another when it is said from God. For the latter is referred to creatures, while the former signifies the divine existence: as when it is said that the Son is from the essence of the Father, it signifies the begotten existence from the Father; and that the Spirit is from the essence of the Father, it signifies the existence produced from the Father by procession. Otherwise, when something is said from the Father, or the Son, or the Spirit, without mention of essence, then it usually indicates created things that are produced. But that the Holy Spirit is from the essence of the Son is found very often in the Fathers and in the Greeks' present-day ritual books. Therefore, since they publicly recite and profess such things, at the same time they hold and profess that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son. Moreover, they say that the Son flows forth, is produced, emanates, springs forth, and similar things from the Father, and they designate the generation of the Son from the Father. They pronounce these same things of the Holy Spirit from the Father, and signify the procession of the Spirit from the Father. Therefore, when they pronounce the same things, and very frequently, of the Holy Spirit from the Son (since the production of the Spirit is not generation, for then the Spirit would be a Son and the Son a Father), they also mark the procession of the Spirit from the Son. So too, where the Fathers decree in express words that the Holy Spirit is from the Son and in the Son. Therefore, if he is from the Son, he has his own existence; and if the existence is essential, then he proceeds essentially from the Son. For if the procession were not essential, the Spirit would be a creature; which is a sacrilegious and impious word in the Greek and Papist Churches, which hold that the Spirit is the true God, consubstantial with the Father and the Son. Read more carefully what we have argued against you on this question, confirmed by the testimonies of the Fathers and the authority of the Greek Church; then judge, and decide seriously. And in essentials, as this article seems to be, you will confess, however unwillingly, that the Greek Church holds the same as the Roman. This truth came from Christ and the Apostles, was repeated by the holy teachers of the Greek and Latin Churches, was confirmed by the Councils, and still flourishes to this our age, whatever the schismatics and heretics bark. Therefore, if you resist these things, you will hear me with good grace, sooner than someone will dislodge you from your whole way of life, than from that opinion of yours, so utterly mad.

units.la: Sed tempus me vocat ad capita illa tua Aphoristica, de quibus inter nos ambigitur, ad quæ tu etiam tandem post tot diuerticula me vocas. & primo ad auctoritatem Papæ in explicatione sanctarum Scripturarum. Dicis, integris tractatibus non diffiteri a Græcis optime ostensum. Probas contra Allatium, cum nihil efferas ad rem, & nos cum de auctoritate Papæ tractabimus, de eadem in exponendis scripturis agemus.
units.tr: But time calls me to those Aphoristic chapters of yours about which we disagree, and to which you too, at last, after so many digressions, summon me. And first to the authority of the Pope in the explanation of the holy Scriptures. You say that the Greeks have shown this very well in complete treatises, which you do not deny. You argue against Allatius, though you bring nothing relevant to the point. When we discuss the authority of the Pope, we will also deal with his authority in expounding the Scriptures.

units.la: Virtutem, & efficaciam ministerij a ministro non suspendunt. Non puto te latere, quæ de hac propositione Pontificij decernant. Nihilominus ne nescius sis. Apud Pontificios certum, atque indubitatum est, virtutem, & efficaciam non pendere a bonitate, vel malitia ministri; Namque sive summa bonitate præditus, sive perditi animi sit, qui ministrat, consecratum ab eo, eiusdem virtutis, & efficaciæ esse, & æque plane persectum, cui nihil admodum deest, dummodo alia necessaria ad sui integritatem non desiderentur. Verba enim Christi sunt, quæ operantur, atque efficiunt. Et hæc Pontificij, quæ porro Græci non alia; & cum duo considerentur, oblatum, & offerens, magis Deus intendit oblato, quam offerenti. ne repetam testimonia. Vide Ioannem Patriarcham Hierosolymitanum, Theophylactum, Euthymium, Nicetam, Nicolaum Cabasilam, Simeonem Thessalonicensem, Hieremiam Patriarcham. Hi non alia dicunt, aperti hostes, si unum excipias Nicetam, de quo non ausim affirmare, Romanæ Ecclesiæ: nec ab his diversus est Bessario itidem Græcus Cardinalis. Sed negant Hæretici, & tu non agnoscens consensum, urvrges diffensum. Si paria paribus reddenda sunt, adde tu, qui tantum sapis, aliquid, quod non cohæreat. Noli tamen æquilam cum noctua,, & cum cygno fulicam comparare. Sed cum addere non possis, recurris ad intentionem ministri, quæ necessario requiritur ad hoc, vt effectum consequatur, quod intendit minister. De intentione ministri eadem dicunt Græci, & Pontificij. Dicis tamen, negare Pontificios, Sacerdotem reum lethalis peccati digne consecrare. Sic amoliris consensum. Ignoras siquidem quantum distat inter fe consecratio absoluta, & digna consecratio. Hoc quidem statum apud Græcos, & Latinos effatum est. Si Sacerdos lethalis peccati reus consecrauerit, tum nouo peccato constringi: nanque ante quam celebret, necesse est sua omnia perspecta habere, & fi quod crimen commiserit, confessario edicendum animo contrito, vel minimum attrito; postquam indoluerit, & pœnitentiam egerit, tum demum ad celebrandum procedet; sin minus delictum nouum, & culpam admittet.
units.tr: The virtue and efficacy of the ministry do not depend on the minister. I do not think you are unaware of what the Papists decree about this proposition. Still, lest you be ignorant, it is certain and beyond doubt among the Papists that virtue and efficacy do not depend on the goodness or wickedness of the minister. For whether the one who ministers is endowed with the highest goodness or has a ruined soul, what he consecrates has the same virtue and efficacy, and it is entirely complete, lacking nothing, provided that the other things necessary for its integrity are not missing. For it is the words of Christ that work and bring about the effect. The Papists hold this, and the Greeks hold nothing different. When two things are considered, the offering and the one offering, God attends more to the offering than to the one offering. I will not repeat the testimonies; see John, Patriarch of Jerusalem, Theophylact, Euthymius, Nicetas, Nicholas Cabasilas, Simeon of Thessalonica, and Jeremiah the Patriarch. These men say nothing different, and they are open enemies of the Roman Church, unless you except Nicetas, of whom I would not venture to say that he belongs to the Roman Church. Bessarion, the Greek cardinal, likewise does not differ from them. But heretics deny it, and you, not recognising the agreement, urge the disagreement. If like must be answered with like, you too, who are so wise, add something that does not hang together. Yet do not compare an eagle with an owl, or a coot with a swan. But since you cannot add anything, you fall back on the intention of the minister, which is necessarily required for the effect the minister intends to follow. The Greeks and the Papists say the same thing about the minister's intention. You say, however, that the Papists deny that a priest guilty of mortal sin consecrates worthily. Thus you remove the agreement. You do not know how far absolute consecration differs from worthy consecration. Indeed, this has been declared as settled among Greeks and Latins: if a priest guilty of mortal sin consecrates, he is then bound by a new sin. For before he celebrates, he must have all his sins clearly before him, and whatever crime he has committed must be declared to the confessor with a contrite heart, or at least an attrite one. Once he has grieved and performed repentance, then at last he may proceed to celebrate; otherwise he will incur a new offence and guilt.

units.la: De Cœna Domini Liturgiarum Græcarum quænam mens sit, exactius suo tempore enucleabimus. Ergo Græci tenent, Sacrificium non esse propitiatorium, expiatorium pro peccatis viuorum & mortuorum; sed tantum mysticum, recordatiuum, commemoratitiuum, eucharisticum. Ergo Graecorum Ecclesia sua partibus Reformatorum fauet phraseologiæ. Annon peracute respondes Allatio? Euge argutiam. In tam leues, ne dicam, in tam ineptas sententias Hottingerum incidisse. Graeci Patres antiqui, recentiores, pappomastiges, demum vniuersa Graecorum Ecclesia in his ipsis Liturgijs vocant hoc Sacrificium propitiatorium, expiatorium pro peccatis viuorum, & mortuorum, & Hottingerus inficere, ac stolide negat id Graecos afferere. Vt leuissime dicam Hottingerus exponere debuerat, quas ecclipses passa sit Ecclesia Graeca in doctrina de Coena. Graeci communicant sub speciebus panis, & vini, & dicunt se verum, & reale Sacrificium propitiatorium offerre pro peccatis, idque tot inculcatis testimonijs demonstrat Allatius adeo, vt Hottingerus ipse prolixam allegatorum pompam agnoscat, & nihilominus negat ita esse. Cui fides tribuenda est, tot Graecorum testimonijs, an Hottingero? Frustra enim ἐπικλήσεως[?] in eo quærit, quod toties Graeci cœnæ Dominicæ nomen προσφορᾶς[?], θυσίας imponunt. Deplorandum hominis ingenium! & tamen permagno æstimabitur, licet in tam apertis, & manifestis deliret: & quod non est, Allatio, vt respondere videatur, apponit. Vnde id expiscatus est, Allatium ex nominibus προσφορᾶς, & θυσίας elicere,
units.tr: What the mind of the Greek Liturgies is on the Lord's Supper, we will explain more exactly in its own time. So the Greeks hold that the sacrifice is not propitiatory or expiatory for the sins of the living and the dead, but only mystical, recollective, commemorative and eucharistic. Therefore the Greek Church, in its own parts, favours the phraseology of the Reformers. Do you not answer Allatius most sharply? Well done, what subtlety! That Hottinger should have fallen into such trivial, not to say such silly, opinions! The ancient Greek Fathers, the more recent ones, the pappomastiges, and finally the whole Greek Church in these very Liturgies call this sacrifice propitiatory and expiatory for the sins of the living and the dead; and Hottinger, staining the truth, foolishly denies that the Greeks assert this. To put it most mildly, Hottinger ought to have explained what eclipses the Greek Church has suffered in its doctrine of the Supper. The Greeks communicate under the species of bread and wine, and they say that they offer a true and real propitiatory sacrifice for sins. Allatius proves this with so many testimonies, pressed home one after another, that Hottinger himself acknowledges the long parade of quotations, and yet denies that it is so. Whom should one believe: so many testimonies of the Greeks, or Hottinger? For he vainly seeks an epiclesis in this, because the Greeks so often give the Lord's Supper the names προσφορᾶς [prosphoras] and θυσίας [thysias]. What a deplorable wit the man has! And yet he will be held in high esteem, although he raves in such open and manifest matters; and he attaches to Allatius what is not there, so that he may seem to answer. From what did he wheedle out that Allatius draws this from the names prosphora and thysia?

units.la: Sacrificium Dominicæ cœnæ dici propitiatorium, & expiatorium? id dicit expressis nominibus propitiatorium, & expiatorium prolixa allegatorum pompa. Si non erit ipsa cæcitate cœcior, & sequatur oculis allegata, aperte prospiciet, quæ attulerit Allatius, & assensum cum Latinis componet. Sed parcendum homini est. In tanta huius disputationis celeritate, atque incredibili festinatione non potuit homo fluxus, & animo vacillans non labi.
units.tr: That the sacrifice of the Lord's Supper is called propitiatory and expiatory? He says so himself, by express names, propitiatory and expiatory, in a long parade of quotations. If he is not blinder than blindness itself, and will follow the quoted passages with his eyes, he will clearly see what Allatius has brought forward, and he will bring his assent into line with the Latins. But the man must be pardoned. In the great haste and incredible speed of this disputation, a shallow man with a wavering mind could not help slipping.

units.la: Communionem sub utraque specie laicam Leo non controuertit. Negat tamen semper illud fieri. De communione Græcorum quid scripserit Allatius, ex eiusdem scriptis iam euulgatis, & usu ipso, & experientia discès. Græci siquidem sub utraque specie communicant, & hoc non controuertitur. Sed illud obseruaueris, diebus Quadragesimæ exceptis Sabbatis, & Dominicis, quibus rem sacram integre peragunt, aliis, cum Præsanctificatorum, vel Præconsecratorum Missam celebrant, si quis laicus communicare voluerit, sub specie unica communicat, illis etenim diebus nulla fit consecratio vini, & per annum qui solitariam vitam agunt, & morti proximi cum communicant, sub unica specie communicant, cum illi non deferant nisi unicam, panem nempe, & vinum illis denegetur ob periculum. Moriturispanis solus consecratus, & si opus est, vinum infunditur cochleari, quod confecratum non est ad panem emolliendum. Negat tamen semper illud fieri. Quid inde? fiat aliquando. apud Pontificios Tridentinos nunquam fit. Manet ergo semper aliquod discrimen. Ne mireris Lector adeo inconcinnam argumentationem, Fit aliquando apud Græcos, apud Pontificios nunquam fit, manet ergo semper aliquod discrimen. Fit & non fit apud Græcos, Ergo Græci, & fieri & non fieri, cum fit ἀ[illegible, ~8 letters], licet discrimen aliquod sit, non id tamen dissidium tanti ducunt, ut Ecclesias separet, & unam ab alia seiungat. Nobis est quæstio de illis discriminibus, quæ Ecclesias discludant, & inimicitias aliquas, & contrarias hominum sententias, & dissimilitudines studiorum, & voluntatem inducunt. Neque Allatius in his, & alijs eiusmodi consensionem investigauit: tum enim Græca, & Latina Ecclesia per omnia una eademque esset. De quibus permulta dici possunt, sed non est necesse omnia commemorare.
units.tr: Leo Allatius does not dispute lay communion under both kinds. He nevertheless denies that this is always done. What Allatius has written about the communion of the Greeks, you will learn from his writings already published, and from the practice itself and experience. For the Greeks indeed communicate under both kinds, and this is not disputed. But you should note this: on the days of Lent, apart from Saturdays and Sundays, on which they perform the sacred rite in full, on other days, when they celebrate the Mass of the Presanctified or Preconsecrated, if any layman wishes to communicate, he communicates under one kind only, for on those days no consecration of wine takes place. Throughout the year, too, those who lead a solitary life, and those who communicate as they approach death, communicate under one kind only, since they receive only one, namely bread, and wine is denied them because of the danger. For the dying only the bread is consecrated, and if need be wine is poured in with a spoon, which has not been consecrated, to soften the bread. He nevertheless denies that this is always done. What follows from that? Let it be done sometimes. Among the Tridentine Papists it is never done. Therefore some difference always remains. Do not be surprised, reader, at so incongruous an argument: it is done sometimes among the Greeks, it is never done among the Papists, therefore a difference always remains. Among the Greeks it is and is not done; therefore the Greeks, both doing and not doing it, although some difference exists, do not regard that disagreement as so great that it separates churches and cuts one from another. Our question concerns those differences which shut churches apart, and which give rise to enmities, contrary opinions of men, dissimilarities of studies and wills. Nor has Allatius investigated consensus in these or other such matters, for then the Greek and Latin Churches would be one and the same in all things. Many things can be said about these, but it is not necessary to recall them all.

units.la: Negat tamen, Allatius, semper illud fieri. Quid inde? Fiat aliquando. Apud Pontificios Tridentinos nunquam fit. Manet ergo aliquod discrimen. Et pernegabis te, melius, pepeius, prosit, obsit nihil videre, nisi quod lubet? Apud Pontificios Tridentinos unquam fit. Et tamen factum esse, fierique quotidie ipsa docet experientia. Nullum Presbyterum sub poena excommunicationis communicare populum sub utraque specie panis, & vini, decretum est in Concilio Constantiensi Seff. 13. & in Tridentino seff. 5. sub Pio, ab inchoata Synodo XXI. post consueta solemnia; Potestatem perpetuo in Ecclesia fuisse, ut in Sacramentorum dispensatione, salua illarum substantia, ea statueret, vel mutaret, qua suscipientium utilitati, seu ipsorum Sacramentorum venerationi pro rerum, temporum, & locorum varietate magis expedire iudicaret: ideoque licet ab initio Christiana religionis non infrequens utriusque speciei usus fuisset, tamen progressu temporis gravibus[?], & iustis causis adductam, consuetudinem sub altera specie communicandi approbare, aut sine ipsius Ecclesia auctoritate pro libito mutare non liceat. Hinc Legatorum industria ad vitandas prolixiores rixas, & quod Cæsari satisfactum vellent, factum est, ut articulus Calicis ad Pontificem remitteretur, apud quem facilius de eo tractare Cæsar posset, quam in Synodo, ubi qui eum concedendum negabant, numero longe potiores erant. Sic anno 1561. a Regina Galliæ Caterina petitus in favorem Hugonotorum, licet Orator Regius apud Pontificem, & Cardinales vehementissime urgeret, repulsam patitur.
units.tr: He nevertheless, Allatius, denies that this is always done. What follows from that? Let it be done sometimes. Among the Tridentine Papists it is never done. Therefore some difference remains. And will you so stubbornly deny it, whether it helps or harms, that you see nothing except what pleases you? Among the Tridentine Papists it is never done. And yet experience itself teaches that it has been done, and is done every day. It was decreed in the Council of Constance, session 13, and in the Tridentine Council, under Pius, from the opening of the twenty-first session after the customary solemnities, that no priest, under penalty of excommunication, should give the people communion under both kinds of bread and wine. The power has always rested in the Church to decree or change, in the dispensing of the sacraments, with their substance preserved, whatever it judges more expedient for the benefit of those who receive them, or for the veneration of the sacraments themselves, according to the variety of things, times and places. Therefore, although the use of both kinds was not infrequent at the beginning of the Christian religion, nevertheless, as time went on, it is not lawful, for grave and just causes, to approve the custom of communicating under one kind, or to change it at will without the authority of the Church itself. Hence, the diligence of the legates to avoid lengthy quarrels, and so that the Emperor might be satisfied, brought it about that the article on the Chalice was referred to the Pope, with whom the Emperor could treat of it more easily than in the Synod, where those who denied that it should be granted were far more numerous. Thus in 1561, sought by Catherine, Queen of France, in favour of the Huguenots, although the royal orator urged it most vehemently before the Pope and the cardinals, she suffered a rebuff.

units.la: Et anno 1564. Ferdinandus Imperator, dum adhuc perduraret Concilium cum Pontifice per suos Oratores Romae, & per se ipsum Oeniponti cum Morono, & Lotaringiae Cardinalibus egerat, pro obtinenda facultate Calicis, & coniugij Sacerdotum, videns nihil eiusmodi concessum fuisse, rursus tam suo, quam Ducis Bavariae generi sui nomine pro ijsdem rebus instituit apud Pontificem Pium IV. scriptis literis decimo quarto Februarij, una cum Commentariolo a nonnullis Doctoribus Catholicis consecto, in quo rationes exponebantur, propter quas considerato statu Germaniae illae res permittendae existimabantur. Idque ipsum post Ferdinandi obitum Maximilianus eius successor prosecutus est, uterque tamen irrito conatu, ob summum periculum, quod ex eiusmodi incertae utilitatis concessionibus omni procul dubio universae Ecclesiae oeconomiae, ac disciplinae eminebat. Sicuti & constabat concessionem Calicis a Paulo III. olim factam longeplus damni, quam commodi attulisse. Et cum alias quoque pro Germanis, Ungaris, aliisque earum regionum populis, non solum Protestantibus, sed etiam Catholicis, Calicis ubique fitibundis Principes Germaniæ, & Oratores Vngarici intercederent, concedendum esse ijsdem conditionibus, quas olim Paulus III. approbaverat, Pontifex Romanus cum Cardinalibus dedit facultatem nonnullis Germaniæ Episcopis, similem ritum non absolute tamen permittendi, sed ubi causas adductas veras invenissent, additis quoque aliis conditionibus. Quod ubi Viennam peruenit, maxima cum lætitia festis clamoribus personatum est a populo. Scribitq; Cardinalis Delphinus tum Internuncius, ut narrat in doctissimo eruditissimoq; suo opere pro Con. Trident. Card. Pallauicinus, maiorem Haereticorum partem eiurata haeresi redactam fuisse in antiquam Ecclesiæ Romanæ concordiam. Sed similem propensionem animi instar fulminis protinus euanuisse compertum est, & aperte agnitum in Calice negando Concilij, & Pontificis rigorem saluti animarum nullo modo impedimento fuisse. Sub Pontificatu postea Gregorij XIII., & Sixti V. cum ex Episcopis aliqui hinc ex vita demigrassent, quibus a Pio similis facultas delegata fuerat, dubitatum fuit, an facultas illa concessa esset dignitati, ideoque adhuc perduraret in successoribus, aut personis, & sic cum eorum morte ipsa quoque extinguereretur, & huic fecundo subscriptum est. Nec licere Sacerdotibus, nisi quibus gratia illa collata esset,a dictis Episcopis antequam diem obijssent, Calicem populo dispensare. & tu negas, Hottingere, parum pudenter, hoc apud Pontificios Tridentinos nunquam factum esse, ut elicias dissidium. Sed uti contra atque tu dicis apud Pontificios Tridentinos factum est, ita dissidium a te dolo malo tentatum euanescit. Sed quis ægre feret tantam inscitiam? Etiam post Tridentinos Pontificios Rex Gallorum in sui auguratione sub utraque communicat, uti & ante Concilium, ut videre est in Ceremoniali rerum Galliæ edito de Ludouico XIII, Henrico IV, & aliis. Hinc Oratores Galli postulârunt in Tridentino, ut si aliter statueretur, Calix nempe prohiberetur, id absque præiudicio fieret præroga-tiuæ Regum suorum, qui in auguratione sua Calicem accipere consueuerunt, quod & assecuti sunt, & Catholici Reges, & cum Ecclesia Romana coniuncti a Sacerdote Catholico post Pontificios Tridentinos sub utraque communicant. Et tu audes dicere Apud Tridentinos Pontifices nunquam fieri ?
units.tr: In 1564 the Emperor Ferdinand, while the Council was still in session, had already pressed the matter through his envoys at Rome and personally at Innsbruck with Moron and the Cardinals of Lorraine, seeking permission for the cup and for marriage among priests. Seeing that nothing of the kind had been granted, he again made the request to Pope Pius IV, in his own name and in that of his son-in-law the Duke of Bavaria, by letter dated 14 February, together with a short memorandum drawn up by some Catholic doctors. It set out the reasons why, given the state of Germany, these concessions seemed advisable. His successor Maximilian pursued the same request after Ferdinand's death, but both attempts failed, because of the great danger that such concessions of doubtful benefit would plainly threaten the whole order and discipline of the universal Church. Indeed, it was established that the concession of the cup made long before by Paul III had caused far more harm than good. Moreover, the princes of Germany and the Hungarian envoys interceded on behalf of the Germans, the Hungarians and other peoples of those regions, not only Protestants but also Catholics who thirsted everywhere for the cup, asking that the same concession be made on the conditions Paul III had once approved. The Roman Pontiff, with the Cardinals, then gave some bishops of Germany the power to permit a similar rite, not absolutely, but where they found the reasons alleged to be true, with other conditions added. When this news reached Vienna, the people celebrated it with great joy and loud shouts. Cardinal Delfino, then Internuncio, wrote, as Cardinal Pallavicino relates in his most learned and erudite work in support of the Council of Trent, that the greater part of the heretics, having abjured their heresy, were brought back into the ancient concord of the Church of Rome. But such an inclination of mind vanished at once, like a lightning flash, as was discovered and openly acknowledged when the Council and the Pontiff refused the cup, the rigour of which was in no way an obstacle to the salvation of souls. Later, under the pontificates of Gregory XIII and Sixtus V, when some of the bishops to whom Pius had delegated this power had departed this life, it was doubted whether that power had been granted to the office, and so continued in their successors, or to the persons, and so would die out with their death. And it was agreed on the second point: that priests, unless those to whom that grace had been granted by the said bishops before their death, may not give the cup to the people. And you deny, Hottinger, with little shame, that this has ever been done among the Tridentine Papists, in order to elicit a quarrel. But just as, contrary to what you say, it has been done among the Tridentine Papists, so the quarrel you have attempted with malicious intent vanishes. But who could bear such ignorance with equanimity? Even after the Tridentine Papists, the King of the French, at his coronation, communicates under both kinds, as he did before the Council, as may be seen in the Ceremonial of French affairs published concerning Louis XIII, Henry IV and others. Hence the French envoys asked at Trent that, if it were decided otherwise and the cup were forbidden, this should be done without prejudice to the prerogative of their kings, who were accustomed to receive the cup at their coronation. This they obtained, and Catholic kings, and those joined to the Roman Church, communicate under both kinds from a Catholic priest after the Tridentine Papists. And do you dare to say Among the Tridentine Pontiffs it is never done?

units.la: Etiamnum hæres, & Allatius tibi suspectus est? euoluè aliorum scripta, quæ certè scio tibi iniucunda futura; Veruntâmen cum Pontificiorum sint, plena fidei fuerint. Henricus Henriquefius lib. 8. de Eucharist. cap. 44. Licet Papa, aut Concilio Generali ex honesta causa concedere id alicui nationi. Clemens Papa VI. legitur concessisse Regi Gallie, quoties vellet, ad cuius imitationem mos fluxit apud quosdam e Gallis non publice, sed in privatis cancellis communicandi sub utraque. Imperator dum coronatur, sumit utramque speciem. Apud quosdam corpus sanguini mixtum, seu intinctum datur omnibus in cochleari. Et supra dixerat; Dum Papa solemniter celebrat, sumpto corpore Christi sedet, & Diaconus Cardinalis defert ei Calicem bibendum, deinde ministrat eum aliis Cardinalibus etiam Diaconis: quod etiam nunc seruatur Parisiis apud Monasterium Cluniacense, & Dionysianum: Id tamen non de omnibus intelligendum est Cardinalibus, sed tantum cum Pontifice celebrantibus. Quod etiam apud Graecorum Collegii Alumnos, nunc ipsum sciente Romano Pontifice indulgenteque, dum solemniter celebratur cum ministrantibus singulis diebus festivis in more est. Franciscus Suarez in 3. partem D. Thomae Quaest. 8. sect. 3. De Clemente VI. refertur, hoc concessisse Regi Gallie Anno 1341. quia cum tota haec res sit iuris Ecclesiastici, per supremam Ecclesiae potestatem dispensationem recipit. Nunc autem pensatis omnibus, vix potest hoc exexpedire, & ad vitandum scandalum, & Haereticis omnem occasionem pertinaciae auferendam, & propter maiorem fidelium vnionem, & conformitatem. Quod tamen non obstat, quod si in aliquo casu consuetudo obtinuit, vt alicui detur vtraque species, talis consuetudo seruetur, vt Romae est consuetudo, vt Diaconus, qui in Missa solemni ministrat Pontifici, sub vtraque specie communicet. Quam tamen interdum praetermissam esse a Paulo II. in odium Hussitarum, & Boemorum refert Turrianus lib. 8. Constit. Clem. cap. 31. & Augustinus Patritius in libello de aduentu Federici Imperatoris Romani. Et, Vnde referunt Auctores citati Paulum III. dispensasse cum Boemis sub conditione, vt ab errore discederent, ipsis autem semper sentientibus, vtramque speciem esse necessariam, dispensatio locum non habuit. Vnde fit, vt remoto errore, possit Ecclesia hoc concedere, vt de Paulo dictum est. Et tandem, ne obruam te, Philippus Gamachaeus Doctor Sorbonicus in eandem partem D. Thomae Tract. de Sacrificio Missae c. 13. agens de Communione sub vtraque specie: Ecclesia non tam seuere hanc legem obseruat, quin aliquando grauissimis de causis in ea dispensat, vt constat ex Tridentino sess. 21. can. 4. & praesertim sess. 22. cap. vltimo, vbi totum hoc dispensationis negotium remittitur ad summum Pontificem, & re vevera summi Pontifices approbarunt, probantque hodie concessionem factam Regi Christianissimo per Clementem VI. vt bis in vita communicet sub utraque specie, semel quando inauguratur Rex, & semel in morte, sicut notat Gaspar Cassalius: Alij etiam extendunt, vt Rex Christianissimus communicet sub utraque specie, quoties libuerit; ita Henricesius lib. 8. cap. 44. Sed fides sit penes Auctorem: Nobis enim Bullam Clementis videre hactenus non licuit. Imperator quoque, dum coronatur, solet communionem accipere sub ambabus speciebus; & Concilium Basiliense voluit concedere calicem Boemis, dummodo haeresim suam abnegarent, de necessitate utriusque speciei, & quibusdam articulis subscriberent, qui habentur apud Taperium tract. de Commun. art. 5. Romae etiam est consuetudo, vt Diaconus ministrans summo Pontifici in Missa solemni, accipiat communionem sub utraque specie, quam tamen consuetudinem Paulus II. in odium Bohemorum aliquando intermisit, vt refert Turrianus 8. Constitut. Apostolic. cap. 31. Denique & in Conuentu Cluniacensi, & sancto Dionysiano prope Lutetiam eadem fertur esse consuetudo, vt qui ministrant ad Altare in Missa solemni, utramque speciem a celebrante accipiant, quemadmodum refert Sanctesius Episcopus de Eucharist. Repet. 10. cap. 2. sub finem, vbi hoc Privilegium refert ad Innocentium IV. Addere etiam possumus casum singularem, quo laicus ambas species accipere queat, si nempe Sacerdos in Missa deficeret post consecrationem, nec posset alius Sacerdos inveniri, qui consecratas species acciperet, Missamque perficeret; tum enim potest laicus calicem bibere, ne species corrumperentur, & acescerent: Idemque iudicium, ubi forte Sacerdos ab Hareticis ex altari per vim traheretur, deberet enim quivis laicus statim accipere, ne venirent in potestatem Hareticorum. Hinc notat Suarez dicto loco, quod non animaduertit Hottingerus. Graeci eundem usum observant, quamuis Graeci in hoc non videantur esse Schismatici, quia non ob eam consuetudinem ab Ecclesia Romana dissentiunt: neque de nostra consuetudine male sentiunt, quantum ego potui, vel audiendo, vel loquendo assequi. Ubi est modo Critopulus ille tuus, vel Sgutopulus, qui te ab infami mendacio, & infscitissima infscitia vindicet? Vim plura & recentiora? Urbanus VIII. in Confirm. Constitut. Collegij Graecorum Anno 1624. eiusdem Collegij Alumnis usum Calicis concedit. Audi verba; Vetus Ecclesiae consuetudo seruetur, ut octauo quoque die confiteantur, & quibus per aetatem licet decimo quoque die communicent. Praterea vero solemnibus diebus festis, ac Dominicis omnibus Adventus, & Quadragesima, idque ordinarie latino ritu, praterquam in Festo Paschatis, Pentecostes, & in festo Nativitatis Domini, aut si quando praeterea iustis de causis visum fuerit Protectori. Docentur autem a Confessario, aut alio spiritualibus rebus Præsecto, quomodo hac cum spirituali fructu peragant. Et ne verba tantum dedisse videretur, in Instructionibus pro dictis Constitutionibus vivae vocis oraculo datis Cardinalis S. Susannæ habetur; Communio ritu Græco ter in anno permittitur, non iubetur. Et potest Protector iustis de causis, hac in re dispensare; si tamen nihil impediat, videtur omnino usurpanda, ut intelligant Orientales, Romana Ecclesia non ritus, sed errores suos displicere. Esset enim hoc sine dubio incentivum dilectionis. Hoc indulto ter in anno dictis diebus festis ritu Græco Alumni publice communicant. Et Annis elapsis Augustissima Suecorum Regina die Divo Athanasio sacro in eiusdem templo, cum in solemni Missae celebratione maxima cum religione, pietateque interesset, & illi ego adhaerens ritus, & ceremonias evulgarem prope finem Missae vidit, ita in illius gratia mandante Protectore, eosdem Alumnos ad soleam procedentes a Metropolita Græco ritu Græco hoc est sub utraque specie Eucharistiam accipere. Et Hottingerus non veretur detecta fronte dicere; Hoc apud Pontificios Tridentinos nunquam fit? I nunc, & similibus fidem adhibe, qui somnia, ac figmenta sua pro oraculis Delphicis venditant, & sciolos decipiunt, salluntque omni fraude, & perfidia.
units.tr: Are you still stubborn, and is Allatius still suspect to you? Turn over the writings of others, which I know will be unwelcome to you, yet since they are Papists', they are certainly full of faith. Henricus Henriquez, book 8 on the Eucharist, chapter 44: The Pope or a General Council may for a good reason grant this to a nation. Pope Clement VI is read to have granted to the King of France that he might communicate under both kinds as often as he wished, and in imitation of this a custom has grown up among some Frenchmen of communicating under both kinds, not publicly but in private chancels. The Emperor, when he is crowned, receives both kinds. Among some, the body mixed or dipped in the blood is given to all on a spoon. And he had said above: When the Pope celebrates solemnly, after taking the body of Christ he sits, and the Cardinal deacon brings him the chalice to drink, then he serves it to the other Cardinals, who are also deacons. This is still observed at Paris in the monasteries of Cluny and Saint-Denis. This is not to be understood of all Cardinals, but only of those who celebrate with the Pope. This also is customary among the students of the Greek College, now indeed with the knowledge and indulgence of the Roman Pontiff, when they serve at a solemn celebration on every feast day. Francisco Suárez, on the third part of St Thomas, question 8, section 3: It is related that Clement VI granted this to the King of France in the year 1341, because the whole matter belongs to ecclesiastical law and admits of dispensation by the supreme power of the Church. But now, weighing all things, it can scarcely be expedient, both to avoid scandal and to remove from heretics every occasion of obstinacy, and for the greater union and conformity of the faithful. Nevertheless, this does not stand in the way: if in some case a custom has prevailed that both kinds be given to someone, such a custom should be kept, as it is the custom at Rome that the deacon who serves the Pope at a solemn Mass communicates under both kinds. Turrianus, book 8 on the Apostolic Constitutions, chapter 31, and Augustinus Patritius in his booklet on the coming of the Emperor Frederick the Roman, relate that this custom was sometimes omitted by Paul II out of hatred for the Hussites and Bohemians. And from the authors cited it appears that Paul III dispensed with the Bohemians on condition that they abandon their error, but since they always held that both kinds are necessary, the dispensation had no effect. Hence it follows that, once the error is removed, the Church can grant this, as was said of Paul. And finally, lest I overwhelm you, Philip Gamache, Doctor of the Sorbonne, in the same part of St Thomas, Tract on the Sacrifice of the Mass, chapter 13, treating of communion under both kinds, says: The Church does not observe this law so strictly that it never dispenses from it on very grave grounds, as is clear from Trent, session 21, canon 4, and especially session 22, last chapter, where the whole business of dispensation is referred to the supreme Pontiff. And in fact the supreme Pontiffs have approved, and today approve, the concession made to the Most Christian King by Clement VI, that he may communicate twice in his life under both kinds, once when the King is inaugurated and once at his death, as Gaspar Cassalius notes. Others extend it so that the Most Christian King may communicate under both kinds as often as he pleases; so Henricesius, book 8, chapter 44. But let the author answer for it, for we have not hitherto been permitted to see Clement's Bull. The Emperor too, when he is crowned, is accustomed to receive communion under both kinds; and the Council of Basel wished to grant the cup to the Bohemians, provided they renounced their heresy about the necessity of both kinds and subscribed to certain articles, which are found in Taperus, tract on communion, article 5. At Rome too there is the custom that the deacon serving the supreme Pontiff at a solemn Mass receives communion under both kinds; yet Paul II sometimes discontinued this custom out of hatred for the Bohemians, as Turrianus relates, book 8 of the Apostolic Constitutions, chapter 31. Finally, at the Cluny monastery and at the church of Saint-Denis near Paris the same custom is said to exist, that those who minister at the altar at a solemn Mass receive both kinds from the celebrant, as Sanctesius, bishop, relates in his Repetition on the Eucharist, book 10, chapter 2, near the end, where he refers this privilege to Innocent IV. We may also add a singular case in which a layman may receive both kinds: namely, if the priest should fail during Mass after the consecration and no other priest could be found to receive the consecrated species and complete the Mass; then a layman may drink from the chalice, so that the species not be corrupted and turn sour. The same judgement applies where perhaps a priest is dragged from the altar by heretics by force, for any layman ought at once to receive, lest the species fall into the power of the heretics. Hence Suárez, in the place cited, observes what Hottinger did not notice. The Greeks observe the same practice, although the Greeks do not seem to be schismatics in this, because they do not dissent from the Roman Church on account of this custom. Nor do they think ill of our custom, as far as I was able to gather, either by hearing or by speaking. Where now is that Critopulus of yours, or Sgouropulos, to clear you of your infamous lie and most ignorant ignorance? Why do I say more, and of more recent date? Urban VIII, in confirming the Constitution of the Greek College in the year 1624, grants the use of the cup to the students of that same College. Hear the words: The ancient custom of the Church shall be kept, so that they confess every eighth day, and those who by age are permitted communicate every tenth day. Moreover, on solemn feast days and all the Sundays of Advent and Lent, and ordinarily in the Latin rite, except on the feast of Easter, Pentecost and the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, or at other times if it seems fitting to the Protector for just reasons. They are taught by their confessor, or by another prefect of spiritual matters, how to carry these out with spiritual fruit. And lest it seem that he had merely given words, the Cardinal of Santa Susanna is found in the Instructions given with the said Constitutions by the living voice of the oracle: Communion in the Greek rite is permitted three times a year, not commanded. And the Protector may dispense in this matter for just reasons; yet if nothing hinders, it seems altogether to be practised, so that the Orientals may understand that the Roman Church dislikes not their rites, but their errors.
