For this would undoubtedly be an incentive to love. By this indult, on the said feast days three times a year, the students of the Greek College communicate publicly in the Greek rite. And in recent years the most august Queen of the Swedes, on the feast of St Athanasius, being present in the same church with the greatest reverence and piety at the solemn celebration of Mass, and I, adhering to that rite, was making known its ceremonies, saw near the end of Mass that, at her request and at the command of the Protector, the same students, advancing to the step, received the Eucharist from the Greek Metropolitan in the Greek rite, that is, under both kinds. And Hottinger does not fear to say with a bare brow: Among the Tridentine Papists this is never done? Go now, and put faith in such things, you who hawk your dreams and fictions as Delphic oracles, and deceive the half-learned, and trick them with every fraud and treachery.

units.la: Vis dicam Hottingere? Miseret me tui, qui Typographum nactus minus accuratiorem, illius incuria subtractione negatiuæ vocula nugatoriæ sententiæ, in crimen vocaris. Puto siquidem te, ne vapules, nonnunquam scripsisse: sicque dedisse Typographo. Hoc apud Pontificios Tridentinos nonnunquam fit. Esto, si tamen gratum accesserit. Sed quo decedet discrimen? inanes in auras. Argumentemur ergo. Allatius negat semper Eucharistiam in Ecclesia Græca cōsumi sub utraque specie, sed id fieri aliquando: sed aliquando etiam fit apud Pontifices Tridentinos, ut sub utraque specie non sacrificantes communicent. Ergo est tamen aliquod discrimen. Ergo Ecclesia Romana a Græca in communionis ritu dissidet. Veruntamen cum ex errore Typographi consensus Ecclesiarum appareat, & scopus sit Hottingero probare dissensum, remanet probatum, in summa omnium rerum, earum etiam, quas vel pueri norunt, ignoratione versari, & præter æquum, & bonum indolere, cum illi Allatius inscitiæ maculam appingit. Non est quod id acceptum referas Allatio: In te culpa residet huius rei. Et tandem cum jam tibi saltandum est, decet audacem esse confidenter pro te, & Typographo proterua loquere, & rota figulari versutior, da verba, falle etiam sciens, vt præruptiorem saltum effugias. O si ex cœnoso illo tuo, putidoque rerum Grammaticarum penu ad hæc aliquando, & nunquam concilianda, vt in hac tua disputatione Apologetica de vernacula Græcorum lingua aliquod acutulum quærendo inuestigaueris! Si memoria non suggerit. concinna illa originaliter, & opposite, ab integro Lectoribus gemina. Fac sis, recoque. Non mouebunt stomacho fastidium.
units.tr: Shall I tell you, Hottinger? I pity you. You got hold of a careless printer, and now you are being called to account for the loss, through his negligence, of one little negative word in a trifling sentence. I suppose you wrote, to keep yourself from a beating, that this sometimes happens among the Tridentine Papists. Very well, if you like. But what difference does that make? It is wind in the air. Let us argue it out. Allatius denies that the Eucharist is always consumed in the Greek Church under both kinds, but says that it sometimes is. Yet among the Tridentine Papists it sometimes also happens that those who are not celebrating communicate under both kinds. So there is still some difference. Therefore the Roman Church differs from the Greek in the rite of communion. Nevertheless, since the agreement of the Churches appears in spite of the printer's error, and Hottinger's aim is to prove disagreement, it remains proved that, in the sum of all things, even those which boys know, he is at fault through ignorance, and grieves beyond what is fair and good, when Allatius charges him with a stain of ignorance. You need not blame Allatius for this: the fault lies in you. And finally, since you must now dance, you should be bold and speak with confidence on your own behalf and the printer's, and be shameless. Like a potter's wheel, be more cunning: give out words, and deceive even knowingly, so that you may escape the steeper leap. Oh, if only you had searched out from that muddy, stinking store of grammar some clever point for reconciling these sometimes and never in your Apologetic Disputation on the vernacular language of the Greeks! If memory does not supply it, those neat phrases originaliter and opposite will serve your readers twice over. Do so, and reheat them. They will not stir disgust in the stomach.

units.la: Quamquam ne hoc quidem largiantur Graci, quorum nomine Leo falsitatis manifestæ convincitur. Critopulus Consef. Ecclesiæ Orientalis nuperrima. An non ridiculus est Hottingerus, qui ad conuellendam universam Græcorum multitudinem, vnum Critopulum in testem adducit? Ego palam edico, me hoc profiteri, & credere verbis expressis, & scripto etiam palam facio. Irrepit nescio quis ex Orci faucibus, vt ita dicam; & scribit, me aliter, atq; pronuncio, vel scribo, sentire. Cui magis adhibenda fides est, mimihi ne, qui in bono lumine meam sententiam effero, an dicenti contrarium? Si impudens non sum, credam absque dubio illi, qui de se sciens loquitur, quam externis, & aduenis. Inquirimus nunc de sententia Ecclesiæ Græcæ; ipsa in suis libris loquitur & exponit plurimum sententiam suam per se, non alieno interprete, & Hottingerus obgannit, & nodum in scyrpo quærit. Ne illi peropportune Terrentius responderet; Dignus es cum tua religione odio. Unum Critopulum universæ Græcorum Ecclesiæ, & consuetudini indubitanter receptæ præponit, quia pro eo esse videtur. Et dicemus, hunc hominem aut non falsum sentire, aut quod non satis explorate perceptum sit, & cognitum, cum aliqua deliberatione defendere non suscepisse? Ego Critopulum istum ad meam rationem usumque nihil æstimo. Sed Hottingerus, ut falsitatis convincat Allatium, ex non intellecto Critopuli dicto, reclamante ratione vera, ratiocinationem adulterat. Et vide; Allatius scribit, non semper Græcos communicare sub utraque specie, Critopulus dicit; omnes utramque speciem communicant, panis inquam, & Calicis, tam Ecclesiastici, quam laici, tam viri, quam fœminæ, quia omnes vitæ indigeant. Allatius unus est, unus est & Critopulus, cuius dictum potius est? Sed esto Critopulus sit fide dignior apud Hottingerum. Quid dicitCritopulus, quod repugnans Allatio sit? Vbi nam illud, semper in Critopulo sub utraque specie, & nunquam sub una, ut falsitatis Allatius convincatur? Rudis hic, ne dicam falsarius, plane arguitur Hottingerus, sicuti etiam alibi saepius in argumentis digerendis,quod aut inertissimae segnitiae est, aut fastidii delicatissimi, nisi mavis dicere, perversi, & malignissimi capitis, improbitatis nequissimae, qua conatur ille fallacias in parum cautos intendere. Sed ut prudentior videaris, adde tu de tuo dictis Critopuli; illud semper, vel quid simile.
units.tr: Although the Greeks do not even grant this, and in their name Leo is convicted of manifest falsehood. Critopulus, in the most recent Confession of the Eastern Church. Is not Hottinger ridiculous, who, to overthrow the whole multitude of the Greeks, brings forward one Critopulus as his witness? I openly declare that I profess this and believe it in express words, and I also make it plain in writing. Someone, I know not who, has crept out of the jaws of Orcus, so to speak, and writes that I think otherwise than I declare or write. Which account deserves more trust: mine, who set out my own opinion in a clear light, or that of one who says the opposite? If I am not shameless, I shall without doubt believe him who speaks knowingly of himself, rather than outsiders and strangers. We are now enquiring into the opinion of the Greek Church. She herself, in her own books, speaks and sets out her opinion very largely by herself, not through an alien interpreter; and Hottinger yaps and seeks a knot in a rush. To him Terence would aptly reply: You deserve to be hated along with your religion. He puts one Critopulus before the whole Greek Church and its undoubtedly received custom, because he seems to favour his view. Shall we say that this man either does not hold a false opinion, or that he did not undertake, with some deliberation, to defend what had not been sufficiently explored and understood? I value that Critopulus at nothing for my reasoning or my practice. But Hottinger, in order to convict Allatius of falsehood, distorts his reasoning on the basis of Critopulus' words, which he has not understood, while true reason cries out against him. And see: Allatius writes that the Greeks do not always communicate under both kinds. Critopulus says: All communicate under both kinds, I mean bread and cup, both ecclesiastical and lay, both men and women, because all need life. Allatius is one, and Critopulus is one: whose statement is more authoritative? But grant that Critopulus is more trustworthy in Hottinger's eyes. What does Critopulus say that contradicts Allatius? Where is that word always in Critopulus, concerning both kinds, and never under one, by which Allatius might be convicted of falsehood? This crude fellow, not to say forger, is plainly shown up as Hottinger, who, as he does elsewhere too in marshalling his arguments, is either most idle in sluggishness or of the most fastidious taste, or, if you prefer to say, of a perverse and most malicious head, of the most wicked dishonesty, by which he tries to direct his fallacies at those who are too little on their guard. But so that you may seem more prudent, add to Critopulus' words, from your own store, the word always, or something like it.

units.la: Discrimen ἀζύμου καὶ ἐζύμῳ[?] multorum ipse probat Allatius auctoritate, sed cui bono? Jam video. Bonum parum, vel nullum est Hottingero, res sacras multorum auctoritate improbari. Et negabis solem meridianum tibi tenebras offudisse, qui in rebus adiaphoris discrimen, & dissidium agnoscis? Graeci, quod primum est, vino aquam miscent, quod faciunt etiam Pontificii. Proba diffensum; & argue, si potes, falsitatis tantorum hominum testimonia. Azymum & fermentatum videntur differre, attamen panis sunt, & in utroque fieri Sacramentum tum Graeci tum Latini fatentur, & usum ilillius nullum inter Ecclesias afferre discrimen. Ergo quod ipse discrimen somniaris, nullũ est. Quod si Græci in Azymo conficerent iam cuiusmodi consensio est.Sed errore typographi mihi ascripsit Allatius. Dicam quid primo intuitu senserim. Putaui, Græcos conficere in Azymo errore esse Typographi. Verumtamen cum te in similibus infantem, & rerum Græcarum inscium in tot alijs offendissem, mutata sententia exclamaui. Hoc quoque mendum sane Hottingeri est. Sed quando vis ita esse, errati veniam. Typographo tuo dabimus, non ideo tamen te negabimus in Ecclesiæ Græcæ, quemadmodum & Latinæ ritibus peregrinari. Quod si, vt tu ais, vnum hoc ex addiaphoris est, qua ratione inter dissidia insulse collocas. ideoque tibi non suffragatur, quod nonnulli ex Pontificijs dicunt, sententiam illam esse erroneam, vel hæreticam.
units.tr: The difference between the unleavened and the leavened [ἀζύμου καὶ ἐζύμου], as Allatius himself proves by the authority of many. But to what good? I see it now. It does Hottinger little or no good to have sacred matters condemned by the authority of many. And will you deny that the noonday sun has shed darkness on you, when you recognise a difference and a dissent in matters indifferent? First, the Greeks mix water with wine, and the Papists do the same. Prove the dissent, and refute, if you can, the testimony of such great men as false. The unleavened and the leavened seem to differ, yet both are bread; and both the Greeks and the Latins confess that the Sacrament is effected in either, and that the use of either introduces no difference between the Churches. Therefore the difference you dream up is nothing. If the Greeks consecrated in unleavened bread, what kind of agreement would that be? But Allatius has ascribed the matter to me as a printer's error. I shall say what I thought at first sight. I thought the Greeks' consecration in unleavened bread was a printer's error. But when I had found you in similar matters, a child and ignorant of Greek affairs, in so many others, I changed my opinion and cried out. This blunder too is certainly Hottinger's own. But, since you want it so, we will grant you pardon for the error. We shall give the credit to your printer. Yet we shall not deny that you wander in the rites of the Greek Church just as you do in the Latin. And if, as you say, this one is among the indifferent matters, then by what reasoning do you foolishly place it among the disputed points? Therefore the claim that some Papists call that opinion erroneous or heretical does not support you.

units.la: De igne Purgatorio, quid ruspatur Allatius? Hodierni Græci diserte testantur eos, qui ab ipso statim tempore ἀναλύσεως[?] beata Dei fruuntur visione, nullam pœnam sustinere neque materialem, neque organicam, neque per ignem, neque per qualemcunque materiam aliam. Quid Græci antiqui, & recentiores testentur, mirum est, quod non legeris in Allatio. Sed quando illa obuia non fuere, audi. Græci omnes pro mortuis non tantum quotidie in Missa orant, & præscriptis etiam diebus per annum, vt Sabbatis omnibus, & potissimum mensis Octobris, & peculiari commemoratione ante magnam Quadragesimam, Deum orant, & defunctorum memoriam religiosissime recolunt: orant & Pontificij, vt illis remittantur peccata, expurgentur, collocentur, vbi iusti quiete perfruuntur, eo consilio, vt a molestijs, horrendisque inferni tormentis, stridore dentium, densa caligine, tenebris exterioribus, vigilante perpetuo verme, lacrymis infructuosis, tristitijs, suspirijs, & quod magis est, igne, & reponantur in sinum Abrahæ, in quietis tabernaculis, vbi festum agentium perpetuum est gaudium, in amoenitatis locis, vnde vitæ fluenta emanant, in loco luminoso, in loco viridi, in loco relaxationis. &c. Eadem pro suis mortuis Latini comprecantur. Et tu Hottingere poenas materiales, & organicas ex opinione Græcæ Ecclesiæ poscis? Poenæ sunt, ignis est, quibus expurgantur a peccatis animæ ἐν τῷ καθαριζομένῳ[?]. vt Græci insinuant, & tu Purgatorium inuestigas? Verbis, sententijsque in Purgatorio exponendo Græci, & Pontificij concordant, & tu dissidium intermisces? Afferentes ista non sunt errones, & & vagi, & stipem emendicantes, vt sunt tuus iste Critopulus, & Zygomala, sed eloquentia, gravitate, honore Ecclesiæ Græcæ florentissimi, & quod magis est, Ecclesia ipsa Græca in suis Ritualibus libris, & expressis verbis largiuntur, & tu audes, quasi legendi nescius sis, affirmare, eos Purgatorium Romanum ignorare, & ritum orandi retinere, vt ex viatoribus fiant spectatores? Opinione Græcorum, iusti ipsi, qui nondum absolute pœnitentiam egerunt, sed remanet illis aliquid expurgandum, plane viatores sunt. Adhuc enim in tormentis & igne peregrinabundi oberrant, & afflictionibus, & igne spurcitiem, & impietatem peccatorum sese spoliant; donec depurgati in peroptatam gloriam introducantur. Vide quæ Epistola ad D. Boineburgium digessi. Plura alia sunt, quæ prætereo, leviter tamen unum tangam. Methodius respondet Theodoræ Imperatrici, quæ rogaverat Patres, vt orarent Deum, vt dimitteret delicta Theophilo marito, quæ ille commiserat pro oppugnatione Imaginum, in vita Michaëlis filij Theophili. Οὔ̓ μὲν οὖν δίκαια ἡ ὀρθόδοξος Ἐκκλησία, καὶ ὁ ταύτης ἐξάρχων Μεθόδιος ἔφασκε διαπονεῖν [?], ἐ δ' ἡμᾶς ἐχρῆν ἀπαναίνεσθαι. Δίκαιον δὲ τῆς ἀρχοῦσι, τὰς ... ἀπιπ-[?] ἀδ̓ς ἀλλ' ἱλῶς, ὅταν μὴ τύραννον ἀρχὴν [?] ἀλλ' ἴσῃ γνώμῃ φιλῆς. ἀλλ' ἔπω Θεοῦ δίκῃ ἡμᾶς τὴν ἀφεῖς ἄλλον βίον ἐξαβεβηκέναι Θωσὶ[?] ἐξαγεῖν δὲ τὰ ἑαυτῶν ἡμᾶς φαντασιώδεις[?]. Διωγμὸς μὲν ἡμᾶς, καὶ κλέας ἐαυτὸν παρὰ θεὸν ἐν τῷ Θεοῦ τὸ βελτιοῦ[?] πᾶσιν αὐτοῖς νικῶσι ἡμᾶς, ἀλλὰ τῆς κῶν τῶν τὸν βίον ἐν οἰκονομικοῖς περιεῖν ἀλλαχοῦ μεταστῶσιν. Ἐπὶ δ' ὅ τε καὶ τοῖς μὴ δισταμένοις ὅσον τι μικρὰ σφάλματα ἡ, καὶ μετάνοια τοῖς θεσμοῖς. Τοῖς δ' ὕδη μὴ πονηρᾶν ἐλπίδων ἀπάτησιν, καὶ πρὸς δόλον φέρειν τῷ καταγωγῇ, ἐχ' εἶ πει τα τῶν ἀθυμίας ἀγαλύειν τέττις ἡμᾶς.
units.tr: On the Purgatorial fire, what does Allatius rake up? The present-day Greeks clearly testify that those who enjoy the blessed vision of God from the moment of their [ἀναλύσεως] departure suffer no punishment, neither material nor organic, neither by fire nor by any other kind of matter. It is surprising that you have not read in Allatius what the ancient and more recent Greeks testify. But since those witnesses were not at hand, listen. All the Greeks pray to God for the dead, not only daily in the Mass, but also on appointed days through the year, such as all Saturdays, and especially in the month of October, and by a special commemoration before Great Lent; and they most devoutly recall the memory of the departed. The Papists also pray that their sins may be forgiven, that they may be purged and placed where the just enjoy rest, with this purpose: that they may be spared the troubles and dreadful torments of hell, the gnashing of teeth, the thick darkness, the outer darkness, the ever-watchful worm, the fruitless tears, sorrows, sighs, and, what is more, fire; and that they may be placed in the bosom of Abraham, in the tabernacles of rest, where those who keep the feast have perpetual joy, in places of pleasantness whence streams of life flow, in a luminous place, in a green place, in a place of refreshment, and so on. The Latins likewise pray in the same words for their dead. And do you, Hottinger, demand material and organic punishments from the opinion of the Greek Church? There are punishments, there is fire, by which souls are purged of their sins [ἐν τῷ καθαριζομένῳ], as the Greeks hint; and do you still look for a Purgatory? Do the Greeks and the Papists agree in their words and statements about explaining Purgatory, and do you still mix in dissent? Those who advance these things are not errant, vagrant beggars soliciting alms, like your Critopulus and Zygomalas, but men flourishing in eloquence, gravity and honour of the Greek Church; and, what is more, the Greek Church herself grants them in her ritual books, in express words. And do you dare, as if you did not know how to read, to affirm that they are ignorant of the Roman Purgatory and keep the practice of prayer, so that from wayfarers they become spectators? In the opinion of the Greeks, the just themselves, who have not yet fully completed repentance but still have something to be purged, are plainly wayfarers. For they still wander as pilgrims in torments and fire, and by afflictions and fire they strip themselves of the filth and impiety of their sins, until, thoroughly cleansed, they are led into the longed-for glory. See what I set out in my letter to Dominus Boineburg. There are many other things which I pass over, but I will touch lightly on one. Methodius answers the Empress Theodora, who had asked the Fathers to pray God to forgive the sins which her husband Theophilus had committed in the persecution of the Images, in the life of Michael, son of Theophilus. [Οὐ μὲν οὖν δίκαια ἡ ὀρθόδοξος Ἐκκλησία καὶ ὁ ταύτης ἐξάρχων Μεθόδιος ἔφασκε] The Orthodox Church and its leader Methodius said that these things were not just; and we ought not to refuse them. It is right for rulers, when they do not rule by tyranny but with an equal and friendly mind, to receive the benefits due to them. But, by God's justice, we who have departed into another life are not free of the disturbances of the flesh [ἐξαγεῖν δὲ τὰ ἑαυτῶν], and we bear the burden of our own failings. Persecution and the prayers of the pious have been granted to those who do not doubt that small faults may still be cleansed, and that there is repentance under the laws; but for those who have now cast away wicked hopes, and bear their sins in deceit, the time of despair is near.

units.la: Iusta itaq; Ecclesia Orthodoxa, & illius Praefes Methodius, Domina, dicit, expostulat, nec nos id possumus abnegare. Iustum enim est de nobis benemeritis, & Principibus condignas gratias affluenter dependere, quando non imperat violenta manus, sed est affensus Deo dilectus. Sed non dum Dei iustitiam nos ab eo, qui ad aliam vitam transmigravit, possumus deflectere, qua supra nos sunt, imaginatione complectentes. Possumus equidem nos, quibus concredita sunt claves Coelorum a Deo volentibus omnibus reserare, sed illis, qui adhuc in hac vita degunt, antequam ad alia transmigrent. quandoque etiam illis, qui extremum diem morte conficiunt, cum errata parua sunt, & de illis poenitentia transfacta est. Qui vero ex hac vita cum spe non bona abierunt, & manifestam cum semetipsis damnationem asportantibus, illis culpam nos dissoluere non possumus.
units.tr: Therefore the Orthodox Church, and its prefect Methodius, rightly complain, and we cannot deny it. It is just to repay our benefactors and princes with fitting thanks, when no violent hand commands it but the consent is one dear to God. Yet we cannot turn God's justice aside from the one who has passed into another life, by picturing him in some imagined place above us. We indeed, to whom the keys of heaven have been entrusted, can unlock it for all who are willing, but only for those who still live in this life, before they pass into another. Sometimes we can do so even for those who finish their last day in death, when their errors were slight and repentance for them has been completed. But those who have departed this life without good hope, carrying with them a manifest damnation, we cannot absolve of their guilt.

units.la: Indulgentiarum mercatum defendere non audet Allatius. Hac tua disputatione Apologetica nihil aliud assequeris Hottingere, nisi ut ab omnibus mortalibus audacia tua atq; improbitas agnoscatur. Non defendit Allatius Indulgentiarum mercatum, quem nunquam defensurus est. Aliud est Indulgentias concedere, aliud est Indulgentias mercari: sicuti aliud est Sacramenta ministrare, aliud vendere. Indulgentias concedunt Pontificii, Sacramenta ministrant, ea nundinantes uti sacrilegos detestantur, & poenis admonent, ijsque grauissimis. Quid in Germania factum sit, quamuis Græcus Allatius, ex ipsis Germanis, eorumque historiis abunde novit, quos impostoribus & falsariis universis præfert, quorum archiva non ea sunt, ut Pontificiis anteponenda veniant. Sed hoc ad rem meam non pertinet, qui consensionem stabilio. Ut tamen in hisquoque appareat consensus, & tu salsus esse in hoc quoque deprehendaris, producam tibi ex ipsis Græcorum monumentis Indulgentiarum formulam, unde argui potest contra atque tu dicis, Græcos ipsas non reijcere Indulgentias. Georgius siue Gregorius Cyprus Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus concessit Indulgentiam Christianis visitantibus partem columnæ, in qua alalligatus fuerat Christus, cuius tenor talis est; Ὁ πάντα ὑπομείνας ἑκὼν κύριος, καὶ Θεὸς ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς δι' ἑαυτοῦ τὴν ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίαν τὰ ἐπονείδιστα πάθη [?] τῆς θείας, καὶ ἀχρὰς αὐτὸς σαρκὸς, καὶ τοῦτο καταδέξατο ἀληθῶς ἐν κίσι [?], καὶ μαστιχθῶν ὑπὸ τῆς ἀνόμων. Ἐπεὶ δὲ οἱ φιλόθεοι Χριστιανοὶ ἐν τῇ κίονι [?] διαλογεῖς μέρη, καὶ ἕκα-στος τῆς ἀνθρώπων προσέρχεσθαι ποιεῖται μεταλαμβάνειν τὸ ἁγιασμὸς τῆς ἀγίας [?] σωματικὴς παραχωρήσεως, καὶ ἀχρεῖτω σῶμα ἐν τῷ πάθει καιρὸς, ἔστιν ἰδεῖν ἐν πολλοῖς τόποις, καὶ χώρας, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἄλλων μερῶν, ἐξ ἀπ' αὐτοῦ τῆς κίονος. Ὅθεν καὶ τὸ μέρος τοῦ ἐκείνῃ λαβόντες φιλόθεοι ἀνθρώποι κατέχον μένει τῷ γυῷ, τῷ ἁγιασμῷ ἀπολαμβάνοντες, καὶ τῆς βοηθείας αὐτῶν. Τὸ γυῦ δὲ κοινὸν ἀγαθὸν ὄν, καὶ κοινῶς προσπωνεῖς ὑπὸ τῆς Χριστιανῶν ὡς εἰκὸς δικαίων. Ὅθεν καὶ προσετέθη, καὶ ἀφιερώθη τῆς ἱερᾶς ναοῦ τῷ ἁγίῳ μὲ παμμάκαρος Νικολάος εἰς Ὁ ὑπὸ παντῶν προσκυνεῖσθαι, ὡς προσελήνιος τῆς παναχράντου, καὶ ἀμωμήτῳ σῶμα τῷ Χριστῷ. Διὸ καὶ οὖν μὴ ἐξομολογήσεως, Ὁ μὴ συνζιβῆς καρδίας προσερχομένους, καὶ προσπωνῆσας τὸ ὀφθῆμον τῆς τιμᾶ τῆς ἱερᾶς κίονος, ἐχθὴ μεζιότης ἡμῶν ἀπὸ τῆς δωθείσης αὐτῇ δωρεᾶς τε, καὶ χαρίτῳ, καὶ ἐξουσίας τῆς παναγίας, καὶ ζωαρχικῇ πνεύματος συγκεχωρημένους τῇ τῶν τῆς Ῥωμαϊκῆς, καὶ ἰσῆς Ἐκκλησίας τάξιν ἡμέρας ἑκάτον. Ὀφείλουσιν οὖν ἅπαντες οἱ προσερχόμενοι μὴ φόβῳ, Ὁ ἐξομολογήσεως, καὶ ἀγάπης Χριστῷ τῷ ἀληθινῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν, τῷ πάντων Δικαιωτῇ, ἵνα ἀφαρπάσῃ ἡμᾶς ἐκ τῆς δελεάσεως τὸ ἐχθρὸν περιέχοντος, ὅπως καὶ ἐλογίας καὶ ἁγιασμῷ ὅπου τύχῃ ἕκαστος αὐτῶν, ἐ τῇ περιτομῶν αὐτῶν βοήθειαν. Εἰδένης καὶ προσενέγκοι τῇ προσπωπήσεως χάριν, ὁ Ζιῶτος πολλῆς ἀμοιβῆς ἀξιωθήσε, τῷ πλεονοδώρῳ, καὶ Δωτῆρι τῆς ἀγαθῶν Θεᾷ, ἐ ἡ χάρεις, καὶ τὸ ἐλεῶν, καὶ ἡ βοήθεια ἐν μὴ πάντων τῆς μὴ πίστεως προσεργαζομένων, καταπάσῃ ἐκ[?]. ἀμὴν. Γεννάδιῳ ἐλέῳ Θεῷ Ἀρχιεπισκόπῳ Κωνσταντινουπολεως, ἐ οἰκουμενικὸς Πατριάρχης. Qui omnes sustinuit libens Dominus, & Deus noster Iesus Christus propter hominum salutem ignominiosas passiones aduersus diuinam, sanctamque suam carnem: & inter eas id quoque perpessus est, columnæ alligari, & flagellis cædi ab impijs.
units.tr: Allatius does not dare to defend the trade in indulgences. By this apologetic disputation of yours, Hottinger, you achieve nothing except to have your audacity and wickedness recognised by all mortals. Allatius does not defend the trade in indulgences, and he never will. It is one thing to grant indulgences and another to trade in them, just as it is one thing to administer the sacraments and another to sell them. The Papists grant indulgences and administer the sacraments. They denounce as sacrilegious those who peddle them and punish them with the severest penalties. Allatius, a Greek, knows well enough from the Germans themselves and from their histories what happened in Germany, and he prefers them to all impostors and forgers. Their archives, however, are not such as to be set before those of the Papists. But this does not bear on my purpose, which is to establish the consensus. So that consensus may appear in this matter too, and so that you may be shown to be false here as well, I will produce for you from the Greeks' own monuments a formula of indulgence. From it one can argue, contrary to what you claim, that the Greeks do not reject indulgences. Georgius, or Gregorius, of Cyprus, Patriarch of Constantinople, granted an indulgence to Christians who visit the part of the column to which Christ was bound. Its wording is as follows: "The Lord who willingly endured all things, our God Jesus Christ, for the salvation of men, through himself underwent shameful sufferings, and in his own flesh, truly undergoing this in the ..., was scourged by the lawless. Since the God-loving Christians have divided the column into parts, and each of those who come wishes to partake of the sanctification of that bodily ... which touched his body at the time of the passion, it is possible to see it in many places and regions, and from other parts, and from the column itself. Whence also the God-loving people who have received a part of it keep it with reverence, receiving sanctification and help from it. The wood, being a common good, is commonly venerated by Christians as is fitting. Whence it was also added to, and dedicated in, the holy temple to the saint Nicholas, to be worshipped by all as having touched the most pure and immaculate body of Christ. Therefore we, the Patriarch, seeing those who come with contrite hearts and kissing the honoured place of the holy column, grant to them, from the gift, grace and authority given to it by the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, the same remission as the order of the Roman and holy Church grants every day. All who come must therefore come with fear, faith and love of Christ our true God, the Judge of all, so that he may snatch us from the snares of the enemy, and each of them, wherever he may obtain the sanctification, may receive help from his veneration. Whoever shall have offered alms for the grace of the veneration shall be deemed worthy of great reward from the bountiful Giver of good things, God, whose grace, mercy and help be with all who labour in faith. Amen. To Gennadius, by the mercy of God Archbishop of Constantinople and ecumenical Patriarch." [Ὁ πάντα ὑπομείνας ἑκὼν κύριος, καὶ Θεὸς ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς δι' ἑαυτοῦ τὴν ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίαν τὰ ἐπονείδιστα πάθη τῆς θείας, καὶ ἀχράντου αὐτοῦ σαρκὸς, καὶ τοῦτο καταδέξατο ἀληθῶς ἐν στήλῃ, καὶ μαστιγωθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνόμων. Ἐπεὶ δὲ οἱ φιλόθεοι Χριστιανοὶ τὴν κίονα διελόντες μέρη, καὶ ἕκαστος τῶν ἀνθρώπων προσέρχεσθαι ποιεῖται μεταλαμβάνειν τὸν ἁγιασμὸν τῆς ἁγίας σωματικῆς παραχωρήσεως, καὶ ἁψαμένου σῶμα ἐν τῷ πάθει καιρὸς, ἔστιν ἰδεῖν ἐν πολλοῖς τόποις, καὶ χώραις, καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἄλλων μερῶν, ἐξ ἀπ' αὐτοῦ τῆς κίονος. Ὅθεν καὶ τὸ μέρος τοῦ ἐκείθεν λαβόντες φιλόθεοι ἄνθρωποι κατέχουσι μετὰ εὐλαβείας, τῷ ἁγιασμῷ ἀπολαμβάνοντες, καὶ τῆς βοηθείας αὐτῶν. Τὸ ξύλον δὲ κοινὸν ἀγαθὸν ὄν, καὶ κοινῶς προσκυνεῖται ὑπὸ τῶν Χριστιανῶν ὡς εἰκὸς δικαίων. Ὅθεν καὶ προσετέθη, καὶ ἀφιερώθη τῷ ἱερῷ ναῷ τῷ ἁγίῳ μὲ παμμάκαρος Νικολάος εἰς Ὁ ὑπὸ πάντων προσκυνεῖσθαι, ὡς προσηνέχθαι τῷ παναχράντῳ, καὶ ἀμωμήτῳ σώματι τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Διὸ καὶ ἡμεῖς οὖν μὴ ἐξομολογήσεως, ὁ μὴ συντριβῆς καρδίας προσερχομένους, καὶ προσκυνήσαντας τὸ ὀφθὲν τῆς τιμῆς τῆς ἱερᾶς κίονος, ἐχθὲς μεζίονα ἡμῶν ἀπὸ τῆς δοθείσης αὐτῇ δωρεᾶς τε, καὶ χάριτος, καὶ ἐξουσίας τῆς παναγίας, καὶ ζωαρχικῆς πνεύματος συγκεχωρημένους τῇ τῶν τῆς Ῥωμαϊκῆς, καὶ ἁγίας Ἐκκλησίας τάξιν ἡμέρας ἑκάστης. Ὀφείλουσιν οὖν ἅπαντες οἱ προσερχόμενοι μετὰ φόβου, πίστεως, καὶ ἀγάπης Χριστῷ τῷ ἀληθινῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν, τῷ πάντων Δικαιωτῇ, ἵνα ἀφαρπάσῃ ἡμᾶς ἐκ τῆς δελεάσεως τοῦ ἐχθροῦ περιέχοντος, ὅπως καὶ ἐλεημοσύνης καὶ ἁγιασμοῦ ὅπου τύχῃ ἕκαστος αὐτῶν, ἐκ τῆς περιποιήσεως αὐτῶν βοήθειαν. Εἴ τις καὶ προσενέγκοι τῆς προσκυνήσεως χάριν, ὁ γὰρ πολλῆς ἀμοιβῆς ἀξιωθήσεται, παρὰ τοῦ πλουσιοδώρου, καὶ Δωτῆρος τῶν ἀγαθῶν Θεοῦ, οὗ ἡ χάρις, καὶ τὸ ἔλεος, καὶ ἡ βοήθεια ἐν μετὰ πάντων τῶν μετὰ πίστεως προσεργαζομένων, ἀμήν. Γεννάδιῳ ἐλέῳ Θεοῦ Ἀρχιεπισκόπῳ Κωνσταντινουπόλεως, καὶ οἰκουμενικῷ Πατριάρχῃ.]

units.la: Quando vero Dei amantes Christiani columnam in partes diuiserunt, & unusquisque eorum nauat operam sedulam particeps fieri sanctificationis eorum, quæ sanctissimum, & immaculatum corpus tempore passionis tetigerunt, & inveniuntur in multis locis, & urbibus particula, & ipsius etiam columna. Unde & partes illius arripientes Dei amantes adhac usque tempora retinebant, & sanctificationis illius, & auxilij participes fiebant. Nunc vero commune bonum cum sit, & communiter adorari a Christianis, ut addecet, decretum est. Quapropter apposita est, & consecrata in sacro templo sancti mei, & beatissimi Nicolai, ut ab omnibus adoretur, tanquam quae tetigit immaculatissimum & innocentissimum corpus Christi. Propterea qui confessi, & corde contrito accesserint, & adorauerint visibilem hanc partem sacrosanctae columnae, eos nostra mediocritas, & concessis sibi munere, gratia, & auctoritate sanctissimi & vitae principis Spiritus secundum Romana, sacraque Ecclesiae usum, absolutionem centumdierum impertitur. Debent itaque omnes accessuri timore, & confessione, & amore Christi Dei nostri, qui omnia sustinuit, ut nos a servitute inimici in libertatem vindicaret, accedere, ut unusquisque & benedictionis, & sanctificationis particeps fiat, & rerum a se patrandarum consequatur adiutorium. Quod si quis obtulerit aliquid adorationis gratia, multa ille remuneratione a munificentissimo, & bonorum datore Deo rependetur cuius gratia & misericordia, & adiutorium fit cum omnibus, qui cum fide accesserint, ut dictum est. Amen. Gregorius miseratione diuina Archiepiscopus Constantinopolitanus, & Oecumenicus Patriarcha.
units.tr: Now when Christians who love God divided the column into parts, each of them took pains to share in the holiness of those parts, which touched the most holy and spotless body at the time of the passion. Pieces of it, and of the column itself, are found in many places and cities. Lovers of God have therefore taken up and kept its parts until the present time, and have shared in its holiness and help. Since this is now a common good and is to be worshipped by Christians in common, as is fitting, it has been decreed that it be set up and consecrated in the sacred temple of my holy and most blessed Nicholas, so that it may be adored by all as that which touched the most spotless and innocent body of Christ. Therefore, those who come to it confessing their sins and with a contrite heart, and who adore this visible part of the most sacred column, our moderation grants them an absolution of one hundred days, by the authority and grace given to us, and by the favour of the most holy and life-giving Spirit, according to the usage of the Roman and sacred Church. All who are about to approach should therefore come with fear, confession, and love of Christ our God, who endured all things so that He might free us from the slavery of the enemy into liberty, so that each one may become a partaker of the blessing and sanctification and obtain help in the matters he undertakes. If anyone offers something as an act of adoration, he will be repaid with a generous reward by God, the most bountiful giver of good things, whose grace and mercy and help are with all who come in faith, as has been said. Amen. Gregory, by divine mercy Archbishop of Constantinople and Ecumenical Patriarch.

units.la: Non reijciunt ergo Graeci Indulgentias, & hortantur, adhortanturque Christianos, ut aliquid de suo offerant, ut non sine senore eoque magno benefactum redeat. Quod affers ex Historia Syropuli, nihil est, tanquam ab homine nihili prolato , ut videbis in Exercitationibus meis aduersus eundem .
units.tr: The Greeks therefore do not reject indulgences, and they exhort and urge Christians to offer something of their own, so that what is done is not returned without reward, and a great reward at that. As for what you bring from the history of Syropulus, it is nothing, being put forward by a man of no account, as you will see in my Exercitations against the same man.

units.la: Horum Imagines, inquit Critopulus, Ecclesia Orientalis non sculptiles faciebat, neque excisas, sed pictas tantum. quid evidentius? Apage tu cum isto tuo Critopulo, ne vna cum illo delirare videaris. Ego video usum, & praxim universalis Ecclesiae Graecae, & Critopulus vult me non videre, quod video; & quod tactu sensuq; percipio, non percipere, & ab ipsa antiqua, florenteque Ecclesia Graeca ad nos traductam consuetudinem, & ad haec tempora conseruatam inter omnes Orientales, & ut aliquid dicat Hottingerus, arculas, & repositoria Iconoclastarum comminiscitur, in quae immittat. Hinc apparet, exiguas amicorum copias Hottingero esse, qui ad Critopulum solum prouocat.
units.tr: "Of these images," says Critopulus, "the Eastern Church made them not carved or sculpted, but only painted." What could be plainer? Away with you and your Critopulus! You will seem to be raving along with him. I see the custom and practice of the whole Greek Church, and Critopulus wants me not to see what I see, and not to perceive what I perceive by touch and sight: a custom handed down to us from the ancient and flourishing Greek Church itself, and preserved to this day among all the Orientals. And, in order to say something, Critopulus invents chests and cupboards of the iconoclasts into which he may put them. From this it appears that the supporters of Hottinger are few, since the one who appeals to Critopulus alone is the one who is left with a small troop of friends.

units.la: Confessionem auricularem Ecclesiam Graecam pridem fecisse missam, ipsorum Pontificiorum querela est, καὶ ἀδιάφορον[?]. Quid alij dicant de Confessione Graecorum, quaerat Hottingerus. Ego habeo testes antiquissimos, recentiores non paucos, qui de recte peragenda confessione auriculari in Ecclesia Graeca praecepta dant, & animorum morbos, & peccata singula, nec non species distinguunt, & Confessario identidem explicant, vt Confessio dicatur esse valida, sic medico requisita ad morbum curandum exhibent. Et Hottingerus Critopulo fidens mendacissimo contrarium asserit. Nonne vidit huius rei testes a me productos Ioannem Ieiunatorem Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum, Ioannem Monachum, & Diaconum magni Basilij discipulum, Simeonem Thessalonicensem, qui Gregorium Nyssenum, & magnum Basilium pro sui dicti confirmatione testes adduxit, Christophorum Angelum, Seuerum Philadelphiensem, ipsos etiam Graecorum Libros rituales, & quod non minimi momenti est, ipsos Vvittembergenses. Quod affers ex Graecia Orthodoxa, plane ridiculum est, cum eo in loco Trapezuntius de idiotis, hominibus sermonem habeat, qui eo amathiæ[?] deuenere, vt ignorent, quid peccatum sit, & longe cum sint a Canonum cognitione disiunctissimi, ideo propter insciti am non discernunt vitium a virtute: sicque non possunt remedia opportuna afferre, quod equidem aliud est: & qui apud hos cofitentur[?], non missam fecere Confessionem, neque confitens, sed approbantes Confessionem, male eam ob ignorantiam peragunt, quod etiam apud Pontificios euenire aliquando verosimillimum est : neque enim omnes sciunt omnia.
units.tr: That the Greek Church long ago abolished auricular confession is a complaint of the Papists themselves [καὶ ἀδιάφορον]. Let Hottinger ask what others say about the confession of the Greeks. I have very ancient witnesses and not a few more recent ones, who give rules for making auricular confession properly in the Greek Church. They distinguish the diseases of souls, the individual sins and their kinds, and repeatedly explain them to the confessor, and they prescribe that confession be made as a physician requires for curing a disease, so that it may be called valid. And Hottinger, trusting the most lying Critopulus, asserts the opposite. Did he not see the witnesses I cited: John the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople; John the Monk, and Deacon, a disciple of the great Basil; Symeon of Thessalonica, who cited Gregory of Nyssa and the great Basil as witnesses to confirm his statement; Christophorus Angelus; Severus of Philadelphia; the ritual books of the Greeks themselves; and, which is of no small weight, the Wittenberg theologians? What you bring from the Orthodox Greece is plainly ridiculous, since Trapezuntius in that passage is speaking of laymen who have come to such ignorance that they do not know what sin is, and, being wholly unacquainted with the knowledge of the canons, for that very ignorance they do not distinguish vice from virtue. So they cannot apply suitable remedies, which is indeed another matter. And those among them who make confession have not abolished confession, nor are they confessing, but approving confession; they perform it badly through ignorance, which is also very likely to happen sometimes among the Papists too, for not everyone knows everything.

units.la: Quæ de Clerogamia affers, plane sunt stultissima. Quid enim est pro Episcoporum matrimonio, si Reformati non paucos Episcopos suos appellant Pastores? Et discrimen, quod tu somnias de Presbyteris, & clericis, insulsissimum, atque inauspicatissimum est. Græci enim ante Photianum schisma matrimonium suis Sacerdotibus non interdicebant, Latini interdicebant & tamen vnio inter ambas Ecclesias continuabatur. Ergo dissidium extra controuersiæ aleam a te positum frustra est, alicuius esse momenti nonnisi a dementissimo, & tui simili reputabitur.
units.tr: What you bring forward about the marriage of clergy is utterly foolish. For what does it prove in favour of marriage for bishops, when the Reformed call many of their bishops ministers? And your distinction, which you dream up between presbyters and clerics, is most silly and most ill-omened. The Greeks did not forbid their priests to marry before the Photian schism, while the Latins did forbid it, and yet the union between the two Churches continued. So the disagreement you have raised, which is beyond dispute, is pointless, and it will be regarded as of any weight only by someone utterly demented and by people like you.

units.la: Scripsi, Sacra Ecclesiastica sua Græcos nonnisi lingua vernacula administrare. Scripsi, fateor. Etiam si negas, papyrus loquitur. Annon coecus es more tuo, qui non vides, neque discernis linguam vernaculam Græcorum a pura illa, & antiqua? Vernaculum, quando cum Grammaticis de grammaticis agere cogor, est quod domi nostræ nascitur, vel in patria, a Verna quod seruum domi nostræ natum ex ancilla, aut seruo notat. Hinc dicitur lingua vernacula, vel seruilis, vel plebeia, qua tanquam communi & naturali omnes loquuntur, & tradunt linguam maternam hodie vocari. Tu qui omnia scis, & me Mercurio opus non habes, vocas linguam vernaculam radicaliter, & oppositè. illo modo linguam Græcorum veterum hodie in Sacris vsitata vernacula vocatur, quia in Græcia orta, & nata est, in Græcia vsurpata, legibus, consuetudine a multis introducta seculis; sed iniuria temporis, & desidia hominum, qui quod tueri mascule debuissent, turpiter neglexerunt. μακάριε τῶ ϑεοπνεύστῳ. Tu ita vocas linguam vernaculam contra atque alij. Eris ne ergo tu auctor linguæ pro arbitrio inuertens, atque immutans omnia? Quare & Lexicon non conscribis, vt omnibus pateat, ista tua noua verborum significatio? Græca lingua in Græcia orta est. plane. in Græcia vsurpata saltem per multa tempora. Sed cum tempore omnia vertantur, & immutentur in peiorem partem, lingua quoque ab illa pura, & primigenia aliam, atque aliam faciem induit nunc elegantiorem, nunc deformiorem; donec deducta est, vt in communibus colloquijs, & familiaribus congressibus in vsu fit. & vernæ etiam & homines nihili eam vsurpent, ita disiunctam, & diuersam ab illa prima, vt primam illam homines pauci, & linguarum studiosi, nec non musarum alumni intelligant, hanc sine literis homines. Et hæc est, quæ vernacula dicitur, in qua tu scripsisti Græcos Sacra facere, quod falsum est, & ex tuo cerebro natum ad componendum dissidium, cum Pontificij antiqua, & qua loquebantur cum Christianum nomen innotuit, in sacris agendis Christiani, quod etiam de Græcis firmissimum est, cum non alia sit, quam quæ cum institutæ fuerunt cerimoniæ, ad libros componendos adhibebatur. Quod si radicaliter hoc tuum locum habet, etiam nunc per te Pontificij in Sacris faciendis, lingua vernacula vtuntur. Et vt magis rideas tuum hoc radicaliter, Hispani, Gallique, qui linguæ suæ originem a Latina pura cognoscunt radicaliter lingua vernacula, & Germani ipsi, qui ab Iaphetica lingua suam deducunt, te iudice lingua Iaphetica Dei laudes concinunt. O miseram Grammattistarum conditionem! Illud & opposite tuum magis in admirationem venit, Græci vtuntur lingua vernacula, quia nec Romanorum more Latinam, nec vllam aliam a vernacula remotiorem admittunt. Si tuum illud radicaliter verum est, quare non & Græci linguam Latinam in Sacris eorum adhibent, cum Latina a Græca ortum suum agnoscat, & radicaliter Græca sic, & sic etiam Latini Græca lingua vtuntur, imo Phoenicia, cum Græca opinione nonnullorum ex Phœnicia fit? Quid tu tandem garrias de lingua Hebræa, & Chaldaica, alij iudicent. Quæ de tribus Græcæ linguæ speciebus ad te tuamque insciitiam excusandam superaddis, inconsultissima sunt, sicut & illa conclusio perridicula. Satis est ad euincendum discrimen inter Orientales Græcas, & Occidentales Latinas, quod illæ Græcam in obeundis Sacris admittunt linguam, Græcis vtique vernaculam non Latinis, non Germanis, &c. Si non omnibus, certe quibusdam, si non hodiernis, veteribus saltem, adeoque Græcam nuncupari vernaculam 1. originaliter 2. oppositè ad Latinos. Sed reliqua pudor est mihi dicere. Antequam finiam, illud mihi respondeas velim. Tu ad confirmanda tua de Græcis Sacra obeuntibus lingua vernacula in testem vocas Edoardum Brewerodum. Ille tamen tibi aduersus est. Inspicito verba. His locis non obstantibus certum est, tantam esse moderna lingua Græca a veteri differentiam, ut Liturgiæ, quæ adhuc hodie in Græcis Ecclesijs leguntur, Basilij diebus Dominicis, & solemnibus, Chrysostomi profestis, a vulgo vel parum, vel plane nihil intelligantur, quod testimonio virorum, qui illis in partibus fuere, habeo; nec veteris linguæ Græcæ periti modernam vulgarem intelligunt. Et alibi; Verum lingua illa non est vulgaris, sed pura Graeca, quam plebs non intelligit. Et post pauca; Ut ut vero ista se habeant, non habere Graecos scripturas in vulgarem linguam versas, certo est. Hinc etiam refellitur mendacium eorum, qui de iisdem Graecis tradunt; Ad orationes plane necessarium esse iudicant, ut quis intelligat preces, ideoque lingua ignota prolatas preces nihil aestimant. Quod tu impudens Graecis ipsis, cum tua lingua vernacula ad probandum dissidium, pro tua humanitate contradere nitebaris. Sed operam, & oleum perdidisti.
units.tr: "I wrote that the Greeks administer their sacred offices only in the vernacular tongue. I wrote it, I admit." Even if you deny it, the paper speaks for itself. Are you blind, as is your habit, that you do not see or distinguish the vernacular tongue of the Greeks from that pure and ancient one? When I am forced to deal with grammarians about grammar, vernacular means what is born in our own household or in our own country, from verna, a slave born in the home of a female slave or a male slave. Hence the vernacular or servile or plebeian tongue is called the language that everyone speaks as common and natural, and which today is called the mother tongue. You, who know everything and have no need of Mercury, call the vernacular tongue radicaliter and oppositè in a sense that no one else does. In that sense the ancient Greek tongue used in the sacred rites today is called vernacular, because it arose and was born in Greece, was used in Greece, and was introduced by laws and custom among many generations; but through the injury of time and the sloth of men, who ought to have defended it manfully, it has been shamefully neglected. Blessed one, inspired by God [μακάριε τῷ θεοπνεύστῳ]. You use the term vernacular tongue differently from everyone else. Will you therefore be the author of a language that you turn and change at will, overturning everything? Why do you not also compile a lexicon, so that your new meaning of these words may be plain to all? The Greek language arose in Greece, that is clear; it was used in Greece, at least for many ages. But since all things are turned and changed for the worse over time, the language too, departing from that pure and primitive form, has taken on one face after another, now more elegant, now more deformed, until it has been brought down to what is in use in common conversation and everyday meetings, and even the slaves and worthless people use it. It is so separated and different from that original speech that only a few people, students of languages and nurslings of the Muses, understand the original, while ordinary people without learning understand this one. And this is the tongue that is called vernacular, and in which you wrote that the Greeks perform their sacred rites. That is false, and born from your own brain to create a dispute, since the Papists, in performing the sacred rites, use the ancient language in which the Christians spoke when the name of Christian became known. This holds most firmly also for the Greeks, since it is no other language than the one in which the ceremonies were instituted and which was used in composing the books. But if your radicaliter has any place here, then even now the Papists, through you, use the vernacular tongue in performing the sacred rites. And so that you may laugh the more at this radicaliter* of yours: the Spaniards and the French, who know that their language derives its origin from pure Latin radicaliter, and the Germans themselves, who derive their tongue from the Japhetic language, sing God's praises in a Japhetic tongue, by your judgment. O the wretched condition of the grammarians! Your and opposite comes to greater wonder: the Greeks use the vernacular tongue, because they admit neither Latin, after the manner of the Romans, nor any other language more remote from the vernacular. If that radicaliter of yours is true, why do the Greeks not also use the Latin language in their sacred rites, since Latin acknowledges its origin from Greek, and radically the Latins use the Greek language in the same way and in the same sense, indeed Phoenician, since according to the opinion of some Greeks it comes from Phoenicia? What you chatter at last about the Hebrew and Chaldaic tongues, let others judge. What you add about the three species of the Greek language, to excuse yourself and your ignorance, is most ill-considered, and that conclusion is most ridiculous: It is enough to prove the difference between the Eastern Greeks and the Western Latins that the former admit the Greek language in performing the sacred rites, which is certainly the vernacular for Greeks, not for Latins, not for Germans, etc. If not for all, certainly for some; if not for the present-day, at least for the ancient; and so Greek may be called vernacular, first, originally, and second, in opposition to the Latins. But it shames me to say the rest. Before I finish, I would like you to answer this. To confirm your claim that the Greeks perform the sacred rites in the vernacular tongue, you call Edward Brerewood as a witness. Yet he is against you. Look at his words: Notwithstanding these passages, it is certain that the modern Greek language differs so greatly from the ancient that the liturgies still read today in the Greek churches, the liturgy of Basil on Sundays and feast days and that of Chrysostom on ordinary days, are understood by the common people either little or not at all, as I have from the testimony of men who were in those parts; nor do those skilled in the ancient Greek tongue understand the modern vulgar speech. And elsewhere: But that language is not vulgar, but pure Greek, which the common people do not understand. And a little after: However these matters stand, it is certain that the Greeks do not have the Scriptures translated into the vulgar tongue. Hence also is refuted the lie of those who write about the same Greeks that they judge it entirely necessary for prayers that a man understand them, and therefore they consider prayers uttered in an unknown tongue to be worth nothing. You, shamelessly, tried to contradict this for the Greeks themselves with your vernacular tongue, to prove your dissent, out of your own humanity. But you have wasted your labour and your oil.

units.la: Papam denique auctoritate excidisse, eosdemque hierarchiam eius, & praeminentiam, ceu superioris omnium Ecclesiarum capitis in spiritualibus auersari, & detestari, non nostra tantum, sed communis Pontificiorum querela est.
units.tr: Finally, that the Papists have fallen from authority, and that they shun and detest his hierarchy and his pre-eminence, as of the head of all the Churches in spiritual matters, is a complaint not only of ours but common to the Papists.

units.la: De auctoritate Papae, & praeminentia in omnes Ecclesias longe longeque plurima sunt a nobis dicta tum alibi, tum etiam in hac Differtatione de Octaua Synodo Photiana. Cum vero tu nihil vltra addas, nos quoque iam dictis contenti, non aliud attexemus. Vnum nihilominus recentioris, sed libris editis in vtraque lingua praestantissimi, & a me primum publicatum apponam. Is est Georgius Trapezuntius, qui ad Cretenses Epistola scribit; Οὕτως Ἐκκλησία μία σωίζει ἢ μηκέτι, παροιμία [illegible, ~12 letters] ἢ [illegible, ~8 letters] τῆς νῦν Λατίνων, παρ' ἡμῖν ἡ ἐνοεία καλουμένη, ὡς ἐν τῷ μικροτάτῳ ὅρῳ ἀξιοχρέως [?]. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἐνοείαι πολλαχοῦ, καὶ πολλαὶ αἱ τοιαῦται Ἐκκλησίαι. ἀλλ' ἡ ἀπόδειξις αὐτὴ εἰς ἓν συνῳκῆσθαι τὸ ὄνομα [?] φυσικῶς καὶ ἀξίως κοινόμυθοι, ταῖς πολλαῖς ἐνοείαις μίαν ἐπισκοπικῶς Ἐκκλησίαν ποιεῖσθαι, τῇ Ἐπισκόπῳ πάσας ἐνωθῆναι. ὁμοίως καὶ ταῖς πολλαῖς Ἐπισκοπαῖς Μητροπολιτῶν μίαν ποιῆσαι, τῇ ἐν Μητροπολίτῃ πάσας εἰς ἓν συνηγμένας. πάλιν ἡ ταῖς Μητροπόλεσι μιᾷ παρχιαρχικῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ συναριθμίζοντες, ἐν Πατριαρχίᾳ εἰς μίαν μεγάλην Ἐκκλησίαν συνάψαντες, ὡς ἐξ τοῦ ἀρχιεπισκόπου Ἐκκλησίαν Ἐκκλησιῶν πλῆθος εἰς μίαν Ἐκκλησίαν δὲ τῷ ἀρχιερέως ἐνώμενον. ἐπὶ δὲ ἡ πέντε πᾶσαί εἰσι μεγάλαι Ἐκκλησίαι, Ῥώμης, Κωνσταντινουπόλεως, Ἀλεξανδρείας, Ἀντιοχείας, Ἱεροσολύμων, δὲ πάντως καὶ ταύταις συνάπτειν, μᾶλλον ἢ αἰσθήκη [?] αἰσθάνεσθαι φυσικῶς εἰς τὸ σωθῆναι. ἵνα μία ἔζα ἡ καθόλου Ἐκκλησία δικαιοῦ τὸν λόγον ἢ ἀληθείας ὀρθοτομῶν, ἡδονῆς ὃ μηδὲν τὸ πλῆθος ἐργάζεσθαι δύναιτο. Τίνι δὲ τῶν πέντε εἰς μίαν αἱ πέντε συνάγονται, δῆλον ὅτι τῇ Φερέτῃ. ἤδη δὲ ἐδιδάχθη Φεροτεδύνῃ ἀεὶ τ' πολλῶν τὸ συνάγον ταῦτα εἰς ἓν καὶ ἐνοῦ. αὕτη δὲ ὅξιν ἡ τῆς Ῥώμης. καὶ τοῦτο ἀδελφαὶ πάντων ἁπλῶς τῆς Χειςιανῶν δόξα. ἐπεὶ δὲ οὖν διὰ ταύτης ἡ καθόλου Ἐκκλησία ἴχθ' τὸ ἓν μίαν, ὅταν μίαν ἀγίαν Καθολικῷ καὶ Ἀποστολικῷ Ἐκκλησίαν λέγομεν, πάντως μίαν ἓν δὲ τὸ ἐπαγόμενον τῆς τῆς Ῥώμης Ἐκκλησίας ὁμο-λο-
units.tr: Very much, and far more, has been said by us about the authority of the Pope and his pre-eminence over all the Churches, both elsewhere and in this Dissertation on the Eighth Council of Photius. Since you add nothing further, we too, content with what has already been said, will add nothing more. Nevertheless, I will set down one passage from a more recent writer, most excellent and published in both languages, which I was the first to make public. It is George of Trebizond, who writes in his letter to the Cretans: Thus the one Church is saved or no longer... [Greek: Οὕτως Ἐκκλησία μία σωίζει] ... as among us, what is called the union, as in the very small boundary, is worthily [?]. Since there are unions in many places, and many such Churches, yet the demonstration itself, that the name is naturally and worthily shared together into one, that the many unions make one Church episcopally, and all are joined to one bishop; likewise also that the many bishoprics make one of the metropolitans, all gathered into one in the metropolitan; again, those who number the metropolises under one patriarchal Church, joining them into one great Church in a patriarchate, as from the archbishop the multitude of Churches is joined into one Church under one chief priest. But there are five great Churches in all: Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem; and it is necessary in every way to join these also, rather than to perceive them naturally for salvation, so that the one universal Church may rightly judge the word of truth, cutting it straight, which the multitude could not accomplish. But to which of the five the five are gathered into one is clear: to Peter. Now it has been taught that Peter always was the one gathering the many into one and one. And this is the glory of Rome, and this is the common opinion of all Christians. Since therefore through this one the universal Church became one, when we say one holy catholic and apostolic Church, certainly one... of the Church of Rome, we should rightly understand, bowing down the word of the Church of Rome.

units.la: [?] Several words in this Greek paragraph are not clear enough to read letter by letter; the accents and the exact spelling of the Greek words are uncertain throughout and should be checked against the scan. λογία νοήσωμεν ὀρθῶς κείνοντες. Οἵς ἂν ἐπὶ τῆς Ῥώμης Ἐκκλησίας, ἐξώκισεν τῆς μιᾶς ἁγίας, ἐ Καθολικῆς καὶ Ἀποστολικῆς Ἐκκλησίας, τρ[?]ἀλαδήμα[?]π ὑποπίπτου[illegible, ~8 letters] εἰς ὅρα[?], καὶ ἐρημίας ὑποπλαιᾶται, ἐ βάεσθαι, ἐ Ὅπον οἰκεῖ, οἷς ἂν ἐπισκοπεῖ κύεικ. βλέπετε δὲ ὡς ἂν ἐμὰ ταῦτα, ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ συμβόλου, καὶ τῆς τῷ Ἐκκλησίαν διαξαγόντων ἀγίων Πατέρων, ἐ τῆς φιλοσοφίας, ἥτις τῆς τῆν θεσλυμάτων σωμήθη φύσεως, ἡ τις μέγα βοᾷ, ἐκ ἄλλως, ἀλλ' ἡ ἑνὶ ὁμοιάδι σωμάτηδαι δώσαδαι τὸ πλῆθος εἰς ἕν. Hac ratione una constituitur minima omnium, quae apud hodiernos Latinos Parœcia, apud nos vero Enoria nomen habet, tanquam quae uno minimo termino circumscribatur. Cum vero Parœciae multae sint, multaque similes Ecclesiae, & nos ostenderimus necesse esse in unam multitudinem congregari, eo quod eiusdem generis est, naturalibus demonstrationibus ducti, multas Parœcias unam Episcopalem Ecclesiam facimus, & Episcopo eas coniungimus. Simili quoque ratione multos Episcopatus in unam Metropolin redactos, uni Metropolitae universos subdimus. Rursusque Metropoles uni Patriarchali Ecclesiae coagmentantes, uni Patriarchae in unam magnam Ecclesiam copulamus. Adeo ut Ecclesia Archieratica dignitate conspicua fit, Ecclesiarum multitudo uni Ecclesiae per Archiprasulem coniuncta. Cum autem quinque sint magnae EcEcclesia, Romana, Constantinopolitana, Alexandrina, Antiochena, Hierosolymitana, necesse est omnino easdem vna aliqua copulari. Imo necessitas naturalis cogit in id compellens, vt vna existens vniuersalis Ecclesia possit recta veritatis dogmata praescribere. Demonstratum siquidem est, nihil posse multitudinem agere. Qua igitur ex his quinque in vnam haec quinque cogentur? Manifestum est non alia, quam prima. Ostendimus enim multo aliis praecellere, quod reliqua in vnum redigit, & vnit. Et haec est Romana, quod ab omnibus Christianis absolute conceditur. Cum itaque per hanc vniuersalis Ecclesia obtineat, vt sit vna, dum vnam sanctam Catholicam, & Apostolicam Ecclesiam dicimus, omnino vnam esse, quod Romana Ecclesia professionem sequatur, nec extra rem iudicantes intelligimus. Quicunque igitur non sequitur Ecclesiam Romanam, extra vnam sanctam, Catholicam, & Apostolicam Ecclesiam est, & anathemati obnoxius, in montibus, & locis solitarijs, ac praeruptis inerrat, & territoria inhabitat, quae non inuisit Dominus. Nanque conspicitis mea haec non esse, sed e sacro Symbolo, & ex Sanctis Patribus, qui Ecclesiam ordinarunt, & Philosophia ipsa, hoc est ex rerum natura recollecta, quae magna voce intonat, non alio, quam vno eiusdem generis posse multitudinem in vnum cogi. Non nego aliquando inter Pontifices Romanos, & Patriarchas dissidia exorta, sed eo quoque tempore recolo, illa intra breve tempus sopita, ac diffidentes in antiquam concordiam offensionibus supressis redactos .
units.tr: ...the one Church, and let us rightly understand the common assent. Whoever is cut off from the Church of Rome, which is cut off from the one holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, falls into [...] and dwells in desolation, [...] where he dwells, wherever he is overseen. See that these things are not mine, but are from the holy Creed, and from the holy Fathers who set the Church in order, and from philosophy itself, which was formed from the nature of things and which cries aloud that a multitude can be brought into one only by a single unifying principle. By this reasoning a unit is constituted, the smallest of all those that today among the Latins are called a parish, and among us an enoria, as being bounded by one smallest limit. Since there are many parishes, and many similar churches, and we have shown that it is necessary for a multitude of the same kind to be gathered into one, led by natural demonstrations, we make many parishes into one episcopal church and join them to a bishop. In the same way we also bring many bishoprics together into one metropolis and subject them all to one metropolitan. Again, joining the metropolises into one patriarchal church, we unite them under one patriarch into one great church. So that the church becomes conspicuous by archiepiscopal dignity, the multitude of churches being joined to one church through its archbishop. But since there are five great churches, Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem, these must of necessity be joined together in some one way. Indeed natural necessity compels toward this, so that the universal Church, being one, may be able to prescribe the right doctrines of truth. For it has been shown that a multitude can accomplish nothing. Into which one of these five, then, will these five be gathered? Clearly into none other than the first. For we have shown that it excels the others by much, since it reduces the remaining ones into one and unites them. And this is Rome, which is absolutely granted by all Christians. Since, then, through this the universal Church obtains that it is one, when we say one holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, we understand that it is wholly one because it follows the profession of the Church of Rome, and we do not judge beside the point. Whoever therefore does not follow the Church of Rome is outside the one holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, is liable to anathema, wanders on mountains, in solitary and precipitous places, and inhabits regions which the Lord has not visited. For you see that these things are not mine, but are taken from the holy Creed and from the holy Fathers who ordered the Church, and from philosophy itself, that is, gathered from the nature of things, which cries aloud that a multitude of one kind can be brought into one only. I do not deny that at times disputes have arisen between the Roman Pontiffs and the Patriarchs, but I recall that at that time those disputes were quieted within a short time, and that the dissenting parties were brought back to the ancient concord with the offences set aside.

units.la: Ecclesias Orientales, etsi iniuria temporum gravem passa sunt cladem, ita tamen hoc commune eorum fuisse fatum, ut cum nostra non sint per omnia, nobis interim in essentialibus propius accedant, quam Pontificiis Tridentinis.. De Ecclesiis Orientalibus, Jacobitarum, Nestorianorum, Dioscorianorum, & aliis, si quae sunt, ipse nihil statuo. Rem optime peregit linguarum Orientalium scientissimus Abraamus Ecchellensis. Ego tantummodo coniectura ducor ad suspicandum, quod & tibi, si solers[?] es ad perspiciendum, arriserit. Nationes illæ omnes Christianis sacris imbutæ, sed quædam Catholicæ Ecclesiæ dogmata impugnantes mutuis odiis conflictantur, & aliam alia irreconciliabili dissensu vexat, & cum necesse est, scriptis etiam editis lacessit, & dogmata damnant. Sunt vero nonnulla, in quibus unis animis conveniunt, quæ ab Ecclesia Græca, & Pontificia non dissonant. Hinc statuendum judico amandatis erroribus, quos eorum mentibus hæresis infudit, reliqua alia ab antiquis temporibus, ex superiorum antiquorumque instituto illis contradita suisse, & communi omnium calculo diffeminata, quæ, licet ringatur Hottingerus, ritibus, ac cerimonijs, nec non dogmatibus Pontificiorum, & Græcorum non absimilia sunt, & hæreticorum recentiorum dictatis maiori ex parte contraria. Quare detonet Hottingerus quidquid de illis vult, ac in mentem venerit, non id efficiet, vt perpetua Orientalium, & Pontificiorum veritas infirmetur: eo enim magis foras pellucebit, quo magis ab infidis occultatur.
units.tr: The Eastern Churches, although they have suffered grievous disaster through the injuries of the times, have nevertheless shared this common fate: that, though they are not in all things the same as ours, they nonetheless come closer to us in essentials than the Tridentine Papists do. As for the Eastern Churches, of the Jacobites, the Nestorians, the Dioscorians and others, if there are any, I myself decide nothing. The most learned Abraham Ecchellensis has done this matter very well, in the Oriental languages. I am only led by conjecture to suspect what, if you are clever enough to see it, may also please you. All those nations, imbued with Christian rites, but attacking certain dogmas of the Catholic Church, are at war with one another in mutual hatreds, and one vexes another with irreconcilable dissension, and when necessary provokes it even with published writings, and they condemn one another's dogmas. There are, however, some points on which they agree with one mind, and in which they do not differ from the Greek and Papist Church. Hence I judge that, setting aside the errors which heresy poured into their minds, the other things handed down to them from ancient times, by the institution of their predecessors and elders, and spread through the common consent of all, are, although Hottinger may scoff at them, not unlike the rites and ceremonies, and also the dogmas of the Papists and the Greeks, and are for the most part contrary to the decrees of recent heretics. Therefore, whatever Hottinger may thunder against them, and whatever comes into his mind, he will not bring it about that the perpetual truth of the Orientals and the Papists is weakened; for it will shine forth all the more, the more it is hidden by the faithless.

units.la: Obseruamus Orientales, vel Reformatis per omnia accedere, vel in circumstantijs tantumvariare, vel vbi Pontificijs videntur fauerepartibus, illud ex principijs fluere Pontificiorum, etiam opinione erroneis. &c. Atque sic non negamus Orientales Ecclesias cum Romana aliquid habere simile, plura tamen nobiscum-. Quis similia audiit? Si saniori mente rem considerasset, Hottingerus, respirasset paululum illius pertinacia, atque temeritas, aliquid loci, & consilio datum fuisset, nec in tantam turpitudinem venisset, vt hoc sibi esset apud integros iudicio viros confitendum. Non erit itaque abs re, si Græcorum præcipua producta, neque enim omnia tempus concedit, conferamus, vt infra.
units.tr: We observe that the Orientals either agree with the Reformed in all things, or differ only in circumstances, or where they seem to favour the Papists, that this flows from the principles of the Papists, even those held in error, etc. And so we do not deny that the Eastern Churches have something similar to the Roman, yet they have more in common with us. Who has ever heard the like? If Hottinger had considered the matter with a saner mind, his obstinacy and rashness would have eased a little, some room and counsel would have been given, and he would not have come to such a disgrace that he must confess this before upright men of judgment. It will therefore not be out of place, if the principal points produced by the Greeks (for time does not allow us to go through everything) are compared, as follows below.

units.la: Sic occurrunt in Orientalium Græcorum cum primis & Syrorum scriptis varia forma ad B. Virginem Mariam concepta, vel etiam ad alios Sanctos, quibus tamen superstitionibus auctissima[?] Pontificiorum ἀγιολατρείᾳ[?] non defenditur. Hæc, & quæ sequuntur ad finem vsque paginæ ex deliro pessimi Hæretici cerebello diducta, refutatione non egent, cum probata sicut, & anteriora omnia, non sint, sed voluntarie ex superiori aluo vti ingurgitata fuerant, refusa. Cum nec nostrum id negotij sit, quibus consensus Græcorum propositus est. Quare cum eadem dicunt Græci, & Pontificij, sive bene, sive male dicant, nil ipse moror, vt sæpius oratione mea prosecutus sum. Nanque sunt viri amplissimi omnium Ciuitatum, & ingenio, & existimatione, & dignitate excellentissimi, & sacris literis instructissimi, qui id cumulatissime peregerunt. Illud præterea observant viri pereruditi, & tantum non inuident ingenij tui adeo feraci fœcunditati. Nam cum Histor. Seculo XVI. duodecim solum dissidij capita inter Ecclesiam Græcam, & Pontificiam numerasses, neque enim plura suppetebant, post Hottingerum Allatij fraudis, & impostura manifestæ conuictum, ita numero creuerint, vel paucissimo tempore, vt iam Orientales Ecclesiae ut cum vestrae non sint, per omnia vobis interim in essentialibus propius accedant, quam Pontificiis Tridentinis. Et; Reformatis per omnia accedere, vel in circumstantiis variare, vel ubi Pontificiis videntur fauere partibus, illud ex principiis fluere Pontificiorum etiam opinione erroneis, aut φανταςιώς[?] potius quam ὀρθῶς, verbis, quam rebus assensum testari maiorem, atque sic non negamus Orientales Ecclesias cum Romana aliquid habere simile, (idem difficulter obtinebunt) Non deest loquendi profluentia in Hottingero, non exceptionum copia in refellendis Catholicorum institutis, inanis citraque delectum verborum sartago. Quid ad hoc Allatius respondet, cui tenues, aut nullae dicendi opes, & exigua verborum ineptissime intermiscendorum facultas? Pauca. confido tamen, certo, & confirmato me posse in hac causa consistere. Horum vel minima pars si in tuis Reformatis consideretur, nae tu una cum aliis stultissime tua confirmabis, & potissimum inscitissima illa; Ecclesias Orientales vobis in essentialibus propius accedere quam Pontificiis Tridentinis, vel tantum in circumstantiis variare, & si quando videantur fauere Pontificiis, id fluere ex opinionibus erroneis Pontificiorum, & φανταςιώς[?] potius quam ὀρθῶς, & verbis, quam rebus testari, & licet non neges aliquod similie cum Romana, habere tamen plura cum vobis. Ad hæc: quæ sunt ista essentialia in tuis, quæ circumstantiæ? Indica circumstantias, in quibus variant a Pontificijs, accedunt ad Reformatos. Enuncia nobis mysteria, quibus illi non φανερῶς [?], sed ὄντως [?], non verbis, sed rebus vobiscum assensum testantur in pluribus. Quam bellum erat Hottingere, confiteri te potius nescire quod nescias, quam similia effutientem temetipsum tibi displicere. Et tandem liceat inter nos, sine fuco, & fallacia; citius me tempus, quam oratio deficeret: tanta est in singulis a te productis materia, ut dies integros ad tua refellenda possim consumere. Ne tamen videar ad te reprehendendum, mihi ansam conquirere, plane tu ἀγοληξία [?] B. Virginis cultus, Monachorum instituta, Patrum in dogmatibus Fidei decernendis auctoritas non conspicis ut altis fixa sint radicibus in Græcorum animis. Quod de Reformatis nonnisi stultissimus, &c, qui veri perdidit, affirmauerit. Hac causa ex ijs, quæ Græci, Pontificijq; profitentur, & in Hottingero proposui, proponam iterum, reddamque incudi, ut magis ac magis colligas dissensum inter Reformatos, & Pontificios, concludasque Græcorum, atque aliorum Orientalium cum Reformamatis consensum. Confer, & compone, si vales.
units.tr: Thus in the writings of the Eastern Greeks, and especially of the Syrians, there occur various forms of devotion conceived toward the Blessed Virgin Mary, or also toward other saints, by which, however, the most extensive superstitions of the Papists' [Greek: ἁγιολατρεία] are not defended. These things, and what follows to the end of the page, drawn out of the raving brain of a most wicked heretic, need no refutation, since they are not proved, as are all the preceding points, but were poured out voluntarily, belched up from his upper belly. For this is not our business, to whom the agreement of the Greeks has been set forth. Therefore, since the Greeks and the Papists say the same things, whether they speak well or badly, I myself do not care, as I have often pursued in my discourse. For there are most distinguished men of all cities, and most excellent in talent, esteem and dignity, and most thoroughly versed in the sacred letters, who have carried this out most abundantly. Moreover, learned men observe this, and they hardly envy the so fruitful fertility of your talent. For when in your History of the sixteenth century you had counted only twelve points of disagreement between the Greek and the Papist Church (for no more were at hand), after Hottinger, convicted of the manifest fraud and imposture of Allatius, they have grown in number, or in a very short time, so that now the Eastern Churches, though they are not the same as yours in all things, nevertheless come closer to you in essentials than the Tridentine Papists do. And: to agree with the Reformed in all things, or to differ in circumstances, or where they seem to favour the Papist side, this flows from the principles of the Papists, even those held in error, or [Greek: φανταστικῶς] rather than [Greek: ὀρθῶς], to bear witness to a greater assent in words than in things; and so we do not deny that the Eastern Churches have something similar to the Roman (which they will hardly maintain). There is no lack of fluency in Hottinger, no abundance of exceptions in refuting the institutions of Catholics, an empty pan without choice of words. What does Allatius reply to this, who has slender or no powers of speech, and a small ability to mix words most unskilfully? Few things. I trust, however, that I can stand firm in this cause, certainly and securely. If even the smallest part of these were considered in your Reformed, indeed you together with others would confirm your own foolishness, and especially that most ignorant saying: the Eastern Churches come closer to you in essentials than to the Tridentine Papists, or differ only in circumstances, and if at any time they seem to favour the Papists, this flows from the erroneous opinions of the Papists, and bears witness [Greek: φανταστικῶς] rather than [Greek: ὀρθῶς], and in words rather than in things; and although you do not deny some similarity with Rome, yet they have more in common with you. To this I ask: what are these essentials in your account, and what are these circumstances? Name the circumstances in which they differ from the Papists and approach the Reformed. Set forth to us the mysteries in which they bear witness to agreement with you in many points not [Greek: φανερῶς], but [Greek: ὄντως], not in words but in things. How well it would have been, Hottinger, to confess that you do not know what you do not know, rather than, by uttering such things, to displease yourself. And finally, let it be permitted between us, without paint and deceit: time would fail me sooner than speech; so great is the matter in each of the points you have produced, that I could spend whole days refuting your claims. Lest, however, I seem to seek an occasion to rebuke you, you plainly do not see that the cult of the Blessed Virgin, the institutions of the monks, and the authority of the Fathers in deciding the dogmas of faith are fixed with deep roots in the minds of the Greeks. Whoever affirms the contrary of the Reformed, except the most foolish man, who has lost the truth, [says it]. For this reason, I will set forth again, from what the Greeks and the Papists profess and what I have set out against Hottinger, and I will put it back on the anvil, so that you may more and more gather the disagreement between the Reformed and the Papists, and conclude the agreement of the Greeks and of the other Orientals with the Reformed. Compare and arrange it, if you are able.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Hæc tenent Romana, & Græca Ecclesia.
units.tr: This is what the Roman and Greek Church hold.

units.la: 1. Diuinam Christi naturam passam non esse. 2. Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum unum Deum omnipotentem. 3. Unum essentia, Trinum personis. 4. Fi-lium æqualem in omnibus Patri, ex Patre genitum, Deum de Deo. 5. Spiritum sanctum in omnibus æqualem Patri, & Filio ex Patre, & Filio, vel per Filium procedentem.
units.tr: 1. That the divine nature of Christ did not suffer. 2. That the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one almighty God. 3. One in essence, three in persons. 4. That the Son is in all things equal to the Father, begotten of the Father, God of God. 5. That the Holy Spirit is in all things equal to the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son, or through the Son.

units.la: Quid Reformati ?
units.tr: What do the Reformed hold?

units.la: 1. Lutherus de Concilijs parte 2. Diuinam in Christo naturam passam esse. Andreas Musculus commendat librum Lutheri, quo ex professo scribit, Diuinam in Christo naturam passam, & mortuam esse: & libro de concordia discipulorum Lutheri testimonijs probat, illum semper sensisse, ac docuisse, quod Christi Diuinitas in cruce passa sit. Iacobus Andreæ Thesi 156. fatetur, pati, & mori nomine & re pertinere ad Diuinitatem. Stephanus Gerlachius contra Bufæum concisè asserit, veras esse has propositiones, Diuinitas est nata, crucifixa, mortua.
units.tr: 1. Luther, On the Councils, part 2: that the divine nature in Christ suffered. Andreas Musculus commends a book of Luther's in which he writes expressly that the divine nature in Christ suffered and died. In his book on the concord of Luther's disciples, he proves from Luther's testimonies that Luther always thought and taught that the divinity of Christ suffered on the cross. Jacobus Andreae, in Thesis 156, admits that to suffer and to die pertain to the Divinity, both in name and in fact. Stephanus Gerlachius, against Bufaeus, briefly asserts that these propositions are true: the Divinity was born, crucified, dead.

units.la: 2. Valentinus Gentilis in suis Prothesibus Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum tres Deos esse æternos, asserit, essentiali numero distinctos; ita tamen ut Pater sit solus Deus ex se, Filius autem & Spiritus sanctus, Dij quidem inferiores, qui a Patre essentiam suam productam habeant, tametsi non ex nihilo, sed ex subsistantia Patris, ut inquit Proth. 1.1. quo circa Patrem essentiatorem, Filium autem, & Spiritum sanctum essentiatos dicit. Beza libro de unitate essentiæ; Legimus idque non sine horrore, quæ Georgius Paulus, Cafanouius, & alij nonnulli a Valentino Gentili fascinati scripserunt, tres personas sive ὑποστάσεις[?], in tres numero ὁμοουσίας[?] sive essentias transformantes, unde fit, ut necessario tres Deos statuant. Titheitæ in Polonia duce Georgio Paulo aiunt, Tres esse Deos, tres æternos, tres omnipotentes. Poloni Epistola ad Senatum Geneuensem. Petrus Statorius Theodori Bezæ discipulus, & Georgius Blandrata publice in Polonia docent, Non unum, sed tres esse Deos haud secus inter se diuersos, ac tres homines, quod a Caluino, Bullingero, Martyre, Musculo se didicisse affirmant. Theodorus Beza Epist. 16. Duitæ in Polonia Petro Goniezio duce, Patrem, & Filium duos esse Deos, asserunt, de Spiritu autem nondum esse revelatum quid sit; Ex Canisio de Corruptelis Verbi Dei, Alphonso Pisano Præfatione in Concilium Nicænum, & alijs.
units.tr: 2. Valentinus Gentilis, in his Prothesis, asserts that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three eternal Gods, distinct in essential number; yet so that the Father alone is God from himself, while the Son and the Holy Spirit are lesser gods, who have their essence produced by the Father, though not out of nothing but out of the subsistence of the Father, as he says in Proth. 1.1. Hence he calls the Father the essentiator, and the Son and the Holy Spirit the essentiated. Beza, in his book on the unity of the essence: "We have read, and not without horror, what George Paul, Cafanouius, and some others, bewitched by Valentinus Gentilis, have written, changing the three persons, or hypostases [ὑποστάσεις], into three essences [ὁμοουσίας] in number, from which it follows that they necessarily posit three Gods." The Tritheites in Poland, under the leadership of George Paul, say that there are three Gods, three eternal, three almighty. The Poles, in a letter to the Senate of Geneva. Peter Statorius, a disciple of Theodore Beza, and George Blandrata publicly teach in Poland that there are not one but three Gods, as different from one another as three men; and they affirm that they learned this from Calvin, Bullinger, Martyr, and Musculus. Theodore Beza, Epistle 16. The Duitae in Poland, under the leadership of Peter Goniezius, assert that the Father and the Son are two Gods, but that it has not yet been revealed what the Spirit is. From Canisius, On the Corruptions of the Word of God; from Alphonsus Pisanus, in his preface to the Council of Nicaea; and from others.

units.la: 3. Lutherus in Confutatione Latomianæ rarationis. Sic odit anima mea vocem Homousion, & nolim ea vti, non ero hæreticus. &c. Nec est quod mihi obiectes aduersus Arianos receptum. Non fuit receptum a multis, quod & Hieronymus optauit aboleri; ideoque non effugerunt periculum hoc inuento vocabulo, vt Hieronymus queratur nescire, quid veneni lateat in syllabis, & litteris, adeo illud Ariani magis quam Scriptores exagitabant. Michaël Seruetus libro 1. contra Trinitatem, Tres illas res incorporeas in vna Deitate distinctas negat posse consistere: omnes qui Trinitatem statuunt in essentia Dei, Tritheitas, & atheos vocat, qui nec Deum nisi tripartitum, & aggregatum habeant. Theodorus Beza Epist. 1. Seruetus Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum Cerberum tricipitem appellauit. Caluinus contra Seruetum. Seruetus Athanasium dicit fuisse Sathanasium, hunc tripartitum Deum inuenisse, Nicænos Patres omnes fuisse cæcos sophistas, ministros bestiæ, mancipia Antichristi, eiusque præstigijs fascinatos. Theodorus Dorschius Francisci Dauidis dogmata defendens. Falsus hic, & fictus Deus, aut ab homine peccati, est Deus trinus, & unus. Nam hic nomine tantum Deus, revera autem Idolum est, de quo Paulus ait, quod nihil sit.
