Nam impossibile omnino est, quod talis aliquis existens, qui unus, & trinus sit, possit, aut debeat verus esse Deus. Nam verus Deus non est tanta potentia, ut possit facere esse eas res, quae sunt impossibiles menti.
units.tr: 3. Luther, against Latomus's Rationes: "So my soul hates the word homoousion, and I would not wish to use it; I shall not be a heretic," etc. Nor can you object to me that it was accepted against the Arians. It was not accepted by many, and Jerome wished it abolished; therefore they did not escape danger by this invented word, so that Jerome complains that he does not know what poison lies hidden in the syllables and letters, so much did the Arians rather than the writers harass it. Michael Servetus, in book 1 against the Trinity: he denies that those three incorporeal things distinguished in one Deity can subsist. He calls all who posit a Trinity in the essence of God Tritheists and atheists, who have no God but one tripartite and aggregated. Theodore Beza, Epistle 1: Servetus called the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit a three-headed Cerberus. Calvin, against Servetus. Servetus says that Athanasius was a Satanasius, who invented this tripartite God; that all the Nicene Fathers were blind sophists, ministers of the beast, slaves of Antichrist, and bewitched by his trickery. Theodore Dorsch, defending the dogmas of Francis David: "This false and fictitious God, a trinity and a unity, is an idol of man's sin. For he is God only in name, but in truth an idol, of which Paul says that it is nothing. For it is altogether impossible that such a being, who is one and three, could be, or ought to be, a true God. For a true God does not have such power that he can make those things be which are impossible to the mind."

units.la: 4. Philippus Melanchthon in locis communibus. Cum aut dubia sit natura Filius, necesse est in eo aliquid esse divinae naturae substantialiter. Quidquid autem est extra personam Patris, quod tamen est aliquid divinae naturae, id necesse est personam esse. Ioannes Calvinus ad cap. 14. Genes. Summa est, Christum ita fore secundum post Deum regem, ut etiam in Sacerdotem ungatur. In Harmonia Euangelica ad Cap. 22. Matthaei. Sessio ad dextram metaphorice accipitur, pro secundo, vel proximo gradu, quem Dei Vicarius occupat. Ad Cap. 26. Matthaei. Dicitur Christus sedere ad dextram Patris, quia summus Rex constitutus, qui eius nomine mundum gubernet, quasi secundam ab eo honoris, & imperij sedem obtinet. Sedet ergo Christus ad Patris dextram, quia eius est Vicarius. Epistola secunda ad Polonos asserit, Christum etiam secundum naturam etiam divinam, Patre minorem esse. Danaeus contra Genebrardum; Dure, & periculose loquitur Augustinus, pace tanti viri dixerim, quando ait; Deus cum Verbum genuit id quod est ipse, genuit. Dure etiam ipse locutus est, cum ait, Christus est Filius substantia Patris, sapientia de sapientia, substantia de substanstantia. Bernardinus Ochinus, Dialogo 2. de Trinitate, Christum Dominum creaturam esse dicit. Fratres familiæ amoris, libro Londini impresso 1579. negant, Christum esse æqualem Patri, quod ipse Christus dixit, Pater maior me est. Præterea addunt, Christum non esse Deum.
units.tr: 4. Philip Melanchthon, in the Loci communes: "Since the nature of the Son is doubtful, it is necessary that there be something of the divine nature in him substantially. Whatever, however, is outside the person of the Father, yet is something of the divine nature, that must necessarily be a person." John Calvin, on Genesis 14: "The sum is that Christ will be the second king after God, so that he is even anointed as priest." In the Gospel Harmony, on Matthew 22: "To sit at the right hand is taken metaphorically for the second or next rank, which God's Vicar occupies." On Matthew 26: "Christ is said to sit at the right hand of the Father, because he is set up as the supreme King, who governs the world in his name, and holds, as it were, the second seat of honour from him. Christ therefore sits at the Father's right hand, because he is his Vicar." In his second letter to the Poles he asserts that Christ, even according to the divine nature, is less than the Father. Daneus, against Genebrardus: "Augustine speaks harshly and dangerously, with respect to so great a man I say it, when he says: God, when he begot the Word, begot what he himself is. He also spoke harshly himself when he said: Christ is the Son of the substance of the Father, wisdom of wisdom, substance of substance." Bernardinus Ochinus, Dialogue 2 On the Trinity: he says that Christ the Lord is a creature. The Brethren of the Family of Love, in a book printed at London in 1579, deny that Christ is equal to the Father, because Christ himself said: "The Father is greater than I." Moreover they add that Christ is not God.

units.la: 5. Philippus Melanchthon in locis communibus; In Spiritu sancto est aliquid essentiæ Dei. &c. In Spiritu sancto est aliquid Dei. Bernardinus Ochinus in Polonia prædicavit, Spiritus sancti hypostasim, & personam nullam esse. Iosias Simletus, in vita Bullingeri, Christianus Francus libro contra sanctam Trinitatem edito; Cum non dum, inquit, contenti duabus divinis personis, tertiam quoque adjicere vellent, quæ Spiritus sanctus vocaretur: non autem ignorarent nullum extare in totis Bibliis de divinitate Spiritus sancti apertum testimonium, imo unigenitum Dei Filium nullam alium Deum admittere, sed prorsus excludere, tertiam personam finxerunt Spiritum sanctum ὁμοούσιον[?] quidem Patri, & Filio, & ab utroque productam: quam tamen commentitiam, fictamque doctrinam communis totius sacræ Scripturæ consensus refellit. Petrus Martyr, in Epist. ad Romanos, ait; Disputationem inter Theologos de processione Spiritus sancti esse meram scholasticam contentionem.
units.tr: 5. Philip Melanchthon, in the Loci communes: "In the Holy Spirit there is something of the essence of God, etc. In the Holy Spirit there is something of God." Bernardinus Ochinus preached in Poland: "The Holy Spirit has no hypostasis and no person." Josias Simlerus, in the life of Bullinger; Christian Franck, in a book published against the Holy Trinity: "Since they were not yet content with two divine persons, and wished to add a third as well, which would be called the Holy Spirit," and since they did not know that there is no clear testimony anywhere in the whole Bible to the divinity of the Holy Spirit, indeed that the only-begotten Son of God admits no other God but altogether excludes one, they invented a third person, the Holy Spirit, consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον] indeed with the Father and the Son, and produced by both. Yet the common agreement of all Holy Scripture refutes this fictitious and made-up doctrine. Peter Martyr, in his Epistle to the Romans, says: "The dispute among the theologians about the procession of the Holy Spirit is mere scholastic contention."

units.la: Ioannes Sommerus contra Petrum Carolium lib. 2. cap. 1. dicit, Carolius quomodo lex Patre, & Filio mutuo se amantibus procedat ὑποστατικὸν[?] πνεῦμα: Filio, & Spiritu, vel Patre se amantibus nihil procedat? Item, Quomodo Spiritus sancti proprietas erit procedere, cum Christus quoque dicatur procedere a Patre: imo cum de pluribus aliis rebus, etiam de Diabolis hoc ipsum verbum dicat?
units.tr: John Sommer, against Peter Carolus, book 2, chapter 1, says: Carolus asks how a spirit subsisting [ὑποστατικὸν] proceeds from the Father and the Son loving each other mutually; does nothing proceed from the Son and the Spirit, or the Father, loving themselves? Likewise, how will it be a property of the Holy Spirit to proceed, when Christ too is said to proceed from the Father? Indeed, when he says this very word of many other things, even of the devils?

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Hæc tenet Romana, & Græca Ecclesia. Christi matrem peccato omnino caruisse, omnibus Sanctis, & Angelis sanctiorem, cuius invocatione multum confidunt: ideoque misericordiam illius implorant, & dies illius festos solemni ritu agunt.
units.tr: This is what the Roman and Greek Church hold: that the mother of Christ was wholly free from sin, holier than all the saints and angels, and that they place great confidence in her intercession; therefore they implore her mercy and celebrate her feast days with solemn rite.

units.la: Quid Reformati?
units.tr: What do the Reformed say?

units.la: Lutherus Serm. de Natiu. Mariæ; Summus[?] pares matri Dei, & æque sancti sicut illa; nisi quod non possumus esse Dei matres sicut illa fuit. Melancht. ad c.2. Ioannis. Christus matrem reiecit, ut æquet eam aliis hominibus, cum inquit: quid mihi tecum est mulier? quasi diceret, quia mater es, ideo videris alicuius prærogatiua merito a me impetratura; ideo scias, te non plus esse apud me, quam vel mulier peccatrix, vel Syrophœniffa. Ioan. Oecolamp.; Uti Maria non eum honorem quærit, qui debetur parentibus, sed etiam ambit honorem Messiæ, & cupit esse— quasi socia administrādi eius officij, quod Christo divinitus mandatum erat, ibi Christus durissime eam alloquitur, ut contineat ipsam intra terminos suae vocationis. Caluinus in Harmonia Euangelica ad Cap. 1. Lucae. Non magnopere laborandum est, ut Mariam ab omni purgemus vitio. Magdeburgenses Centuriae primae lib. 1. Utraque delicta, Eva & Maria non sunt exigua. Sed tamen non tantum secundum obiecta discernuntur peccata, verum magis principaliter secundum interiores causas, nempe iudicium, & assensum voluntatis. Eva sciens, & volens facit contra mandatum Dei: Maria insciens, & contra voluntatem amittit Filium, sed nihilominus grauiter peccat. Ioannes Caluinus in Harmonia Euangelica ad cap. 1. Lucae. Quod suspicati sunt quidam, Mariam perpetuae Virginitatis conceptum habuisse votum, nimis infirmum est, imo prorsus absurdum. Perfidum enim fuisset se marito collocare, sanctumque coniugij foedus non sine Dei ludibrio spreuisset. Lucas Stembergius tanto flagrauit Mariae odio, ut eam Virginitatis gloria omnique honore spoliandam putaret, utpote quam ex Iosepb [?] coniuge multos filios peperisse, & a reliquis non differre, spurcissime sinxit, & tradidit. Theodorus Beza in novum Testamentum; Perpetuam Mariae ad mortem usque virginitatem, & si pie & libenter credo, tamen nihil hoc ad salutis nostrae mysterium pertinet. Joannes Riccius libro de Abusibus Ecclesiasticis; Nullo modo affirmare vult, Mariam una cum corpore assumptam esse: quoniam in Sacra Scriptura nullus de ea re locus extat. Nicolaus Selneuerus in Disputatione Euangelica de festis Sanctorum, Virginis Mariae invocationem tetrum errorem appellat. Christianus Rodingus contra Scholas Jesuitarum, Virginem sic loquentem inducit: Define me salutare, & salutando venerari, istam tuam salutationem, & preces execror. Tu ubi terrarum fis, quid agas, denique an mortuus fis, neque scio, neque curo, tantum abest, ut te peccatorem exaudiam. Henricus Bullingerus adversus Anabaptistas lib. 2. capite 13. narrat Melchiorem Hoffmannum Argentinae in publica disputatione asseruisse, Christum non sumpsisse carnem ex Maria Virgine, eoque processisse, ut libere diceret, maledicta fit caro Mariae. Joannes Oecolampadius in Concione de omnibus Sanctis, dixit. Mariae veneratione, cultum Idolorum esse. Rodulphus Gualterus ad Cap. 3. Marci. Salutationem Angelicam, quasi magicum murmur existimat. Jacobus Heerbrandus, in Disputatione de Semine Abrahae; Turpissime errant Pontificii dum D. Virgini hoc tribuunt, quod sit fons ineuacuabilis misericordiarum, & venia, imo ipsa misericordia, & venia. Martinus Lutherus in Euangelium, de Festo Natiuitatis Mariae. Peruelim hoc festum omitti, cum nullo Scripturae testimonio nitatur. Et libro de pijs cerimonijs obseruandis; Assumptionis, & Natiuitatis Mariae festa plane reijcimus.
units.tr: Luther, Sermon on the Nativity of Mary: "The saints are equal to the mother of God, and as holy as she is; except that we cannot be mothers of God as she was." Melanchthon on John 2: "Christ rejected his mother in order to put her on a level with other people, when he said: 'What have I to do with you, woman?' as if he meant: 'Because you are my mother, you seem to be going to obtain something by the merit of some prerogative from me; therefore know that you count for no more with me than a sinful woman or a Syrophoenician.'" Johannes Oecolampadius: "Mary does not seek the honour that is owed to parents, but even aspires to the honour of the Messiah, and wants to be, as it were, the partner in the office which was divinely entrusted to Christ; there Christ addresses her very harshly, so as to keep her within the limits of her calling." Calvin, in his Harmony of the Gospels on Luke 1: We need not labour greatly to cleanse Mary of every fault. The Magdeburg Centuries, Century 1, book 1: Both the sins of Eve and of Mary are not small. Yet sins are distinguished not only by their objects but still more chiefly by their inner causes, namely the judgement and assent of the will. Eve, knowingly and willingly, acts against the command of God; Mary, unknowingly and against her will, loses her Son, yet nonetheless sins grievously. John Calvin, in his Harmony of the Gospels on Luke 1: That some have suspected that Mary had a vow of perpetual virginity is far too weak, indeed utterly absurd. For it would have been treacherous to bind herself to a husband, and she would have despised the holy covenant of marriage without mocking God. Lucas Stemberger burned with such hatred of Mary that he thought she should be stripped of the glory of virginity and of all honour, and he shamefully invented and handed down that she bore many sons from her husband Joseph and did not differ from the rest. Theodore Beza, on the New Testament: I believe, piously and gladly, in Mary's perpetual virginity until death; yet this has nothing to do with the mystery of our salvation. Johannes Riccius, in his book on Ecclesiastical Abuses: He does not wish to affirm in any way that Mary was taken up together with her body, since there is no passage about this matter in Holy Scripture. Nicolaus Selnecker, in his Evangelical Disputation on the Feasts of the Saints, calls the invocation of the Virgin Mary a foul error. Christian Roding, against the Jesuit schools, introduces the Virgin speaking thus: Do not greet me with a salutation, and do not honour me by greeting; I curse that salutation of yours and those prayers. Where you are on earth, what you are doing, and whether you are even dead, I neither know nor care, so far am I from hearing you as a sinner. Henry Bullinger, against the Anabaptists, book 2, chapter 13, relates that Melchior Hoffmann asserted in a public disputation at Strasbourg that Christ did not take flesh from the Virgin Mary, and proceeded so far as to say freely: "Cursed be the flesh of Mary." Johannes Oecolampadius, in a sermon on All Saints, said: The veneration of Mary is the worship of idols. Rudolf Gwalther, on Mark 3: He considers the angelic salutation to be like a magical mumbling. Jacob Heerbrand, in his disputation on the Seed of Abraham: The Papists err most shamefully when they attribute to the Blessed Virgin that she is an inexhaustible fount of mercies and pardon, indeed mercy and pardon itself. Martin Luther, in a gospel sermon on the Feast of the Nativity of Mary: I would gladly have this feast omitted, since it rests on no testimony of Scripture. And in his book on the good works to be observed: We plainly reject the feasts of the Assumption and of the Nativity of Mary.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Haec tenent Romana, & Graeca Ecclesia.
units.tr: The Roman and Greek Church hold these things.

units.la: 1. Pios homines huius vitae afflictionibus & molestijs aeterna gaudia promereri.
units.tr: 1. Pious people earn eternal joys through the afflictions and troubles of this life.

units.la: 2. Post hanc vitam ab omnibus malis exemptos visione beatifica frui. 3. Ideoque illos inuocant, & intensissimis precibus eorum—, apud Deum auxilia implorant, 4. Templis, atque Basilicis in eorum honorem sumptuosissime exaedificatis, 5. Et eorum dies festos agunt, 6. Et Reliquias, 7. atque Imagines veneratione prosequuntur.
units.tr: 2. Once free after this life from all evils, they enjoy the beatific vision. 3. And therefore they invoke them, and with the most intense prayers implore their help with God. 4. They build temples and basilicas in their honour at great expense. 5. And they celebrate their feast days. 6. And they honour relics 7. and images with veneration.

units.la: Quid Reformati ?
units.tr: What do the Reformed say?

units.la: 1. Martinus Lutherus de Inuentione S. Crucis. Non cogites tua afflictione, e Cruce te salutem consequi, si patienter, & late tolerras; sicut vecordes aliqui Seductores suadent. Quemadmodum enim nos opera nostra non salvos faciunt: ita ne cruce, nec afflictionibus nostris salus nobis constat. Georgius Dauid asserebat; Stultos fuisse Apostolos, & Martyres, quod tormenta, mortemque propter Christi consessiofissionem passi sint. Magdeburgenses Cent. 3. cap. 4. reprehendunt Tertullianum, Origenem & Cyprianum, quod immodicis laudibus extulerint Martyrium.
units.tr: 1. Martin Luther, on the Invention of the Holy Cross: Do not imagine that you obtain salvation through your affliction and the Cross, if you bear it patiently and calmly, as some foolish seducers persuade. For just as our works do not save us, so neither does salvation come to us through the Cross or our afflictions. Georg David maintained: The Apostles and Martyrs were foolish, because they suffered torments and death for the confession of Christ. The Magdeburg Centuries, Century 3, chapter 4, rebuke Tertullian, Origen and Cyprian, because they extolled martyrdom with immoderate praise.

units.la: 2. Martinus Lutherus ad cap. 25. Genes. Sancti dormiunt, & nesciunt quid hic agatur, & tamen quiescunt. Cornelius Agrippa de Occulta Philosophia lib. 3. asserit, Sanctorum animas non dum esse in Caelo. Ioannes Calvinus lib. 3. Institutionum, capite 25. Stultum, & temerarium est inquirere, in quo loco sint animae Iustorum, & an gloria fruantur, nec ne[?].
units.tr: 2. Martin Luther, on Genesis 25: The saints sleep and do not know what is going on here, and yet they rest. Cornelius Agrippa, in De occulta philosophia book 3, asserts that the souls of the saints are not yet in heaven. John Calvin, Institutes book 3, chapter 25: It is foolish and rash to inquire in what place the souls of the righteous are, and whether they enjoy glory or not.

units.la: 3. Martinus Lutherus, de Adoratione Sacramenti ad waldenses; Non possum vos pro haereticis habere, quemadmodum Sophistae nostri faciunt, quod neque Dei matrem, neque quemquam Sanctorum invocatis, sed in solo, & unico mediatore Christo acquiescitis. Et si hic alius pro alio intercedere debet, tamen de Sanctorum mortuorum intercessione, & invocatione nihil in Scripturis extat. Philippus Melanchthon in antithesi verae doctrinae, & Pontificiae. Manifesta Idolomania est omnis invocatio mortuorum, qualis est in cultu Sanctorum. Nicolaus Henningus in Explicatione Euangelii in festo Annunciationis Mariae; Invocatio Sanctorum est cultus Diabolicus, in Ecclesiam a Diabolo invectus. Ioannes Brentius in Apologia Confessionis wirtembergensis; Concedimus Sanctos in Cælo pro viuentibus orare in terra, num idcirco sunt inuocandi? nihil minus &c. Quis iussit nos inuocare Sanctos, vt Dei amicos? Nam hic ipse sanctos inuocandi cultus Idololatricus est, propterea quod solus Deus sit inuocandus. Theodorus Beza Responsione ad Nicolai Selneueri calumnias; Sanctorum mortuorum inuocatio, non tantum stulta, & inanis, sed etiam impia esse conuincitur.
units.tr: 3. Martin Luther, on the Adoration of the Sacrament, to the Waldensians: I cannot regard you as heretics, as our Sophists do, because you invoke neither the Mother of God nor any of the saints, but rest in Christ alone, the one Mediator. And even if one must intercede for another, still nothing is found in Scripture about the intercession and invocation of the dead saints. Philip Melanchthon, in his antithesis of true and Papist doctrine: Every invocation of the dead, such as is found in the cult of the saints, is manifest idolatry. Nicolaus Henning, in his explanation of the Gospel on the Feast of the Annunciation of Mary: The invocation of the saints is a diabolical worship, brought into the Church by the Devil. Johannes Brenz, in the Apology of the Württemberg Confession: We grant that the saints in heaven pray for the living on earth; does it follow that they are to be invoked? By no means &c. Who commanded us to invoke the saints as God's friends? For this very cult of invoking the saints is idolatrous, because God alone is to be invoked. Theodore Beza, in his Response to the calumnies of Nicolaus Selnecker: The invocation of the dead saints is shown to be not only foolish and vain, but also impious.

units.la: 4. Martinus Lutherus, in Euangelium Dominicæ 23. Trinitatis; Et tali falsa, & impia confidentia in homines collocata damnum quoq; illud in Christianismum irrepsit, Sanctorum nempe cultus, & veneratio. Vnde Christiana Ecclesia maximum sane damnum, & tantum non incomparabilem ruinam perpessa est. Quid enim Sanctorum cultus, & veneratio aliud fuit, nisi diabolica res? Epistola ad Erphordienses; Non necessarium est Sanctos colere, sed sufficit Christiano nosse solum Christum esse colendum. Quanquam sit superuacaneum Sanctos colere, non tamen eos putarim respuendos, qui Sanctos adhuc colunt. Ioannes Caluinus lib. 1. Institut. cap. 11. & 12. Non patitur vllum cultum exhiberi Sanctis, vel Angelis, vel hominibus defunctis, nec magnum, nec parum. Martinus Lutherus ad Euangelium Dominicæ primæ Aduentus; Bona opera appellant[?]; quæ haudquaquam Deus præcepit, vt sint peregrinari ad excelsa illa diuorum, ieiunare, in honorem Sanctorum extruere, & ornare templa. &c. Ecquis enumeret abominandas illas abominationes, & spurcissimas, atque perniciosissimas imposturas? Et ad Euangelium in die Natiuitatis Mariæ; Hic honor e medio sublatus est, & in eius locum insani boatus, & Sanctorum, qui in Cœlum subuecti sint, veneratio inducta est. Hinc tot templa, & altaria substructa sunt. Hic Petro, hic Paulo ædes electa est, vt omnes fere anguli Diuorum phanis pleni sint. At cui vsui ipsis illa? His sumptibus indotatis Virginibus consuli poterat, & alia maioris momenti opera patrari. &c.
units.tr: 4. Martin Luther, on the Gospel for the 23rd Sunday after Trinity: And by such false and impious trust placed in men, that damage also crept into Christianity, namely the cult and veneration of the saints. Hence the Christian Church has suffered a very great loss and an almost incomparable ruin. For what else was the cult and veneration of the saints but a diabolical thing? Letter to the Erfurters: It is not necessary to honour the saints, but it suffices for a Christian to know that Christ alone is to be worshipped. Although it is superfluous to honour the saints, I would not think that those who still honour the saints should be rejected. John Calvin, Institutes book 1, chapters 11 and 12: He allows no cult to be offered to saints, or angels, or departed men, neither great nor small. Martin Luther, on the Gospel for the First Sunday of Advent: They call good works those things which God by no means commanded, such as going on pilgrimages to those lofty shrines of the saints, fasting, building in honour of the saints, and adorning churches. &c. Who could count those abominable abominations, and most filthy and most pernicious impostures? And on the Gospel for the day of the Nativity of Mary: This honour has been removed from the midst, and in its place a mad clamour and the veneration of the saints, who have been carried up into heaven, has been introduced. Hence so many temples and altars have been built. Here a house has been chosen for Peter, here one for Paul, so that almost all the corners are full of temples of the saints. But to what use are they? With these expenses, poor virgins could have been provided for, and other works of greater importance could have been carried out. &c.

units.la: 5. Martinus Lutherus, De Cerimonijs Ecclesiæ seruandis, Festa Sanctorum in vniuersum aboleantur. Libello de formula Missæ; Omnium Sanctorum festa prorsus abroganda putamus. Libro contra Ambrosium Catharinum; Duodecima facies Antichristi est festorum dierum obseruatio, cum omnes dies liberi sint, & ad feriandum, & ad laborandum. In hac autem facie insignius lucent, magni illi festi dies, Visitationis, Corporis Christi, Apostolorum, Conceptionis, & similium; & necesse est peccare, & perire animas, si quæ non seruant, vel inuite seruant hæc stulta, inutilia, & vana præcepta. Confessio ministrorum Ecclesiae in Heluetia, & Tiguri cap. 24. Festa hominibus, aut Diuis instituta non probamus.
units.tr: 5. Martin Luther, On the Ceremonies of the Church to Be Kept: We think the festivals of all the saints should be utterly abolished. In the booklet on the form of the Mass: We think the festivals of all the saints should be utterly abrogated. In the book against Ambrosius Catharinus: The twelfth face of Antichrist is the observance of festival days, when all days are free both for resting and for working. In this face the great festival days of the Visitation, of Corpus Christi, of the Apostles, of the Conception, and the like, shine out more conspicuously; and souls must sin and perish if they keep, or unwillingly keep, these foolish, useless and vain precepts. Confession of the Ministers of the Church in Helvetia and Zurich, ch. 24: We do not approve of festivals instituted by men or in honour of saints.

units.la: 6. Martinus Lutherus, Postilla in die Exaltationis S. Crucis. Quidquid de S. Crucedixi, intelligi debet de omnibus Sanctorum reliquijs. Reliquiae enim nihil aliud sunt, quam fraudes, & seductiones fidelium; quare omnino infra terram defodiantur. Hoc de explodendis & exfibilandis Sanctorum reliquijs olim pertractauit & Vigilantius, cui se fortiter, & acriter opposuit Hieronymus. Quod si adhuc Vigilantij monumenta superessent, quemadmodum Hieronymi etiamnum extant, facile crediderim eum multo christianius super hoc scripsisse, quam ipsum Hieronymum. Vellem terra omnes istas reliquias contectas esse. Ioannes Calvinus, Admonitione de Reliquijs; Itaque ut paucis dicam. Reliquiarum desiderium nunquam superstitione caret, imo, quod deterius est, mater est, idololatriae. Christianorum officij erat, Sanctorum corpora in sepulchris suis relinquere: non erigere ipsa opere magnifico, & sumptuoso, quo praemature corporum resurrectionem fabricarent. Hoc quidem minime intellectum fuit, sed e diuerso, contra decretum Dei fidelium corpora effossa sunt, ut magnifice extollerentur; cum in sepulchro suo velut in lectulo ad extremum diem quiescere debuissent.
units.tr: 6. Martin Luther, Postil on the day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross: Whatever I have said of the Holy Cross must be understood of all the relics of the saints. For relics are nothing other than frauds and deceptions of the faithful; therefore they should be buried entirely beneath the earth. The matter of rejecting and hissing down the relics of the saints was once also treated by Vigilantius, against whom Jerome opposed himself strongly and bitterly. But if the writings of Vigilantius survived, as those of Jerome still do, I would readily believe he wrote much more Christianly on this than Jerome himself. I wish all those relics were covered over by the earth. John Calvin, Admonition on Relics: So, to say it briefly. The desire for relics is never free of superstition; indeed, what is worse, it is the mother of idolatry. It was the duty of Christians to leave the bodies of the saints in their tombs, not to raise them with magnificent and costly work, by which they would prematurely build up the resurrection of bodies. This was by no means understood, but on the contrary, against the decree of God, the bodies of the faithful were dug up so that they might be magnificently exalted, whereas they ought to have rested in their own sepulchre as on a bed until the last day.

units.la: 7. Andreas Carlostadius primus in Germania Imaginum hostis, Eas templo abstulit: quod quia nescio & non confulto Luthero fecerat, acriter propterea ab eodem fuit reprehensus. Philippus Melanchthon in locis communibus, Cap. de Decalogo, reprehendit omnem Imaginum venerationem. Ioannes Caluinus libro 1. Instit., capite 11. Insanire eos minime obscurum est, qui simulacra Dei, & Sanctorum exemplo Cherubim defendere conantur. Confessio Ministrorum Ecclesiae in Heluetia ca. 4. Reijcimus non modo gentium idola, sed & Christianorum Simulacra.
units.tr: 7. Andreas Carlstadt, the first enemy of images in Germany, removed them from the church; because he did this without knowledge and without consulting Luther, he was for that reason sharply rebuked by him. Philip Melanchthon, in the Loci communes, chapter on the Decalogue, condemns all veneration of images. John Calvin, Institutes book 1, chapter 11: It is not at all obscure that they are mad who try to defend the images of God and of the saints by the example of the cherubim. Confession of the Ministers of the Church in Helvetia, ch. 4: We reject not only the idols of the Gentiles but also the images of Christians.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Hæc tenent Romana, & Græca Ecclesia.
units.tr: These things are held by the Roman and Greek Church.

units.la: 1. Monastica vita non recens excogitata, sed inde usque a Christi temporibus ad nos deducta,
units.tr: 1. Monastic life, not recently devised but handed down to us from the times of Christ onward,

units.la: 2. Peculiari amictu; 3. Tonsuraque nomina scribunt, 4. Et proprijs abnegatis, 5. Voto se mancipant, 6. Pauperta-tis, 7. Et castitati operam dant, 8. Et Prælatis suis obediunt, neque postmodum in seculum impune redeunt.
units.tr: 2. a peculiar garb; 3. and they write down names with the tonsure; 4. and, having renounced their own possessions, 5. they bind themselves by vow; 6. to poverty, 7. and devote their efforts to chastity, 8. and obey their prelates, nor afterwards return to the world with impunity.

units.la: Quid Reformati?
units.tr: What do the Reformed say?

units.la: 1. Martinus Lutherus de votis Monasticis; Cupio eradicata, & extincta, & abolita esse universa Monasteria, qua utinam Dominus igne, & sulphure cælesti ad exemplum Sodoma, & Gomorrhæ demergat, adeo, ut ne memoria quidem illorum superfit : Neque satis fuerit illis anathema imprecari. &c. Vota monastica sunt impia, Gentilia, Iudaica, Sacrilega, mendacia, erronea, daemoniaca, hypocritica, Apostatica, etiam Sanctorum exemplis aduersaria. Quare cum omni fiducia renocanda, & discernenda sunt, etiam si pia, & seria opinione emissa fuerint. In prioris ad Corinth. cap. 7. Qui coelibem in Monasterijs vitam degunt, Idolo Moloch corpora sua cremant. Philippus Melanchthon in Apologia Confessionis Augustanae, dicit; Monasticam vitam recens esse excogitatam: Vota, atque opera Monachorum nunc hypocriticas simulationes, nunc etiam traditiones Pharisaicas, atque Mahumeticas appellat. Ioannes Calvinus lib. 4. Instit. capite 13. Monasteria dicit esse lupanaria, vota monastica dicit esse retia Satanae, Monachos omnes appellat Sophistas cucullatos, qui ab Ecclesia defecerunt, & se totos Diabolo consecrarunt. Magdeburgenses Centuria 10. cap. 4. Si quis haec hominum monstra non execretur, ut inimicos humanae societatis, & contra secundam tabulam delinquentes.
units.tr: 1. Martin Luther, on monastic vows: I wish all monasteries uprooted, extinguished and abolished, which I pray the Lord would sink with heavenly fire and brimstone, as Sodom and Gomorrah, so that not even the memory of them would remain. Nor would it be enough to call down a curse upon them. Etc. Monastic vows are impious, Gentile, Jewish, sacrilegious, lying, erroneous, demonic, hypocritical, apostate, and even opposed to the examples of the saints. Therefore they must be revoked and rejected with all confidence, even if they were uttered with a pious and earnest opinion. On 1 Corinthians ch. 7: Those who live a celibate life in monasteries burn their bodies to the idol Moloch. Philip Melanchthon, in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, says: Monastic life has been recently devised. The vows and works of the monks he calls now hypocritical pretences, now also Pharisaic and Mahometan traditions. John Calvin, Institutes book 4, chapter 13: He calls monasteries brothels, calls monastic vows the nets of Satan, and calls all monks hooded sophists who have fallen away from the Church and wholly consecrated themselves to the Devil. Magdeburg Centuries, century 10, ch. 4: If anyone does not execrate these monstrosities of men, as enemies of human society and transgressors of the second table.

units.la: 2. Martinus Lutherus excusso cucullo, Passim in suis scriptis, habitum monasticum ludibrio proscindit. Volfgangus Musculus in locis communibus, cap. de Voto; Respondeant Monachi, quo loco cucullos suos habeant, & quomodo ab hypocrisi, & superstitione tueantur, quod singulari & colore, & forma a consueto sese, ac populari amictu disiunxerunt. Sunt qui praeferant, nescio quae humilitatis, & innocentiae indicia.
units.tr: 2. Martin Luther, having shaken off the cowl: Throughout his writings he mocks and tears apart the monastic habit. Wolfgang Musculus, in the Loci communes, chapter on Vows: Let the monks answer where they keep their hoods, and how they defend them from hypocrisy and superstition, since they have separated themselves by a singular colour and form from the customary and common dress. There are those who put forward I know not what signs of humility and innocence.

units.la: Lutherus libro de Votis Monasticis, & ista [?] priuata, & alibi, Tonsuram Clericorum, & Monachorum miris sannis, & ludibrijs proscindit. Ioannes Caluinus lib. 4. institut. cap. 19. Radunt eos in vertice, ut corona regale decus significet: assignant & alias rationes. Summitas capitis denudatur, ut mens ad Dominum libere demonstretur, omnia in figuris scilicet, quia velum templi non dum scissum est. Quo usque nos talibus fucis, & praestigijs ludunt? Cur non magis sanctitatem vere exhibent, quam falsis mendacibusque signis ipsius speciem simulant? Hortensius Landus tonsurae monachalis desertor, libellum emisit in lucem, quem inscripsit: De perfecutione barbarum, in quo miris sannis Clericorum, & Monachorum tonsuram persequitur. Magdebugrenses, Centuria 4. cap. 6. ad dictum Dionysij Areopagitae de habitu, & tonsura Monachi, inquiunt, Haec superstítiosa sunt, non consentanea Sacris literis, nec observationi purioris Ecclesiae.
units.tr: Luther, in his book on Monastic Vows, and these [?] privately, and elsewhere, tears apart the tonsure of clerics and monks with wondrous sneers and mockery. John Calvin, Institutes book 4, chapter 19: They shave them on the crown so that the royal ornament of a crown may signify it; they assign also other reasons. The top of the head is bared so that the mind may be freely shown to the Lord, all in figures, of course, because the veil of the temple is not yet torn. How long will they mock us with such paints and tricks? Why do they not rather display real holiness, rather than pretend its appearance by false and lying signs? Hortensius Landus, a deserter of the monastic tonsure, put out a little book which he entitled On the Persecution of Beards, in which he pursues the tonsure of clerics and monks with wondrous sneers. The Magdeburg Centuries, century 4, ch. 6, on the statement of Dionysius the Areopagite about the habit and tonsure of the monk, say: These things are superstitious, not consistent with the Sacred Letters, nor with the observance of the purer Church.

units.la: 4. Lutherus contra triginta duos articulos Louanienfium Thesi 59. Paupertas, quam vouent, est rapina Orbis terrarum, & opes mundi sicut scriptum est; Ecce peccatores abundantes in seculo, obtinuerunt diuitias. De votis Monasticis; Votum paupertatis videtur a Satana in hoc effectum, ut religiosi pretextus eius liberi fiant a iuuanda pauperum aliorum, & ab impendendis operibus misericordie[?]. Philippus Melanchthon in locis communibus; Euangelium nec consulit, nec præci[?]pit, discedere a facultatibus, nisi eripiantur: nec præcipit, nec consulit res in commune conferre.
units.tr: 4. Luther, against the thirty-two articles of the Louvain theologians, Thesis 59: The poverty which they vow is a robbery of the whole world and its wealth, as it is written: Behold, sinners abounding in the world have obtained riches. On monastic vows: The vow of poverty seems to have been brought about by Satan to this effect, that the religious, under the pretext of it, become free from helping other poor people and from performing works of mercy [?]. Philip Melanchthon, in the Loci communes: The Gospel neither counsels nor commands giving up one's goods, unless they are taken away; it neither commands nor counsels putting goods into a common fund.

units.la: 5. Martinus Lutherus, lib. de Votis monasticis, de obedientia Monachorum; Peccant hic eadem insania Monastici, qua & in paupertatem. Primo quod consilium eam faciunt: deinde quod solis sibi arrogant. Ideo dum eam vouent, & impie negant mandatum Dei, & sacrilege damnant votum Baptismi sui. Si vero aliqui pie vouent, nonnisi corporalem vouent. At nisi Spiritus in eis fit, & tandem alijs quoq; subdat, nihil vouetur, nisi contrarium Euangelicæ obedientiæ. Inter omnia vota monastica nullum est minus substantiale, quam obedientiæ votum. Igitur fiat conclusio. Obedientiam Monasticam, esse rudem, & puerilem obedientiam pro rudimento dumtaxat iuuentutis institutam, nec aliter apud Deum acceptam, nec aliter voueri possibilem, nisi impiam, & sacrilegam facere velis. Lutherani in colloquio Aldeburgensi; Opera bona legis, & bona obedientia non ad regnum Christi, sed ad mundum pertinent. Qui credit Christianus, supra omnem est obedientiam, & supra omnem legem.
units.tr: 5. Martin Luther, book on Monastic Vows, on the obedience of monks: Monks commit the same folly here as in poverty. First, because they make it a counsel; then, because they claim it for themselves alone. Therefore, while they vow it, they impiously deny God's command and sacrilegiously condemn the vow of their own baptism. If some do vow it piously, they vow only a bodily obedience. But unless the Spirit is in them, and they subject themselves to others also in the end, nothing is vowed except what is contrary to evangelical obedience. Among all monastic vows there is none less substantial than the vow of obedience. Therefore let this conclusion stand: monastic obedience is a crude and childish obedience, instituted merely as the rudiment of youth, neither accepted by God in any other way nor possible to vow in any other way, unless you wish to make it impious and sacrilegious. The Lutherans at the Colloquy of Aldenburg: Good works of the law and good obedience pertain not to the kingdom of Christ but to the world. The Christian who believes is above all obedience and above all law.

units.la: 6. Martinus Lutherus de vita coniugali. Crescite, & multiplicamini, non est praeceptum, sed plusquam praeceptum, quod nos non possumus impedire, vel praetermittere, & perinde necessarium est ac edere, & bibere, purgare, & expurgare, dormire, & vigilare, sicut in mea potestate non est, quo minus sim mas, ita minime situm in me est, quo minus sim sine muliere. Contra Ambrosium Catharinum. Decima facies Antichristi est, insignis ille coelibatus, & castitatis Monastica multitudo, plane Angelica facies, sed diabolica res. Huldaricus Zwinglius in Cap, 1. Matthaei. Quod Maria perpetuo mansit Virgo, ne tu trahas temere in exemplum, quod imitari velis, nisi singulari quadam revelatione ad id vocata, & electa. Inter omnes mortales hanc unam ad hoc elegit, ut casto, intactoque corpore Christum filium Dei gestaret, & mater esset, sine virginitatis, & castitatis iactura. Hoc privilegium nulli creaturae concessum est. Ad instructionem ergo Dei nobis respiciendum erit, & videndum, ut debito tempore matrimonio nos iungamus, nisi certi sumus, aliud Deum nobis statuisse. Ne ergo dicas, Christus non duxit uxorem. Ergo nec ego ducam: neque enim est similis ratio. Similia habet Conradus Pellicanus, & Martinus Bucerus in cap. 1. Matth.
units.tr: 6. Martin Luther, on the married life: Increase and multiply is not a precept but more than a precept, which we cannot prevent or omit, and it is just as necessary as eating and drinking, purging and emptying out, sleeping and waking. Just as it is not in my power not to be a man, so it is not in me not to be without a woman. Against Ambrosius Catharinus: The tenth face of Antichrist is that famous celibacy and the great multitude of monastic chastity, a plainly angelic face, but a diabolical thing. Huldrych Zwingli on chapter 1 of Matthew: That Mary remained a virgin forever, do not rashly draw this as an example you wish to imitate, unless you are called and chosen for it by some singular revelation. Among all mortals she alone was chosen for this, that with a chaste and untouched body she should bear Christ the Son of God and be a mother, without loss of virginity and chastity. This privilege has been granted to no creature. Therefore for our instruction we must look to God and see that at the proper time we join ourselves in marriage, unless we are certain that God has appointed something else for us. So do not say: Christ did not take a wife; therefore neither shall I; for the reason is not similar. Conrad Pellican and Martin Bucer have similar things on chapter 1 of Matthew.

units.la: 7. Lutherus de votis Monasticis; Quod ad ipsam voti rationem attinet, neque praecipit, neq; consulit Scriptura, ut quicquam devoveatur. Non probat autem Deus, nisi quod praecipit, vel consulit. Quare non video, quid accedat pietati propter votum. Et de vita coniugali; Et adversum haec nihil te movebit etiam si decies iuraveris, voveris, mera ferrea, & adamantina pacta peregeris. Nam ut nihil minus vovere potes, quam ut non sis mas, aut foemina: (& si voveres, stultum esset votum, nec quicquam valeret: non enim potes te alium formare) tanto minus etiam potes vovere, quod non velis coire, & multiplicare terram. Philippus Melanchthon Disput. 16. de iureiurando. Non valent Monachorum vota, quæ sine peccato non possunt præstari.
units.tr: 7. Luther, on monastic vows: As far as the very nature of a vow goes, Scripture neither commands nor advises that anything be vowed. But God approves only what he commands or advises. So I do not see what piety is added by a vow. And on married life: Nothing will move you against these things, even if you have sworn and vowed ten times and made iron and adamantine pacts. For just as you can vow nothing less than that you will not be male or female (and if you did vow it, the vow would be foolish and worth nothing, for you cannot form yourself otherwise), so much less can you vow that you will not wish to couple and multiply the earth. Philip Melanchthon, Disputation 16 on oaths: The vows of monks are not valid, since they cannot be fulfilled without sin.

units.la: Jam habes; quæ Græci, & Pontificii sentiant de his Capitibus, quæ Reformati. Et est nè hoc in essentialibus Reformatis propius accedere per omnia, quam Pontisicijs Tridentinis, & licet Pontificijs videantur fauere partibus, verbis, quam rebus assensum testari maiorem, & habere plura vobiscum? quo ore? qua fronte?
units.tr: Now you have what the Greeks and the Papists think about these heads, and what the Reformed think. Is it not the case that in essentials the Reformed come closer to them in every way than the Tridentine Papists do? And although the Papists seem to favour your side in words, do they show a greater agreement in things, and do they have more in common with you? With what mouth? With what brow?

units.la: Ut vero dissidium, vel consensus Graecorum luculentius cum Reformatis appareat, dicito non dissimulanter, sed candide, si potes; Cuias es tu, Lutheranus ne, an Calvinista, vel aliquod simile præter naturam in religione, cultuque diuino monstrum? Sic enim dissidium hoc & consen-sus Græcorum obijcietur oculis. Alias cum inter eos confusa sint omnia, & unus alium impugnet, & injurijs lacessat, quid ipse sis, nondum exploratum est. Theologi Mansfeldenses, Suspectam habent Sacramentariorum doctrinam propter nouitatem : extitit nanque recens eorum tempore, & ignota fuit vetusta Ecclesia. Secundo quia Sacramentarij non definite in eadem sententia sunt concordes, sed in se ipsos diversi, ut inter eos sint Carlostadiani, Zwingliani, Oecolampadiani, Swenckfeldiani, Campanista, Calviniani, & similes. Nicolaus Amsdorffius in publica confutatione purae doctrinae; Nos Zwinglianam_, & Osiandrinam Hæresim, & errores tranquilla conscientia amplecti non possumus: nec eorum_, qui se a Luthero segregarunt, successioni, aut novationi subscribere, & astipulari. Matthias Illyricus, in Defensione Confessionis Martinistarum, Calvinistarum. Liturgia non uno sacrilegio vitiata est, contaminataque, eaque, proh dolor! innumeras animas æterno exitio in-voluit. Conradus Clusselbergius scripsit Theologiæ Caluinistarum libros tres, in quibus ceu in tabella quadam, quasi ad oculum plusquam ducentos viginti tres errores Sacramentariorum publicis scriptis, verbis proprijs, & auctorum nominibus indicatis, demonstratur, eos de nullo fere doctrinæ Christianæ articulo recte sentire, addita simul veræ sententiæ assertione, & contrariæ opinionis refutatione. Francofurti 1592. in 4. Dies me deficeret, & charta, si vellem omnia, quæ Martinus Lutherus, Philippus Melanchthon, Franciscus Stanckarus, alijq; scripserunt, ediderunt[?]que contra Caluinistas, & contra Lutheranos Caluinistæ, in medium proferre. Præ manibus omnium sunt certa dogmata, in quibus Lutherani a Caluinistis, seu Sacramentarijs dissentiunt, & Sacramentarij a Lutheranis ingrauissimis fidei dogmatibus. Vin plura ? Non eadem dicunt, tenentque inter se Trinitarij. Sacramentarij Sacramentarios mutuis scriptis damnant, Anabaptistæ Anabaptistas, Lutherani Lutheranos. Et quod manifeste perridiculum est, Caluinus, Melanchthon, Luthe rus a se ipsis in potissimis discordant: nec quid inter ipsos certum fit, nec ipsi sciunt, nec alij capiunt. Ita tenebrarum potestas inter eos conualuit, ueaiant, negent eodem ipso momento, & dum sua sustinere conantur, infamiori lapsu in perniciosiora præcipitantur. Hinc Hottingere, nisi quæ certa sunt apud te, ut Reformatos tuos enuncias, nunquam id assequeris, ut consensum tibi Græcorum concilies. Aude, dic aliquid, si verum non suppetit, saltem vero proximum, & si id quoque in promptu non est, aliquid quod sit vero simile, & si id quoque deficit, quod non dubito defuturum, contechna aliquid, contexe mendacium. Interim concedas necesse est, cum vestra dissidia inter vos ab exorta hæresi non dum sedata sint, imo in dies de novo pullulent nova, accrescantq; non posse dijudicari, nec ferri sententiam de consensu Græcorum, & Reformatorum, & an Græci vobis, vel aliis accedant. Nolo hic alios testes, te ipsum Hottingere produco, qui in hac tua Disputatione tantum non Reformatorum dissensum deploras. Vident[?] & ex nostris non pauci triste inter Reformatos Schisma hominum malitia, quam ipsius rei natura, & capitum controversorum pondere, maius esse, nec tamen hactenus post tot vota, & molimina tolli potuit animorum distractio. Domesticas turbas vides, fluctuantes animos, nutantes, omnia absque ulla certitudine dubia, & consensum Græcorum ad hæc incerta pertrahis? Quid, cum quod stabile fit, comparatur? Græcorum sive bona, sive mala, neque enim de hoc modo agitur, stabilia sunt; Reformatorum ambigua, & sic nulla. Compone tua, firma. dein enuncia; tum alij judicabunt, & statuent.
units.tr: So that the disagreement or agreement of the Greeks with the Reformed may appear more clearly, tell me, not evasively but candidly, if you can: whose are you, a Lutheran or a Calvinist, or some monster in religion and divine worship, contrary to nature? For in that way this disagreement and agreement of the Greeks will be set before the eyes. Otherwise, since everything is confused among them, and one attacks another and assails him with insults, what you yourself are has not yet been established. The Mansfeld theologians: They hold the doctrine of the Sacramentarians suspect on account of its novelty: it arose recently in their time, and the ancient Church did not know it. Secondly, because the Sacramentarians are not agreed definitely on one opinion, but are divided among themselves, so that among them there are Carlstadtians, Zwinglians, Oecolampadians, Schwenckfeldians, Campanists, Calvinists, and others like them. Nicolaus Amsdorf, in the public refutation of pure doctrine: "We cannot embrace with a quiet conscience the Zwinglian and Osiandrian heresies and errors, nor subscribe to and agree with the succession or innovation of those who have separated themselves from Luther." Matthias Illyricus, in the Defence of the Confession, against the Martinists and Calvinists: "The liturgy has been defiled and contaminated by more than one sacrilege, and that, alas, has drawn innumerable souls into eternal ruin." Conrad Clusselbergius wrote three books on the Theology of the Calvinists, in which, as if on a tablet set before the eye, more than two hundred and twenty-three errors of the Sacramentarians are shown, indicated from their public writings, in their own words and with the names of their authors. He demonstrates that they hold rightly almost no article of Christian doctrine, adding at the same time an affirmation of the true opinion and a refutation of the contrary one. Frankfurt, 1592, 4to. The day would fail me, and the paper too, if I wished to bring forward everything that Martin Luther, Philip Melanchthon, Franciscus Stancarus and others have written and published against the Calvinists, and what the Calvinists have written against the Lutherans. Everyone has in hand the definite dogmas on which Lutherans differ from Calvinists or Sacramentarians, and Sacramentarians from Lutherans, on most serious articles of faith. Do you want more? The Trinitarians do not say the same things or hold the same things among themselves. Sacramentarians condemn Sacramentarians in mutual writings, Anabaptists condemn Anabaptists, Lutherans condemn Lutherans. And what is plainly most ridiculous: Calvin, Melanchthon and Luther disagree with themselves on the chief points. Nothing certain is fixed among them, and they do not know it themselves, nor do others grasp it. So the power of darkness has prevailed among them: they affirm and deny in the same moment, and while they try to sustain their own positions, they are hurled into more pernicious falls by a more shameful lapse. Hence, Hottinger, unless you state what is certain among you, as you set out your Reformed, you will never manage to win over the consensus of the Greeks. Dare to say something. If the truth is not at hand, say something near the truth; and if that too is not ready, something that is likely to be true; and if that too fails, as I do not doubt it will, make something up, weave a lie. Meanwhile you must concede, since your disputes among yourselves have not been calmed since the heresy arose, and indeed new ones spring up and multiply daily, that it cannot be judged, nor can a sentence be pronounced, on the consensus of the Greeks and the Reformed, or on whether the Greeks agree with you or with others. I do not want other witnesses here; I bring forward you yourself, Hottinger, who in this Disputation of yours all but lament the dissent of the Reformed. Many of our own see that the sad schism among the Reformed is greater through the malice of men than through the nature of the thing and the weight of the controverted heads, and yet so far, after so many vows and efforts, the division of minds has not been able to be removed. You see domestic troubles, wavering minds, everything doubtful and without any certainty, and yet you drag the consensus of the Greeks into these uncertain matters? What is this, when what is stable is compared? The Greeks' things, whether good or bad (for that is not the point here), are stable; the Reformed things are ambiguous, and so are nothing. Arrange your own firm points, then state them; then others will judge and decide.

units.la: Nolo morosus esse. Id tamen adijciendum necessarium est. Joannes Conradus Dannhauerus, Præfatione ad Lectorem ante exercitationem Historico-Theologicam Eliæ Veielij scribit: Post extincta prisca Græcia lumina, Athanasios, Chrysostomos, Theodoretos, Cyrillos, alios, Græcorum fidem sublestam, & Apostaticam in religione Christiana fuisse. Affirmat id quoq; Veielius in eadem Exercitat., Præceptoris sui Dannhauerí verba referens: Omnis inquam illa gens Eoa olim a sacris literis recte damnatis hæresibus, Judaica fermenti mixtura infamata, lucem verbi obscurat, legem non tenet, pacem non habet. Et infra de suo: In Ecclesia Græcanica sequiore, occurrit nihilominus, & proh dolor? apostasia a veteri orthodoxa, quod in subsequentibus clarum faciemus. Neq; id agimus insultandi Græcis gratia, quorum potius miseremur, & judicamus, eos partim neglectu Scripturæ, & cæco obedientiæ studio, partim tyrannide Turcica pressos de via discessisse. Et si Apostasia illa deprehenditur in Antichristiana articulorum quorundam, in fundamentum impingente acaccessione una cum pertinacia. Horum itaque judicio fides Græcorum post Athanasium, Chrysostomum, & alios, fides est sublesta, & Apostatica. Sed hæc Græcorum fides, & earum gentium in essentialibus propius accedit Hottingeranæ fidei: neque enim innotescit, cujus fidei ille sit, quam Pontificijs Tridentinis, vel tantum in circumstantijs variat; & si quando favere videtur Pontificijs verbis, quam rebus testari; & licet aliquod habeat simile cum Romana, habere tamen plura cum Reformatis. Hæc tua sunt Hottingere. tum conclude. Ergo fides Hottingerana, & ea, quæ est Reformatorum fides, sublesta, & Apostatica, & Judaici fermenti mixtura infamata lucem Verbi obscurat, legem non tenet, pacem non habet: quia configuratur ad similitudinem Græcæ, & gentis Eoæ, sublesta, & Apostaticæ, &quæ lucem Verbi obscurat, legem non tenet, pacem non habet.
units.tr: I do not want to be fussy, but the following must necessarily be added. Johann Conrad Dannhauer, in his Preface to the Reader before the Historical-Theological Exercises of Elias Veiel, writes: After the ancient lights of Greece were extinguished, Athanasius, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Cyril and others, the faith of the Greeks was shaky and apostate in the Christian religion. Veiel affirms the same thing in the same Exercise, quoting the words of his teacher Dannhauer: "That whole Eastern nation, I say, once infamous for the Jewish admixture of leaven, with heresies rightly condemned by the sacred letters, obscures the light of the Word, does not hold the law, and does not have peace." And further on, in his own voice: "In the later Greek Church, nevertheless, there occurs, alas, an apostasy from the old orthodoxy, which we shall make clear in what follows." Nor do we say this to insult the Greeks, whom we rather pity; we judge that they, partly through neglect of Scripture and a blind zeal for obedience, and partly oppressed by Turkish tyranny, have departed from the way. And if that apostasy is found in certain articles of an Antichristian kind, striking at the foundation, it is joined with obstinacy. Therefore, by their judgment, the faith of the Greeks after Athanasius, Chrysostom and the others is shaky and apostate. But this faith of the Greeks and of those peoples comes closer in essentials to Hottinger's faith, for it is not known whose faith he holds: he differs from the Tridentine Papists only in circumstances; and if at any time he seems to favour the Papists in words rather than to bear witness in things; and although he has something in common with the Roman Church, he has more in common with the Reformed. These are your words, Hottinger. Then conclude: therefore Hottinger's faith, and that which is the faith of the Reformed, is shaky and apostate, and infamous through the Jewish admixture of leaven, obscures the light of the Word, does not hold the law, does not have peace, because it is conformed to the likeness of the Greek and Eastern nation, which is shaky and apostate, obscures the light of the Word, does not hold the law, and does not have peace.

units.la: Si dicas, te id non de recentiorum Græcorum sed antiquorum sermonem habere: tum stultiora effers. Quis enim dubitat, fidem, quam illis temporibus Græcorum Ecclesia prositebatur, eandem in essentialibus cum Romana fuisse, & Patres omnes, & Doctores illius tum Græcos, tum Latinos eadem dixisse, verbis, rebusque testatos? Si fides Græcorum, sublesta, & Apostatica est. &c. quam ob causam eam in vestram infunditis, & & in communionem illius vosmetipsos insi-nuatis, & eorum consensum tam anxie concupiscitis? Imprudentis stolidique est, argentum, vel aurum in scoriam vertere. Pellite flagitium, amouete scelus. Si quis non defendit iniuriam, ut aiebat ille, neque propulsat a suis, cum potest, iniuste facit. Vel si tibi non displicet, argumentare. Inter Romanam Ecclesiam, & Græcam, Eoasque disconuenit: nanque cum Græca, Eoæque Reformatis coniunguntur sententiis, nullus consensus, neque unitas inter Græcam Eoas, & Romanam est. Ergo Romana fides non est neque sublesta, neque Apostatica: esset enim talis, si cum Reformatis conueniret, ad quos propius accedunt Græca, Eoæque Ecclesiæ. Adde etiam; Græca fides, antequam dicta lumina prisca Ecclesiæ extinguerentur, non erat neque sublesta, neque Apostatica, sed recta, integraque, cum maculam, neque rugam haberet, quam postmodum extinctis illis luminibus contraxit. Sed tum illa agnoscebat Ecclesiam Romanam unam, Catholicam, & Apostolicam, tenebatq; omnia quæ tum tenebat, & modo tenet Ecclesia Romana, & non dicebatur a veritate deerrare. Ergo Ecclesia Romana est illa, quæ dicitur una Catholica, & Apostolica. Adde Pontificiam, cum discordet a Reformatis in omnibus, nec illis accedat, & hæreses eorum detestatur, non esse Iudaici fermenti mixtura infamatam, lucem verbi non obscurare, legem tenere, pacem habere. Hæc tota Hottingeri ratiocinatio est, ex fundamentis dirimentibus consensum depromta. Maior est Præceptoris Veieliani, & ipsius Veielij. Minor tua Hottingere. Conclusio illius, qui logica methodo, & rationibus exquisitis, non amenti furore disputat, nec ex rebus dubijs captat assentionem.
units.tr: If you say that you are speaking not of the recent Greeks but of the ancient ones, you bring out something even more foolish. For who doubts that the faith which the Greek Church professed in those times was the same as the Roman faith in essentials, and that all the Fathers and Doctors of that time, both Greek and Latin, said the same things and bore witness to them in words and in substance? If the faith of the Greeks is shaky and apostate, etc., why do you pour it into your own cup, and insinuate yourselves into its communion, and so anxiously long for their consensus? It is the mark of a foolish and senseless person to turn silver or gold into dross. Drive out the disgrace, put away the crime. "If someone does not defend an injustice," as that man used to say, "nor ward it off from his own when he can, he acts unjustly." Or, if you do not mind, argue it this way: between the Roman Church and the Greek and Eastern Church there is disagreement; for while the Greek and Eastern churches are united with the Reformed in their opinions, there is no consensus or unity between the Greek and Eastern churches and the Roman. Therefore the Roman faith is neither shaky nor apostate; for it would be so only if it agreed with the Reformed, to whom the Greek and Eastern churches come closer. Add also: the Greek faith, before those ancient lights of the Church were extinguished, was neither shaky nor apostate, but right and whole, having neither stain nor wrinkle, which it later contracted when those lights were extinguished. But at that time it acknowledged the Roman Church as one, Catholic and Apostolic, and held everything that the Roman Church then held and now holds, and it was not said to err from the truth. Therefore the Roman Church is that which is called one, Catholic and Apostolic. Add that the Papist Church, since it disagrees with the Reformed in everything, does not come near them, and detests their heresies, is not infamous through the Jewish admixture of leaven, does not obscure the light of the Word, holds the law, and has peace. This is the whole reasoning of Hottinger, drawn from premises that rule out consensus. The major premise is that of Veiel's teacher and of Veiel himself; the minor is yours, Hottinger; the conclusion is his who disputes by a logical method and by carefully chosen arguments, not in the frenzy of a madman, and does not seek assent from doubtful matters.

units.la: Neque est hic supina Hottingeri ἀνισοεισία[?] obticenda: nanque inter Auctores, qui de vnione Græcorum facta in Concilio Florentino, & eorundem post Concilium ad pristinos errores regreffione aliquid narrant, interponit Ioannem Veccum Præsulem Constantinopolitanum, Cui, ait, concordia studium ita fraudi fuit, ut plurima solo illo nomine ei exantlata fuerint ærumnæ. Veccum multum operæ, laborisque insumpsisse pro vnione Græcorum, & Latinorum, & propter eam causam multa dira, atque atrocia pertulisse, tandemque extorrem anno decimo quarto exilij in carceribus vitam posuisse, verum est. Sed eum post Florentinam Synodum concordiam procurasse, hoc vero salsissimum est. Vixit ille sub Michaële le[?] Palæologo primo, sub quo similis Græcorum vnio agitata, & absoluta est sub tribus Capitulis, de quo alibi fusius. A Vecci promotione ad Patriarchatum ad Florentini Concilij celebrationem anni interlapsi sunt centum sexaginta quatuor. Hæc adnotaui, vt posthac in discernendis temporibus oculatior sis,
units.tr: Nor should Hottinger's careless ... be passed over here. Among the authors who relate something about the union of the Greeks made at the Council of Florence, and about their return to their former errors after the Council, he cites John Veccus, Patriarch of Constantinople: "For him," he says, "zeal for concord was so costly that very many hardships were suffered by him on that ground alone." That Veccus spent much effort and labour on the union of Greeks and Latins, and on that account endured many dire and atrocious things, and at last, in exile, ended his life in prison in the fourteenth year of his banishment, is true. But that he secured concord after the Synod of Florence is most absurd. He lived under Michael Palaeologus the First, under whom a similar union of the Greeks was debated and concluded in three chapters, about which I shall write more fully elsewhere. From Veccus's promotion to the patriarchate to the celebration of the Council of Florence, one hundred and sixty-four years elapsed. I have noted this so that you may be more careful hereafter in distinguishing the dates.

units.la: Semper de tua fide, & sæpe numero te deprehendi falsiloquum; at nunc in his, quæ de Allatio scribis, falsificum. Nec mirum. sorex tuo indicio peris, Scribis; Sed frustra numerus obijcitur contradicentium, Allatius Græcus est. Inter Græcos enutritus. huic uni maior adhibenda fides, quam sexcentis alijs. Caeteri remotiores & a regione, & religione Græcorum rumore potius abrepti, quam de rei veritate edocti scripserunt, Subdis; ita sibi blanditur Allatius. Ita assentitur, vel assentatur potius Forerus. Assentatur Forerus; ergo ita sibi blanditur, assentitur, & assentatur Allatius. Vnde nam hoc habes? Ita hic assensum Allatij probas, vti dissidium Ecclesiarum. Despicit sua Allatius: alij laudant, & suspiciunt, & apud Hottingerum malignæ mentis hominem Leo in vitio est, & admittit in se culpam castigabilem. Quid vero de se scripsit Allatius? Allatius a puero in sacris aliisque divinis ritibus versatus est, &
units.tr: You have always been unreliable about your faith, and I have often caught you being a liar; but now, in what you write about Allatius, you are a forger. Nor is this surprising: "The shrew perishes by your own judgment," you write. "But the number of those who contradict him is raised in vain: Allatius is a Greek, brought up among the Greeks. To him alone greater trust must be given than to six hundred others. The rest, more remote both in region and in religion from the Greeks, were carried away by rumour rather than taught the truth of the matter, and wrote." You add: "So Allatius flatters himself." Thus Forerus assents, or rather flatters. Forerus flatters; therefore Allatius flatters himself, assents, and fawns. Where did you get this? You approve Allatius's assent just as you approve the disagreement of the Churches. Allatius despises his own people, while others praise and admire him; and before Hottinger, a man of malicious mind, Leo is at fault and admits a blameworthy fault. But what did Allatius write about himself? "Allatius from boyhood was trained in sacred and other divine rites, and

units.la: [catchword follows] innutritus, & libros tum Pontificios, tum Græcos de his ijsdem rebus tractantes diligenter, accurateque euoluit, & cum de illis scripsit, de rebus sibi bene cognitis scripsit, non aliunde emendicando notitias, sed de suis promens: nec vnquam adeo fuit incogitans, atque impudens, vt præsumpserit, dictis suis, nisi testimonijs Doctorum Ecclesiæ confirmatis, & stabilitis credendum esse. Et hanc animi moderationem Allatij aliunde repetitis illius laudibus in crimen vertere conaris, tantum, vt odium in illum apud doctos viros concites. Quasi vero Leo suis plus tribuat, quam sexcentorum aliorum dictis. Et non erit Hottingerus salsificius, & alienorum dictorum adulterator manifestus? Scripsit Allatius, se Græcum esse, & inter Græcos enutritum. Hoc si noxia est, repetat iterum, & sæpius. Eo siquidem nomine quodammodo superbit Allatius, & sibi longe, longeque plurimum complacet. Non ita tamen insanit, vt maiorem sibi fidem, quam sexcentis alijs adhiberi præsumat, qui sibi vel soli fidem habendam abnegat, quam alijs & minori numero præstat, imo si lecta intelligis, fidem sibi prorsus demit, nisi testimonijs Doctorum Ecclesiæ confirmentur, & stabiliantur. Et plane talpa est coecior Hottingerus, qui non videt dicta Allatij ab aliis scriptoribus publice ce scriptis editis, & ab ipsa Ecclesia Græca, nec non Latina, quibus in hoc negotio, cum res earum agitur, indubitate credendum est, apertissime testata, in quorum copia ipse tenebris crassis circumfusus cæcutit, & neglecta testimoniorum auctoritate, quando reliqua deficiunt, ad unum Critopulum, sive Syropulum, sive etiam Creyghtonum confugit. Quod ipse subdit de remotioribus a religione Christiana, id quoq; de alienis est. Licet enim in Græcorum ritibus exercitus sit, non ita tamen in illis se profecisse æstimat, ut alios in illis instructiores negat, & semetipso versatiores esse nolit. Veruntamen, cum ibi agat de notitia rerum Ecclesiasticarum Hottingeri, fatetur se Græca tenere, & Græcum inter Græcos enutritum, melius res Græcas callere ipso Hottingero, qui nihil ipse sciens afferre de suo, ab aliis notitias emendicans, non quod re ipsa est, sed quæ ab aliis traduntur aliter atque sunt, absque ullo examine in medium profert. Et hoc ne est, maiorem sibi fidem, quam sexcentis aliis adhibendam? Hisce suæ inscitiæ socios alios de virtute, & literis benemeritos homines coniungens, quod illi soli attribuerat Allatius, aliis communicat, ut Allatio nulla causa confidentiæ famam inurat. Et sic falsifici, non tantum falsidici ipse nota tenetur. cum dicti alieni & verba, & sententiam immutando, in alium, atq; alium intellectum, quantum libido fert, improbe pertrahat.
units.tr: was brought up in them, and has read diligently and carefully both Papist and Greek books treating these same matters; and when he wrote about them he wrote about things well known to him, not begging his knowledge from elsewhere but drawing it from his own store. Nor was he ever so thoughtless and shameless as to presume that his words should be believed unless they were confirmed and established by the testimonies of the teachers of the Church." And this moderation of spirit in Allatius you try to turn into a charge, dragging his praises in from elsewhere, so that you may stir up hatred against him among learned men. As if Leo gave more weight to his own words than to the sayings of six hundred others! And will Hottinger not be a forger and a manifest corrupter of other men's words? "Allatius wrote that he is a Greek and was brought up among the Greeks." If this is harmful, let him repeat it again and more often. For under this title Allatius does, in a way, take pride, and he is very, very much pleased with himself. Yet he is not so mad as to presume that greater trust should be given to himself than to six hundred others. He who denies that trust should be given to himself alone grants it to others, and to a smaller number. Indeed, if you read carefully, he withdraws trust from himself entirely unless it is confirmed and established by the testimonies of the teachers of the Church. Hottinger is plainly blinder than a mole, for he does not see that Allatius's statements are openly attested by other writers in published books, and by the Greek Church itself as well as the Latin, to whom, when these matters are at issue, one must without doubt give credence. Wrapped in thick darkness, he stumbles blindly amid this abundance, and, neglecting the authority of the testimonies when the rest fail, he flees to Critopulus alone, or Syropulus, or even Creyghton. What he adds about those more remote from the Christian religion applies also to foreigners. For although Allatius was trained in the rites of the Greeks, he does not judge himself so advanced in them that he denies others are better instructed, and he is unwilling to be thought more experienced than himself. Yet when he there treats of Hottinger's knowledge of ecclesiastical matters, he confesses that he holds Greek things, and that a Greek brought up among Greeks understands Greek matters better than Hottinger himself. Hottinger, knowing nothing of his own, begs his information from others and brings it forward without any examination, not as the thing really is but as others hand it down, and often differently than it is. And is this the man who ought to have greater trust than six hundred others? By joining to his own ignorance other men who have deserved well of virtue and letters, Hottinger shares among them what Allatius had attributed to them alone, so that he may brand Allatius with a charge that has no basis for confidence. And so he is held to the mark not merely of a liar but of a forger, since by changing the words and the sense of others' statements he drags them, as lust leads him, into one meaning after another.

units.la: Tuum est etiam Hottingere, nec mirum est, cum inter has Ecclesias dissidium, quod aliquid fit, comperis, ad illa confugere; Quid si ritibus tantum differrent, differrent tamen. Negat, tamen illud semper fieri. Quid inde? fiat aliquando. Apud Pontificios Tridentinos nunquam fit. Manet ergo semper aliquod discrimen. Et similia. Et non vides, cum dissidium urges, vires tuas accisas, rationes attritas, & totam domum Hottingeri una rheda componi, qui minutiora ista precario colligit, ad probandum dissensum. Est tamen aliquod discrimen, si ritibus tantum differunt, differrent tamen. Hinc garris; Schismata certe, non tam ex dogmatum, quam rituum, & regiminis pullulare discrimine notius est, quam quod prolixe probari a me debeat. Certum itaque est Hottingero, ritus ipsos atque regimen in minori pretio esse ipso dogmate, qui dissidium ex rituum ac regiminis discrimine potius pullulare discrimina religionis edicit: quia id tamen stultissimum ipse iudicat, uti notissimum praeterit, & ab eo probando declinat. Prolixe lixe nos alibi demonstrauimus, ipsum, aliosque, qui similia tradunt, loqui pugnantia. Sed in re tam clara quid Græca cum Romana teneat, inuestigemus; vt discat Hottingerus verum a falso discernere. Niceta Byzantius pro Concilio Chalcedonensi contra Armeniæ Principem, Οʹπ ὁ καλῶς φρονῶν τὸ μικρὸν, κατ' ὀλίγον [?]πισπάτω. πᾶν ἢ τὸ εἰς [?]πίστιν ἀπόρον, καὶ [?]πίστων ἀπὸ Θεοῦ, μίσους, καὶ ὑποστροφῆς ἄξιον. Qui parum negligit, paulatim cadit; quodcunque vero in casum adducit, & casum a Deo, execrationis, auersionisque dignum est. Nec aliud sonant verba Eulogij Alexandrini; Ἐʼπὶς τῆς ἀκουώντων τοῖς θεοφόροις [?]παῤῥήσιας ἐχαλῶν, ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκουμένης κλητέον, ἀλλὰ ἀμφιβαίην, καὶ [?]θεοσέβειας δόγματος, καὶ περὶ τὸ θεῖον ἀσέβειαν. Ex illis, quæ diuini Patres approbarunt, aliquid præuertere, nullo modo dispositio appellanda est, sed prævaricatio, & proditio dogmatis, & circa res diuinas impietas. Diuersum itaque dogma diuersitatem fidei generat: potest tamen diuersos ritus sub vna fide vnitatem Ecclesiæ conseruare. Irenæus lib. 5. cap. 21. cum varias ieiuniorum formas enumerasset. Καὶ ὑδὲν ἔλαττον πάντες ἔτοι ἀφλωδοσάν τε καὶ ἐφλωδοσάμων θεὸς ἀλλήλως, καὶ ἡ διαφωνία τῆς νηστείας τῷ ὁμόνοιαν τῆς πίστεως συνίσησαν.
units.tr: It is also your habit, Hottinger, and no wonder, since you find that there is some disagreement between these Churches, to take refuge in such things: "What if they differed only in rites? Yet they would still differ." He denies that this "yet" always holds. So what? Let it hold sometimes. Among the Tridentine Papists it never does. So some difference always remains. And so on. Do you not see that when you press the disagreement, your strength is weakened, your arguments are worn down, and the whole house of Hottinger is packed into one carriage, which gathers these trifles on sufferance to prove dissent? "There is, however, some difference, if they differ only in rites; yet they would differ." Hence you chatter: "That schisms arise from a difference of rites and government, no less than of dogmas, is certainly more widely known than that it should be proved at length by me." It is therefore certain to Hottinger that rites and government are of less worth than doctrine itself, since he declares that division arises from a difference of rites and government rather than from differences of religion. Yet he himself judges this most foolish, and, passing over what is very well known, he shrinks from proving it. We have shown elsewhere at length that he and others who teach similar things talk self-contradiction. But in a matter so clear, let us examine what the Greeks hold together with the Romans, so that Hottinger may learn to distinguish true from false. Nicetas of Byzantium, defending the Council of Chalcedon against the Prince of Armenia, says: "He who thinks rightly and neglects the small matters gradually falls away; but whatever brings the faith into doubt, and falling away from God, is worthy of hatred and aversion." [Οʹπ ὁ καλῶς φρονῶν τὸ μικρὸν, κατ' ὀλίγον πισπάτω. πᾶν ἢ τὸ εἰς πίστιν ἀπόρον, καὶ πίστων ἀπὸ Θεοῦ, μίσους, καὶ ὑποστροφῆς ἄξιον.] The words of Eulogius of Alexandria sound no different: "To deviate in any respect from those things which the divine Fathers approved cannot in any way be called arrangement, but is prevarication and betrayal of doctrine, and impiety concerning divine things." [Ἐπὶς τῆς ἀκουόντων τοῖς θεοφόροις παῤῥήσιας ἐχαλῶν, ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκουμένης κλητέον, ἀλλὰ ἀμφιβαίην, καὶ θεοσέβειας δόγματος, καὶ περὶ τὸ θεῖον ἀσέβειαν.] Thus a different doctrine produces a diversity of faith; yet diverse rites can preserve the unity of the Church under one faith. Irenaeus, book 5, chapter 21, after listing the various forms of fasting, says: "And nonetheless they all, both those who fast and those who do not, are at peace with one another; and the disagreement over fasting commends the concord of faith." [Καὶ ὑδὲν ἔλαττον πάντες ἔτοι ἀφλωδοσάν τε καὶ ἐφλωδοσάμων θεὸς ἀλλήλως, καὶ ἡ διαφωνία τῆς νηστείας τῷ ὁμόνοιαν τῆς πίστεως συνίσησαν.]

units.la: Atque nihilominus, cum isti inter se pacem tranquillam retinuerunt, tum nos etiam ininter nos retinemus, ficque varia, ac difcrepans ieiunij ratio concordiam fidei plurimum commendat. Nec defunt alij, quibus addere potes Gregorium Nazianzenum Orat. 1. de Pace; Ἐάν ἕ τι καὶ παρ' οἷς ἀνθρώπων, ὥσπερ ἡ καὶ μέγιστον τῆς ἀληθείας ἐλέγχος, οὐδ' ὑπὸ τῆς καιρῷ νικωμένης, οὐδὲ τῆς ἐχθρας παντελῶς τὸν ἀπιν[?]δ[?]έα τῆς ἐν ἡμῖν ἀγάπης καὶ ζαλυσμός. ὅτι τὸ μέγιστον ὑπὲρ τῶν ἡμῖν, καὶ σαπαζόμενον ἡ ὁμοδοξία, καὶ τὸ συμφέρινα, μὴ ἐπεξυγχύσῃ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ, μὴ δ' ἐναντίως διαχ[?]ἄρ, ἀλλὰ τῇ αὐτῇ χαρακτῆρι μεταφορωμένοις τῆς πίστεως, καὶ τῆς ἐλπίδος ἡμῶν ἐλπίδα. Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἔτως ἰσχυρὸν πρὸς ὁμοιότητα τοῖς γνησίοις τὸ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, ὡς ἡ πρὸς Θεῷ συμφωνία. Καὶ ἐὰν οὕτως ἴσιμον πρὸς διάστασιν ὡς ἡ πρὸς τὸ διαφωνία. Atque hæc vigente etiam ipso diffidio mutuo de nobis quandoque, & apud quosdam homines praedicabamus, quod scilicet maximum etiam veritatis argumentum erat: quippe cum ipsa ne a tempore quidem vincereretur, nec inimicitia charitas eius, quae in nobis erat, igniculum prorsus extinguueret. Praeterea quod nobis etiam diffidentibus, id, quod maximum erat, nimirum eadem de fide sententia fuberat, illudque nobis conscij eramus, nos in veritatis negotio, minime inter nos differentire, ac contrario modo affici. Verum eodem fidei, & primae nostrae Spei charactere formatos, & consignatos esse, Nihil enim eos, qui sincero animi affectu Deum colunt, aeque inter se conciliat, atque consentiens de Deo doctrina, quemadmodum contra, nihil ad diffidium ita promptum, ac paratum est, ut diversa in hac re animorum sententia. Vides? Concordia in rebus fidei, & de Deo doctrina Christianos maxime inter se conciliat: e contrario, diversa in hac re animorum sententia ad dissidium concitat, non quaecunque in aliis rebus differentia. Nec aliud est, quod secunda Oratione de pace insinuat; Ὅταν ἁλῶμεν ὑπὸ ἐλέγχου, καὶ ὀρθόδοξοι ὦμεν, ψευδόμεθα [?] πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ὡς ὑπὲρ πίστεως σπουδάζοντες. Ἔτι τοῦτο μόνον ἐπαγγελτὸν ποιοῦμεν, ὡς ἐν κακοῖς, εἰ μὴ καὶ λίαν αἰσχρὸν [?], ὅτι τὴν καίριον εὐδοξίαν [?] ὀνόματα [?] μεταβαίνομεν [?] τὸ ὀρθόδοξον [?]. Nam cum deprehendimur, pij atque orthodoxi sumus, falsoque ad veritatem confugimus, tanquam— pro fide contendentes. Idque unum, & in malis laude dignum, imo turpe in primis facimus, quod vitium erubescentes ad speciosius honestiusque nomen, hoc est ad pietatem transfimus.
units.tr: And yet, just as those churches kept peaceful tranquillity among themselves, so we too keep it among ourselves; and thus a varied and discordant practice of fasting greatly commends the concord of faith. Nor are there lacking others, to whom you may add Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 1 on Peace: "If among some men, as is the greatest proof of the truth, neither is love overcome by time, nor is the charity in us wholly extinguished by enmity... so that agreement in opinion and fellowship be not confounded with the truth, nor be shaped in contrary ways, but be formed with the same character of faith and of our hope. For nothing so strongly unites genuine worshippers, in their likeness toward God, as agreement with God; and if such [agreement] is harmful to division, so is discord." And again: "While we were still disagreeing with one another, we used to declare this about one another, and among certain people, as the greatest argument for the truth: for it was not conquered even by time, nor did enmity wholly extinguish the little spark of charity which was in us. Moreover, although we disagreed, the greatest thing, namely the same opinion about the faith, remained; and we were conscious that we did not at all differ among ourselves in the matter of truth, nor were we affected in opposite ways, but were formed and sealed with the same character of faith and of our first hope.
