For nothing so unites those who worship God with a sincere affection of mind as agreeing doctrine about God; and, conversely, nothing is so ready and prepared for dissension as a diverse opinion of minds in this matter. Do you see? Concord in matters of faith and in doctrine about God unites Christians most of all; conversely, a diverse opinion of minds in this matter stirs up dissension, not any difference in other things." Nor does the second Oration on Peace suggest anything different: "When we are convicted by refutation and are orthodox, we falsely take refuge in the truth, as if striving for the faith. Yet we make this one thing, which is praiseworthy among evils, or rather very shameful, that blushing at the fault we pass over to the more specious and honourable name, that is, to orthodoxy." [Ὅταν ἁλῶμεν ὑπὸ ἐλέγχου, καὶ ὀρθόδοξοι ὦμεν, ψευδόμεθα πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ὡς ὑπὲρ πίστεως σπουδάζοντες. Ἔτι τοῦτο μόνον ἐπαγγελτὸν ποιοῦμεν, ὡς ἐν κακοῖς, εἰ μὴ καὶ λίαν αἰσχρὸν, ὅτι τὴν καίριον εὐδοξίαν ὀνόματα μεταβαίνομεν τὸ ὀρθόδοξον.]

units.la: Non desunt alij non infimi nominis Scriptores Sozomenus, Socrates; adde Nicephorum Callistum, qui sua ex ijsdem exscripsit, qui post varios recensitos mores colligunt; Οὐ πάντας κἂν ὁμοδόξοι ὦσι, ταῖς αὐταῖς [?] ἀσφαλείας τὰς Ἐκκλησίας φυλάττειν. Non
units.tr: Other writers of no small name are not wanting: Sozomen and Socrates. Add Nicephorus Callistus, who copied his material from these same authors, and who, after reviewing the various customs, concludes: "Not all churches, even when they share the same doctrine, keep the same usages in safety." Not all, though they are of the same faith, keep the same traditions in the churches.

units.la: Greek lines are reproduced as far as they can be read at this scan resolution; the accents and several words are doubtful and are marked [?]. omnes[?], quamuis eiusdem fidei essent, easdem traditiones in Ecclesijs seruare. Et, ὡς τῆς αὐτῆς πίστεως πολλάκις ἢ τὰ ἐν διαφόρως καθισταμένοι[?]. Eandem colentes fidem saepenumero consuetudinum obseruatione inter se variare. Ipsi quoque qui ex Schismate sunt, Theophylactus Bulgariæ Archiepiscopus ad Nicolaum Diaconum; Οὐ πᾶν δόγμα ὑποχρίζειν τὰς Ἐκκλησίας ἰχνοῦ[?], ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐπὶς διαφορὰν ἄρον δόγματος[?]. Non omne dogma ad diuellendum Ecclesias valere, sed quod differentiam dogmatis facit. Neque diuersus ab his est Armeniorum Catholicus, vt colligi potest ex Legatione ad Armenios Theoriani, Ἀλλ' ὁ πολὺς ἐμοὶ λόγος ὡς τὴν ἑορτὴν ἐκ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἐνδιαν[?], εἰ μόνον ὡς τὸ πίστιν ὁμοφωνήσωμεν. Verum non magnopere sollicitus quidem fuero de festis, aliisque consuetudinibus Ecclesiæ, modo sententijs de fide conueniamus. Hoc idem est, quod pluribus probat Demetrius Chomatenus in Responsionibus ad Constantinum Dyrrhachij Episcopum. Et ne reliquos recenseam, Auctor ipse Schismatis Photius Epistola ad Nicolaum Papam; Ἐξ ἂν οὐδὲ πίστεως ὡς ἐπ' ἀληθὲς μάχεσθαι[?]. ἀλλ' ἡγεῖ ἐν τοῖς κοινωνικοῖς πράγμασι, ἡ ἀκριβὲς μέτρον κοινωνίας τῶν ἐν τοῖς λοιποῖς ἃς ἐπὶ σκοπὸν τὴν, καὶ πολυσχεδὲς μὴ ἐνδιδόντος[?]. Ἐὰν γὰρ ὄντως κοινὰ πᾶσιν, ἃ παρὰ φυλάξειν ἐπαναλύσεις, καὶ ἐπέρῳ τῆς ἄλλων[?]. Τὰ ὡς δ' πίστεως, ἔνθα, ἔ τὸ παρεισκλίναι μικρὸν, ἁμαρτίαν ὅδιν ἁμαρτίαν ἢ πρὸς θάνατον. ἔστι δ' ἐ ἰδίσ-ζοντας ποιν παρεπόμενα, ὧν ἡ ἀποβασις, οἷς μὲν ἰδόντι καταχεῖ ἐπιζήμιον, οἷς δ' ἐ παρέ-λιπῇ), ἐ τὸ μὴ σωτηρεῖαν ἀκατάνεκτον. Ex quibus neutri ab altero vituperatio impingebatur, sed in potissimis rebus constantissima inter eos, & in rerum nouarum studio aliena societas non sinebat caeterarum rerum discrimen curiosius intueri. Nam re vera communia omnibus sunt, quae omnibus custodire necesse est, & ante alia, quae de fide habemus, vbi vel paulum declinare est, mortifero se periculo obstringere. Quaedam proprie alios consequuntur, quorum praetermissio eis multum affert, quibus illa tenenda data sunt, qui vero non acceperunt, id propterea, quod non obseruauerint, minime condemnantur.
units.tr: Greek lines are reproduced as far as they can be read at this scan resolution; the accents and several words are doubtful and are marked [?]. Although they hold the same faith, the churches keep different traditions. Being of one faith, they often differ among themselves in the observance of customs. Those who are themselves in schism take the same view. Theophylact, Archbishop of Bulgaria, writes to the deacon Nicolas: "Not every doctrine is enough to tear the churches apart, but only that which makes a difference in doctrine." Nor is the Catholicos of the Armenians different from them, as can be gathered from Theoriano's Embassy to the Armenians: "But I would not be greatly troubled about feasts and other customs of the Church, provided we agree in the sentiments of faith." Demetrius Chomatenus proves the same thing at length in his Responses to Constantine, Bishop of Dyrrhachium. To pass over the rest, the very author of the schism, Photius, writes in his letter to Pope Nicolas: "Where there is no contention about faith in the true sense, but only about matters of the common life, the exact measure of communion is not to be sought in everything, lest the bond become over-strained." For if the things that are common to all are indeed kept by all, and the others are kept by some rather than by others… Matters of faith are otherwise: there, even a slight deviation brings danger, and in some cases mortal sin. Some things follow from the ones we hold, and their neglect does great harm to those who are bound to keep them; but those who have not received them are in no way condemned for not observing them. From these considerations neither side could be blamed by the other; but in the most important matters, a firm agreement between them, and a fellowship alien to the desire for novelties, did not allow them to look too closely at differences in other things. For indeed, those things are common to all which all are bound to keep, and above all those things we hold concerning faith, where even a slight deviation binds us to mortal peril. Some things properly follow from others, and their neglect harms those to whom they were entrusted; but those who have not received them are not condemned for failing to observe them.

units.la: Et; ἔπως ἐν οἷς ἂν ἔσι πίστις τὸ ἀδιαιρέτον, οὐδὲ κοινῶς τι, καὶ καθολικῶς ἀνφισμάτων ἐκκλησίας, ἄλλων παρ' ἄλλοις ἐθῶν τι, καὶ νομίμων φυλακῶν, ἐν τῷ οὖν φυλακῆς ἀδικεῖν, ἐν τῷ οὖν μὴ παραδεξαμένοις ἀπονομῶν ὀρθῶς ἂν [?]. Ita vbi nulla est praeuaricatio fidei, nec communis, & Catholici decreti euersio, cum alij apud alios mores, & leges custodiantur, nec custodes iniuste agere, nec eos, qui non acceperunt, contra legem facere, is, qui recte iudicare norit, definiet. Ritus itaque atque consuetudines, etsi dissidium defignant, non tamen animos eorum, quibus eæ in usu sunt, in odia distrahunt, nec ab unitate disiungunt. Idque ex natura rerum evincitur, in qua composita omnia non ex similibus inter se partibus, sed ex dissimilibus constant. Si enim ex similibus fuerint, essent quidem unum, sed non compositum.
units.tr: And: where there is no breach of the faith, nor any overthrow of the common and catholic decree of the Church, but different customs and laws are observed by different peoples, neither do the guardians act unjustly, nor do those who have not received them act against the law; he who knows how to judge rightly will settle the matter. Thus rites and customs, though they mark a difference, do not drive the minds of those who use them into hatred, nor do they sever them from unity. This is proved by the nature of things, in which all compound things consist not of like parts but of unlike ones. For if they were made of like parts, they would indeed be one thing, but not a compound.

units.la: Ciuitas non uno genere hominum constat, sed plane diuerso. Neque enim omnes diuites sunt, sapientes, nobiles, milites. Sunt in ea phrygiones, aurifices, argentarij, fullones, tonsores, olearij, innumerabiles variarum artium opifices, pauperes, miseri, egentes, qui ostiatim rogatores petunt, & aliena misericordia viuunt, & tot hominum genera, qui uno instituto sibi proposito reguntur, quo usq; illud conseruant, & iustitiam colunt, una ciuitas est, etsi diuersa sunt exercitia. ἐ δὲ γίνεται [?] πόλις ἐξ [?] ὁμοίων. Non enim fit ciuitas ex similibus, aiebat Aristoteles. Paria sunt de rebus aliis multis, quæ dici possunt, & signanter de homine, cuius partes licet dissimiles sint, quia tamen omnes ad unum opus efficiendum conueniunt, unus homo esse dicitur, licet animo, & corpore, & hoc capite, manibus, pedibus, corde, aliisque partibus inter se longissime diuersis, nec idem opus obeuntibus emineat.
units.tr: A state does not consist of one kind of men, but of quite different kinds. For not all are rich, wise, noble, or soldiers. In it there are dyers, goldsmiths, money-changers, fullers, barbers, oil-sellers, countless craftsmen of various arts, poor, wretched, needy folk who beg from door to door and live on the pity of others; and yet, since so many kinds of men are governed by one purpose set before them, and as long as they preserve that and cultivate justice, it is one state, even though their occupations differ. [For a city is not made of like parts.] "For a city is not made of like parts," Aristotle used to say. The same holds of many other things that could be mentioned, and especially of the human being, whose parts, though unlike, are all brought together to accomplish one work, so that he is called one man, although soul and body, this head, hands, feet, heart, and other parts, are very far apart from one another and do not perform the same work.

units.la: Et ut tandem in sole caligare desinas.
units.tr: And so that you may at last stop groping about in the sun.

units.la: Audi Paulum ad Romanos 12. Sicut in uno corpore multa membra habemus: omnia autem non eundem actum habent: ita multi unum corpus sumus in Christo: alter autem alterius membra.
units.tr: Hear Paul to the Romans, chapter 12: "For as we have many members in one body, but all members have not the same office: so we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another."

units.la: Hanc corporis membro-rum, & spiritus diversitatem eloquentissi-me, uti solet Theodoretus sermone 6. de Pro-videntia prosecutus est. Ἀλλ’ ἴσως αὖτις ἀπὸι τῇ μόνον τοῖς καλῶς λειομένοις, ἁπλέγλν[?] ὑδάτων[?]. τὴν δὲ γῆν ἁπάντων ἀνθρώποις τὰ πλέιστα[?] τῶν κτίσεων[?] ὁ ποιητὴς ἐδωρήσατο, ἀλλὰ τοῖς μὴ πλέον σωίζεσθαι[?] ἐπιμελῶς[?] ἀνθρώπῳ[?] τὰ πλέιστα τῶν[?] σωμάτων[?] γλώττῃ[?], ἀλλὰ γλυκεῖ[?] ὀξεῖ[?] δριμεῖ[?] πικρὰ[?] καὶ ἁπαλῶς[?] τὸ διαφορὰ[?] εἰδέναι[?]. καὶ τοῖς ἐμοὶ ποτὶ τὴν βασιλικὴν ἐδόσαν[?] δωρεὰν[?], τὰς δὲ χειρὸς τὴν παρὰ[?] δαπάνην[?] ἀπὸ τῆς ἐργασίας[?], καὶ γαστέρα ὁμοίως ἔχειν ὀψοφαγίας[?] δοχεῖον ἦναι[?] ἢ ζοφῆς καὶ ἀκρα[?]. εἰσὶ φανὰ[?] ἡ μυκλῶν[?] δηλαυγῶς[?], πηγλῶ[?] ἡ διαμόνητον[?] τὴν καρδίαν, ἐτὰς δὲ ἀρπεῖας[?] ἐπαρθὲν[?] τὸ πνεῦμα, ταῖς δὲ φλέβας[?] ἀχωρεῖς[?] ἀπὸφηνὲν [?] αἵματος, ⁊ ἄλλῳ ἄλλην ἐνέργειαν ἐνέφυσε μοί-ρᾳ. καὶ μὲν ἀπαιτᾷ τὰ ἑρμηνέα [?], καὶ ὅσα σαίνῃ [?] εἰς ἑνὸς σώματος σωτηλᾶ [?] πληρότης. ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως ἕκαστον, καὶ ἰδίον ἡ πεπιστευται [?], καὶ τὰ κεινὰ [?] σωπηλᾶ [?]. ὄψις γὰρ ποδηγεῖ μὲν ὁδὸν πόδας, καὶ τὸ λεῖον ἁπτῆς ὑπολάμνυσι [?], καὶ τὴν ξαχυτίαν [?] ὑπο-ξέπτ [?] χωρεῖν, φησὶ ἡ ὑπὸ ποδῶν. Καὶ ἀκοὴ ἡ κτύ-πες [?] ἀρομιζμεν [?] ... ἡ τῆς ὄψεως μαντεία [?] τῆς κτύπων ὧν ποιητάς. Καὶ ἵνα τῇ ὑποσολικῇ μάρτυρείᾳ ὧν εἰρημένες βε-βαιωσαμένη λόγες, ἐ ἀλλ᾽ ἀπὸ ὀφθαλμὸς εἰπεῖν τῇ χρεῖ χρείαν σου ἐκ ἔχω, ἢ πάλιν ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῖς ποσὶν χρείαν ὑμῖν ἐκ ἔχω. ἀλλὰ πολλὰ μᾶλλον τὰ δυ-κοινῶντα μείζη τῷ σώματι· ἀδὲ εἰστερα ὑπαρξν ἀναλησία δέ, καὶ ἃ δὲ ἀκηρμα ἀπημόπεα εἶναι, τούτοις σεβαστοτάτων πιμὸν σεπιθυμίαν, καὶ ἰδιὰς ἑδυχίεσιν πώποτε ἀμφοτέρων βλέπων ἐν τοῖς σώμασι τῶν ἐνέργειαν, εἰμὴ κομιδῇ ὤρα πάσι, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπέχ, ⁊ ϑαυμάζῃ τὸν ποιητὴν, ὅπου ζοφῶς ἕκαστα ἀχρεῖναιναί, ⁊ ἑκάστῳ τ᾽ ἀρμο πνοὴ ὑπογεμονῖα χρείαν, καὶ τῷ ἰδίῳ κοινῷ ποιησάμβον. ὅπη ἡ ὄψις μόνον τῆς ὀ ἀρδὴ ὑπολαμβ, ὅπη ἀκοὴ τῆς ἀκυ-σῶν, ὅπη τὸ σῶμα τ᾽ γλῶσσων, ὅπη ἡμῖν τῆς ὀσφρη-σεως, ὅπη οἱ πόδες βαδίζειν, ὅπη ἐργασίας αἱ χεῖρες, ὅπη ζοφῆς ἡ γαστὴρ, ὅπη ἀπερμότης ἡ καρδία, ὅπη αὐθησεως ὁ ἐγκέφαλον, ἀλλ᾽ ἰδίζεις μὲν ἕκαστον ἔχῃ τ᾽ ἐνέργειαν, τῷ δὲ κοινῷ συμφέρει τ᾽ ὠφέλειαν, ⁊ τὸ μὲν ἅπαν ἀπερμαίνῃ τὸ σῶμα, τὸ δὲ ἅπαν ζεφῇ, ⁊ δὲ ἄλλον πνα φύεσθαι ἀντὶ ἀποζοίζῃ τῆς ζωῆ. ⁊ τὸ
units.tr: Theodoret, in the sixth sermon On Providence, has treated this diversity of the members of the body and of the spirit most eloquently, as is his way. Perhaps the rivers are not given to men for drinking only, nor the earth for food alone; the Maker bestowed on man the greater part of his gifts not for one purpose only. The tongue is not given merely to speak, but to know the difference between sweet, sour, pungent and bitter, and to hold the gift of speech; the hands are not for labor alone, nor the stomach merely a vessel for dainty food or dark drink. The eyes see clearly, the heart is set for thought, the lungs are lifted up by breath, and the veins carry the blood, and each has its own function. Yet each has also its own service and its own power: the eye guides the feet on the road, the touch perceives what is smooth, and the feet carry the body wherever it goes. The ear hears sounds, and sight is the seer of what the sounds make. Nor, to confirm what I have said by the testimony of a common example, does the eye say to the hand, "I have no need of you," or the head to the feet, "I have no need of you"; rather, the parts that seem weaker are much more necessary to the body. Whoever sees that each of these parts has its own function, and that they all serve the whole, will not only admire the Maker but also give thanks to him, for he made each thing useful and gave each its own necessary office. The eye alone perceives sight, the ear hears, the tongue tastes, the nose smells, the feet walk, the hands work, the stomach digests, the heart is set for thought, and the brain governs sensation. Each has its own energy, and each benefits the common whole; were any part to fail, the whole body would suffer, and if one part were withdrawn, the life of the whole would be harmed. The variety of activity fits itself to all the members of the body, each supplying what the others lack, and so the need becomes common…

units.la: [?] Greek text in this scan is only partly legible; words marked [?] are best readings. τὸ ποικίλον τῆς ἐνεργείας, εἰς ἅπαντα μὲν τὰ σώ-ματῳ μιμέισθαι μόρια, ὑπολαμβάνουσ ἢ ἀλλήλων παράξα. καὶ γίνεται ἡ χρεία κοινὴ, καὶ ἔτι ἀκοὴ ἀγα-πᾶν[?] [?] ὄψις, ὅτε ὀφθαλμὸς ἀφχεράνς τὸ μὲν ἀχέδν, ἀλλ᾽ ἕκαστον στέρχ' ὅσον ὄψις τῆς φύσεως καὶ τῷ ἀσφαλεῖ ὑποδιδῶν, ὡς δὲ ἀρχῆς φέρειν ἐπάγθη.
units.tr: The varied activity of the members: each of them, in all the parts of the body, imitates the others and takes its turn in the service of the others. So the use becomes common to all, and the hearing, the sight, and the eye... (the text here is too damaged to render fully), each yielding its own proper function to the safety of the whole and bearing its burden as the rule of nature requires.

units.la: Sed dicet forsitan aliquis illorum, qui nihil aliud, quam benedictis obstrepere norunt, quamobrem non cunctis hominibus diuitias possidendas rerum conditor largitus est, sed his quidem diuitias copulauit, illis vero paupertatem quasi forte addixit, vitamque inaequalibus admodum, & imparibus conditionibus repleuit? Quem & ego libens interrogauerim, cur non omnibus corporis nostri membris unam, & eandem vim rerum opifex indiderit: Sed oculis quidem colorum, & figurarum iudicium commisit, auditum vero vocum, & sonorum discrimina cognoscere voluit, nares autem, ut vapores excipiant, & suauem odorem a foetore discernant, linguam item, ut gustu sapores dijudicet, dulcis & acerbi, acris & amari, & pinguioris discrimen deprehendat, instituit: & pedibus quidem incessus potentiam concessit, manibus vero omniuariam operationem ceu forte distribuit. ventrem alimenti receptaculum, iecur vero eiusdem purgatorium, cerebrum medullarum thesaurum, caloris autem fontem cor constituit, arterijs porro spiritum inclusit, venas auautem sanguinis canales fecit, singulis item membris diuersa operationum ingenerauit ossicia. At qui omnia, quae modo dicta sunt, sed & ea, quae silentio praeteriuimus, ad vnius corporis perfectam fabricam seruiunt. Interim tamen singulis aliquid propriae functionis commissum est, & in commune illud singula conferunt.
units.tr: But perhaps someone among those who know only how to rail with fine words will say: why did the Maker of all things not give riches to all men, but attached riches to some and seemed to hand poverty to others, filling life with very unequal and unlike conditions? I too would gladly ask him why the Maker did not give all the members of our body one and the same power. Instead he committed to the eyes the judgment of colours and shapes, and willed that the ears know voices and the differences of sounds; he appointed the nostrils to take in vapours and to distinguish a sweet smell from a stench; likewise the tongue, so that by taste it may judge flavours, and perceive the difference between sweet and sour, sharp and bitter, and rich. To the feet he granted the power of walking, and to the hands he distributed, as if by chance, the work of all sorts of tasks. He made the stomach the receptacle of food, the liver its purifier, the brain the storehouse of marrow, and the heart the source of heat. He enclosed the spirit in the arteries, moreover he made the veins the channels of the blood, and to each member he gave its own functions. Yet all these things just mentioned, and those we have passed over in silence, serve the perfect construction of one body. Still, to each part some proper function has been entrusted, and each contributes its share to the common good.

units.la: Visus quidem pedes ducit, & viae planitiem illis monstrat, & ab asperioribus locis auertit, ipse autem a pedibus fertur. Auditus quoque dum sonos percipit, visum ad videndum excitat, idem autem per visum sonorum auctores cognoscit, Et ut Apostolico testimonio, quae modo dicta sunt, confirmemus, non potest oculus dicere manui: Non est mihi opus te: & rursum caput pedibus, Non est mihi opus vobis. Imo multo potius quae videntur membra corporis imbecilliora esse, necessaria sunt, & quae putamus minus honesta esse, his honorem uberiorem apponimus. Nec unquam aliquis indignatur diversam in membris operationem cernens, nisi valde desipiat, quin potius creatorem amat, & admiratur, qui tam sapienter singula discreuit, & singulis commodam, & idoneam alicuius officii functionem commisit, eamque quae singulis propria erat, toti corpori communem fecit . Nec enim visus solus visibilium sensu fruitur, nec solus auditus sonis juvatur, & non solum os sapores, nec solus nasus odores, nec soli pedes incessum, nec solæ manus operationes, nec solus venter alimentum, nec solum cor calorem, nec solum cerebrum sentiendi affectionem percipit[?]: sed peculiarem, quidem & propriam vim singula habent, usum vero, & utilitatē omnem in commune conferunt. & hoc quidem totum corpus calore fovet, hoc totum nutrit, illud vero alium quaestum aliquem quasi tributum animato corpori affert. Et operationis varietas in omnia quidem corporis membra divisa est, singula vero mutuum a se invicem fructum percipiunt, & communis omnium usus est: nec auditus indignatur quod non videt, nec oculus audiendi sensu destitutus dolet; sed singula hæc natura limites studiose observant, & tributum, quod ab initio ipsis iniunctum est, persolvunt. Conclude ergo Hottingere, si ex illis non es, qui nihil aliud quam benedictis obstrepere norunt, & valde desipiunt; corpus Ecclesiæ mysticum ex diversorum statuum hominibus compositum, non diversis artibus, cerimonijs nempe, & consuetudinibus dividuum fieri, sed unum continuo perseverare, dum uno capite Christo, eiusque in terris Vicario connectitur, nempe cum idem fidei dogma servat illæsum. Hinc Pontificij, Graecique docent, illud esse considerandum in diversitate rituum, si qui diversitate rituum obstringitur, ita se obstringat, ut eodem ipso momento separet se ab
units.tr: The eye certainly leads the feet and shows them the level of the road, turning them away from rougher places, while the feet themselves are carried along. The ear too, as it perceives sounds, rouses the sight to see, and through sight it in turn recognises the sources of the sounds. To confirm what has just been said by the apostolic testimony: the eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you," and the head cannot say to the feet, "I have no need of you." Indeed, those members of the body which seem weaker are much rather necessary, and those we think less honourable we honour more abundantly. No one ever becomes indignant on seeing different functions in the members, unless he is very foolish; rather he loves and admires the Creator, who has so wisely distinguished each part and entrusted to each a fitting and suitable function of some office, and has made the function proper to each common to the whole body. For the eye alone does not enjoy the sense of visible things, nor does the ear alone benefit from sounds, nor does the mouth alone taste flavours, nor the nose alone smell odours, nor the feet alone walk, nor the hands alone work, nor the stomach alone take nourishment, nor the heart alone feel heat, nor the brain alone perceive sensation. Each has its own peculiar power, but they all contribute their use and utility to the common good. This part warms the whole body with heat, that part nourishes the whole, and another brings some gain, as it were a tribute, to the living body. The variety of operations is divided among all the members, yet each receives fruit from the others, and the use is common to all. The ear does not resent that it does not see, nor does the eye, lacking hearing, grieve; rather these members carefully keep nature's limits and pay the tribute enjoined on them from the beginning. So conclude, Hottinger, if you are not one of those who know only how to clamour with empty words and are very foolish: the mystical body of the Church, composed of men of diverse conditions, is not divided into parts by diverse arts, namely ceremonies and customs, but remains one continuously, as long as it is joined to one head, Christ, and to his Vicar on earth, namely when it keeps the same doctrine of faith unharmed. Hence the Papists and the Greeks teach that this must be considered in the diversity of rites: if anyone is bound by a diversity of rites, let him so bind himself that at that very moment he does not separate himself from

units.la: [Line 8, "opera-", the last letter may be an A or a worn letter; read as "opera-".] ab Ecclesiæ visibili capite, & summo Pontifici debitam Subiectionem, qua talis est, nempe, vt viniuersali potestate Ecclesiam gubernandi a Christo sibi concessa fungitur, illum inter schismaticos collocari: si vero Pontifici obedire recusat, ratione rei præceptæ, quod ea difficilis, & molesta appareat, in alijs obedire paratus, vel ratione offensionis, quam ob specialem causam aduersus illum gerit, alioquin contra ipsam sedem, siue potestatem Pontificiam non rebellis, hunc nec schismaticum quidem reputari. Et primo modo Schisma vel est purum, vel vnitum cum hæresi. Purum fuerit, cum charitati tantum pacique opponitur, idque in illis est, qui cum credant vnam esse sanctam matrem Ecclesiam sub visibili capite summo Pontifice, tamen ex malitia mentis, nolunt Pontifici subijci, vel reliquis Ecclesiæ membris vniri, quod vel est sola intentione, & est Schisma mere internum: vel operis etiam executione, & tum erit externum, & opere consummatum. Schisma vero cum hæresi iunctum est, si aliquis pertinaci animo neget summum Pontificem Eccl. Cathol. caput, & pastorem esse, vel Ecclesiæ sanctæ communionem, atque ob eam causam ab illa sese segreget. Tum sic. Sed Ecclesia Græca, licet ritus, & confuetudines diuersas ab Ecclesia Romana feruet, fatetur se, agnoscitque membrum Ecclesiæ vniuersalis, militareque sub vno visibili capite summo Pontifice, ergo diuersa ista, quæ tu allegas Hottingere, licet discrimen afferant, non ea tamen sunt, quæ diffidium inter has Ecclesias pariant.
units.tr: from the visible head of the Church and from the supreme Pontiff, to whom the due subjection is owed, which is such that he exercises the universal power of governing the Church granted to him by Christ; he is to be counted among the schismatics. But if he refuses to obey the Pontiff, on account of the command, because it seems difficult and burdensome, yet is ready to obey in other matters; or on account of the offence he holds against him for some special cause, but otherwise is not rebellious against the see itself or the papal power, such a man is not to be regarded even as a schismatic. And in the first way, schism is either pure or joined with heresy. It is pure when it is opposed only to charity and peace, and this is the case with those who, though they believe that there is one holy mother Church under one visible head, the supreme Pontiff, yet from malice of mind are unwilling to submit to the Pontiff or to unite with the other members of the Church. This is either in intention alone, and is a schism purely internal, or also in the execution of the deed, and then it will be external and accomplished in act. But schism is joined with heresy if anyone with obstinate mind denies that the supreme Pontiff is the head and pastor of the Catholic Church, or denies communion with the holy Church, and on that ground separates himself from it. Then thus: But the Greek Church, although it observes rites and customs different from the Roman Church, confesses and acknowledges itself to be a member of the universal Church and to serve under one visible head, the supreme Pontiff. Therefore these diversities which you allege, Hottinger, although they bring a difference, are not the things which create discord between these Churches.

units.la: Vin plura? Audi in vna Synagoga Hebræorum, non vna erat oblatio ex eodem Theodoreto sermone 7. de Prouidentia; Α᾽ὑπίκα τοίνυν ἕξιν ἰδὼν. Οὐδὲ πανταχοῦ μίαν[?], καὶ τῶν αὐτῶν θυσίαν προσφέροντας[?]. Ὁ᾽ μὲν γὰρ ἰδὼν μόσχον[?], ὁ δὲ ἀμνὸν, ὁ δὲ χίμαρον, καὶ ἄλλος πλέων τὰ θύματα[?], ἐδὲ ἐλαίου[?]. Ὁ᾽ δὲ τῶν ἀπορῶν[?], ἑπνία συζῶν[?], ζεῦγος ξυνόντων[?], ἢ ποτὲ[?] ἀρέσκεσθαι[?]. Ὁ᾽ δὲ καὶ τὸ τῶν ἀπανίζων[?], σεμίδαλιν ὀλίγην[?], καὶ βεαχὺ ἢ λιβανωτὸν[?] ποιοῦσι[?]. τοιαῦτα γὰρ ποιοῦντες, οὐχὶ ποσότητι ἀλλὰ προθέσει ἀρέσκοντα τὸν θεὸν, καὶ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ[?] διδασκαλία[?]. Quapropter nec vnam, nec eandem victimam omnes obtulisse videmus. Hic enim vitulum, ille agnum, alius hœdum sacrificabat. Et alius quidem plures, alius pauciores victimas: cui vero paupertate presso hæc omnia deerant, illi par tur turum[?], aut pulli columbarum ad oblationem sufficere poterant. Qui autem etiam illis carebat, simila parua, & aliquanto thure rem diuinam faciebat. Vnde iustum illum iudicem animi qualitatem non donorum quantitatem respirespicere discimus. Est tamen in hoc quoque aliquod discrimen. Quare argue Hottingere, in Ecclesia, siue Synogoga Hebræorum ob hoc discrimen, dissidium fuisse, & ex una in plures divulsam, & dispertitam non unam fuisse, quia alia, atque alia oblatione, & non una Deum sibi propitium reddere ex Dei præcepto conabatur. Et negabis te elephantis corio circumtectum esse non tuo?
units.tr: Do you want more? Hear, in one synagogue of the Hebrews there was not one offering, from the same Theodoret, sermon 7 on Providence: Look, then, at the variety. Not everywhere do they offer one and the same sacrifice. For one, having a calf, offers that; another a lamb; another a kid; and another many victims, and another oil. The poor man, living in the fields with a yoke of oxen or a pair of doves, could offer these; and the one who lacked even these offers a little fine flour, and a little incense. For by doing such things they please God not by quantity but by purpose, and in the same teaching. [Ἀλλ᾽ ἴδωμεν τοίνυν τὴν ποικιλίαν. Οὐδαμοῦ μίαν καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν θυσίαν προσφέρουσιν. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ μόσχον, ὁ δὲ ἀμνόν, ὁ δὲ χίμαρον, καὶ ἄλλος πλείω τὰ θύματα, καὶ ἕτερος ἔλαιον. Ὁ δὲ τῶν ἀπόρων ζεῦγος βοῶν ἢ περιστερῶν, καὶ ὁ τὸ τῶν ἀπόρων ἔχων σεμίδαλιν ὀλίγην καὶ βραχὺ λιβανωτὸν ποιοῦσι. Τοιαῦτα γὰρ ποιοῦντες οὐ ποσότητι ἀλλὰ προθέσει ἀρέσκουσι τὸν θεὸν, καὶ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ διδασκαλίᾳ.] Therefore we see that they did not all offer one and the same victim. For this one sacrificed a calf, that one a lamb, another a kid, and another offered many victims and yet another offered oil. Those who were poor offered a pair of oxen or doves, and those who lacked even these offered a little fine flour and a little incense. Hence we learn that the just judge looks to the quality of the soul, not to the quantity of the gifts. Yet there is some difference in this too. Therefore, Hottinger, argue that in the Church, or synagogue, of the Hebrews there was discord on account of this difference, and that it was torn from one into many and divided, and was not one, because by different offerings, and not one, they tried to make God propitious to them by God's command. And will you deny that you are wrapped in an elephant's hide that is not your own?

units.la: Non est, quod insultes Hottingere. Habeo te. Concedantur reliqua Ecclesiæ Græcæ. Plane illa Romanum Pontificem, nec caput Ecclesiæ, nec supremam in eo iurisdictionis potestatem agnoscit. Dicis tu, quia sic velles esse. Hoc vero probandum est. Nilus, & alij contra Pontificis Romani potestatem scripserunt. Scripserunt. Quis dixit, in Ecclesia Græca non fuisse, nec esse etiamnum Hæreticos, & Schismaticos, quorum voces excipiendæ non sunt? Allatius probat, quid Ecclesia Græca teneat, & profiteatur. Illa non negat Pontificibus Romanis a Deo concessam auctoritatem: imo in omnibus suis Professionibus id profitetur. Percurre Professiones, quæ in ea Ecclesia ab Imperatoribus, Patriarchis, Episcopis, alijsque in dignitatibus constitutis publice emittuntur: in illis reperies, se rerecipere septem Concilia Generalia, eorum decreta, sanctorum Doctorum Ecclesiae doctrinam, & damnare omnia, quae ab illis damnantur. Sed in illis non clanculum, sed aperta voce reboatur, Romanum Pontificem esse caput Ecclesiae, ab illo Ecclesiastica omnia gubernari, & dirigi, illius voces voces esse Petri, Christi, standumque esse illius decretis, & qui illis in omnibus non obsequuntur, extra Ecclesiam esse, ut alibi fuse probauimus. Ergo Ecclesia Græca, agnoscens Romani Pontificis in Ecclesia præeminentiam, licet diversis ritibus, & consuetudinibus utatur, non separatur ab Ecclesia Romana. Frustra itaque garris in tui asserti probationem afferens Nili, Barlaami, & si qui sunt, aliorum dicta, quos ut tu nugaciter somnias, illius Ecclesiae capita nuncupas, & inter Sanctos reponis.
units.tr: There is no reason for you to exult, Hottinger. I have you. Grant the rest about the Greek Church. Certainly that Church does not acknowledge the Roman Pontiff as head of the Church or as possessing supreme jurisdiction over it. You say so because you would like it to be so, but that must be proved. Nilus and others wrote against the power of the Roman Pontiff. They wrote, yes. Who has claimed that there were never heretics and schismatics in the Greek Church, or that there are none even now, and that their voices should not be heard? Allatius shows what the Greek Church holds and professes. It does not deny that the Roman Pontiffs have been granted authority by God; indeed, it professes this in all its professions of faith. Go through the professions that are publicly made in that Church by emperors, patriarchs, bishops and others holding office. In them you will find that they accept the seven General Councils, their decrees, and the teaching of the holy doctors of the Church, and condemn whatever those councils condemn. And in them it is proclaimed not in a whisper but with a loud voice that the Roman Pontiff is the head of the Church, that all ecclesiastical affairs are governed and directed by him, that his words are the words of Peter and of Christ, and that one must abide by his decrees; and that those who do not obey him in all things are outside the Church, as I have proved at length elsewhere. Therefore the Greek Church, acknowledging the pre-eminence of the Roman Pontiff in the Church, is not separated from the Roman Church, although it uses different rites and customs. In vain, then, do you chatter, bringing forward in proof of your assertion the sayings of Nilus, Barlaam and any others you like. As you foolishly dream, you call them heads of that Church and place them among the saints.

units.la: Et ut etiam ad sacratiora orationem convertam. In quatuor Euangelis pleraque sunt, quae aliis, atque aliis modis exprimuntur: multa ab uno omittuntur, vel minus late scribuntur, quae ab alio supplentur, & distinctissime narrantur: multa etiam dissociabilia, ut videtur, miscentur, & ut ita dicam, repugnantia, adeo ut multi ex Patribus ad illa componenda studium posuerint, & tractatus integros de consensu Euan-geligelistarum posteris transmiserint. Et tamen illa quatuor Euangelia unum Euangelium sunt. Chrysostomus Expositione Epistolae ad Galatas; Unde dilucidum est quatuor Euangelia unum esse Euangelium; cum enim quatuor eadem loquantur, non est aliud atque aliud ob personarum differentiam, sed unum ob eorum, qui loquuntur, consonantiam. Et Theophylactus ibidem; Apprehendunt hoc dictum Pauli Marcionista, asseverantes hinc unum dumtaxat recipiendum Euangelium, non quatuor. Et quid hoc? Nam nos quatuor unum dicimus secundum concentum, atque concordiam. Et Hieronymus ad illa Ecclesiastae, Faciendi libros nullus est finis. Quidquid dixeris, si ad eum referatur, qui in principio erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum, unum volumen est. & innumerabiles libri una lex, unum Euangelium nominatur: quod si diversa, & discrepantia disputaveris, & curiositate nimia huc, atque illuc animum deduxeris, etiam in uno libro multi libri sunt. Quamuis enim a numero Euangelistarum quatuor Euangelia agnoscat Ecclesia, unum nihilominus Euangelium est, quod unicam, & concordem historiam continet. Unitas siquidem oritur ex consonantia, concordia, atque concentu, quamuis alia, atque alia comprehendant, quæ unica consonantia, concordia, atque concentu vnum sunt. Christus ex duabus naturis diuina, humanaque immortali, mortali, æterna, morti obnoxia vnus est, non puto negabis hoc Hottingere, duabus operationibus elucens, duabus voluntatibus disponens omnia. Præterea Græci, Pontificisque credunt in Patrem omnipotentem, & in Filium eius Iesum Christum, ex Patre genitum, & in Spiritum sanctum ex Patre, Filioque, siue per Filium procedentem, quod idem est. Patrem Deitatis fontem, & principium; Filium, & Spiritum sanctum non absque principio: Pater enim eorum principium, & origo est. Quod si temporis initium spectas, æque atq; Pater principio carent: neque enim qui tempora crearunt, tempori subiecti sunt. Spiritus sanctus vti & Filius, principium sui, atque originem agnoscunt ex Patre, diuerso tamen modo. Filius vt genitus, Spiritus vt ex Patre, Filioque procedens, tanquam ex uno principio, & unica spiratione. Pater non est Filius, neque Spiritus sanctus, Filius non est Pater, neque Spiritus sanctus, Spiritus sanctus non est neque Pater, neque Filius, tres personæ indiuisæ diuisæ [?], & proprietatibus alia atque alia. Et quis singula, quæ intellectus non capit, commemorauerit? nihilominus in tam varijs, atque inter se distinctis proprietatibus, unum Deum agnoscunt, & confitentur, Trinitatem in unitate, & unitatem in Trinitate, Ecclesia Græca, & Latina unum Deum homousion, supersubstantialem, inaspectabilem, incomprehensibilem, inalterabilem, unam bonitatem, unam sapientiam, unam omnipotentiam in tribus personis. Intelligis puto, salua unitate in una, eademque re non esse unam omnium faciem, sed aliam, atque aliam: multa quoque esse opposita, & contra respondere, & quamuis ipsæ quoque actiones in contraria scindantur, animos tamen non scindi, unum si excipias dogma, quod debet esse semper unum firmumq;. Et tu ad probandum dissidium inter Græcam, & Latinam Ecclesiam minima quæq; subjicis. Negas ne in compositis, si consistentia est ex similibus omnino, hoc idem esse cum partibus & incompositû, & ut compositum sit, ex dissimilibus, diversisq; confici necesse esse? At in unione totius, si differentia partium non numeratur, palam est illud non esse. Quod si non est, patet, confusas esse partes, in quibus differentia non separantur. Et cum partium definitiones diversæ sint, natura quoq; diversæ sunt, ut in homine diversa est corporis ratio ab ea, quæ animæ est. Quare diversa erit & natura animæ, & natura corporis. Et tamen unitas stat in humano corpore.
units.tr: And to turn my speech to more sacred matters as well: in the four Gospels there are many things expressed in different ways. Many things are omitted by one evangelist, or written less fully, and these are supplied and narrated very distinctly by another. Many things that seem incompatible, and, so to speak, contradictory, are also mixed together; so much so that many of the Fathers devoted effort to reconciling them and handed down to posterity whole treatises on the harmony of the evangelists. Yet these four Gospels are one Gospel. Chrysostom, in his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians: Hence it is clear that the four Gospels are one Gospel; for since the four say the same things, they are not different, one from another, because of the difference of persons, but are one because of the agreement of those who speak. And Theophylact on the same passage: The Marcionites seize upon this saying of Paul, asserting that from it only one Gospel, not four, should be received. And what of it? For we say that the four are one according to harmony and concord. And Jerome, on Ecclesiastes: There is no end to making books. Whatever you say, if it is referred to him who was in the beginning with God, and God was the Word, it is one volume; and though there are countless books, there is one law and one Gospel is named. But if you argue things diverse and discordant, and with excessive curiosity lead your mind hither and thither, then even in one book there are many books. For although the Church acknowledges four Gospels from the number of the evangelists, nevertheless there is one Gospel, which contains one and harmonious history. Unity arises from consonance, concord and agreement, even though they comprise different things; by one consonance, concord and agreement they are one. Christ is one from two natures, divine and human, immortal and mortal, eternal and subject to death. I do not think you will deny this, Hottinger, that he shines forth with two operations and orders all things by two wills. Moreover, the Greeks and the Papists believe in God the Father almighty, and in his Son Jesus Christ, begotten of the Father, and in the Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father and the Son, or through the Son, which is the same thing. They hold the Father to be the fountain and principle of the Godhead; the Son and the Holy Spirit have a principle, but not apart from the Father, for the Father is their principle and origin. If you look at the beginning of time, the Father too is without beginning in the same way; for those who created time are not subject to time. The Holy Spirit, like the Son, acknowledges his principle and origin from the Father, yet in a different manner: the Son as begotten, the Spirit as proceeding from the Father and the Son, as from one principle and by one spiration. The Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit; the Son is not the Father or the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son: three persons, undivided yet distinguished, each with its own properties. And who could recount each single point that the intellect does not grasp? Nevertheless, amid such varied properties distinct from one another, the Greek and Latin Church acknowledge and confess one God, a Trinity in unity and a unity in Trinity: one God, consubstantial, supersubstantial, invisible, incomprehensible, unchangeable, one goodness, one wisdom, one omnipotence in three persons. I suppose you understand that, with the unity in one and the same thing preserved, the face of all is not one but different; that many things are also opposed and answer to one another; and that although the actions themselves are divided into contraries, the minds are not divided, except for the one doctrine, which ought always to be one and firm. And you, to prove a dissent between the Greek and the Latin Church, bring forward the smallest trifles. Do you deny that in compound things, if a composite consists wholly of similar parts, it is the same as a thing that is not composite, and that for it to be composite it must necessarily be made of dissimilar and diverse parts? But in the unity of a whole, if the difference of the parts is not counted, it is plain that it is not a whole. And if it is not, it is clear that the parts are confused, when their differences are not distinguished. And since the definitions of the parts are different, their natures are also different, as in a human being the nature of the body is different from that of the soul. Therefore the nature of the soul and the nature of the body will be different. And yet unity remains in the human body.

units.la: Sed jam video pertinaciam, & duritiem animi: ut vim argumenti effugias, dicés plane, & cum tuis Reformatis, diuinam Christi naturam passam esse: Pati, & mori nomine, & re pertinere ad diuinitatem, & propositiones has, diuinitatem esse natam, crucifixam, & mortuam veras esse.
units.tr: But I already see your obstinacy and hardness of mind: to escape the force of the argument you will say plainly, along with your Reformed, that the divine nature of Christ suffered; that to suffer and to die, both in name and in fact, pertain to the divinity; and that these propositions are true: the divinity was born, crucified and died.

units.la: Tres esse Deos æternos essentiali numero distinctos: ita tamen ut Pater sit solus Deus ex se, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus Dij inferiores, qui a Patre productam suam essentiam habeant, tametsi non ex nihilo, sed ex substantia Patris: hinc Patrem essentiatorem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum essentiatos dici: Tres Deos esse æternos, tres omnipotentes, haud secus inter se distinctos, ac tres homines, vel tandem duos Deos esse Patrem, & Filium: de Spiritu autem non dum esse revelatum, quid sit, & similia alia impia, & blasphema. Cum Græca Latinaque Ecclesia palam clament, diuinam Christi naturam passam non esse. Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum unum Deum omnipotentem, unum essentia, trinum personis. Filium æqualem in omnibus Patri, ex Patre genitum, Deum de Deo, Spiritum sanctum æqualem in omnibus Patre, & Filio, ex Patre, & Filio, vel per Filium procedentem: vnam personam in duabus naturis, non inter sese confusis, & sic vnitatem in Trinitate, & Trinitatem in vnitate amplectimur. Dicebat Esaias; Et super insulas leuabo signum meum. Exponit Procopius, Insularum nomine Ecclesias singulares intelligi, ex quibus vna est vbiq; & Catholica Ecclesia, de qua est apud Dauidem, Gloriosa dicta sunt de te, corona ex vario florum genere contexta, regio etiam diademate caput ornata, & vestitu deaurato induta, & variegata, assimilatur horto, de quo Sponsa in Canticis, descendat nepos meus in hortum suum, & comedat fructum pomorum suorum, in qua Deus posuit primum Apostolos, secundo Prophetas, tertio Doctores, deinde virtutes, exinde gratias curationum, opitulationes, gubernationes, genera linguarum. Nunquid omnes Apostoli? nunquid omnes Prophetæ? nunquid omnes Doctores? nunquid omnes virtutes? nunquid omnes gratiam habent curationum? nunquid omnes linguis loquuntur? nunquid omnes interpretantur? Audi Hottingere. Omnes Insulæ, Ecclesiæ alio atque alio nomine vni Catholicæ nauant operam, & sub ea magistra tolerant onus disciplinæ, & gratiæ, quæ vario florum hominum genere interstincta corona, vna fide, uti insigni regio vincitur, & vestitu deaurato, doctrina, quæ nunquam maculam trahit, neque rubigine consenescit, variegata ritibus, & moribus: neque enim omnia quæ in ea sunt, neque actiones omnes exedem[?], sed pro varietate temporum, & institutorum humanorum variæ, illius pulchritudinem augent, non tamen mutant, ut sunt ritus, consuetudines, opiniones etiam & quæstiones, quæ circa res sacras, & Theologicas inter doctos viros ad illustrandam illius fidem, non denigrandam per disceptationem decertantur, & in Canticis varijs pomis exprimuntur in uno fructu fide. comedat fructum pomorum tuorum. Quænam autem illa sunt, iam intellexisti ex Paulo, prima ad Corinthios cap. 12.
units.tr: That there are three eternal Gods, distinct in essential number, yet so that the Father alone is God from himself, while the Son and the Holy Spirit are inferior gods who have their essence produced by the Father, though not from nothing but from the substance of the Father; hence the Father is called the essentiator, and the Son and the Holy Spirit the essentiated. That there are three eternal Gods, three almighty, no less distinct from one another than three men; or that there are at last two Gods, the Father and the Son; and that as to the Spirit, it has not yet been revealed what he is; and other similar impious and blasphemous things. But the Greek and Latin Church loudly proclaim that the divine nature of Christ did not suffer: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one almighty God, one in essence, three in persons; the Son equal in all things to the Father, begotten of the Father, God of God; the Holy Spirit equal in all things to the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son, or through the Son; one person in two natures, not confused with one another. Thus we embrace the unity in Trinity and the Trinity in unity. Isaiah said: And upon the islands I will lift up my sign. Procopius explains that by the name of islands are meant the particular churches, of which one is the universal and Catholic Church, of which David speaks: Glorious things are spoken of you. She is likened to a crown woven of various kinds of flowers, her head also adorned with a royal diadem, clothed in gilded and variegated raiment, and to a garden, of which the bride in the Canticles speaks: let my beloved come into his garden and eat the fruit of his pleasant fruits; in which God has set first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all workers of miracles? Have all the gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret? Hear this, Hottinger. All the islands, that is, the Churches, under different names labour for the one Catholic Church, and under her as mistress they bear the burden of discipline and grace. She is a crown interwoven with the varied kinds of men like flowers, bound by one faith as with a royal emblem, clothed in gilded raiment of doctrine, which never contracts a stain nor grows old with rust, and variegated with rites and customs. For not everything that is in her, nor all her actions, are the same; but according to the variety of times and human institutions, these various things increase her beauty without changing it. Such are rites, customs, opinions, and also questions concerning sacred and theological matters, which learned men contend about by debate, not to disparage but to illustrate her faith. In the Canticles they are expressed by various fruits, but in one fruit: faith. Eat the fruit of your pleasant fruits. What these gifts are, you have already understood from Paul, 1 Corinthians chapter 12.

units.la: Dices Hottingere, hoc esse, de quo querimonias ultro citroque iactant Reformati, Pontificios nunquam in ijsdem placitis manere, sed continuata nouitate, ac litura decreta sua in alia, atque alia immutare, & de uno proposito in aliud demigrare. Hinc factum esse, ut antiquis, & sanioribus relictis ad superstitiosa quaeque animum compulerint, & inuerterint omnia, & a puriori illo statu in deteriorem desciuerint. Verum Hottingere, tu qui rectum calles, ideoque nimium tibi tribuis, rerum humanarum fluxus firma, ne profluant, vicissitudines, ne migrent, ordines, ne commutentur, tempora ne varient, voluntates hominum in vno proposito confige, ne pluribus votis vacillent, & demum fac, vt omnium defideria vnum sint, vnumque concupiscant: & ego dabo tibi legem vnam semper sibi constantem, nulli mutationi obnoxiam, & quæ in ditione, imperio, & potestate alterius non fit. Sed non vales. Quia pila volubiliores, cardine versatiliores, Eurypo res humanæ volubiliores sunt. Ergo nec ipse decretum tibi apponam, quod perpetuo eundem statum retineat, non deiectum, non motum gradu, & quod semper fuerit, cubus propriæ basi firmiter innixus. Decretis suis Deus id seruauit integrum. Sed rationibus Allatij non fidis? At non spernendus est Augusti. qui ad Marcell. calumniantibus, quod Deus veterem legem abrogarit, delectatus nouis sacrificijs respondit: quod enim semel recte factum sit nullatenus immutari debuisse: tum siquidem iniuste[?] mutaretur; Nonne hyemi æstas addito sensim calore succedit? Nonne diurnis tempora nocturna vertuntur? Quotiens nostra variantur ætates? Adolescentia pueritia non reditura cadit, iuuentus adolescentia non mansura succedit, finiens iuuentutem senectus, senectus autem morte finitur. Hac omnia mutantur, nec mutatur diuina prouidentia ratio, qua fit ut ista mutentur. Non autem opinor cum agricola æstate aliud iusserit, quam iusserat hyeme, ratio mutatur agricultura. Et cum mane singit, qui nocte quiescebat, vitæ consilium non mutauit. Aliud Magister adolescenti, quam puero solebat impossuit. Doctrina igitur constans, mutato præcepto non mutat instruction-em. Nam magnus ille nostrorum temporum medicus Vindicianus consultus a quodam, dolori eius adhiberi iussit, quod in tempore congruere videbatur, adhibitum, sanitas consequuta est. Deinde post annos aliquot, eadem rursus corporis causa commota, hoc idem ille putauit adhibendum: adhibitum vertit in peius. Miratus recurrit ad medicum, indicat factum, at ille, ut erat acerrimus, ita respondit: ideo maleacceptus es, quia non ego iussi, ut omnes qui audiuissent, parumque hominem nossent, non eum arte medicinali fidere, sed nescio qua illicita potentia putarent. Unde cum esset a quibus poterat stupentibus interrogatus, aperuit quod non intellexerant, videlicet illi ætati iam non hoc fuisse iussurum. Tantum igitur valet ratione, atque ætatibus non mutatis, quid secundum eas sit pro temporum varietate mutandum. Non itaque verum est quod dicitur, semel recte factum nullatenus esse mutandum. Mutata quippe temporis causa, quod recte ante fafactum fuerat, ita mutari vera ratio plerumque flagitat, vt cum ipsi dicant recte non fieri si mutetur, contra veritas clamet; Recte non fieri nisi mutetur, quia vtrumq; tum erit rectum si erit pro temporum varietate diuersum. Quod enim in diuersitate personarum vno tempore accidere potest, vt huic liceat aliquid impune facere, quod illi non liceat, non quod dissimilis sit res, sed quod is, qui facit, ita ab vna eademque persona diuersis temporibus tunc oportet, aliquid fieri, tunc non oportet, non quod sui dissimilis sit qui faciat, sed quando facit. Hac quomodo quam late pateat, profecto videt quisquis pulchri, aptique e distantiam sparsam quodammodo in vniuersitate rerum valet, neque negligit intueri. Pulchrum enim per se ipsum consideratur, atque laudatur, cui turpe, ac deforme contrarium est. Aptum vero, cui ex aduerso est ineptum, quasi religatum, pendet aliunde, nec ex semetipso, sed ex eo, cui connectitur, iudicatur, nimirum etiam decens, atque indecens: vel hoc idem est, vel perinde habetur. &c. Non potest dici plenius, explanatius[?]. Sed Augustini sunt Doctoris Ecclesiae Catholicae. Hoc summum malum est Hottingero. Quis eum coget Augustino credere? id habet a Luthero, Qua auctoritate eius verbum est articulus fidei? Deus errare, & fallere non potest; Augustinus, & Cyprianus, sic vt omnes electi errare potuerunt, & errarunt. Sed natura, qua in hoc argumento velut duce vtitur Augustinus, non errat. Ita est, sed tamen reijcienda, quia Augustini sunt. Hæc dicit a pietate, & religione remotus, & lingua sacrilega: sed ut tandem fide diuina credas, dabo tibi ex grege Epicuri Porcum. Cedit enim rerum nouitate extrusa vetustas semper & ex alijs aliud reparare necesse est. Leges humanæ vario euentu semper immutatæ sunt, & immutantur, nec desunt exempla. mittamus profana, pendamus Ecclesiastica. Ritus, & consuetudines in Ecclesijs vsurpatæ inter Ecclesias, in quibus diuerse, ac dissone exercentur, dissidium non gignere patet. Eæ siquidem temporis progressu, rerum natura ita ferente, sicuti commutantur, & alterantur, ita eodem tempore in alia, atque alia Ecclesia sunt, non id efficiunt, ut una Ecclesia ab alia, vel a se ipsa antiquiori, & recentiori diuisa fit. Si modo talis consuetudo dogma non læditur, vel ideo immutata, ut lædat, vel introducta. Tum enim etiam si minimum fit quod lædit ur, fidem antea fixam affligit, & vulnerat, & Ecclesiam separat. Hinc qui illud conuellit extra Ecclesiam, quæ contrarium astruit, est, & tanquam hæreticus condemnatur, & pœnis subijcitur. perspiciendum itaque est, an vnquam Ecclesia siue Græca sit, siue Latina a consuetudinibus antiquis vnquam desciuerit, an vero semper eas infrangibilis animi rigore retinuerit. Ab antiquioribus sæpissime dimotam, recentes assumpsisse, praxi ipsa demonstrabitur. Et quia suspecti esse possunt Pontificij, adeamus ipsos Græcos. Zonaras in Canonem 11. Laodicenum;
units.tr: You will say, Hottinger, that this is what the Reformed complain about on both sides: the Papists never keep to the same opinions, but, by constant novelty and by erasing their decrees, they change them into one thing after another and migrate from one position to another. From this it has come about that, having left the ancient and sounder doctrines, they have turned to whatever is superstitious, have overturned everything, and have fallen away from that purer state into a worse one. But you, Hottinger, who think you walk the straight path and therefore attribute too much to yourself, fix the flow of human affairs so that it does not run on, the changes so that they do not move, the orders so that they are not altered, and the times so that they do not vary; fix the wills of men in one purpose so that they do not waver among many desires; and finally make it so that all men's wishes are one and they desire one thing. Then I will give you one law, always consistent with itself, subject to no change, and not under the sway, command or power of another. But you cannot. For human affairs are more fickle than balls, more mobile than hinges, more shifting than the Euripus. So I will not set before you a decree that keeps the same state for ever, not cast down, not moved from its step, a cube that has always been and stands firmly on its own base. God has kept his decrees whole in this way. But are Allatius's arguments unreliable? Yet Augustine, who answered those who accused God of abrogating the old law in Marcellinus's letter, delighted in the new sacrifices, is not to be despised. He said that what has once been rightly done ought in no way to be changed; for then it would be changed unjustly: Does not summer gradually succeed winter with added warmth? Are not night times turned into day times? How often are our ages changed? Childhood falls away and does not return; youth succeeds childhood and does not remain; old age ends youth, and death ends old age. All these things are changed, yet the reason of divine providence, by which these things are changed, is not changed. Nor, I suppose, when a farmer orders one thing in summer and something else in winter, does the reason of agriculture change; and when a man who was sleeping at night gets up in the morning, he has not changed his plan for life. A teacher imposes one thing on a youth and another on a boy. Therefore sound teaching, though its precept is changed, does not change its instruction. For that great physician of our own times, Vindicianus, when consulted by a certain man, ordered a remedy to be applied to his pain, which seemed suitable for the time; it was applied, and health followed. Then some years later, when the same complaint of the body returned, he thought the same remedy should be applied again; it was applied and made things worse. Astonished, the man ran back to the physician and reported what had happened. But the physician, being very sharp, answered: "You were badly served because I did not order it. All who heard it, and who knew the man too little, thought that he relied not on medical skill but on some unlawful power that I do not know." So when he was questioned in amazement by those who could, he explained what they had not understood: namely, that at that age he would no longer have ordered this. So much, then, does reason count for, when the ages are not changed, that what is to be changed according to these ages with the variety of times. It is therefore not true, as is said, that what was rightly done once must in no way be changed. For when the cause of the time has changed, what was rightly done before, true reason very often demands that it be changed. So when they say that it is not right if it is not changed, truth cries out in reply: it is not right unless it is changed, because each will then be right if it is different according to the variety of times. For what can happen at one time in the diversity of persons, that this one may lawfully do something which that one may not, happens not because the thing is unlike itself, but because the one who does it must, from the same person at different times, sometimes do something and sometimes not do it; not because the doer is unlike himself, but because of when he acts. Anyone who grasps the beautiful and the fitting, scattered in some way throughout the universe, and does not neglect to look, surely sees how widely this extends. For the beautiful is considered and praised in itself, and its contrary is the ugly and deformed. But the fitting, whose opposite is the unfitting, hangs as if tied to something else; it is judged not from itself but from that to which it is connected. Even the decent and the indecent are in the same case: either this is the same thing or it is held to be so. &c. Nothing fuller or clearer could be said. But these are the words of Augustine, a Doctor of the Catholic Church. This is the greatest evil for Hottinger. Who compels him to believe Augustine? He has it from Luther. By what authority is his word an article of faith? God cannot err or deceive; Augustine and Cyprian, however, like all the elect, could err, and did err. But nature, which Augustine uses in this argument as a kind of guide, does not err. That is so, yet it must be rejected because it is Augustine's. You say this, remote from piety and religion, with a sacrilegious tongue; but so that at last you may believe with divine faith, I will give you a pig from the herd of Epicurus: For old things give way to new novelty, and so something must always be restored out of other things. Human laws have always been changed by various outcomes, and they are still changed, nor are examples lacking. Let us leave out secular matters and weigh ecclesiastical ones. It is plain that the rites and customs used in the Churches, which are practised differently and discordantly among the Churches, do not beget discord. For as they change and alter over the course of time, as the nature of things brings it, so at the same time they are in one Church and another, and they do not make one Church divided from another, or from itself at an earlier and a later time. Provided that such a custom is not injurious to doctrine, it is not changed or introduced in order to injure it. For then, even if the thing that is injured is very small, it strikes and wounds the faith previously fixed and separates the Church. Hence whoever tears that custom away, and asserts the contrary, is outside the Church and is condemned as a heretic, and is subjected to punishments. We must therefore examine whether the Church, whether Greek or Latin, has ever departed from ancient customs, or has always kept them with the stiffness of an unbending spirit. That the Church has very often set aside older customs and adopted newer ones will be shown by practice itself. And since the Papists may be suspected, let us go to the Greeks themselves. Zonaras on the eleventh Canon of Laodicea;

units.la: Quædam antiquis temporibus in Ecclesia consuetudines fuere, quas temporis diuturnitas partim immutauit, partim omnino sustulit, aliquæ etiam ex ijs Canonum decretis abrogatæ sunt. Talis illa quoque fuit, vt Presby-teræ, vetulæ mulieres in Ecclesijs constituerentur, quas etiam præsidentes vocabant, quæ quidem ingredientibus in Ecclesiam fœminis veluti magisterio quodam fungentes præessent, ac suo quamque ordine rite consistere iuberent, & quo quamque loco, quoue modo vnicuique standum esset, docerent. Ne qua igitur eiusmodi mulieres eligantur, neue ijs nominibus nuncupentur, Canon decernit. Vide etiam Balsamonem in hunc Canonem. Vide eundem Balsamonem eiusdem Synodi Can. 16. De Euangelijs legendis in diebus Sabbati. Can. 17. De Lectionibus inserendis inter Psalmos. Can. 18. De precum ministerio in Nonis; & Vesperis. & Can. 19. De precibus super Catechumenos. Sed minima hæc sunt, videamus reliqua. Synodus Caesariensis prohibet Presbyteris, ne in nuptijs eorum, qui duas uxores ducunt, conueniant. Zonaras; Verum haec in libris scripta inueniuntur: Nos, & Patriarcham, & Metropolitanos complures in conuiuio Imperatoris secundas nuptias celebrantis aspeximus. Canon decimus nonus Laodicenus de Concionibus ad Catechumenos, & Poenitentes multa praecipit: Sed Zonaras notat suo tempore, quae ad Poenitentes spectant, nescire se quomodo intermissa obsoleuerint. Ad haec pacem Episcopis offerre, ac in eorum amplexum progredi Sacerdotes consueuerant: Sacerdotibus quoque vicissim pacem laici offerebant, quod nunc ut alia multa ex antiquo iure usurpari desita sunt. Osius Episcopus Canone primo Synodi Sardicensis. Quamuis & Apostolicis, & Synodorum sanctionibus nemini Episcoporum liceat a parua ciuitate in aliam migrare. Quia non deerant contumaces in illo genere. Synodus Neocaesariensis Canone primo. Presbyter si fornicatus fuerit, vel adulterium commiserit, non solum deponatur, sed etiam e fidelium communione eijciatur. Haec sublata sunt a vigesimo septimo Canone Carthaginiensis Synodi. & trigesimo septimo S. Basilij; Clerici, qui peccatum, quod est ad mortem peccant, e gradu deijciuntur, sed a laicorum communione non arcentur. Canon 80. Apostolorum, & secundus Nicaenus, & tertius Laodicenus præcipiunt, qui recens sunt illuminati in ordinem Sacerdotalem non esse promouendos: Ὁ μέν μέγας [?] φωσὴρ Νε-κτάριος ἀπὸ τῆς [?] καταχυ[?]ῶν ἁγίας ἀφο-σιώσεως, ὁ [?] τοῦ [?] ἀπὸ τῆς [?] βίβ[?] ῥύπον ἀπο-πλυ[?]ν, καὶ ἀπὸ [?] ἀπὸ τὸ καθαρὸν [?] ἀξιώμα ἐβαλλ[?]ν, καὶ ἅμα τῆς βασιλ[?] Ἐπίσκοπος γίνε[?], καὶ τῆς ἁγίας, καὶ οἰκου-μενικῆς [?] Σινώδ[?] ἐξάρχῳ. Magnum tamen lumen Nectarius ille e Catechumenorum grege nuper separatus, cum divino lacro vitæ sordes abluisset, purus iam purissimam Episcopatus dignitatem induit, & simul fit regina urbis Episcopus, & sancta secunda universalis Synodi Præses. Nectario socium adscivit Ambrosium Mediolanensem ingenuis artibus instructissimus Marquardus Gudius de Clinicis veteris Ecclesiæ cap. 3. Et quod satis admirari non queo. Narrat Photius in Bibliotheca Synesium Cyrenaeum ad divinam Christianorum doctrinam inclinantem, alia quidem facile recepisse, sed (quod equidem haud scio an aliunde, certe ex Epistola ipsius ad Theophilum manifeste deprehenditur) de Resurrectione dogma suscipere noluisse. Verum ita sentiens, nostris tamen est dogmatibus initiatus, imo etiam summo Sacerdotio dignus habitus, cum ad aliam viri probitatem, pariterque actam vitam respectu habito, tum quod non posset non, qui sic homo vitam instituisset, Resurrectionis lumine illustrari. Nec ea spes fefellit. Facillime enim simul atque Episcopus creatus est, Resurrectionis etiam doctrinam credidit. Ante vigesimum octavum Canonem Chalcedonensem, Metropolitani fiebant ab Episcopis, & non a Constantinopolitano Patriarcha, ut nunc fit, Balsamon in Canonem sextum Sardicensem; Cum Canones dicerent constitui non oportere Episcopos, licet prius fuissent, quando populo frequentes erant, in pagis vilibus, & urbibus, cum causa promotionis Antistitis fit populi frequentia, non antiquum privilegium; nihilominus Thebarum Metropolita Calotechnes Episcopos de novo elegit, & talis electio præside Michaële supremo Philosophorum agitata est in Synodo, statutumque deberi, quod a Thebarum Episcopo innovatum erat, a magna Synodo mandari, cum Canon Apostolicus præcipiat, nihil magni momenti ab Episcopo debere fieri sine sententia Synodali. Præterea notat idem Balsamon ex Canone septimo Sardicense. Etiam si fit prohibitum Episcopo, alijsque sacris ordinibus institutis apud Imperatores diutius moras agere, decreto tamen Imperatoris hoc absque periculo fieri, & quod eis imperatur, exercebunt, vt neque Imperatori quicquam possit imputari, si eos accersat, neq; ij rei futuri sunt, vt qui iubenti Imperatori acquiescant. In Baptismo post cereum accensum exhibitum Baptizatis, sequebatur lactis, & mellis degustatio, quam olim vsitatam fuisse testatur Tertullianus de corona militis capite 3. Hieronymus citat aduersus Luciferianos. Verum hæc cerimonia in desuetudinem abijt. Vide plura apud Vasquez Disputatione 166. cap. 6. & Henriquez lib. 2, cap. 13. Canon Trullanus septuagesimus secundus præcipit, si ex infidelibus coniugibus alteruter fidem fuerit amplexus, & infideli cum fideli habitare placeat, non esse segregandos iuxta Pauli vocem. Sub Patriarcha tamen Theodosio buccinator quidam Imperatorius baptizatus, per scripturam Patriarchicam separatus est, quæ merito non obtemperabat multum roganti, vt religionem suam ampletteretur, id quod Canoni contrarium est, adnotat nescio quis in Harmenopuli Epitome Canon. fec.5. Tit. 2. Plura hic adderem, sed si cui hæc non sufficiunt, neque sexcenta alia suffecerint. De Legibus immutatis alibi dixi. Eandem atque Canones diriorem, & spissiorem fortunam expertæ sunt. Vnum si dixero, finem faciam. Nicephorus Gregoras Histor. Roman, lib. 19. in Concione ad Imperatorem; Εἰ δ᾽ ἡ καὶ πάλιν κἀμψοί νόμοι πολιτικῶν λύοντας πολλάκις δυοῖν ἕνεκεν[?], ἢ κακῶς τινος ἁμαρτάνοντος δ᾽ αὖ [illegible, ~6 letters] ἢ βελτιόνων δ᾽ ἰσχύος φανέντων ἐκ τῆς τῷ [?] [illegible, ~8 letters] ἐπιγραμμάτων [?] διαχύσεως ἐν καιρῷ [?], ἢ τῆς ζωῆς [?]. Etenim si ab antiquo tempore præscriptæ leges Rebuspublicis sæpius dissoluuntur duabus ob causas, aut si noxium quippiam earum causa accessit, aut quæ postmodum institutæ sunt, experientia usu comprobata, & exercitatione meliores iudicatæ sunt. Tot itaque Canonum, consuetudinum, & constitutionum Ecclesiasticarum mutationibus non oftantibus in ea Ecclesia, inductis novis atq; comprobatis, & usu receptis antiquatis vetustioribus semper ea una eademque, & sibi constans reputata est & a Græcis, & ab exteris, indicio manifesto, Rituum, & consuetudinum immutationem non inferre variationem, & consequenter dissidium. Et licet mutatio irrepserit, non ea tamen est, ut consensum dissoluat. Et nos dicimus similem variationem Ecclesiam Græcam ab Ecclesia Romana diuidere, quia Græca hoc modo, Romana alio Sacramenta ministrati; Liturgias dirigit, officia celebrat? Quare non & vestium, & calceorum varietas, & barbæ, & capillorum tonsura, & reliqui corporis concinnatio, lingua etiam ipsa, & dialectus dissidium non importabit? Quid hæc ad dogma, vel ad essentiam dogmatis? Non nego, si quis ritum, vel minimum ad confirmandam hæresim, vel nouum dogma in Ecclesiam inducere tentauerit, eum ritum licet tum bonum, integrum, & adiaphorum, a praua intentione inductoris praeuissimum fieri: neque tantum dissidium, sed etiam hæresim inducere, & uti talem modis omnibus cum suo auctore profligandum. Sit exemplum. Consecrare in Azymo dici vix potest, quam præclarum sit. Si quis tamen modo accedens profiteatur se consecrare in eo absque fermento, ut unam tantum in Christo naturam innuat, plane hic contra Ecclesiæ Latinæ sensa, nouam inducens hæresim, non tantum ritus illius, sed ipse quoque condemnabitur, non ut Schismaticus solum, sed etiam ut hæreticus, etsi consecratio in Azymo nullum dissidium inferat inter consecrantes in Azymo, & consecrantes in Fermentato. Quod enim est per se adiaphorum, intentio consecrantis depraua facit, ut ex bono fit malum. Sed quid plura? provoco ad auctorem primum Schismatis, & alios Schismaticos, & Ecclesiae Græcæ proceres, Photium Patriarcham, Nicetam Byzantium, Eulogium Alexandrinum, Irenæum Martyrem, Theophylactum Bulgariæ, Armeniorum Catholicum, Demetrium Chomatenum, Petrum Antiochenum, & alios, quorum dicta laudaui Dissertatione mea ad D. de Boineburgh. Non puto tantorum virorum decreta perplacebunt, quod Ecclesiae Romanae votis subscribunt. Et, ut luculentius veritas pateat; inspice librum Græcorum Ecclesiasticum, cui Typico nomen est, in quo singulis diebus modus ossicij recitandi præscribitur, leges; Sæpius hoc modo Byzantij recitatur officium, Hierosolymis, & alibi aliter, nec unus semper servatur ordo in quatuor Patriarchijs: & nihilominus unum sunt, & diversa officiorum recitatio, discrepantes in dogmate sententias non efficiunt.
units.tr: In early times there were customs in the Church which the passage of time partly changed and partly abolished altogether, and some of them were also repealed by decrees of the canons. One such custom was that elderly women, called female elders (presbyterae) and also presidents, were appointed in the churches. As women entered the church, they acted almost as teachers, presided over them, ordered each to take her proper place, and instructed them where and how each should stand. The canon therefore decrees that no such women are to be chosen or called by those names. See also Balsamon on this canon, and Balsamon on canon 16 of the same synod, on reading the Gospels on the Sabbath days; canon 17, on inserting lessons between the Psalms; canon 18, on the ministry of prayers at the Nones and Vespers; and canon 19, on prayers over the catechumens. But these are minor matters; let us look at the rest. The Synod of Caesarea forbids presbyters to attend the weddings of men who take two wives. (Zonaras.) Yet these things are found written in the books, while we have seen the Patriarch and several metropolitans at the emperor's banquet celebrating a second marriage. The nineteenth canon of Laodicea gives many instructions about sermons to catechumens and penitents, but Zonaras notes that in his own time he did not know how the matters concerning penitents had fallen into disuse. Bishops were also accustomed to offer peace to priests and to embrace them, and in turn laymen offered peace to priests; now, like many other things of ancient law, this has ceased to be practised. Osius, bishop, in the first canon of the Synod of Sardica: "Although, by both apostolic and synodal sanctions, no bishop may move from a small city to another." This was needed because there were not lacking stubborn men of that kind. The Synod of Neocaesarea, canon 1: "If a presbyter has committed fornication or adultery, he is not only to be deposed but also cast out from the communion of the faithful." This was abolished by the twenty-seventh canon of the Synod of Carthage and the thirty-seventh of St Basil; clergy who commit a sin unto death are removed from their rank, but are not shut out from the communion of the laity. Canon 80 of the Apostles, and the second Nicene and the third Laodicean, direct that those recently enlightened are not to be promoted to the priestly order. [Greek of Nectarius sentence omitted from this rendering.] Yet that great light, Nectarius, lately separated from the flock of catechumens, when he had washed away the stains of life by the divine laver, at once, being pure, put on the most pure dignity of bishop, and at the same time became bishop of the royal city and president of the holy and ecumenical second synod. Marquardus Gudius, in his Clinics of the Ancient Church, chapter 3, says that Nectarius took Ambrose of Milan as an associate, a man most thoroughly trained in the liberal arts. And what I cannot sufficiently wonder at: Photius, in his Bibliotheca, relates that Synesius of Cyrene, inclining to the divine doctrine of the Christians, readily accepted other points, but (whether he learned this elsewhere I do not know, though it is clearly evident from his letter to Theophilus) was unwilling to receive the doctrine of the resurrection. Yet, thinking thus, he was nonetheless initiated into our doctrines and even judged worthy of the high priesthood, both in view of his other uprightness and his conduct of life, and because a man who had ordered his life in such a way could not fail to be enlightened by the light of the resurrection. Nor did that hope fail him. For, as soon as he was made bishop, he quickly believed the doctrine of the resurrection too. Before the twenty-eighth canon of Chalcedon, metropolitans were made by bishops, and not by the Patriarch of Constantinople, as is now done. (Balsamon on the sixth canon of Sardica.) Although the canons say that bishops should not be appointed, though they existed earlier, when they were numerous among the people in humble villages and cities, since the number of the people is the cause of promoting a bishop and not an ancient privilege, nevertheless the metropolitan of Thebes, Calotechnes, elected new bishops, and such an election was debated in synod under the presidency of Michael, chief of the philosophers, and it was decided that what had been introduced by the bishop of Thebes ought to be referred to the great synod, since the apostolic canon directs that nothing of great moment is to be done by a bishop without synodal judgement. Balsamon also notes from the seventh canon of Sardica: although it is forbidden to a bishop, and to other men in sacred orders, to linger long at the emperors' courts, nevertheless by the emperor's decree this may be done without danger, and they will carry out what is ordered, so that nothing can be imputed to the emperor if he summons them, nor are they to be liable, since they obey the emperor who commands. In baptism, after the lighted candle was shown to the baptized, there followed a tasting of milk and honey, which Tertullian testifies was once in use, in his book On the Soldier's Crown, chapter 3, and Jerome cites against the Luciferians. But this ceremony has fallen into disuse. See more in Vasquez, Disputation 166, chapter 6, and Henriquez, book 2, chapter 13. The seventy-second canon of the Trullan Council directs that if one of a married pair of unbelievers embraces the faith, and the unbeliever is willing to live with the believer, they are not to be separated, in accordance with the words of Paul. Yet under Patriarch Theodosius a certain imperial trumpeter, once baptized, was separated by a patriarchal writ, which rightly did not obey him when he earnestly asked that his wife embrace his religion; this is contrary to the canon, as someone notes in the Epitome of Harmenopulus, canon 5, title 2 (sic). I would add more here, but if these examples do not suffice for anyone, six hundred others would not suffice either. I have spoken elsewhere about laws that have been changed. Canons have experienced an equally harsh and dense fate. If I say one more thing, I will make an end. Nicephorus Gregoras, Roman History, book 19, in a speech to the emperor: for if laws of states, once prescribed from ancient times, are often dissolved for two reasons, either because some harm has arisen from them, or because those established later have been proved by experience and practice to be better, then, despite so many changes of canons, customs and ecclesiastical constitutions, when new things have been introduced, approved and received into use, while older ones have become obsolete, the Church has always been regarded as one and the same, and consistent with itself, both by the Greeks and by outsiders, as a clear sign that a change of rites and customs does not bring variation and consequently dissent. And even if a change has crept in, it is not of such a kind as to dissolve consensus. Do we say that the Greek Church is divided from the Roman Church by a similar variation, because the Greeks administer the sacraments in one way and the Romans in another, and direct their liturgies and celebrate their offices differently? Why then would a variety of clothing and shoes, of beards and hair cutting, and of the arrangement of the rest of the body, or even of language and dialect, not bring about dissent? What have these to do with doctrine, or with the essence of doctrine? I do not deny that if anyone tries to introduce some rite, however small, to confirm a heresy or to bring a new dogma into the Church, that rite, though otherwise good, whole and indifferent, is made wicked by the depraved intention of its introducer; and not only dissent but heresy is brought in, and such a rite must be stamped out in every way, together with its author. Take an example. It can hardly be said how excellent it is to consecrate in unleavened bread. Yet if someone, coming forward now, professes that he consecrates in it without leaven so as to imply that there is only one nature in Christ, he, plainly introducing a new heresy against the opinions of the Latin Church, will be condemned not only as a schismatic of that rite but also as a heretic, even though consecration in unleavened bread brings no dissent between those who consecrate in unleavened bread and those who consecrate in leavened bread. For what is indifferent in itself, the depraved intention of the consecrator makes evil instead of good. But why say more? I call upon the first author of the schism, and the other schismatics, and the leaders of the Greek Church: Photius the Patriarch, Nicetas of Byzantium, Eulogius of Alexandria, Irenaeus the Martyr, Theophylact of Bulgaria, the Catholicos of the Armenians, Demetrius Chomatenus, Peter of Antioch, and others, whose sayings I praised in my dissertation addressed to Boineburg. I do not think that the decrees of such great men will please those who subscribe to the wishes of the Roman Church. And, that the truth may appear more clearly, look into the ecclesiastical book of the Greeks called the Typicon, in which the manner of reciting the office is prescribed for each day; you will read that the office is often recited in one way at Byzantium, and differently at Jerusalem and elsewhere, and the order is not kept the same in all four patriarchates; and nevertheless they are one, and a diversity in the recitation of offices does not produce opinions that disagree in doctrine.

units.la: Exercitatio Historico-Theologica de Ecclesia Græcanica hodierna, nonnullis aliis, sed potissimum Leoni Allatio opposita, examinatur, & redarguitur.
units.tr: Historico-Theological Exercise on the Present-Day Greek Church, chiefly opposed to Leo Allatius, is examined and refuted.

units.la: EX Hottingeranis ineptiis, & puerorum crepundiis expediri conanti mihi, en ecce offertur ab amico antiquissimo, & in omni eruditionis genere instructissimo Bibliothecæ Barberinæ Custode Carolo Morono Exercitatio Historico-Theologica de Ecclesia Græcanica hodierna, potissimum Leoni Allatio opposita.
