Verum fateor, assentatiuncula quadam blandius sum mihi, cum me vidi inter versatissimos in omni studio Arcudium, Nihusium, aliosque collocari, tantique mea dicta æstimari, ut in Athenis Germanicis digna iudicata sint exponi, & exposita in solemnem congressum produci, productaque oppositis obiectionibus expendi, quot pondo sint. Concupiscebam tamen, & avidissime, æquam in illis expendendis lancem. Sed cum mentis incitatione, & propriæ religionis affectu, alienæ odio plusquâ nouercali pensata sint, non intellecta parte, factum est, ut potior Allatii causa, peior non nemini, qui in rebus bus Græcorum, atque consuetudinibus Ecclesiasticis ieiunus est, videri poterit. Sed de his ipse nihil laboro. Dicta Allatij multos ab hinc annos publico iudicio exposita sunt. Laudatores non defuerunt. Iudicabunt posteri. Aduersarij dicunt, nihil Allatium dicere. Quare vero nihil Allatius dicit, nulla est ratio, quæ appareat. Exsibilandus est Allatius. Quare vero hæc Allatio? Quia sic placet aduersario. Inconstans est Allatius, contrarius sibi: indicium inconstantiæ quodnam est? contrarietatis fundamentum in quo situm est? Ita vult aduersarius, ita sibi commodum ducit. Si doctis ac cordatis hominibus responsiones similes contra asserentes gratæ sunt, iam actum est de Allatio. Verum Allatius ad eosdem provocat, & de disciplina non bona sibi tradita cum illis conqueritur, qui docuerunt, contra rationes rationibus, & contra argumenta argumentis agendum esse: si vero non suppetunt, deuinci ab aduersario, & fateri victoriam non esse dedignandum. Hinc solutionis ille modus, quo sæpissime utitur opponens, nullo modo probabitur a laudatissimis viris. Deficientibus siquidem omnibus, cum neq; quid respondeas, neq; rationes, & testimonia ad probandum dogma suppetūt, satisfuperq; aduersarium convelles, si dicas; Possem pro Cauco multa dicere, & singulis obiectionibus Allatianis respondere, verum breuitatis studium illam operam in aliam occasionem reijcere nos iubet. Et vbi monetur Allatius, ex immani odio totum illud Caput Chytraeo opposuisse, eumque praeter illius mentem, institutum, & meritum tam inique, & non raro calumniose tractaffe, quod fortasse alias ostendetur. De visione deifica Sanctorum; Leo Allatius, & copiosius in Epistola ad Boineburgium a f. 26. ad 41. vbi magno conatu dissensionem in hoc argumento Graecorum a Latinis amoliri conatur, sed quo successu, alibi, si opus erit, ostendetur. De Consensione Allatij, & Epistola ad D. Boineburgium. Nec fortassis contrarium persuadebit D. Boineburgio viro non tam dignatione, quam eruditione illustri. Ast in his diutius immorari non conuenit cū id in praesentia nobis propositum sit, statum Ecclesiae Graecanicae hodiernum aliquatenus delineare. De falsis Graecorum opinionibus; Neq; tamen falsas Graecorum opiniones ad examen revocare, vel omnia, quae hic a Pontificijs obiiciuntur, excutere animus est: id enim alius laboris erit. Differtationem nanq; nudā damus, & quasi excerpta quaedam ex ijs, quae uberius congesta sunt. De visione beatifica, cum probandum erat contra Allatium, alia Graecos, alia Latinos determinare, quod magno conatu amoliri conatur Allatius, de quo successu alibi, si opus erit, ostendemus. Et ubi nam opportunius, & commodius fieri poterat? De scripto contra Purgatorium oblato Basiliensi Concilio. Allatius hariolatur desumptum esse ex penu Hæreticorū, quos vocat Luteranorum: quam vero in suahariolatione eruditus vir hallucinetur, haud difficulter monstrari aliquando poterit. De Tract. contra Coringium de Purgat. Ego autem contra dico, tam nihil egisse Allatium in illo tractatu, ut causam suam si non prodidit, exsibilandam saltem propinauerit. Contendunt modo inuicem ea, quae ὁ πασίν[?] Coringius scripserat, cum iis, quae Allatius reposuit, & patebit unicuique praeiudicijs non fascinato, nihil aliud de scripto Allatij pronunciandum esse, quam ἄρρητα ἀμένω[?]. Et de Artolatria; Arguit hunc ritum Arcudius ipse tanquam idololatricum: excusare autem conantur Goar, & Allatius, sed conantur tantum. Et alia: neque enim omnia reportanda sunt. Vides qua methodo, quibus rationibus, illisque ineluctabili vi, & perlecui momento concinnatis dicta Allatij refelluntur, & obiecta diluuntur, ut nihil iam remaneat Allatio in sui patrocinium reponendum, & putant se responsis similibus bene sanis hominibus satisfacere? o iudices ingenuos! o strenuos antagonistas! unica inficiatione, vel affirmatione, vel in aliud tempus remissione responsi sua probasse, aduersarij reprobasse, o quam felicissimum est Hæc tamen non curat Allatius, qui prolatis dictis vtriusque Ecclesiæ conformibus, quidquid de eorum veritate disputent alij siue Catholici, siue Heterodoxi, consensionem firmat. Hörum continua sunt pleraque, in Hottingerana Disputatione Apologetica, quem admonitum peruelim, vt sua putida, insuauia, atque inerudite ingurgitata, quæ se repositurum minatur Allatio,citius reuomat, ne in ventriculo putrefacta pestilentiam afferant, & mox exitum Hottingero. Qui itaque hac ratione argumentis aduersariorum respondent, non soluunt argumenta, sed incertis occultisque responsis Lectores implicant. Quæ cum considero, vellere mihi sentio aures dicta Firmiani Lactantij lib. 3. de ijs qui Antipodes esse putant; Num aliquid loquuntur? aut est quisquam tam ineptus, qui credat esse homines, quorum vestigia sint superiora, quamcapita? aut ibi quæ apud nos iacent inuersa pendere? fruges, & arbores deorsum versus crescere? pluuias, & nines, & grandinem sursum versus cadere in terram? Et miratur aliquis hortos pensiles inter septem mira narrari; cumPhilosophi, & agros, & maria, & vrbes, & montes pensiles faciant? Et infra; At ego multis argumentis probare possem, nullo modo fieri posse, ut calum terra sit inferius; nisi & liber jam concludendus esset, & adhuc aliqua restarent, quae magis sunt praesenti operi necessaria, & quoniam singulorum errores percurrere non est unius libri opus: satis sit pauca enumerasse, ex quibus possit, qualia sint cetera, intelligi.
units.tr: I was trying to free myself from Hottinger's silly trifles and children's rattles when my most ancient friend, Carlo Moroni, Custodian of the Barberini Library and a man equipped in every kind of learning, offered me An Historico-Theological Exercise on the Present-Day Greek Church, chiefly opposed to Leo Allatius. I admit I was rather pleased with myself, a little vain, when I saw myself placed among the most accomplished scholars in every field, Arcudius, Nihusius and others, and my own sayings valued so highly that they were judged worth setting out in the German Athens, and once set out were brought before a solemn assembly, and, once brought there, were weighed against opposing objections to see how much they weigh. I was eager, very eager, for a fair balance in weighing them. But since they have been weighed with the spur of ambition and zeal for one's own religion, and with more than step-motherly hatred of another's view, and since one side has not been understood, it has come about that the cause of Allatius may seem the stronger, and to some who are ignorant of Greek affairs and ecclesiastical customs, the weaker. But I am not troubled about these things myself. Allatius's sayings were exposed to public judgment many years ago. Praisers were not lacking. Posterity will judge. The adversaries say that Allatius says nothing. Why Allatius says nothing, there is no reason that appears. Allatius must be hissed off. Why Allatius in particular? Because it pleases the adversary. Allatius is inconsistent and contrary to himself: what is the evidence of his inconsistency? On what foundation is the contradiction based? That is what the adversary wants, and that is what he thinks advantageous to himself. If replies of this sort against those who assert are pleasing to learned and sensible men, then it is all over for Allatius. But Allatius appeals to those same men, and complains of the poor discipline handed down to him by those who taught that arguments must be met with arguments and proofs with proofs; and if these are not available, one must be defeated by the adversary and not disdain to confess the victory. Hence that method of answering, which the objector uses most often, will in no way be approved by the most praiseworthy men. For when everything fails, and you have neither an answer nor reasons and testimonies to prove your doctrine, it is quite enough to overturn the adversary by saying: I could say much for Caucus and reply to each of Allatius's objections, but the desire for brevity bids me put that labour off to another occasion. And where Allatius is warned that out of immense hatred he opposed that whole chapter to Chytraeus, and treated his purpose and merit, beyond his intention, so unjustly and not infrequently calumniously, which perhaps will be shown elsewhere. On the Beatific Vision of the Saints; Leo Allatius, and more fully in the letter to Boineburg from pages 26 to 41, where with great effort he tries to remove the Greeks' disagreement with the Latins on this question, but with what success will be shown elsewhere, if need be. On the Consent of Allatius, and the Letter to Mr. Boineburg. Nor perhaps will he persuade Boineburg, a man illustrious not so much by rank as by learning. But it is not fitting to linger longer on these matters, since it is now our purpose to outline in some measure the present state of the Greek Church. On the false opinions of the Greeks; Nor is it my intention to examine the false opinions of the Greeks, or to go through everything the Papists object here; that would be a separate labour. For I give a bare dissertation, as it were excerpts from those things that have been gathered at greater length. On the beatific vision, when it had to be proved against Allatius that the Greeks determine one thing and the Latins another, which Allatius strives with great effort to remove, on what success elsewhere, if need be, we will show. And where could this have been done more fittingly and conveniently? On the writing against Purgatory offered to the Council of Basel. Allatius guesses that it was taken from the store of the heretics whom he calls Lutherans; how far the learned man is mistaken in his guess can be shown at some time without much difficulty. On the treatise against Coringius on Purgatory. But I for my part maintain that Allatius achieved so little in that treatise that, if he did not betray his cause, he at least offered it to be hissed at. They only contend with one another, what Coringius wrote and what Allatius replied, and it will be plain to anyone not bewitched by prejudice that nothing else is to be pronounced about Allatius's writing than [ἄρρητα ἀμείνω], better left unspoken. And on Artolatry: Arcudius himself argues that this rite is idolatrous; Goar and Allatius try to excuse it, but only try. And other matters, for not everything need be carried back. You see by what method, by what arguments, and by what irresistible force and well-wrought weight Allatius's sayings are refuted and the objections dissolved, so that nothing remains for Allatius to put forward in his defence, and they think they satisfy well-minded men with such replies! O generous judges! O vigorous antagonists! By a single denial, or affirmation, or deferral of the reply to another time, to have proved one's own answer and disproved the adversary's: how very fortunate that is! Allatius, however, does not worry about this, but, having produced sayings in agreement with both Churches, he confirms the consensus, whatever others, whether Catholic or heterodox, dispute about their truth. Most of this is in Hottinger's Apologetic Disputation, which I would very much like to warn to vomit up quickly its foul, unpleasant and unlearnedly gorged stuff, which it threatens to restore against Allatius, lest, rotting in the stomach, it bring pestilence and soon an end to Hottinger. Those who answer the arguments of their adversaries in this way do not solve the arguments, but entangle the readers in uncertain and obscure replies. When I consider these things, I feel my ears tingle at the words of Lactantius Firmianus, book 3, on those who think there are Antipodes: Do they say anything? Or is there anyone so foolish as to believe that there are men whose feet are higher than their heads? Or that things lying upside down here hang there? That crops and trees grow downwards, that rain and snow and hail fall upwards to the earth? And does anyone wonder that gardens hanging in the air are counted among the seven wonders, when philosophers make fields, seas, cities and mountains hang in the air? And below: But I could prove by many arguments that it is in no way possible for the sky to be below the earth; but the book is already to be concluded, and some things remain that are more necessary to the present work, and since to run through each person's errors is not the task of one book, it is enough to have listed a few, from which it may be understood what the rest are like.

units.la: An non Lactantius, nullos esse Antipodas clavo trabali fixit? Falsum in principio sumpserunt qui Antipodas asserunt, verisimilitudine inducti. Necesse est eos in ea, quae consequuntur, incurrere. Sic incidunt in multa ridicula, quia necesse est falsa esse, quae rebus falsis congruunt. Sic edicto sancit, qui Antipodas subvertere nititur, quod & multis argumentis probare potest, nihilominus & libri conclusio, & aliqua praesenti operi magis necessaria restant, nec est unius operis, singulorum errores percurrere: satis est enumerasse, ex quibus possit, qualia sint cetera, intelligi. Quid ergo? Concludamus, Antipodes nulli sunt. Et tamen, mi Lactanti, sunt. Plura itaque contradicentis asseveratio, vel in aliud tempus ad probandum id quod praetenditur, dilatio, non facit, ut quod non est, sit, & adversa sententia destruatur. Quare quaecunque in hunc modum in scripto retuleris, nisi subsequatur clarum documentum, & oculis comperta non proferantur, nulla sunt, nec repugnantium mentem destruunt, nisi tu eodem veftigio temporis verisimiliora, siue credibiliora produxeris. Multa ergo ab Allatio asserta, & ab opponentibus hunc in modum reiecta, certissima, & perfuasissima pluribus erunt, quam quae promittuntur dicenda in posterum.
units.tr: Did not Lactantius nail down with a beam that there are no Antipodes? Those who assert Antipodes, led by plausibility, assumed a falsehood at the start. They are bound to fall into what follows from it. Thus they stumble into many absurdities, because whatever agrees with false things must itself be false. So he who strives to overthrow the Antipodes decrees, and who could prove this by many arguments, nevertheless has the conclusion of his book and some things more necessary to the present work still left to do, and it is not the task of one work to run through each person's errors: it is enough to have listed a few, from which the rest may be understood. What then? Let us conclude that there are no Antipodes. And yet, my dear Lactantius, there are. So the mere assertion of the contrary, or a postponement to another time of the proof of what is put forward, does not make what is not, be, nor destroy the opposing opinion. Therefore whatever you have set down in writing in this way, unless a clear proof follows and things seen with one's own eyes are not produced, are nothing, nor do they destroy the minds of those who disagree, unless you in the same breath produce things more probable or more credible. Therefore many things asserted by Allatius, and rejected by his opponents in this way, will be more certain and more persuasive to many than those promised to be said in future.

units.la: Sed ad optatam dictorum constantiam perveniamus, statuendi sunt testes, quorum auctoritate veluti indubitata rem comprobemus. Tu Pontificios reijcis, vti Pontificiae dignitatis vindices, adfers adversarios, & eorum testimonio tua constabilire niteris: ego vero eosdem, & merito reijcio. qui enim Pontificatum perditum ire, &, si fieri posset, memoriam illius penitus obliterare conantur, quod ad illius laudem est, confirmatque dominium, vel silebunt, vel imminuent, saepius etiam in contrarium, & exitium convertent. Æquum itaque fuerit, vel utrisque fidem negare, vel exhibere, dummodo verosimilia dicant. Tum vero proxime ad verum accedent, & loquentur credibiliter, cum reiectis calumnijs eorum dicta, vel facta non ad vituperationem, nec ad laudem, sed ad simplicem rerum narrationem adducunt. Sed Reformati non probant. Hoc vero est e terris fidei ac veritati fugam injcere. Sed ero tibi æquior. Res, de quibus inter nos agitur, non in theoria, sed in praxi consistunt; Neque enim de eorum natura, sive veritate disputamus, quod alij peragunt, sed tantum de consensu, & dissidio inter Græcam, & Romanam Ecclesiam, utcumque se habeat ista fides, vel veritas. Modo inter nos id, tantum disputatur: & tu dissidium, ego consensum arguo. Consensus est voluntatum coniunctio, sententiarum conuenientia, & dictorum congruentia. An vero voluntates coniungantur, vel sententiæ congruant, cum intimis præcordijs lateant, foras verbis egeruntur, quæ sæpius si ad præsentes non eiaculantur, in auras euanescunt, neq; an unquam fuerint, dignoscuntur. Quod aliter euenit, si monumentis prodantur memoriæ. Tum siquidem fixa remanent, & firmiter retinentur. Si ex alia parte animi proni sint ad religionem, præter reuerentiam, quam Deo, rebusque sacris inuiolatam conseruant, proferenda in divino cultu cautissime circumspectant, ne fallant, vel fallantur. Quare ad dicta Græcorum probanda nulla ratio probabilior occurrit, quam eorundem inter preces effata, ex quibus indubitata mens eorum habebitur. Quare exempli causa dubium sit, An Græcorum Ecclesia teneat: Iustos post hanc vitam illico in regnum Coelorum transfuectos visione beatifica perfrui, & Deum videre non in speculo, & in aenigmate, sed facie ad faciem? opponens nihil dicit, si prouocet ad hos, & alios, qui afferunt Graecos visionem beatificam ante iudicium Iustis negare; nanq; recurrendum est ad eorumdem dicta scripto tradita, & quae solemniter venerantur, recitantque in Ecclesia, in quibus si affirmatur, iam tenemus sententiam. Tum addit Leo; Sed Ecclesia Romana de visione beatifica haec eadem pronunciat, ergo inter Ecclesiam Graecam, & Latinam est consensus, & non dissidium. Et argumentum simile nunquam dissoluetur, etiam si quamplurimi sint, qui dicant, visionem beatificam illam Ecclesiam negare. Quis enim melius Ecclesiae Graecae mentem sciuerit, vel explicauerit, quam ipsa Ecclesia Graeca? dicit hoc Casalius, Azorius, alij. Dicunt. Ergo ita est: Hoc vero nego. Contrarium video, lego, verba non sunt obscura, vel difficilia, & ego fidem oculis meis negauero? Sed dicunt Ephesius, Cabasila, alij Graeci. Dicunt. Quis fide,dignior est, Ecclesia ne Graeca an Ephesius, vel Cabasila? Multa dicebant Ariani, Nestoriani, alij: quia tamen Ecclesia non erant, dicta eorum reiecta sunt, Ecclesiae probata. Quod si Nilus, & Ephesius[?] veritatis lumine compulsi congruenter cum Ecclesia loquantur, tum fides Ecclesiae testimonio aduersariorum corroborata potior fuerit, & sic ab Ecclesia Romana eadem afferente confirmabitur, & tum diffidio omni de medio sublato consensus erit illustrior. Sic quoque de aliis philosophandum est.
units.tr: But let us come to the constancy of the points we have raised. Witnesses must be named, whose authority will confirm the matter as beyond doubt. You reject the Papists as defenders of papal dignity, and you bring forward adversaries and try to establish your case by their testimony. I, for my part, reject those people too, and rightly so. Those who try to have the papacy destroyed and, if it were possible, its memory wholly erased, will either be silent about what praises it and confirms its dominion, or they will diminish it, and quite often they will turn it into the opposite and into ruin. It would be fair, then, either to deny credence to both sides, or to allow it to both, provided they say what is plausible. Then indeed they will come closest to the truth and speak credibly, when they set aside their slanders and report their words or deeds not to blame or praise, but as a plain account of events. But the Reformed do not approve this. To do so would be to flee from the lands of faith and truth. Yet I will be fairer to you. The matters under dispute between us do not rest on theory but on practice. For we are not disputing their nature or truth, which others may do, but only the agreement and disagreement between the Greek and the Roman Church, however that faith or truth may stand. Between us this alone is being argued: you assert dissent, and I assert agreement. Agreement is the joining of wills, the harmony of opinions, and the congruence of words. But whether wills are joined or opinions agree, while they lie hidden in the innermost heart, cannot be known unless they are brought forth in words. And these words, if they are not uttered to those present, often vanish into the air, and it is not known whether they were ever spoken. It is otherwise if they are handed down in written records. For then they remain fixed and are firmly held. If, on the other hand, minds are inclined to religion, they keep, besides reverence for God and for sacred things inviolate, and in the worship of God they take the greatest care that they neither deceive nor be deceived. Therefore, to prove the statements of the Greeks, no more probable method occurs than the sayings they utter in their prayers, from which their settled mind may be known. So, for example, let it be doubtful whether the Greek Church holds that the righteous, after this life, are at once carried into the kingdom of heaven and enjoy the beatific vision, seeing God not in a mirror or in an enigma, but face to face. The opponent says nothing if he appeals to those others who assert that the Greeks deny the beatific vision to the righteous before judgment. For one must have recourse to the statements of the Greeks handed down in writing, which they solemnly venerate and recite in the Church, and if in these it is affirmed, we already hold the opinion. Then Leo adds: But the Roman Church pronounces these same things about the beatific vision; therefore there is agreement, and not dissent, between the Greek and Latin Churches. And an argument of this kind is never refuted, even if there are very many who say that the Greek Church denies that beatific vision. For who could know or explain the mind of the Greek Church better than the Greek Church itself? Casalius, Azorius and others say otherwise. They say it. Therefore it is so? This I deny. I see the contrary, I read it, the words are neither obscure nor difficult, and shall I deny the evidence of my own eyes? But Ephesius, Cabasila and other Greeks say otherwise. They say it. Which is more worthy of trust, the Greek Church or Ephesius or Cabasila? The Arians and Nestorians said many things, but because they were not the Church, their statements were rejected and the Church's were approved. But if Nilus and Ephesius, compelled by the light of truth, speak in agreement with the Church, then the faith of the Church, confirmed by the testimony of its adversaries, will be the stronger, and so it will be confirmed by the Roman Church affirming the same; and then, with all dissent removed, the consensus will be the clearer. So too must one reason about other matters.

units.la: Sed opponens Schismaticorum auctoritatem requirit, & testimonium ambit. At omnino videndum est, quid Schismatici dicant: nam si pro consensu tuo producas Latinos mercatura gratia in Graecia habitantes advenas quosdam captiuos, & subditos Romani Pontificis, qui recensentur O. P. nihil ages. Certe hercle. Quid Schismatici ipsi dicant, examinauimus alibi. Vbi Ecclesiam habes, cuius res interest, loquentem, tu Schismaticos euocas? Res salua iam est. Cum causa Reformatorum agitur, ex Pontificijs argumenta petantur. Sunt in Graecia plerique Pontificiae religionis indigenae multo ab hinc tempore; sunt etiam advenae, res inter se contrahentes, emendo, vendendo, permutando, alijs, atque alijs negotijs occupati, qui Pontificiam dignitatem colunt, & ad illius praecepta vitam accommodant, parumque curant, quid Graeci dicant, vel profiteantur. Cum consensum urgeo, nullius ex his testimonium sumpsi. Nomina vel unum. Græci sunt fere omnes in Græcia nati, ritibus, ac religioni Græcorum addictissimi, qui sua narrant, non aliena. Et quod magis est, Ecclesiæ ipsius libri Rituales clamant, & digito monstrant decreta illius Ecclesiæ, quæ, ut videre est, eadem quæ & Pontificij concinunt. Sed tu Schismaticos quæritas, quare non potius illius Ecclesiæ Patres, ac Doctores integerrimos, & scientiarum omni genere cumulatissimos, qui eadem ipsa insinuant? Si male Reformatis olent ingentia illa Ecclesiæ Græcæ culmina, ideoque eorum effata in minimis ponuntur, in Ecclesia nihilominus Græca inter veritatis arcana, & rectæ fidei stabilia fundamenta recensentur. Ne tamen Allatio consensus argumenta, & in processione Spiritus ex Filio, de quo nunc sermo est, deesse videantur, in hoc quoque argumento votis opponentis respondens testimonium proferam ex Concilio Constantinopolitano a Schismaticis contra Barlaamum, Acindynum, & Niceph. Gregoram a Calixto Patriarcha, & Ioanne Cantacuzeno, & Ioanne Palæologo Imperatoribus coacto, in Triclinio Alexiaco sacrarum Blachernarum. Conuenerant vna Metropolitæ Philotheus Coccinus Heracleensis postmodum Patriarcha Constitinopolitanus, Gregorius Palama Thessalonicensis, Arsenius Cyzicenus, Macarius Philadelphiensis, Iacobus Chalcedonensis, Metrophanes Melenicen. sis, Methodius Pontoëracleensis, Georgius Pegarum, & Parij, Dionysius Berrhoensis, Nipho Trapezuntius, Germanus Traianopolitanus, Esaias Selybriensis, Gabriel Apri, Callinicus Amastridis, Daniel Æni, Eusebius Sugdaiæ, Theodorus Bryseos, Iacobus Madytorum, Neophytus Byziæ, Ioannicius Garellæ, Euthymius Mediæ, Iosephus Tenedi, Theodosius Sozopolis, Theoleptus Metropolita Didymotechi, Tum præterea Adrianopolitanus, & Chrysopolitanus, Amasiensis, Examilij. Episcopi, Heracleæ, Panis, Chariupolis, Pamphyli, Athyræ, Campaniæ, Sardium, Traianopolis, Eleutheropolis: nec non alij Ecclesiæ Constantinopolitanæ proceres, Chartophylax magnæ Ecclesiæ, & Philosophorum Hypatus Ambaris, Magnus Sceuophylax Euthymius Apocaucus, Sacellarius magnæ Ecclesiæ Michaël Cabasila, Magnæ Ecclesiæ Referendarius Manuel Siluefter, Magnæ Ecclesiæ a supplicationibus Theodorus Perdicca, Sceuophylax Imperatorij Cleri Georgius Perdicca, Magnæ Ecclesiæ a Sacra Constitutione Michaël Maniaces, Præfes Monasteriorum Diaconus Choniata. En tibi quæréti gregem Schismaticorum, & globum Hæreticorum, tanquam qui Gregoram Palamam, & schismatis, & hæreseon Patronum pertinacissimum sequuntur, & illius male sanas opiniones tutantes, contrarias, rectas, atque integras oppugnant: hi omnes gregatim, conglobatimq; etiam perinviti, atque adversissimi, veritatis radio compulsi processionem Spiritus ex Filio confitentur, & additionem, cum suam defendere nituntur in Tomo Synodico probant. Si his non conquiescis, neque si Graecos alios omnes nemine excepto acervatim uno signo convenientes produxero, non conquiesces. Sed non puto te adeo litigiosum hominem esse. Hi itaque Schismatici in Tomo; Ἡ δὲ Θεία Σύνοδος ὀχώρισον μὲν ἰσομὴν ἔφη τῷ Θεῷ οὐσίαν, καὶ τὴν Θείαν, καὶ Φυσικὴν ἐνέργειαν. ἡ γὰρ ποτὲ ἐνέργεια ἂν ἀπὸ τῆς ἑαυτῆς οὐσίας χωρεῖς. ἆρα μὴ ἀρχῆς [?] τὸ Θεοῦ ἀδημιουργήματος [?] ἐν [?]. τῆς ἐκ οἰκίας, εἰμὴ καὶ Θεὸν ἀπολείπουσα τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ Θεοτόκοι [?], ὅν πῶν ἀδημιούργημα τῆς ἐνεργείας τὸ ἀδημιουργήσαντος, ἀλλ᾽ ἡ τῆς οὐσίας μεταλήψις [?]. ἡ δὲ εἰκόνα τῆς τὸ οἰκονομίας, ἡδὲ ταῦτ᾽ αὐτῆς ἀναγνωρίσεως μετείληφε [?] τῆς οὐσίας, ἀλλὰ τῆς τέχνης, καὶ τῆς ἐνεργείας καὶ τῶν Νύσσης θεολόγου. Sacra Synodus dixit, indimisam cognoscimus divinam essentiam, & sacram cram, & naturalem actionem. Neque enim unquam actio assignabitur a sua essentia divisa. De iis vero quae ab initio a Deo creata fuere dixit. Quis nescit, nisi uti qui Ecclesiae contradi- cunt, insaniat. Quidquid creatum est, actionis Creatoris, non vero essentiae particeps esse? Domus enim non aedificatoris, neque nauis nauipegi essentiae, sed artis, & actionis, ut Nyssenus Theologus decernit, particeps est. Et explanatius. Τῷ Θεῷ ἐνέργειαν ἐκ τῆς Θείας οὐσίας [illegible, ~30 letters] ἀγίων βοώντων [illegible, ~40 letters] ἐν τῷ Θεῷ, καὶ ταύτῃ [illegible, ~35 letters] τοῖς διαφερομένοις [illegible, ~30 letters] τὸ δοκεῖ. [illegible, ~60 letters] τῆς οὐσίας τὸ Θεοῦ [illegible, ~50 letters] τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας [illegible, ~45 letters] ἐν τῇ οὐσίᾳ [illegible, ~40 letters] καὶ πάλιν, κτίσις ἡ οὐ ποίησις τὸ ἐξωθεν, ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας τὸ κτίζοντος, ἡ ποιοῦντος γενέσθω κτιζόμενον ἡ ποιήματος ἀνόμοιον παντελῶς. ἡμῖν ἀλλ' ἡδ' ὡς ἐξωθεν ἡ Θείας οὐσίας ὥστε ἐν τῇ Θείας οὐσίας ὑπάλληλα [illegible, ~30 letters]. ὥσπερ ἡ τῆς ληρεῖν ἡ τοσοῦτον ἀσεβῶς, ὅσον ἀμαθῶς τοῖς ἐκ ἐναντίας ἐπῆλθε, μή ποτε τῆς ἡμῶν φρενῶν ἐκσαίνῃ, ἀλλ' ἡσυχάσῃ, ἡ φυσικῶς ταύτῳ τῷ Θεῷ κτίσιν ἐᾶς ἡ ἑαυτὸν ἐν Θεολόγως ἀδύπτος, ὡς πηγὴς ἀνυπάρχω φυσικῶς ἡ Θείας οὐσίας ἀφέρχωσ, καὶ [?]
units.tr: But the opponent demands the authority of the Schismatics and seeks their testimony. Yet one must certainly see what the Schismatics say, for if you bring forward in support of your consensus some Latins, strangers living in Greece for the sake of trade, some captives and subjects of the Roman Pontiff, who are listed as O.P., you will achieve nothing. Certainly, by Hercules! What the Schismatics themselves say we have examined elsewhere. When you have a Church whose interest is at stake speaking, do you summon the Schismatics? The matter is already safe. When the cause of the Reformed is under discussion, arguments must be sought from the Papists. There are in Greece, for a long time now, many natives of the Papist religion, and there are also foreigners who make contracts with one another, buying, selling, exchanging, and busy with various other business, who honour the Papal dignity, accommodate their lives to its precepts, and care little what the Greeks say or profess. When I press the consensus, I have taken the testimony of none of these. Name even one. Almost all the Greeks are born in Greece, most devoted to the rites and religion of the Greeks, and they report their own affairs, not those of others. And what is more, the Church's own ritual books cry out and point with a finger to the decrees of that Church, which, as can be seen, agree with the Papists too. But you seek out the Schismatics. Why do you not rather seek the Fathers and most upright Doctors of that Church, most richly furnished with every kind of learning, who themselves put forward the same things? If those great pillars of the Greek Church give off a bad smell to the Reformed, and therefore their sayings are set down among the least important, nevertheless in the Greek Church they are counted among the secrets of truth and the firm foundations of right faith. Still, lest the arguments for consensus on the procession of the Spirit from the Son, which is now the subject, seem to be lacking to Allatius, I shall answer the opponent's wishes in this matter too, by producing testimony from the Council of Constantinople, convened by the Patriarch Callistus and the Emperors John Cantacuzenus and John Palaeologus in the Alexian Triclinium of the sacred Blachernae, against the Schismatics Barlaam, Acindynus and Nicephorus Gregoras. Gathered together there were the Metropolitans: Philotheus Coccinus of Heraclea, afterwards Patriarch of Constantinople; Gregory Palamas of Thessalonica; Arsenius of Cyzicus; Macarius of Philadelphia; James of Chalcedon; Metrophanes of Melenikon; Methodius of Pontoheracleia; George of Pegae and Paros; Dionysius of Berrhoea; Nipho of Trebizond; Germanus of Trajanopolis; Isaiah of Selymbria; Gabriel of Aprus; Callinicus of Amastris; Daniel of Aenus; Eusebius of Sugdaea; Theodore of Bryses; James of Madytus; Neophytus of Byzia; Ioannicius of Garella; Euthymius of Media; Joseph of Tenedos; Theodosius of Sozopolis; and Theoleptus, Metropolitan of Didymoteichon. In addition were the Bishops of Adrianople and Chrysopolis, of Amasia, of Examilia, of Heraclea, of Panis, of Chariupolis, of Pamphylia, of Athyra, of Campania, of Sardis, of Trajanopolis and of Eleutheropolis; and the other leading men of the Church of Constantinople: the Chartophylax of the Great Church and Hypatus of the Philosophers, Ambaris; Euthymius Apocaucus, Great Skevophylax; Michael Cabasilas, Sacellarius of the Great Church; Manuel Silvester, Referendary of the Great Church; Theodore Perdiccas, of the Supplications of the Great Church; George Perdiccas, Skevophylax of the Imperial Clergy; Michael Maniakes, of the Sacred Constitution of the Great Church; and Diaconus Choniates, Prefect of the Monasteries. Behold, for you who seek the flock of Schismatics and the crowd of Heretics, as those who follow Gregory Palamas, a most obstinate patron of schism and heresies, and who defend and uphold his ill-sane opinions, attacking the contrary, the right and the sound: all these, gathered in a flock and in a crowd, even against their will and most hostile, compelled by the ray of truth, confess the procession of the Spirit from the Son, and in the Synodal Tome they approve the addition, which they strive to defend. If you will not rest content with these, nor will you rest content if I bring forward all the other Greeks, without exception, assembled in a heap under one sign. But I do not think you are so quarrelsome a man. So these Schismatics say in the Tome: "The divine Synod distinguished the divine essence, which is indivisible, from the divine and natural operation. For an operation can never be separated from its own essence. Surely whatever has been created by God from the beginning does not partake of the Creator's essence but of his operation. For a house does not partake of the essence of the builder, nor a ship of the essence of the shipwright, but of the art and the operation, as the Theologian of Nyssa decides." And more explicitly: [the Greek of this passage is largely illegible in the scan; the legible parts speak of the divine operation as coming from the divine essence, of the saints crying out, and of creation as something external, which is not made from the essence of the Creator, nor is the created thing wholly unlike the maker. As the Latin rendering has it: ...] Who does not know that anyone who contradicts the Church talks such nonsense, and is as impious as he is ignorant, and would rather that those words do not wound our minds, but keep silent, or that God should be left to create nature, or that he himself should be made by the Theologian... [the remainder of the Greek is illegible in the scan].

units.la: [the Greek remainder is too faint to read reliably] καὶ ταύτης χωρὶς ὑπόστασιν θεωρεῖσθαι, ἀλλ' ἀδιαί-ρέτως αὐτῆς ἀεὶ διαμένον ἐξ ἀϊδίου τε τῇ θεᾷ συν-[illegible, ~20 letters] σωτηρίας. Diuinam essentiam, seu operationem ex diuina essentia esse cum a Patribus id aperte clamantibus audiuerimus, non vt omnia ex Deo, & hanc non alia ratione concipimus, vti illis, qui a nobis dissident, inter alia multa absurda, & hoc quoque videtur: nanque ex Deo, & de rebus creatis dicitur; veruntamen ex essentia Dei de nulla creatura vnquam dictum est; quinimo hoc prorsus prohibetur a Sanctis Patribus. Etenim magnus Basilius; Quod fit, inquit, non ex essentia factoris est. Et diuinus Damascenus; Creatio licet postmodum fuerit, veruntamen non ex essentia Dei. Rursusque: Creatio, & factio extra est, & non ex essentiacreatoris, & factoris, quod creatur, & fit, cum prorsus dissimile sit, fit. Non tamen extra diuinam essentiam, ex diuina essentia esse intelligimus, sicuti illud blaterare, non solum impie, sed ignoranter aduersarijs venit in mentem, (non sit, qui ita insaniat) sed essentialem, & naturalem hanc Dei motionem existentem-, Theologis ita decernentibus, scientes, quasi ex fonte dicimus, diuina essentia progredi, & effundi, & absque ea nunquam intelligi, sed indiuisam ab ea perpetuo perseuerare, & ab æterno simul cum diuina essentia existere, & inseparabiliter unitam esse, quæ nec sæculo, nec temporario, aut locali aliquo interuallo a diuina essentia separari unquam valet: sed absque tempore, & ante sæcula ex ipso procedit, & indiuisibiliter illi inhæret. Præter iam dictos, & supra commemoratos, hæc omnia confirmata sunt, & approbata a Monachis Hagioritanis. Vides? Schismatici docent, aliud notare, esse ex Deo & aliud, esse ex essentia Dei: esse ex Deo sæpe ad creaturas, quæ sunt ad extra, & non sunt eiusdem cum Deo essentiæ: esse ex essentia ad internam, naturalem, & essentialem actionem, & processionem referri: tum enim ex ea progreditur, & effunditur ab æterno inseparabiliter, non temporario, non locali interuallo, ante sæcula, quod ex essentia Dei est. Sed Spiritus a Patribus Græcis dicitur esse ex essentia Filij. Conclude tu cum Schismaticis, quando Catholicos excludis. Et contendes, Ecclesiam Græcam non æque atque Pontificios in processione Spiritus sentire? Spiritum esse ex essentia Filij, tradunt Cyrillus Orat. Prosphonetica ad Imperatorem Theodosium, Secundo libro Thesaurorum sæpius, & Expositione in Ioannem, Epiphanius in Ancyroto, Athanasius in Orat. de incarnata Dei Verbi Oeconomia; & ex Schismaticis Georgius Cyprius in Tomo, Demetrius Chrysolora Dialogo Antirrhetico contra Demetrium Cydonium pro Nilo Theffalonicensi, quorum testimonia habes in Hottingero cap. 18. Et hæc de Dogmate, quid de ditione? Non alia. Idem Schismatici in eodem Tomo. Καὶ ἀεσοπήνας, καὶ οἱ Στρυβουλίτες, ἐ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας καταφρονήσαντες ἔπει. Καὶ ἠσπιάδας, τὸν [?]ενεκεν Βασιλέως ἀποσβᾶς ζῶντ[?] παρ' αὐτῶν, Ταυ[?] τῆς ἀσεβείας τολμῶντι. οἱ δὲ ὑπάσαντο [?] ἐν τῇ ὁμολογίᾳ τῶν [?]ρδίων [?]. ἐν αὐτῇ ἡ ἐποιοῦντο καὶ τὸν Θεσαλονίκης. ἐπειδὴ συναλίζεσθαι ἔλεγον κατ' αὐτῶν ἐν πᾳ τ' ἐκ[?] τῆς Βαρλαὰμ, καὶ Ἀ'χίνδυνον ἀπορρήτως ἐνωάθων. Adducti sunt, qui tumultuabantur, & scindebant Ecclesiam, interrogatique, quam ob causam, Imperatore vitam pie agente, ab ipsis contra pietatem similia auderentur. Illi criminati sunt quandam additionem factam in professione Fidei eorum, qui Præsules ordinantur. Insuper accusabant Thessalonicensem, nanque scandalizari sese dicebant de nonnullis, quæ ille aduersus Barlaamum, & Acindynum scribens dixerat. His se culpa liberans Synodus respondit. Ἐπὶ τούτοις ἡ Θεία Σύνοδος πρὸς τὰ φατὰ ἀρχιεράσιν, φησί, πρὸς τὴν ΘήΘήκλω, ἢ τῆς ὑδὲ ἀρεσκήνη ἀπ καλοῖς δικαίως, ὡς αἰάπηξις ἕζα τῆς ἁγίας, καὶ οἰκυμενικῆς ἐκ- τῆς Σωσόδε, οὐδὲν ἔπεσν ἔσιν, ἡ ἀποκήρυξις Βαρλαὰμ τε, καὶ Ἀκινδύνου. Ἰωὶ οἱ μεμφόμενοι δίκαιοι παῦτες τῆς καὶ ἐπιοσουῦ σωιεῖσιν τῇ τὰ Βαρλαὰμ, ἕ Ἀκινδύνου ἀπηπιεύμενοι. Ad hæc sancta Synodus, ad illam additionem, quam vos æquo animo ferre non posse affirmatis, dicit; immerito eam vocari additionem, tanquam quæ expositio est sanctæ & Oecumenicæ Sextæ Synodi, quæ nihil aliud est quam rerum Barlaami, & Acindyni abdicatio. Eam qui criminantur, manifesto deprehenduntur, etiam illis qui non ita cordati sunt, Barlaami, atque Acindyni res tutari. Horum itaque Schismaticorum decreto, additio, quæ expositio fit, non condemnatur. Nihil ergo concluditur, cum effertur, Græcos ad hæc usque tempora illas particulas in Symbolo non apposuisse, causam esse non consensum cum Latinis, sed reverentia maiorum suorum, & metus anathematismi Ephesini, licet præposteri. Nam si tanta esset reverentia, & metus anathematismi, non addidissent in suis, & postquam addidere, excusassent, additionem illam non esse novum, aut alienum dogma, sed expositionem dogmatis. quod posse absque læsione dogmatis fieri, Synodum Chalcedonensem Patres defendentes adversus eam culculpantes statuerunt: & quod magis est Synodus ipsa Chalcedonenfis . Nilus praeterea schismaticus additionem improbat, eo folum nomine, quod absque conuentu Graecorum consentientium facta fit. Ergo non simpliciter prohibetur additio per Nilum, sed quae facta est non consentientibus Graecis. Sed an ita necessaria fit in Dioecesi saltem Romana ista Graecorum assensio, decernent alij. Ego consensionem urgeo. Parthenij Synodus, cum universalis non fit, fidem parum, aut nullam apud Graecos meretur, nisi in quibus cum alijs Patribus, & Conciliis concordat. Et Parthenius unus est, non praeferendus tot alijs: etsi praeponendus Cyrillo Lucari ob hoc solum, quod processionem ex Filio negat, praeferendus etiam est in alijs, quae ipse cum alijs sua Synodo damnat; & Reformatorum fere omnes, eaeque praecipue opiniones, & haeretica hae-reses una simul exploduntur, & improbantur. Et sic quoque Ecclesia Graeca in quamplurimis accedet ad Pontificiam, recedet a Reformatis, contra insanissimi Hottingeri praecipitem confidentiam. Tu vero testimonia Schismaticorum emendicas, ego tibi ipsius Ecclesiae Graecae dicta apponam, quibus non negabis fidem, existimo. Simon Constantinopolitanus Epistola ad Joannem
units.tr: ...and that it is not to be considered as having subsistence apart from it, but as always remaining indivisibly from it, from eternity, together with the divine ... of salvation. Since we have heard the Fathers openly proclaiming that the divine essence, or the operation from the divine essence, is so, we do not conceive it in the way that those who dissent from us do, and among their many absurdities this also appears. For "from God" is said of created things, but "from the essence of God" has never been said of any creature; indeed the holy Fathers absolutely forbid it. For the great Basil says: "What is made is not from the essence of the maker." And the divine Damascene: "Creation, though it came into being afterwards, is not from the essence of God." And again: "Creation and making are outside God, and not from the essence of the creator and maker; what is created and made is entirely unlike him." Yet we do not understand that which is outside the divine essence to be from the divine essence, as that babbling, which has come into the minds of our opponents not only impiously but also ignorantly (let no one be so mad), would have it. Rather, the theologians decree this essential and natural motion of God to exist, knowing that we speak of the divine essence as proceeding and flowing out, as from a fountain, and that it is never understood apart from it, but remains perpetually undivided from it, and from eternity exists together with the divine essence and is inseparably united to it. It can never be separated from the divine essence by any interval of time, place or any other kind of distance; but without time, and before the ages, it proceeds from him and cleaves to him indivisibly. Besides the authorities already named and cited above, all these things have been confirmed and approved by the Monks of Hagion Oros. Do you see? The schismatics teach that "to be from God" signifies one thing and "to be from the essence of God" another: "to be from God" often refers to creatures, which are outside God and are not of the same essence as God; "to be from the essence" refers to the internal, natural and essential action and procession, for from it something proceeds and flows out from eternity, inseparably, not by any temporal or local interval, before the ages, and this is from the essence of God. But the Spirit is said by the Greek Fathers to be from the essence of the Son. Conclude with the schismatics, then, since you exclude the Catholics. And will you contend that the Greek Church does not think the same as the Papists about the procession of the Spirit? That the Spirit is from the essence of the Son is taught by Cyril in his Prosphonetic Oration to the Emperor Theodosius, in the second book of his Thesaurus very often, and in his Exposition on John; by Epiphanius in the Ancoratus; by Athanasius in his Oration on the Incarnate Economy of the Word of God; and among the schismatics by George of Cyprus in his Tome, and by Demetrius Chrysoloras in his Antirrhetic Dialogue against Demetrius Cydones on behalf of Nilus of Thessalonica. You have their testimonies in Hottinger, chapter 18. And this is concerning doctrine; what of discipline? Nothing different. The same schismatics, in the same Tome, say: "And Aesopenas, and the Strybulites, who despised the Church..." and "Ishpiadas, on account of the Emperor..., having been ... by them, dared such impiety..." And they [the Synod] ... in the confession of the hearts ... in it they also made [accusations] against the Thessalonian, since they said that they were being gathered together against them... of Barlaam, and Acindynus, secretly ... [the Greek here is too corrupt to render exactly]. "Those who were disturbing things and rending the Church were brought forward and asked why, while the Emperor lived piously, similar things were dared against piety by them." They charged that a certain addition had been made to the profession of faith of those who are ordained bishops. Moreover they accused the Thessalonian, for they said they were scandalized by some things he had written against Barlaam and Acindynus. Freeing himself from this fault, the Synod answered: "To these things the holy Synod, to the additions, which you affirm you cannot bear with equanimity, says: it is unjustly called an addition, since it is an explanation of the holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod, which is nothing other than the renunciation of the teachings of Barlaam and Acindynus. Those who accuse it are manifestly shown to be defending the views of Barlaam and Acindynus, even if they are not so sound in mind." Therefore by the decree of these schismatics, the addition, which is made as an explanation, is not condemned. Nothing is concluded, then, when it is put forward that the Greeks until these times did not insert those particles into the Creed, and that the cause was not agreement with the Latins but reverence for their ancestors and fear of the Anathematism of Ephesus, though that was misguided. For if there were such reverence and fear of the anathematism, they would not have added it in their own works, and after adding it, they would have excused the addition, saying that it was not a new or foreign dogma but an explanation of the dogma, which can be made without injury to the dogma: the Fathers defending the Council of Chalcedon against those who blamed it so decided, and, what is more, the Council of Chalcedon itself. Moreover the schismatic Nilus disapproves of the addition on this ground alone, that it was made without the agreement of the consenting Greeks. So it is not simply the addition that is forbidden by Nilus, but the addition that was made without the consent of the Greeks. But whether such assent of the Greeks is so necessary, at least in the Roman diocese, let others decide. I insist on consent. The Synod of Parthenius, since it is not universal, deserves little or no faith among the Greeks, except where it agrees with other Fathers and Councils. And Parthenius is one man, not to be preferred to so many others; though he is to be preferred to Cyril Lucaris on this alone, that he denies the procession from the Son, he is not to be preferred in other matters which he himself, with his Synod, condemns. And almost all the Reformed, and especially their opinions and heretical heresies, are at once exploded and rejected together. And thus also the Greek Church will in very many things draw near to the Papist, and withdraw from the Reformed, contrary to the headlong confidence of the most insane Hottinger. But you beg for the testimonies of schismatics; I will set before you the sayings of the Greek Church itself, which I think you will not deny to be trustworthy. Simon of Constantinople, letter to John.

units.la: Αἷς οἰκουμενικῆς ἀρχῆς Σωσόβις ἡ ὀρθοδοξότατος τῆς Γραικῶν Ἐκκλησίας ἐν ἅπασιν ἀκολουθήσασα δόγμα τῆς Θείων μάλιστα ποιητὴς τ' καλλιώνταν [?] ὡραϊσάντων αὐτῷ Θεοῖς ἑαυτῆς μεταφράσματα, τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον αἰνέκα [?] μέχρι τῆς σήμερον· ἀλλ' ἡμῖν ἐκ τῆς ἐν παρρησίᾳ ζῶσα τῆς φωνῆς Θεολογεῖ ἐκπορεύεσθαι, ὡς λέγει Φώτιος ὁ Βεκλᾶς, ὁ τότε Ἰδιάσκαλος Θεοδώρητος. Καὶ γὰρ ἡ αὐτὴ εἰς ἀκραφνῆ πανέσχασιν τῆς Ἰδίας φυσικῶς ὕπαρξιν τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι ἐκπορεύσεως ἐν μὲν τῇ ἑκτῇ φωνῇ τῷ κανόνι τῆς δόντος ἐβλασφήμησε τῆς Θεοῖς ἱερὸν, Σπλαγχνων Ἰωάννου, ἐν βιβλίῳ Τεωσδίῳ τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἀποτελοῦμεν, ἐπὶ τὸ ῥῆμα μελωδοῦσα Θεολογεῖ.
units.tr: Which the most orthodox Church of the Greeks, holding to the teaching of the ecumenical authority in all things, and, following the divine (chiefly the Fathers) and the translations made for it by its own, has confessed the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Son up to the present day; but, living among us in freedom of speech, it theologizes that he proceeds from the mouth, as Photius the Bekkos says, who was then the teacher Theodoretus. For the same [Church], in the pure and clear profession of its natural existence of the procession of the Holy Spirit, in the sixth anathema of the canon of the holy council, blasphemed the holy Spirit... and in the book of Theodoret says the same Holy Spirit is from the Son [ἐκπορεύεσθαι], singing the word again, theologizes.

units.la: Τ'Ἡμεῖς ἡμᾶς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, μετέχουσα τῆς σῆς ἀπερ[?]ζόμενον ἀγιότητος, καὶ φωτὸς ἀνεπέρας καὶ Θέας ζωῆς, ἐκ τῆς ὠδηλεύτου δῆλος ὑπάρχει ἐκ προκηρύξεως.
units.tr: We, the Holy Spirit participating in your holiness, the one who is from the Son and is the light of unapproachable life and vision, is clearly manifest from the proclamation...

units.la: οὐ γὰρ πολαμὸς Θεότητι ἐκ τῆς παῤῥῆς δὲ ἡ ἐκπορεύομενον. ἐν δὲ πῆ ἔχων ἡ Ὀκτωήχη ἐκ τὸν Σωτῆρα ἡμῶν μελπουζα ἔτι ἐπὶ λέγει. Ἐ' ἐν ἡμῖν ἀναταίχωσιν φρέσβυ τλὸ ἐ πιχᾶς, Χεισὲ, ταύτης τὰς ἐντολὰς ἔλεω νόμοις ὑμῖν πνεῦμα μεγαδοσικὸν ἀγαθότητος, ἐκ παῤῥός δὲ σοῦ φερεχόμενον. Καὶ ταῦτα ἡ αὐτὴ δὲ τῆ Θεῷ Ἰωάννη τῆ Δαμασκηνῷ.
units.tr: For the Spirit is not from the Son by nature, but proceeds from the Father. In the Octoechos, the hymn addressed to our Saviour, the author sings again: "Lord, Christ, you who send us the Spirit of goodness, the Spirit who proceeds from the Father." These are the words of John Damascene, the same author.

units.la: Δὲ δὲ τῇ Θεοτόκῳ Μεταφράσῃ Συμεὼν ἐν τῷ φερομένῳ, τὲ ἐν τῇ ἕκτῃ ἡμέρᾳ τὸ κατ' αὐτὸ ταῖς μὲν ὡς παντὸς ἀνόμου [illegible, ~9 letters] ἀπαγγέλματος τὸ μαρτυρίας τὸ ἐν ἀχέιοις Διαγνῶσι
units.tr: In the Metaphrastes' Life of the Mother of God, Symeon, in the work attributed to him, says on the sixth day, with respect to the same matter, that the testimony of the Spirit in the (?) ... [the text here is too corrupt to be recovered].

units.la: τῷ Ἀρεοπαγίτῃ ὑπὸ πως δολμοτίζει ἐθὴ λέξεως[?].
units.tr: Dionysius the Areopagite, in some way, (?) ... [the text here is too corrupt to be recovered].

units.la: Πάλαι μὲν ἐν τύποις ὧ τῆς πίστεως, καὶ αἰνιγμα-τα, καὶ τὸ τῆς ἀληθείας φέγγος τῆς σκιᾶς νέφη σωσεκαλύπτετο[?]. ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ μέγα τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῖν ἐμφανισμάτων μυστήριον, καὶ ὁ πλάζας τὰς μόνας ταῖς καρδίας ἡμῶν, παρὰ τῆς οἰκείας αὐτοῦ ἡμᾶς οἴκτῳ χρηστότητι ἀναμαρτήτως[?], γάρ ἡμῖν τὰ ἄλλα πε ὑπηλθεν ὅλα ἢ ἀνθρωπίνης ἐξ ἀσθενέ-ας, ἵνα ἐγὼ τὸν θεὸν τῷ φωτὶ ἀπολάβω δίχῇ[?], ἐ πλεῖ τὸν δὲ σαυτοῦ θάνατον καζακείνῃ[?].
units.tr: In former times, in the types of faith, in riddles, and in the shadows, the light of truth was veiled by clouds. But at the great mystery of our salvation, now made manifest, the one who has shaped our hearts, out of his own kindness and goodness, took upon himself our other human weaknesses, so that ... the light of the Father, and ... death.

units.la: Καὶ ἵνα μὴ τὰ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον λέγω, πολλὰ τὰ ἐν μίσῳ ἢ οἰκονομίας αὐτοῦ μυστήρια πέρας τὰ τῆς σωματικῆς ἐνδημίας δίχει[?].
units.tr: And not to speak of each point separately: many mysteries of his dispensation, in the midst of which the limits of his bodily sojourn ... .

units.la: Τὰ δὲ τὰ πνεύματος ἀρχῇ, καὶ ὡς ἑαυτὸν ὁ ἡμῶς Χριστὸς ἀφέρει, ἐ φως τὸν παζικὸν ἐπάνῃ θεόγονον, ἐ τὸ ἐκπορεδόμενον αὐτὸ πνεῦμα ὅπι τὸ τῆς ἀπίστων ἰδιῶν καταπέμ-πει τοῖς μαθηταῖς ὁδηγίαν[?].
units.tr: Concerning the beginning of the Spirit, and how Christ our Lord himself sent him forth, not the ... God-begotten light, but the Spirit who proceeds from him, he sends to his disciples as a guide (?) ... .

units.la: Δ᾽ ἐ ἐ ὁ μακάριος Παῦλος ὅπι ἡ σκιᾶς ἐχθεχωρήθη ὡς τὸ τῆς ἀλήθειας[?].
units.tr: But the blessed Paul also says that the shadow has given way to the truth.

units.la: Εἰ γὰρ ὁ Σωτὴρ ἡμῖν μὴ ὡς ἐκπορευόμενον αὐτὸ τὸ πνεῦμα ὅπι τὸ τῆς ἀπίστων ἰδιῶν ὁδηγίαν αὐτὸ καταπέμψει τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ μαθηταῖς, ἀλλ᾽ αὐ-τὸς πῶς παρέξει, ὥσπερ πινὲς δήξας βιάζονται, παρ-εχηγκλυκοί τε τῷ ἴδιῷ ἱερῷ θεολογίαν τῆς θεΐας Μεταθέσεως, ἐ δολματίζοντες, ὡς ἔδηλον, ἐξ ὧν αἰσθήτως λέγουσιν, ὡς τὸ ἡμῶν παῖδος ἐκπέμπει ὡς συμφυΐς ἐκείνῳ, ἐ ὁμοούσιον, ὅτι ὡς ἐκπορευόμενον ἐκεῖθεν φυσικῶς, ταῦτῃ ἀπεσαλῇ, ἕω δὲ ἡ ἀμμουσιω, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἱπερφυεῖς τε, ἐ ὑπαχρέιον, ὅτι ἡχ ὡς ἐκεῖνο ἐκπορευόμενον καθὼ-πε[?]
units.tr: For if the Saviour did not send the Spirit to his own disciples as proceeding from himself, as a guide, but himself gave him as some men, forcing their words, reshape the theology of the divine mission, (...) not daring, as is clear from what they say, that the Son sends the Spirit as one who is by nature of the same substance with the Father; not consubstantial, but as one who proceeds from the Father naturally, and is sent by him ... not as one who is not of the same substance, but as one who is above nature and not subordinate ... (?) ...

units.la: περὶ δὲ τὸ παχὺς, ἀλλ' ἐξωθεν ἡ οὐσίας αὐτῆ, καθάπερ δὲ τὰς δικαιοσύνας ὑποστελλόμενα ἐπόθεν λέγει, τῆς ψυχικῆς πνεύματος, ἔσχ τὸ παντάπασιν ὑβρισ-βέσθαι, δὲ βλάσφημον. ἀλλ' ὅπ ἡ̈χ ἡ̈τως, ἀλλ' ἐκεῖθεν ὡς ἐξ οἰκείας φωτὸς ἡ ἀληθείας αὐτοῦ φύσεως φυσικῶς τι, δ' ἀμείσως ἐκφαγόμενον, παρ' αὐτοῦ τῆς ποιήματος πέμπτῃ), [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐν μιᾷ τῇ ἐβδόμῃ ὡδῇ τὸ κανόν[?] τὰ ἁγία Ἰωαννης τῇ θεολόγῳ, τὸ φαλλομένῳ ἐν τῇ οὐρανῷ ἡμέρᾳ, τὰ Μαΐα μικρὸς ἔφεις εἰμὶ, Θεὸς συγκαταβαίνειν, ἐφεὶς αὐτὸν τὸν μονογενῆ Θεὸν λόγον τῆς παχὺς ἀδελφὰ ὑπαυτίως θεολογεῖ. Τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον παχὺς αἰ ἀρχῆς ἐκπορευόμενον, καὶ ἐκ σὲ ἀμεί-σως ἐκλάμψαν μονογενὴς λόγῳ Θεῦ τοῖς Ἀπο-στόλοις κραυγάζειν αἰνήγειλε, ὁ τὴν πατέρων Θεὸς ἀὐτόργητος ἑ· ἐν ᾗ μιᾷ τῇ μυστικῶν ἀρχῶν τῆς Θεῖας λειτουργίας τὸ ἐν ἁγίοις μεγάλῳ Βασιλείᾳ πρὸς Θεὸν τὸν πατέρα ἀποτελούμενον, ὅπως ἀφεὶ ἐιρηνῆς, ἑ ἐκ τὸ φωτὸς τῆς ἀληθινῆς ἡλαδὴ τῆς ἐκφανσεως τὸ ἁγίᾳ πνεύματος κῇ ῥῆμα ἀνέξειν, Ἀ ἀρχῆς, ἀξιαται, ἀκαταλήπτε ὁ πατὴρ τῆς κυρίᾳ ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, τῷ μεγάλῳ Θεῷ, καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, ὅς ἐστιν εἰκὼν ἑ τῆς ἀγαθότητος, σφραγὶς ἰσότυπος, ἐν ἐωυτῷ δύκινος σε τὸν πατέρα, λόγος ζῶν, Θεὸς ἀληθινὸς, ἡ περὶ αἰώνων σοφία, ζωὴ, ἁγιασμὸς, δύναμις, τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινὸν, παρ' οὗ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐξεφάνη, τὸ ἑ ἀληθείας πνεῦμα, τὸ ἑ υἱοθεσίας χάρισμα, ὁ ἀρραβὼν ἑ μελλούσης κληρονομίας. καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. καὶ ὥσει ταῦτα σκέπτεσθ[?]
units.tr: But concerning the thick (?) and external substance itself, just as they shrink from the righteousness (?) of the Spirit, they dare to say that it is wholly outrageous and blasphemous. But he does not come thus, rather he comes from the Father as from his own light, and naturally, and comes forth from him without intermediary, as the Spirit of his truth and nature, sent by the Son. In the seventh ode of the canon, sung on the holy day of Pentecost, John the Theologian (?) ... Whence the Only-begotten Word of God, who in the Father's bosom ... so-called "I am a little one", the God who condescends, as to the Son, the Only-begotten God, the Word of God, ... theologizes: The Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father, and shines forth from the Son without intermediary, the Only-begotten Son of God proclaimed to the Apostles. ... In the first of the mystical prayers of the divine liturgy, the great Basil, in the Saints' service, prays to God the Father, that the Holy Spirit may be sent forth from the Son, ... the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the great God and our Saviour, who is the image of his goodness, the exact seal, who in himself shows forth the Father, the living Word, true God, the wisdom of the ages, life, sanctification, power, the true light, from whom the Holy Spirit was made manifest, the Spirit of truth, the gift of sonship, the pledge of the inheritance to come. And so forth. And as they consider these things ...

units.la: Ff
units.tr: Ff

units.la: ὅπ ὁ Σωτὴρ ἡμῶν Θεάνθρωπος ὢν, καὶ ὁ Θεὸς λόγος ὁ αὐτὸς ἐξ οἰκίας φωτὸς ἡ ὑπερφυῦς μακαρίας αὐτοῦ φύσεως; ἐκφαίνων φυσικῶς κατ' ἰδίαν ὕπαρξιν τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, καὶ ὃ ἀδιά[?]ον τι ὡς ἐκ φωτὸς φαῦλ' τὴν· ἐκφαίνεσθαι μὴ φυσικῶς τι, καὶ ἀμεί-σως δ' αἰξαντλήτως ἐνδὲν πηγάζεσθαι, ὡς ἐκείνῳ συνυπάρχοντ τι, δ συγχρόνον.
units.tr: Our Saviour, being God-man, and the same God the Word, from the light of his own ineffable and blessed nature, naturally manifests the Holy Spirit according to his own subsistence; and he does not shine forth naturally from some other light, nor is he poured out without intermediary and inexhaustibly from some other source, as a co-existing thing, with him, co-eternal.

units.la: Καὶ καὶ δὲ ἀληθῶς αὐ-θεροπῶν ὁ αὐτὸς τῷ Θεῷ ὑποχωρῶ τῷ τοιοῦδε ἀγίῳ πνεύματος εἰς ζωῆς φωτὸς πολυξόπως ἐφανέρωσε τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ μαθηταῖς, ἢ ἐλλογιμώς ἢ, ὡς ἕκας τὴν καθ' ἡμᾶς ἀγίων, ὅτι ἀ φιλῶς αὐθεντικῶς ὁ αὐτὸς, ἀλλὰ Θεὸς λόγος σαρκωθεὶς ὢν θεοπρεπῶς, ὡς δὲ οἰκίας φωτὸς ἢ ὑπερφυῆς αὐτοῦ θεότητος πηγάζων αὐτὸ, ἡμῶν ἐκφαίνων αὐτὸ φυσικῶς. ἅπερ ἀμφότερα δηλῇ ἡ, φαίνω, φωτή. φαίνω γὰρ τὸ λάμπω φασί, καὶ Φαίνω τὸ φανερῶ. Διὸ καὶ ὁ Θεολόγος Γεννήσεις ἐν τῇ πνεύματος λόγῳ.
units.tr: And indeed, the same one, truly becoming man, submitting himself to God, showed the Holy Spirit to his disciples in the form of the light of life, in many ways, either in speech or in deed, as the Holy Fathers say, that the same one, not by himself but as God the Word made flesh, divinely, and from the light of his own ineffable divinity, causes the Spirit to flow and naturally manifests him to us. Both of these things the Greek word "phaino" signifies: for "phaino" is said to mean "shine", and "phaino" to mean "make manifest". Therefore also the Theologian (Gregory) speaks of the Spirit as begotten... [the rest is corrupt].

units.la: Τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα φησὶ τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἢ μέρος δηλήμα τὴν τῆς ἀληθείας ἀποστόλων ἀνάμεσον, ἐν ἀρχῇ τῆς Εὐαγγελίου μὴ τὸ πάθος, μὴ τῶν αὐτοῦ ὁδὸν ταῖς ἀποστολαῖς ἐπιπλοῦν, ἐμφυσῶ-μενον, ἐν γλώσσης πυρέναις φαινόμενον, καὶ ὡς Ἰησοῦ καὶ ὀλίγον ἐκφαίνει), αὐτὴ τῆς, ὡς ἀληθὲς Σωτῆρος ἐκφαίνει). Καζαλίγον ἡ τῇ τῆς ἀληθείας ἀληθινὸν ἁμαρτωλόν ἀναμιξάμενον.
units.tr: The same Spirit, as the Gospel says, appeared to the disciples, as a part of the truth, breathed upon the apostles at the beginning of the Gospel ... in the form of tongues of fire, and as Jesus, shining a little, ... as the true Saviour shines forth. Thus, in the light of the truth, the true (?) ...

units.la: Ὅπ ἐλαχίστως καὶ δίζων οἱ αὐτὰ μαθηταὶ οἷ π ... Πεντηκοστῆς λόγῳ, ἐν εἰ δοξασθῆναι Χριστὸν πρὸς πάθος, μὴ τὸ δοξασθῆναι τῇ ἀναστάσει, μὴ τῶν εἰς ἐρῆμος ἀναβαῖνον, ἢ ἀπο-καταῖ-
units.tr: That the disciples (?) ... at the feast of Pentecost, ... Christ ... to be glorified by the passion, not to be glorified by the resurrection, not to ascend into the desert, or to ... [corrupt].

units.la: κατάσαιν, ἤ ὅπ χρὴ λέγειν. Δηλοῖ ἡ πρώτη τῆς γύσεων, καὶ ἡ τῆς πνευμάτων κάθαρσις, ἐκ αὐτοῦ πνεύματος δηλαδὴ ψυχωδύη[?], ἐ τὸ μὴ τῶν οἰκο-νομίαν ἐμφύσημα ζαφῶς ὃν ἔμπνευσις ἀφοτέρα[?], ἡ-χου ζαφῶς ὡν ἀπέκοισμα ἐμπνεύσεως ἀφοτάτῳ τῷ πνεύματος. καὶ ὁ νῦν μερισμὸς τῶν πνεύων γλωσσῶν, ὢ καὶ παυγνείζομεν, ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν θεῖον ἀμυθρῶς, τὸ δὲ ἀδύτερον ἐκπυπώτερον, τὸ δὲ νῦν, ἡ χου τῶν πνεύων γλωσσῶν, τγεώτερον, ὡς ὡ τῷ Σωτῆρῳ ἡμῶν, δηλονότι κ̣ῃ φύσιν ἑαυτὸν ὡς ἐπηγγείλατο τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἐκπεμπό-μενον. ὅθεν ἡ ὕστερὸς τῆς Γραικῶν Ἐκκλησία ἐν ἐνὶ ζοπαιείῳ τῆς ἀὲὶ τὲ ἀγίῳ πνεύματος κανόνων ὡς ἐξ ἀὐτὸν τὸν Σωτῆρα ἡμῶν μελωδῆσαι ἐπὶ μίλτῳ[?].
units.tr: The first Pentecost of the nations shows the purification of the spirits, of the spirit itself, namely, that it is not an inspiration in the dispensation, but clearly a breathing forth from the Spirit's own inspiration. And the present division of tongues (which we also call wonderful), the one divine and marvellous, the other more ..., the present division of tongues being more ..., as our Saviour himself promised, namely that he himself would send him forth from his own nature to the disciples. Whence the Greek Church, in one of its hymns about the Holy Spirit, sings from the Saviour himself, ... the Spirit's mission, in the chant ...

units.la: Ἀνὰξ ἀνάκτων, οἱ ὃς ἐξ οἶου μόνος, λόγῳ ὡς ψυθὼν παξὸς ἐξ αἰμάτε, Ἰσοσδεύες σου πνεῦμα τῆς Ἀποστόλοις, Νημερτὴς ἐξέπεμψας ὡς ἐξερχόμενος, ἀπὸ τὸ, νημερτὴς, ὅ ὄντως, καὶ φύσει καὶ ἀληθεία τὸ ἰσοσδενὲς σου πνεῦμα τῆς Ἀποστόλοις κατ᾽ ἰδίαν ὑπόχεσιν ἐξ ἑαυτὸν ἐπεμψας, ὡς ὁ Θεοπέσιος Πέτρος δημηγορῶν ἐν τῆς Πεντήκοστῆς ἡμέρας ἱδῶν ἀκούειν λέγων, Ἐξ ἑαυτὸς ἔχεις τὸ ὑμᾶς ἀκοῦσαι καὶ βλέπειν. αὐτὸ γὰρ ὅτι τὸ ἐξέχεις καὶ ὑμῶν ἐξωθεν, ὡς νοῶν διδωσὶν, ὃς ὧν λέγει ὁ Βαλσαμείας Θεοφύλαχτος. ὅθεν ἡ Ἐκκλησία ἐν ἐνὶ τῷ τοῦ Πεντηκοστῆς Ἀπολυτικῷ αὐτῆς πρὸς ἐναρχῇ ταῦθε μείας ἀληθείας ὑπῶσι τῷ λαῷ ἐκφωνεῖ. Ὁ ἐν ἀδῇ πνεύων γλωσσῶν καὶ ἐπέμψας ἐπὶ ἐξ αὐτ ἀγίας σου Ἀποστόλε, καὶ μαθητὰς τὸ πνεῦπνεῦμά σου τὸ ἅγιον Χριστὸς ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς; ἡμῖν τὰς προσβάσεις [?] παναχράντου μητρός σου. Καὶ τὰ λοιπά. ἐν ἕδρᾳ [?] Σωτὴρ ἡμῶν [?] τῆς ἑαυτοῦ μαθητὰς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, ὡς ἐταῖς [?] θεολογεῖ ἡ ἀεὶ ὀρθόδοξος [?] ἐν ἅπασιν ἐκκλησίαις τῆς Γραικῶν Ἐκκλησίας, ἵνα μάθοιμεν ὅτι ἐκ ἑτέρως ἐκ ἑαυτοῦ πέμπει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, ἢ ὡς ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου ἀπὸ τῆς φύσεως αὐτοῦ τὴν, καὶ τῷ παρῳδῷ [?] ἀναλόγως, οὐδὲ φῶς ἐπέφθην [?] πέμπειν [?] ἀκολουθίᾳ φυσικῆς πέμψεως, ἧς ἐκ ἐν τῇ ζωῇ νομίζεται, ἢ ὡς πῦρ ἐκ πυρὸς [?] τὸ ἀδόμενον, ταῦτα ἐκ ζωαῖς ἐκκλησίας αὐτὴ τὸ πιστὸν ἁγίῳ πνεύματι· πῦρ ἐκ πυρὸς θεοῦ, καὶ ζῶ θεόφων [?] ἐκ παιδὸς, καὶ ὑιὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, φησὶν ὁ τῆς Ἀλεξανδρέων ποιμὴν, ὁ μέγας Κύριλλος ἐν τῇ τριακοστῇ πέμπτῃ κεφαλαίῳ τῶν Θησαυρῶν, ἕ ὅτι τῆλωμα, ἐκ τῆς ἀσίας παιδὸς, καὶ ὑιὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον. καὶ ἐμφύτως καὶ ἐκ ὑιὸς, καὶ ἐκ τῆς ὑιὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον. ἕ μόνον ὁ αὐτὸς, ἀλλὰ ἐ ὁμῷ ἡ ἀπαζα διάλεκτον σύλλογον τῆς Θεῶν διδασκάλων τ Ἐκκλησίας, καὶ οἱ αὐτῆς ἅγιοι ποιοῦσι, ὡς ἐν τῷ σεφῷ τῷ πρὸς τὸ σὸν ἀμωσωλίω ἡμετέρῳ Συνταγμα σαφῶς ἐξ τῆς ἱερῶν αὐτῶν σιγῇ μάτων διδάσκειν [?] ἐξαπουσίως θεολογοῦσιν.
units.tr: O King of kings, who alone from the Father's bosom ... and from the Father, the Spirit whom you send to the Apostles, the Unerring one (nemertes), who came forth ... from "nemertes", which truly and by nature and in truth, your co-equal Spirit sent to the Apostles according to his own subsistence from himself, as the divine Peter, preaching on the day of Pentecost, said, "You have from yourselves that you hear and see". For "from yourselves" is said to signify that you have it from outside, as Theophylact the Bulgarian says. Whence the Church, in its Pentecost apolytikion, proclaims to the people at the beginning of the feast ... "O Christ, true God, you who sent the Spirit to your holy apostles, and the Holy Spirit to your disciples ..." And the Greek Church, always orthodox, theologizes in all its churches that the Saviour sends the Holy Spirit to his disciples from himself, so that we may learn that the Holy Spirit is sent from himself and not otherwise than from the nature of the Father. Nor is it like light sent from light, by a natural sending, which is thought to exist in life, nor like fire kindled from fire; so the Church teaches. ... "Fire from fire, God from God, and life from life, and the Holy Spirit is the Son's," says Cyril, the great shepherd of Alexandria, in the thirty-fifth chapter of the Thesaurus, where he says that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, and is in the Son, and proceeds from the Son. Not only does he say this, but the whole company of the divine teachers of the Church, and its holy ones, say the same, as in the Synodal Tome, which our synod sets forth, they clearly teach from their holy writings and, by no means silently, speak of God.

units.la: Quas vniuersales sanctas Synodos rectis dogmatibus quam maxime addicta Graecorum Ecclesia in omnibus secuta per diuinos potissimum Poëtas, qui eam adornarunt, & & per quam speciosam reddiderunt suis diuinis Poëmatibus, Spiritum sanctum iam dudum, & ad hunc diem per Filium, & ex Filio publicè, & confidenter apertis verbis fatetur procedere, & non ex solo Patre, vt Photius Beclas, illiusque magister Theodoretus asserunt: Nanque ipsa in claram affirmationem per Filium secundum propriam exi-stentiam ex Patre Spiritus sancti processionem in septima secunda hebdomadis Canonis Ode, quæ concinnitur ad Hirmum, Interiorum Ionan, modulatur; in libro Triodio nuncupato ad Spiritum sanctum sermone conuerso, hunc in modum ipsissimis verbis concineus decernit; Veni ad nos Spiritus sancte, tua sanctitatis nos participes faciens, & luminis nunquam occidentis, & diuinæ vitæ & odoratissimæ distributionis. Tu siquidem es fluuius Deitatis ex Patre per Filium procedens. In tertio vero tono Octoëchi ad Saluatorem nostrum canens, sic effatur; Posuisti nobis legatum, quam non pudet, tuam genitricem Christe: huius supplicationibus propitium tribue nobis Spiritum communicatiuum bonitatis ex Patre per te progredientem. Et hæc eadem ipsa per Ioannem Damascenum: Sed per diuinissimum Simeonem Metaphrastem in prooemio Lectionis Martyrij sancti Dionysij Areopagitæ, quæ legitur tertio Octobris die, hisce verbis decernit; Antiquitus quidem res fidei in figuris erant, & ænigmatibus, & veritatis lumen umbra nebula occultabantur, cum vero magnum nostræ salutis mysterium absolutum est, & qui corda nostra creauerat propria bonitatis circa nos misericordia absque peccato, uti nos factus est, aliaque subiyt, quæ humanæ infirmitatis sunt, ut ego pristinam nobilitatem recuperarem, tandemque morte per crucem multatur. & ne singula persequar, quæ in sua œconomia medio peregit, tandem, quæ corporei descessus sunt, subiyt, & quæ Spiritus sunt, initium capiunt, & in cælos meus Christus transmigrat, & ad paternum solium reuertitur, & procedentem ab ipso Spiritum in infidelium gentilium ducem ablegat, per quem beatus Paulus ex umbra ad veritatem manuductus est. Etenim si Saluator, non ut ab ipso procedentem Spiritum infidelibus gentilibus ducem prabuisset suis discipulis, non uti Pater, quemadmodum nonnulli demonstrare nituntur, male hanc sacram Theologiam diuini Metaphrasta interpretantes, & decernentes, ut planum est, ex iis quæ inconsideratè effutiunt, a Patre quidem mitti, uti illi connaturalem, & confubstantialem, tanquam qui ex eo procedat naturaliter, hoc est mittatur: a Filio vero alio modo, uti alienæ naturæ, & subditum, quod non tanquam ex ipso procedens, sicuti ex Patre, sed extra essentiam eius, quemadmodum, & qui mittuntur Spiritus a Deo in ministerium spiritus; quod est prorsus impium blasphemumque. At hoc non ita se habet, Apparens siquidem ex Filio, uti ex proprio lumine diuina illius natura naturaliter & induisse ex ipso mittitur ad creaturas. Hocque manifestum est ex iis, quae eadem Ecclesia in septima Ode Canonis in S. Ioannem Theologum, qui die octauo mensis Maij canitur ad Hirmum Dei condescensionem[?], ad ipsum Unigenitum Deum Verbum Patris concinens, ita decernit: Spiritus sanctus ex Patre absque principio procedens, & ex te induisse elucens, Unigenitum Verbum Dei Apostolis clamare denunciauit, Patrum Deus benedictus es. Et in una mystica oratione diuinae Missae sancti magni Basilii ad Deum Patrem orationem convertens hunc in modum de iam dicta ex lumine vero, Filio nempe, apparitione Spiritus sancti haec ad verbum edisserit: Absque principio, invisibilis, incomprehensibilis Pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, magni Dei, & Salvatoris nostri, qui est imago tuae bonitatis, sigillum aequale, in se ipso te Patrem ostendens, Verbum viuens, Deus verus, ante secula sapientia, vita, sanctificatio, virtus, lumen verum, ex quo Spiritus sanctus apparuit, veritatis Spiritus, adoptionis donum, futura hereditatis arrhabo. &c. Considerandum porro est in his, quod Salvator noster, Deus atque homo existens, uti Deus Verbum ipse ex proprio lumine supernaturalis, beatæque suæ naturæ emittit naturaliter secundum propriam existentiam Spiritum sanctum. Nanque haud fieri potest, vt aliquid ex lumine alicuius appareat, & non naturaliter, & indiuise, & inexhauste inde effundatur, & tanquam illi coëxistens, & coœuum, & vti verus homo hic idem diuinam præeminentiam huius sancti Spiritus viua voce multimode reuelauit suis discipulis, sed non seruili modo, vti quicunque ex nostris sanctus, quod non purus homo erat ipse, sed Deus Verbum incarnatum diuino quodam modo, vti ex proprio lumine superdiuinæ suæ Deitatis effundens illum, vt ex fonte, promens nempe illum naturaliter. quæ duo vox φαίνω significat, φαίνω siquidem eluceo notat, & reuelo. Quapropter & Theologus Gregorius Oratione de Spiritu, Idem Spiritus, ait, ad Apostolos, ad Discipulos quoq; sigillatim se confert ad excipientium videlicet captum, modulumque sese impertiens, nimirum in Euangelij principio virtutes perficiens, post Christi passionem infusflatus, post ascensum in igneis linguis apparens, quod idem est atque a Saluatore promittitur, sed paulatim recipientium facultati commensuratus. Quin etiam ab ipso Iesu paulatim declaratur, vt ipse quoq; coperiens, Quod in Christi Discipulis ijsque [?] triфariam, prout ipsorum captus ferebat, tribus temporibus, ut ipse ait Oratione de Pentecoste, antequam Christus per passionem glorificatus esset, postquam per resurrectionem glorificatus fuit, & denique post eius ad Coelos Ascensionem, sive restitutionem, sive quocunque alio nomine res ea sit appellanda. Haec autem perspicue ostendit tum prima illa morborum, Spirituumque depulsio, quae scilicet non absque Spiritus numine fiebat, tum illa insufflatio, quae divinioris procul dubio inspirationis speciem habebat, tum postremo praesens ignearum linguarum divisio, quarum primo quidem obscure, secundo expressius, nunc vero perfectius, uti e Salvatore nostro, secundum naturam, nempe, de Coelo, sicut promiserat, missus Discipulis. Hinc pia Gracorum Ecclesia in uno Tropario Canonum in Spiritum sanctum ad ipsum Salvatorem nostrum concinens, ita canit, Rex regum, unus ex uno solus, manens ex Patre absque causa, aequalem tuum virtute Spiritum Apostolis, uti de illis bene meritus, quasi diceret; vere, & re ipsa, & natura, & veritate aequalem tuum virtute Spiritum Apostolis uti promiseras ex temetipso misisti, uti & divinus Petrus concione habita ad Iudaeos in Actis dicendo contendebat; ex semetipso effudit hunc, quem vos auditis, & videtis: id enim notat, illud, effudit; & non extrinsecus, ut dant intelligere dicta Bulgaria Theophylacti. Hinc
units.tr: The Greek Church, most firmly devoted to the sound doctrines of those universal holy Synods, follows them in all things, chiefly through the divine poets who adorned it and made it so splendid with their divine poems. It openly and confidently confesses in plain words that the Holy Spirit has long proceeded, and still proceeds to this day, through the Son and from the Son, and not from the Father alone, as Photius, Beclas, and his teacher Theodoret maintain. For in the seventh ode of the second week's Canon, which is sung to the Hirmus "Interiorum Ionan", in the book called the Triodion, in an address to the Holy Spirit, it sings and decrees in these very words: "Come to us, Holy Spirit, making us partakers of your holiness, of your never-setting light, of your divine life and of your most fragrant distribution. For you are the stream of the Godhead, proceeding from the Father through the Son." In the third tone of the Octoechos, singing to our Saviour, it speaks thus: "You have set before us a mediator, Christ; do not be ashamed of your Mother. At her entreaties grant us, favourably, the Spirit who imparts goodness, proceeding from the Father through you." The same things are said by John of Damascus. But also through the most divine Simeon Metaphrastes, in the preface to the lection on the martyrdom of St Dionysius the Areopagite, which is read on the third day of October, he decrees in these words: "In ancient times the matters of faith were in figures and enigmas, and the light of truth was hidden in shadow and cloud. But when the great mystery of our salvation was accomplished, He who had created our hearts, out of his own goodness and mercy towards us, without sin became as we are and underwent the other things that belong to human weakness, so that I might recover my former nobility; and at last he was punished by death on the cross." And, not to pursue each thing he did in the midst of his economy, at last he underwent those things that belong to bodily departure and took up those that belong to the Spirit, and my Christ migrates into the heavens and returns to the Father's throne, and sends away the Spirit proceeding from himself as leader to the unbelieving Gentiles, through whom the blessed Paul was led from shadow to truth. For if the Saviour had not made the Spirit proceeding from himself a leader for his disciples among the unbelieving Gentiles, not as from the Father, as some try to show, wrongly interpreting this sacred theology of the divine Metaphrastes, and deciding (as is plain from what they rashly babble) that he is indeed sent from the Father, as being connatural and consubstantial with him, as one who proceeds from him naturally, that is, is sent; but from the Son in another way, as of an alien nature and subordinate, not as proceeding from him as from the Father, but outside his essence, just as those spirits who are sent by God into ministry are sent; this is utterly impious and blasphemous. But it is not so. For shining forth from the Son, as from his own light, that divine nature is naturally sent from him to creatures. This is manifest from what the same Church, in the seventh ode of the Canon concerning St John the Theologian, which is sung on the eighth day of May to the Hirmus "Dei condescensionem", singing to the Only-begotten God, the Word of the Father, decrees in this way: "The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father without beginning and shining forth from you, the Only-begotten Word of God, proclaimed to the Apostles: Blessed are you, God of our fathers." And in one mystical prayer of the divine Liturgy of St Basil the Great, turning his prayer to God the Father, he sets forth the same thing about the aforesaid manifestation of the Holy Spirit from the true light, namely the Son, word for word: "Without beginning, invisible, incomprehensible Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the great God and our Saviour, who is the image of your goodness, the equal seal, showing yourself as Father in himself, the living Word, true God, wisdom, life, sanctification, power, the true light before the ages, from whom the Holy Spirit appeared, the Spirit of truth, the gift of adoption, the pledge of the future inheritance," etc. Moreover, it must be considered in these words that our Saviour, being God and man, as the Word of God himself, from his own supernatural and blessed light, naturally sends forth the Holy Spirit according to his own existence. For it cannot happen that something should appear from the light of someone and not be poured forth from it naturally, indivisibly and inexhaustibly, and be co-existing and co-eternal with it. And as true man he revealed the divine pre-eminence of this Holy Spirit to his disciples by his living voice in many ways, not in a servile manner, as any of our holy men did, because he was not a mere man, but God the Word incarnate, pouring him out in a divine way, as from his own light of his superdivine Godhead, bringing him forth as from a fountain, that is, naturally. The one word phainō [φαίνω] signifies these two things: phainō means both to shine forth and to reveal. Therefore the theologian Gregory, in his Oration on the Spirit, says: "The same Spirit comes to the Apostles and also to the disciples one by one, adapting himself to the capacity of those who receive him, and fitting himself to their measure: at the beginning of the Gospel working miracles, after Christ's passion breathed upon them, after the ascension appearing in tongues of fire, which is the same as what the Saviour promised, but gradually as the capacity of the recipients allowed." Indeed he was gradually made known by Jesus himself, so that he too might cover up... In the disciples of Christ, that is, in three ways, according to the capacity they had, in three times, as he himself says in his Oration on Pentecost: before Christ was glorified through the passion, after he was glorified through the resurrection, and finally after his ascension to heaven or restoration, or whatever other name the thing should be called. But that first casting out of diseases and spirits, which surely was not done without the power of the Spirit, clearly shows this, as does that breathing upon them, which surely had the appearance of a more divine inspiration, and finally the present division of tongues of fire, first obscurely, then more clearly, and now more perfectly, as sent to the disciples from our Saviour according to nature, namely from heaven, as he had promised. Hence the pious Greek Church, in one troparion of the Canons concerning the Holy Spirit, sings to our Saviour himself: "King of kings, one from one alone, remaining from the Father without cause, you sent your Spirit, equal to you in power, to the Apostles, as to those who had deserved well of you," as if to say: truly, in deed, in nature and in truth, you sent from yourself the Spirit equal to you in power to the Apostles, as you had promised; just as the divine Peter, in the sermon he gave to the Jews in Acts, argued, saying: he poured out from himself this Spirit whom you hear and see. For that word "poured out" signifies this, and not from outside, as the Bulgarian remarks of Theophylact seem to suggest. Hence

units.la: Ecclesia in vno Petecostes Apolyticio ad apertam confirmationem huiusce veritatis, sic ad populum alta voce pronunciat. Qui in specie ignearum linguarum misisti ad sanctos tuos Apostolos, & Discipulos Spiritum sanctum tuum, Christus verus Deus noster, precibus immaculatissimae matris tuae. &c. in specie ignearum linguarum de Cœlo misit Saluator noster suis discipulis Spiritum sanctum, ut hoc in loco decernit, quae semper in omnibus recte credit pia Graecorum Ecclesia, ut discamus, non alia ratione mittere ex semetipso Spiritum sanctum, quam veluti ex igne spirante, facultate divinae naturae suae, & Patris, quemadmodum congruente analogia, neque flamma loco ex alio mitti potest, secundum naturalis missionis consequentiam, quae in Triade modis omnibus ponenda est, quam ut ignis ex igne, iuxta illud quod canit eadem Ecclesia de hoc eodem Spiritu sancto, ignis ex igne progrediens. & tamen progreditur ex Patre, & Filio Spiritus sanctus, ait Alexandrinorum Pastor, magnus nempe Cyrillus in trigesimo quinto Thesaurorum capite, cuius ille titulus est. Ex essentia Patris & Filij Spiritus sanctus. Ad haec & ex Filio, & per Filium Spiritus sanctus, non solum ipse, sed universus simul a Deo congregatus congressus divinorum Ecclesiae Doctorum, & omnes illius sancti Poëtae, ut in primo ad tuam sanctitatem Commentario nostro fatis clare, ex sacris eorundem scriptionibus demonstrauimus, luculenter decernunt.
units.tr: The Church, in one Pentecost Apolytikion, pronounces to the people in a loud voice, in order to confirm this truth openly: "You who sent your Holy Spirit in the form of fiery tongues to your holy Apostles and disciples, Christ our true God, through the prayers of your most immaculate Mother..."
