The Saviour sent the Holy Spirit to his disciples from heaven in the form of fiery tongues, as the pious Greek Church, which always believes rightly in all things, decrees in this place; so that we may learn that the Holy Spirit is sent from himself in no other way than as from a breathing fire, by the power of his divine nature and of the Father, as by a fitting analogy: for a flame cannot be sent from one place to another except according to the consequence of natural mission, which in the Trinity must be posited in every way, as fire from fire. Accordingly the same Church sings of this same Holy Spirit: "fire proceeding from fire." And yet the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, says the minister of the Alexandrians, namely the great Cyril, in the thirty-fifth chapter of his Thesaurus, whose title is: "The Holy Spirit from the essence of the Father and the Son." Moreover, not only he himself, but the whole united assembly of the divine teachers of the Church, and all those holy poets, as we have clearly demonstrated from their sacred writings in our first commentary to your holiness, decide plainly that the Spirit proceeds also from the Son and through the Son.

units.la: Concludamus ergo; processionem Spiritus Ecclesia Græca æque atque Latina, & quod magis est, quos desideras, Schismatici, etiam ex Filio expressis verbis asseuerât, ergo una eorundem est sententia, & consequenter consensus, licet non exprimant in Symbolo. Ergo insulse inculcatur illa Allatio. Scripsit Allatius; differunt in eo a Latinis, quod ipsi de Spiritu sancto dicunt, qui ex Patre procedit, Latini, qui ex Patre, Filioque, id cum Græci non negent, idem cum Latinis dicere existimandi sunt. Respondet; Sed quale hoc argumentum; non negant, ergo affirmant? Photiniani quando Symbolum Apostolicum recitant, non negant Christum, & Spiritum sanctum esse æternum Deum, ergo ne idem nobiscum dicere existimandi sunt? Non est par ratio de Photinianis, & Græcis. Quamuis enim Photiniani diuinitatem Spiritus, & Filij non negabant, attamen in quæstione de ijsdem eosdem non esse Deum contendebant. Græci vero post altercationes non negantes id, de quo tandiu disputatum est, si non negant, cum opus est, vel videntur non dissentire, vel nouo consensu sententiam approbare. Quid vero dices, cum hi ijsdem palam, & aperte in eorum Ritualibus libris processionem etiam ex Filio profitentur. Discitoque, cum veritas ab hostibus veritatis extorquetur, veritatis lumen clarius apparere, tanquam quod ab aduersarijs, & illud occultare contendentibus prolatum est. Ideoque Allatius consensum suum ut plurimum ex ipsis Ecclesiasticæ veritatis hostibus, & potissimum Schismaticis confirmat, ut egit in tractatu de Purgatorio, afferendo testimonia ex Hebræis, & Mohammedanis ipsis, quod tibi non multum arrisisse videtur.
units.tr: Let us therefore conclude: the Greek Church, just as the Latin, and what is more, the schismatics you yourself desire, expressly affirm that the Spirit proceeds also from the Son. Their opinion is therefore one and the same, and consequently there is agreement, even if they do not state it in the Creed. So that argument of Allatius is pointless. Allatius wrote: They differ from the Latins in this, that they say of the Holy Spirit that he proceeds from the Father, whereas the Latins say that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Since the Greeks do not deny this, they are to be thought to say the same as the Latins. You reply: "But what sort of argument is this: they do not deny it, therefore they affirm it? When the Photinians recite the Apostles' Creed, they do not deny that Christ and the Holy Spirit are eternal God. Are they therefore to be thought to say the same as we do?" The case of the Photinians is not parallel to that of the Greeks. For although the Photinians did not deny the divinity of the Spirit and of the Son, they nevertheless contended, on the very question in dispute, that these were not God. The Greeks, however, after their controversies, do not deny the point over which they have disputed so long; if they do not deny it when it is needful, they either seem not to dissent, or they approve the opinion by a new agreement. But what will you say, when these same men openly and plainly profess in their ritual books that the procession is also from the Son? Learn also that when the truth is wrung from the enemies of the truth, the light of the truth shines more clearly, as something brought forth by adversaries who strive to hide it. Therefore Allatius confirms his agreement mostly from the very enemies of ecclesiastical truth, and especially from schismatics, as he did in his treatise on Purgatory, by bringing forward testimonies from the Hebrews and from the Mohammedans themselves, which does not seem to have pleased you much.

units.la: Cum scribis: Sed parum fuisset, nisi etiam Mahummedani, tanquam Patroni causæ Pontificiæ advocarentur. Idem Mahummedani cum Iudæis producuntur ad firmanda pro defunctis suffragia; quamuis hæc argumentandi ratio Bellarmino quoque, & Allatio arriserit, ut inde aliquis suspicari queat, fore aliquando, ut ad testimonia patris mendaciorum recurrant. Opponens ex aliorum suspicione loquitur: neque enim puto, hominem rerum iudicem callidum similia pronuntiasse. Quam valida sint in comprobanda causa inimicorum vel exterorum testimonia, norunt vel pueri.
units.tr: You write: But it would have been of little use, unless the Mohammedans too were summoned as patrons of the Papist cause. The same Mohammedans are produced along with the Jews to support prayers for the dead; although this method of argument has pleased Bellarmine too, and Allatius, so that one may suspect that at some time they will have recourse to the testimonies of the father of lies. You speak here on the basis of someone else's suspicion, for I do not think a man skilled in judging such things would pronounce something of this kind. How strong the testimonies of enemies or outsiders are in confirming a cause, even boys know.

units.la: Ab ipso Ecclesiæ primordio Paulus Apostolus contra gentes nouam suam doctrinam, & verum Deum probans Iesum Christum, & illius resurrectionem in Areopago ex Inscriptione aræ Ignoto Deo, & Dei omnipotentiam ex antiqui Poëtæ carmine, In ipso enim viuimus, & sumus, &, Ipsius genus sumus, confirmauit. Et 1. Corint. 15. euellens prauas consuetudines, Corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia prava, & ad Titum mores Cretensium redarguens, Cretenses semper mendaces, malæ bestiæ, ventres pigri. Quinimo Christus ipse suæ diuinitatis, & diuinæ generationis doctrinam, & declarationem minime abhorrens ab ipso Diabolo publica proclamatione vult recognosci; Quid nobis, & tibi Iesu fili Dei? Et hoc uti Χεῖσοαπποϛολπεσπεραδδώϛ[?] fuit in usu semper in Ecclesia Orientali, atque Occidentali seruatum, non quod ab dictis testimonijs dogma Catholicum suam firmitatem habeat, nemo siquidem dat, quod non habet, sed dogmatis certitudinem adeo claram, ut iam dicebam, patentemque esse, ut ab ipsis etiam hostibus, & aduersarijs agnita fuerit, & per vim etiam a veritate extorta. Audi Lactantium Firmianum Instit. lib. 1. Sed cum defendamus causam veritatis apud eos, qui aberrantes a veritate, falsis religionibus seruiunt, quod genus probationis aduersus eos magis adhibere debemus, quam ut eos Deorum sacrorum testimonijs seiungamus? Et infra; Nec difficile sane fuit paucorum hominum prava sentientium redarguere mendacia testimonio populorum, atque gentium in hac una re non diffidentium. Et infra; Sed omittam sane testimonia Prophetarum: ne minus idonea probatio videatur esse ab his, quibus omnino non creditur. Veniamus ad Auctores, & eos ipsos ad veri probationem testes citemus, quibus contra nos uti solent: Poëtas dico, ac Philosophos. Ex his unum Deum probemus necesse est, non quod illi habuerint cognitam veritatem: sed quod veritatis ipsius tanta est vis, ut nemo possit esse tam caecus, qui non videat ingerentem se oculis divinam claritatem. Augustinus contra Iudæos, Paganos, & Arianos; Demonstremus etiam nos ex gentibus testimonium Christo fuisse prolatum: quoniam veritas non tacuit clamando etiam per linguas inimicorum suorum. Nonne quando Poëta ille facundissimus inter sua carmina, Jam nova progenies caelo demittitur alto, dicebat, Christo testimonium perhibebat? In dubium hoc veniet, nisi alios ex gentibus idoneos testes, pluraque dicentes in medium introducam. Illum Regem, qui vestram superbiam captivando perdomuit, Nabuchodonosor regem scilicet Babylonis non praetermittam. Dic Nabuchodonosor, quid in fornace, quo tres viros iniustos iniuste immiseras: dic, dic, quid tibi fuerit revelatum. Nonne inquit tres viros misimus in fornacem ligatos? Et aiunt ei, Vere rex. Ecce, inquit, ego video quatuor viros solutos deambulantes in medio ignis, & corruptio nulla est in eis, & aspectus quarto similis est Filio Dei. O alienigena, unde tibi hoc? Quis tibi annunciauit Filium Dei? non dumquidem mundo nascitur, & similitudo nascentis a te cognoscitur. Unde tibi hoc? Quis tibi istud annunciauit, nisi quia sic te diuinus ignis intus illuminauit, ut cum illi apud te captiui tenerentur inimici Iudaei, sic diceres testimonium Filio Dei, &c. Cicero in Oratione pro P. Quintio; Tuum testimonium, quod in aliena re lene esset, id in tua-, quoniam contra te est, grauissimum debet esse. Et tu Iudaeorum, ac Muhammedanorum testimonia ad corroborandā Fidei dogmata, æque atque Diaboli forent, Bellarmino, & Allatio in crimen vertis? o tempora! o accisam verae religionis perspicientiam!
units.tr: From the very beginning of the Church, the Apostle Paul, when he set forth his new doctrine against the Gentiles and proved the true God and Jesus Christ and his resurrection, confirmed it at the Areopagus from the inscription on an altar, To the Unknown God, and from the saying of an ancient poet, For in him we live, and move, and have our being, for we are also his offspring. And in 1 Corinthians 15 he uprooted bad customs with the words, Evil communications corrupt good manners, and in his letter to Titus, rebuking the morals of the Cretans, he wrote, The Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, slow bellies. Indeed Christ himself wished the doctrine of his divinity and divine generation to be acknowledged by a public proclamation even from the Devil, who by no means shrank from declaring it: What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? This way of speaking has always been kept in use in the Eastern and the Western Church. Not that the Catholic dogma gains its firmness from these testimonies, for no one gives what he does not have; rather, the certainty of the dogma is so clear and so evident, as I was saying, that it has been acknowledged even by its enemies and adversaries, and has been wrung from them by force of truth. Hear Lactantius Firmianus, Institutes book 1: "But since we defend the cause of truth before those who, straying from the truth, serve false religions, what kind of proof ought we rather to use against them than to separate them by the testimonies of their own sacred gods?" And below: "Nor was it really difficult to refute the lies of a few men who held perverse views by the testimony of peoples and nations, who in this one matter are not distrustful." And below: "But I will certainly omit the testimonies of the Prophets, lest the proof seem less suitable, since it comes from men whom they do not believe at all. Let us come to the authors, and let us cite as witnesses to the proof of truth those very men whom they are accustomed to use against us: I mean the poets and the philosophers. From these it is necessary for us to prove one God, not because they had knowledge of the truth, but because the power of truth itself is so great that no one can be so blind as not to see the divine brightness thrust upon his eyes." Augustine, against the Jews, Pagans and Arians: "Let us also show that testimony was given to Christ by the Gentiles, since truth has not been silent, but has cried out even through the tongues of its enemies. Did not that most eloquent poet, when among his verses he said, Now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven, bear witness to Christ? This will be doubted, unless I bring forward other suitable witnesses from the Gentiles, saying more. I will not pass over that king who by taking captives subdued your pride, namely Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Say, Nebuchadnezzar, what in the furnace, into which you had unjustly thrown three unjust men: say, say, what was revealed to you. Did we not, he says, cast three men bound into the furnace? And they say to him, 'Truly, O king.' Behold, he says, I see four men loosed walking in the midst of the fire, and no corruption is in them, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God. O foreigner, whence did you have this? Who announced to you the Son of God? For he is not yet born into the world, and the likeness of the one to be born is known by you. Whence did you have this? Who announced this to you, unless the divine fire so illuminated you within, that while those enemies, the Jews, were held captive by you, you would speak thus to bear witness to the Son of God," etc. Cicero in his speech for P. Quinctius: Your testimony, which in another's affair would be mild, in your own, since it is against you, ought to be very weighty. And do you turn the testimonies of the Jews and Mohammedans, which are used to strengthen the dogmas of the faith, into a crime against Bellarmine and Allatius, as if they were equally the devil's? O the times! O the blunted insight into the true religion!

units.la: Pergit ad ea, quae cum Reformatis Græci consentiunt. In negatione descensus Christi e Cælo in Sacramento Eucharistiæ. Descensum Christi e Cælo in Sacramentum Eucharistiæ nunquam somniauit Græca Ecclesia, quæ veram, & realem transubstantiationem panis in corpus, & vini in sanguinem Christi tenet. Siquidem verba consecrationis operatoria esse illius, quod significant, sentit: & sic per omnipotentiam Dei effici, ut, quod antea panis erat, & vinum, fiat corpus, & sanguis Christi, quae est vera transfubstantiatio, & conuersio panis, & vini in corpus, & sanguinem Christi; Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Catechesi Mystag. 4. Aquam aliquando mutauit in vinum &c. Et non erit dignus, cui credamus, quod vinum in sanguinem transfinutarit? Et infra. Pro certissimo habeas, panem hunc, qui videtur a nobis, non esse panem, etiam si gustus panem esse sentiat; sed esse corpus Christi. Chrysostomus Homil. 8. in Matthaeum. Non sunt humana virtutis opera, quae tunc in coena confecit: ipse nunc quoque operatur, ipse perficit. Ministrorum nos ordinem tenemus, qui vero hoc sanctificat, & transfinutat, ipse est. Idem Oratione de Coena Dominica, & proditione; Πάρεσιν ὁ Χειστὸς, ὁ νῦν ἐκάνῳ ὁ τὴν ζάμισιν ἐκείνῳ κοσμήσας, οὐκ ἐκ ταύτην [?] ἁγιασμῶ νῦν. ὁ γὰρ ὄντως ἀνθρώπου ὁ ποιῶν τὰ προκείμενα ἡμῖν σῶμα, καὶ αἷμα Χριστοῦ. ἀλλ' ὁ σαυτοῦ ἀπὸ ἡμῶν Χριστός. Σῆμα γὰρ πλεῖον ἔσμεν ὁ ἱερεὺς τὰ ῥήματα ἐκεῖνα φθεγγόμενος τῆς σωτηρίας. ἡ δὲ δύναμις ἐκ ἡ χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστιν. τοῦτό μου τὸ σῶμα, φησί. τοῦτο τὸ ῥῆμα ἐκ τοῦ προκείμενα μεταβρυθμίζει, καὶ καθάπερ ἐκεῖνα ἡ λέγεσθαι, αὐξανέσθω, καὶ πληθυνέσθω, καὶ πληρούσθω τὸ γλῶ, ἐρρήθη μὲν ἅπαξ. δὲ πάντως ἡ τοῦ χρόνου γίνεται ἐξω δυναμικῶς τοῦ φύσιν τοῦ ἡμετέραν τοῖς παιδοτροφίαν, ἔτι καὶ αὕτη ἡ φωνὴ ἡ ἅπαξ λεγθα-[?] Ϲα ϗαδ᾽ ἐκάσλω ξ ἀπίζαν ἐν ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις ἐξ ἐκείνου μέχρι σήμερον, ἐ μέχρι τῆς αὐτῆ παρουσίας τὴν θυσίαν ἀνάδζ[?]. Adest & nunc Christus ipse, qui mensam illam ornauerat, ipse & hanc nunc ornat. Non enim homo est, qui proposita facit corpus & sanguinem Christi, sed ille, qui pro nobis crucifixus est Christus. Nam Sacerdos proferens deprecationis verba figuram illius praefert, sed potestas, & gratia a Deo est. Hoc est, ait, corpus meum. Hoc verbum proposita permutat. Et quemadmodum vox illa dicens, Crescite, & multiplicamini, & replete terram, semel quidem dicta est, semper autem facit operes confortans ipsam naturam in filiorum propagationem; sic & haec semel dicta in qualibet mensa apud Ecclesias ab illo usque ad hoc temporis, & usque ad eius aduentum sanctificat sacrificium. Gregorius Nyssenus apud Euthymium in Panoplia Tit. 11. ait; Quod panis per Verbum Dei, Hoc est corpus meum, sanctificatur, & in corpus Christi mutatur. Ioannes Damascenus libro 4. Fidei Orthodoxae cap. 14. Panis, ac vinum, & aqua per sancti Spiritus invocationem, & aduentum mirabili modo in Christi corpus, & sanguinem vertuntur. Theophylactus in cap. 16. Matth. Non dixit Christus hoc est figura, sed hoc est corpus meum: ineffabili enim operatione transformatur, etiam si nobis videatur panis. Ad hanc conversionem non rerequiritur, ut corpus Christi de nouo producatur, seu reproducatur, neque ut de loco in locum adducatur, tanquam quæ substantialis ista conuersio in eo consistat, quod in locum substantiæ panis accidentia sustentantis, nunc autem omnino definentis per omnipotentiam Dei succedat corpus Christi, ibidem sustentans accidentia panis; quamuis non ut formas sibi inhærentes, sed altiore tamen proprie dicto sustentationis modo. Non obstat, quod secundum hanc doctrinam, neque substantia Christi, neque ulla eius pars producatur: & modus Christi existendi sacramentaliter sub speciebus, seu accidentibus panis, sit absque extensione partium in ordine ad locum. Nanque sicuti per omnipotentiam Dei fieri potest, & non semel factum est, ut duo corpora se mutuo penetrarent, eodemque loco existerent: Christus nanque Dominus ex utero illæso prodijt, per ianuas clausas ad discipulos ingressus est: ita etiam eadem Dei virtute fieri potest, ut omnes partes corporis Christi sine extensione sint, sine positione unius partis extra alteram in ordine ad locum. Neque similiter obstat, quod Christi corporea substantia in Cælis existens, etiam in terris non uno loco tantum, sed ubicunque sacrificium offertur, vel Eucharistia asseruatur, realem præsentiam habeat: quia præsentia ista localis, cum accidens quoddam substantiæ sit, per divinam omnipotentiam multiplicari potest non multiplicato subiecto. Quemadmodum itaque plura corpora in uno loco existentia, non ideo definunt esse plura, & substantialiter diversa, ita etiam unum corpus in plurimis locis existens non ideo definit esse unum, seu substantialiter indivisum. Vide Ioannem Chrysostomum lib. 3. de Sacerdotio. Et panis hic & vinum verbis Christi consecrata sunt vere corpus, & sanguis Christi, & non figura, & typus. Hæc doctrina Romanæ, nec alia Græcæ Ecclesiæ est. Quæ vero Reformatorum? Panem esse corpus Christi, & vinum sanguineum significatiue, non aliter ac clavis tradita sit domus, sceptrum sit Imperium, & annulus hæreditas: Hic panis me, & nullum alium significat: Vera præsentia corporis, & sanguinis Christi in Eucharistia esse vere Capernaiticam Christi manducationem: Christum a nobis abesse corpore, spiritu in nobis habitare: Impanationem, suppanationem, phantasias huius sæculi delitescentis corporis Christi: Carnem Christi tam situ ipso abesse ab ipsis signis, quam Cæli, in quos ascendit a terris, in quibus versamur, absunt: Symbola panis, & vini, si locorum interualla spectes, tanto spatio corpora nostra a Christi carne absunt, quanto summi Cœli, in quos ascendit, & ad extremum vsque diem permansurus est, absunt a nobis in terra versantibus. Immota manet illa regula; verum corpus pluribus in locis esse simul non potest: Hoc est corpus meum, perinde est ac si sponsus abiens det sponsæ annulum, & dicat, Hoc est sponsus,& maritus tuus, quoties hunc annulum exosculata fueris, facito in mei memoriam. & quis omnes de hoc Sacramento Reformatorum ineptias undique cogeret? Et nihilominus confidenter non verentur dicere Reformati cum illis consentire Græcos in negatione descensus Christi e Cœlo in Sacramentum Eucharistiæ.
units.tr: He goes on to the points on which the Greeks agree with the Reformed. On the denial that Christ descends from heaven in the sacrament of the Eucharist. The Greek Church never dreamed that Christ descends from heaven into the sacrament of the Eucharist. It holds a true and real transubstantiation of the bread into the body and of the wine into the blood of Christ. It holds that the words of consecration are operative and effect what they signify, so that by the omnipotence of God what was bread and wine before becomes the body and blood of Christ. That is the true transubstantiation and conversion of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ. Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Catechesis 4: He once changed water into wine, etc. And shall we not believe that he changed wine into blood? And below: Be assured that this bread, which appears to us, is not bread, even though taste perceives it as bread, but is the body of Christ. Chrysostom, Homily 8 on Matthew: The works of human power are not what then accomplished the supper; he himself now also works, he himself completes it. We hold the order of ministers, but he who sanctifies and transforms this is himself. The same, in his Oration on the Lord's Supper and the betrayal: "Christ is present now, who adorned that table, he himself also now adorns this one. For it is not a man who makes the things set forth the body and blood of Christ, but Christ who was crucified for us. For the priest, pronouncing those words, stands in the place of the Saviour; but the power and grace is of God. 'This is my body,' he says. This word transforms the things set forth. And as that voice, 'Increase and multiply and fill the earth', once spoken, yet always works, strengthening nature for the begetting of children, so also this word, spoken once, at every table in the churches from that time until now, and until his coming, makes the sacrifice holy." [Ἔστι δὲ καὶ νῦν ὁ Χριστὸς ... τοῦτό μου τὸ σῶμα, φησί. τοῦτο τὸ ῥῆμα τὰ προκείμενα μεταρρυθμίζει ...] Gregory of Nyssa, cited by Euthymius in the Panoplia, title 11: "That the bread is sanctified through the Word of God, 'This is my body', and is changed into the body of Christ." John of Damascus, Orthodox Faith, book 4, ch. 14: "Bread and wine and water are changed in a wonderful manner into the body and blood of Christ through the invocation and coming of the Holy Spirit." Theophylact on Matthew 26: "Christ did not say 'this is a figure', but 'this is my body'; for it is transformed by an ineffable operation, even though it seems to us to be bread." For this conversion it is not required that the body of Christ be newly produced or reproduced, nor that it be brought from place to place, as if this substantial conversion consisted in this: that in the place of the substance of the bread, which sustained the accidents and now wholly ceases, the body of Christ succeeds through the omnipotence of God, sustaining there the accidents of the bread, though not as forms inhering in it but by a higher mode of sustaining, properly so called. It is no objection that according to this doctrine neither the substance of Christ nor any part of it is produced, and that the mode of Christ's existing sacramentally under the species, or accidents, of bread is without extension of parts in relation to place. For just as by the omnipotence of God it can happen, and has happened more than once, that two bodies penetrate one another and exist in the same place (Christ the Lord came forth from the unharmed womb and entered to his disciples through closed doors), so by the same power of God it can happen that all the parts of Christ's body are without extension, without the position of one part outside another in relation to place. Nor is it an objection that the corporeal substance of Christ, existing in the heavens, has a real presence on earth not only in one place but wherever the sacrifice is offered or the Eucharist is reserved; for this local presence, being a certain accident of the substance, can be multiplied by divine omnipotence without multiplying the subject. Just as several bodies existing in one place do not for that reason cease to be several and substantially different, so also one body existing in very many places does not for that reason cease to be one, or substantially undivided. See John Chrysostom, book 3 On the Priesthood. And this bread and wine, consecrated by the words of Christ, are truly the body and blood of Christ, and not a figure or type. This is the doctrine of the Roman Church, and no other doctrine of the Greek Church. But what of the Reformed? That the bread is the body of Christ and the wine is blood only in a signifying way, just as a key is handed over as the house, a sceptre is the empire, and a ring is the inheritance; that this bread signifies me and nothing else; that the true presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist is the Capernaitic eating of Christ; that Christ is absent from us in body and present in us in spirit; the impanation, the suppanation, the phantasies of this age about a hidden body of Christ; that the flesh of Christ is as far away from the very signs in place as the heavens, into which he ascended from the earth where we dwell, are distant: The symbols of the bread and wine, if you consider the intervals of place, are as far from the flesh of Christ as our bodies are, as far as the highest heavens, into which he ascended and where he will remain until the last day, are distant from us who dwell on earth. That rule remains unshaken: a true body cannot be in many places at once. "This is my body" is just as if a bridegroom, departing, gave his bride a ring and said, "This is your bridegroom and husband; as often as you kiss this ring, do so in memory of me." And who could gather together all the absurdities of the Reformed about this sacrament from every side? Yet the Reformed do not hesitate to say confidently that the Greeks agree with them in denying that Christ descends from heaven into the sacrament of the Eucharist.

units.la: In aperta Communionis sub utraque specie necessitate. Quid hic, vel alii dixerit de Communione sub utraque specie judicabunt alii. Allatius apertissimis rationibus docuit, Græcos ipsos non semper sub utraque specie mysterium consummare. Pueri siquidem, infirmi, Sacerdotes ipsi in quadragesimali ieiunio, cum celebrant diebus ferialibus, qui solitariam vitam agunt, omnes hi sub unica specie communicant. Conclude, ergo non est apud ipsos usus inviolabilis de utraque specie: & cum toties sub unica communicant, signum est eos Communionem tam sub utraque specie, quam sub unica non condemnare, nec alterum excipere uti sibi praecepto Ecclesiae impositam, quae cum libera sit, & usu comprobata, si quis est, qui utramque speciem praeferat, unicam convellat, nae ille adversus Graecae Ecclesiae statuta militat, cum inter ἀδιάφορα ponenda sit. Et Arcudius, quidquid ex verbis suis colligunt alij, satis aperte intonat, non Orientalis Ecclesiae, sed aliquorum recentiorum Graecorum sententia ea in re necessitatem praecepti imponere. Innuis, Allatium, Non dum probasse Graecos non ea fini panem in vinum intingere, quanos volumus id fieri. Lapsus forte in his Grammaticus. Quis sit finis vester in eo ritu, cum ritum non observatis, nondum capio. Proba tu prius vos id efficere, prome finem, tum examinabitur, prodendo Graecorum finem, an conveniat. Sic posset & Mahumedanus dicere de sua coena, Allatium non dum probasse, non ea fine panem in vinum intingere, quo nos volumus id fieri. Sed haec ludicra sunt, & a multis derisa. Ad faniora reuertamur. Nunquam tamen effugiet Allatius, ut non invitus etiam deprehendere cogatur, Graecos propterea panem vino tingere, ut sub utraque communicent. Institutor similis intinctionis, quis nam fuerit, adhuc ignoratur, sicuti & fcopus illius: Græci tamen ex posterioribus nonnulli, ne viderentur inconsiderate rem agere, hanc sibi ritus rationem, uti accommodiorem quærendo investigarunt, quam & produxit Allatius, ut sub utraque dicerentur communicare: sed hoc stultissimum est. Qua enim ratione quis dicetur sub tali, vel tali specie communicare, quæ nusquam apparet, vel nusquam est. Sic etiam ille dicendus veniet, communicare sub utraque specie, qui sub specie sola vini, in quo mica panis fuerit proiecta, & postmodum extracta, communicaret. Ego certe riderem hominem, qui scio, cessantibus illis speciebus, statim, & eodem temporis vestigio corpus, sanguinemque Christi esse desinere. Quidquid opinetur communicans, cum falsa illa existimatio sit, non communicat id, quod non est. Et conquestio nulla est de Pontificijs, quod nihil certi illi referunt: cum quidquid certi referunt Pontificij, Reformati aut cauillis, aut peruersis expositionibus, & corruptelis incertum reddunt, & referentes in Doctorum numero ponere recusant. Et vide. Sionita unus est, nec Græcus; Arcudius, Caryophilus, Ecchellensis, Holstenius plures, Græci, Maronita, Germanus, doctrina, & erudiditione Sionita excellentiores : & tamen creditur vni Sionitæ , reijciuntur plures . Absque ratione ergo conqueruntur Reformati, nihil certi referri a Pontificijs, cum quæ certa referuntur, ipsi vel non intelligunt , vel nolunt intelligere ; vel nolunt omnia credere , quæ Proselyti Romani ad fauoris aucupium dicunt . Neque id mirum est , cum qui hic vocantur Proselyti Pontificij , neque sciunt Reformatis lenocinari; neque sermonem ad illorum gratiam singere : sed rem factaque , vt sunt, exponere; alijsque , vt exponant , auctores sunt. Et cum scripsisset Allatius de modico illo vino; quo panis intingitur, eo exsiccato , & vini quidquid fuerit, deperdito , non amplius vtramque speciem esse, sed vnam tantummodo, & qui panem absumit, Sacramentum Eucharistiæ , corporis scilicet, sub una tantum specie absumere , cum ibi nulla vini substantia remaneat, non sine admiratione interrogat Opponens. Quid? quorsum abijt sanguis ille Christi, vt vt in superficie tantum hærens, in tenues ne reuoluitur auras sanguis Christi incorruptibilis? Dictum est, specie vini exsiccata , cum tum nulla species vini est, desinere esse, quemadmodum & specie panis sublata corpus. Hoc enim axioma apud Catholicos commune est. Quare ridiculum est quærere, An in tenues revoluitur auras sanguis Christi incorruptibilis? Sed id nolunt Græci, qui panem consecratum ab omni corruptione, & putrescentia vindicant, cumque id aliquando contigisse narret Pachymerius, instar prodigij, & futurorum malorum prænuncium fuit. Sunt in ea existimatione Græci, res naturales benedictione Sacerdotis, sive Episcopi subactas, non solum ea benedictione, mala, & noxia averruncandi, sed etiam sese conservandi facultatem acquirere: Hinc aquam, quam ipsi die Epiphaniæ sacro, cum laudibus, & precibus Deum venerantes benedicunt, nusquam corrumpi vulgata apud eos opinio est, quod cum videretur incredibile nonnullis hic Romæ, & falso prodi, doctissimus, ac clarissimus Collega meus Stephanus Gradius, eo ipso benedictionis die guttulum ea implens experimento didicit ad triginta annos incorruptam conservatam fuisse, quam ipse, & plerique alij indepravatam conspeximus. Sic multo firmius de speciebus consecratis opinantur; non quod illæ prorsus incorruptibiles sint, sed quod illæsæ diutius perennant. Ideo ætate Pachymerij cum illas immutatas vidissent, malorum prænuncium reputarunt, non quod illas plane incorruptas existimarent, sed quod præter consuetum id contigisset. Quare non videtur absurdum Allatio, vinum, qui erat vere sanguis, exsiccari, & panem, qui erat vere corpus, consumi. cum illa quamuis supra naturā, non tamen extra naturam consecratione sustollantur, & de hoc tenet, quidquid Reformati sentiant, etiam post transubstantiationem sensibus relinqui judicium, cum palam species illæ sensibus objiciantur. Et quod additur de incorruptibilitate, & corruptibilitate corporis Christi, sub Alexio Angelo enata, non est ad rem. Aliud enim est de corruptibilitate corporis Christi, aliud de specierum corruptibilitate sermonē esse. Corpus Christi incorruptibile est, species corruptibilis, tempore enim, vel a fidelibus absumptas corrumpi necesse est, & argumentū contra Allatium cadit. Ubi nulla vini substantia remanet, ibi sanguis non sumitur. in bibitione sacrificuli nulla vini substantia remanet, ergo nescio, an hoc sint concessuri. Concludere ignorantiam, non est argumentari contra Allatium, qui plane dicit, sanguinem Christi sub speciebus vini conservari, donec species intacta, atq; integra est, qua læsa definit & sanguis esse. Quis enim unquam Catholicus dixit, in substantia vini remanere sanguinem, cum post consecrationem vini nulla amplius substantia vini sit, sed sub specie vini sanguis. Et propterea argumentaris; Ubi est odor, color, sapor, humor, fluiditas ipsa vini, ibi etiam est substantia vini. ergo non mera accidentia. Quis dubitat, ante consecrationem? post consecrationem adest odor, color, sapor, humor fluiditas vini, & reliqua, quae speciem vini constituunt ut mera accidentia. Ergo nulla transubstantiatio. Hoc vero negatur, uti ineptissimum, cum substantia vini post consecrationem nulla remaneat, sed sub specie vini sanguis Christi, qui sub illis speciebus latet. Ergo corruit nobilis illa exceptio, Laicos accipiendo corpus Christi, accipere etiam sanguinem, quia corpus non fit absque sanguine. Nego ex assertione, quoniam sanguis non editur sed bibitur. Mi homo tu ex tua hæresi separas sanguinem a corpore. Pontificij, Græcique, qui corpus Christi sub speciebus agnoscunt vitaliter animatum, in speciebus panis, & vini, etiam si vinum separatum a pane est; & sanguinem item vivum spirantemque, sub speciebus panis totum Christum, & sub speciebus vini totum Christum latere opinantur. licet sanguis bibatur, in illa bibitione etiam comestio est, quemadmodum in comestione bibitio, & sic exceptio illa, quae apud Pontificios certissima est, non corruit, & argumenta tua nihil concludunt. & Græcos huiusce sententiae esse, ex libris eorundem Ritualibus memini me fuse alibi ostendisse.
units.tr: The open necessity of communion under both kinds. What Hottinger or others may say about communion under both kinds, others will judge. Allatius has shown by very clear arguments that the Greeks themselves do not always complete the mystery under both kinds. Children, the sick, and the priests themselves, when they celebrate on ordinary days during the Lenten fast, and those who lead a solitary life, all communicate under one kind alone. It follows that among them there is no unbreakable custom of both kinds. Since they so often communicate under one kind, this is a sign that they do not condemn communion under both kinds or under one alone, and that they do not impose one on the other as a precept of the Church. Since that practice is free and approved by use, whoever prefers both kinds and rejects the single kind fights against the statutes of the Greek Church, because it must be counted among indifferent things [ἀδιάφορα]. And Arcudius, whatever others may gather from his words, clearly thunders that it is not the view of the Eastern Church but of some more recent Greeks that imposes the necessity of a precept in this matter. You hint that Allatius has not yet proved that the Greeks do not dip the bread in the wine for the purpose for which we want this done. Perhaps the grammarian slipped here. What your purpose is in that rite, since you do not observe the rite, I still do not grasp. Prove first that you accomplish this, state your purpose, and then it will be examined, by setting out the purpose of the Greeks, whether it agrees. In this way a Muslim could also say of his own supper, that Allatius has not yet proved that they do not dip the bread in the wine for the purpose for which we want this done. But these are trifles, and many have mocked them. Let us return to more serious matters. Nevertheless, Allatius will never escape being forced, even against his will, to admit that the Greeks dip the bread in wine so that they may communicate under both kinds. Who the originator of this similar intinction was is still unknown, and so is its aim. Yet some of the later Greeks, lest they seem to act thoughtlessly in the matter, sought out this rationale for the rite as more suitable, and Allatius brings it forward, so that they may be said to communicate under both kinds. But this is most foolish. For by what reasoning will someone be said to communicate under a kind that nowhere appears, or nowhere exists? In this way, too, a man would be said to communicate under both kinds who received only the species of wine, into which a crumb of bread had been thrown and afterwards removed. I would certainly laugh at a man who, as I know, believes that when those species cease, the body and blood of Christ at once and in the same instant cease to be. Whatever the communicant thinks, since that opinion is false, he does not receive what is not there. And there is no complaint that the Papists report nothing certain to them, since whatever certain things the Papists report, the Reformed make uncertain by quibbles, perverse expositions and corruptions, and they refuse to count those who report them among the teachers. And consider this: Sionita is one man, and not a Greek; Arcudius, Caryophilus, Ecchellensis, and Holstenius, several Greeks, Maronites, and Germans, are more distinguished than Sionita in learning and erudition; yet Sionita is believed alone, and the many are rejected. The Reformed therefore complain without reason that nothing certain is reported by the Papists, since they either do not understand, or do not wish to understand, the certain things that are reported; or they do not wish to believe everything that the Roman proselytes say to win favour. Nor is this surprising, since those who are here called Papist proselytes neither know how to flatter the Reformed, nor do they shape their speech to please them, but set out things and deeds as they are, and they are the authorities for others to set them out too. And when Allatius had written that, once the small amount of wine into which the bread is dipped has dried up, and whatever wine there was has been lost, there is no longer both kinds but only one, and that whoever consumes the bread consumes the sacrament of the Eucharist, namely the body, under one kind alone, since no substance of wine remains there, he asks with wonder: Objector. What? Whither has that blood of Christ gone, that, clinging only to the surface, the incorruptible blood of Christ is not dissolved into thin air? It has been said that when the species of wine has dried up, it ceases to be, since then there is no species of wine, just as the body ceases when the species of bread is removed. For this axiom is common among Catholics. Therefore it is ridiculous to ask, whether the incorruptible blood of Christ dissolves into thin air? But the Greeks, who protect the consecrated bread from all corruption and putrefaction, do not want this; and when Pachymeres relates that this once happened, it was taken as a prodigy and a forewarning of coming evils. The Greeks hold the opinion that natural things, brought under the blessing of a priest or bishop, acquire not only the power to ward off harmful and noxious things by that blessing, but also the power to preserve themselves. Hence the common belief among them is that the water which they bless on the holy day of Epiphany, honouring God with praises and prayers, never spoils. Since this seemed incredible to some here in Rome and was reported falsely, my most learned and distinguished colleague Stephanus Gradius, on that very day of blessing, filling a small drop of it, learned by experiment that it had been kept uncorrupted for thirty years, and he and many others saw it undamaged. They think in the same way, and much more firmly, about the consecrated species; not that these are absolutely incorruptible, but that, unharmed, they last longer. So in the time of Pachymeres, when they saw those species altered, they considered it a forewarning of evils, not because they thought them wholly incorruptible, but because this had happened contrary to the usual course. Hence it does not seem absurd to Allatius that the wine, which was truly blood, dries up, and that the bread, which was truly body, is consumed; since those things, though raised above nature by consecration, are not nevertheless outside nature, and he holds that, whatever the Reformed think, judgment is left to the senses even after transubstantiation, since those species are plainly presented to the senses. And what is added about the incorruptibility and corruptibility of the body of Christ, brought forth under Alexius Angelus, is beside the point. For one thing is the discussion of the corruptibility of the body of Christ, another of the corruptibility of the species. The body of Christ is incorruptible; the species is corruptible, for in time, or once consumed by the faithful, it must corrupt; and your argument against Allatius falls. Where no substance of wine remains, there the blood is not taken. In the drinking of the little sacrifice no substance of wine remains; therefore I do not know whether they will concede this. To conclude from ignorance is not to argue against Allatius, who plainly says that the blood of Christ is preserved under the species of wine as long as the species is intact and whole, and when it is damaged, it ceases to be blood. For who among Catholics has ever said that the blood remains in the substance of wine, when after consecration there is no longer any substance of wine, but the blood of Christ is under the species of wine? And therefore you argue: Where there is the smell, colour, taste, moisture, and the very fluidity of wine, there also is the substance of wine; therefore not mere accidents. Who doubts this before consecration? After consecration the smell, colour, taste, moisture, fluidity of wine, and the rest that constitute the species of wine, are present as mere accidents. Therefore no transubstantiation. This is denied, as most absurd, since after consecration no substance of wine remains, but under the species of wine is the blood of Christ, which lies hidden under those species. Therefore that famous exception falls: that the laity, receiving the body of Christ, also receive the blood, because the body is not made without blood. I deny the assertion, since blood is not eaten but drunk. My good man, by your heresy you separate the blood from the body. The Papists and the Greeks, who acknowledge the body of Christ under the species as living and animated, believe that under the species of bread, even if the wine is separated from the bread, the whole Christ is present, and likewise that under the species of wine the whole Christ is present, with living and breathing blood. Although the blood is drunk, in that drinking there is also eating, just as in eating there is drinking; and so that exception, which is most certain among the Papists, does not fall, and your arguments conclude nothing. I remember having shown at length elsewhere, from the Ritual books of the same Greeks, that they hold this opinion.

units.la: Interim quaero ex Nihusio, An quando Graeci confitentur se in praesanctificatis accipere τὰ ἄζυμα λεπτά[?], ἄζυμα[?] in plurali, id efferant propterea, quia plura simul sunt consecrata, an quia non unum, sed duo sunt Symbola, quorum fuerunt participes facti? Si non displicet, sit a me responsum pro Nihusio. Graeci confitentur in praesanctificatis accipere se in plurali numero ἄζυμα[?] λεπτά[?], ἄζυμα[?], non quia plura sunt consecrata, aut plures particulae, neque; quia panis, vinique symbola accipiunt, sed quia corpus, & sanguinem sub una specie absumunt: nanque ipsi aeque atque Pontifici cum corpus Christi vivum teneant, sub specie panis consecrati, licet una species sit, corpus & sanguinem accipiunt, ideoque plurali numero efferunt. Poterat Graecus id efferre in singulari, cum unum corpus absumat, sed quia in Missa separata intelliguntur, ne unum absque alio participare reputaretur, quod recte intendit, verbis exprimit, licet sanguis ibi sub sua propria specie non adsit, ipse tamen absumendo corpus, quod sine sanguine non est, absumit eodem momento sub specie unica panis corpus, & sanguinem. Quare in Graecis male concluditur, accipi sacra dona in plurali, quia utroque symbolo vtuntur. Tum enim falsum diceret vnicam tantum speciem, & utramque vsurpans, vt praxis ipsa manifeste docet, cui contra pugnare, esset sensibus fidem adimere.
units.tr: Meanwhile I ask Nihusius: when the Greeks confess that in the presanctified rite they receive the unleavened little loaves [τὰ ἄζυμα λεπτά] and the unleavened [ἄζυμα] in the plural, do they say this because several things are consecrated at once, or because there are not one but two symbols of which they have become partakers? If it does not displease, let my answer be given on Nihusius's behalf. The Greeks confess that in the presanctified rite they receive [ἄζυμα] in the plural, not because several things are consecrated or there are several particles, nor because they receive the symbols of bread and wine, but because they consume the body and blood under one species. For they, just as the Papist does, hold that the living body of Christ is under the species of consecrated bread; although there is only one species, they receive body and blood, and therefore they express it in the plural. A Greek could have said it in the singular, since he consumes one body; but because in the separate Mass the two are understood, lest one be thought to partake without the other, he rightly intends it and expresses it in words. Although the blood is not there under its own proper species, by consuming the body, which is not without blood, he consumes at the same moment, under the single species of bread, both body and blood. Therefore it is wrongly concluded from the Greeks that the holy gifts are received in the plural because they use two symbols. For then he would be saying falsely that there is only one species, and that he uses both; practice itself clearly teaches otherwise, and to fight against it would be to rob the senses of their trust.

units.la: Quam autem Pontificiorum causæ hac inparte nihil accedat, satis ex superioribus contra Nihufium disputatis constare potest. Si causæ Pontificiorum nihil accedit, at accedit causæ Allatij probantis consensum; si in hac etiam solemnitate, quæ infrequenter fit, Græci cum Pontificijs conspirant: vt enim hi die Parasceues magnæ sacro, ab integra Missa abstinentes, anteconsecratis vtuntur, & Missam celebrant, absque eo quod vinum consecrent; ita Græci diebus ferialibus in quadragesima Missã præ-sanctificatorum, cum libuerit, recitantes, sola præsanctificata vsurpant, illaq; absumunt absq; vini consecratione, ergo probatur in hoc quoque consensio, improbatur dissensio.
units.tr: How little the cause of the Papists gains in this respect can sufficiently be established from what has been argued above against Nihusius. If the cause of the Papists gains nothing, yet the cause of Allatius, who proves agreement, does gain: if in this solemnity also, which occurs infrequently, the Greeks agree with the Papists. For as the latter on the great sacred day of Good Friday, abstaining from the full Mass, use pre-consecrated elements and celebrate Mass without consecrating wine, so the Greeks, reciting the presanctified Mass on ferial days in Lent whenever they wish, use only the presanctified elements and consume them without consecration of wine. Therefore agreement is proved in this point too, and disagreement is refuted.

units.la: Admissa Clerogamia. De clerogamia plura scripsi contra Hottingerum, qui Episcopos cum Presbyteris confundit, quod nec Græci, nec Pontificij faciunt. Græcorum Episcopi continentiam seruant, Hottingerani non item, Græci ante sacrum ordinem vxores ducunt, Virgines, virgines ipsi, non autem post: Hottingerani vxores ex tritriuio, ex triuio & ipsi. Et ridiculum est, quod insinuant Reformati, In re ipsa conuenimus, licet in Rituali aliquo discrepemus. Iam ergo ipse quoque ex Reformatis disco, in re Rituali discrepantiam, non parere dissidium. Adde etiam, Synodus Trullana, ubi renunciatus fuerit aliquis, Episcopo, uxoris ante quam renunciaretur ductæ commercio, & consuetudine interdicit, seuerioribus vitam Episcoporum continentiæ legibus astringens, non modo, ut ab aliorum uxoribus abstineant, sed & ab ijs quoque, quas tori confortes habuere, neque solum lecti socias non admittant, sed nec sub eodem tecto, aut ijsdem ædibus degere patiantur. Nam etsi fieri potest, ut castos se nihilominus, atque integros seruent, offendi tamen alios exemplo, atque abduci ad deteriora necesse est. Quod licuit Synodo incertæ, & cuius auctoritas etiamnum in dubium vertitur, negabunt Photius, Græcique, Romanæ Synodo in suâ Dioecesi licuisse in suis Presbyteris, Diaconis, & Subdiaconis? Trullani profitentur se obseruare antiquum Canonem Apostolicæ per. sectionis, & ordinis; quare potius illum in Subdiaconis, Diaconis, & Presbyteris, & non in Episcopis seruant? Quod est persectionis, & ordinis Apostolici in Sacerdotibus, quare non & in Episcopis fuerit? si Presbyteri, & reliqui sacris initiati dimittant uxores, tum enim ex illa dimissione nuptiæ, quas ipse conspectu suo Dominus honestauit, & miraculis ibidem editis consecrauit, & quarum sanctitas aliis quoque sacrarum literarum testimoniis asseritur, improbari videntur. Episcopi vero non item, si honestatis, & religionis obtentu dimittant, non improbantur. Eadem amborum conditio est, & quod in uno locum habebit hoc diuortium ob eandem perfectionem, & ordinem, quare non & in altero locum habebit?
units.tr: Admitting clerical marriage. I have written much on clerical marriage against Hottinger, who confuses bishops with presbyters, which neither the Greeks nor the Papists do. Greek bishops keep continence; Hottingerans do not. The Greeks take wives before sacred ordination, virgins as virgins, but not after; Hottingerans take wives from the crossroads, and they too from the crossroads. And it is ridiculous what the Reformed insinuate: We agree in the thing itself, though we differ in some ritual point. So I too learn from the Reformed that a difference in ritual is no sign of dissent. Add also the Trullan Synod, which forbids, when someone has been elected bishop, intercourse and cohabitation with a wife married before the election. It binds the lives of bishops by stricter laws of continence, so that they must abstain not only from the wives of others but also from those whom they once had as bedfellows; they may not keep as companions in bed, nor suffer them to live under the same roof or in the same house. For although it may happen that they nonetheless keep themselves chaste and unblemished, it is necessary that others be offended by the example and drawn to worse things. Will Photius and the Greeks deny that what was allowed by an uncertain Synod, whose authority is still in doubt, was allowed to the Roman Synod in its own diocese regarding its presbyters, deacons and subdeacons? The Trullans profess that they observe the ancient canon of apostolic perfection and order. Why, then, do they keep it for subdeacons, deacons and presbyters, and not for bishops? If it is a matter of perfection and apostolic order in priests, why should it not be so in bishops? If presbyters and the rest who are initiated into sacred orders dismiss their wives, then the marriages which the Lord himself honoured in his presence, and consecrated by the miracles performed there, and whose holiness is asserted by other testimonies of Sacred Letters, seem to be condemned by that dismissal. But if bishops dismiss them under a pretext of decency and religion, they are not condemned in the same way. The condition of both is the same; and if this divorce takes place in the one case on account of the same perfection and order, why should it not take place in the other?

units.la: Non omittenda grauissima controuersia inter Græcos, & Latinos. De insolubilitate Matrimonij dicemus in Exercitationibus nostris aduersus Creyghtonum, & Syropulum in Historia Concilij Florentini.
units.tr: The very grave controversy between the Greeks and the Latins must not be omitted. We shall speak of the indissolubility of marriage in our Exercitations against Creighton and Sylvester Syropulus in the History of the Council of Florence.

units.la: Purgatorij negatio, quod apparet ex Concilio Florentino, ex tractatu Græcorum edito Allatius hariolatur. quam vero in sua hariolatione eruditus vir hallucinetur, haud difficulter monstrari aliquando poterit. Expecto demonstrationem. Iis vero inconstantior Allatius, vbi ex Gabriele Philadelphiensi, Josepho Bryennio, Georgio Coresio, videre est, Græcos a flammis istis ustulatorijs tantopere abhorrere, ut malint in perniciosissimum, & Origenicum errorem inincidere. Verum est inter Græcos Schismaticos, & hæreticos fuisse nonnullos, qui negarunt: at eos potius amplexatos errorem Origenis, hoc vero falsum est. Vitant siquidem errorem Origenis, & illius sententias cum Origene anathemate feriunt, Leo ipse sibi contrarius id dicit. Pace tua dixerim. Allatium non intellexisti. Agit Allatius contra Græcos schismaticos, Purgatorium negantes, contra quos evidentissime probat, si Purgatorium non concedunt, necessario in errorem Origenis cadere, & argumentatur. Mortuorum secundum Græcos tria sunt genera, Iustorum, Damnatorum, & eorum, qui non dum perfecta poenitentia e viuis excedunt. Preces pro Iustis salutares non sunt, sicuti, nec damnatis, Oraculo siquidem Christi didicimus, in Inferno nullam esse redemptionem. Ergo si tertius locus non est, in quo preces fructuosæ sint, necessario, ne inutiles eas esse dicamus, condemnatis visui esse fatendum est. Quod postremum nunquam dicent Græci: ideoque necessario fateri debent Purgatorium. Sed de hoc, si plura cupis, attente legito tractatum nostrum de Purgatorio, in quo precibus illis Deum exorare Ecclesiam Græcam, confspicies[?], ut mortuorum animæ liberentur a tenebris, mœstitia, tormentis, poenis, & expurgentur etiam flammis, & poenis vltulatorijs. Et Conringius non dum respondit. Quod contra Allatium absq; vlla probatione dicitur ridiculum est; Nihil egisse Allatium in illo tractatu, vt causam suam, fi non prodidit, exfibilandam saltem propinauerit. Contendantur modo inuicem ea, quae ὁ πάνυ Conringius scripserat cum ijs, quae Allatius reposuit, & patebit vnicuique praeiudicijs non fascinato, nihil aliud de scripto Allatij pronunciandum esse, quam ἀῤῥήτῳ ἀμάνω. Iam triumphat Conringius. Habuit suæ causæ tutissimum patronum. Quis hisce obiectionibus, & argumentis contra Allatium respondebit?
units.tr: The denial of Purgatory, which appears from the Council of Florence and from the treatise of the Greeks published by Allatius, he conjectures. How much the learned man goes astray in his conjecture can, not with much difficulty, be shown at some time. I await the demonstration. Allatius is more inconsistent in this, where one may see from Gabriel of Philadelphia, Joseph Bryennius and George Coresius that the Greeks shrink so greatly from those burning cleansing flames that they prefer to fall into the most pernicious and Origenist error. It is true that among the Greek schismatics and heretics there were some who denied it; but they rather embraced the error of Origen, and this is false. For they avoid the error of Origen, and strike his opinions with anathema along with Origen. Leo himself says the opposite of himself. With your leave, I would say: you have not understood Allatius. Allatius is arguing against the Greek schismatics who deny Purgatory, and against them he proves most evidently that if they do not concede Purgatory, they necessarily fall into the error of Origen, and he argues thus. According to the Greeks there are three kinds of the dead: the just, the damned, and those who depart from the living without having completed repentance. Prayers for the just are not beneficial, nor for the damned, for we have learned from the oracle of Christ that there is no redemption in Hell. Therefore, if there is no third place in which prayers are fruitful, then, lest we say they are useless, we must admit that they are of benefit to the condemned. The Greeks will never say this last point; therefore they must necessarily admit Purgatory. But if you want more on this, read attentively our treatise on Purgatory, in which you will see that the Greek Church beseeches God with those prayers that the souls of the dead may be freed from darkness, sorrow, torments and punishments, and purged even by flames and cleansing punishments. And Conringius has not yet replied. What is said against Allatius without any proof is ridiculous: that Allatius accomplished nothing in that treatise, so that, if he did not betray his cause, at least he offered it to be hissed off. Let only what the most distinguished [ὁ πάνυ] Conringius wrote be set against what Allatius replied, and it will be plain to anyone not bewitched by prejudice that nothing else is to be pronounced about Allatius's writing than [ἀῤῥήτῳ ἀμάνω], an unspeakable and unbearable thing. Now Conringius triumphs. He has had the safest patron for his cause. Who will answer these objections and arguments against Allatius?

units.la: In Ecclesia Graecanica sequiore occurrit nihilominus, & prob dolor! Apostasia a veteri orthodoxa, quod in subsequentibus clarum faciemus. Neque id agimus insultandi Graecis gratia, quorum potius miseremur, & iudicamus eos partim neglectu scripturae, & coeco obedientiae studio, partim tyrannide Turcica pressos in dewia discessisse, hodieque nimis rerum aliarum imperitis, imprudentesque sine vlterioricura, & indagine in antiquam siluam doctoribus ijsdem morbis laborantibus ire: quanquam sex illa ipsa Orthodoxia multa adhuc retinuerint. Et haec ne faciunt ad probandum schisma cum Pontificijs? Sed antequam examinentur, proponantur singula; Mutabilitas Infernalis, miseriæ non corporalis, sed tantum in tenebris, nescio quibus, Dei priuatione, & animarum per conscientiæ stimulos afflictione, & consumptione constitutæ suffragijs vinorum, Sanctorum, Angelorum, & B. Virginis releuabiles, releuatæ actu ipse non tantum a Christo in eius ad inferos descensu omnibus tum hominibus, qui in monumentis erant, ad vitam reuocatis, adeoque vniuersali aliqua illo tempore resurrectione facta, quam reuelationem, & redemptionem Ioannes Baptista præcursor Christi prædicarit, ac prope esse prænunciarit, sed etiam per solutionem vinculi excommunicatorij. Considerentur sed maturo iudicio.
units.tr: In the later Greek Church, however, there occurs, and to our grief, an apostasy from the old orthodoxy, which we shall make clear in what follows. Nor do we do this to insult the Greeks, whom we rather pity; we judge that they, partly through neglect of Scripture and a blind zeal for obedience, and partly oppressed by Turkish tyranny, have wandered into error, and that today their teachers, too ignorant of other matters and too imprudent, without further care and inquiry, go into the ancient forest afflicted with these same diseases; although that old Orthodoxy has still retained much. And do these things not serve to prove schism with the Papists? But before they are examined, let each point be set forth. The mutability of Hell: its misery is not bodily but only in certain darkness, the deprivation of God and the affliction and consumption of souls by the stings of conscience, and it is relieved by the suffrages of the living, of the saints, of the angels and of the Blessed Virgin. It was actually relieved not only by Christ's descent into Hell, when all the men who were in the tombs were called back to life, so that some universal resurrection took place at that time, a revelation and redemption which John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ, proclaimed and announced as near; but also by the loosing of the bond of excommunication. Let these things be considered with mature judgement.

units.la: Triodion hortatur fideles, Christum exorare, ut animas fidelium mortuorum ex igne sempiterno liberet. Id ipsum facit Ecclesia Romana, & tamen non dicitur, mutabilitatem Inferni tenere, Ergo vtrique Ecclesiæ conuenit: & certe ex confusa ista variarum opinionum colluuie, quidquid elicitur, confusum, atque coenosum esse necesse est. Nec excusandus est Allatius, sed eius verba consideranda: nam tum nulla illius μνημονικὰ ἀμφιβολίας[?] comperies, imo firmam doctrinæ Catholicæ soliditatem, qua consensio inter Græcam, & Latinam Ecclesiam constabilitur. nullaque est inconstantia; cum ex opinione de excommunicatis, quam vocat stultissimam, & absurdam, dum Græci ex ea probare satagunt liberationem impiorum ex Inferno, opinationem, postremo autem eandem pro astructione[?] Purgatorij assumit.
units.tr: The Triodion urges the faithful to pray that Christ would free the souls of the faithful dead from everlasting fire. The Roman Church does the same, and yet no one says that it holds that Hell is changeable. So the point applies equally to both Churches. Certainly whatever is drawn out of this muddled sludge of differing opinions must itself be muddled and filthy. Nor should Allatius be excused, but his words must be weighed. For then you will find no ambiguity in him, but rather the firm solidity of Catholic doctrine, by which agreement between the Greek and Latin Churches is established. Nor is there any inconsistency, since he calls the opinion about the excommunicated foolish and absurd, while the Greeks strive to prove from it the release of the impious from Hell, and yet he himself finally takes up the same opinion to support Purgatory.

units.la: Omnia Allatiana disputata in lib. de Purgatorio ex hisce everti, & penitus destruis, neminemq; tam clare Allatio potuisse contradicere, quam fecit ipse met. Certe nec auctor Exercitationis, nec alij mentem Allatij assecuti sunt. Allatius siquidem tractans contra Græcos schismaticos de Purgatorio, probansq; illos vi veritatis coactos, quod verbis negat, in suis Ritualibus libris palam expresse fateri, Purgatorium scilicet; sinminus in opinionem Origenis ire ab Ecclesia Græca damnatam, ita argumentabatur. Oratur in Ecclesia pro defunctorum animis, ut ab igne, & sæpe etiā ab igne æterno liberentur. Istæ preces non sunt pro iustorum animis, quibus illæ non indigent, neq; pro damnatorum, quibus proficuæ nullo modo sunt; In inferno enim nulla est redemptio. Ergo necessario tertius locus est asserendus in quo animæ illæ degunt, quibus illæ supplicationes quæstuosæ esse possunt ad minuendos dolores, subleuandas molestias, clarificandas tenebras, & expurganda reliqua inquinamenta, quorum causa in tormentis similibus detinentur; quod erit ipsissimum Purgatorium. Idsi abnuunt in errorem Origenis, quem ipsi tantopere detestantur, coincidere necesse est. Hinc deceptus opponens mutabilitatem Inferni Ecclesiae Graecae appingit, ut dissidium augeat.
units.tr: All the arguments Allatius makes in his book on Purgatory are overturned and wholly destroyed by these points, and no one could have contradicted Allatius so clearly as he himself did. Certainly neither the author of the Exercitatio nor anyone else has grasped Allatius's meaning. For when Allatius, dealing with the schismatic Greeks on Purgatory, argued that they, compelled by the force of truth, openly and expressly confess in their Ritual books what they deny in words, namely Purgatory, lest they fall into the opinion of Origen condemned by the Greek Church, he reasoned thus. Prayers are offered in the Church for the souls of the dead, that they may be freed from fire, and often even from everlasting fire. These prayers are not for the souls of the just, who have no need of them, nor for the souls of the damned, for whom they are in no way of use, since there is no redemption in Hell. Therefore a third place must necessarily be asserted, in which those souls dwell, for whom such supplications can be of profit in lessening their pains, relieving their distresses, clearing their darkness and cleansing the remaining stains for which they are held in similar torments. This will be Purgatory itself. If they deny this, they must necessarily fall into the error of Origen, which they so greatly detest. Hence the objector, deceived, charges the Greek Church with the changeability of Hell, in order to enlarge the quarrel.

units.la: Nimia exaltatio Traditionum Synodicarum, septem praesertim Synodorum, & Patrum, Ecclesiaeq; infallibilitas. Ita opponitur Graecis, quasi illi aspernentur sacras Scripturas. Sed quã firmo argumento, Opponens viderit. Graeci siquidem primo loco venerantur sacra Biblia, & potissimum nouum Testamentum, ex quibus statis diebus legunt pericopas, Veteris testamenti in medio Ecclesiae Lectores, & Clerici, reliquis auditoribus sedentibus, Apostoli in medio Ecclesiae Lector, vel Diaconus, reliquis stantibus operto capite, Euangelii non nisi Sacerdos, vel Diaconus, vel Episcopus intra sanctum Bema. Neque necesse fuit in Professionibus Fidei apponere illa, de quibus nullo unquam tempore dubitatum est. Et male arguitur hic nulla mentio fit Bibliorum: ergo excluduntur a veneratione, & fide illis deferenda.
units.tr: Excessive exaltation of the synodical traditions, especially of the seven Synods, and of the Fathers, and the infallibility of the Church. He objects this to the Greeks as though they despised the holy Scriptures. But with what solid argument the objector has seen this! For the Greeks first of all venerate the holy Bibles, and above all the New Testament, from which on appointed days they read the pericopes: the readers and clergy read from the Old Testament in the middle of the Church while the other hearers sit; a reader or deacon reads from the Apostles in the middle of the Church while the rest stand with heads covered; and the Gospel is read only by a priest, a deacon or a bishop within the holy Bema. Nor was it necessary to insert in the professions of faith those things about which no doubt has ever been raised. And it is a poor argument to say: here no mention is made of the Bibles, therefore they are excluded from veneration and from the faith to be given them.

units.la: Tu praeterea addis; Differentia realis operationum divinarum a substantia Dei, quae fuit opinio Gregorii Palamae, Philothei Coccini Patriarchae, & aliorum, condemnata tamen ab iisdem Graecis, & Patriarchis: sed cui bono? Tu videris. An unquam audisti Grae-
units.tr: You further add: the real difference between the divine operations and the substance of God, which was the opinion of Gregory Palamas, of Philotheus Coccinus the Patriarch, and of others, yet condemned by the same Greeks and Patriarchs. But to what purpose? You must see to that. Have you ever heard of the Greek

units.la: Græcos omnes semper tum antiquos, tum recentiores, continuatim a fronte simul, & occipitio oculatos adeo fuisse, vt nunquam a recto aberrauerint? Fuerunt in eo genere hominum pleriq; experti, ad disciplinas periti, natura sagacissimi, rerum Ecclesiasticarum experientissimi. Non nego, Sicuti nec inter eos fuisse tyrones, indociles, inscios rerum omnium, Glauco stupidiores, Corœbo stultiores, quorum si effata in vnum colligere, & singula ab illis contra Ecclesiam Romanam dictata tentaveris, vt dissidium comprobes, næ tu illis stultior, pace tua dixerim, reputareris. Non facit dissidium, quidquid vnusquisque inconfiderate, & secreto ab alijs coquit, sed quod sapientiorum, & doctiorum Præsulum consensus non sine sui Patriarchæ approbatione ab omnibus excipitur, & defenditur, quæ paucissima admodum fuerint. Et hæc regula sit cuicunque similia dijudicandi in se onus assumenti.
units.tr: that all the Greeks, both ancient and more recent, have always had eyes at the front and back of the head, so that they never strayed from the right path? Among that race of men there were many who were experienced, skilled in the disciplines, most keen by nature, and very experienced in ecclesiastical affairs. I do not deny that among them there were also novices, the untaught, the ignorant of everything, more dull than Glaucus and more foolish than Coroebus. If you should gather their sayings into one heap, and try to prove the quarrel by taking each thing they said against the Roman Church, then, with respect to you, I would think you more foolish than them. What creates a quarrel is not whatever each man thinks up carelessly and privately on his own, but what is received and defended by all as the agreed view of the wiser and more learned prelates, with the approval of their Patriarch; and such views are very few indeed. Let this be the rule for anyone who takes on himself the task of judging such matters.

units.la: Quid porro deseruiunt illa annexa; Fiducia propria iustitia, ac operum merita præcipue eleemosynarum. &c. An hæc etiam diffidium augent? Fortasse tibi oculatissimo. Ita est. Nos qui non ita præacute conspicimus, iudicamus hæc, consensionem Allatij, non Heterodoxorum dissidia cum Romana Ecclesia magis, ac magis corroborare, ac stabilire. Cui enim clam non est, Græcos vniuersos, siue illi Schismati, siue recto dogmati addicti sunt, corpus Christi sub speciebus panis, & vini,Crucem, Deum Trinum, atque vnum veneratione latriæ, Deiparam Virginem hyperduliæ, Sanctorum imagines, siue Lipsana, & Sanctos ipsos dulię adorare, reliqua autem ad sacra ministeria deseruientia in maximo honore habere, quod itidem eodem consilio facit Romana Ecclesia. Hinc poteras parcere similia exscribendi, notandique labori. Præterea illud quoque adnoto commilites hosce, tuos, quibus tu innixus, cum aliquid, quod arriserit contra Romanam Ecclesiam, vel ab ipsa diuersum occinunt, quasi votis tuis respondentes pergratos accedere venerandos augustosque, cum silent, vel contra te tinniunt, molles, eneruesque, quasi quassabilia quædam iacere, ac si nullius essent nominis, despectabiles. Hinc statuo in constituendis rebus fidei, non quod verum est, sed quod volupe est, & arriserit, inquiri. Amamus nos, vt verum fatear, non dogmata, ex quo animi propensio vniuscuiusque dignoscitur. De bonis operibus, de libero arbitrio, nullum vnquam reperi, qui variationem inter Græcos, & Latinos alicuius momenti commemoret .
units.tr: Moreover, what do those added phrases serve? Trust in one's own righteousness, and the merits of works, especially of almsgiving, etc. Do these too increase the quarrel? Perhaps so to you, who see most sharply. Indeed so. We who do not see so keenly judge that these things, and not the disagreements of the heterodox with the Roman Church, strengthen and establish more and more the agreement of Allatius. For who does not know that all the Greeks, whether they are attached to that schism or to sound doctrine, adore the body of Christ under the species of bread and wine, the Cross, the triune and one God with the worship of latria, the Virgin Mother of God with hyperdulia, and the images of the saints, or their relics, and the saints themselves with dulia; and that they hold the other things that serve the sacred ministries in the highest honour, which the Roman Church likewise does with the same purpose? Hence you could have spared yourself the labour of copying out and noting such things. I further observe that these fellow soldiers of yours, on whom you lean, when they sing out something that pleases them against the Roman Church, or something different from it, come forward as venerable and august, as if answering your wishes, most welcome; but when they are silent, or ring against you, they are feeble and effete, like missiles that are thrown but are of no account, and are despicable. Hence I determine that in settling matters of faith, what is inquired after is not what is true but what is pleasing and agreeable. To tell the truth, we love not doctrines, but this shows the bent of each man's mind. On good works and on free will I have never found anyone who records any difference of importance between the Greeks and the Latins.

units.la: Nimia exaltatio Traditionum Synodicarum, septem praeterea Synodorum, & Patrum Ecclesiaeque infallibilitas. Et post verba Ieremiae subdit; Vide imperitiam, & infscitiam Patriarchae linguam sanctam non aspernentis modo, verum etiam schismata eidem imputantis. Vide quomodo tractat testem suum alias facundissimum, cuius auctoritate toties consensum Allatij conuellere nisus est. Dicat porro Opponens, quomodo Græci vel schismatici excludant scripturas, cum dicunt se recipere Synodos, Doctores Ecclesiae, Interpretesq; divinitus inspiratae scripturae. & unde nam elicitur id ex verbis Patriarchae ;
units.tr: Excessive exaltation of the synodical traditions, moreover of the seven Synods and of the Fathers, and the infallibility of the Church. And after the words of Jeremiah he adds: See the inexperience and ignorance of a Patriarch who not only does not despise the holy language but even imputes schisms to it. See how he handles his own witness, otherwise most eloquent, by whose authority he has so often tried to overthrow Allatius's agreement. Let the objector say further how the Greeks, or schismatics, exclude the Scriptures, when they say that they receive the Synods, the teachers of the Church, and the interpreters of divinely inspired Scripture. And whence is that drawn from the words of the Patriarch?

units.la: Contentio sanctarum Imaginum in hac Urbe, & divinarum reliquiarum ab Hebrais initium habuit, & schismata, quae apud nos sunt, quae multa varijque generis sunt, Lutheranorum[?], ut fama fert, pietatis simulatione introduxerunt, ac disseminarunt. Hic apponit Iudaeis contemptum Imaginum, & Reliquiarum, & schismatum inter Græcos, & Lutheranos appingit, quod plane verum est, si historiae non fallunt. Repete ab initio Iconoclastarum historiam, perpendeque Lutheranorum dogmata. Ergo Patriarcha linguam sanctam non aspernatur modo, verum etiam schismata eidem inepte imputat. Et hoc ne est ex principiis veris conclusionem elicere? Quidquid sit de sequentibus capitibus de differentia reali operationum, & proprietatum divinarum a substantia Dei, fiducia propriæ iustitiæ, ac operum meritis, præcipue eleemosynarum. qui bene verba admetitur,Græcam Ecclesiam cum Pontificiis, non cum Reformatis convenire reperiet.
units.tr: The contention over the holy images in this city, and over the divine relics, had its beginning among the Hebrews, and the schisms that are among us, which are many and of various kinds, the Lutherans, as report has it, introduced and spread under a pretence of piety. Here he charges the Jews with contempt for images and relics, and charges the Greeks and the Lutherans with schisms, which is plainly true, if histories do not lie. Go back to the beginning of the history of the Iconoclasts, and weigh the doctrines of the Lutherans. So the Patriarch not only does not despise the holy language, but also foolishly imputes schisms to it. And is this not drawing a conclusion from true premises? Whatever be said of the following chapters on the real difference between the operations and properties of God and the substance of God, on trust in one's own righteousness and the merits of works, especially of almsgiving, whoever weighs the words well will find that the Greek Church agrees with the Papists, not with the Reformed.

units.la: Septenarius Sacramentorum numerus. Ieremias Patriarcha hunc numerum inportunius defendit. Non effugit autem censuram Allatij, eo quod reliqua præter Baptismum, & sacram cœnam Sacramenta instituto Ecclesiæ tantum assignat. De Sacramentorum numero, & de eorum institutione, & gratia, Græca, & Latina Ecclesia consentiunt. Quare discursus hic ad convellendum consensum non adeo iuvat oppositorem. Sed hoc est non veterum, sed recentiorum Græcorum dogma. Ioannes quidam Damascenus vir octavi[?] seculi, cum Christianam omnem Theologiam, eo opere, quod de Orthodoxa fide scripsit, complexus sit, illam [illegible, ~2 words] divisionem nullus tradidit. Latinorum aliqua fortasse æmulatio eos ad hunc septenarium mysteriorum numerum, ne aliquare illis inferiores esse viderentur, deduxit. Sunt verba Dallæi. Ergo Græci etiam recentiores, ut Latinis non sint inferiores in aliquo. ergo conformant se cum illis, & procurant consensum. De Sacramentis, & eorum antiquitate diximus supra contra Hottingerum; nunc in gratiam opponentium nonnulla addemus, ut quam antiqua sit mysteriorum in Ecclesia traditio dignoscatur: Tertullianus lib. de Refurrect. cap. 9. ubi explicat, quid homini in carne fit, cum anima eius Deo allegitur. Caro abluitur, ut anima in-maculetur. En Baptismum. Caro unguitur, ut anima consecretur, Caro signatur, ut anima muniatur, Caro manus impositione obunbratur, ut eo anima illius illuminetur. En Confirmationem. Caro corpore, & sanguine Christi vescitur, ut & anima de Deo saginetur. En Eucharistiam. &c cap. 9. Caro hominis, quam Deus manibus suis ad imaginem suam struxit. &c. quam Sacramentis suis, disciplinisque vestiuit, haeccine non resurget? Et libro de Praescriptionibus adversus Haereticos capite 40. Tingit, & ipse quosdam utique credentes, & fideles suos: expiationem peccatorum de lauacro repromittit, & sic adhuc initiat mythrae: signat illic in frontibus milites suos: celebrat, & panis oblationem. Ambrosius libro de iis, qui mysteriis initiantur cap. 7. Repete quia accepisti, signaculum Spirituale, Spiritum sapientiae, & intellectus, Spiritum consilij, & virtutis, Spiritum cognitionis, & piepietatis, Spiritum sancti timoris, & serua quod accepisti. Signauit te Deus Pater, confirmauit te Christus Dominus, & dedit pignus Spiritus in cordibus tuis. Et cap. sequenti. His abluta plebs dues insignibus ad Christi contendit altaria, depositis inueterati erroris exuuijs, renouata in Aquilae iuuentutem coeleste illud festinat adire conuiuium. Et lib. 3. de Sacramentis. Sequitur Speciale signaculum, quod audistis hodie legi: quia post fontem superest, vt persectio fiat, quando ad inuocationem Sacerdotis Spiritus sanctus infunditur. Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Catechesi Mystagogica 3. Nobis, postquam ex aquis sacri lauacri ascendimus, datum est Chrisma, quod imaginem gerit illius, quo vnctus est Christus: Et Catechesi 4. Beati Pauli doctrina satis poterit vos efficere certissimos de diuinis mysteriis, quae vobis donata sunt, qui facti estis Christi corporis, & sanguinis compartices. De Chrismate Origenes ad caput 6. Epistolae ad Romanos; Omnes baptizati sumus secundum typum Ecclesiae traditum in aquis ipsis visibilibus, & Chrismate visibili: Eusebius Caesariensis Hist. libro 6. cap. 35. Nouatus morbo tandem elapsus, neque cetera, quibus post Baptismum secundum Ecclesiae canonem imbui oportuerat, acquisiuit, neque sigillo ab Episcopo obsignatus fuit. Quae quidem nequaquam potitus, quomodo quaeso Spiritum sanctum Elum[?] adeptus? Synodus Laodicena Can. 39. Oportet eos, qui illuminantur, post Baptisma inungi supercoelesti Chrismate, & esse regni coelestis participes. Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Catechesi 3. Mystagogica. Sicut panis Eucharistiae post illam sancti Spiritus invocationem non est amplius panis communis, sed Christi corpus; sic-sacrum hoc unguentum non amplius est unguentum nudum, neque si quis appellare velit commune, postquam iam consecratum est, sed est Chrisma Christi, quod adventu Spiritus sancti per ipsius divinitatem energiam habet. quo frons, & alij sensus corporis tui symbolice inunguntur: & corpus quidem isto visibili unguento perungitur, anima vero sacro vivificoque Spiritu sanctificatur. Ac primum quidem —fronti illinitur, ut eum abstergat a vobis pudorem, quem primus homo transgressor perpetuo circumferebat, simulque efficiat, ut possitis vultu non velato gloriam Domini intueri. Theodoretus ad caput i. Canticorum; Sacri Baptismatis mysterium recordare, in quo qui initiantur, post Sathana abnegationem, & Dei consessionem, veluti signo, & nota quadam regiae spiritualis unguenti Chrismate inuncti, sub ea visibili unguenti specie invisibilem sanctissimi Spiritus gratiam suscipiunt.
