But now it has become the usage in the Roman Church that infants are not confirmed until they reach the use of reason, which happens about the seventh year of age. For in the early Church, when confirmation was customarily conferred on little children outside danger of death, as well as on adults at Easter and Pentecost, and when bishops were present, afterwards, as the Church grew and baptism began to be administered at all seasons of the year, it came about that infants were confirmed at a more convenient time immediately after baptism. The bishop blesses the matter of this confirmation, both in the Greek and in the Latin Church. Granted; but in the Greek Church a priest anoints, whereas in the Latin this is forbidden to a priest and claimed for the bishop. When the minister has the faculty, the sacrament conferred by him is valid. And that the Pontiffs have granted this faculty to certain churches, I learn from the decree of Eugenius IV in the Council of Florence: It is read that sometimes, by dispensation of the Apostolic See, for a reasonable and very urgent cause, a simple priest has administered the sacrament of confirmation with chrism consecrated by a bishop. See the passage of Gregory the Great. This is the doctrine of the Greek and Latin theologians, and since it is the same, we draw from it a unanimous agreement on the conferring of chrism, not a dissension. But here one may be astonished at Luther, Melanchthon, Calvin, the Magdeburg Centuriators, and the rest, who remove the sacrament of chrism from the number of sacraments of the Eastern and Western Church, on the ground that it was made by the laying on of hands, that it is a wholly idle ceremony, that its power is invented, that it contributes to the increase of grace conferred in baptism for innocence, that the Word of God does not promise the presence of the Holy Spirit in it, and that it is not read in any but Western writers. And yet that it confers grace, like the other sacraments, is read in Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius of Caesarea, the Synod of Laodicea, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory Nazianzen, Epiphanius, John Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Isidore of Pelusium, Theodoret, and among more recent writers, Theophylact, Oecumenius, Balsamon, Nicetas Choniates, Symeon of Thessalonica, Jeremias, Patriarch of Constantinople, and others, whose words, since they are in the public domain, each may seek for himself if he likes. But there is a difference in this as well. Indeed, rather an agreement. For since it does not harm the essence of the sacrament, it matters little whether it is conferred immediately after baptism, or after six years or more. For it is said that even today in Spain boys of two or three years old are confirmed. So children and infants in danger of death before the age of seven are most rightly confirmed, since they are capable of confirmation and worthy of it.

units.la: Panis enzymi necessitas. Non attendit Allatius, quid hic vel ille contra Græcæ Eclesiæ asserta verà pronunciet, & potissimum si ex eorum genere sint, qui eiurata Græcorum religione, novis sese opinionibus manciparunt, quorum præcipuorum catalogum, scriptis etiam indicatis, loco opportuno intexuit. Hoc apud Græcos certum est, in Azymo, & in Enzymo verum corpus Christi effici: idem tradunt Latini. Et hæc concordia non est, etiam si nonnulli in ea Ecclesia negant, quos uti Schismaticos, & Hæreticos reiicimus? Sed Allatius vocat hoc septimum in Triodio errorem. Et nunc iterum repeto. & qui possum respondere huic dicto, cum plane hæresis sit? Sed auctoritatem libri cum aliter respondere idonee nequit, elevare studet. Et auctoritatem libri elevare, in quo similis error continetur, respondere quæstióni non est? Quæstio est inter Græcos schismaticos, & Latinos Pontificios, in Azymo ne an in Enzymo Cristus confecerit. In hac quæstione Græci Schismatici argumentantur; si Cristus confecit in Enzymo, ergo Enzymus de necessitate Sacramenti est, inde sequi Azymum non esse materiam accommodam, tanquam contra institutum Christi introductam ad consecrandum. Pontificius licet praetendat, nec praeter rem, Christum in Azymo confecisse, moderatiorem se gerit, & pronunciat, cum utrumque panis Enzymus & Azymus panis sit, utrumque, sive acceptum a Christo, sive non acceptum æquebene consecrandum venire. Expunxi, signauiq; errorem recentis Schismatici Xanthopuli, qui Synaxaria illa concinnauit, & inspersis erroribus, & hæresibus proprijs commaculauit. Illa Synaxaria, cum laterent in tenebris, tandem his postremis temporibus e latebris eruta, nebulone quopiam, sive Xanthopulus ita, ut sunt, ea composuerit, sive ab hoc impostore erroribus illis conspurcata, procurante, in lucem prodierunt, in usum Græcæ Ecclesiæ. Quod probaui firmiter, eo potissimum, quod in Synaxario post diem Pentecostes sermonem habens de Spiritu sancto dicit, illum procedere ex Patre solo; in alia postmodum eiusdem Synaxarij editione omissa est vocula, solo. Quæ hæc infantia est, si erat in Archetypo, quare in una editione omissum est, si non erat, quare additum? Hinc arguebam, Synaxarijs illis ita peruersis nullam fidem habendam esse. notauique errores in illis contentos. Sic eleuauit auctor[?]-ritaritatem errorum adiunctorum, non Triodij, cuius habentur pluribus in locis, & vrbibus antiquissima exemplaria, in quibus similes errores nunquam conspexeris. Adde præterea dictorum Synaxariorum ob similes errores pessimam eorum famam apud Græcos esse, vt in nullis Ecclesijs, saltem paucis eorum lectio admittatur. Quæ adnectis ex Verino, non sunt tanti, vt responsionem mereantur. Habebit argutulus ille Grammatista ab illis, quorum res agitur, suas notas. cum illa non pertineant ad Allatij consensum. De suffocati abstinentia indaizante, nihil est quod dicam. Sed eam obiecisti tuis Græcis. Græcis nempe stultissimis, qui similibus delirijs in vniuersam Ecclesiam excitant tragœdias, & inanibus tumultibus concutiunt omnia. Adde, similem suffocatorum abstinentium non fuisse apud omnes Græcos in vsu, vt refert Petrus Patriarcha Antiochenus Epistola ad Michaelem Cerularium.
units.tr: The necessity of unleavened bread. Allatius does not consider what this or that man says against the assertions of the Greek Church, especially when they belong to the sort who, having renounced the religion of the Greeks, gave themselves over to new opinions. Allatius has woven a catalogue of the chief of these into his work, with their writings indicated, in a suitable place. It is certain among the Greeks that the true body of Christ is made both in azymos and in enzymos, and the Latins teach the same. Is this not agreement, even if some in that Church deny it, and we reject them as schismatics and heretics? But Allatius calls this the seventh error in the Triodion. And again I repeat: how can I answer this statement, since it is plainly a heresy? But since he cannot answer properly in any other way, he strives to discredit the authority of the book. Is it an answer to the question to discredit the authority of a book in which a similar error is contained? The question is between the schismatic Greeks and the Papists, the Latins, whether Christ consecrated in azymos or in enzymos. On this question the Greek schismatics argue: if Christ consecrated in enzymos, then enzymos is necessary to the sacrament, and it follows that azymos is not a suitable matter, being introduced for consecration contrary to the institution of Christ. The Papist, though he claims, and not without reason, that Christ consecrated in azymos, conducts himself more moderately and declares that, since both enzymos and azymos are bread, both can be consecrated equally well, whether or not they were received from Christ. I have struck out and marked the error of the recent schismatic Xanthopulus, who compiled those Synaxaria and stained them with his own errors and heresies. Those Synaxaria lay hidden in darkness, and in these last times were at length dragged out of their hiding places and came to light for the use of the Greek Church, whether some rogue composed them as they are, or they were defiled with those errors by this impostor, who arranged it. I have firmly proved this, chiefly because in the Synaxarion, speaking of the Holy Spirit after the day of Pentecost, it says that he proceeds from the Father alone; in a later edition of the same Synaxarion the little word alone has been omitted. What childishness is this? If it was in the archetype, why was it omitted in one edition? If it was not, why was it added? From this I argued that no trust should be placed in those Synaxaria, so perverted, and I noted the errors contained in them. Thus the author has discredited the authority of the added errors, not of the Triodion, of which very old copies are held in many places and cities, in which you will never find similar errors. Add also that these Synaxaria have a very bad reputation among the Greeks because of similar errors, so that in no churches, or in only a few, are they admitted to be read. What you add from Verinus is not worth an answer. That quibbling little grammarian will have his marks from those whose affair it is, since those things do not pertain to Allatius' consensus. As for abstinence from what has been strangled, I have nothing to say. But you have objected it to your Greeks. Indeed to the most foolish Greeks, who stir up tragedies throughout the whole Church over similar delusions, and throw everything into confusion with empty tumults. Add that a similar abstinence from strangled meat was not in use among all the Greeks, as Peter, Patriarch of Antioch, reports in his letter to Michael Cerularius.

units.la: Grana aquæ calidæ in sacro Calice jam confecrato. Allatius notans in Ecclesia Græca bis aquam Calici immiscceri, frigidam ante consecrationem, calidam post consecrationem. Praxim in Ecclesia Græca de aqua feruida immiscenda sacris Mysterijs vere accurateque adnotauit Allatius, Opponens tamen alia omnia, non dissidium tentat. Quid enim refert, si ea in sacris vtuntur Græci, Latini non item? Quod articulum fidei lædit? Qua ratione iugulantur Pontificij sub fulmine anathematis, vrgentes mixtionem aquæ? Annon hoc idem faciunt Græci, qui sub anathematis fulmine iugulant Armenos, aliosque, qui in sacris celebrandis mysterijs vino aquam non miscent? Adeatur Canon sexagesimus secundus Trullanus, & in eum Commentaria Zonaræ, & Balsamonis, quibus addi potest Alexius Aristenus. Nec dum capio, quid hoc ad dissidium faciat. Quæ adduntur de signis, & figuris ex Chemnitio prorsus sunt [illegible, ~10 letters].
units.tr: Grains of hot water in the sacred chalice already consecrated. Allatius, noting that in the Greek Church water is mixed into the chalice twice, cold before consecration and hot after consecration. Allatius has truly and accurately recorded the practice in the Greek Church of mixing hot water into the sacred mysteries. But while opposing all the other things, he does not attempt a dissent. For what does it matter if the Greeks use this in the sacred rites and the Latins do not? Does it harm an article of faith? On what ground are the Papists slaughtered under the thunderbolt of anathema, urging the mixing of water? Do not the Greeks do the same, who under the thunderbolt of anathema slaughter the Armenians and others who do not mix water with wine in celebrating the sacred mysteries? Let the sixty-second Canon of Trullo be consulted, and the commentaries of Zonaras and Balsamon on it, to which Alexius Aristenus may be added. I still do not see what this has to do with dissent. What is added about signs and figures is entirely from Chemnitz [illegible, about ten letters].

units.la: Ieiunij præcipue quadragesimalis non sine Latinorum reprehensione rigidior celebratio.
units.tr: A rather rigid celebration of the fast, especially of Lent, not without the reproach of the Latins.

units.la: Rigidiora esse apud Græcos ieiunia, & maiora, non nego. Quid tum? Etiam antiquis temporibus, cum Ecclesiæ non scindebantur, ieiuniorum modus non erat vnus, sed diuersus pro religione Ecclesiarum. Videndus est Irenæus, Socrates, alij, quorum testimonia alias ad diuersas ieiuniorum consuetudines adduximus. Videri etiam potest Philostorgius de rigida apud antiquos ieiuniorum obseruatione. Addo nunc Gregorium Proto-syncellum aduersus Marcum Ephesium. Οὐκ οἶδεν ὅτω ὡς ἔοικεν, ὁ ἡμῶς[?] ἐξῆς, ὅτι καὶ ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ μεγαλοπόλει διάφορον ἔθη εἰσὶ, νησεία τι[?], καὶ ἐκκλησιαστικὴ τάξις παρα-λαμβάνομεν. καὶ γὰρ οἱ μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς δεκάτης τετάρτης τὸ νοεμβρίου ἀρχὴν νηστεύειν τὸ πασαρεκοντάμερον, οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς ἑκτῆς τὸ δεκεμβρίου, οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς εἰκοστῆς, καὶ ἑτέροι ἢ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς τὸ μαῖε ἕως τῶν ἑορτὴν τῆς Χριστοῦ ἀναλήψεως, καὶ ἄλλοι ἄλλας νη-στείας. καὶ οἱ μὲν τὰ Σάββατα ἢ τὰς κυριακὰς τῆς ἁγίας καὶ μεγάλης πασαρεκοστῆς ἰχθύας ἐσθίουσιν, ἑτέρῳ ἢ, καὶ ἄλλας ἡμέρας, ἄλλοι ἢ τέτων ἀπο-χνῇ. τί οὖν; ἀσυμφώνως, ἢ ᾧ τὸ πίστιν ἐρεμῷ[?]; ὁμοίως, καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησιαστικαῖς τάξεσιν διαφο-ρὰν ἔχειν ἐρίν. καὶ γὰρ ἡ καθολικὴ Ἐκκλησία ἐν ταῖς ἀλμφοδίαις ἄλλῳ τάξιν ἔχει, καὶ ἄλλῳ αἱ μεγάλαι μοναὶ, καὶ ἄλλῳ τὰ πουχασήεια, καὶ ἄλλῳ αἱ κοσμικαὶ Ἐκκλησίαι. Ϛ οἱ Ταβεννησιώ-ται δὲ ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ, Ϛ μιᾷ μονῇ διαφόρως νησείας, διαφόρως φαλμωδίας ἐπιτέλουν. Καὶ οἱμὲν αὐτῶν δύο ἡμερῶν ἐνηστεύουν, οἱ δὲ ἐβδομά-δα. καὶ οἱμὲν ἀφ' ἑσπέρας, οἱ ἢ ἀπὸ μίσης νυκτὸς τὴν ὑμνωδίαν ἐπιτέλουν. ὁμοίως καὶ ἐν τῇ τῶν ἀκειμήτων μονῇ. Καὶ ὁ ἁγιώ ἢ Συμεὼν ὁ συλίτης πασαρεκοντα ἡμερῶν νησεῖαν ἐπιτέλεσε, μηδὲ-οὐ γὰρ ἀγγελμος[?]. Ο μοίως Ϛ Δανιὴλ ὁ ὅσιο. ἀλλ' ἐδῆς ταῦτα ἐνεκάλεσέ ποτε μίχρι Ϛ τήμερον. τὰ Καινόνος ἢ λέγοντος τὰς ὁδηγοκαλάς πάσας νησεύειν, ἡμᾶς καταλύομεν ὅσας δὴ καὶ καλύομεν. Λαπῖνοι ἢ πάσας νησεύσιν, εἰ μὴ τῶν Χειτουγῶν ἡμέρα τύχῃ. Καὶ πάλιν τὸ Καν ὁν ὁ λέγοντος, τὰ Σάββάζε μὴ νηστεύειν, Σωκράτης ὁ ἱστορικὸς τῆς Ἐκκλησίας Σωζο-μένος δὲ ὢν φησὶν ἐν τοῖς ἐκκλησίαις τὰ Σάββατα νηστεύ-σιν. ἀλλ' οἱ ταῦτα τότε ὄντες τῷ ἐκ ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ [?] ἐνεκάλεσε[?]. ἤδη δὲ ὅτι τὸ ἐξαφοσον τὴν νηστῶν, καὶ τὴν ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ [?] ἐξ ἀ[?]ζάγ[?]. Θαυμάζει δ' αὐτῆς τὸ τὸν, πῶς καὶ τὸ ἐξαφοσον τῆς γλωσσης, καὶ τὸ τῆς ἐνδυμάτων ἐκ ἐνεκάλεσιν, ἡ πῶς ἐκεῖνοι τὸ χόνυ κλίνονται. ἀνεσσυνδεῖσθαι, καὶ ἀνεσσ... τῷ ἀρχαίᾳ τάξιν, ἡμᾶς ἢ ἐκ ἔτος. Nescit ergo, ut plane videtur, eximius hic vir, varios in hac etiam urbe magna Constantinopoli servari mores, ieiuniorumque, ac ritum Ecclesiasticorum esse diversitates. Nanque ante Christi natalem sunt, qui ordiuntur ieiunium ex die decimo quinto Novembris, alij ex die sexto Decembris, alij ex vicesimo. Ad honorem quoque Ascensionis Christi quidam ieiunare incipiunt ex Kalendis Maij, & alia ab alijs ieiunia observantur. Nam & ipso sancta, ac magna Quadragesimae tempore diebus Sabbati, ac Dominica multi vescuntur piscibus, alijs quoque alij diebus. sunt etiam, qui ijs omnino se abstinent. Quid ergo? Dicemus ne illos fide etiam inter se differentire? In ritibus quoque Ecclesiasticis consuetudo est varia. Nam Constantinopolitana maior Ecclesia in celebrandis officijs alio more utitur, alio vero maiora monasteria, alio minora ad quietem accommodata, denique alia Sacerdotum secularium Ecclesia. Quin Tabernaenesiotæ in uno eodemque Cœnobio varios ieiunandi, psallendique modos habebant, alijs per biduum ieiunantibus, alijs per hebdomadam: & his quidem ad vesperam, illis vero de media nocte sacros hymnos canentibus: quod siebat etiam in Monasterio Acœmetorum. Sanctus Simeon Stylita quadraginta diebus ieiunium nihil omnino degustans compleuit: idem beatus quoqs Daniel præstitit, hæc tamen nemo ad hunc diem in crimen vocauit. Iubet Canon, omnibus sextis feriis esse ieiunandum: nos quibusdam non ieiunamus: Latini vero nunquam eius diei soluunt ieiunium, nisi Natalis Domini dies contingat. Rursus præcipiente Canone, non esse ieiunandum Sabbato, Socrates, qui fuit ante Synodum tertiam; in occiduis, inquit, partibus ieiunant diebus Sabbati: nec tamen qui illis fuere temporibus crimini hoc dederunt: quod scirent varios ieiuniorum & rituum mores non inferre differentiam fidei. Mirum porro fuerit, cur ipse vir, & linguæ diuersitatem, & varium indumentorum genus vitio non verterit, aut quod illi flectant genua, cum adorant, & orant, seruantes morem antiquitatis, nos minime. Scite responsum ad tua. Dic tu aptius, accommodatius, cohærentius. Ne turberis animo: tum enim ad suum munus fungendum non bene affectus, aduersus rigidiora ieiunia, & mitiora non sine reprehensione LaLatinorü insonabit. Sed Proto-syncellus iste Pontificius est. scripsit pro Romano contra Ephesium. Quasi Pontificij, quia Pontificij nihil dicant ad rem, omniaque eorum, vel sola ista exceptione Pontificiorum reijcienda, & fides eorum abigenda sit. Ubi res ipsa loquitur, & Historici eam classico buccinant, morose Pontificiorum errata repudiantur. Allega tu contraria, si potes, & palmarium habe. Licet prima Synodus Sisinnium Nauatianum, uti non bene sentientem in nonnullis improbauerat, eius tamen auxilio ad compescendos Arianos utebatur. Origenes ob errores suos in antiqua Ecclesia improbatus est, veruntamen libri eius contra Celsum, & in sacras Scripturas Commentaria probabantur. Pötificijs a Reformatis nihil conceditur. Sed Reformati sive aiant, sive negent, parum curant Pontificij, qui veritatem quærunt, & comprehensam mordicus tenent, neque Iamijs[?] hæreticorum, neque sepulchrorum spectris territantur. Sed quid ieiunia ad dissidium? Etiamnum in Ecclesia Romana varia apud pios religiososque viros ieiunia mitiora rigidioraque passim obseruantur, non ideo tamen Ecclesia illa diuisa a semetipsa reputatur, nec pars ieiunans non ieiunantes a se excludit. Redige in memoriam illa Pauli ad Romanos; Is qui manducat non manducantem non spernat; & qui non manducat, manducantem non iudicet: Deus enim illum assumpsit. Et, qui manducat, Domino manducat: gratias enim agit Deo: & qui non manducat, Domino non manducat, & gratias agit Deo. Mirum te uini pocula, & offarum condimenta ad probandum diffidium in medium non attulisse.
units.tr: I do not deny that the fasts among the Greeks are stricter and greater. So what? Even in ancient times, when the Churches were not divided, the manner of fasting was not one, but differed according to the custom of the Churches. Irenaeus and Socrates should be consulted, and others whose testimonies I have elsewhere adduced concerning the diverse customs of fasting. Philostorgius may also be seen on the strict observance of fasts among the ancients. Now I add Gregory the Protosyncellus against Mark of Ephesus. [Greek passage] Evidently he does not know that even in this great city there are different customs, and we receive various ecclesiastical orders. For some begin to fast the whole forty days from the fourteenth of November, others from the sixth of December, others from the twentieth, and others from the beginning of May until the feast of Christ's Ascension, and others keep other fasts. Some eat fish on the Saturdays and Sundays of the holy and great Quadragesima, others on other days, and others abstain from these altogether. What then? Shall we say that they differ in faith among themselves? Likewise there is variety also in ecclesiastical orders. For the universal Church follows one order in the vigils, the great monasteries another, the parish churches another, and the secular churches another. The Tabernesiotes, in one and the same monastery, performed the fasting and psalmody in different ways, some fasting for two days, others for a week, and some singing the hymns in the evening, others from midnight. The same was done in the monastery of the Akoimetoi. Saint Symeon Stylites completed a fast of forty days, tasting nothing at all; the blessed Daniel did the same. Yet no one has brought these things into accusation to this day. The Canon of Trullo commands that every Friday be fasted; we do not fast on certain of them; the Latins, indeed, never relax the fast of that day unless it falls on the Lord's Nativity. Again, although the Canon forbids fasting on the Sabbath, Socrates, who lived before the third Synod, says that in the western parts they fast on the Sabbath days; yet those who lived in those times did not charge them with this crime, because they knew that diverse customs of fasting and rites do not introduce a difference of faith. Indeed it would be strange why this man did not find fault with the diversity of language and the varied kinds of garments, or with the fact that they bend their knees when they adore and pray, keeping the custom of antiquity, while we do not. A fitting answer to your objections. Say something more apt, more suitable, more coherent. Do not be disturbed in mind: for a man not well disposed to performing his own duty will keep sounding out, not without reproach, against the stricter and milder fasts of the Latins. But this Protosyncellus is a Papist; he wrote for the Roman side against the Ephesian. As if the Papists' opinions were to be rejected simply because they are Papists, and everything they say should be cast out by this one exception, and their faith driven away. When the matter itself speaks, and the historians sound it with a trumpet, the errors of the Papists are rejected with peevishness. Adduce contrary evidence, if you can, and take the prize. Although the first Synod had disapproved Sisinnius the Novatian as not holding sound views in some matters, it nevertheless used his help in suppressing the Arians. Origen was condemned in the ancient Church for his errors, yet his books against Celsus and his commentaries on the sacred Scriptures were approved. Nothing is conceded by the Reformed to the Papists. But the Reformed, whether they affirm or deny, care little for the Papists, who seek the truth and hold fast what they have grasped, and are frightened neither by the gleanings of heretics nor by the specters of tombs. But what do fasts have to do with dissent? Even now in the Roman Church, among pious and religious men, milder and stricter fasts are everywhere observed, yet that Church is not regarded as divided from itself, nor does the fasting part exclude the non-fasting from itself. Recall those words of Paul to the Romans: He who eats, let him not despise him who does not eat; and he who does not eat, let him not judge him who eats: for God has received him. And, He who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who does not eat, does not eat to the Lord, and gives thanks to God. It is strange that you have not brought forward the cups of wine and the seasoning of morsels to prove the dissent.

units.la: Ad dogmata refero animarum παννυχισμὸν [?], seu peruigilationem. Concludatur, ergo ex dictis, omnia ad usque a principio dicta pro dissidio, cum dogma non attingerent, nullius momenti, & frustra, invitisque Musis consarcinata sunt, quæ erat melius silentio texisse, ut laborem legentibus diminueret. Veruntamen ritus, consuetudines, ceremonias, contra atque prætendit Opponens, dissidium non parere, Græci ipsi æque atque Pontificij cognoscunt, & tenent.
units.tr: I refer to the doctrines the all-night vigil of souls [παννυχισμόν], or keeping vigil. It follows, then, from what has been said that everything argued so far in support of the dissent, since it did not touch doctrine, is of no weight. It was stitched together in vain and against the wishes of the Muses, and it would have been better to pass over it in silence and spare the reader the labour. Yet ceremonies, customs and rites, contrary to what the Objector pretends, do not produce dissent. The Greeks themselves, no less than the Papists, recognise and hold them.

units.la: Legendus est inter alios Photius, Demetrius Chomatenus, Theophylactus, & alij, quos alibi laudavimus. Sed quando iam ad dogmata peruenimus videamus, an solidius, feliciusque cursum absoluerit. Peruigilationem in catalogo hæreticorum accenset Bellarminus. Et iure merito. Quis enim inter Catholicos eam tenuit? Multi Joannem Papam XXII. huius erroris insimulant. Sed ininsimulant. Contrarium siquidem tenuisse, luce meridiana clarius est. Quid de ea Marcus Ephesius, & alij Græci Schismatici asseruerint, alibi a nobis dictum est. Illam assignauit Græcis suis Caleca. Assignauerit. Legenda erant, quæ in contrarium attulit Allatius ex Patribus, nec non etiam Schismaticis Ecclesiæ Græcæ antiquioribus, & recentioribus in Tractatu de Purgatorio, & ex aliis eiusdem Ecclesiæ Doctoribus in Hottingero. quod ut probe intelligas, nomina hic apponam. units.tr: Photius, Demetrius Chomatenus, Theophylactus and others, whom we have praised elsewhere, should be read among the rest. But now that we have come to doctrines, let us see whether he has finished the course more solidly and happily. Bellarmine counts the vigil of souls among the heresies. And rightly so. For who among the Catholics held it? Many accuse Pope John XXII of this error. But that he held the contrary is clearer than the noonday light. What Mark of Ephesus and other Greek schismatics asserted about it I have said elsewhere. Caleca assigned it to his Greeks. Let him have assigned it. Rather, the things Allatius brought to the contrary should have been read: from the Fathers, from the older and more recent schismatic writers of the Greek Church in his Treatise on Purgatory, and from other teachers of the same Church collected in Hottinger. So that you may understand this clearly, I shall set down the names here. Anastasius, Patriarch of Antioch, Anagoge on the Hexaemeron, Oration 1. Andreas of Crete, Oration on St Nicholas, bishop of Myra in Lycia. Andreas the Hymnographer, Canon on St Nicholas. Angelus the Hymnographer, Canon on Holy Parasceve. An anonymous author, a poem on Mary, consort of the Roman emperor. Arsenius, Archbishop of Corfu, in praise of St Barbara. The author of the Life of Cosmas the Melodist. The author of the Life of Gregory of Decapolis. The author of the Commentary on the translation of the relics of St John Chrysostom. The author of the Life of St Maximus the Confessor. The author of the Life of St Pachomius. The author of the Praise of St Paul of Latros. The author of the Praise of St Procopius the Martyr. The author of the Life of St Theodore the Studite. units.tr: These things might suffice even for men of obstinate will, who have already come forth and been spread among the public. Nevertheless, at another time and for your benefit, so that stubbornness of mind may be laid down more and more, I will add the works of other teachers of the same Church who were not of the lowest rank: Athanasius of Alexandria, in the life and deeds of St Syncletica; Joseph the Monk, the least of men, in the praise of the holy Apostle Bartholomew; Ammonius the Monk, on the holy Sinaite monks; Sabas the Monk, in the life of St Joannicius; Theodore the Studite, in his Catechetical Oration on the Lord's day of Easter; Theodulus, Master of Thessalonica, in his Oration on St John the Baptist; the Emperor Manuel Palaeologus, in his Praise of Gabriel, Bishop of Thessalonica, his Praise of St Euphemia the martyr, his Praise of our holy Fathers and universal Teachers who took part in the seven holy and universal Synods, his Praise of David, Bishop of Thessalonica, and his Consolatory Oration on the death of his brother John; To these I will add the composers of hymns: Joseph, in his Canon on St Abercius; Isidore, on St Demetrius; Bartholomew, on the martyr Theodore; Basil, on St Nicholas; German, on St Mary of Egypt; John, on the hymn-writer Romanus; and Athanasius, on the holy martyrs Theodore and on St Joannicius the Younger.

units.la: Nihilominus nunc quoque, cum similis argumenti prodigus campus, ex effertissima similium opimitate plene, & cumulate exultaret, duorum in ea gente pannychismum hunc afferentium principum, & quorum auctoritatem non configet, neque proteret Opponens, Marci Ephesij, cuius alibi de eodem pro Pontificijs sententiam adduximus, diversam tamen ab his, & Nicetæ Stethati testimonijs evincam, pannychismum hunc nullum esse in Orientali Ecclesia, sed somnium, atque intemperiem Schismaticorum, non sibi usquequaque constantium. Marcus Ephesius Epistola ad Io-annem Palaeologum Imperatorem, quæ in-cipit; Δεξὸν τοι τὸ μικρὸν[?], scribit; τὰ αὐτὰ τὸ περιττὸν ἔχει, Ἀλλὰ ἡ λόγῳ παρεῖσα, καὶ φιλήσουν[?], ἵνα δὲ ἐν τύτοις ἄσωτον, καὶ ὠκύμορον ἐννοήσαντας, τ ἀληθὲς καὶ μόνιμον ἡδονὴν ζωτάλλυ[?], τ μαγεία[?], τ διδυκὴ[?], τ ἀνωλεθρον, ὧν ἐν-ταῦτα ὧδ' ἡ ψυχὴ θείοις λόγοις ξεφουλύν[?], καὶ θεωρήματα, ἐ καταφυσωσα τὸ κυέις ἐφὶ παντὸς, τῇ τε τῇ μελλόντων ἔπιδη χαίρειν. Μετὰ δὲ τὸ παρὸς ζωὴν ἐπιτυχεῖα τῆς τοῦ ἑαυτῶν εἰς ἀιω-νας ἀγαλλεῖ. φωνὴ γὰρ φησιν ἀγαλλιάσεως, καὶ σωτηρίας ἐν οικωνάις δηλῶν. Flores intuentibus voluptatem creant, sed verbo ocyus praetereunt, & expirant, ut in his instabilitatem, cito perituram considerantes, veram & perpetuo sibi constantem voluptatem conquiramus, beatam, sempiternam, & in omni ævo duraturam, qua perfruitur anima diuinis sermonibus, & speculationibus innutrita, & perpetuo in Domino delectatur, & futurorum bonorum spe gaudio completur. Veruntamen post hanc vitam quæ desiderauerat consecuta in omne tempus lætitiæ omnibus exultat. Vox siquidem, dicitur exultationis, & salutis in tabernaculis iustorum.
units.tr: Nevertheless, even now, since a field of a similar kind, lavish with the abundant richness of such authors, rejoices fully and abundantly in them, the Opponent cannot shake or overthrow the authority of two leading men of that nation who affirm this pannychism. One is Mark of Ephesus, whose opinion on the same matter, favourable to the Papists, we have cited elsewhere; yet it differs from theirs, and I will prove by the testimonies of Mark and of Nicetas Stethatus that this pannychism does not exist in the Eastern Church, but is a dream and an excess of the Schismatics, who are not consistent with themselves at all. Mark of Ephesus, in his letter to the Emperor John Palaeologus, which begins with the words "It is good...", writes: "Flowers create pleasure for those who look upon them, but they pass away more swiftly than a word and perish. So let us, considering in these things their instability and their swift ruin, seek out the true and enduring joy, the blessed and everlasting one that lasts through all ages, which the soul enjoys when it is nourished by divine words and contemplations and rejoices perpetually in the Lord, and is filled with joy in the hope of the good things to come. And after this life, the soul that has longed for these things obtains them and exults for all time in joy. For it is the voice of exultation and salvation in the tabernacles of the just."

units.la: Et in Ecphrasi animam agentis non inele-ganter descripta; Ὁ σοι ἡ δεβανικώπεοι[?], καὶ Φόδην ὀξὰς τὸ ἱερὸν ὅμμα ἐ τὸ ὁσίε ψυχὴν ἀνιῶ-ζαν εἰς ἡ ἐγνῆν ὄρθ[?], ἐ ἡμῖν ἐπεύχονταχ κοινωνῆ-ζαι καὶ τῆς θέας· ἢ οὐχ ὁρᾶς ἁρπάσας[?] ἀμβλέψας, οἶμαι, καὶ τῆς ἀχλύος αἰσθάνη κεκαθαρμένος.
units.tr: And in his vivid description of a soul in its death-agony, not inelegantly written: "O you who ... with the sacred eye ... the holy soul ascending to the place where it is known ... and we pray to share in the sight. Do you not see? Looking up, I think, and having been freed from the mist, you perceive it cleansed."

units.la: κόρην δὲ δόπτω περιστοιχῶν, μέσῳ τε ἀλοιν αἰγλέ-λοιν διαλημμένῳ, καὶ νεφῶν πνα ἰδλαν ἔχρᾶν ὁ τεχνίτης, καὶ ἐεαγὸν αὐτὸν κυανοειδῆ π ἀρδο,
units.tr: "... surrounding the pupil of the eye, held in the middle between two shining lights, and the artist made a kind of clouds, and sky dark blue ..."

units.la: Qui vero acriori, atque attentiori animo res contemplantur, & penetrant, & perspicaciores sunt a Deo sibi concesso sacro lumine, Sancti, animam in Cælum progredientem intuentur, orantque, ut nos quoque illius spectaculi participes efficiamur. Annon vides nunc? Vsurpas enim oculis, ut reor, & perspentisicis ex tenebris evolutus, eam puellæ eximiæ pulchritudine, venustaque forma prædita non absimilem, inter duos Angelos deprehensam. & speciem quandam nebularum effinxit artifex, & Cælum ipsum flore cærulei conspicuum. Qui pie sanctèq; vixit, post hanc vitam nancisciturea, quæ vitam agens desiderauerat in omne tempus duratura. sed nullus desiderat moerores, lacrymas, tormenta, flammas, quæ etiam si essent, non sunt sempiterna, & statim atque excesserit e vita ab Angelis veluti puella pura, munda in Cælum deportatur. Ruit ergo sententia Ephesij Pannychismus similis. Quid vero Stethatus in Tractatu suo de anima cap. 14.? fixis oculis excipe.
units.tr: Those who contemplate and penetrate things with a keener and more attentive mind, and who, by the sacred light granted them by God, are more perceptive, behold the soul as it progresses into heaven, and they pray that we too may be made partakers of that sight. Do you see it now? For, as I suppose, you take hold of it with your eyes, and, released from the darkness by your insight, you see it, not unlike a maiden of remarkable beauty and graceful form, caught between two angels; and the artist has fashioned a kind of cloud, and heaven itself, visible with the bloom of its blue. He who has lived piously and holily obtains after this life that which he desired while living, a good that will last for all time. But no one desires mourning, tears, torments, or flames; and even if these existed, they are not everlasting, and as soon as the soul departs from life it is carried up into heaven by the angels like a pure and clean maiden. Thus the pannychism of the Ephesian falls to the ground, being of a similar kind. But what does Stethatus say in his Treatise on the Soul, chapter 14? Take it in with fixed eyes.

units.la: Ποῖ φέρει; ἡ ψυχὴ μὴ θάνατον; ἢ τῶν ἐκδημούντων ψυχῶν ἀμὲν εἶσι καθαρεῖ, εὐώδης, Θεοειδῆς τε καὶ πληρεφορημένῳ δόξης ἐνδύσει, καὶ ἀκραφνεστάτῳ φω-τὸς, αἱ τῆς ἁγίων. καὶ λάμπτωσιν ἐκδημίως τὸ σῶ-ματος ὡς ἥλιος, ἐξ ἔργων δικαιοσύνης, καὶ σοφίας, καὶ κυδαγωγῆς. αὐτοὶ δὲ διὰ τῆς ἀπα-γόντων φίλων ἀγγέλων πρὸς τὸ πρῶτον φῶς τὸ ἅσπρον ἐόνιον, τὸ ἄυλον, τὸ καὶ ἀγγέλοις ἀκαταπόντων, αὐτὸν τὸν Θεὸν τὸν ἐν παρῇ, καὶ ὑφ' καὶ ἁγίῳ πνεύ-ματι δοξαζόμενον τε, καὶ φεσπωμένον ὑπὸ ἀπείρων δυνάμεων, οἷα δὴ ἄωρα φανὰ ζήτης τάξεως διὰ ἀπείρων φώτων ἀνέρχονται. ἐ ἐμυ-μύναι φεσπωθῶ τῷ Θεῷ τῆς δίξης αὐτῶ ἐν ἁγίῳ φόβῳ, καὶ χαρᾷ Θεῶ πνεύματος, παισα-μένων τὸν Χερουβὶμ τε, καὶ τὸν Σεραφὶμ, καὶ πασῶν τὸ ἄνω ἐν ζόμω, καὶ φόβῳ δυνάμεων, καὶ θαρ-σες πληρωσῶν ἀνερχομένας αὐτὰς. ΕΙΘ' ἅπως οἰ-κείως, ἐ καθαρῶς ἑκάστῃ τύπων ὡς φίλῳ φίλῃ σωμα-πεν ν ὑμαι Θεῷ ἑκάνῳ τοῦ τάγματος, ἐ τῆς δόξης καὶ σάτεως χαρισμα ἔλαβε διὰ τῆς τὲ ἁγίᾳ πνευ-ματῶ μετυσίας ἐν τῇ παρὰ ἔνσῃ ζωῇ, καὶ μεθ' ἔ τῇ τῶ πιστῶν ἐφανερώθη εἰς οἰκοδομίαν τὸ σώματος τὲ Χριστὲ. τύτῳ ἢ σωσάπτει), ὡς σωδιαιτᾶς αὐτὸ, καὶ συμφρᾶνεις, καὶ ἐπαναπαύσεως μέλ-λες (ἀ ἐν τῇ σκιᾷ τὴν πεύζων αὐτὸ μέχρι τῆς μελ-λόσης κοινῆς ἀποκατασώσεως πρὸς Θεὸν. αἱ ἢ ζω-φάδις, ἐ δεινῶς σκοτεινα ἐν φαύλων ἔργων, ἐ λόγων, ἐ νοημάτων, ἡδῆ τε ἐ ἐπὶ τῆς μάτων, καὶ διαθέσεων, αἱ τῆ ἀμβρωλῶν, ἐ δυσοδίας ἀποπνίσει, βιαίως τὸ σῶματος ἀποπώμυαι ἢ αὐτὸ σὺν ἀνδρὶ πάση ἐ μεταδιδόασιν ἐξερχε-μύμαι. μδυαι. αὖται ὡς πλήρεις ζόφε[?], Ϲ δυσομίας, Ϲ ῥύπε ῶδᾳ κολασῶν[?], Ϲ σκοτεινῶν ἀληθῶν[?], ἀβυ-λήτως[?], Ϲ μὴ φόβε δεινῶ[?], ζόμε π[?], Ϲ διλίας εἰς ἁδὲ μυχοὺς ὡς φρεκεὶν φοβιεῖν[?], ἡ ἀπαρεμύ-σπητον ἀπαγόμενα[?] ᾠδᾳ δίδωσι φεσυεκέρχος[?] πνεύ-μασιν ἀκαθάρτοις[?], Ϲ πονηρῖς, ἔνθα ὁ τῶ σκότους ἀ-χων[?] δισμοῖς εἰς πυρὸς αἰωνίω τηρῆται ὑπέκκαυμα μῆ τῆ σκοτεινῶν Ἀγγέλων τῆ ὁμοίων αὐτῶ[?]. Τούτοις ἢ ᾠδᾳ δίδωσι[?], ὡς συνίσῃ μέλλυσι αὐτοῖς αἰωνίως, οἷς ὡς φίλοις τῆ ζῶν βίου, ἔντε τοῖς ἔργοις, Ϲ τοῖς λόγοις ἐχρήσαντο, Ϲ ὧν ταῖς ὑποθῆκας ἀ-πήΖαζαι εἰς ἔργα θεοῖς λύμλω ἑαυτῶ[?], Ϲ ἄλλων ἐξήγαγον, κακὸν ὑπόδειγμα ἐν τῆ ζωῇ ταύτῃ ἡυό-μένοι, Ϲ χαλεπώτερος κακὸς ἐς φαῦλον μνημό-συνον καταλείλαβαι[?].
units.tr: "Whither does it go? Does the soul not die? Indeed the souls of those who depart from the body go into the pure, fragrant, God-like place, clothed in full glory, and in the purest light, those of the saints; and they shine forth like the sun, from works of righteousness, wisdom and holiness. Led by the friendly angels through the sacred light, they are brought to the first light, the infinite, the immaterial, which is beyond comprehension even to the angels, where God himself is glorified by the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and is praised by infinite powers. Thus, as in a flame of light of an order of sacred powers, they ascend through infinite lights, and they sing, with holy fear and joy in the Spirit, the praise of God, glorifying the Cherubim and Seraphim and all the powers above in heaven, and filling them with fear and courage as they ascend. And how, in a manner fitting and pure, each soul, as a friend to a friend, is united to God, according to the rank of its order, and receives the gift of glory and grace through its participation in the Holy Spirit in this present life, and is then made manifest to the building up of the body of Christ, the faithful; these souls are then preserved, as in a shadow, for a time of rest and refreshment, until the common restoration to God in the future. But those souls which are wholly darkened by evil deeds, words and thoughts, and which have been stained by evil in their dispositions, are violently torn from the body, or go out with it, even against their will, and are not given to the good. These, being full of darkness, of ill-favour, of the filth of the punishments, and of dark ..., are cast into the depths of the abyss, filled with fear and terror, and are handed over to unclean and wicked spirits, where the leader of darkness, bound in chains, is kept as fuel for the eternal fire together with the dark angels like himself. These souls are given to be consumed eternally, as they were friends to the wicked, in their deeds and in their words, and they have led others astray by their counsels, and have become a bad example in this life, and have left behind a worse memory of evil."

units.la: Quæ egrediuntur e corpore animæ, hæ quidem sunt puræ, suaueolentes, Deo similes, & diuina gloria, & purissimo lumine replete, Sanctorum scilicet, & excedentes e corpore æque atque Sol propter opera misericordiæ, sapientiæ, & mundiciei splendescunt. Hæ per amicos Angelos deportatæ, ad primum supercæleste lumen, immateriatum, ipsis etiam Angelis incomprehensibile, Deum ipsum in Patre, & Filio, & Spiritu sancto glorificatum, & adoratum ab innumera multitudine Virtutum, quæ tanquam clara lumina ordinis tertij per secunda lumina ascendunt: quo cum accesserint, Thronum gloriæ eius venerantur in sancto timore, & spiritus diuini lætitia, adstantibus Cherubim, & Seraphim, & omnibus superioribus Virtutibus in tremore, & metu, & ipsas ascendentes confidentia replentibus. Postmodum familiariter pureque earum quaelibet uti amica amico coniungitur nutu diuino Ordini, cuius gloriae, & stationis gratia donata est per sancti Spiritus participationem in vita praesenti, & cum quo inter fidelium coetum apparuit in aedificationem corporis Christi. Illi porro coniungitur, ut una cum eo insimul aetatem agat, & collatetur, & requiescat sub umbra alarum illius usq; ad futuram, & a Deo faciendam communemrestitutionem. Tenebricosae vero, atque insigniter obscura ob iniquae gesta, sermones, cogitationes, consuetudines, studia, & affectiones, Peccatorum nempe, graveolentes violenter e corpore discerpuntur, quem acrem odorem illi cum ingenti, atque insuaui molestia communicant. Hæ uti caligine, & foetore, & inquinamentis conferta a punientibus tenebrosisque Angelis coacte, et cum ingenti metu tremoreque in Inferni profunda, tanquam in custodiam perobscuram, & inconsolabilem deducta, traduntur custodibus, spiritibus immundis, & peruersis; tenebrarum princeps in vinculis sempiternis in igni ad aeternitatem stabilis suscitabulum cum caliginosis Angelis illi similibus conferuat[?]. Hi vero traduntur in omne aeuum, cum illis conuictura[?], quibus veluti amicis, cum vixerunt, & & operibus, & sermonibus adhaeserunt, & quorum suggestionibus acquiescentes in actiones in sui, aliorumque noxam adacta sunt, perniciosum exemplum in hac vita facta, & notis pessimis ad sui memoriam infamandam posteris relinquentes. Non potuerunt exprimi luculentius, enodatius: Non alia Pontificius[?] syllabatim dictat.
units.tr: The souls that go forth from the body are indeed pure, sweet-smelling, like God, and filled with divine glory and the purest light, namely those of the saints; and as they leave the body they shine like the sun because of their works of mercy, wisdom and purity. Carried up by friendly angels, they are brought to the first supercelestial light, immaterial and incomprehensible even to the angels, to God himself, glorified and adored in Father, Son and Holy Spirit by the innumerable multitude of Powers, who ascend through the second lights like bright lights of the third order. When they have arrived, they venerate the throne of his glory in holy fear and in the joy of the divine Spirit, with the Cherubim and Seraphim standing by and all the higher Powers trembling and fearing, and filling them with confidence as they ascend. Afterwards each of them is joined, as friend to friend, familiarly and purely, by the divine will to that Order whose glory and station was granted to them through participation in the Holy Spirit in the present life, and with which they appeared among the assembly of the faithful for the building up of the body of Christ. They are joined to it so that they may live and converse together with it, and rest under the shadow of its wings until the future common restoration to be effected by God. But the dark souls, remarkably obscure because of the wicked deeds, words, thoughts, habits, pursuits and affections of sinners, foul-smelling, are violently torn from the body, communicating to those present a sharp odour with great and unpleasant distress. These, weighed down with darkness, stench and defilements, are compelled by punishing and gloomy angels, with great fear and trembling, to be led into the depths of Hell, as into a most dark and inconsolable prison, and are handed over to guards, unclean and perverse spirits; the prince of darkness, in everlasting chains and in fire established for eternity, keeps them with the gloomy angels like themselves. These are handed over for all ages, to live together with those to whom, as friends while they lived, they clung in both deeds and words, and by whose suggestions, acquiescing, they were driven to actions harmful to themselves and to others, leaving behind a pernicious example in this life and wicked marks to defame their memory among posterity. These things could not have been expressed more clearly or more plainly: no Papist could dictate them more exactly, syllable by syllable.

units.la: Vides ? Communis hic consensus est, & fere praeter paucos Schismatici addictissimos, neminem invenies adversantem. Ideoque qui haec negare visi sunt, cum de alicuius iusti obitu sermonem faciunt, statim, & illico in Coelum assumptum, facie ad faciem, non in speculo, neque in aenigmate Deum videre, & visione beatifica perfrui scribunt. Imo ipsa Graecorum Ecclesia in suis Officiis singulis horis, atque momentis hoc idem asseuerat, ut plane ridendus veniat, qui contrarium dicit. Ecclesiam Graecam universam, cum suis fere omnibus stultam esse; & aliud ore proferre, aliud corde tenere, non nisi stultissimus asseveraverit. Utiam tibi opus sit, si non comprobas consensum, defensionem facere dissidii tui, quod tot modis exterminat Allatius.
units.tr: Do you see? Here is a common consensus, and, apart from a few most committed Schismatics, you will find no one opposing it. Therefore those who seem to deny these things, when they speak of the death of any righteous man, at once and straightaway write that he has been taken up into Heaven, sees God face to face, not in a mirror nor in an enigma, and enjoys the beatific vision. Indeed the Greek Church itself, in its Offices at every hour and moment, asserts the same thing, so that whoever says the contrary would plainly deserve to be laughed at. That the whole Greek Church, with almost all its members, is foolish, and says one thing with its mouth while holding another in its heart, only the most foolish man would assert. Would that you had no need, if you do not approve the consensus, to make a defence of your dissent, which Allatius refutes in so many ways.

units.la: Primatum Papa oecumenicum. Gracos suisse semper detestatos hanc doctrinam. Hoc ex criptis Allatij colligi falsum est. Illis enim plane contrarium constabilitur; auctoritatem scilicet, & praeeminentiam Romani Pontificis in universam Ecclesiam, & potissimum Graecam agnitam fuisse ab Ecclesia Graeca ad tempora usque Photij, ante schisma, in schismate, & postmodum. Idque ex ipsa praxi, exercitio, testimonijs antiquis medij, & posterioris aevi Patrum comprobatur, & tum potissimum, cum a Graecis Schismaticis infensissime oppugnaretur, qui extra Ecclesiam militant. Petantur scripta Allatij. Et quod hic affertur de Patriarchis Constantinopolitanis post Acacium Catholicis, Romanam, & Catholicam fidem, etiam scripto profitentibus, a Romanis Pontificibus nunquam in communionem admissis, si bene intelligantur iurisdictionem, & praeeminentiam in Romano arguit, & probat. Quare enim isti, Catholici licet, non admittuntur a Romano? Quia Romano non obediunt. Qui nō audit iussa, non admittitur. Hinc Opponens absq; iudicio & modo colligit, & nō sine omnium admiratione veritatem extorquet: Quidquid igitur agas, patiarisue pro fide Orthodoxa, Papa autem iussa non adores in communionem Sanctorum admitti nequis. Nihil potest esse hac veritate verius. Cuius rei consequendæ gratia, nullis parcitum est impendijs; Collegium Romæ pueris Græcis munificentissime erectum est, & instructum, in quo religionem Pontificiam doceantur, quo facile fit, ut flexiles puerorum ad superstitionem tanto splendore vestitas animi vincantur. Ex illo deinde Collegio, &c. Verum id est. Tu dicis ea elaborasse, ut Ecclesiæ Græcæ non tam consensum, quam subiectionem obtineant. Hoc vero non dum probatum est.
units.tr: The Pope is the oecumenical primate. The Greeks have always detested this doctrine. That this is to be inferred from the writings of Allatius is false. For the opposite is plainly established by them: that the authority and pre-eminence of the Roman Pontiff over the whole Church, and especially over the Greek Church, was acknowledged by the Greek Church up to the times of Photius, before the schism, during the schism, and afterwards. This is proved from the practice itself, from its exercise, and from the ancient testimonies of the Fathers of the middle and later ages, and most of all at the time when it was most bitterly attacked by the Greek Schismatics, who fight outside the Church. Let the writings of Allatius be sought out. And what is brought forward here about the Patriarchs of Constantinople after Acacius, who were Catholics and professed the Roman and Catholic faith even in writing, but were never admitted to communion by the Roman Pontiffs, if rightly understood, argues for and proves the jurisdiction and pre-eminence of the Roman See. Why, though they were Catholics, are they not admitted by the Roman? Because they do not obey Rome. He who does not hear the commands is not admitted. Hence the Opponent, without judgement or method, draws his conclusion, and to the astonishment of all wrings out the truth: Whatever you do, and whatever you suffer for the Orthodox faith, unless you adore the Pope's commands you cannot be admitted into the communion of the Saints. Nothing can be truer than this. To achieve this aim no expense has been spared: a college for Greek boys has been erected and equipped most generously in Rome, in which they are taught the Papist religion, so that the pliable minds of boys clothed in such splendour are easily won over to superstition. From that college then, etc. That is true. You say that they have laboured at these things so as to obtain from the Greek Church not so much agreement as subjection. But this has not yet been proved.

units.la: similibus laboribus, ac studijs summi Pontifices nullis parcentes sumptibus, non Græcorum modo, sed aliarum quoque nobilissimarum nationum, Germanorum, Gallorum, Hispanorum, Anglorum, & Orientalium Armenorum, Maronitarum, & nunc demum Collegio Fidei propagandæ nationum promiscua congerie vniuersi Orbis terrarum animos sibi devinxerunt. Dicis hac arte, earundem nationum subiectionem sibi procurasse. Quare non dicis subiectionem vero Deo procurare, cuius ipsi vices in terris gerunt? Inter illas nationes pleriq; peruersorum hominum fraudibus, atque improbitate seducti, & ad praua dogmata pellecti captiui sub Diabolo tenentur, & Dæmonibus seruiunt, alij dissoluta consuetudine ex immodica Magistrorum facultate sibi concessa, redditi deteriores peccatis, sese continuo implicant, qui quodlibet sibi licere opinantur. Alij ignorantiæ tenebris cæci, & rerum omnium ignari, nec, Deus an sit, nondum didicerunt, idque malitia eorundem hominum, qui vendere possunt, redimere non possunt. Et opem ferre reducereque a fide sublesta, & noxia ad rectam, a vitijs ad virtutes, ab obtusa, & obtenebrata mente ad pellucidam, & limpidissimam erit obtinere subiectionem? Non est quærendum quid vendat, consid-era, quid emat, & invenies, quod emat. Profundit suos thesauros. omnia suo confert sumptu, eoque continuo, non alieno, augendo aliena, minuendo sua. Et subiectio illa Romano Pontifici facta, mera libertas est. Animus eximitur a seruitute Diaboli, & libertatis præmio, non seruitutis, conformatur. Ideoq; qui in deditionem illius concedunt, non amittunt ius suum, sed in idem restituuntur. excipiunt dogma reconciliati, non mutant consuetudines, non mutant ritus: quæ rata sunt, nec dogma lædunt, permittuntur, idque non tremore, e supercilio Campano, sed exemplo Christi agitur, Qui pro salute animorum, teste Augustino, omnia passus est, & sanguine suo redemit nos, & a vitijs, atque criminibus, non solum doctrinæ auxilio, & & gratiæ, sed etiam exemplo ad studium sanctitatis accendit. Hæc Græcorum, & Latinorum effata sunt. Et hac eadem ratione Pontifex Romanus, cum non posset sanguine, impendijs, ac sumptibus Christianorum saluti Collegijs munificentissime erectis prouidet, vt videmus iam factum in Orientalibus Ecclesijs.
units.tr: With similar labours and zeal, the supreme Pontiffs, sparing no expense, have bound to themselves the minds of the whole world, not only of the Greeks but also of other most noble nations: the Germans, the French, the Spanish, the English, and the Eastern Armenians and Maronites, and now at last, by the mixed multitude of the College for the Propagation of the Faith among the nations. You say that by this art they have secured the subjection of these same nations to themselves. Why do you not say that they secure subjection to the true God, whose vicars they are on earth? Among those nations many, seduced by the deceits and wickedness of perverse men and enticed into depraved doctrines, are held captive under the Devil and serve demons; others, made worse by a loose way of life, from the immoderate licence granted to them by their teachers, entangle themselves continually in sins, thinking that whatever they please is allowed to them. Others, blind in the darkness of ignorance and ignorant of all things, have not yet learned whether God exists, and this through the malice of those men who can sell but cannot redeem. And will it be a subjection to bring help and to lead back from a weak and harmful faith to the right one, from vices to virtues, from a dull and darkened mind to a clear and most limpid one? One should not ask what he sells; consider what he buys, and you will find that he buys what he sells. He pours out his treasures, he gives everything at his own expense, and continually so, not at another's, enriching others and diminishing his own. And that subjection made to the Roman Pontiff is pure liberty. The soul is freed from the slavery of the Devil and is shaped for the reward of liberty, not of servitude. Therefore those who yield themselves to his surrender do not lose their own right, but are restored to it. They accept the doctrine of reconciliation, they do not change their customs or their rites: what is sound and does not harm the doctrine is permitted, and this is done not with trembling and a Campanian frown, but by the example of Christ, who, as Augustine testifies, suffered everything for the salvation of souls and redeemed us with his blood, and kindled us to the pursuit of holiness not only by the aid of teaching and grace but also by example, and from vices and crimes. These are the words of Greeks and Latins. And by this same reasoning the Roman Pontiff, since he cannot provide for the salvation of Christians with blood, does so with the expense and outlay of most generously erected colleges, as we now see has been done in the Eastern Churches.

units.la: Horum diligentiam prætergressus est Leo Allatius, Vir alioqui doctissimus, & de multis Græcis Scriptoribus præclare meritus, quam laudem ei admetitur [?] G. I. Vossius, quod aggressus est in opere de Ecclesia Occidentali, atque Orientalis consensione. Huc enim scopus Operis Allatiani tendit. Res ex primo Consensionis libro redditur manifesta. Non est insumendum multum laboris in expiscando Allatiano in libris de Consensione consilio. Iam edico, ne curiosius id quæras. Scopus illi fuit, & præcipuus, dissensum, quem alij inter has Ecclesias disseminant, in concordiam reducere, demonstrareque vtramque eadem profiteri, eadem verbis etiam ipsissimis dicere: & cum vnam Catholicam, & Apostolicam Ecclesiam ipse profiteatur in Symbolo, & duæ sint Græca, & Latina, quænam sit prima, & superior, ad cuius nutus altera subiaceat, vt ductrici pedisequa, dum duo capita visibilia in vna Ecclefia esse non possint, & vbi acrius momenta vtriusque examinat, ex Patrum Orientalium, & Occidentalium, necnon Conciliorum, Sacrorumque eloquiorum penu Pontificiam cognouit esse caput, & magistram veritatis infallibilem, &, non machinis, neque artificijs, neque inuentis, neq; alijs Pontificale Palladium, vt tu loqueris, & omnipotentiam Papalem extruxit, & firmauit, quam & multi alij ante ipsum melius, fortunatiufque prouexerunt. Nec fraudem prodit, dum scribit, Conciliorum cogendorum potestatem uno Pontifici Romano transcribens, & Principes, & extraneos ab ijs audacissime reijcit. & id contra veterum auctoritatem. Imo id totum peregit, demonstrauitque ita esse veterum Doctorum Ecclesiæ tum Græcæ tum Latinæ testimonijs, quibus ad hæc tempora nullum vidit responsum. Nisi negare auctoritates Patrum, Conciliorum, ipsiusque Ecclesiæ, ampliter respondere est. Allatius scripsit, probauit: tu vero negas, nihil contra opponens, cuius causa potior est, negantisne nullis productis rationibus, an affirmantis, & dictum stabilientis auctoritatibus sanctorum Doctorum omni exceptione maiorum, & Conciliorum? Tu quoq; eadé fi diceres, excluderetur a tuis tua ipsius auctoritas vel eo solo nomine, quod Pontificibus fauet. Hæc conditio, quam mihi alias præscripsit Hottingerus, stolida, dura, atque intractabilis est, ne quid peius dicam. Altercandum est vel alijs rationibus, vel aliorum testimonijs, non temere affirmandum, & negandum, si iura tua aliquo præsidio defendere, & propugnare religionis commoda cupis, quod non ita ex sententia prouenturum puto.
units.tr: Leo Allatius, a man otherwise most learned and deserving well of many Greek writers, has passed over their diligence, a praise which G. J. Vossius grants him, because he undertook the work on the agreement of the Western and Eastern Church. For the aim of the Allatian work tends in this direction. The matter is made plain from the first book of the Agreement. There is no need to spend much labour in fishing out the design of Allatius in the books On the Agreement. Now I declare that you should not seek it more curiously. His aim was chiefly to reduce to concord the dissent which others spread between these Churches, and to demonstrate that both profess the same things and say the same things in the very same words; and since he himself professes one Catholic and Apostolic Church in the Creed, and there are two, the Greek and the Latin, he examines most keenly which of them is first and superior, to whose nods the other is subject as a leading handmaid, since two visible heads cannot exist in one Church. And from the storehouse of the Eastern and Western Fathers, of the Councils and of the sacred oracles, he learned that the Pontifical is the head and infallible teacher of truth, and he built up and established the papal omnipotence, not with machines, nor with devices, nor with inventions, nor with other things, as you say, the Pontifical Palladium, which many others before him have promoted, more happily and more successfully. Nor does he betray any deceit when he writes, transferring to the one Roman Pontiff the power of convoking Councils, and most audaciously rejects princes and outsiders from it; and he does this against the authority of the ancients. Indeed he carried through the whole matter and demonstrated that it is so by the testimonies of the ancient Doctors of the Church, both Greek and Latin, to which up to the present time he has seen no answer. Unless to deny the authorities of the Fathers, of the Councils and of the Church itself is to answer at large. Allatius wrote and proved; but you deny, offering nothing against him. Which side has the stronger case: that of the man who denies without producing any reasons, or that of the one who affirms and establishes what has been said by the authorities of holy Doctors, above all exception, and of Councils? If you too were to say the same things, your own authority would be excluded by your own people on this ground alone, that you favour the Pontiffs. This condition, which Hottinger has prescribed to me elsewhere, is foolish, harsh and intractable, not to say worse. One must dispute either with other arguments or with the testimonies of others; one should not rashly affirm and deny, if you wish to defend your rights with any protection and to champion the advantages of religion, which I do not think will turn out so well as you would like.

units.la: Unum addo, ex quo mens Allatij perdisci potest, quod hactenus inaudito, & temerario elogio Papam Liberium ornat, dum ita-[?] philosophatur: Sedes alia errare possunt, & errant. &c. Sola Romana est, quæ nec sibi unquam fucum fecit, nec alijs. &c. Sola Romana veritatis vindex, cum paucis alijs, qua sedibus pulsis, qua exilio multatis inconcussa stabat, & oppugnabat hæresim. Quid igitur Adversariorum phalanx comminiscitur? Unum nobis adsciscamus Liberium, & reliquorum machinæ cadent: unus ille præomnibus est. nutante illo solo, nutabunt reliqui. ille itaque solus adeatur. Hinc postea Opponens concludit. Quid audimus? Liberius ne talis fuit? & quid solus solus, intidem ingeminans hanc vocem. Expendamus singula, sed æqua lance; ne iterum, atque iterum anhelandum tibi sit.
units.tr: I add one thing, from which Allatius's meaning can be fully learned, namely that he adorns Pope Liberius with an unheard-of and rash eulogy, when he thus philosophizes: Other sees can err, and do err, etc. Only the Roman See is one that has never deceived itself or others, etc. The Roman See alone, the champion of truth, together with a few others, stood unshaken, some with their seats overthrown, some punished with exile, and opposed heresy. What, then, does the phalanx of our opponents devise? Let us take up Liberius alone, and the machines of the rest will fall: he is first of all. If he wavers alone, the rest will waver. Let him alone, then, be approached. From this the Objector afterwards concludes: What do we hear? Was Liberius really such a man? And why only, only, repeating this word again and again. Let us weigh each point, but with an even scale, lest you have to gasp for breath again and again.

units.la: Unum addo, ex quo mens Allatij perdisci potest. Perdis hic quoque vocem & scripta, & ut proprouerbio fertur, Leonem larua territas. Non est Allatij mens perdiscenda, cum illa ex eiusdem scriptis, & ex volumine de Confenfione, non uno loco, sed pluribus apertiffime, vel cæco pateat. Unum illi institutum, & deliberatum cum animo fuit, veritatis partes agere aduersus rebellium falsas criminationes, & dignitatem, ac præeminentiam Romani Pontificis tutari eo potissimū præfidio, si uni sententiæ verba congruentia Ecclesiæ Græcæ, quam sciebam antiquum suorum dogmatum decus, ac voluntatem incolumem, integramq; etiamnum pugnaciffime conseruare, in medium producerem. Nec est quod frigidam suffundas, ut soles, Ecclesiam illam, Græcam intelligo, quæ ab antiquo suæ religionis statu sanctorum illius Ecclesiæ studio, atq; diligentia Patrum constabilito, nunquam deerrauit. & attento animo excipe. Non omnes, qui in ea Ecclesia fuerunt, Ecclesiam Græcam dici, sed eos tantum, qui illius Ecclesiæ instituta secuti sunt. qui vero dispares dogmatibus fuerunt, ac dissoni moribus, licet Græci, Græcorum fuisse Ecclesiam nonnisi dementiffimus dixerit. Quis enim in ea Ecclesia ampliter ingeminasse Hæreticos, & defertores Fidei pernegabit? Quare qui confenfionem inter has duas Ecclesias inficiantur, quæ Ecclesia Græca, & quæ Romana fit, plane summa rerum Ecclesiasticarum ignoratione nesciunt. Adde sis[?] hoc etiam, quod sæpius Allatius professus est, Allatium haud in magno ponere discrimine, quid de veritate dogmatis fit. Sit verum, aut falsum Ecclesiæ Latinæ, vel Græcæ dogma publice expositum. fit quidquid fit. Quamuis sciam dogmata Latinæ Ecclesiæ abunde satis, & rationibus, & testimoniis sanctorum Patrum tuta esse. Hinc mens Allatio fuit ipsa Ecclesiarum consensio. Quare consideranda sunt Græcæ Ecclesiæ placita, si cum Romanæ conformia sunt, si conformia sunt, ergo consensio stat, & tenet locum. Si non cohærent, iam adversarij, & unionis oppugnatores triumphent. Et hoc ante alia in scriptis Allatij, uti præcipuum considerandum est, ante quam impugnetur Allatij consensus.
units.tr: I add one thing, from which Allatius's meaning can be fully learned. Here too you lose both the word and the writings, and, as the proverb goes, you frighten a lion with a mask. Allatius's meaning is not something to be learned with difficulty, since it is plain, in many places and most openly, even to a blind man, from his own writings and from the volume On the Consensus. His one purpose and settled resolve was to play the part of truth against the rebels' false accusations, and to defend the dignity and pre-eminence of the Roman Pontiff chiefly by this safeguard: to bring forward into the open words that agree with one opinion from the Greek Church, which I knew to be the ancient glory of its doctrines and which it still preserves, unimpaired and whole, with the utmost tenacity. Nor have you any reason to pour cold water on it, as you usually do. By the Greek Church I mean that church which, from the ancient state of its religion, established by the zeal of that church's saints and the diligence of the Fathers, has never gone astray. And listen with an attentive mind: not everyone who was in that church is to be called the Greek Church, but only those who followed its institutions. Those who differed in doctrine and were discordant in morals, though Greeks, were not the Greek Church, as only a madman would say. For who will deny that in that church heretics and deserters of the faith multiplied abundantly? Therefore, those who deny the agreement between these two churches, which is the Greek Church and which the Roman, plainly do not know the sum of ecclesiastical matters. Add this too, which Allatius has professed more than once: Allatius does not attach great importance to whether a doctrine is true. Whether the doctrine publicly set out by the Latin or the Greek Church is true or false, let it be whatever it is. Although I know that the doctrines of the Latin Church are sufficiently secure, both by reasons and by the testimonies of the holy Fathers. Hence Allatius's intention was the very agreement of the churches. Therefore the opinions of the Greek Church must be considered: if they agree with the Roman, then the consensus stands and holds its place; if they do not cohere, then our adversaries and the opponents of union may triumph. And this, before anything else in Allatius's writings, must be considered as the chief point, before Allatius's consensus is attacked.

units.la: Et ne in posterum frustra quæritando labores de intentione Allatij, iterū edico, non alium illius esse propositum, nec conatus suos in aliud dirigi, nisi ad extruendam, firmandamque præeminentiam, & auctoritatem Romani Pontificis in alias Ecclesias, quarum regimen ad ipsum solum, uti Ecclesiarum caput, & petram infallibilem Fidei pertinet, vel hoc solo argumento, quod Liberius ne talis fuit? Et quid solus, solus intidem ingeminans hanc vocem, Papistis alias tam exosam? Et denuo pugnam integro. Solus, solus, ut audias Papistas alias vocem tam exosam. Hoc vero certe apud Papistas nugatorium est, qui pro se, & in sui fauorem dicta, cum vera sint, libenter excipiunt; cum falsa, non sine stomacho reiectant. Et ut scias, Papistae, quae sua non sunt, non ambiunt: sua tutantur, & mordicus. Quare illis iucundissime tangit aures, si Liberius a calumniis vindicatus, sua dignitate, & praeeminentia praefulgeat, tantum abest, ut vocem Leonis exosam habeant. Obtestor vos, qui estis ex Pontificijs cordati viri, an unquam legistis, Athanasium cessisse, Arrio furente? Annon videtis plana Allatij verba, Opponenti quoque non inexplorata esse? Sola Romana veritatis vindex cum paucis alijs, qua sedibus pulsis, qua exilio multatus inconcussa stabat. Inter hos paucos Athanasius, qui neque haeresim amplexus, neque homoufion unquam insectatus est, ergo purumputum mendacium est, id Alia tium dixisse. Sed solus Liberius propugnauit homoufion. ergo iam excluditur Athanasius. Itane argumentantur hodie Haeretici. Solus Liberius propugnauit homoufion, sed ut caput Ecclesiae, ut dogmatum Ecclesiasticorum cognitor, ut iudex : Athanasius, ut membrum, ut obnoxius, ut supplex ; ideoque eiectus, excommunicatusque ad Liberium recurrit, ut ille causam recognoscat, apud quem fidei suae professionem emittit, ut Liberius indicet, & recta ne, an prava fit, iudicium ferat, quod alij quoque Præsules vi Arianorum de sedibus pulsi pari voce cum Athanasio peraguntʼ, & discussa causa a Liberio innocentes pronunciati, sedibus suis restituuntur : & tu negas Liberium solum Catholicorum causam tutatum : & verba Athanasij, & Basilij, si recte iudicas, etiam si distinguas tempora, quæ prorsus officij tui erat distinxisse, sultem, ut aliquid dixisse existimareris, confusa adhæc, & propugnantia veritatem Allatianam indistincta intermisisti. Quare consensionem Allatij puramputa esse dissensionem concludis; tibiq; plaudis, quod hoc tuū iudicium aliis quoque doctis perplacuerit. Quare ergo hi docti Viri non ausi sunt publice aliquid decantare? Quare de hoc negotio scripta Salmasij tanti Viri ad hunc diem reprimùntur? Quid de ea senserit Boineburgii[?], vir & dignatione, & eruditione illustri, & alij Germanorum proceres, literæ eorum ad Allatium datæ non obscure extricant. De mea vero dissensione, sive consensione, quidquid Hæretici, quid alij adversarij sentiant, parum mihi curæ est. Antequam calamum ad scribendum assumpsissem iam præuideram aduersantium, & repugnantium Fidei Catholicæ ingeniorum calumnias, maledicta, insulsas oppositiones, & pessime confecta mendacia, tantum vt tenebras veritati offundant. Sic nunc cum video, vt ipse tum conceperam, ita animatos, atque solicitos ad euertenda mea quæcunque sunt studia, eodem ipso tempore recepto animo in iocos transfusus, vt ita dicam, risu emorior, & deplorandam mifereor[?] similium cæcitatem, & conatus infelicissimos, qui in tanto veritatis splendore tenebras quærunt, & rebus clarissimis nubes offundere tentant. Ergo labente Liberio, reliqui etiam lapsi sunt. Quis dubitat eos omnes, qui secuti sunt Liberium, si Liberius lapsus est, eos quoque lapsos fuisse? Sed quid tum indead[?] refellenda dicta Allatij, qui negat ipsum Liberium lapsum fuisse, sic nutante inter varias opiniones historiæ fide? Quidam aiunt Liberium, & aduersus homoufion, & aduersus Athanasium subscripsisse. Nihil alij de Liberij lapsu memorant. Veruntamen ex recentioribus Cardinales Baronius, & Perronius, & ex alijs Petauius ad Epiphanium, Iodocus Coccius in Thesauro, & alij defendunt. Qui tamen lapsus, siue verus sit, siue falsus, præter institutum Allatij est, cum de consensione tantum discernat. Quare sic argumentatur, quod etiam super innuit. Eustathius Sebastenus sæpius in hæresim lapsus, decreto Synodi deponitur, cuma suis restitutionem in integrum desperat, ad sinum Romani Episcopi, veluti ad tutum asylum, qui tum Liberius erat, diuertit. Quid apud ipsum egerit, ignoratur, & in summa rerum caligine versatur. Hoc certum est a Liberio suæ restitutionis in sedem, ex qua fuerat per Synodum reiectus literas impetrasse, illisque patefactis Synodo Orientali eiusdem Synodi decreto, absque vllo suæ causæ examine in pristinum statum ac dignitatem restitutum esse. Hoc non scribunt sequioris seculi scriptores, sed Basilius magnus, cui si fidem non adhibeas, & dicta recipias, impius es. Sed dicit, se causam nescire, quare id Liberius egerit, & hoc admirabilius est, cum fecerit, & factum apud Orientales ad effectum datum est. Conclude in Romano, vt tu vis, etiam suspecto de hæresi tanta eminet auctoritas, vt in eius decreta contra Synodum lata indiscussa causa Orientalis alia Synodus cursu vadat, illiusque dicto acquiescat, illique[?] veluti magistro, & superiori iudici affigatur, tandemque obediat. Et maiora de præeminentia Romani peruestigamus? Adde fis notulas nostras super hoc eodem argumento supra expositas. Et turpissime labente Liberio lapsus est. Certum est, fi lapsus fuisset Liberius, Athanasius, fi eius vestigijs instituisset, lapsus fuisset. Quis hoc nisi stipes in dubium verterit. Nonne inter lapsos ponimus, qui lapsum sequuntur? Dic tu quoque, & audacter, Athanasius secutus est lapsum Liberium, ergo Athanasius etiam lapsus est. Tum ad hoc attexe. sed Liberius lapsus non est: Ergo nec Athanasius sequens Liberium lapsus est; vel si manis, Athanasius semper secutus Liberium lapsus non est. ergo neq; Liberius lapsus est, cuius via pergebat Athanasius. & plane hunc in modum sermocinatus, non eris iniurius in hunc sanctissimum virum, si tamen collegeris, vt Allatius iubet. Adducit quidem verba Athanasij, & Basilij de Liberio, sed distingue tempora, & Allatium nihil dixisse deprehendes. Et quare tempora notioni omnium a te substrata non sunt, vt Allatius nihil dixisse deprehenderetur? Poteras tuo studio, ac labori parcere, si statim initio Exercitationis id solum dixisses? Adducit quidem Leo multa pro hac consensione, sed distingue tempora, & Allatium nihil dixisse deprehendes. Tum siquidem protinus, & abiecta omni cunctatione difficultatibus omnibus Allatianis ingeniosissime respondisses, triumphasseque apud tuos; sed apud callidos vsu viros parum prudens, ne quid peius dicam, habereris.[?] Ex quo nanq; fonte simile responsionis genus promanauit in publicum? Quisunquam in disciplinis versatus hoc modo tantopere erudito Disputationum discrimen transmittere edocuit? quis hanc viam concertationis inter doctos viros enatas effugiendi aperuit? Gaudeo itaque mihi, qui ψευδόχων[?] ἀεὶ [illegible, ~7 letters] noua hæc ab his hominibus ἀδικομαγ[?]. Vti & illud quod mihi sæpius in hoc opere ingeminatur. Cum argumento prompta responsio nulla fit, quæ vim illius eludere valeat, responsionem in aliud tempus transmittere. Sunt hæc Opponentis. Quid audiuimus? Liberius ne talis fuit? & quid? Solus solus itidem ingeminans hanc vocem Papistis adeo excsam[?]. Audi toleranter: id nanque inter nos liceat. Non illa sunt, quæ tu tibi fingis Allatij placita, & aliena tanquam Allatij sint, oppugnas. Lege si tibi animus est, cautius: neque, enim explanatio interpretis opus est. Catholicæ veritatis hostium Arianorum nempe, verba illa sunt, qui Liberij auctoritatem, & in rebus Ecclesiasticis præeminentiam bene noscentes, id vnum[?] tantum sibi, & hæresi suæ commodum esse reputantes; si vnum Liberium sibi ducem, vel comitem adscisscrent, ea enunciabant: Vnum nobis adscisca-mus Liberium, & reliquorum machinæ cadent. Vnus ille præ omnibus est, &c. Tanta erat tum Romani Pontificis maiestas, ipsis etiam aduersarijs cognita, vt vel solo illius assensu, atque probatione in religionis negotio rem suam augere possent, & illius improbatione rursus affligere; ideoque machinis, vi etiam imperatoria, ac necessitate illum ad se allicere conati sunt. Quid βασιλικὴ δυναστεία[?] ꝏactus[?] egerit, non est præsentis temporis, nec loci. Ex his tamen manifestum, compertumque redditur supremum in Ecclesiam regimen Romani. Fuit ergo talis Liberius iudicibus Catholicorum infensissimis hostibus: neque semel id dicunt, sed indidem ingeminant hanc vocem. Tu obtestaris cordatos ex Pontificijs viros, si vnquam legerunt, Athanasium cessisse Ario furente, hæresim amplexum, homoufion insectatum esse? respondent Pontificij, se nihil tale vspiam legisse, vel audisse. At Allatius dicit. Hæ vero germanæ gerræ sunt, & purumputum mendacium, ne quid peius dicam. Quis enim tum fuit Episcopus Alexandrinus? Athanasius. Triumphas, vt video, sed extra rem, sed pedaneus, & cursu destitutus. Audi, non est lapsus in haeresim Athanasius. Cessit Alexandrinus. Alexandrinus Athanasius est. Ergo cessit Athanasius. Quis negauerit? Allatius. Ita colligere tu iubes ex tua Dialectica; & praeterea iubes, distinguere tempora: tum enim Allatium nihil dixisse deprehendes. Geram morem, distinguam tempora.
units.tr: And so that you do not labour in vain in future over Allatius's intention, I say again that his purpose was nothing other than to build up and confirm the pre-eminence and authority of the Roman Pontiff over the other Churches, whose governance belongs to him alone, as head of the Churches and the infallible rock of the faith. This is shown by this argument alone: Was Liberius not such a man? And what of only, only, repeating this word again and again, a word so hateful to the Papists elsewhere? And again he renews the fight in full: Only, only, so that you may hear the Papists' word, so hateful elsewhere. Yet this is certainly trifling on the part of the Papists, who gladly accept sayings in their own favour and their own defence when they are true, and reject them with indignation when they are false. And so that you may know, Papists, they do not seek what is not theirs; they defend what is theirs, and tooth and nail. Therefore it sounds most pleasant in their ears if Liberius, cleared of slanders, shines forth in his dignity and pre-eminence; so far are they from finding the word of Leo hateful. I beg you, who are the sensible men among the Papists: have you ever read that Athanasius gave way when Arius raged? Do you not see that Allatius's plain words were not unknown even to his opponent? The sole champion of Roman truth, with a few others, stood unshaken, some driven from their sees, some punished with exile. Among these few was Athanasius, who neither embraced heresy nor ever attacked the homoousion; therefore it is a downright lie that Allatius said this. But Liberius alone defended the homoousion. Therefore Athanasius is now excluded. Is this how the heretics argue today? Liberius alone defended the homoousion, but as head of the Church, as judge and examiner of ecclesiastical doctrines; Athanasius as a member, as one under obligation, as a suppliant. Therefore, cast out and excommunicated, he runs back to Liberius, that he might review the case, before whom he makes his profession of faith, so that Liberius might declare and pass judgment on whether it is right or wrong. The other bishops also, driven from their sees by the violence of the Arians, pleaded their cause with Athanasius in one voice; and when the case had been examined, they were pronounced innocent by Liberius and restored to their sees. And you deny that Liberius alone defended the cause of the Catholics! If you judge the words of Athanasius and Basil rightly, even if you distinguish the times, which was entirely the business of your office to do, at least so that you might seem to have said something, you have passed over in silence, mixing them up with confused and defensive arguments, the points that favour Allatius's position. Therefore you conclude that Allatius's agreement is nothing but disagreement, and you applaud yourself that this judgment of yours has pleased other learned men too. Why then have these learned men not dared to sing anything publicly? Why have the writings of Salmasius, so great a man, been suppressed to this day on this matter? What Boineburg thought of it, a man of distinguished rank and learning, and other leading Germans, their letters written to Allatius make plain enough. As for my own dissent or agreement, I care little what heretics or other adversaries think of it. Before I took up my pen to write, I had already foreseen the calumnies, the insults, the foolish objections and the very badly made-up lies of those men who oppose and resist the Catholic faith, which are meant only to cast darkness over the truth. So now, when I see them stirred up and anxious to overturn all my efforts, just as I had conceived them at the time, my spirit is turned to jesting, as it were, and I die of laughter, and I pity the blindness, to be deplored, of such people, and their most unhappy efforts, which seek darkness in the midst of so great a splendour of truth and try to throw clouds over the clearest things. Therefore, when Liberius fell, the others too fell. Who doubts that all who followed Liberius fell as well, if Liberius fell? But what then is the point of refuting Allatius's statements, when he denies that Liberius himself fell, the historical record wavering among various opinions? Some say that Liberius subscribed both against the homoousion and against Athanasius. Others report nothing about Liberius's fall. Yet among more recent writers, the cardinals Baronius and Perronius, and among others Petavius in his edition of Epiphanius, and Jodocus Coccius in his Thesaurus, defend it. However, whether that fall was true or false, it lies outside Allatius's purpose, since he is discussing only agreement. Therefore he argues as he also remarks above: Eustathius of Sebaste, who often fell into heresy and was deposed by a decree of the Synod, when he despaired of being restored in full with his followers, turned aside to the bosom of the Roman bishop, as to a safe refuge, who at that time was Liberius. What he did there is not known, and it lies in deep obscurity. This is certain: he obtained letters from Liberius for his restoration to the see from which he had been removed by the Synod, and when these were produced to the Eastern Synod, he was restored to his former state and dignity by a decree of that same Synod, without any examination of his case. Later writers of a lesser age do not record this, but Basil the Great does, and if you do not give him credence and accept what he says, you are impious. But he says that he does not know the reason why Liberius did this, and this is more remarkable still, since he did it, and what was done was given effect among the Easterners. Conclude about the Roman church as you wish: even a bishop suspected of such heresy holds such authority that, against the decrees issued against the Synod, without any discussion of the case, another Eastern Synod proceeds on its course, acquiesces in his word, and submits to him as to a master and superior judge. And shall we investigate greater things about the pre-eminence of Rome? Add to this our notes above, set out on this same argument. And Liberius fell most shamefully.
