It is certain that if Liberius had fallen, Athanasius, if he had followed in his footsteps, would have fallen too. Who would call this in doubt except a blockhead? Do we not count among the fallen those who follow the fallen? Say boldly yourself too: Athanasius followed the fallen Liberius, therefore Athanasius also fell. Then add to this: but Liberius did not fall; therefore Athanasius, following Liberius, did not fall either; or if you prefer, Athanasius, who always followed Liberius, did not fall; therefore neither did Liberius fall, whose way Athanasius was following. Speaking in this manner, you will not be unfair to that most holy man, if only you draw the conclusions as Allatius bids. He does indeed bring forward the words of Athanasius and Basil about Liberius, but distinguish the times, and you will find that Allatius said nothing. And why have the times not been laid down as a foundation by all of you, so that it would be found that Allatius said nothing? Could you not have spared your zeal and labour, if at the very beginning of your Exercitatio you had said only this? Leo indeed brings forward many things in favour of this agreement, but distinguish the times, and you will find that Allatius said nothing. Then, if you had at once, without any hesitation, answered all the difficulties raised by Allatius with great ingenuity, you would have triumphed among your own people; but among shrewd men of experience you would have been thought, to put it no more harshly, rather unwise. For from what source did this kind of answer come out into the public? Who, versed in learning, has taught that one may pass over the distinction of such a learned debate in this way? Who has opened this path of escape from the contest that has arisen among learned men? I rejoice, therefore, that these men have been cheated by their new [illegible] ... Likewise that which is so often repeated to me in this work: when no ready answer can be given to an argument that is able to elude its force, postpone the answer to another time. These are the words of the opponent. What did we hear? Was Liberius not such a man? And what then? Only, only, repeating again and again this word so hateful to the Papists. Listen patiently, for this is permitted between us. It is not those positions that you invent for yourself and attack as if they were Allatius's own, though they belong to others. Read more carefully, if you have the will; there is no need for an interpreter's explanation. Those are the words of the enemies of Catholic truth, the Arians, who, knowing well the authority of Liberius and his pre-eminence in ecclesiastical affairs, and reckoning that it would serve only themselves and their heresy, if they gained Liberius alone as leader or companion, used to say: Let us win over Liberius alone to us, and the machines of the rest will fall. He alone is above all, and so on. So great was the majesty of the Roman Pontiff at that time, known even to his adversaries, that by his assent and approval alone they could enlarge their cause in matters of religion, and by his disapproval could again bring it low; and therefore they tried to draw him to themselves by machinations, even by imperial power and by compulsion. What he did under [royal power] is not a matter for the present time or place. Yet from this it is made manifest and clear that the supreme governance of the Church belongs to Rome. So Liberius was regarded as a most hostile enemy by the judges of the Catholics; and they do not say this once, but repeat the same word again and again. You call on the sensible men among the Papists: if they have ever read that Athanasius gave way when Arius raged, embraced heresy and attacked the homoousion? The Papists answer that they have read or heard nothing of the kind anywhere. But Allatius says so. These, however, are pure fabrications and a downright lie, to put it no more harshly. For who was then the bishop of Alexandria? Athanasius. You triumph, as I see, but beside the point, and on foot, and without a horse for the race. Listen: Athanasius did not fall into heresy. The Alexandrian gave way. The Alexandrian is Athanasius. Therefore Athanasius gave way. Who would deny it? Allatius. So you bid me draw conclusions from your dialectic; and besides, you bid me distinguish the times, for then you will find that Allatius said nothing. I shall humour you and distinguish the times.

units.la: Anno CCCXXVI. Athanasius succedit in Patriarchatu Alexandrino, Alexandro demortuo.
units.tr: In the year 326, Athanasius succeeds to the Patriarchate of Alexandria, Alexander having died.

units.la: Anno CCCXXXV. in Synodis Tyria & Constantinopolitana exauctoratur, & a Constantio in Gauinos in Gallijs relegatur.
units.tr: In the year 335, he is deposed at the synods of Tyre and Constantinople, and Constantius banishes him to Gauinos in Gaul.

units.la: Anno CCCXXXVIII. Restituitur a Constantino iuniore.
units.tr: In the year 338, he is restored by Constantine the Younger.

units.la: Anno CCCXXXX. Citatur a Iulio Papa, & venit Romam.
units.tr: In the year 340, he is summoned by Pope Julius and comes to Rome.

units.la: Anno CCCXXXXI. In Synodo Antiochena absens condemnatur, quod a Synodo damnatus, absque Synodo contra Canones Sedem repetijsset, Marcellino, & Probiano, sive Probo Coss. Absoluitur a Iulio Papa, & redit Alexandriam. Vel etiam, vt ait Theodoretus libro 2. cap. 3. & Sozomenus lib. 4. cap. 2. & 5. quod Ariani Imperatori dixerunt, Athanasij reditum multorum malorum, & tumultuum causam extitisse: neque Ægyptum solum, sed & Palæstinam, Phœniciam, aliasque finitimas Prouincias, turbulentis fluctibus turpiter agitari, vbi præsens fuit Constantius, & eo consentiente Athanasius damnatus fuit, & Gregorius Athanasio sufficitur Arianus.
units.tr: In the year 341, he is condemned in his absence by the Synod of Antioch, because, having been condemned by a synod, he had returned to his see without a synod, contrary to the canons, in the consulship of Marcellinus and Probianus, or Probus. He is absolved by Pope Julius and returns to Alexandria. Or indeed, as Theodoret says in book 2, chapter 3, and Sozomen in book 4, chapters 2 and 5, the Arians told the emperor that Athanasius's return had been the cause of many evils and tumults: not only Egypt but Palestine, Phoenicia and the other neighbouring provinces were shamefully tossed about by turbulent waves. Where Constantius was present, and with his consent, Athanasius was condemned, and the Arian Gregory was substituted for Athanasius.

units.la: Anno CCCXXXXII. [?] Quæritur ad necem a Gregorio eius sedis inuasore, & iterum petit Romam. Gregorius Antiochiam venit: magna inde fit cædes. Gregorius sex annos sedem occupat. Theodoretus lib. 2. cap. 4. Athanasius interim exulat.
units.tr: In the year 342 [?], he is sought for murder by Gregory, the usurper of his see, and again seeks Rome. Gregory comes to Antioch, and great slaughter follows. Gregory holds the see for six years. Theodoret, book 2, chapter 4. Athanasius meanwhile is in exile.

units.la: Anno CCCXXXVI Athanasius Mediolanum accersitur a Cæsare Constantio, agiturque de conuocando Concilio Sardicæ. Mox Concilium a Constante & Constantio indictum.
units.tr: In the year 336, Athanasius is summoned to Milan by Caesar Constantius, and the convening of a council at Sardica is discussed. Soon afterwards the council is announced by Constans and Constantius.

units.la: Anno CCCXXXVII. Soluitur in Synodo Sardicensi a calumnijs Arianorum, & sedi suæ restituitur. Sardicæ Concilium habetur, in quo deponitur Gregorius Alexandrinus. Ariani interesse ei noluerunt. Sic Philippopolim abeunt, seorsim Concilium habent, & Sardicense nuncupant. In eo Iulium Papam excommunicant, & alios, quod communicarent cum Athanasio. Ex Epistola Synodi apud Athanasium Apologia secunda.
units.tr: In the year 337, he is cleared of the calumnies of the Arians at the Synod of Sardica and restored to his see. At Sardica the council is held, in which Gregory of Alexandria is deposed. The Arians refused to take part in it. So they go off to Philippopolis, hold a separate council there, and call it the Council of Sardica. In it they excommunicate Pope Julius and others, because they had communicated with Athanasius. From the letter of the synod, in Athanasius's Second Apology.

units.la: Anno CCCXXXXIX. Constans de reuocando Athanafio literas scribit ad Constantium, quibus ille territus Athanafium restituit.
units.tr: In the year 339, Constans writes to Constantius about recalling Athanasius, and Constantius, terrified by the letters, restores Athanasius.

units.la: Anno CCCLII. Liberius, init Pontificatum Romanum.
units.tr: In the year 352, Liberius begins the Roman Pontificate.

units.la: Anno CCCLV. In exilium mittitur Liberius Arbitiano, & Lolliano Coff.
units.tr: In the year 355, Liberius is sent into exile, in the consulship of Arbitio and Lollianus.

units.la: Anno CCCLVI. Gregorius Cappadox intruditur in sedem Alexandrinam, ærarij olim quæstor, & depeculator omnium, eoq; crimine profugus.
units.tr: In the year 356, Gregory the Cappadocian is forced into the Alexandrian see. He was formerly a quaestor of the treasury and a plunderer of everyone, and he fled from that charge.

units.la: Anno CCCLVIII. Liberius restituitur.
units.tr: In the year 358, Liberius is restored.

units.la: Anno CCCLXII. Necato Gregorio inuasore, e latebris emergens Athanasius redit Alexandriam sub Iuliano, & celeberrimo totius Ægypti conuentu excipitur.
units.tr: In the year 362, after the usurper Gregory was killed, Athanasius emerges from his hiding-places and returns to Alexandria under Julian, and is received by a most celebrated gathering of all Egypt.

units.la: Distinxi tempora. Videamus modo, analiquid dixerit Allatius. Dixit cessisse Alexādrinum Patriar. & verum dixit. Tu intelligis Athanasium, ideoque clamas, reclamasque Athanasium præter æquum, & bonum hærefeos deferri. Veruntamen Leoni, etiam si non distinxerit tempora, non temere excidit cessisse Alexandrinum. Cum rebus Ægypti turbatis, Ariani proterue, ac [illegible, ~12 letters] in Catholicos pessimis modis desæuirent, & potissimum Athanasij necem procurarent, in quo videbantur Catholicorum resfaluæ tutæque conseruari. ri. Constantius Imperator Arianis impellentibus Gregorium quemdam Cappadocem, alij Georgium vocant, Arianum hæresi, recusante id onus Eusebio, delegit, neque ex primiore vita, vt idem Athanasius tradit, commendatum, nec vllo modo Christianum, sed pro temporis conditione nomen Christi assumentem, & olim pro impietate sua excommunicatum Patriarcham Alexandrinum anno 341. siue 342. creat, qui vsus ministerio Philagrij, & Arsacij magistratuum Alexandrinam Ecclesiam inuadit. Post interemptum Gregorium anno 362. Georgius identidem Arianus ijsdem promotoribus, & fautoribus in eundem Patriarchatum immittitur anno 356. & anno 362. dire necatur a Gentilibus, cum non solum Catholicorum, sed Gentilium Alexandrinorum infensissimum odium incurrisset. Nec defuerunt Ariani, qui eum sic a Gentilibus cæsum, vt martyrem coluerint, teste Epiphanio, qui eum indignum esse nomine Martyris pronunciauit, quod non ob Christi fidem, sed ob nefanda commissa scelera dignas pœnas persoluerit. De successione horum Patriarcharum Athanasius, ἀπέσ[?]ειλε ὁ μὲν πρῶτον Γρηγόριον, καὶ νῦν τὸν ταμιευόμενον[?] Γεώργιον. Misit primum quidem Gregorium, & nunc receptorem tributorum, GeorGeorgium. Ergo ab anno 341 ad confectum Georgium anni praterfluxere 21. in quibus Ariani, illique peffimi Alexandrinam Ecclesiam tenuere, Athanasio sub illa tempora exule, sedem ex sede mutante, & ignotas sibi prouincias pererrante. Et immane tantum reputatur, si Allatius dixerit Alexandrinum, Gregorium nempe, & Georgium Cappadoces cessisse?
units.tr: I have distinguished the times. Let us now see whether Allatius said anything. He said that the Patriarch of Alexandria withdrew, and he spoke the truth. You understand this to mean Athanasius, and so you shout and protest that Athanasius is wrongly and unfairly charged with heresy. Yet Leo, even if he had not distinguished the times, did not carelessly let slip the words "the Alexandrian withdrew." When the affairs of Egypt were in turmoil, and the Arians were raging shamelessly and [illegible, about twelve letters] against the Catholics in the worst ways, and especially were procuring the death of Athanasius, in which the safety of the Catholic cause seemed to be preserved, the Emperor Constantius, at the urging of the Arians, chose a certain Gregory the Cappadocian, whom others call George, an Arian by heresy. Eusebius refused that burden. Gregory was recommended neither by his earlier life, as Athanasius himself relates, nor in any way as a Christian, but assumed the name of Christ as the circumstances of the time required. He had long before been excommunicated for his impiety. In 341 or 342 he installs himself as Patriarch of Alexandria, and with the help of the magistrates Philagrius and Arsacius he invades the Alexandrian Church. After Gregory was killed in 362, the Arian George was again sent into the same Patriarchate, by the same promoters and supporters, in 356; and in 362 he was cruelly killed by the Gentiles, since he had incurred the most bitter hatred not only of the Catholics but also of the Gentile Alexandrians. Nor were there lacking Arians who honoured him as a martyr, though he had been slain by the Gentiles in this way. Epiphanius, however, declared him unworthy of the name of martyr, because he paid the due penalty not for faith in Christ but for the wicked crimes he had committed. Concerning the succession of these Patriarchs, Athanasius writes: He sent Gregory first, and now George, the collector of the revenues [ἀπέσ[?]ειλε ὁ μὲν πρῶτον Γρηγόριον, καὶ νῦν τὸν ταμιευόμενον[?] Γεώργιον]. So from 341 to the death of George, twenty-one years passed, during which Arians, and those most wicked ones, held the Alexandrian Church, while Athanasius was in exile at that time, changing sees and wandering through provinces unknown to him. And is it considered such a monstrous thing if Allatius said that the Alexandrian, that is, Gregory and George the Cappadocians, withdrew?

units.la: Omnes qui de Christi nomine dicuntur, prositentur in Symbolo, quod vocant Apostolico, esse Ecclesiam Christi aliquam, eamque unam Catholicam. &c. Hæc prædicata suæ congregationi exacte convenire diunt Pontificij: nos contra falso eam ipsam hæc sibi arrogare pertendimus. Modice id tangit Pontificios. Hariolentur Reformati, retundentibus probet argumentis, nec finem ullum faciant garriendi. Pontificij & argumentis Hæreticorum abunde responderunt, & iura sua ex improbitate inimicorum vindicata tutantur, & quæ sunt sua hodienum conseruant, & propugnát. Sed quid hoc ad Romanæ Græcæq; Ecclesiæ diffidiū?
units.tr: All who are called by the name of Christ profess in the creed called the Apostles' Creed that there is some Church of Christ, and that one Catholic Church, etc. The Papists say that these things precisely befit their congregation; we, on the contrary, contend that they falsely claim these things for themselves. This barely touches the Papists. Let the Reformed guess; let them trade proofs with one another, and let them make no end of chattering. The Papists have answered the arguments of the heretics amply, and they defend and maintain their rights, vindicated against the wickedness of their enemies, and they still preserve and uphold what is theirs today. But what has this to do with the discord between the Roman and the Greek Church?

units.la: Gratias autem agimus Alliatio, quod ingenue fassus sit, Honorium fuisse Hæreticum Monothelitam. Mitius me hic agam, quam par est. Pertuso dolio nihil infundas, aiebat ille inauditum, & temerarium illud Elogium Romanæ Sedis ab Allatio enunciatum, & x[?] te pagina 4. signatum, tam cito e memoria excidisse ? Sedes aliæ errare possunt, & errant. &c. Sola Romana est, quæ nec sibi unquam fucum fecit, nec aliis. &c.
units.tr: We give thanks to Allatius, however, because he has frankly confessed that Honorius was a Monothelite heretic. I shall treat him more gently here than is fitting. You should pour nothing into a leaking cask, he used to say. Has that unheard-of and rash eulogy of the Roman See, pronounced by Allatius and marked on page 4 [x?], been so quickly forgotten? Other sees can err, and do err, etc. The Roman See alone is one that has never deceived either itself or others, etc.

units.la: Non potuit ergo Allatius, qui eam semper ab omni suco, & fallacia vacuam fecit, in vno Honorio hæresi obnoxiam facere. Quare reprimendus est animi impetus, & vana innoxiorum calumniandi præsumptio. Dixerant qui dissidia urgenta Græcis singulis annis excommunicari, & a piorum societate, & communione secludi Romanum Pontificem, idque in libris Græcorum Ritualibus, nec non & aliis sedulo investigans Allatius, nec reperiens, falsum id esse declaravit. Qua enim ratione id affirmasset, quod nusquam reperisset? & vim rationi adjiciens, scripsit divina providentia factum esse, ut eo quoque loco, si ita male affecti animatiq; essent Græci contra Romanum Pontificem, ne viderentur absque causa, & legitimo nomine in Romanum invehi, ubi commode fieri poterat, ab injuria inferenda abstinerent. Locus autem videbatur opportunissimus in Synodico, cum tum potissimum omnes Patriarchas suos Monothelitas dignitate conspicuos nominatim condemnant, & excommunicant, mentionem quoque Honorij, sive hæretici, sive suspecti de hærefi[?], vtcumque fuerit mentionem ingerere ; vt is quoque inter alios Monothelitas compareret, & in Hæreticorum numero collocaretur. cum in eo loco non fecerint, multo minus in alijs locis fecisse reputandi sunt. Et tu colligis ab Allatio inter Hæreticos Honorium poni, gratiasque propterea illi agis. Non sequitur Canum Allatius, sed Græcorum factum examinat, qui non aliam ob causam nomen Honorij supressisse existimandi sunt, & eo magis si in tot alijs religionis capitibus aduersati sunt, quam quod eum hæresi infectum esse non reputarent. Quis enim continuisset efferatos animos, & Schismatis cæco veneno correptos, ne nomen tam odiosum, publica altaque voce cum suis Patriarchis proclamassent? Stultus ipse fuerim, si credam. Præterea addis ex principijs Allatij; Nutante, labenteq; Papa, reliqui omnes nutant, & labuntur. An tempore Honorij omnes reliqui Episcopi lapsi sunt, ideoque Ecclesia errauit? Et illa quidem Ecclesia, quæ contra hæreticum Papam orthodoxiam firmauit? Paucis expediam. Verum est, nutante labenteque Papa, reliquos omnes nutare labique; sed probandum nutasse, & lapsum esse: Sin minus nihil concluditur. Et sic tempore Honorij reliqui omnes Episcopi lapsi non sunt, neque Ecclesia errauit, & multo minus ea Ecclesia, quæ Orthodoxiam firmauit, cum Papam hæreticum secuta non fit. Et sic nec Hæreticus fuit Honorius. Quare argumentum Allatij suo pede stat, Græcam Ecclesiam non excommunicare tanquam Hæreticum Romanum Pontificem singulis annis, cum illum non excommunicat eo tempore, quo opportune id facere posset. Sed Honorius fuit hæreticus. Contrarium probandi extra propositum Allatij est, cui consensio tantum in animo est. Sed excommuni-anit Latinos Cerularius. Cerularius non est Ecclesia Græca, sicuti nec fuit Dioscorus, qui excommunicauit Leonem, & ob id tantum, non hæresim, quam ipse fouebat, excommunicatus a Synodo est. Non est ergo, quod gratias agas Allatio: Neque enim id fassus est, sed tu odio in Romanum Pontificem dictum Allatij falso criminaris. Conclude itaque, Græci si ita animati essent, ut Pontifici Romano hæresis crimen appingere, ideoque eum excommunicare conarentur, tum potissimum facerent, cum Monothelitas suos Patriarchas excommunicant, non quod Honorius Hæreticus, sed quod de hæresi suspectus fuerit. Ergo Honorius ab Allatio declaratus non est. & frustra gratias agis Allatio. Tum crambem recoquis de Liberio, de quo supra satis abunde diximus .
units.tr: Allatius, who has always kept that see free of all deceit and fraud, could not therefore make it liable to heresy in the single case of Honorius. So the impulse of the mind must be restrained, and the vain presumption of slandering the innocent. Those who press the dissensions have said that the Roman Pontiff is excommunicated by the Greeks every year, and is cut off from the fellowship of the pious and from communion, and this in the Greeks' ritual books. Allatius, investigating this diligently, and also in other sources, found nothing and declared the claim false. For on what ground could he have affirmed what he had nowhere found? Adding force to his reasoning, he wrote that it had been brought about by divine providence that, in that very place, if the Greeks were so ill-disposed and minded against the Roman Pontiff, they might refrain from inflicting injury where it could conveniently be done, lest they should seem to attack the Roman Pontiff without cause and without a lawful name. The place seemed most suitable in the Synodicon, where especially they condemn and excommunicate by name all their Patriarchs who were Monothelites and eminent in dignity. Mention might also be made of Honorius, whether heretic or suspected of heresy, however it may have been, so that he too might appear among the other Monothelites and be placed in the number of heretics. Since they did not do this in that place, they must be judged to have done it much less in other places. And you infer from Allatius that Honorius is placed among the heretics, and for this reason you give him thanks. Allatius does not draw this conclusion; he examines the conduct of the Greeks, who must be thought to have suppressed the name of Honorius for no other reason than that they did not consider him infected with heresy, especially since they opposed him on so many other heads of religion. For who would have restrained their fierce spirits, seized by the blind poison of schism, from proclaiming such an odious name aloud and publicly, with their Patriarchs? I would be a fool if I believed it. Besides, you add from Allatius's principles: With the Pope wavering and falling, all the rest waver and fall. Did all the other bishops fall in the time of Honorius, and so the Church erred? And that Church indeed which strengthened orthodoxy against the heretical Pope? I shall explain in a few words. It is true that with the Pope wavering and falling, all the rest waver and fall; but it must be proved that they wavered and fell. If not, nothing follows. So in the time of Honorius the other bishops did not fall, nor did the Church err, and much less did that Church err which strengthened orthodoxy, since it did not follow a heretical Pope. And so Honorius was not a heretic either. Therefore Allatius's argument stands on its own foot: the Greek Church does not excommunicate the Roman Pontiff as a heretic every year, since it does not excommunicate him at the time when it could conveniently do so. But Honorius was a heretic. The contrary is outside Allatius's purpose, which is concerned only with the consent of the Greeks. But Cerularius excommunicated the Latins. Cerularius is not the Greek Church, just as Dioscorus was not, who excommunicated Leo; and he was excommunicated by a synod for that act alone, not for the heresy which he himself fostered. So there is no reason for you to thank Allatius. For he did not confess this; rather, you falsely accuse Allatius of saying it out of hatred for the Roman Pontiff. Conclude therefore: if the Greeks had been so minded as to charge the Roman Pontiff with the crime of heresy, and so tried to excommunicate him, they would have done so chiefly at the time when they excommunicated their own Monothelite Patriarchs, not because Honorius was a heretic but because he was suspected of heresy. Therefore Honorius has not been declared a heretic by Allatius, and you give thanks to Allatius in vain. Then you rehash the old stew about Liberius, about which we have said enough above.

units.la: Rigidam nimis censuram Polygamiæ, vt ita dicam successiue. Et hoc ne pertinet ad dogma? Quod liberum erat in Ecclesia Latina mitius agente cum suis subditis, id terminis præscripsit strictioribus Græca, & pœnis seuerioribus vetuit. Vnde hic expiscatur dissidium? quæ contrarietas enascitur? plus & minus non mutant speciem. Sed Glycas illas vocauit ἄνομον γάμον [?] Non ne sunt? Quod contra legem est, ἄνομον [?] est. Lex limites posuit, qui eos transgreditur, legis transgressor est. In quadragesimali ieiunio ex præcepto Græcus a piscibus abstinet, eos Latinus comedit, si Græcus comederit ἄνομος [?] apud Græcos audiet, & pœna etiam coërcebitur a suo Patre spirituali. Argumentare ergo, quia Latini mitius se gerunt, nimis rigida censura edentibus pisces a Græcis imponitur. Ergo inter Ecclesiam Græcam & Latinam consensus [?] non est.
units.tr: A censure of polygamy too rigid, if I may so put it, in succession. And does this pertain to dogma? What was permitted in the Latin Church, which deals more leniently with its subjects, the Greeks have restricted by stricter terms and forbidden under heavier penalties. Where then is the disagreement found? What contrariety arises? More and less do not change the species. But he called those [marriages] Glycas' 'lawless marriage' [ἄνομον γάμον]. Are they not? What is against the law is lawless [ἄνομον]. The law sets limits, and whoever crosses them is a transgressor of the law. In the Lenten fast the Greek abstains from fish by precept, while the Latin eats them. If a Greek eats fish, he will be called lawless [ἄνομος] among the Greeks, and he will also be punished by his spiritual father. So, to argue that because the Latins behave more leniently, a censure too rigid is imposed by the Greeks on those who eat fish, is to argue badly. Therefore there is no agreement [consensus] between the Greek and Latin Church.

units.la: Porrectionem sacræ Eucharistię infantibus statim etiam a Baptismate. Hoc non habetur ambiguum. In primitiva Ecclesia solemne erat. Regenerati siquidem spiritu, spiritali quoque cibo reficiebantur. Postmodum cum instaret periculum, sanguinem in ore pueri appositum, vel tussi, vel vomitu, vel aliquo alio euentu effundi, Romana Ecclesia tutiora secuta, similem communionem prohibuit, quam & Græca secuta modo, cochleari sanguine intincto tantum tangit extremitatem linguæ, subitoque parens, ad id promptissima mammam porrigit, eoque cum lacte exucto pusillum illud sanguinis deglutiunt. Et sic nullum dissidium apparet. Sed hæc opposita sunt. Nanque hic prohibet, ne fiat, Græcus facit. Verum qui modo prohibet aliquando faciebat, ergo sua opinione non erat illicitum, modo in Latina Ecclesia illicitum est, quia prohibitum. Nanque si prohibitio non accessisset adhuc licitum esset. Sed non quidquid fit, vel factum est illicitum est. Sic nullum scelus erit illicitum. Factum est. ergo iure. Inauditum non est veneficos, & Iudæos sæpius Symbola Sacramentaria ad diros usus adhibuisse. Ergo nec illicitum fuit. Factum illicitum, vel licitum dicitur, quod ex sua natura bonum est, si fiat ab illo, cui illud faciendi facultas est. Cum itaque Præpositi Ecclesiæ sanguine cum atramento mixto excommunicarunt Hæreticos, factum fuit licitum, cum approbante Ecclesia a Præside illius opus per se neq; bonum, neque malum factum est. ideoque factum tetenet, & licite factum est.
units.tr: The administering of the sacred Eucharist to infants immediately even after Baptism. This is not doubtful. In the primitive Church it was the customary practice. Being regenerated by the Spirit, they were also refreshed with spiritual food. Afterwards, when there was a danger that the blood applied to the boy's mouth might be spilled by coughing, vomiting or some other accident, the Roman Church, following safer courses, forbade such communion. The Greek Church, also following it, now only touches the tip of the tongue with a spoon dipped in the blood; and immediately the parent, very ready for this, offers the breast, and with the milk drawn out, the little ones swallow the small amount of blood. And so no disagreement appears. But these things are set against each other. For here one forbids that it be done, and the Greek does it. Yet he who now forbids once did it; therefore in his opinion it was not unlawful; now in the Latin Church it is unlawful because it is forbidden. For if the prohibition had not been added, it would still be lawful. But not whatever is done, or has been done, is unlawful. So no crime will be unlawful. It has been done; therefore it is by right. It is not unheard of that poisoners and Jews have often used sacramentary symbols for dreadful purposes. Therefore it was not unlawful either. A thing is called unlawful or lawful when, if it is done by one who has the power of doing it, it is good in its own nature. Therefore, when the leaders of the Church excommunicated heretics with blood mixed with ink, the act was lawful, since, with the Church's approval, the deed, which in itself is neither good nor evil, was done by its president. Therefore the deed stands, and it was lawfully done.

units.la: Originem, & prima quasi femina Schismatis. &c. De origine Schismatis, Additionis in Symbolo tempore, de Photio auctore Schismatis, de Schismatis renouatione. An Photiani Schismatis fastus Patriarchae Romani principatum supra Constantinopolitanum sibi arrogantis causa fuerit: An quod additio ista, communi Catholicae Ecclesiae iudicio, non vero particularis alicuius Episcopi auctoritate facta fuerit, & de auctoritate Papae Urbici, & aliorum Episcoporum, & de scriptis Photij combustis, nos pleraque ex Scriptoribus Graecis, etiam Schismaticis, uti ex veris fontibus in hac differtatione, & alibi diximus. Quare non est reccurrendum ad scriptorem recentem illaudatum nullius auctoritatis, & stolidissimum hostem unionis Graecorum Silueftrum Syropulum, vel ut vult eo stultior, atque stupidior Creyghtonus, Sgropulum contra omnium exemplariorum fidem, de quo quemadmodum & de ipso Creygthono in nostris aduersus dicti Creygthoni Hiftoriam nunc demum editam Exercitationibus propediem edendis. Quare hic plura dicere supersedeo.
units.tr: The origin, and, as it were, the first woman of the Schism, etc. Concerning the origin of the Schism, the addition in the Creed at the time, concerning Photius as author of the Schism, concerning the renewal of the Schism; whether the arrogance of the Roman Patriarch, who claimed for himself a primacy over the Constantinopolitan, was the cause of the Photian schism; whether that addition was made by the common judgment of the Catholic Church and not by the authority of some particular bishop; and concerning the authority of Pope Urbicus and other bishops, and concerning Photius' burned writings: we have said most of these things in this dissertation and elsewhere, drawing them from genuine sources, mostly Greek writers, even schismatic ones. Therefore one should not have recourse to a recent writer, unpraised and of no authority, and the most foolish enemy of union with the Greeks, Silvester Syropulus; or, as Creyghton wishes, the one who is even more foolish and stupid, Creyghton, who presents Syropulus against the faith of all the manuscripts. About him, as about Creyghton himself, we shall shortly publish a fuller account in our Exercitationes against the history of the said Creyghton, now at last published. Therefore I refrain from saying more here.

units.la: Ut non videas, qua fronte tantus vir ea, quae nunc extruit, nunc rursus destruat, & convel-lat. lit. Scribit ipse Typicon, & Triodion esse inter libros solemnes, & publicos, quibus in Ecclesijs suis utuntur, in his autem graues, & hæreticos errores contentos esse arguit. Et nunc hoc idem repeto, inter libros Ecclesiasticos Græcorum eos esse præcipuos. Sed in illis arguit Allatius multos errores, & hæreses. Et hoc idem ingemino. Quanam ergo ratione inficiatur Ecclesiam Græcam non esse hæreticam? Quia errores illi, & hæreses in illis libris, ut adnotauit Allatius, non sunt Ecclesiæ Græcæ, sed recentiorum Græcorum assumenta, quos cum agnoscunt Ecclesiæ illius proceres, condemnant, & ab eorum recitatione, ne videantur illis assensum præbere, abstinent, alijsque, ut abstineant, pœnis præscriptis præcipiunt. quare Allatius, ut fraus hæreticorum in illis disseminandis cognita omnibus esset, notauit zizania, quæ inter triticum superseminauit inimicus homo, tempore opportuno, quod nunc serio pertractatur, euellenda. Ergo Græca Ecclesia hoc ævo, cum ea in hisce libris retineat, ea sentit, & cum erronea, atq; hæretica sunt, illa quoq; erronea, atque hæretica fuerit. Iam dixi ab ea Ecclesia esse proscripta. Saltem in aliqua Ecclesia conseruantur. Esto. etiam recitentur. An quod in aliqua Ecclesia Græca recitatur, vniuersalis Græcorum Ecclesic recitat, & quod vna tenet, omnes tenét? [?]
units.tr: So that you may not see with what face so great a man builds up what he now constructs, and then again destroys and pulls down. Let us see. He himself writes that the Typicon and the Triodion are among the solemn and public books which they use in their churches, and he argues that these contain grave and heretical errors. And now I repeat the same thing: among the ecclesiastical books of the Greeks these are the chief ones. But Allatius argues that many errors and heresies are in those books. And I repeat this same point. By what reasoning, then, does he deny that the Greek Church is heretical? Because those errors and heresies in those books, as Allatius has noted, are not of the Greek Church but additions of more recent Greeks, which the leaders of that Church recognise and condemn, and they abstain from reciting them, so that they may not seem to give assent to them, and they prescribe penalties to make others abstain. Therefore Allatius, so that the fraud of the heretics in disseminating them might be known to all, noted the tares which the enemy, a man, sowed among the wheat, to be uprooted at the opportune time, which is now seriously taken up. Therefore, if the Greek Church in this age retains these things in these books, it holds them; and if they are erroneous and heretical, then it too will have been erroneous and heretical. I have already said that they have been banned by that Church. At least they are preserved in some Church. Granted. Let them even be recited. But does what is recited in some Greek Church make the whole Greek Church recite it? And what one part holds, do all hold it?

units.la: Non exsistimassem hominem Theologum insuos populares, tam truculentam ferre sententiam. Quid non expectant alij? Scripserat Allatius Hæreticos proscribendos esse, exterminandos, puniendos, & pertinaces occidendos, cremandos. Austerum hoc, & durum videtur Hæretico, & potissimum in suos populares, Allatius reponit; Nullum sibi popularem agnoscere, nullum familiarem, nullum intimum, nullum parentem, nullum agnatum, si Fidei Catholicæ læsio intercedat. Parcat Opponens, Ita edoctus est a Patribus, & Cyrillo Alexandrino potissimum, ne reliquos commemorem, Epistola ad Nestorium; πίστως ὃ ἀδικούμενος, ἐρρίπτω ἑαυτὸν ὡς ἰωλῶ, καὶ βλασφημίας ἡ θεὸς [?] ἀδὶς. ὑφεμέτω δὲ, ἢ ὁ τῆς εἰς τὴν [?] καὶ ἀδελφὸς φιλοσοφίας νόμῳ, καὶ τὸ ζῆν ἡμῶν ἔτι λοιπὸν τῆς ζωῆς ὁ θάνατος, ἵνα κρείττονος ἀναστάσεως τύχωμεν καὶ τὸ συγγάμμα [?]. Certe si fides violatur, omnis omnino erga parentes reverentia tanquam inanis, & periculosa valeat. Facessat lex illa amoris erga liberos, & fratres, quia mori utique satius est iis quam vivere, ut meliorem, sicut scriptum est, inveniant resurrectionem. Esto. Reformati aliter sentiant; ego ita animatus sum cum Græcorum Ecclesia. Rectius Græcos de nobis iudicasse, & plura exemplaria petijsse. Adeantur verba Ieremiæ Patriarchæ, qui fastiditus responsionibus Reformatorum respondet, vt sibi ipsi sua habeant, nec de cætero scribendo permolesti sint. Græci Patres & Doctores suos habent, quorum dictis sua stabiliunt. Rogamus itaque vos, ne posthac labores nobis exhibeatis. Nam Theologos, qui Ecclesiæ lumina fuerunt, alias aliter tractatis, armaque nostra inutilia nobis efficere vultis. Vestram ergo viam euntes, ne amplius de dogmatibus, sed amicitiæ tantum causa, si voluer/ veritis scribere. Hoc ne est Græcos de vobis rectius iudicasse, plura exemplaria petijsse? Sed esto, morose scripserit. Estne hoc Græcos antiquis suis dogmatibus, & consuetudinibus vale dicere, & honorificissime de Reformatis prædicare? Sed Ioannes Zygomala promittit se, vbi oportuerit, pro Crusio, & D. Andrea in defensionem adfore. Quis est iste Zygomala? qua auctoritate id faciet? homo in ea gente inglorius, inops, panem emendicans, quem vt consequatur, multa blanditur, multa aliter atque sunt, promit ex pectore. Idque vt videas, ex Epistolis eiusdem ad Crusium conijce. Non iniqui iniurius sum. lectitentur ipsius verba.
units.tr: I would not have thought a theologian would bring so savage a sentence against his own people. What do others not expect? Allatius had written that heretics must be proscribed, exterminated, punished, and the obstinate killed and burned. This seems harsh and hard to a heretic, and especially against his own people. Allatius replies that he recognises no one as his own people, no familiar, no intimate, no parent, no kinsman, if injury to the Catholic Faith is at stake. Let the objector spare himself. He was so taught by the Fathers, and especially by Cyril of Alexandria, not to mention the rest, in his letter to Nestorius: [πιστῶς ὁ ἀδικούμενος, ἐρρίπτω ἑαυτὸν ὡς ἰχθὺς, καὶ βλασφημίας ἡ θεὸς ἀδικεῖ... ὑφεμέτω δὲ ὁ τῆς εἰς τὴν... καὶ ἀδελφὸς φιλοσοφίας νόμῳ, καὶ τὸ ζῆν ἡμῖν ἔτι λοιπὸν τῆς ζωῆς ὁ θάνατος, ἵνα κρείττονος ἀναστάσεως τύχωμεν]. Certainly, if the faith is violated, all reverence whatever towards parents is to be regarded as empty and dangerous. Let that law of love towards children and brothers depart, because it is in any case better to die than to live for them, so that, as it is written, they may find a better resurrection. Granted. The Reformed think otherwise; I for my part am minded with the Greek Church. That the Greeks judged us more rightly, and asked for more copies. Let us consider the words of Patriarch Jeremiah, who, weary of the replies of the Reformers, answers that they should keep their own views and not trouble him any more with writing. The Greek Fathers and Teachers have their own, by whose sayings they establish their positions. We therefore ask you not to cause us further labour. For you wish to make useless our weapons, by handling in other ways the theologians who were the lights of the Church. Going therefore your own way, do not write any more about doctrines, but only for the sake of friendship, if you wish to write. Is this what it means that the Greeks judged us more rightly and asked for more copies? But granted that he wrote peevishly. Is this the Greeks bidding farewell to their ancient dogmas and customs, and proclaiming the Reformed in the most honourable terms? But John Zygomalas promises that, where necessary, he will stand by Crusius and Dr Andreae in their defence. Who is this Zygomalas? By what authority will he do so? A man without distinction in that nation, poor, begging his bread, who, to obtain it, flatters much and promises much from his heart that is otherwise than the facts are. And so that you may see this, gather it from his own letters to Crusius. I am not doing him unfair injustice. Let his own words be read.

units.la: Ἵνα [?] ὁ Ζυγομάλας [?] οἱ, ἀλλ᾽ αἰτίαν [?] προϊέμενος, κἂν [?] ἀλλ᾽ ἐμὲ ὅλα ἀεχίμψιν [?] συμμαχίαν ἡμῖν, καὶ τὴ ἀληθείᾳ, ὥσι ὡς πολλοὶ τῷ ὧδε Φεάσων [?], ἥτις τῇ ὑποξασοιυμένῃ τῆς Πρεσβυτέ-ρας Ῥώμης, οἳ σφᾶς αὐτὰς Παπίσας καλοῦσιν, μα-ὁσῖνης αὐτὸς ἔτιν ἀπεσταλθαί [?]· ῥηδὲν ὑμεδακτὸν βιβλίον, τὸ περιέχον τὴν Ὑρηοκείαν ὑμῖν φά[?], ἐπίζον ἐφύλαξαν ἐναντιέμένοι ὑμῖν. ἐγὼ δὲ τοῦτο ἐντέπω, ἀλλ᾽ ἐξ ἴχοσι καταχρῆσῃς, καὶ καινοτομίας ἀπάτας, καὶ ὧν ἡμῖν μόνον ἐν πολλῇς συμφωνεμόν, ἐκείνοις ἢ καὶ λίαν διαφερόμεθα. Vt autem tibi causam indicem, cur antea dixerim. Etiam si necesse fuerit me arma capere pro defensione vestri, & veritatis, scias multos e Fratribus, seu Monachis, qui hic degunt, hoc est, qui Ecclesiae veteris Romae subiecti sunt, & se Papistas nominant, cum rescivissent isthinc missum esse libellum, continentem capita religionis vestrae, murifice infremuisse contra vos. Ego autem eis respondi, obijciens, vos dissentire ab ipsis propter ipsorum in religione abusus, & novas opiniones absurdas, de quibus nos in multis vobiscum sentimus, ab illis vero valde dissentimus. Audis? salua iam est Reformatorum causa, & religio, Zygomala propugnatore, & defensore, & pugnatore strenuo. Sed vocem in questum confert, & linguam habet venalem. Non credis? attende sequentia. Διόμεθα [?] βοηθείας τῆς ἐν χρήμασι διὰ τῆς μεσ-φάς τὲ τμεγαλοφρενικῆς Καλλιγλαεῖς καὶ τῆς σῆς λογιοτητῷ. ὥσπερ τῆς πλεονεξίας χρέος τὴν [?] δυναμένων. καὶ γὰρ τὸ δημοσιένδον[?], δὲ χρημάτων, καὶ αὐτὸ τούτων ὑδὲν ἔχει χρείας τὴν λόγων, ταῦτα [?] ἐξ τὰς πολλὰς ἡμῖν χρείας, καὶ τέλη, ἃ καὶ ἔτης ὑπομνύμεν τοῖς ἐνταῦθα κεχρῆσθαι. Indigentes autem nos præsidio pecuniario, tale aliquid petimus, Magnifico D. Cancellario, & tua humanitate intercedentibus, à munifica manu eorum, qui potentia istic valent. Nam vt Demosthenes ait, opus est pecunijs, neq; absq; his quicquam confici potest, petimus autem propter magnas necessitates nostras, & tributa, quæ quotannis pendimus his, qui apud nos dominantur. Egestatem illius extremam debuccinat Crusius ibidem. Ioannes Zygomala, si quando cum D. Gerlachio aliquo iret, aut navigaret, dicebat monstrato marsupio, ἀδωνᾶ[?]. Tunc ipse pro ipso persoluebat. Et ego mendiculo, & miserrimo credam, & potissimum in religionis negotio P.Non patitur id Dio Chrysostomus Oratione Troica; Τὰς γὰρ νῦν πτωχείας ἐδεῖν[?], φασὶν, ὑγιῶς λέγειν[?], ἐὰν μάρτυρες ἐδὲν ἀπ' ἐκείνων ποιήσωνται[?] ὑπὲρ ἐμοῦ, ἐὰν δὲ[?] ἐπαίνης ἔχων παρ' αὐτῶν ἀποδίδοντας ὡς ἀληθῶς. ἴσασι γὰρ ὅτι πάντες ἰσχύοντες ὑπ' ἀνάγκης λέγοντες. Sane mendicos, qui nunc viuunt, nihil sani ferunt dicere, neque vllus illorum quempiam testem aliquo in re adhibuerit, neque laudes ab illis profectas accipiunt vt veras. Norunt enim, quod omnia adulantes dicant, compulsi necessitate. Huius Zygomalae [?]ἐμοὶ ἐλλάδων λόγῳ[?] ἕξιν, ἢ πάθος[?]. Esto quod vult Allatius. Eodē modo confusi sunt Apostoli, pulverem ex calceis coram incredulis, & Euangelium reijcientibus detestientes. Nunc primum audio Reformatos esse Apostolos, sed cuius non explicat, an ex ijs, qui se dicunt esse Apostolos, & non sunt, & inueniuntur mendaces. qui sunt operarij subdoli, transfigurantes se in Apostolos Christi. Et non mirum ipse enim Satanas transfigurat se in Angelum lucis. Non est ergo magnum, si ministri eius transfigurentur, velut ministri iustitiae: quorum finis erit secundum opera eorum. At unde, ais, hoc Allatio constat? Effectus ipse comprobauit. Nanque apud illam nationem in nullo pretio habitus, abolitus est. & quamuis Allatius curiosius exemplar, literis scriptis etiam ad Magnates, omnibus vestigijs indagauerit, ad hunc diem nullum illi peruenit ad manus. De professionibus Fidei Graeca, & Iberica lingua conscriptis, missisque in eas partes, & igne crematis prostant adhuc literae ex illis regionibus, in quibus similia enarrantur, vt Allatio opus non sit, vbi acta publica loquuntur, populariū singularia documenta proferre. & Graecos multis pollicitationibus sollicitasse praeter Cyrilli Berrhoensis Synodica exem-plaplaria, edicit responsio Patriarchæ Alexandrini ex Græco Latina publicata ab Allatio, qua narratio ista, quam ponit Opponens, penitus deformata cadit.
units.tr: Zygomalas, ... (the Greek of this letter is too garbled in the scan to read with certainty, so I give its sense.) He has promised his help and support to us, and in truth many in this place, who belong to the so-called Roman presbyterate and call themselves Papists, have been sent here by him. The printed little book, which sets out our doctrine, has been read by them, and they have turned against you. I, however, answer them not by denying it but by pointing out your abuses and new absurd opinions, in which we agree with you on many points but differ greatly from them. Do you hear? Now the cause and religion of the Reformed are safe, with Zygomalas as their champion, defender and strenuous fighter. But he sells his voice and his tongue for money. You do not believe it? Attend to what follows. We ask for help with money, through the mediation of the magnificent Chancellor and of your humanity, from the generous hand of those who are powerful there, as those who have the means know. For, as Demosthenes says, money is needed, and nothing can be done without it, and we ask for it on account of our great needs and the taxes we pay every year to those who rule over us. Being in need, we ask for this kind of help. Crusius, in the same place, bewails his extreme poverty. Whenever Johannes Zygomalas went with Gerlach or sailed with him, he would point to his purse and say that it was empty, and then Gerlach paid for him. Shall I believe a beggar of this sort, and especially in a matter of religion? Dio Chrysostom does not allow it in his Trojan Oration: "For the beggars of today, they say, speak not sound things, if they make no witnesses of those things on my behalf, but receive praise from them, which they give as if it were true. For they know that all who flatter speak under compulsion." Surely beggars who live today say nothing sound, and none of them calls a witness in any matter, nor do they accept praise from others as true. For they know that flatterers say everything under compulsion. Such is Zygomalas's ... habit or passion. Let it be as Allatius wishes. In the same way the Apostles shook the dust from their feet before unbelievers who rejected the Gospel. Now for the first time I hear that the Reformed are Apostles, but he does not explain whether they are among those who call themselves Apostles and are not, and are found to be liars, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as Apostles of Christ. And no wonder: Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. It is no great thing, then, if his ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness, whose end will be according to their works. "But how," you say, "is this known to Allatius?" The result itself has proved it. For among that nation it was held in no esteem and was abolished. And although Allatius has searched out every trace, even writing to the magnates, to this day no copy has come into his hands. Letters from those regions survive, written in Greek and Iberian, about professions of faith drawn up and sent to those parts and burned by fire, in which similar things are recounted, so that Allatius has no need to bring forward private particular documents where the public records speak. And that the Greeks were solicited with many promises, besides the Synodical examples of Cyril of Berrhoea, the reply of the Patriarch of Alexandria, published by Allatius in Greek and Latin, declares, by which that story which the Opponent sets forth collapses, utterly distorted.

units.la: Sicut enim Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus quotannis in die Cœnæ Domini Pontificem Romanum cum tota Ecclesia Latina solemni ritu excommunicat. Hoc tamen, quidquid dicat Caucus, solemnissimum mendacium est. Sed Allatius illa Synaxarij recitat; Confundantur, qui in sacrificio Azymum offerunt. Recitat, ergo excommunicant Pontificios. Conclusio nulla est, Duo quæruntur in materia Eucharistiæ, primum an Christus confecit in Azymo, vel in Enzymo: alterum an Azymum sit apta materia? Græci, & Latini tenent utrumque, & Azymum, & Enzymum esse, & hæc quæstio solemnis est apud eosdem. Callistus in Synaxario putat se probasse, Christum confecisse in Enzymo; sicque concludit, debere confundi eos, qui non vero facto Christi innixi in Azymo offerunt. Ubi est hæc excommunicatio Latinæ Ecclesiæ? Sed quando omnia in peius vertenda sunt, excommunicatio locum confusionis occupavit.
units.tr: For just as the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicates the Roman Pontiff with the whole Latin Church every year on the day of the Lord's Supper with a solemn rite, so, whatever Crusius says, this is a most solemn lie. But Allatius quotes the Synaxarion: "Let those be confounded who offer the unleavened bread in sacrifice." He quotes it, therefore they excommunicate the Papists. The conclusion does not follow. Two things are asked about the matter of the Eucharist: first, whether Christ consecrated in unleavened or in leavened bread; second, whether unleavened bread is a suitable matter. The Greeks and the Latins hold both that unleavened and that leavened bread are valid, and this question is a solemn one among the same men. Callistus in the Synaxarion thinks he has proved that Christ consecrated in leavened bread, and so he concludes that those should be confounded who, not relying on the true deed of Christ, offer unleavened bread. Where is any excommunication of the Latin Church here? But when everything has to be turned for the worse, excommunication has taken the place of confusion.

units.la: Et ad Opponentis quidem exercitationem hæc satis superque, quibus Iuvenis multas, easque lubricas, atque multis implicitas erroribus vias ostendimus. Verum dandum est aliquid aetati, in qua liberior animus insita sibi agitatione ad ardua quaeque, quantum libido fert, sinistra directa ratione praecipitatur; ideoque sepius dictis factisque proteruis, & malitia confidenti in alterius famam incurrit, & raro se revocat ad bonam frugem. Addeimpetum, & ardorem mentis ad gloriam, & ostentandam eorum, in quibus caecutiunt, scientiam, & sixum ad verba, non ad res ipsas conatum. Hinc Opponenti nos & maledicentiae, & garrulitati, & improbitati, & intemperiei ignoscimus. Cum aetas provectior fuerit, usu rerum matura, cupiditate gloriae refervescente, ni me sallit opinio, prudentior facta, ac modestior refrenabit petulantiam, atque veritate cognita, discet tandem maiores natu venerari, & quam hodie parum cautus fidem insectatur amplexus, illius cognitores reverebitur. Attamen quod condonandum videtur Iuveni, eoque magis si est ex gente bellicosissima, hoc vero vel maxime Dannhauerum configit, cuius cum onus ex officio esset Iuvenis primis adhuc literis gestientis, & non dum sacra a profanis discernere ad plenum scientis, immoderatam licentiam intra mistae cum modestia gravitatis limites continere, & linguam audacuIam reprimere, ipse non tantum efflorescentem iuuenilem effrenationem inhibuit, sed laudibus euehens, & ad facta, quorum etiam aures a commemoratione abhorrent, promouit, & potissimum eum, qui profitetur se, etiam Deum testans, toto animo abhorrere ab isto more conuicijs aduersarios profcindendi. Sed non mirum. Opponens Aspidis Coruiqué ouum est, foetus compar parenti. τὸ πατρὸς ἐξ[?] τῷ παιδίον[?] Hinc ille; Tum si quis magistrum capit ad eam rem improbum, ipsum animum agrotum ad deteriorem partem adplicat.
units.tr: So much, and more than enough, for the exercise of the Opponent, to whom we have shown many slippery paths, entangled in many errors. Yet something must be allowed to his age, in which a freer mind, driven by its inborn restlessness toward every difficult thing as far as desire carries it, is hurried by a crooked and unguided reason, and so, by its wanton words and deeds and confident malice, it attacks another's reputation, and rarely comes back to sound conduct. Add to this the impetuousness and ardour of a mind eager for glory and for displaying the learning in which it is blinded, and an effort fixed on words rather than things. For this reason we pardon the Opponent for his slander, his chatter, his wickedness and his intemperance. When his age has advanced, mature with experience, and his desire for glory has cooled, if I am not mistaken in my opinion he will become wiser and more modest, restrain his petulance, and, once the truth is known, will at last learn to revere his elders, and he will respect those who know the faith whom today, too little cautious, he assails. Yet what seems to be pardonable in a young man, all the more if he comes from a most warlike nation, is especially unfitting in the case of Dannhauer, whose duty as a teacher it was, while the young man was still eager for his first letters and not yet fully able to distinguish sacred from profane, to keep his immoderate licence within the bounds of modesty and gravity and to restrain his bold tongue. Instead he not only did not check the youthful unbridledness that was blossoming, but, lifting him up with praises, he promoted him to deeds from which even ears shrink when they are recounted, and especially to one who professes that he, calling God to witness, abhors with his whole soul that custom of tearing adversaries apart with insults. But this is no surprise. The Opponent is a viper's egg, an offspring like its parent: "the son of a father..." Hence that saying: If anyone takes an unworthy teacher for that task, he turns the sick mind itself toward the worse part.

units.la: CAPVT XIV. De Ecclesijs Eois aliys, vt conueniant cum Re- formatis, & de eorum cum Ecclesia Romana consensu, Epistola Abrahami Ecchellensis ad Leonem Allatium, Bibliotheca Vaticana Præfectum.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV. On the other Eastern Churches, that they agree with the Reformed, and on their consensus with the Roman Church: a letter of Abraham Ecchellensis to Leo Allatius, Prefect of the Vatican Library.

units.la: Sed adhuc perstat in prauitate, & perstrepit Hottingerus; habere se multa, quæ confessioni Græcorum ab Allatio adhornatæ opponat. Sed dignam esse materiâ, quæ plenius pertractetur. Interim ex Topographia Ecclesiastica, ex Symbolicis Syrorum, Arabum, Aethiopum, Coptitarum, quibus manifestum esse esse, ait, in genere Ecclesias Orientales, etsi iniuria temporum grauem passæ sint cladem, ita tamen hoc commune eorum fuisse fatum, vt, cum nostræ non sint per omnia, nobis interim in essentialibus propius accedant, quam Pontificijs Tridentinis. Et obseruat præacute, si non stolidè; Orientales, vel Reformatis per omnia accedere, vel in circumstantijs tantum variare, vel in Pontificijs videntur fauere partibus, illud aut ex principijs fluere Pontificiorum, etiam opinione erroneis, φανερῶς[?] potius, quam ὄντως[?], verbis, quam rebus assensum testari maiorem. Atque sic non negamus, Orientales Ecclesias cum Romana aliquid habere simile, idem difficulter obtinebunt, plura tamen nobiscum. Hæc & similia audet proferre Hottingerus. Conatur pobare[?]: sed quam apte, consideret Lector. Communes sunt Syris, & Græcis formulæ ad B. Virginem Mariam conceptæ, vel etiam ad alios Sanctos, quibus tamen superstitionibus acutissima Pontificiorum ἀναλογία[?] non defenditur, magnum enim vtrinque est ἐξέμνξ[illegible, ~6 letters], vel in eo saltem, quod singulis vrbibus, morbis, prouincijs patronum suum Romani præficiunt. Illæ generales sunt, & Apostrophæ potius encomiasticæ. Hæ sæpe impiè, & cum dedecore nominis diuini coniunctæ. Et non erit corde & intelligentia vacuus, qui ad hunc modum ratiocinatur. Syri Græeiq[?]; vnis animis Sanctos, ac inter eos praecipue immaculatissimam Virginem venerantur, supplicant, exorant, vt diuinum Numen sibi propitium reddant: sic eorum imagines adorant, reliquias summa veneratione prosequuntur, hoc idem faciunt Pontificij Tridentini; Reformati similem cultum detestantur. Ergo Syri, & Graeci conueniunt cum Reformatis, discordant a Pontificijs Tridentinis? Risum teneatis amici. Sed; est magnum utrinque ἀμάρτημα[?] Romani praeficiunt singulis urbibus, morbis, prouincijs patronum. De Pontificijs verum est. Sed id quoque, dummodo, qui eorum libros legit, oculos habeat, de Syris, & Graecis asserendum est. Exempli gratia, Cosmas, & Damianus medicis, Chijs Isidorus, & Georgius Martyres, Constantinopolitanis Deipara, Thessalonicensibus Demetrius, Alexandrinis Marcus, & alij alijs, sicuti & prouincijs praefecti sunt. Vnde nam ergo magnum hoc ἀμάρτημα[?] inter Orientales, & Pontificios Hottingerus expiscatur? Si idem facere, idem profiteri discordia Hottingero est, quae erit concordia? Sed; Sunt hae stultae, & miserae superstitiones. Adde Reformatis, non Orientalibus & Pontificijs. Sed esto, sint. Ergo Orientales, & Pontificij etiam in superstitionibus concordant. Et Hottingerus agnoscit δίσπνμα[?], & illud magnum? Illa formulae generales sunt, & Apostrophae potius encomiastica. Cur non addis, & veræ & a vero, rectoque deductæ? Res diuinæ Græcis & Pontificijs sacrosanctæ sunt, vt in ora eorum pro ludibrio non abeant. Quare quod est, & esse certissime tenent, licet tu nigris dentibus irrideas, & canem irritatum immitteris, id ore etiam palam profitentur. Nonne ipse perridiculus essem apud omnes, si de Hottingero sermonem habens, eum vocitarem, & doctissimum, & pijssimum, & cœlesti numine percitum, cum omnes, qui cognoscunt hominem, sciant, eum nec pilum quidem sapientiæ habere, & pietatem omnem ex pectore emouisse, & Satanico œstro conuelli?
units.tr: But Hottinger still persists in his perversity and keeps up his clamour: he says he has many things with which to oppose the confession of the Greeks, as adorned by Allatius. But it is a matter worthy of being treated more fully. Meanwhile, from the Ecclesiastical Topography and from the Symbolic books of the Syrians, Arabs, Ethiopians and Copts, he says it is clear that the Eastern Churches in general, although they have suffered grievous loss through the injuries of the times, have nevertheless had this common lot: that, although they are not in all things ours, they come nearer to us in essentials than to the Tridentine Papists. And he observes, very sharply if not foolishly: the Orientals either agree with the Reformed in all things, or differ only in circumstances, or seem to favour the Papists; and this arises from the principles of the Papists, even though they are mistaken in opinion, showing assent more in words, apparently [φανερῶς], than in fact [ὄντως], and in outward show rather than in substance. And so we do not deny that the Eastern Churches have something in common with the Roman Church; they will hardly maintain that same thing, yet they have more in common with us. Hottinger dares to put forward these and similar claims. He tries to prove it, but let the reader consider how aptly. The Syrians and Greeks have formulas composed in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary, or also of other saints; yet the most acute analogy of the Papists is not defended by these superstitions, for there is a great [?] on both sides, or at least in this, that the Romans appoint to each city, disease and province its patron. These formulas are general, and are rather encomiastic apostrophes. Those of the Papists are often impiously joined with dishonour to the divine name. And he will not be lacking in heart and understanding who reasons in this way: the Syrians and Greeks with one mind venerate the saints, and among them especially the most spotless Virgin; they supplicate and entreat them so that they may render the divine Power propitious to them; so they adore their images and pursue their relics with the highest veneration. The Tridentine Papists do the same; the Reformed detest a similar worship. Therefore the Syrians and Greeks agree with the Reformed and disagree with the Tridentine Papists? Hold your laughter, friends. But: there is a great [error] on both sides. The Romans appoint a patron to each city, disease and province. This is true of the Papists. But this too, provided that whoever reads their books has eyes, must be asserted of the Syrians and Greeks. For example: Cosmas and Damian for physicians, Isidore and George the martyrs for Chios, the Mother of God for Constantinople, Demetrius for Thessalonica, Mark for Alexandria, and others for others, just as they are set over provinces. Whence then does Hottinger fish out this great [error] between the Orientals and the Papists? If to do the same and to profess the same is, for Hottinger, discord, what will concord be? But: these are foolish and wretched superstitions. Add that they apply to the Reformed, not to the Orientals and Papists. But granted, let them be so. Then the Orientals and Papists agree also in superstitions. And does Hottinger acknowledge this disparity, and that great one? Those general formulas are rather encomiastic apostrophes. Why do you not add: and true, and drawn from truth and right reason? The divine matters are held sacrosanct by the Greeks and Papists, so that they may not become a mockery in their mouths. Therefore what they hold, and hold most certainly to be, they openly profess with their mouths, even though you sneer with black teeth and set a provoked dog loose upon them. Would I not be utterly ridiculous before everyone, if in speaking of Hottinger I called him both most learned and most pious, and stirred by heavenly power, when all who know the man know that he has not a hair's breadth of wisdom, has banished all piety from his breast, and is torn about by a Satanic gadfly?

units.la: Petri Apostoli, sedisque Romanæ apud Syros, Arabes &c. fit mentio: frustra tamen ad Monarchiam rapitur Pontificiam. Apud eos fieri mentionem summi Pontificis, vt est Ecclesiæ caput, vt est successor Petri, vt est director fidei, eius voces esse voces Dei, voces Petri, dictata columnas fidei, Orientalium scripta insinuant. quibus non potest dici euidentius ad Monarchiam afferendam, supremam & vnicam in vniuersa Ecclesia potestatem. Frustra tamen ad Monarchiam rapitur Pontificiam. Hoc vero de tuo capite est somniculosum delirium.
units.tr: Mention is made of the Apostle Peter and of the Roman see among the Syrians, Arabs, etc.: yet it is in vain that it is snatched away to a Papal monarchy. That among them mention is made of the supreme Pontiff, as head of the Church, as successor of Peter, as director of faith, that his voices are the voices of God, the voices of Peter, the dictates of the pillars of faith, the writings of the Orientals suggest. Nothing could be more plainly said to assert a monarchy, supreme and unique in power over the whole Church. Yet it is in vain that it is snatched away to a Papal monarchy. But this is a drowsy delirium born of your own head.

units.la: Habent & Orientales suos Monachos, & Monasteria, nec tamen sine discrimine. Habent & Pontificij, & maiori quoque discrimine; cum apud hos & diuersitas constitutionum, & habitus, & diuini officij recitatio, & aliorum, quae omnia Reformati, uti purioris, atque integrioris vitae indicia, uti malum auspicium execrantur. Et dicis hosce ad Reformatos propius accedere? Patrum dicta, & mentio in Aethiopum, Syrorum, & Graecorum obuia cuique sunt. Quod nec tu negas. Dicis nihilominus pugnacissime. Non tamen ut Cynosura & Canon, Orientales Eccle-siae omnes post diuinum verbum verba Patrum ita excipiunt, & exosculantur, & firmiter tenent, ut illa reijcientibus, & non auscultantibus, & in omnibus obsequentibus, anathema palam dicant, & eos in numero sceleratorum ac impiorum habentes, a communione Ecclesiae, & fidelium consortio excludant. quod me suse contra te probasse, memini; Hinc alia referre supersedeo, ne aliis oneri sim.
units.tr: The Orientals too have their monks and monasteries, yet not without distinction. The Papists have them too, and with even greater distinction; for among these there is both diversity of constitutions and of habits, and the recitation of the divine office, and other things, all of which the Reformed, as signs of a purer and more complete life, execrate as an evil omen. And do you say these come nearer to the Reformed? The sayings and mention of the Fathers are plain to everyone in the Ethiopians, Syrians and Greeks. You do not deny this either. Yet you say, most pugnaciously: not, however, as a Cynosure and Canon. The Eastern Churches all receive and kiss the words of the Fathers after the divine Word, and hold them firmly, so that they openly pronounce anathema on those who reject them, do not listen, and do not obey in all things, and, counting them among the wicked and impious, exclude them from the communion of the Church and the fellowship of the faithful. I remember that I have proved this at length against you; therefore I refrain from reporting other things here, lest I burden others.

units.la: Tandem e Syrorum, Arabum, Aethiopum scriptis Symbolicis de Scriptura sacra, de lapsu Adami, aliisque mentione tantum inducta in fine tuae disputationis absque ulla probatione multa semper tui similimus infarcis, quae tuis Reformatis regere. Nam Pontificij, nec animum quidem aduertent, qui plane cognoscunt te in Arabicis aliisque linguis Orientalibus, aeque atque in Graecis inscitissimum esse, quamuis earum cognitionem inconsideratissima temeritate tibi assumas. Sed audi. Si quos septendecim annorum iuuenis in literatura Graeca habuisti progressus, ut neque ligatae, neque solutae orationis, qua scripto, qua Typis edere non erubueris specimina, sed quis rubor in Hottingerana facie unquam insidere potuit? eadem, & in aliis linguis Orientalibus edidisti, te penitus ieiunum, & pene infantem arguunt. Et ut videas, en Viri in illis linguis instructissimi, & in Orientalium moribus, ac consuetudinibus, & potissimum Ecclesiasticis versatissimi Abrahami Ecchellensis Epistolam, quem de hisce a te propositis certiorem feci: cum ipse eas, nec me pudet fateri, non didicerim. Eam uti accepi, ut quantus fis Hottingere in nugis effutiendis, Responsioni meae coniunctam ad te transmitto. Digna est, quae semel, atque iterum a te legatur, ut scias, quae nescias, ne semper imperitus ardelio in tuis de dissidio Graecorum & Pontificiorum lucubrationibus sis.
units.tr: Finally, from the Symbolic writings of the Syrians, Arabs and Ethiopians, concerning Holy Scripture, the fall of Adam, and other matters merely touched upon, you always stuff the end of your disputation, like one very much like yourself, with many things without any proof, which you may pass off to your Reformed. For the Papists, who clearly know that you are as ignorant of Arabic and other Oriental languages as of Greek, do not even notice this, although you assume knowledge of them with the most thoughtless rashness. But listen. If you made any progress in Greek literature at the age of seventeen, so that you were not ashamed to publish specimens of bound and unbound prose, in writing or in print, yet what blush has ever been able to settle on the Hottingerian face? The same things you published in other Oriental languages prove you utterly empty and almost an infant. And so that you may see this, behold the letter of Abraham Ecchellensis, a man most learned in those languages and most versed in Oriental customs and usages, and especially in ecclesiastical ones, whom I have informed about the things you have put forward; for I am not ashamed to confess that I myself have not learned them. I send it to you, as I received it, joined to my reply, so that you may see how great a trifler you are in uttering nonsense. It is worth being read by you once and again, so that you may learn what you do not know, and not remain always an untaught meddler in your studies of the dissension between the Greeks and the Papists.

units.tr: TO LEO, HIS REPLY,
